items.title: Why Are We So Good at Feeling Bad?
items.description: Charles Darwin was not a well man. As a youth, he suffered from scarlet fever and eczema. He couldn’t stand the sight of blood at medical school, and his five-year voyage on the Beagle brought seasickness, headaches, and infections. After returning to England,
items.author: Louis Menand
paragraphs: Charles Darwin was not a well man. As a youth, he suffered from scarlet fever and eczema. He couldn’t stand the sight of blood at medical school, and his five-year voyage on the Beagle brought seasickness, headaches, and infections. After returning to England, in 1836, he developed severe anxiety and gastrointestinal issues, including bouts of vomiting and flatulence. He also suffered from insomnia, fatigue, and depression.

In 1849, ten years before he published “On the Origin of Species,” he wrote to a friend of “dreadful vomiting every week” and reported, “I was not able to do anything one day out of three.” He thought that he was “rapidly going the way of all flesh.” In fact, he lived another thirty-three years, though the ailments never left him. Giving a scientific paper, or even attending a party, could overwhelm him. By then, he had moved to a village in Kent, rarely venturing out without his wife, Emma.

From 1849 to 1855, Darwin kept a “diary of health,” recording his conditions as “goodish,” “poorish,” and “very bad fl[atulence] with fright.” He consulted some twenty doctors and tried Victorian cures, including hydrotherapy, which offered some relief, and galvanism. Diagnoses included nervous dyspepsia, water brash (acid reflux), and “suppressed gout” (whatever that is).

What was the problem? Retrospective diagnoses range from Chagas’ disease, a parasitic illness he might have contracted in South America, to lactose intolerance. He may have suffered from some combination of diseases and allergies, and possibly Crohn’s. But some symptoms suggest a psychological condition. Agoraphobia with panic disorder is a plausible diagnosis.

Whatever the cause or causes, Darwin must, at some point, have asked himself, I got naturally selected for this? Of course, not every affliction has an evolutionary purpose. People get sick. But our extraordinary susceptibility to misery does raise a question about what kind of creatures natural selection has made us. We get depressed when we win the lottery; we lie awake worrying about whether the car needs new tires; we feel jealous when our girlfriend talks too long with the barista.

Anxiety might have adaptive utility when we are in danger of being eaten by a sabre-toothed tiger. But there are not a lot of sabre-toothed tigers around anymore, and we still get anxious, frequently for no very good reason. We don’t just react emotionally to things. We overreact. Why have genes for emotional overreaction, rather than genes for being cool, calm, and collected, been passed along? Wouldn’t we be reproductively fitter if we weren’t unhappy so much of the time?

These are questions George Loewenstein tries to answer in “The Opposite of Happiness: How Bad Feelings Make and Break Us” (Harper). Loewenstein, who teaches at Carnegie Mellon, is a leader in the field of behavioral economics. Neoclassical economics relied on the fiction of the rational actor, someone who makes decisions by way of a judicious calculation of self-interest. Behavioral economics, by contrast, emphasizes the nonrational factors in economic decision-making. Whatever human beings are rational about, it’s not money. We overspend it; we under-save it; we buy stuff on impulse. We generally don’t do the math. Why it took so long for this to dawn on economists is mystifying. Didn’t those people ever read a novel? Virtually every famous nineteenth-century novel is about people behaving badly around money.

Still, figuring out why we act foolishly when we could, or should, or want to act otherwise is a worthy academic pursuit. Among Loewenstein’s contributions is the identification of what he calls “empathy gaps,” our inability to imagine how we would feel or behave in an emotional state different from the one we’re in. When we’re pain-free, we can’t really remember what pain feels like. When we’re angry, we can’t imagine being calm. Emotions, Loewenstein argues, can reprogram our whole psyche. He gives a personal example: learning that it is better to wait a day before responding to an annoying e-mail.

Didn’t we know this already, though? Adam Smith made similar observations in “The Theory of Moral Sentiments” (1759). And some of Loewenstein’s work does seem to amount to a confirmation of common sense. One of his experiments, for instance, measured the effect of sexual arousal on judgment and decision-making in male students. Guess what? A sexually aroused young man reported a greater willingness to engage in morally questionable behavior to obtain sexual gratification.

Explaining how feelings affect our judgment is one thing. Why so many emotions make us unhappy is another. That’s the larger question Loewenstein takes up. His thesis is that these emotions “were built to keep us alive and reproducing, not to keep us happy.”

Loewenstein is hardly alone in proposing evolutionary explanations for misery. Randolph M. Nesse, a psychiatrist, made a similar case in “Good Reasons for Bad Feelings: Insights from the Frontier of Evolutionary Psychiatry” (2019), a work Loewenstein discusses. Such arguments recall the “selfish gene” model. Evolution is not about the reproduction of persons, is the idea. It’s about the reproduction of genes. And, from a gene’s point of view, the body is just a disposable gene container. It can fret about the tires, climb the Matterhorn, write “On the Origin of Species”—whatever, as long as the genes keep getting passed along. Darwin may have been wretched much of the time, but he had ten children. He checked the evolutionary box. Was he also farting and throwing up a lot? Sure. His genes didn’t care.

But Loewenstein thinks that negative emotions aren’t simply a design flaw or a regrettable by-product of natural selection. On the contrary, he thinks that we have good evolutionary reasons for being able to feel bad. Our ancestors would have been less “fit” to pass their genes along if they hadn’t been equipped with negative emotions. Fear could save us from predators; guilt could help us maintain the social bonds on which survival depended.

Knowing this, Loewenstein warns, won’t make us feel any less unhappy. “I offer in these pages no tips and precious little advice,” he writes. “This is not a self-help book.” (I wonder whether his publishers tried to talk him out of that.) Loewenstein describes the book as, instead, “one scientist’s bird’s-eye view of the subject, shaped by broad reading, personal experience, and, in many cases, my own research.”

“The Opposite of Happiness” is fairly nontechnical. There is no talk of neurotransmitters, and Loewenstein, who has himself conducted brain-imaging research, thinks that the interpretation of functional-MRI scans is often “not much more reliable than reading tea leaves.” The book is also quite personal, although selectively so. Loewenstein lets us know, for example, that he suffers from paruresis (shy-bladder syndrome) but neglects to mention that he is a great-grandson of Sigmund Freud, whose theories of unconscious drives bear some family resemblance to Loewenstein’s account of our emotional programming.

The problem with a lot of evolutionary psychology is that its explanations are hard to verify. It undertakes to explain an observable fact (we fret about bald tires) with an unobservable one (cavemen worried that a mastodon might trample them). Loewenstein is alert to the danger of producing “just-so” stories, accounts of human attributes based on unconfirmable hunches about what life was like in the Paleolithic era. But they’re hard to avoid.

Even if we accept these evolutionary explanations, they leave a further puzzle. Why do negative emotions so often persist long after they’ve served their purpose? Like the earworms of cheesy pop songs, they can get stuck in our heads. Our brains continue pumping them out even when the occasions for them have passed.

We also have the unfortunate ability to reëxperience some negative feelings just by remembering the occasions for them. We may find it hard to recall what physical pain felt like once it has stopped, but, when we remember something shameful we did, we can feel the shame all over again. Most of us could use an empathy gap there.

“At the heart of so many of our miseries,” Loewenstein says, “is not the fact that we feel bad, but the belief that we should feel otherwise.” Our brains fight with themselves. We feel ashamed of our shame, angry about our anger. The wish to escape an unpleasant emotion becomes another source of misery. Who’s running the show in there?

Not “us.” We may resolve, after firing off an intemperate e-mail, to respond more calmly the next time. But, when the next provocation arrives, our anger can make the resolution seem lame. As Loewenstein explains, we are adept at psychological self-sabotage. Sometimes our very efforts to gain control make things worse, as when athletes concentrate too intently on not trying so hard.

In the second half of “The Opposite of Happiness,” Loewenstein lets unhappiness sufferers speak for themselves. He has gathered their stories through what he calls the Misery Survey, in which more than five hundred respondents were asked about their experiences of negative emotions. Each was assigned an emotion at random and asked whether it had caused them misery. If it had, they were invited to describe the experience; if not, they were assigned another emotion. The stories make for fun reading (more or less), not so much because they hold surprises but because we recognize ourselves in so many of them. Misery, it turns out, loves company.

Loewenstein devotes a chapter to each of twelve varieties of misery. It’s a bit like Dante’s Inferno if Dante had modelled his work on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders rather than the “Summa Theologiae” of Thomas Aquinas. The first two circles in Loewenstein’s hell are Impatience and Boredom, followed by Anger, Envy, Jealousy, Rejection, Guilt, Shame, Anxiety, Regret, Loneliness, and, in the last circle, Depression, which he deems “a fitting finale to this Hieronymus Bosch underworld of psychic torments—not just because it is so supremely awful, but because nearly all the other miseries, when they persist and accumulate, can give rise to it.” (Hate, a resurgent political emotion across much of the planet, did not make the list. Neither did grief.)

Loewenstein suspects that depression, unlike some other negative emotions, has no adaptive function of its own. It arises, he thinks, as a by-product of other psychological systems in distress. That’s close to what Peter D. Kramer concluded in his 2005 book, “Against Depression,” where he defines depression as “a disease in which a host of injuries combine to cause a common downstream process that becomes self-sustaining.” It is hard to see how suicidality conduces to reproductive success. And depression can create what Loewenstein terms “the ultimate empathy gap”: people in its grip find it almost impossible to imagine what life without it would feel like.

At the other end of his inferno is boredom. We might not think of boredom as an emotion. It seems more like the absence of emotion. But, in a study tracking the daily feelings of some four thousand adults, Loewenstein and his colleagues found that boredom frequently accompanied strong negative feelings, including anger and anxiety. “We found that boredom was 4.2 times more likely to occur in the presence of another negative emotion than a positive one,” he says.

Two places where people commonly report being bored are doctors’ waiting rooms and airport terminals. We sit there fiddling with our smartphones, and with nothing else to do, running scary or angry scenarios through our heads—the medical news will not be good, the flight will be cancelled, they will close the gate while I’m in line at Starbucks—and composing powerfully cogent letters to the airline about the incompetence of the gate crew. We get mad when we are forced to wait for something for which there are no substitutes, and then we complain that we’re bored. (In a section titled “Why Are Dreams So Boring?,” Loewenstein says that one of the most “excruciatingly boring” things we can do is listen to someone describe a dream they had. This reads like a barely veiled put-down of his famous forebear.)

But how did we acquire the capacity for boredom? There don’t seem to have been airports or doctors’ offices back in Paleolithic times, when men just hunted and gathered (and, we hope, partied). Loewenstein suggests that the ability to become bored developed as a way of budgeting attention. “If early humans didn’t feel the urge to redirect their attention when staring at the same patch of woods,” he says, “they might have missed important opportunities—a rustle in the bush that signaled prey, or an approaching threat. Our ancestors who were better at reallocating attention had an adaptive advantage: they probably avoided more predators, found more food, and pursued more socially or intellectually engaging activities.” This might be a little just-so-y. It’s hard to see how the humans or proto-humans who never got bored were the ones who got selected out. Maybe sabre-toothed tigers ate them all.

Other evolutionary explanations seem more persuasive. Loewenstein agrees with many people who have written about negative emotions that feelings like shame and guilt perform a regulatory social function. They help enforce the norms of the group. Shame, in particular, encourages submission rather than confrontation, a response “designed to protect us from one of the greatest threats to our survival—being cast out.”

Explaining why negative emotions might have evolved, though, still leaves that problem of why they can become so consuming, so hard to toggle off. Why do we spiral? Is it because we inherited emotions like anxiety which evolved in response to genuine threats to survival and can now be triggered by the prospect of missing the bus? Or were our emotions always liable to become excessive? Did our Stone Age ancestors lie awake wondering whether they had remembered to put out the fire pit?

Loewenstein thinks that it’s at least partly the latter. Our emotional system, he says, “is prone, almost by design, to malfunction.” To protect us against threats, it has to be highly sensitive, prone to false alarms rather than risk missing a real danger. But this sensitivity also makes the system unstable. He believes our psyches are poised on a “razor’s edge” between negative feedback, which allows an emotion to subside when the threat has passed, and positive feedback, in which an emotion amplifies itself. Anxiety, for example, makes us more alert to threats, which can make us perceive more threats, which heightens our anxiety. It’s like driving on an icy road: the harder we brake, the more we lose control of the car.

Of course, an emotion that makes us miserable is not necessarily an irrational response to our circumstances. One question we can ask about psychological diagnoses is whether some states we classify as symptoms of mental disorders are responses to a world that’s genuinely frightening or depressing. What if life really is meaningless? What if other people really are out to get us? What if the barista really is hitting on our girlfriend? Then feelings like sadness, anger, and jealousy might be perfectly understandable, and the emotions that need to be explained are optimism, tolerance, and a sense of humor. Maybe it’s the optimists who are the crazy ones.

In the list of books that helped replace a theological understanding of the universe with a secular one, “On the Origin of Species” is near the top. One theory about Darwin’s poor health, in fact, was that he was horrified by the implications of his own discoveries—that our species was not a special creation and that no providence dictated its characteristics. Natural selection is a blind process. There is no being out there or up there that oversees its course.

Still, there is a way in which evolutionary psychology belongs to a religious tradition, the tradition of theodicy. This was the effort of theologians to explain why, given an omnipotent and beneficent God, there is evil in the world. Transposed to a Darwinian world view, this becomes the question: If natural selection has equipped us to survive and reproduce, why has it burdened us with so much misery? There is a temptation to assume that every form of suffering must have served some evolutionary purpose, just as God must have had a reason for earthquakes in Lisbon. The problem of why bad things happen kept intellectuals busy for centuries. The problem of unhappiness promises to do the same. It may be that both depend on a shared illusion: that it all makes sense. ♦

items.title: Changing Our Relationship to Technology Will Require Collective Action
items.description: At noon, at six-thirty, and at ten at night, before I shuffle off to bed, my phone automatically shuts off access to all social-media sites. If I want to restore my ability to mindlessly scroll, I have to walk sheepishly to my kitchen and press my phone up aga
items.author: Jay Caspian Kang
paragraphs: At noon, at six-thirty, and at ten at night, before I shuffle off to bed, my phone automatically shuts off access to all social-media sites. If I want to restore my ability to mindlessly scroll, I have to walk sheepishly to my kitchen and press my phone up against a little plastic square that sits on a high shelf. This humiliation device, called the Brick, limits my screen time to the apps that, in an earlier moment of clarity, I deemed essential: text messages and Apple Books, which, during these Bricked hours, I have been using to dutifully reread “The Brothers Karamazov,” prompted more by a sense of shame than by a sincere interest in revisiting the great novels. (If I’m still going to be on my phone, it should be for something ostensibly edifying.) In the past year, the Brick has represented the only real resistance I’ve mustered against the continual creep of the online world into my daily life. My screen time hasn’t decreased, but it’s better, I suppose, to read Ivan Fyodorovich’s rants about God than to watch endless reels about the latest revolution in shin-guard technology or whatever.

I have been thinking and writing about resistance to technology for a while, spurred by an unresolved alarm that Americans have not put up much of a fight against the sense of alienation caused by our growing dependence on screens. It’s increasingly clear to me that we will not survive as a society without some seismic intervention that separates us from our screens, our algorithms, and our little simulacra of social life. I believe that such a rupture will come—but what will it look like? Will it resemble the dropout movement of the late nineteen-sixties and early seventies, with waves of young people refusing to abide by convention? Or will we eventually see a government anti-screen initiative, one that “raises awareness” and issues stiff penalties against tech companies, similar to the ones levelled against tobacco companies in the nineties? Perhaps we will shed our phone addiction the way we have gradually shed cigarettes.

Whatever the solution may be, it feels, at the moment, impossibly far away. In the immediate aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, which had glued us all more tightly than ever to our phones, many people, I’m sure, crafted some limp armistice like mine, buying a Brick or muting notifications or stashing their phones in other rooms at bedtime, or even just leaving them on “Do Not Disturb” throughout the day. But, in most cases, that was about the extent of their protests. If there is a local initiative to ban the use of devices in their children’s schools, they will support it, but they will probably not do much to rip the phones out of their children’s hands. Most of us have settled into a persistent but passive discontent.

During the next few weeks, I’ll be exploring, in a series of columns, whether this malaise is finally breaking. There is some evidence that it is. For example: the American public has coalesced into what the election forecaster Nate Silver calls a “super-majority” against data centers. That opposition began in raucous protests at town halls and building sites, but it has metastasized into something of a national movement. (According to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project, there have been more than three hundred protests against data centers in the U.S. this year.) Data centers now feature in the electoral platforms of numerous officeholders and candidates, including the Democratic Presidential hopeful Ruben Gallego, who recently announced a tax plan that would shift the construction and energy costs of data centers away from the public and onto the tech companies that benefit from them. Gallego is a relatively moderate and somewhat heterodox candidate, and although his plan isn’t exactly a Luddite call to smash the robots, he might be seen as a bellwether for what the left side of the aisle will be thinking in the coming years. People in the streets and politicians in Congress aren’t the only ones demonstrating a tech backlash: the courts have handed down a set of billion-dollar rulings against tech giants, including in a recent case in New Mexico in which Meta was found guilty of forty-three million violations of the state’s laws.

These days, resistance to tech is typically framed in terms of individual choices: if we buy the Brick, limit our children’s screen time, delete the worst apps from our phones, stop doomscrolling, and refuse to use ChatGPT for anything other than the most mundane searches, we will be released from the grasp of Big Tech. Freedom becomes a question of your own will power. In 2022, the Times published a charming story about “Luddite” teens in Brooklyn who met up in Prospect Park once a week to draw, whittle, and read “The Consolation of Philosophy.” The teens, many of them inspired by the D.I.Y. punk scene and Jon Krakauer’s “Into the Wild,” had decided to drop out of digitized life and start noticing the world outside their phones. Like these kids, I usually think about tech resistance in terms of my own attention and that of my family. I worry constantly about whether the iPad is rotting my children’s brains; I celebrate every reduction in my weekly screen-time reports. But I think this individual focus has a lot to do with why we feel so helpless against Big Tech, and I wonder whether those of us who want to free ourselves from our phones might be better off thinking more collectively.

One of the longest-running and most significant ongoing political actions against A.I. has come from nurses, who, since at least the spring of 2024, have been protesting the technology’s incursion into their profession. Their concerns are numerous and rooted in both present practices and future possibilities. This past March, more than two thousand mental-health professionals at the health-care consortium Kaiser Permanente went on a one-day strike over concerns that they would eventually be replaced by artificial intelligence. Four months later, a story in CalMatters detailed new surveillance layers that had been placed on nurses at Kaiser, including an A.I. program that allegedly assessed their empathy and the tone of their voices when they answered calls from patients. Last year, HCA Healthcare, one of the largest hospital providers in the country, released a joint program with Palantir called Timpani, which promised to streamline the scheduling of nurses by using A.I. to spot inefficiencies. This past August, the National Nurses United (N.N.U.) union led a day of nationwide demonstrations against Palantir.

Americans, in general, like nurses and don’t trust A.I. companies, much less Palantir, to make potentially life-saving decisions. And although hospital efficiency measures are nothing new—almost every labor fight in the health-care sector arises out of issues around head count and hours—A.I. represents a different type of invasion. The N.N.U. is not demanding a full removal of A.I. technology from workplaces, or suggesting a return to a time when all scheduling was done by hand and all consultations were aided only by a nurse’s hard-earned experience. Rather, the union is drawing a line at A.I. supremacy in staffing, decision-making, and clinical assessments. “What makes A.I. even more dangerous is the insistence of health-care companies and these billionaires to use it as a technology to override the judgment of nurses, and to override their clinical decision-making,” Puneet Maharaj, the executive director of the N.N.U., told me.

Maharaj said that A.I. has infiltrated many parts of a nurse’s workday. In the past, nurses’ schedules were partly automated but overseen by a human manager, who could be aware of, and responsive to, personal issues. Now schedules are run entirely by A.I., which, according to Maharaj, will always understaff nurses’ posts. When nurses arrive at their shifts, they may be asked to use A.I. tools that listen to their interactions with patients, and A.I. may also be used to evaluate medical records. These programs have been known to make mistakes in their automated assessments. For example, Maharaj said, in the course of describing the details of their day, a patient might mention battling pine needles in yardwork, and an A.I. might mislabel the patient as having an opioid problem. The listening machines also raise real questions about patient privacy. “With A.I., we don’t always know where that information is going and whether it will be protected or not,” Maharaj said. (A.I. phone-monitoring is of particular concern among mental-health professionals. This was another reason for the Kaiser Permanente strike in March.)

The ultimate concern, though, is that A.I. will replace the relationship between nurse and patient and turn medical professionals into meat puppets who do the machine’s bidding. “Maybe you can look at efficiency when you’re looking at widgets,” Maharaj said. “But when you’re talking about patients, and you’re talking about the relationship between a nurse and her patient—that is extremely important, and that is reserved for the judgment of the nurse, and not some technology that is going to override their judgment.”

The nurses’ protests are intriguing in part because organized labor has the capacity, the experience, and the public approval necessary to secure support outside of a single industry. And the N.N.U. protests go beyond the direct workplace concerns of nurses. Palantir was chosen specifically as a target of protest not just for its incursion into health care but for its role in surveillance and military technology. “A corporation that is invested in killing people should have no space in health care, where the goal is to keep people healthy and alive,” Maharaj said. She pointed out that Palantir was making inroads into a wide range of industries, and that this, in turn, presented a “great opportunity for allies, labor and non-labor alike.” The playbook, then, seems to be high-profile strikes and demonstrations that not only spotlight nuts-and-bolts questions about staffing but also address the more existential and perhaps still somewhat abstract fear that A.I. will become a replacement for nurses everywhere. A confrontation with Palantir, the mere name of which causes many Americans to recoil, can bring in other labor unions and also political activists who opposed Palantir’s more notorious work. Solidarity is easier when there’s a common enemy; there are few better ones than Palantir.

Is this a more productive path to resisting technology than our individual efforts? The sentimental lefty in me would say that the answer, obviously, is yes: rallying together against a powerful villain to address material and workplace harms offers both the clarity and the social support that we’ll need to beat back some of the most pernicious and anti-human excesses of the tech industry. Still, I’m not sure that such actions will entirely satisfy the Luddite teens who desire a separation from the digital world rather than worker control over inevitable technological change. Of course, that has no bearing on the merits of the nurses’ union’s actions—I only want to point out that the dissatisfaction with our screen lives is uniquely personal, for the simple reason that we mostly look at our devices alone, and whatever we bury inside them is generally accessed only by us. In the past decade, nobody, not even my parents or my kids or my wife, has looked upon my face more than has my phone’s camera, which, without comment, scans my features a hundred times a day. If that camera were always on, and someone were watching the feeds, what range of emotions would they witness passing through its narrow frame? Next week, I will write about this modern narcissism and what we might be able to do about it. ♦

items.title: The Death Knell of Digital Search
items.description: Lately, I’ve been having trouble finding stuff in my Gmail inbox. The Search function has become overzealous, jumping to summarize my conversations using artificial intelligence and skipping the actual addresses I’m attempting to search. It’s not just e-mail a
items.author: Kyle Chayka
paragraphs: Lately, I’ve been having trouble finding stuff in my Gmail inbox. The Search function has become overzealous, jumping to summarize my conversations using artificial intelligence and skipping the actual addresses I’m attempting to search. It’s not just e-mail accounts, though; search is in crisis everywhere. Google Maps guesses where I want to go at a given time of day instead of simply listing places I’ve just searched for. When I try to use Google Search, the A.I.-overview function sometimes occupies my entire browser window, generating its own, not always correct, answers rather than directing me to relevant websites. Full-on A.I. mode skips the old blue links entirely.

Search has gotten so annoying, in fact, that it has become a problem for Google’s very business model. Companies pay Google to splash ads into search results that are relevant to their businesses—advertising stoves, say, to someone searching for kitchen-renovation tips. More than half of Google’s revenue comes from those ads. But, if users aren’t clicking through to external sites, because they’re relying on A.I. to answer their queries, then the ads that Google hosts are suddenly much less valuable. In a recent earnings call, Google’s chief business officer, Philipp Schindler, admitted that the company has been seeing “lower monetization” on A.I. searches. After the call, the stock of Alphabet, Google’s parent company, fell by nearly a quarter, down five hundred billion dollars, the largest single-day drop in its history. Even Google may not be too big to fail, as pessimism mounts about the possibility of Search ever again working the way it used to.

Just as Google has faltered in Search, use of OpenAI’s ChatGPT has surged. OpenAI’s consumer-product lead, Adam Fry, recently told the tech journalist Alex Kantrowitz that ChatGPT is siphoning users away from the older company: over the past year and a half, it has grown to handle one-fifth the volume of “search-like queries” that Google does. This acceleration only makes sense: a growing number of people now rely on A.I. chatbots as their primary windows to the internet, and they’re less likely to click out of those apps to ask the kinds of simple questions that they might once have turned to Google to answer. It doesn’t help that bots have lately grown much better at browsing the internet in real time, using virtual browsers and plug-ins, rather than simply generating answers from preëxisting data. Google has its own suite of A.I. products, Gemini, but they’ve lagged in popularity behind Anthropic’s Claude and ChatGPT. The investment firm Menlo Ventures found that Gemini accounts for only nine per cent of A.I. spending for businesses in 2026, down from twenty-one per cent last year.

Can the internet as we know it survive without a reliable flood of search traffic? Chatbots treat websites as databases of information to draw from, but since they divert traffic from those sites they don’t provide much impetus for creators to keep posting new content. The end state we’re heading toward seems to be an internet both generated and traversed by bots—in which case, it will no longer matter how annoying it is for a mere human being to find information. Some websites are already moving defensively to keep out the trawling bots attempting to digest their content. Reddit, one of the internet’s major remaining repositories of human-generated knowledge and opinions, is moving toward “a primarily logged-in experience,” as its C.E.O., Steve Huffman, recently announced. In a third-quarter letter to shareholders, Huffman noted that Reddit’s search traffic “dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week” during October. The letter explained, “Web search is evolving from a gateway to the web to becoming an AI-powered destination itself.” In a recent earnings call, Huffman said that “people still want Reddit” but that “Google is not sending them to Reddit the way they used to.” Requiring users to log in is the equivalent of pulling up the drawbridge to keep away the A.I. models roaming outside. But it also means that the casual human searcher will be less likely to see the full conversations happening on Reddit.

In 2019, before the A.I. boom, the entrepreneur Yancey Strickler presciently outlined a “dark-forest theory of the internet.” As the web experience got worse, Strickler argued—because of “the ads, the tracking, the trolling, the hype, and other predatory behaviors”—users would retreat to more private, hidden online spaces, or “dark forests,” in search of human interaction. We once used search to find those dark forests and find the humans on the internet who were doing whatever we were interested in. Now those old tricks of Boolean operators and half-remembered keywords don’t work, because we’re meant to trust a robot to do the navigating for us instead. I often feel that the internet isn’t built for us human users anymore.

One prominent tech-commentator account on X has described companies as locked in “a knife fight for the remaining and dwindling volume of human traffic on the internet.” Many seem to have bought into the narrative that the old-school open internet is done for, so they’re scrambling to lock users into their own, A.I.-automated walled gardens. (Not to be left behind, Reddit is introducing an algorithmic For You feed and A.I.-generated short-form videos based on its content.) Google recently inspired a public backlash when it announced that it would make A.I. functions optional, rather than permanently accessible, on its software suite for schools and students, but with a catch: if schools turned off the Gemini A.I. functions, they would lose access to Google Search, too. This policy amounts to a threat: use generative A.I. or use nothing. The largest tech companies are investing so much capital in A.I. infrastructure—chips, data centers, intensively trained models—that they must make the bet pay off, one way or another.

The upshot is that, more often than not, I find myself using A.I. to fight back against aggressive A.I. Instead of using the Gmail app on my phone, I’ve been texting my questions about my own inbox to an A.I. agent called Instinct, which I recently granted access to my account. (It’s a security risk, to be sure, but one I was willing to take to see if the product is any good for techno-normies.) In a matter of seconds, Instinct can dig up an event invitation or a note from someone whose name I can’t quite remember. Instead of Googling potential interview subjects, I have Claude scrape for their contact information. But I would really prefer if Search just worked the way it did in the first place. ♦

items.title: “Wicker” and What Straight Women Want
items.description: “Being Straight Is Great, Actually” is the original title of an opinion piece published in the Times earlier this year, by Magdalene Taylor, a senior editor at Playboy. Timing is everything; the piece ran on May 31st, on the precipice of Pride Month, and that
items.author: Doreen St Félix
paragraphs: “Being Straight Is Great, Actually” is the original title of an opinion piece published in the Times earlier this year, by Magdalene Taylor, a senior editor at Playboy. Timing is everything; the piece ran on May 31st, on the precipice of Pride Month, and that gave it an incendiary lift. The essay was addressed to a certain kind of heterosexual woman, one with whom we’ve all become familiar. A loathing has rotted her heart, a loathing directed at the subpar men who surround her, and at herself. She is a smart woman. She is enraged by the recession of gender equality, she is appalled by the prominence of Andrew Tate and his misogyny gospel, and she is alarmed by the proliferation of the trad wife. She has removed herself from the apps, and perhaps from men altogether. And yet she still wants them, these men, or at least the idea of them. She keeps wanting them, all while not wanting them.

Taylor cheerily argues against this prevailing “bad mood” that is all the rage these days—that mood being heteropessimism, a cultural condition first explored, and named, by the writer and scholar Asa Seresin, in The New Inquiry, back in 2019. Seresin was trying to work out a knot. He used the framework of Afropessimism, which he described as “a school of thought that takes antiblackness to be the transhistorical structuring force of the world,” to understand an emergent form of internet-era ennui: “performative disaffiliations with heterosexuality, usually expressed in the form of regret, embarrassment, or hopelessness about straight experience.” Coinage is deadening. “Heteropessimism” had the appeal of new jargon, and it launched about a million confessionals that, maddeningly, had the effect of narrowing questions about desire—political desire, romantic desire, what have you—instead of opening them up.

The second title of Taylor’s essay, the Times’ fix after the initial blowback, is “There’s Nothing Wrong With Wanting Men.” This permissiveness—the permission to desire—is one theme of the new film “Wicker,” a romp directed by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson. The movie’s essence is Chaucerian; the pacing is taut, jaunty, like a fairy tale, helped along by a twinkling score composed by Anna Meredith. In a medieval village, men are named by their occupations—the Tailor (Nabhaan Rizwan), the Bottle Washer (Gustav Lindh)—and the women, by their affiliation to their husbands—the Tailor’s Wife (Elizabeth Debicki), the Bottle Washer’s Wife (Marli Siu). The film delights in the slippage between satire and historical accuracy, laying out before us a wheat-colored, barely civilized civilization. Lewdness rules. The people are ritualistic. The men are boors. The women are sour. At marriage, the maiden bends her head and joyfully receives a collar, this universe’s version of a “ring,” and the union is pronounced “man and his wife.” At the reception for one such marriage, that of the Bottle Washer and his wife, the whole town spills out to celebrate. One woman, an outcast, the Fisherwoman, played by Olivia Colman—a performer whose gift of interpretation allows her to enliven the one-dimensional, matronly characters she often chooses to play—looks off scoffingly, but not uninterested.

“Wicker” is a hybridized movie, a comedy/horror/romance. It basically sustains itself on a pun, that of hard wood, but its recombinations of the joke don’t get old. We meet the Fisherwoman on the outskirts of town, by the water, where she expertly guts and cleans her fish, shelters in a modest hut, and pisses in a bucket by her bed. The women in town ridicule her for her fish stench, which is also the smell of being unchosen. But isn’t the Fisherwoman, a kind of sister to Chaucer’s working woman—the five-times married Alison, the beloved first sovereign woman of English literature—content to be alone? The film, which is based on a short story by Ursula Wills called “The Wicker Husband,” tees up a proto-feminist refusal: “Love seems more a burden than a prize,” the Fisherwoman replies to her bullies, who sarcastically ask if she has yet to catch a lover. What do they know about love? The time for the familiar beat, the wish-fulfillment moment, soon arrives. The Fisherwoman appeals to the Basketmaker (Peter Dinklage), a fellow-outcast, to cure her loneliness by making her a wicker husband.

The op-ed-informed mind luxuriates in the resonances that this movie continuously lobs at it. And the lightness of “Wicker” prevents us from ever feeling lectured at. For too short a time, it is a sexy movie. Alexander Skarsgård—his enormous form covered in an intricately knitted suit meant to mimic the wave and stroke of soft willow, all the way down to lashes drawn from flax fibre—takes the role of the Fisherwoman’s husband as his raison d’être, because it is. He is a dream man because he is not a man; he is made from earth, never baptized in the swamp of patriarchy. Wicker Husband and the Fisherwoman enter a haze of domestic bliss. Their sex breaks the bed. Wicker Husband is happy to fix it, and also to fix the roof, after he notices water dripping from the ceiling and onto the Fisherwoman’s foot, as she lies underneath him spread-eagle. The sound of their pleasure wakes up the whole town; it awakens a jealousy, confusion, and anger not only in the other women but in the men, with both camps amazed that marriage could ever beget something like pleasure. A culture war explodes. I won’t spoil the conflict, but know that it is not too dissimilar from the zealotry you might see on a manosphere message board.

The monster romance is as old as Pasiphaë tricking the white bull into bedding her, but a spate of recent offerings, across film and literature, especially, have come to form something less like a genre and more like a drug. The straight woman is in crisis, we’re told, and so she lightens her pain by engorging herself on works of romantasy, in which nonhuman creatures satisfy very human wants. The author Sarah J. Maas, known for her “A Court of Thorns and Roses” series, which devotees lovingly claim as fairy smut, has sold more than a hundred million books worldwide. In Hollywood, a certain ur-monster is getting notably and problematically hotter: Jacob Elordi’s Creature, as painstakingly imagined by the fable obsessive Guillermo del Toro, in his version of “Frankenstein,” is a soulful giant, with a shattered-pottery body and a long stare. In Maggie Gyllenhaal’s millennial update, “The Bride!,” Christian Bale reinvents the creature as a tall, dark, and handsome cinephile. You can imagine a version of “Wicker” that’s braver, accepting of the implicit queerness of its central couple, that does not make this monster so debonair and forthright and Skarsgårdian, to communicate something more real about the grotesque, and how, counterintuitively, it drives attraction.

The straight woman must find her love. I wasn’t expecting to think of Ingmar Bergman’s masterpiece “Scenes from a Marriage” after I watched “Wicker,” but, as I left the theatre, it came up. Bergman’s exploration of divorce, of the emotional alienation a marriage can bring, was blamed, in Sweden and elsewhere in Europe, for a spike in divorce rates. Causation seems dubious, but the point is about an outside force facilitating enlightenment. When the heteropessimist doubt begins to take over, in “Wicker,” when the Fisherwomen lets her mind be poisoned by rumor and gossip, the union starts to crumble. It’s the outside world, the ideological world, that introduces issues. “Wicker” ends with the promise of gender equality. As a marriage movie, it believes too deeply in the institution as a potentially liberating event in a woman’s life. The Husband is nothing more than hot; his undeveloped and cloistered psychology gives the marriage its ultimate peace. The film has to meet the needs of romance, but isn’t that the problem, the expectation that life moves like genre? ♦

items.title: Donald Trump’s Repudiation, America’s Revenge in the Midterms
items.description: It wasn’t even 11 P.M. on Election Night—the worst Election Night for an incumbent President’s party pretty much ever—when Donald Trump weighed in for the first time. For weeks he had travelled the country, insisting that voters act as though he were on the ba
items.author: Susan B Glasser
paragraphs: It wasn’t even 11 P.M. on Election Night—the worst Election Night for an incumbent President’s party pretty much ever—when Donald Trump weighed in for the first time. For weeks he had travelled the country, insisting that voters act as though he were on the ballot and that the campaign should be a referendum on him and his policies. But Trump’s first response was to disclaim all responsibility. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he posted defiantly. A few minutes later, he blamed the governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, for losing his own race, claiming that one of the most conservative politicians in the country had been defeated because Abbott had become “a RINO”—a Republican in name only. A few minutes after that, Trump posted an image of a red baseball cap with the word “VETO” emblazoned on it. By just before midnight, he was saying it was all because of his formerly favorite TV network. “Fox News,” he complained, “bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse.”
Yes, we get it. He’s not going to go quietly. He’s not going to accept blame. Trump in defeat is still Trump. “I shouldn’t feel guilty,” he told Bret Baier, of Fox News. “It’s just a point in time.”

But the scale of Tuesday night’s reckoning defies even his ability to lie, dissemble, and generally squirm his way out of it. It is really hard to steal an election when voters all across America reject you. These were the President’s own voters, in states where he won by huge margins just a couple of years ago. By Wednesday morning, J. D. Vance admitted it wasn’t that Republicans failed to show up but that they did. “The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026,” he wrote on social media. Reality, if only temporarily, burst the White House bubble. Even Trump and his cronies know that Iowa and Kansas and Michigan and North Carolina and South Carolina and Texas did not all conspire together to rig the outcome. This righteous blue wave was made in red America.

Whatever he may say later—and I have no doubt he will spend years pretending that what just happened somehow did not just happen—Trump knows it, too. Even as the scale of the disaster for him was still becoming clear, he told the Times that he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results that he’d spent the past two years preparing to contest.

For now and for forever, the midterm election of 2026 will be known as one of the most decisive rejections of an American President since long before Richard Nixon got on that helicopter in 1974. Republicans losing both the House by thirty-five or more seats and the Senate by as many as eight seats—which now seems like a very real possibility—has happened only once since the Second World War: in 1958. And that campaign wasn’t anything close to the 2026 referendum on the dangerous words, disruptive actions, and bizarre personal preferences of the man in the White House.

Trump’s insistence on making the election so singularly about himself was not a surprise, but it was an error right out of a Greek tragedy—an epic self-own by the Narcissus of the National Mall that could be read only as a direct disavowal of the President. Republicans in Washington these past two years failed spectacularly when it came to defending the nation from the depredations of their party’s leader, but Republican voters around the country—enough of them, at least—admitted their mistake and did something big to rectify it. As the MAGA pundits on Fox News struggled for words to explain the calamity that they had not wanted to admit was coming, there was much clarity to be found in the viral clips of regular Republican voters interviewed at the polls, clarity and the clearest possible sense of moral revulsion: they did not want Trump, his policies, or his party anymore.

Was it because of the Iran war, as many here in Washington are already starting to argue? (“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote on X. “The president himself said so last night.”) Maybe, but I think not only that. Results like this don’t happen just because diesel is pushing seven dollars a gallon at the pump. The scale of this is so large because the scale of Trump’s offenses has been so vast. Tariffs and trade wars, Canada-bashing, Europe-bashing, the betrayal of Ukraine and embrace of Vladimir Putin, the grotesque self-enrichment of himself and his circle, the unleashing of an armed militia of ICE goons on our streets. People voted for Alex Pretti and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. They voted against data centers and Elon Musk buying elections. They voted against the cost of everything being too damn high. They voted because so much of what is happening in Trump’s America seems so very un-American.

Trump’s own role in this cannot be discounted. I know that structural factors are often considered the most important ones by political scientists. They will perform their regression analyses and examine the economic data and conclude that the results were probably baked in months ago. But, still, I hope they study the President’s last month of campaigning, too, an orgy of foolishness and mean-spirited lies that included twenty-one rallies in twenty-one days, where he talked about Jon Husted’s ass, the glories of his golden ballroom, and the algae in the Reflecting Pool while dismissing and demeaning voters’ concerns about practically everything. He said that affordability was a Democratic hoax and that the war he started and has failed to win wasn’t really a war at all and that the other guys were so awful that they would allow men to play in women’s sports. It speaks to the utter debasement of those around the President that they allowed him to keep saying these things—and to the terrifying emptiness of Trump’s soul that he thought these were winning sentiments at all.

As the magnitude of the election began to hit on Tuesday, I started to keep track of all the different words being used to describe it: blue wave, blue tsunami, blue-nami, bloodbath, extinction-level event, flood, landslide, obliteration, once in a generation, once in a lifetime, rebuke, rejection, repudiation. As early as 9:58 P.M., John King announced on CNN, clearly, unequivocally, “This is the collapse of the President’s party, on live television.” He was right. This was more clear than Trump’s 2018 midterm defeat, more clear even than his ouster in 2020, amid COVID and Trump-created chaos—which is why it doesn’t matter what you call it.

By Wednesday morning, the White House was reduced to sending out pictures of their guy behind the Resolute desk, under the caption, “PSA: TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT.” He was glaring. If it seemed like a threat, I’m sure that was the intent. But so what? That’s a tomorrow problem. As Senator Jon Ossoff, of Georgia, said in a victory speech that might have been the opening lines of the 2028 Presidential campaign, “The first light of dawn is on the horizon.”
Whatever happens next, the American people have finally and definitively told Donald Trump that enough is enough. ♦

items.title: Stephen Miller’s Big Plan Is to Bring Back Men
items.description: Newly promoted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller has a new — or at least renewed — plan to return Trump and the GOP to glory: He wants to win back the men. Or more specifically, per Axios, he wants the administration to remind the young and minority me
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: Newly promoted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller has a new — or at least renewed — plan to return Trump and the GOP to glory: He wants to win back the men. Or more specifically, per Axios, he wants the administration to remind the young and minority men who swung nearly 40 points toward Democrats in the midterms why Trump is still the leader for them.

Miller has, of course, always been a fan of man. He repeatedly promoted Trump as the only real choice for real men during the 2024 presidential campaign, and at one point even suggested to young men that being loud and proud for Trump would get them laid:

If you’re a young man — it’s very important in an election season — who’s looking to impress ladies, to be the alpha, to be attractive, the best thing you can do is to wear your Trump support on your sleeve. Show that you are a real man. Show that you are not a beta, right? Be a proud and loud Trump supporter and your dating life will be fantastic.

Like all other midterm swing voters, young men were primarily motivated by economic concerns created, overlooked, or greatly exacerbated by the Trump administration. Axios reports that Miller thinks refocusing on culture-war issues and affordability will do the job:

Miller wants to spend more time highlighting administration policies he believes haven’t gotten enough attention, and that will appeal to working-class voters concerned about the economy, insiders tell Axios.

His priorities will sound familiar to Trump watchers: eliminating what the administration considers “woke” policies from colleges and workplaces, lowering prescription drug prices, and rooting out government and health-care fraud. He also wants to emphasize reducing the federal bureaucracy and push for permitting reform, while highlighting how those efforts could help address affordability.

Those policies may also sound familiar to anyone who has paid any attention to what Trump and his allies have pushed and blamed others for over the past several years. And they seem to indicate that Miller believes a back-to-MAGA-basics approach — minus the Iran war, plus more lip service to costs of living — will somehow magically restore Trump’s 2024 coalition. It might, however, be hard to be alpha on affordability without the Democrat-controlled Congress onboard.

items.title: Trump Was Twice Warned About Huang’s Spy Lover
items.description: Back in May, while President Donald Trump was en route to Beijing for his big summit in China, he abruptly decided to invite and then pick up Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang along the way so that he could come, too. When Air Force One stopped to refuel in Alaska, Huan
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: Back in May, while President Donald Trump was en route to Beijing for his big summit in China, he abruptly decided to invite and then pick up Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang along the way so that he could come, too. When Air Force One stopped to refuel in Alaska, Huang met them there and came aboard. Up to that point, he had been conspicuously left off the list of big tech leaders invited to accompany Trump on the trip, and it’s not yet confirmed whether his girlfriend probably being a Chinese spy was the reason why.

This week, Trump was asked whether he knew about Huang’s affair with the spy at the time, and he replied, “No, I didn’t hear about it then.” Turns out he had been informed about it — twice, including once on that very flight.

The New York Times reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed (or actually reminded) Trump aboard Air Force One about the intelligence regarding Huang’s spy lover after learning they were on their way to pick up the CEO. And it was the second time Trump had been informed that Huang may be compromised, having been previously briefed on the matter. It either didn’t register or didn’t matter.

Trump has repeatedly defended Huang but has now changed his mind about bringing him to Beijing again next week. The closest Trump got to admitting he had heard anything about the spy lover was when he said this on Monday:
I’d certainly check with the intelligence people They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.

It’s all okay, though: The same government official who confirmed Trump was made aware of Huang’s spy connection said he only briefly saw Trump while aboard and and was otherwise relegated to a “separate part of the plane for almost all of the trip.”

items.title: Pete Hegseth Is Doing His Best ‘Impeached Trump’ Impression
items.description: Pete Hegseth staged his first news conference in more than half a year on Tuesday — and what he wanted to talk about was the abominable persecution of Pete Hegseth. The embattled so-called secretary of War is facing an impeachment vote by the House of Represen
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: Pete Hegseth staged his first news conference in more than half a year on Tuesday — and what he wanted to talk about was the abominable persecution of Pete Hegseth. The embattled so-called secretary of War is facing an impeachment vote by the House of Representatives, which as of now seems all but certain to succeed. The war in Iran he continues to champion just helped fuel a nationwide political reckoning against Trump and the Republican Party to the point that Vice-President J.D. Vance has blamed the GOP’s midterms disaster on the war. He has run the Pentagon like a tin-pot dictator and blustered his way through dozens of scandals.

But despite all of it, Hegseth still has his job and it’s clear he desperately wants to keep it. On Tuesday morning, while Hegseth didn’t try to nail himself to a cross onstage, he did compare himself to another well-known innocent victim of political persecution.
See? I’m just like Donald Trump! Hegseth told reporters (and Trump):

Hegseth singled out Thomas Massie, the renegade House Republican who has led the (bipartisan) effort to impeach him, framing the whole situation as a “farce and a stunt” perpetrated by “one disgruntled and defeated congressman.” And the secretary of Defense insisted that he was being attacked not for doing anything wrong but for doing so much right, following orders so well, and being so victorious against America’s enemies:
He also claimed the impeachment was an attack not just on him, and not just on the greatest commander-in-chief of all time, but on all American servicemembers:

Before the press event, a member of Hegseth’s security team threatened to physically remove any unruly reporters. When he was done with his speech, Hegseth mostly called on reporters from sympathetic right-wing news organizations. But he was still asked if he agreed with Vance that the Iran war was a mistake that cost the GOP the midterms. No, he responded:

While President Trump has reportedly privately asked around about whether he should get rid of Hegseth in the aftermath of the midterms, publicly he’s fully supported his Defense secretary. After the press conference, Trump gave Hegseth the highest possible grade for his performance.
“Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” he wrote in a Truth Social post.
Trump and his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, have reportedly encouraged Hegseth to fight the impeachment and have told him they’ll stand by him. Others seem less convinced, per CNN:

[T]here are many senior advisers throughout the administration who have grown skeptical of whether the defense secretary will be able to hang onto his position for much longer, arguing his goodwill with the president will last until it becomes a serious liability.

“The president will back him to a point,” one Trump ally, a former adviser to the president, told CNN. “But he may be forced to remove him once it’s no longer tenable. There are varying views in the West Wing on how long that will be.”

In addition, two Republican senators on Tuesday signaled their lack of support for Hegseth. Iowa’s Joni Ernst suggested Hegseth was lying to the White House and Congress about the Iran war. Another outgoing lame duck, Bill Cassidy, said he was open to the idea of an impeachment trial.

items.title: Why Didn’t Democrats Help Scott Colom?
items.description: The Associated Press and others have made it official: Democrat Scott Colom is going to become the next U.S. senator from Mississippi, and the first Black senator from the state since Reconstruction. The prediction markets had already been certain Colom won, b
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: The Associated Press and others have made it official: Democrat Scott Colom is going to become the next U.S. senator from Mississippi, and the first Black senator from the state since Reconstruction. The prediction markets had already been certain Colom won, but it took a week for his victory to be called while some absentee ballots and provisional votes were still outstanding. Now there should be hard questions about why national Democrats did not see this result coming and didn’t do more than the very little they did to help Colom upset the evidently weak Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Yes, several leading Black politicians, plus Rhode Island senator Sheldon Whitehouse, offered Colom some hands-on assistance, which drew some needed national attention. And, yes, during the final two weeks of the campaign, the national Senate Democratic PAC bought some ads and threw some money Colom’s way. But compared to what the party was committing to other Senate races, it was sofa-cushion money. Early on, Democrats targeted national spending on races their candidates eventually won easily, like Georgia and North Carolina, and later, they focused on late-breaking opportunities like Kansas and even South Carolina while spending to shore up Democratic-leaning races in Maine and Michigan. They spent heavily on Ohio and Texas nonstop. A little more in Mississippi might have eliminated any doubt about one of the most remarkable political upsets in living memory. And even a little more effort in Louisiana, where Jamie Davis came within 25,000 votes of upsetting Republican incumbent Julia Letlow, could have produced an equally shocking result. And Florida Democrats believe more national help could have lifted Senate candidate Angie Nixon and gubernatorial candidate David Jolly to victory in races that wound up being very close.

So what was the problem? Colom understandably doesn’t want to blame Chuck Schumer and his likely future colleagues in the Senate Democratic Conference. But he’s clearly annoyed with the Beltway conventional wisdom and the institutions that help define it:

In defense of the Cook analysts, they typically base their ratings on polls, electoral history, and interviews with candidates, party leaders, and journalists on the ground in the places where the races are underway. So there may be some shooting-the-messenger in Colom’s complaints about Cook, which did move his race from “Solid R” to “Likely R” (a category where upsets are considered possible). But he’s right that Cook and most of the other experts, along with the national Democratic Party, underestimated the strength of their southern wing.

Perhaps there was an unconscious racial element in this myopia, since Colom, Davis, and Nixon were all Black candidates in red states that have not elected Black statewide candidates in living memory. But it seems to be more of a regional issue. White southern Democrats like the gubernatorial candidates in Alabama (Doug Jones), Florida (Jolly), and Tennessee (Jerri Green) were also written off and came very close to huge upsets. Meanwhile, the Beltway Establishment did not underrate Georgia’s Black Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms (whose race was rated a toss-up by Cook), despite her terrible fundraising disadvantage against billionaire Rick Jackson, for the simple reason that abundant polling showed her in a close race all along. So one very clear lesson of 2026 is that the national parties should do a lot more polling of states on the periphery of their vision, particularly in a “wave” election year. Even if the polling itself underestimated Democratic voting strength, as it did nationally by about 4 percent, it would have shown that a combination of strong Black turnout and swing-voter unhappiness with Donald Trump put much of the South within reach.

Perhaps the most difficult problem is that party strategists, like military strategists, have a strong tendency to fight the last war, basing their calculations on what happened in the last election. There is in fact no more reliable indicator of electoral outcomes in any given place than how that place has voted in the recent past. But there was abundant evidence throughout the 2026 cycle that the GOP’s 2024 coalition was falling apart. National Democrats (and the “prognosticators” they inform) should have been more open to the fresh opportunities Trump’s intense unpopularity presented for them. And strong “under-the-radar” candidates like Scott Colom should not have been forced to beg for attention and win an unequal fight on his own.
This post has been updated following Colom’s victory.
