items.title: Madonna Really Does Love New York
items.description: There I was minding my business (by not minding my business) when I get the email of a lifetime: "What are you up to Thursday night? Wanna spend it with Madonna?"
items.author: Paper Magazine
paragraphs: There I was minding my business (by not minding my business) when I get the email of a lifetime: "What are you up to Thursday night? Wanna spend it with Madonna?"

You know me by now... and if you’re pretending you don’t: I’m Linux, New York’s premiere downtown it-girl. I spend my nights either attending or throwing Scene City’s hottest parties. This week in particular is madness, being New York Pride. It's the Thursday of NYC’s Gay Marathon and, "What are you up to Thursday night?", was a question I'm more than prepared to answer.
At the end of the day, I’m a human being on planet Earth. And around these parts, when Madonna calls... you answer!

So I did just that (after waiting about 30 minutes to respond, of course... I didn’t want to come off too desperate). They told me to meet at the Moxy in Chelsea at 10 PM. A bus would be there waiting to take me and a hundred drag queens to a very proud and very gay night with Madonna at Terminal 5.

My Uber pulled up to the trendy hotel to a Jean Paul Gaultier-emblazoned double decker bus already boarding the world’s hottest gaylebrities: Symone, GiGi Goode, Shea Coulee, Aquaria, Gottmik, Detox and Kylie Sonique Love all posed for photos as the Gaultier team smoked cigarettes on the sidewalk. The bus driver honked his horn and we all screamed, knowing that noise meant it was time to leave towards Hells Kitchen to party with Madonna.

A DJ on the bus blasted Madonna's deep cuts as we drove through Times Square — a moment when all of us asked ourselves, "Is this real life?" Once we pulled up to Terminal 5, the marquee with Madonna’s name in flashing lights made it all too real that we were really about to see the Queen MDNA herself. So, what was this Madonna event all for anyways?

Madonna, who has been a leader in the NFT space, partnered for another time with WoW (World of Women), a thriving community celebrating representation, inclusivity and equal opportunities. The entire event was sponsored by The Sandbox, who has partnered with WoW to create the WoW Foundation, which will invest $25 million over five years in education and mentorship through programs across the metaverse.

Finally Enough Love, Madonna's 16-track career-spanning remix compilation album, was also released on streaming at midnight. To put it in simpler terms: Madonna was doing God’s work for the LGBTQ+ and wrapped it all up into a sickening Pride party.

As I entered the venue, I was immediately welcomed by teams of artists from MAC Viva Glam, who were offering guests Madonna-inspired touch ups (MAC Viva Glam has raised more than a half billion dollars to end HIV/AIDS). My makeup was already flawless, so I didn’t need anything done, but it's always nice to kiki with a MAC girlie.

I scammed my VIP bracelet from Geordon Nicol of the Misshapes, who was helping produce the night, and ran upstairs to Terminal 5’s VIP rooftop. I needed a cocktail and, luckily, Belvedere was offering free vodka, keeping the kids all liquored up. Next to the bar sat boxes and boxes of pizza from Made in NY (so Italian). But we’re not here for Pizza, we’re here for Madonna! So I ran back downstairs to get a good spot for the show.

Bob the Drag Queen served as MC. The icon Laganja Estranja performed "Vogue," where she was joined by Jose Xtravaganza, one of Madonna's dancers on the Blond Ambition tour. After that, we were all blindsided by Saucy Santana appearing on stage to perform "Walk," before "Material Girl" started playing and Madonna came out to perform it with him. Girl, when I tell you the crowd went wild! Herstory in the making. Madonna then premiered a "Hung Up" remix with Tokischa, which ended with the two of them making out on stage... it was really hot.
Joined by all of the performers, Madonna ended the night with a show-stopping performance of "Celebration" while rainbow confetti flooded the venue.

It was the best way to celebrate Pride imaginable. There was only one problem: I didn’t want it to end! Luckily, Madonna didn’t want it to either. For those with VIP bracelets, the party continued on the third floor of Terminal 5, where all the Ru Girls, it-kids and fashion peeps partied until the early morning.
Photography: Ricardo Gomes

items.title: Meet the Future of American Fashion
items.description: This is the November 4, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.
items.author: José Criales-Unzueta
paragraphs: This is the November 4, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

The United States has been overtaken by a blue wave following last night’s midterm elections. James Talarico flipped Texas to make it to the Senate, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire became the first out gay man to be elected to the Senate, and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia is now the first Black woman to be elected governor in the history of the US. There were great memes about what this could mean for the country—largely, the comeback of woke—and some fashion moments worth discussing. Scroll down for a midterm-fashion verdict, including notes on the curious case of a seemingly AI-generated picture featuring Chanel and Valentino products supposedly spotted at a Michigan Democratic Party election night event in support of Abdul El-Sayed.

In other news, Ye is staging a comeback Yeezy show in Los Angeles tonight at the brand’s flagship—keep an eye out tomorrow for a report from my Angeleno colleague Maxwell Adler. Congratulations are in order for Schiaparelli’s Daniel Roseberry, who is having a great week after running the New York City Marathon on Sunday, posting a much-discussed thirst trap on Monday morning, and receiving the Leader in the Arts Award at the Smithsonian’s annual Hirshhorn New York Gala on Monday night. Congratulations as well to the winners and honorees at the 2026 CFDA Awards. More on that very curious evening below, including an interview with Colleen Allen, certified fashion darling and Emerging Designer of the Year winner.

Mentioned in this issue: Jon Ossoff and his tight suit, Colleen Allen, Ralph Lauren, Jill Biden, Melania Trump, Hasan Piker, Zohran Mamdani and Rama Duwaji, and Tim Burton and his new Loewe collaboration.

The CFDA Fashion Awards on Monday night brought some star power to the American Museum of Natural History: Keke Palmer hosted, and presenters included Matt Damon, Cole Escola, Lupita Nyong’o, Laufey, and Demi Moore. And yet the mood of the evening was somewhat tentative. The Council of Fashion Designers of America is under something of a renovation: Steven Kolb, its former CEO, resigned in September following an altercation with PETA protesters at New York Fashion Week. Serving in his stead is Hildy Kuryk, a comms expert who spent four years at Vogue as its executive director of communications following a career in politics. Kuryk is serving as interim CEO and heading up the search for Kolb’s permanent replacement. On Monday night, she stayed out of the spotlight, leaving most of the audience wondering—and gossiping about—who the new face of the CFDA could and should be.

Rachel Scott of Diotima took the main award of the night as womenswear designer of the year, and Anthony Vaccarello, who just left Saint Laurent, was presented with the International Designer of the Year Award by muses Zoë Kravitz, Hailey Bieber, and Rosé. Ralph Lauren was named menswear designer of the year, securing his place as the most awarded designer in CFDA history. Mr. Lauren himself made an appearance—a crowd-pleaser that also left me wondering if the American industry often puts too much emphasis on its past and not enough on its future. In that spirit, I called up Colleen Allen, who took the prize for emerging designer of the year, and asked her to introduce herself to those of you who haven’t met her yet.
José Criales-Unzueta: What would you say is the most important thing for people to know about your background?

Colleen Allen: I often lead with that I always was a menswear designer and was never intending on doing womenswear. That point of view has really guided my work and who I’ve become. I just love the process of making. I did menswear because there wasn’t an identity of women that I saw that I connected with, really, with brands when I was first going to school. And I just loved the craft of tailoring and learning the physical process of cutting a pattern. I think there’s such an ephemerality in making womenswear, in a way. Draping on a mannequin is quite abstract to me. A huge part of my identity is thinking like a tailor.
Where did you go to school, and where did you work before starting your brand?

I did half at Parsons, half at Central Saint Martins. I consider Parsons to be quite technical, and Saint Martins sort of opened up the world conceptually for me and gave me a lot of freedom and thinking about world-building. I was at The Row doing menswear for three years, and then I also interned at Vogue for a minute [and] Calvin Klein 205W39NYC was a very formative experience. When I was an intern there, I was full-time. I was there for eight months, but it was just so cool because it was all in the same room with Raf [Simons, now at Prada], Pieter [Mulier, now at Versace], Matthieu Blazy [now at Chanel]. You knew at that moment how special it was and how crazy it was. I think the world didn’t process it, but when you were in the room, you knew these people were all so important. And so I think being around that every day and absorbing the way that they worked together and they’re such world-builders, all three of them are very conceptual. I think that was a huge informative experience for me.
What is your claim to fame?

I think that people know me for color. The feedback that I get from people who buy the clothes is that when you’re wearing a big velvet coat in a color, or even just a dress or a top, people get stopped on the street just because it’s so visually impactful. Velvet is also a signature. That duality of color and texture, and also a bit of a historical Victorian sensibility.
Where do you think that interest in Victorian garments comes from?

There’s an emotional, aesthetic love for it. There’s a bit of a groundedness and a weight to it, and a bit of that period of time was quite spiritual thinking about the afterlife and death, but there was a sense of romance around that that I think really seeped into the clothes in a way that I don’t know if other periods of time really reflect. On the other side of it, it isn’t Victorian specifically, but a lot of historical dress for women is incredible tailoring—thinking about those bodice jackets that have a lot of tiny little panels with lots of little grosgrain finishing on the seams on the inside—and it’s all about molding to the female body. As a menswear designer, I love wearing men’s clothes and wearing a tailored jacket, but I think that the idea of having that sensibility and also reflecting femininity is the perfect storm for me. A lot of that just got lost in a certain period of time once women were able to wear pants, and in the transition of women being able to access menswear, women’s tailoring never got back to that sort of technical level of fitting the body or the female form.
You’ve never done a runway show, which is something that many young designers feel signals their arrival. Why is that?

I love fashion and wanted to work in fashion because I loved watching fashion shows. And specifically, I loved shows that were immersive. I always go back to [Alexander] McQueen [that signaled] fashion is more than product. It is this world-building, cinematic performance art, and you can take it just so much further emotionally. If I’m going to do a show, I want it to carry that level of weight. For me, at my scale, it just feels like the most manageable way to encapsulate a sense of emotion is to do it through a [photo] shoot and showroom appointments for now, just in truly a practical sense. But it is my dream, and I’m working towards having a show. But when I do it, I want it to feel special.
What does this recognition mean to you?

It’s a bit surreal, in a way. It’s especially cool that it’s voted by the industry, and it sounds maybe kind of cheesy, but I do just feel like that is the best reward. That all these people that I’ve worked with are acknowledging [me]. It feels solidifying, grounding. It feels like I’ve been doing this forever, and it’s also going by so fast at the same exact time. It lets me be present and acknowledge myself for how much work has been put into it and that I did it and it’s real and it’s something I dreamed about for so long.
Do you feel like a fashion-industry darling?

[Laugh] Oh my God, how does one answer that question? Gosh, I think that three years ago I was entering these rooms knowing absolutely no one... I think the showroom has actually really fostered real relationships and friendships in the industry, and a sense of community that just feels really good. I work as hard as I can to support whatever the stylists are doing or the editors, I’m always physically running around to make sure that they get the clothes because I love what they do. I love that I know the photographer and the stylist and all the people, and know that if my clothes are in it, it will be amazing for me and they made the effort to reach out to me, to include me in it. The word darling is such an ick word [laugh]. I feel like the word I want to say is camaraderie, because everyone just works so hard. Nobody is flouncing around being a darling. We are all hustling together, and if I can support your hustle and you support mine, that’s the best thing. And when it works, it’s just so satisfying.

Tim Burton, iconoclast filmmaker extraordinaire, has a new capsule with Loewe, which has recreated characters and vignettes from The Nightmare Before Christmas as bags and charms. These kinds of collabs were a staple when Jonathan Anderson was at the brand, and Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez seem to be game to keep them coming with the same endearing whimsy.

In the age of artificial intelligence, the film has become a symbol of human craft and ingenuity. “The more it keeps going that way,” Burton told me yesterday, calling from London and answering a question about the proliferation of AI in film, “the more I appreciate [the human] side of it. I think it’s something that’s very important to keep in the world, the tactile, not being on a screen all the time and doing all that sort of thing. To me, [humanity] is very important to life and art and anything, really.” We also spoke about his collaboration with A$AP Rocky and whether he’d ever do a live-action remake of 2005’s Corpse Bride.
To subscribe to José Criales-Unzueta's weekly Fit Check newsletter, click here.

items.title: “I Hate My Fucking Life Right Now”: A Night Out With DC Republicans as the Blue Wave Crashed Down
items.description: It’s not easy to throw an election night party in Washington when your side is bracing for a wipeout. But at Butterworth’s, the bistro that has been a hub of MAGA Washington in Donald Trump’s second term, the DC Republicans were intent on trying. Women in busi
items.author: Aidan McLaughlin
paragraphs: It’s not easy to throw an election night party in Washington when your side is bracing for a wipeout. But at Butterworth’s, the bistro that has been a hub of MAGA Washington in Donald Trump’s second term, the DC Republicans were intent on trying. Women in business casual and men in the party uniform—blue suits, white shirts, and red ties taut to the collar—drank specialty cocktails including “The Elephant in the Room” and “The Senate Majority Martini.” The bar might have been busy, but the mood was precarious. As Dua Lipa blasted from the speakers inside, a man on a smoke break out on the street took big gulps of a pint of lager and stared down at his phone. “Darline Graham just plummeted on Polymarket,” he said, exhaling from his cigarette. “I hate my fucking life right now. Everything just sucks. Jesus Christ, we’re gonna lose it all.” A car drove past Butterworth’s with the windows down. A woman leaning out of an open window screamed, “Oh yeah, Democrats!”

Inside, at first, revelers were upbeat. It was early enough that the rising of the blue tide had yet to inspire fear—to an extent. A man waiting for drinks at the bar monitored the results in Florida, one of the few bright spots for Republicans. When informed that Senate candidate Ken Paxton and incumbent governor Greg Abbott were down bad in Texas, he clutched his head dramatically. “Oh my God! I just got here. I need to go home.” He looked at his phone in anguish. Within minutes, he darted for the door. A White House staffer wearing a red hat emblazoned with “45/47” on the side and “WINNING” on the front made the rounds. “Optimistic? I was a lot more earlier,” he said. “If we lose Texas, it’s a catastrophe.” Minutes later, Decision Desk called Texas for James Talarico, the first Democrat to be elected to the Senate in the Lone Star State since 1988.

As Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” blared through the speakers, two men at the bar lamented the cruel irony of the song playing as Talarico’s comfortable lead expanded over Paxton, his Republican challenger.

“I’m not trying to crash out,” said one of the men, a Republican volunteer. “But we nominated Hitler with Down syndrome. And guess what?! He lost! He lost! And now we lose a Supreme Court justice. It is a fucking disaster.”

It was a fucking disaster indeed. Republicans lost almost every Senate seat that mattered, with the small consolation of Florida quickly washed away by the titanic loss of South Carolina. Trump had spent the election telling voters, “Pretend that I’m on the ballot.” By all measures, they had. By 10:40 p.m., Trump offered his verdict on the night: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

Trump only has himself to blame for the Republican wipeout. The executive decisions that have defined his second administration were like something cooked up in #Resistance laboratories to alienate the vast majority of Americans from his political project. The candidates he backed in these midterm elections, against the wishes of the Republican establishment, are those who wiped out the hardest. Darline Graham, the political-neophyte sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Texas attorney general whom Trump backed in the primary against incumbent senator John Cornyn, lost to young Democrat James Talarico.
“We got SMOKED. BIGLY,” one source close to Trump texted me. “He’s not the kingmaker he was, or still thinks he is. This is a referendum on him.”

In the 1994 midterms, when Bill Clinton’s presidency was bludgeoned half to death by the Newt Gingrich revolution, The New Yorker’s Michael Kelly described the punch-drunk shock inside the White House. “No one can be expected to grasp immediately the full implications of being struck between the eyes by a two-by-four,” he wrote in the wake of the Gingrichian curb stomp, “so it was not surprising that the initial White House response to what had happened, and why it had happened, contained an element of stunned denial.”

The train that flattened Trump and Republicans this year had been barreling down the track for some time. No one could claim to be blindsided. Never in history has a party tethered itself so helplessly to one man, much less such a historically unpopular one. In December of last year, The Washington Post reported that Vice President JD Vance invited a conservative pollster to the White House to deliver an urgent message to the president: Americans don’t feel like you are fighting for them, Mark Mitchell of Rasmussen Reports explained as Trump ate a crab cake lunch. Mitchell urged him to focus on a message of “pragmatic economic populism.”

Trump ignored all that. Soon after the meeting, he started a war with Iran that triggered a global energy shock and by one study’s estimate has cost the average American household $2,000. “The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least,” pro-Trump pundit Matt Walsh wrote on X. “A catastrophically stupid decision. An unforgivable betrayal of America First principles.”

A year after the calamity he dubbed “Liberation Day,” Trump conjured up a new plot to liberate Americans from economic security: an escalated trade war with Canada that battered states in the upper Midwest that Republicans needed to hold the Senate. All the while, the president dismissed concerns about the cost of living in his public statements. He referred to “affordability” as a hoax, and fixated on lavish renovation projects, like the $600 million ballroom and the messy renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The pool, of all things, ended up anchoring Trump’s closing argument. In a press conference held there on Monday, Trump spent more than 20 minutes regaling reporters with war stories from his summer campaign against algae. “They’re brand-new pipes put in, and the pipes being very important in terms of the algae and other things,” he said sternly, brandishing a poster board with photos of the pool base. The next day, gasoline and diesel prices hit their highest national average in history. The president’s approval ratings sat firmly at a record bottom. “I don’t think Trump cares,” said the source close to Trump.

The White House line on these elections is that Trump did all he could to help the party, holding a blitz of rallies in the run-up to Election Day and deploying more than $350 million of his sizable MAGA Inc. war chest to boost Republican candidates. The money might have helped, but it isn’t clear that the rallying did. Trump’s unpopularity is now seismic, and there’s a growing feeling that his movement, after a decade of dominating the frontal lobe of the American mind, is petering out. Even the president’s very generous offer to every American—$5,000 each if Republicans held both chambers of Congress—didn’t seem to sway our particularly plutomanic populace. Seventy-one percent of Americans, according to one poll, said they didn’t believe they would ever receive the money.

Trump’s approval among young men, a key voting bloc that ensured his return to power, has plummeted, and popular podcasters who cater to a younger audience have abandoned him. CNN’s exit poll on Election Day found Democrats won young white men by 17 points, two years after Trump won the same group by 28 points. “We all have to move to Florida,” said a dejected young Republican wearing a tie covered in elephants at Butterworth’s. “It’s a disaster.” Doja Cat’s “Paint the Town Red” was blasting.

Around 20 minutes north, at Metrobar, a few hundred Democrats assembled in the garden for a victory party. Emerging from a taxi, I was met with the roar of the crowd. NBC News had just announced that Democrats had won the Senate. As Steve Kornacki broke down the results from Ohio on a jumbotron erected in the garden of the bar, the crowd chanted, “USA!”

Michelle Meoh, a young Democratic volunteer, told me the night had gone “extremely well” for her party. “Basically every race, even races that I hadn’t thought would go in our favor, were wins.” What does she want Democrats to do with their newfound power? “I guess show that we’re worthy of the trust that the voters are placing in us. I want us to prove that we’re tapped into the feelings of ordinary Americans and that we really do feel their pain. And that we don’t take that support for granted.”
Two burly men embraced. “Susan Collins is fucking gone!” one shouted.

I made my way to the exit as the hysterical celebrations died down, and Kornacki on the jumbotron read the latest results in Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed held a narrow lead over Republican Mike Rogers. “How am I feeling?!” asked a visibly overserved woman. I hadn’t asked. “Fucking great!”
This story has been updated.

items.title: The Curious Case of Olivia Reingold’s AI Photo at a Democratic Victory Party: Valentino, Chanel, and a Free Press Mystery
items.description: On Monday night, the eve of the 2026 midterm elections, the fashion crowd celebrated at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, colloquially referred to as the Oscars of American fashion. Tory Burch was honored with the Positive Change Award, which was presented to her
items.author: José Criales-Unzueta
paragraphs: On Monday night, the eve of the 2026 midterm elections, the fashion crowd celebrated at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, colloquially referred to as the Oscars of American fashion. Tory Burch was honored with the Positive Change Award, which was presented to her by Anna Wintour, the global editorial director of Vogue and chief content officer of Condé Nast. In her remarks, Wintour made the evening’s only direct reference to the midterms, reminiscing about attending a fundraising event for James Talarico, who successfully flipped Texas in the race for the Senate last night, alongside Burch. After applause from the audience, Wintour, a prolific Democratic fundraiser herself, looked up and addressed the room: “Let’s hope all of Texas feels the way you do,” she said.

The American fashion crowd has largely distanced itself from politics since the 2024 election. During their time in the White House as first ladies, Michelle Obama and Jill Biden were staunch supporters of the American fashion industry, often wearing American designers for public appearances. Melania Trump, in contrast, has more often preferred European labels. It’s an MO that trickles down into the political parties they represent.

There were many headlines that came out of last night’s midterms: Talarico flipped Texas, Annie Andrews flipped South Carolina, New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas became the first out gay man to be elected to the Senate, and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia and Deb Haaland of New Mexico became the first Black and Native American women, respectively, to be elected governor in the history of the US.

And yet it wasn’t just good news (and many great memes) that circulated in my group chats last night; there were also some fashion choices worth noting. First, the most pressing: Where were Steve Kornacki’s khakis? And what was the reasoning behind Haley Stevens’s ludicrously capacious hat? Some questions in life simply go unanswered.

Kornacki, a national political correspondent for NBC News, does not make his political affiliations public. But men in his age range (he is 47) and in the generations that follow—millennials and Gen Z—have been contending with what formalwear means and signals today.

Democratic men have been hard at work on their public image since the 2024 election, largely distancing themselves from the MAGA look and its too-large suits and extra-wide ties. In separating themselves from the manosphere, men like Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Senate race in Michigan, and Jon Ossoff, who was reelected to the Senate in Georgia, have been dressing more like the less buttoned up, progressive men they represent and less like the old establishment politicians on both the right and the left.

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed often sported tees and sweaters rather than button-downs and ties, frequently wearing taut sweaters and henleys under his suit jacket, while Ossoff largely opted for rolled cuffs and no jacket. As the two delivered victory speeches last night, they each wore a tailored suit—a little too tight in the arms; these are men who seem to eat their fair share of protein—and ditched their tie.

It’s a familiar image of a more laid-back look, but one in stark contrast to that of the faces of the right: Donald Trump, JD Vance, et al. Ossoff and El-Sayed, similarly to Kamala Harris during her presidential bid, also leaned into what was happening on the internet. These days, netizens are happy to objectify men and christen a new internet boyfriend every week. Ossoff’s and El-Sayed’s campaigns seemed to understand the power of thirst—that their suits were too tight was most likely not completely intentional, but it did help underscore a simple fact: that they are fit, and that their virility can be both attractive and nonthreatening all at once.

It is worth noting, however, that there are some men further to the left, both in politics and around it, who have reembraced the suit: Zohran Mamdani and Hasan Piker. On one hand, this has served a similar purpose as Ossoff’s and El-Sayed’s choices: It has distanced them from looksmaxxers and other conservative-leaning young men. On the other hand, a suit for Mamdani and Piker signifies what suits have always represented: that these are grown men doing important things.

The men are not the full story, however. Bottoms and Haaland came as they are, nodding to the communities they represent. The former wore a bright fuchsia suit and matching blouse, a callback to the lively and monochromatic dressing that is a deeply embedded and celebrated tradition in Black church culture. Haaland’s jewelry—firefly earrings and a beaded necklace—nodded at the style of accessories that is representative of Native style and fashion. If there is something that fashion clearly signifies, it’s community and belonging.

It is a running punch line that the left is more closely connected to fashion—it’s the wine-and-cheese crowd, the elites. (Hillary Clinton, during her bid for the presidency in 2016, was dragged online and by the press for wearing an Armani jacket that reportedly retailed for some $12,000 while delivering a speech that touched on income inequality.) While it’s true that fashion designers are often more enthusiastic about dressing progressives than they are about dressing conservatives, in the era of Trump and the MAGA look, this has become a half-baked story.

Olivia Reingold, a staff writer at The Free Press, made a post on X last night while reporting from an event for the Michigan Democratic Party. “So far at Abdul El-Sayed’s election night event I’ve spotted, Valentino heels, a Chanel bag, a Moncler jacket, Rolex watches, and a YSL bag among other designer items,” Reingold wrote, captioning an image of a woman holding a gold quilted Chanel handbag and a pair of Valentino Rockstud leather pumps.

When one takes a closer look, however, the image has several discrepancies. The style and make of the Chanel Flap bag is inconsistent with others the brand has sold, and the Valentino shoes in question appear askew in proportion; their straps have several punched holes that the authentic Valentino style does not. This could mean that the products in the image are not authentic, but there is another suggestive tell: The bottom strap on the left shoe appears to cut through its connecting strap rather than around, a classic mistake made when artificial intelligence is used to create or alter an image. A run of the image through several AI detectors, including SynthID, a digital watermarking approach created by Google DeepMind that detects media generated by OpenAI, Google, Nvidia, and Kakao, suggests the use of AI. SynthID detected that “this media was made or edited with OpenAI.” (Vanity Fair has reached out to Chanel and Valentino to advise on the authenticity of the products.)

Reingold did not reply to a request for comment, but on Thursday afternoon followed up with a new post on X, admitting to using AI “to brighten and sharpen an image of a woman in Valentino shoes and a Chanel bag.”

It’s become too easy to try to make a point about the left’s fashion choices: that Rama Duwaji, wife of Mamdani, should not wear pricey shoes, even if borrowed, because of her political beliefs; or that Democratic women should not carry Valentino or Chanel and vote for a candidate seeking to tax the wealthy. Therein lies the crux of the argument: Does this mean that luxury shoppers should align themselves with MAGA because it’s a party associated with billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos and logo-clad celebs like Nicki Minaj, who wore Chanel to the polls in New Hampshire? The answer is simple: no.

Our fashion choices say much about our values, identity, and aspirations. And while politicians have oftentimes utilized fashion to align themselves with specific groups or appear friendly to voters, they, in broad strokes, do not define our political affiliations. A Chanel bag does not make a Democrat, just as a red tie does not make a Republican.
This story has been updated.

items.title: Gay People (Mostly) Explain Gay Halloween
items.description: When you see a post that begins with “I hate gay Halloween, what do you mean you’re dressed as…” you know you’re in for a good laugh, or perhaps the feeling that you’re completely out of the loop. Trick-or-treating isn’t until this weekend, but in the age of s
items.author: José Criales-Unzueta
paragraphs: When you see a post that begins with “I hate gay Halloween, what do you mean you’re dressed as…” you know you’re in for a good laugh, or perhaps the feeling that you’re completely out of the loop. Trick-or-treating isn’t until this weekend, but in the age of social media the day itself has taken the back seat—it’s online where the battle for the best costumes takes place, and it’s happening earlier every year.

The trend began taking shape in the late 2010s and gained strength during the pandemic: celebrities—most notably the Kardashian-Jenner clan—began re-creating memorable moments from pop culture, mostly old film posters or iconic music album covers, and staging elaborate costume shoots for their Instagrams. The closer the re-creation would get to the original the better—and worthier of likes.

The idea of gay Halloween exists somewhere in this realm, though it’s inevitably more lo-fi, and the most successful looks aim for laughs rather than mere online clout. Plainly, it’s when people—mostly gay men—pick a niche pop culture moment or meme and re-create it in a costume. Forget witches and Scream masks. In 2004, Mean Girls declared, “In girl world, Halloween is the one night of the year when a girl can dress like a total slut and no other girls can say anything about it.” The 2026 equivalent is less about horny devils. Halloween is now the one night of the year when you can let out your inner freak or geek: Now you can be the breakup Post-it from a 2003 episode of Sex and the City, or Marc Jacobs when he wore a neck brace. Two years ago, a friend dressed as Antonio, a character played by Ariana Grande on Saturday Night Live. Another at the same party went as Rihanna as a nun for an Interview magazine cover.

Once upon a time, Halloween was about being as frightening as possible. Sure, there is something indeed terrifying about being broken up with via Post-it, and some less-online people are still attached to the classics—a zombie, a devil, et cetera—but Halloween has been co-opted by the internet, and by celebrity culture, in a way that has made it entirely self-indulgent.

Consider Heidi Klum’s famous annual Halloween bash, which she started in 2000. Early on, her costumes evolved from classic (a dominatrix the first year, a vampire in 2005) to more complex (a skinless person in 2011) to complete cosplay. In 2015, Klum appeared as Jessica Rabbit; in 2018, as the ogre version of Fiona from Shrek. Last year, she was a Medusa, and her husband, Tom Kaulitz, a hoplite turned into stone. There are Hollywood-level prosthetics, and, largely, it appears as if her costumes are made more for an image than for a party. Klum, in this space, is both the trendsetter and the shining example of the way our collective take on the holiday has evolved to adjust to our online-first lifestyles.

“Someone I just started working with recently said, ‘We live in a reference economy,’” says stylist Ron Hartleben, who works with Camila Cabello and Tyla, among others. “That really struck me,” he says. “Everything has been done. Everyone has access to all the same images now.” So much so that people in the queer community “have gone about seeking the most niche, obscure reference from a show or pop culture moment and making that their Halloween costume” so that a mere mortal, in this case a cis, heterosexual person, may not understand it. “Gay Halloween is exploiting that obscure moment in pop culture and running with it to create one of the most stupid and entertaining outfits imaginable,” Hartleben says. “As long as you think it’s funny and you get it, you’re doing gay Halloween right.” Consider Benito Skinner and Mary Beth Barone’s costume this year as a shining example of gay Halloween: they dressed as Dakota Johnson and Ellen DeGeneres and even recreated their infamous, viral interview about the actor’s birthday party.

But gay Halloween has now broken past its own internet bubble. Celebrities and straight normies alike have adopted the reference-first language popular in queer and adjacent subcultures—from drag to ballroom and beyond—and made it mainstream to come off as more in-the-know.

Last year, Mandy Lee, a trend forecaster known as @oldloserinbrooklyn on TikTok and Instagram, dressed as Jonathan Anderson smoking a cigarette by the Seine, a video she reposted this year next to the original clip of Anderson to much online buzz (hers was taken by the Gowanus Canal in Brooklyn). “It’s a format that works particularly well online versus IRL because you’re able to [have] text onscreen or even throw up reference images to make it click,” Lee says. She categorizes her costumes as “fashion Halloween,” which she says lives under the same umbrella as gay Halloween. She’s dressed as Lynn Yaeger and Miuccia Prada before, and also the “tabi swiper.” The trick is that they are, as she says, “low effort.” They’re costumes that rely on what’s already in Lee’s closet—no production value, just a sense of humor. “It’s just fun to get hyper specific and granular,” Lee says. “[The costumes] are also not for everyone; they are for fashion people, and that’s what makes it fun.”

Earlier this week, stylist and creative director Chris Horan, who works with the likes of Charli xcx, Demi Lovato, and Christina Aguilera, reposted clips he’d been tagged in on Instagram of fans dressed as Adéla, for whom he is both stylist and creative director. “I obviously love when people dress up or reference any of the looks we’ve worked on,” Horan says. “It takes a lot of effort to make any sort of look on our part or [the fans’], so it always makes me happy to see it.”

Last year Horan worked with Lovato on her costume, for which she dressed as Poot Lovato, her fictional twin sister that originated from a Tumblr post in 2015. Poot had long been a gay Halloween staple, but her fans would have never imagined that Lovato herself would bring her back to the forefront in such a way. Horan thinks these costumes also speak to something bigger: “I don’t think you’re really hitting as a pop star if you don’t have an immediately identifiable look.”

The internet has changed the way we do most things, particularly getting dressed, so it’s no surprise that it would affect how we get dressed up. We do things not just for ourselves, or even the people who will see the costume IRL, but for our circles, or “followers,” to congratulate us. Social media may not have ruined Halloween—it’s made it funnier and perhaps less spooky—but it’s altered its spirit.

items.title: As “Black October” Comes to a Close, the Cybersecurity World Is on Edge
items.description: For months, the heads of frontier AI labs have been warning us that incidents like this summer’s Hugging Face hack could represent “early warning shots” before more menacing attacks in the years to come. Equipped with their own doomsday bunkers, some CEOs have
items.author: Julia Black
paragraphs: For months, the heads of frontier AI labs have been warning us that incidents like this summer’s Hugging Face hack could represent “early warning shots” before more menacing attacks in the years to come. Equipped with their own doomsday bunkers, some CEOs have begun instructing their teams to run preparedness scenarios for the day after a “catastrophic AI incident.”

“We are willing to accept some things going wrong,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Vanity Fair’s global editorial director, Mark Guiducci, last month, adding that “there is a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems that are going to come from these open-source models.”

Just in time for spooky season, those warning shots got a little louder. On Wednesday, October 21, two serious security vulnerabilities were revealed in PHP, the programming language behind more than 70% of the internet’s web pages. Some cybersecurity professionals have already begun to call this “Black October,” thanks to the unprecedented spate of hacks across the globe.

AI did play a role in all this—but perhaps not the one you’d expect. Security researchers had actually used tools developed by OpenAI to discover the bugs months ago—and had been rushing to patch them up before they got into the hands of bad actors. Unfortunately, those vulnerabilities leaked last week, sending governments and businesses scrambling to protect their websites before hackers—perhaps armed with some of the very same AI tools as those defending against them—moved in.

Yet even the frontier labs’ ability to keep pace was called into question on Monday morning, when The Washington Post published a story about how Cathedral, a new cybersecurity company founded by four ex-DOGE staffers, successfully infiltrated some of Anthropic’s internal systems in just 12 hours. The article dropped just hours before Anthropic filed pre-IPO documentation detailing the potential risks to its own revenues and the world at large if its cybersecurity game were found to be lacking.

To the cybersecurity community, this was just the latest in a series of startling escalations. Joshua Achiam, who resigned from his post as OpenAI’s chief futurist this summer after nine years at the company, wrote on X: “Feels like March 1, 2020 for Cyber. Not normal, something is happening. Internet lockdowns in a couple of months?”

While these anxieties may not have reached your average American yet, business leaders have been growing increasingly concerned. In mid-September, executives from some of the world’s largest companies gathered for a special meeting of the Partnership for New York City. Their special guests that day were Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon and former Department of Defense official Mark Beall, who had come to warn them about the threats posed by emerging AI capabilities.

The co-chairs, Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla and Tishman Speyer CEO Rob Speyer, looked out at their screens full of anxious CEOs from hedge funds and banks, as well as insurance, real estate, and pharmaceutical companies, and noted that it was one of their largest gatherings in years. One big topic on the minds of those gathered: AI-enabled cyberattacks.

During the Q&A portion of the talk, a representative from Coinbase raised his hand to ask what companies like his could do to combat the threat of “open-weight models in the hands of bad actors,” from cybercriminals to nation-states. (Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, meanwhile, has been one of the more outspoken advocates of deregulated, open-source AI.)

Earlier this month, Japan declared a “state of emergency” following sweeping cyberattacks on more than 20 major companies, from financial firms to rail operators. French authorities are still piecing together the mystery of how and why hackers targeted supermarket refrigerators around the country, spoiling millions of euros’ worth of food. Meanwhile, a new report from CrowdStrike suggests that recent attacks on South Korea’s financial sector were allegedly carried out by a single 26-year-old in China using an open-source AI tool.

Even here, cyberattacks have become so commonplace that you may have missed them in the flurry of headlines. (Did you catch this month’s massive breach of FBI employees’ personal details? Iran’s hit on more than 30 water systems in Minnesota this summer? And that’s to say nothing of mounting efforts by Russia to influence the midterm elections.)
“Feels like March 1, 2020 for Cyber.”

I was surprised to learn that the concerns of most cybersecurity experts are both less apocalyptic and more present than the kinds of visions filling the heads of AI CEOs. In short, they believe that AI systems haven’t yet caused a paradigm shift in terms of the scale of damage they can inflict. What increased access to AI tools has done is lower the barrier to entry for even unskilled hackers to target low-hanging fruit.

“Over the coming weeks and months, the more likely scenario is a local hospital network in Ohio losing power and patients on life support dying as a result; a utility network in Texas taken offline; the lights going out across half of Wisconsin,” says Hamza Chaudhry, the AI and national security lead at the Future of Life Institute.

“We’re just in an exceptionally unresilient moment, coming up against systems which are designed to exploit that lack of resilience,” he tells me. “The largest providers,” however, “also have the most resources to defend themselves, including early access to frontier AI models for defense.”
He concedes that there is one more scenario that is keeping him up at night. “I’m very concerned about the so-called geopolitical Hugging Face moment.”

At the Munich Security Conference earlier this year, his group ran a simulation for an audience of national security officials from across the West: Imagine China develops a Mythos-level cyber-capability, which then gets into the hands of the mercenaries at the Wagner Group, who deploy it in Mali to target French military infrastructure. Then, much like in the Hugging Face incident, the agents go on an unintended side quest and attack mainland military infrastructure inside Europe. And that’s when things spiral out of control. “There was a real chance that Article 5 would be invoked and NATO would declare war on Russia” in this simulation, Chaudhry tells me.

A high-level executive at one of the world’s largest energy suppliers tells me he’s been losing sleep over aging infrastructure, budget cuts, and staffing shortages. Small utilities, he says, are plagued by “patches that might be easy to fix given the resources necessary.” But for now, “operators are running on Windows NT,” he says, referring to Microsoft’s 1990s operating system. New infrastructure coming online to support data center buildouts isn’t much better off. This infrastructure is “being built at such a speed [that] there’s no regulation and there are no hard standards,” says the energy executive. “Security is an afterthought, and that scares me a whole lot.”

This is the part of the story where I’d love to reassure you that the powers that be have been hard at work bolstering our defensive systems. The reality is, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has lost nearly a third of its workforce and hundreds of millions of dollars in funding, and it has failed to appoint an official director to lead the agency since the Trump administration took office in January of last year. But things at the state and local levels are what really worry the experts I spoke with. A recent Deloitte survey of state chief information security officers (CISOs) found that their budgets are failing to keep pace with growing threats—and have even faced cuts in 16% of the country.
“For some reason, amidst increasing cyber-capabilities, our defenders are running out of money,” Soham Mehta, a research fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, tells me. “Great.”
“Security is an afterthought, and that scares me a whole lot.”

There is at least some indication that authorities are beginning to wake up. Earlier this month, the new White House AI task force met for the first time to discuss cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection, among other topics. Many are hopeful that frontier AI will do more to help companies and governments defend themselves than it will to help their attackers—as in the case of OpenAI’s assistance in discovering the PHP flaws. In a survey of more than a hundred national security officials last month, 81% said that defensive capabilities are very likely to improve with the help of AI.

None of the experts I spoke with advised me to load up the bug-out bag just yet. For now, our fate is largely in the hands of the government officials and executives who have to make the choice to invest in updated security systems.

They largely gave the same advice I’ve been working off for years. Set up a password manager, as well as two-factor authentication wherever it’s available. Beware of any unusual messages, and don’t drop your credit card details into any suspicious websites. And perhaps most importantly: Contact your local representatives to nudge them on updating that 1990s software.

items.title: Hegseth and Advisers Yelled at for Disrespecting Tomb of Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day
items.description: Pete Hegseth was in a celebratory mood after Republicans successfully blocked his impeachment in the House of Representatives on Tuesday night, gloating with Donald Trump about the failed effort to boot him from the Pentagon. The following day called for a mor
items.author: Ryan Bort
paragraphs: Pete Hegseth was in a celebratory mood after Republicans successfully blocked his impeachment in the House of Representatives on Tuesday night, gloating with Donald Trump about the failed effort to boot him from the Pentagon. The following day called for a more solemn demeanor, however, as Hegseth and Trump visited Arlington National Cemetery to commemorate Veterans Day.

Hegseth’s party didn’t get the memo. On Wednesday afternoon, CNN released footage of an Army sentinel castigating Hegseth and his advisers when they started laughing after taking photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Solider, one of the nation’s most sacred war memorials.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!” the sentinel yelled shortly after laughter emanated from Hegseth’s group, before the group continued up the steps in front of the memorial.

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery is a burial site for an American soldier who died during World War I. An Army sentinel from the Third Infantry has guarded the tomb 24 hours a day since 1948, with a guard-changing taking place every half hour.

Hegseth was standing in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, his chief of staff, Ricky Buria, his deputy chief of staff, Patrick Weaver, and his senior adviser and deputy assistant, Tami Radabaugh, following a Veterans Day ceremony at the site, per CNN.

“The secretary and the entire department have always honored — and will always honor — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe,” chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement provided to Rolling Stone. “While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”

Hegseth narrowly survived impeachment in the House of Representatives on Tuesday night when Republicans passed a bill to send the resolution to committee, effectively killing it. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, accusing the Pentagon chief of offenses including violations of the War Powers Agreement of 1973, failing to minimize civilian casualties, and conducting extrajudicial killings.

items.title: Kai Cenat on Creating Boundaries With His Streaming Audience: 'I Got to Clock Certain Things'
items.description: Kai Cenat is figuring out his boundaries. The 24-year-old rose to fame as a teenager in his mom’s house in the Bronx, posting YouTube videos of himself gaming, doing pranks, or just chatting with his friends. But in the past few years he’s shot to a kind of fa
items.author: Elisabeth Garber-Paul
paragraphs: Kai Cenat is figuring out his boundaries. The 24-year-old rose to fame as a teenager in his mom’s house in the Bronx, posting YouTube videos of himself gaming, doing pranks, or just chatting with his friends. But in the past few years he’s shot to a kind of fame that used to be reserved for movie stars and pop icons, raking in almost 22 million Twitch followers and 16 million subscribers on YouTube. In VIBE’s Fall 2026 cover story, he reveals that, after taking a step back from streaming last summer, he’s figuring out just how much of his personal self he wants to share with his fans — and what he’s keeping for himself. “I got to clock certain things. It was like, ‘Yeah, maybe I shouldn’t go to the internet for this,’ or, ‘Maybe I shouldn’t show them this,’” he told VIBE.

For the feature, VIBE (and Rolling Stone) senior writer Jeff Ihaza — who had profiled the AMP collective, which includes Cenat, last year — spent time with Cenat at his fashion show in Manhattan in September. As the megastar streamer prepared for the event for his line, Vivet, he talked about building the brand. “The show was a representation of my two worlds colliding,” he told VIBE. “It was a staple moment for the world of streaming and the world of fashion to collab on a platform that I’ve been able to build.”

Last fall, after a breakneck few years building followers and stacking cash, thanks to seemingly limitless brand deals, he “abruptly hit stop on the stream,” Ihaza wrote in the cover story, “vanishing from Twitch without explanation.” But he didn’t stay off the platform for very long, and has since streamed from around the world, including from inside a volcano in Iceland. He also launched his second year of Streamer U, where he brings together content creators from across the globe to learn from one another and, of course, show up in one anothers’ streams. “You get to see how these storylines play out, and also you get to see how they collaborate,” he said.

Cenat also addressed controversy he’s faced, both because of fallouts with other streamers and from his own decisions, like when he was charged with inciting a riot after announcing an impromptu PlayStation 5 giveaway in Union Square in 2023. (He paid a $55,000 fine, and the charges were dropped.) He told VIBE that back then, he didn’t understand what the problem was. Now, though, he said he realizes that his influence is also his responsibility. “Why is it my fault? Why is it my fault? What did I do?” he asked himself at the time. “Whole time, bro, your influence is just so big, so you got to know.”
