items.title: Thom Yorke and Harry Styles Come Together in Epic Conversation
items.description: T wo years ago, in the summer of 2024, Harry Styles was strolling down a small cobblestone side street in Rome, when he suddenly noticed a face he recognized. It was Radiohead’s Thom Yorke, one of his biggest musical heroes. He introduced himself — just two st
items.author: Rob Sheffield
paragraphs: T wo years ago, in the summer of 2024, Harry Styles was strolling down a small cobblestone side street in Rome, when he suddenly noticed a face he recognized. It was Radiohead’s Thom Yorke, one of his biggest musical heroes. He introduced himself — just two stars walking the streets incognito, with no entourage. As Styles confesses to Yorke now, with a shy grin, “You, to me, had always been that person that I was scared of meeting.”

Yorke and Styles might seem like they’re from two different worlds — the planet’s most dazzling glam-pop prince versus the high priest of art-rock angst. But today, they’re busy making each other laugh on a sunny July afternoon in London, at a studio near Camden Town. Yorke has been known to be a thorny interview subject, ever since the early days of Radiohead. Yet today he lets down his guard, as he basks in the presence of the equally notorious charm of Harry Edward Styles. They crack each other up like mischievous schoolboys.

In May of this year, Yorke was honored at the U.K.’s prestigious Ivor Novello Awards, where Styles gave a heartfelt tribute, saying, “Radiohead is my favorite band.” He also made a surprise admission about one of the band’s B sides.
“I lost my virginity to ‘Talk Show Host,’” he declared, then corrected himself. “I lost my virginity to the intro of ‘Talk Show Host.’”

Radiohead released their first album in 1993 — the year before Styles was born. But both have built their careers around defying expectations and refusing to repeat their successes. Styles could be said to be going through his own Kid A moment right now, with the experimental electro-pop of Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally. This summer, when he did a record-breaking 12-night residency at London’s Wembley Stadium, Yorke came the very first night — he was up and dancing right from the opening song.

Yorke has been on a creative roll lately. In his conversation with Styles, he reveals that he’s working on an upcoming solo album, although it hasn’t been officially announced. He dropped two acclaimed 2024 albums with the Smile, his band with Radiohead guitarist Jonny Greenwood. Hamlet Hail to the Thief, a production of the Shakespeare play featuring music from Radiohead’s 2003 album, runs at the Barbican Theatre in London from Oct. 31 to Jan. 23. And Radiohead recently answered the world’s prayers with their first live shows in seven years. They return in mid-2027 for residencies in Australia and Japan.

Styles and Yorke are both famously magnetic performers, but famously private offstage — shy of giving anything away, wary of outsiders. Yet face-to-face for their Musicians on Musicians cover story today, they bring out different sides of each other that the world doesn’t always get to see. In this wide-ranging two-hour conversation, they go deep on fame, fandom, songwriting, suffering from impostor syndrome, the inspirational power of walking, and the emotional intensity of weeping onstage.
Watch the video interview below
Styles: We met for the first time in Rome, on a small street. You were playing in Rome that week with the Smile. I was going to that show.
Yorke: Was it before the show?

Styles: It was before the show, yeah. A friend of mine had asked me if we’d ever met, and I had said that we hadn’t. So I was walking down the street, and I noticed you because you were wearing a hat that said “Acid” on it. I thought, “Oh, that’s a cool hat.” And then I was like, “Oh, it’s you.” I had A Moon Shaped Pool [the 2016 Radiohead album] playing in my headphones, and I stopped it. “Oh, hello—”
Styles: “Mr. Yorke, hello.” You said, “Oh, hi.”
Yorke: No, I said, “What the fuck [laughs] are you doing standing in the street?”
Styles: Then I came to the show, and we met properly.
Yorke: I didn’t know you were living in Rome a lot. I had no idea. So I was doubly confused.
Styles: You, to me, had always been that person that I was scared of meeting.
Yorke: Oh, yeah. I’ve got a whole list.
Styles: Yeah, totally. And I remember feeling so light afterwards. “Oh, people are kind, and they’re nice.”
Yorke: I was also impressed that you were just walking down the street. I was like, “Where’s his security?” Because I mean, I know I can do it, but I didn’t know you could do it. Is that a choice?

Styles: I think in the early days, when I was in the band [One Direction], so much of the hotel experience felt very locked-in. When I’d be home, it felt like, “Oh, it’s not safe for me to be out.” Then I had a girlfriend who was very outgoing, and she was coming to London and I was like, “Oh, if we just sit in my house for three days, she’s gonna think I’m nuts.” So we walked everywhere, and it was this realization for me: “Oh, it’s fine to be outside.” It kind of broke that thing. Now, it’s changed my life in such a big way, because it’s how you stay connected to the world.
Styles: I read something about walking being the artist’s kind of perspective, because you’re at ground level and you see things that you just don’t see if you’re driving everywhere.

Yorke: It’s also a good way to write. I wrote “A Wolf at the Door” — I was going through a really bad moment and I walked for like two-and-a-half days, rain, didn’t matter. A notebook in my hand, and just wrote it all. I felt so much better at the end of it.

But also it’s not just the walking — it’s the walking past people. The simple thing of people-watching, playing that game of imagining as someone walks by — where they’re going, what they’re doing, all that stuff. It brings you out of yourself, brings you out of your troubles. I mean, without it, see, it’s really easy to get lost.

I remember when we were on tour with R.E.M. [in 1995] and Michael Stipe figuring out that I would just hide in the dressing room, and never went out anywhere. So he started dragging me out, and he gave me this trick. He said, “If you don’t care, they don’t care. If you’re not looking, they’re not looking.” And it works. I remember being in Stockholm going to some really busy club, and he said, “Try it.” And it worked. Nobody bothered us.

There are moments when you will feel vulnerable. There are moments when shit will happen, or The Sun will be printing your picture one too many times. I’ve had that. So it’s not easy. It’s not an easy decision to make, but it’s better than the alternative. I know people who got death threats, and then wouldn’t leave the house and had security patrolling their house. You don’t want that.
“If you write ‘Everything in Its Right Place,’ do you think, ‘Yeah, I’ll write another one’? You can’t. I’ve tried.”

RS: You both have a history of leaving your comfort zones behind. That’s a pattern for you as artists — after you do something hugely successful, you say, “OK, I did that already. I’m not doing that again.” How do you avoid repeating yourself?

Yorke: I can’t, even if I wanted to. I couldn’t do it again. If you write “Everything in Its Right Place,” do you think, “Yeah, I’ll write another one of them”? It doesn’t make sense. You can’t. I’ve tried.

I think if you have something that’s very successful, there’s a lot of pressure to repeat that, which I’m sure you’ll probably feel, or you do feel sometimes. Or you will feel. It doesn’t go anywhere, because that’s like working to commission.
Styles: “Paint that again.”
Yorke: Yeah. It’s a commercial art form, so you’re always going to get people asking you to do that.

Styles: It’s an interesting cycle, I think. You make something that connects with people, because you’ve captured something about the human experience, whether it’s a vulnerability or a sensitivity that comes with being human. And then any kind of success around that thing makes it take on this life of its own. Then everything around you makes your experience incredibly not human.

Styles. Yeah. The goal is how you shut that out when you’re making stuff, so you can still be making music about the human experience. I’ve always thought if I was to make music about being in a studio, and touring, and all of the shiny things that come with that—
Yorke: Shiny for you, mate. It’s not shiny for everyone.
Styles: That’s definitely not interesting to me, so it can’t possibly be interesting to anyone else.

What I love about your work, for example, so many people look at you in this kind of godlike status — to still be someone who looks at it like, “This is the gritty part of life.” I think that’s what’s so impressive about your work — for people to revere you and to still be looking at what’s under the fingernails.

Yorke: I think the reason for that was having to learn quite a difficult lesson. Around Kid A, Amnesiac, before that, I really struggled every time I had to try to do something new. I was explaining it to myself while I was doing it, literally. It’s like a form of madness, and I couldn’t get out of it. I felt I needed to justify it somehow — not apologize, but justify it in an intellectual way.

The reason for that was I needed to get out of it. I needed to just get out of the studio, and I needed to just walk. I used to just walk on the cliffs in Cornwall, for example. And a lot of that was down to the fact that nobody cares, man. Nobody cares that it’s difficult. If you’re bummed out that it’s difficult, fucking stop. Go and do something else — go dancing. Also, later on, as you have kids, the choice to carry on doing this kind of work, you have to enjoy it. And the enjoyment comes from having to start again from scratch every time. Whatever you learn, you’ve got to unlearn.

Also, songwriting is very odd. Going to the Ivor Novello thing — I don’t hang out with songwriters, but apparently I am one. And you realize that songwriting is quite a naive thing. You can’t be savvy about it. You can work really hard on it — but the good stuff just happens, and you don’t know why. And you’ve got to be honest with yourself that you don’t know why. When stuff forms that you like, you just grab onto it and you don’t let go. “Pyramid Song” — I mean, it’s three chords over and over again, and the same lyric. How does that make sense? But you like it, and you’re not bothered about if anyone else likes it.
“The thing that excites me the most is when I start a record, I have no idea how it’s going to end up sounding.”
Styles: I’ve always wondered if that’s part of why the impostor syndrome that can come with that commercial success exists.

Styles: If you write in that way, it almost feels like you’re not responsible for it. So then if people are like, “Oh, you’ve made this thing and that means that you’re this,” there’s something in there that feels like, “Oh, I can’t take credit for it. It just happened to me.” Like you were saying, the best things tend to just happen. I’ve always found the things that I end up liking the most, or have been the most special things to me, are the ones where you write it, and then as you’re listening back, you’re learning something about yourself. You’re realizing that you’ve said something, rather than, “I’m going to sit down — I’m going to say this.”
Yorke. Yeah, and you might not realize. You might record it and track it and everything, and not realize until you’ve mastered it — and then you suddenly hear, “Oh, shit, that’s what I meant.”

But it’s not divine intervention or anything like that. You’ve got to show up. You have to learn to accept the months of impostor syndrome, where you’re like, “I don’t have anything to justify all this amazing equipment in my studio.” And then you’ll pick up your notebook, and there’ll be one line in it that sets you off. But the point is, you showed up. Because it’s really easy not to show up.

Styles: Someone once described it to me as like surfing, where you can practice getting up on the board. Sometimes there’s no waves. If a wave comes but you haven’t practiced enough, you’re not going to be able to surf it. When they happen, it’s the combination that you’ve practiced being able to capture it, and something is happening at the right time.
Yorke: Yeah, you’re ready enough. Or if I’m surfing, you’re not ready, ever. You’re on the rock going, “Fuck!”
Styles: I’ve had a big shift — I used to feel labor-focused about art in general. I felt like to justify it, I had to be in the studio months at a time.

Yorke: That’s your impostor syndrome speaking. I’m the same — sometimes it’s fun, but sometimes you’re doing it because you feel you should do it, because you need to stay ahead of the game. Or you need to keep proving that you are who you say you are, or other people say you are.

Styles: I feel like it’s a real line to ride with that. Because I still feel like I get it onstage sometimes. The sweet spot is where you’re relaxed, in that flow state where it feels like, “Oh, this feels really easy. It feels like it’s just happening, and this is great.” And then I click over to “Oh, it feels too easy. Am I not working hard enough?” When it feels most natural is when I think the show is at its best, but then I have this voice of “It shouldn’t be this easy.”

Yorke: That’s completely normal. The joke with Radiohead is always, like, we’ll have moments in the show like, “Oh, my God, we’re so great!” And exactly that moment, someone fucks up. Every time, without fail.
“I’m jealous of people who can just free flow onto a mic and put it out. All my hip-hop heroes freestyling.”

Styles: How different is it for you in terms of how much you enjoy making music with the band, versus making stuff by yourself? Do you like what the friction can make in that scenario? Or do you tend to enjoy, like, “Oh, I’m going to have this idea, and I’m going to just see this all the way through.” Because it’s both, I’m sure.

Yorke: It’s both. There’s a kind of mad history to that. It wasn’t until after Kid A that I remember quietly saying to Nigel [Godrich], “I’ve got all these things. I just want to do them on my own with you, because it doesn’t make sense to try and include anybody else.” Up until that point, it was a really alien concept.

We’ve known each other a mind-boggling number of years now. [Radiohead met in 1985.] We all know each other’s musical strengths and musical weaknesses. So you’re spending a lot of the time working around that. I mean, we haven’t worked. We haven’t been in the studio together for a long time, so I don’t know how it would actually feel now.

With the Smile, it’s totally different because Jonny [Greenwood] just generates ideas all the time. [Drummer Tom] Skinner works faster than any human being I’ve ever met and can respond to literally, as you probably know, anything you throw at him. I’m in the middle going, “All right, why don’t you guys record this, because I don’t understand what’s going on?” My favorite experiences in the studio are something that’s good, and I don’t understand why it’s good, but I pick up a mic and respond to it. I will listen back to it like, “I have no idea who that was. Is that us?” Yeah, that’s us. And you only get that when you have other people.
Styles: Do you find it more vulnerable to be putting out your own stuff?

Yorke: It’s all vulnerable. But at the same time, I don’t know about you, but if I’m finishing a record, if I can’t sit down and listen to it and be comfortable with it and happy with it, it’s not going out. So the vulnerable bit happens …
Styles: When you’re writing it?
Yorke: Yeah. When you’re trying to finish the fucking lyrics. That’s when it’s the worst. Words, right? How do you do words?

Styles: I think what I’ve always found so exciting is that I’ve never found the one method. It’s never been like, “I’ll write a poem, and then I put it to music.” The good stuff tends to come from a few weeks or a couple months of “Oh, I’ve got nothing. I don’t have anything. It’s all gone.” Then all of a sudden you write something and you’re like, “I really like this. I don’t know why.” And that comes in lots of different ways — I have a line, or I have a piano thing, or a melody that’s mumbled. I’m building a song around these three words that sound great over this thing.

Yorke: That is the correct process, in my opinion. If you’ve got a few words that you hang everything off, and you don’t understand why, then that’s the most exciting. Even though it’s painful, because then you have to spend weeks trying to fill in the blanks.

Styles: Sometimes, with some of the best stuff, I think it’s more difficult to be concise. I know I like a melody when I overwrite the song — I’ll write a bunch of verses, a bunch of lyrics. Then I think, “Oh, you take these three verses, take these lines, and make them one verse — it’s actually much more powerful in what it’s saying.” It’s better than explaining everything.
Yorke: Honestly, the thing I’m most jealous of will always be people who can just free flow onto a mic, and put it out. All my hip-hop heroes freestyling. I wish I had that brain.

Styles: I listened to a podcast you were on. You said you think of your vocal as one of the instruments in the song, and that’s how you tend to approach composition now. Is that something you noticed, when that changed for you? Because you say you don’t so much sit and write a song, like, “I’m going to sit here, and this is a song and this is how it goes” — you think of how it sits in the production. But obviously, if you go back to The Bends, for example, like “High and Dry,” that is a song.
Yorke: Yeah, a guy with an acoustic guitar. Singing his song. That particular one I wish I hadn’t [winces in pain], but there’s nothing wrong with that.

I don’t listen to a lot of singer-songwriters. I listen to a lot of mad old folk music, or I listen to film music, or I listen to electronic music. The banging away on the guitar thing is sometimes when it really speaks to me, but not a lot. I’m not quite sure why that is — probably because we grew up when there was a real renaissance of that, and The Bends was that.

But by the time we got to Kid A, I was excited about what else you could do with your voice, really. Jonny and Nigel set up this thing where Jonny’s playing the Martenot [a vintage electronic keyboard] and I’m just picking out random lines from my top hat. And that became the vocal. I’m not singing that at all — I’m literally speaking it.
“I remember watching the ‘Karma Police’ video thinking, ‘This is so brilliant.’ So much of your music has that weight.”

One of my favorite singers ever is Michael Stipe, who for the first two or three [R.E.M.] records didn’t even bother writing the lyrics. Or if he did, it was stream of consciousness. “I’m not going to make this explicit. I’m just the human sound in the middle of all these amazing jangling guitars.” Sometimes I don’t like the lyrics being the point. Sometimes it’s really exciting that there’s just this sound. [Yorke pulls out a notebook full of his questions.] I’ve got notes.
Styles: [In mock horror.] Homework!
Yorke: Do you travel with a laptop?
Styles: My laptop has been dead for about six years [laughs]. I don’t know where the charger is.
Yorke: We can help you with that. Where are your ideas? In your pocket?
Yorke: On your phone. You know your phone is basically a computer?
Styles: But just a phone. I use GarageBand a lot, and voice notes.
Yorke: Really? Wow. Fuck a duck.
Yorke: No, I mean in a way that’s good. I remember my MiniDisc. That was my best friend.
Styles: Yes, I remember being in primary school. [Both are laughing too hard to continue.]
Yorke: OK, let’s try it again.
Styles: The voice-note thing, I like something about it being its blankest version.
Yorke: Yeah. It’s the pencil drawing.
Styles: I think I like that. The thing that excites me the most is when I start a record, or before I’ve started something, and I have no idea how this is going to end up sounding.
Yorke: I’m surprised, because the last album [Kiss All the Time] very much sounds like it was developed in the studio. It doesn’t sound like it comes from voice notes.

Styles: That one was less from voice notes. There were a few moments — the orchestral thing [“Coming Up Roses”], or the piano songs. There’s a couple of much more straightforward songs. There’s probably three or four moments that are the most down the middle like that.
Yorke: So the rest are worked up in the studio?

Styles: A lot of it, yeah. Probably two-thirds of this one. I think it was just where I felt like I was at in my life, and the music that I was experiencing. I wanted to meld the parts of my life together. I’d started going out dancing a lot more. I really didn’t want it to be like, “Oh, I’m listening to this music — this is where I’m at,” but then I go in the studio and say, “Well, I have to make this sort of music instead.”
“Being open and exposed to people doesn’t bother me now. It used to.”
Yorke: I know that feeling. I know that feeling very well.
Styles: It was really like, “I’ve just come from this place. I want that beat to keep going. I want to be onstage feeling in the middle of it.” That was the kind of thing that informed the record.

Yorke: I think you did that. That’s my favorite part of the show, where you literally do that. There was a generosity to that, where I thought, “Yeah, that’s really cool. That is clearly someone who’s discovering this thing and wants to share it.” The honesty of it was very cool. I was really into that. I mean, it’s very difficult to take that kind of music into those places. It’s much easier to just make yourself totally deaf DJ’ing in a club in Berlin.
I was going to ask you: Where’s home? Because you have more than one.
Styles: I think when I’m in London, it feels the most like home. And I’m not from here.
Yorke: Where’s your stuff? Your important stuff?

Styles: London. Because I’ve lived in my house for 12 years or something. That’s the place where I feel like I’ve been through so many versions of myself, even in the same space. I feel like I really grew up in this house, in a big way. I remember moving in — right after my 19th birthday. It’s been through a lot of changes, but in there, in my kitchen, is the most like “This is where I live.”
Yorke: You’re probably pretty good, aren’t you?
Yorke: I’m fucking terrible.

Styles: To stay on you for a second, if I may. [Yorke snaps his fingers in disappointment.] I was curious about doing this interview, for example, or the Ivors thing — I think everyone communicated a surprise that you were willing to be celebrated. I’m curious about how your relationship with that has changed over time. In terms of someone who’s so innovative, how much of it has always been a need to reject any sort of nostalgia, to assure yourself that you’re moving forward?

To me, it feels like maybe just being in a happier place, to realize that you can do both: You can still innovate, and also allow people to celebrate things you’ve done, whether it be the Ivors, or touring and playing a deep selection from your catalog. To be able to play those songs and not feel “We’re living in the past right now,” but just be like, “We made something really beautiful. I’m going to play it, and that’s beautiful. And I can now also still be moving forward.”

Yorke: You’re answering this better than I can do. You’re right, that I’m in a slightly better place nowadays, but I’d be lying if I didn’t say that something like getting an Ivor Novello fellowship was not deeply confusing for me. I admire a lot of the people that they’ve given those awards to. Some of these people are my heroes. But I have a very, very strange relationship to … God, this is really hard to explain. I have a very strange relationship to that element of my work.
“Playing live is where you embrace that your music has connected with People”
Yorke: I find it hard to believe in it. The moving-forward thing, that’s what I believe in. That’s easy to believe in, because it’s new. I don’t have to explain it, so I’m happy.

After the [2025 reunion] Radiohead tour — even though in the middle of it, it was really fun — my response to it afterwards was to crash, like massively crash, in terms of self-confidence. It took me months.… It took me starting on my own record again two months later to go, “Oh, OK. I’m good now. I’m fine.” I just have a really odd relationship with it. And I’ve just grown used to that.

The Ivors, to be honest, your speech was great, because it was really honest and personal, and I could relate to it. Whereas when it feels like a business, and you’re part of a business, and the cameras are running … I don’t know, man. I got this legacy feeling about all of it.
Styles: Something I’m curious about: I wonder if it’s something that maybe happens when you have children, then keep creating.

Yorke: It’s really important they all integrate, and keep informing who you are. You probably saw Agnes and Noah at the Ivors. They were very emotional about it, and Dajana, my wife, was as well. I do it for them, because if they’re emotional about it, OK, that’s why I’m here. Because for me, I feel quite numb about it.

One of the things I’m most proud of is, some of the attitude that I have has rubbed off on [Agnes and Noah] as they grow up. I can see they have that kind of attitude in what they’re doing. Quite fearless about being creative, and quite open. Not embarrassed. Because I mean, obviously, when your kid’s a teenager, they’re like, “Oh, God, my father’s blah, blah, blah.” But now it’s really nice. It’s a good thing. I feel super lucky about that, because it wasn’t easy, for a long time.

Styles: The “Karma Police” video — I remember watching that and thinking, “Oh, this is so brilliant.” I feel like so much of your music has that weight where you just remember hearing it. It’s so inspiring just to see someone be so consistently great, in so many different ways. I’ve always really been drawn to stuff like “Codex” or “True Love Waits.” “Everything in Its Right Place” is it for me.

Yorke: “Everything in Its Right Place” was my response to not being able to write. We had an empty house. We had a grand piano, and we had a mattress. And that’s the first thing I did when we moved into this house. I’d felt lost since the OK Computer thing. It was like a mantra. I wasn’t thinking, “Oh, I’m writing a song.” I was really enjoying playing piano in this empty house; I just had one CD, [minimalist composer] Arvo Pärt, and that’s it. It was during the winter, there were storms all the time, and it was so great — playing this riff over and over and over again to make myself feel better.
RS: Harry, you just finished your massive run at Wembley Stadium, and on the final night, people were so moved to see you in tears. For both of you, what’s it like to get emotional onstage?

Styles: For me, so much of the studio experience of making something is almost trying to block out the fact anyone’s going to listen to it. You have to be “What do I want to listen to at this time in my life? What is it that I feel like I want to do, say, make?” The fact people are going to hear it — that realization happens later. Playing live is the part where you’re embracing that people listen to it, that it’s connected with people.

The kind of emotion that happened at the end of the London shows — I think it was a realization that these shows felt like a culmination of so many people’s support. I felt supported, in a way that’s more than like, “We’re here because we want to hear this song that you’ve done.” It just felt like, “We’re here because we believe in what you’re doing.” That’s why I found it so emotional.

Yorke: Also, you have to give a lot of yourself, and that makes you very … what’s the word? Open. You’re exposed to all these people. It doesn’t bother me now. It did, it used to — it doesn’t bother me any more. But it makes you very open.

Styles: A lot of the time, when you’re making stuff, you’re trying to reject what’s coming back at you, to remain in a beginner’s mind. You’re always trying to get back to a sense of starting again. Those moments where you let go and open up and allow it all to come in, and you get to feel that — it’s a wave of something that you don’t live with every day.

Yorke: When we did the first Radiohead show, in Madrid last year, we did this thing where we had to walk through the audience. Never done that before. Then we had to stand on the stage getting prepped before we went up. It was the first time we did that [going onstage together], after I don’t know how many years. All of us, the whole band, were like, “OK, keep it together. Keep it together.” Because I wanted to burst into tears, and we hadn’t even played a note. I hadn’t been exposed to whatever that was for so long, and to walk through the middle of it … I mean, all of us, we were like, “Holy shit. Holy shit.”
Styles: Which brings us back to walking — the artist’s perspective, where we began. There’s the bow. There’s the seal.

Styling by HARRY LAMBERT at BRYANT ARTISTS. Hair by MALCOLM EDWARDS at LGA MANAGEMENT. Makeup by NIAMH QUINN at LGA MANAGEMENT. Set Design by PATIENCE HARDING. Production by FARAGO PROJECTS. Lighting Director: KAI NARINS. Photo Assistance: GEORGE HUTTON and BENEDICT MOORE. Digital Technician: GILES SMITH. Styling Assistance: NAOMI PHILLIPS and ELLA BACON.  Set Design Assistance: MIRANDA LATIMER, EDDIE AMOS, and JACK SHORT. Video Interview Director of Photography: NICK CARTER. Video Interview Camera Operators: STEPHAN KNIGHT and ISSEY RIDER. Video Interview Gaffer: JACK GOULD. Video Interview Camera and Lighting Assistant: TOM WOOD. Video Interview Sound Operator: JAVIER CARLES. Video Interview Production Assistant: ALCIA WOODS. Photographed and filmed at BIG SKY.

YORKE: Artist’s own clothing.

items.title: The 200 Greatest Rock Songs of the 21st Century So Far
items.description: “Rock & roll can never die,” Neil Young sang deep in the 20th century. Guess what: Neil wasn’t lying. Nearly 50 years later, rock is thriving the way it always has — by mutating, diversifying, evolving into the future. Now that we’re deep into the 21st century
items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: “Rock & roll can never die,” Neil Young sang deep in the 20th century. Guess what: Neil wasn’t lying. Nearly 50 years later, rock is thriving the way it always has — by mutating, diversifying, evolving into the future. Now that we’re deep into the 21st century, it’s a perfect time to celebrate the songs that have made this a golden age for rock fans. But as always, rock & roll keeps moving too fast to get pinned down, which is why it remains defiantly, unrepentantly vibrant a century after Chuck Berry was born.

That’s the spirit behind this list — the 200 best rock songs of the 21st century so far. It’s a companion piece to our recent Reasons to Love Rock feature. The list is a wide-ranging mix of different rock styles, different generations, different voices. Some of these tunes are universally beloved classics, known and sung worldwide; others are deep cuts or underground cult faves. But from Bruce to Boygenius to Bombino, from Dylan to D’Angelo to Deftones, from Wilco to Wednesday to the White Stripes, we’ve got artists from around the world and all over the stylistic map.

This is an era when rock can’t be contained — it travels everywhere. In our Top 10 alone, we’ve got the blues, we’ve got dance-floor glam, we’ve got gritty punk and psychedelic jams and high-tech dystopia and acoustic storytellers, along with loads of air-guitar riffs. We’ve got metal warriors from Black Sabbath to Mastodon. We’ve got pop-punk and emo. We’ve got sex and drugs and black leather jackets. We’ve got riot grrrls, rock en español, indie upstarts, rootsy twang, African desert grooves, virtuoso guitar heroes, garage bands, electro experiments, grunge, deep soul. We’ve got Nineties legends from Fiona Apple to Sonic Youth. We’ve got the grizzled veterans who learned new tricks instead of going quietly: David Bowie, Prince, even Neil “Time Fades Away” Young himself.

We’ve got country rebels. We’ve got hip-hop headbanger anthems from OutKast and Jay-Z. (You know, the guy who called himself “rap’s Grateful Dead.”) We’ve got ambitious pop rockers from Olivia Rodrigo to Harry Styles to Taylor Swift, who’ve kept their unabashedly rock moves at the top of the charts. We’ve got the skinny-tie postpunk club commandos of the Meet Me in the Bathroom era. We ramble from the U.S.A. to Colombia, Tokyo, Versailles, Niger, Dublin, CDMX, and YYZ. Some of these songs are innovative and complex; others are three-chord bangers to make you jump up and down. Their only thing in common is that they rock. You can listen to it all here.

It’s a list of songs, not artists, so we mostly avoid repeating songs by the same artist. But a handful of legends simply had too many classics to deny. (How could you pick just one Radiohead song from this century?) The toughest part was cutting it down to a mere 200, with so many more worthy artists than we could cram into one list. But it’s a tribute to the vitality, diversity, and energy of rock in our modern age. There will always be folks asking why it can’t stay like the old days, but that question has been around since Buddy Holly’s plane went down, and the answer is the same as it ever was — rock keeps growing because rock keeps changing. The only way to deny the music’s irrepressible health is to stop listening, and what fun would that be? Keep reading for 200 excellent reasons to pump up the volume and let it blast.

- Yellowcard, ‘Ocean Avenue'(2003) Yellowcard managed to capture the ephemera of teenage summers of yore — and the angsty yearning for those days — in this violin-driven pop-punk classic. It wasn’t an easy feat. As the band finalized recording its debut, Ocean Avenue, lead singer Ryan Key couldn’t find a melody for the title track’s chorus. “One day I walked in, exhausted and almost defeated … and I sang, ‘if I could find you now, things will get better,’” Key told Rolling Stone for Ocean Avenue’s 20th anniversary. It was just what producer and pop-punk architect Neal Avron was looking for. “I tracked it on the spot, and our lives were changed forever.” —Maya Georgi

- Noah Kahan, ‘American Cars’ (2026) On his 2026 album, The Great Divide, Vermont songwriter Noah Kahan broadened his palette beyond the indie-folk magic of “Stick Season.” On “American Cars,” he dug deep into heartland rock, channeling Bruce Springsteen, John Mellencamp, and the War on Drugs. He likens drinking to a profession (“If drinkin’ was a day job/I’d be askin’ for more money”), while begging his sister to come fix the latest kerfuffle in the family. “The song was basically like, ‘You’ve got to get your ass home, we really need you this time,’” Kahan told us in his Rolling Stone cover story. It’s a propulsive stunner unlike anything in Kahan’s catalog — and proves he’s a genuine rock star. —Angie Martoccio
- Speedy Ortiz, ‘The Graduates’ (2015)

Sadie Dupuis’ pen was never sharper than on this 2015 song, which spins an alt-rock anthem out of a complaint about feeling overlooked: “I was the best at being second place, but now I’m just the silver you dread.” Her witty, literate lyrics and her twist-and-turn chords somersault over one another until she hits the bridge and flies even higher. (“Someone tweeted that I looked bored onstage,” she told RS. “I’m like, ‘I’m just focusing so I don’t fuck up this guitar part!’”) It’s a gem from a moment when indie rock was heating up again, and it seemed like all you needed was a distinct perspective and a distortion pedal to get the world’s attention. —Simon Vozick-Levinson

- Mogwai, ‘2 Rights Make 1 Wrong’ (2001) Thirty years in the noise game, and the Scottish punk lads in Mogwai have yet to go stale. They rose up in Glasgow, after getting their minds blown by My Bloody Valentine and Slint, blasting their own massively emotional — yet ear-bleedingly loud — style of worshipful feedback devotionals on their 1997 debut, Young Team. “2 Rights Make 1 Wrong” is their apex, from the 2001 gem Rock Action, around the time Stephen Malkmus was declaring them “the best band of the 21st century.” It’s a swirl of banjos, a vintage 1970s Vocoder, heavy guitar fuzz, distorted strings and horns, barking dogs — a psychedelic hymn, building for nearly 10 cathartic minutes. —Rob Sheffield

- Incubus, ‘Circles’ (2001) Incubus broke through in the final breath of the 20th century with Make Yourself in the fall of 1999 — a cosmic rock odyssey that featured their meditative acoustic hit “Drive.” They carried that momentum into the 2000s with Morning View, an ultra-chill California masterpiece that glistened with rockers like “Wish You Were Here” and “Mexico.” The album’s hardest-rocking moment was the head-banging kiss-off “Circles,” complete with guitarist Mike Einziger’s fiery riffs. When they rerecorded Morning View in 2024, the songs were less an exact replica of the originals and more a reflection of how they’d evolved in live settings over the years. Unsurprisingly, “Circles” sounded more ferocious than ever. —Angie Martoccio

- The Mountain Goats, ‘This Year’ (2005) Singer, songwriter, and guitarist John Darnielle’s look back at “playing video games in a drunken haze” when he was “17 years young” and acting out against an abusive stepfather brims with the sort of warts-and-all autobiography that feels uncomfortably intimate. And then you get to the chorus, in which the Mountain Goats founder vows that “I am going to make it through this year/if it kills me.” This track from the Goats’ stellar The Sunset Tree has long been a fan favorite before becoming an unexpected viral hit in 2020, when the notion vowing to make it through a shit time became unexpectedly resonant. —David Fear

- Old 97’s, ‘Rollerskate Skinny’ (2001) Dallas’ Old 97’s were initially lumped in with the alt-country scene, but by 2001’s Satellite Rides, they had turned into something else: an ace pop-rock band. Inspired by a brief romance with Winona Ryder, “Rollerskate Skinny” finds frontman Rhett Miller piling up lines both boyishly endearing (“You’re pretty as a penny”) and caustic (“Wouldn’t be here if the Athenia hadn’t sunk”). It’s joyfully buoyant, but with an ache at its center, summed up by its final line, which Miller stretches out till it sounds almost like an affirmation: “I believe in love, but it don’t believe in me.” —Jon Dolan

- Momma, ‘Speeding 72’ (2022) The Brooklyn-by-way-of-Los-Angeles band Momma was born out of the tight-knit friendship between childhood pals Etta Friedman and Allegra Weingarten, who met in grade school. Their longtime connection is all over the group’s wistful melodies, often hidden in under blankets of distortion, as no song might be as reflective of what they’re good at than “Speeding 72,” off their 2022 album, Household Name. It’s a dreamy, riff-heavy joy ride that brings in more and more overlapping guitars, swelling into a bit of chaos that sounds like the whole band moving around each other without ever stepping on each other’s toes. —Julyssa Lopez

- Juanes, ‘Es Por Ti’ (2002) Back in the late 1990s, Medellín, Colombia native Juanes left Ekhymosis, his heavy metal band, and decamped in Los Angeles in search of pop-rock stardom. He found it almost immediately thanks to a superlative ear for comforting hooks, and the guidance of producer Gustavo Santaolalla, By the time his second album, Un Día Normal, dropped in 2002, Juanes was a Latin Grammy winner and concert favorite. “Es Por Ti” sums up the Zen beauty of his spiraling, guitar-based melodies, the supple comfort of his guy-next-door vocals, and a sunny cosmovision of disarming sincerity. —Ernesto Lechner

- Wolf Parade, ‘I’ll Believe in Anything’ (2005) Spencer Krug’s baroque and surprisingly hopeful rock anthem has had a few lives now, the most recent being the endlessly charming needle drop from HBO’s Heated Rivalry. Krug actually wrote the first version of the song, a low-fi take on an upright piano, for his side project Sunset Rubdown back in 2005, calling it a “kooky” experiment. “For me, it was a scrappy little love song about two people willing to take a chance on their young relationship,” Krug said. He eventually rerecorded it into the billowing version that’s become the enduring Wolf Parade classic that saw a 2,650 percent steaming jump and peaked at Number Seven on the Billboard U.S. rock chart 20 years later. —J.L.
- Alex G, ‘After Ur Gone’ (2014)

Alex Giannascoli was a college kid making music in between term papers when he wrote, recorded, and produced this two-and-a-half-minute stunner. Released as the first track on his breakthrough album, DSU, it has all the qualities that would make him a star — the haunting falsetto, the piercing guitar lead, the cryptic words alluding to an unnamed loss. “I guess some kids do model cars or skateboarding,”  Giannascoli told Rolling Stone at the time, describing how he developed his DIY methods. “I’d go to the basement after everyone was asleep and record all fuckin’ night.” Many years later, he’s still doing more or less the same thing, for an audience so huge you can hardly call it a cult anymore. It all starts here. —S.V.L.

- Baroness, ‘Isak’ (2007) A surface read of the lyrics to “Isak” makes this song seem to be about living an unfulfilling existence on a farm. But singer-guitarist John Baizley hollers couplets like, “Isak, tender the swine, carry the hare and barrow home,” in a way that suggests there’s something deeper going on. Ultimately, it’s the overall feel of this Red Album standout that made “Isak” an instant classic. Baizley and Brian Blickle play swinging blues-metal riffs, each guitarist dutifully stacking his part over the other’s, with two great solo breaks — the first echoing Pink Floyd space rock, the second summoning Tony Iommi–like metal miasmas. And drummer Allen Blickle somehow holds them together with unusual, jazzy rhythms.—Kory Grow

- The Raconteurs, ‘Steady, As She Goes’ (2006) “Steady, As She Goes” was the first song Jack White and Brendan Benson wrote together before forming the Raconteurs in 2005 with Patrick Keeler of the Afghan Whigs and Jack Lawrence of the Greenhornes. They had an alt-rock hit with “Steady, As She Goes,” a catchy garage-blues tune with a bassline that recalled Joe Jackson’s 1979 hit “Is She Really Going Out With Him?” This song has two very different videos, each directed by notable filmmakers. The first was more traditional, directed by Jim Jarmusch, with the band playing in a barn, and another directed by the Malloys that featured Paul Reubens as a cartoonish villain. —Alison Weinflash

- Slipknot, ‘People = Shit’ (2001) “I’m in this band because of everything that I hate about everything in the world,” Slipknot drummer Joey Jordison told Rolling Stone in 2000. Actual children of the corn, the nine mutants of Slipknot came out of Iowa in the late Nineties with their scary masks and bone-breaking live shows, and made their eye-popping extremism the most explosive attraction on Ozzfest. They summed up their hate-everything worldview with succinct fury on the nu-metal maelstrom “People = Shit,” an undeniable statement of tribal misanthropy and outcast self-determination. —J.D.

- Tame Impala, ‘Elephant’ (2012) On “Elephant,” Tame Impala’s Kevin Parker took some of rock’s most familiar pleasures — fuzzed-out Sabbath chug, high-heeled glam stomp, mind-melting psychedelia — and fused them into a sonic funhouse of his own. The lead single from his sophomore album, Lonerism, builds a whole world around Parker’s supersized riff. The song’s wonderfully wiggy midsection — a fantastic voyage of proggy synths, heavily distorted guitar, and burbling electronics — blasts into the cosmos before snapping back into its big dumb riff, showing Parker’s knack for indulging headphone listeners without losing the arena crowd. —Jason Roth

- Velvet Revolver, ‘Slither’ (2004) Unlike so many other Frankenstein bands, the mashup of Stone Temple Pilots and Guns N’ Roses known as Velvet Revolver wasn’t a cringey lark. The group actually turned out kick-ass, relevant hard rock songs, and “Slither” is chief among them. Driven by the river-bottom bass of Duff McKagan, the song twists and turns like its serpentine title, with Scott Weiland’s keening vocals cutting through the din. It climaxes with an eruptive Slash solo that ranks right up there with the guitarist’s best. Even Axl Rose seems to like the song: It’s become a staple of the reunited GNR’s set list. —Joseph Hudak

- Mudcrutch, ‘Crystal River’ (2008) After an incredible run of in the 1990s, Tom Petty hit a creative rough patch in the 2000s, with underwhelming albums like The Last DJ and Mojo. But he rediscovered something in 2008 when he made the unlikely decision to reform his pre-Heartbreakers band Mudcrutch and record a new album with them. Unlike Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, this was a democratic unit where all members wrote songs and even sang lead. But their best song, “Crystal River,” was a Petty original that clocked in at nearly 10 minutes. (In concert, it stretched out to 15.) Though considerably longer than just about anything else in Petty’s catalog, it’s a mellow journey that never gets boring or repetitive. —Andy Greene

- Bombino, ‘Amidinine’ (2013) A member of the nomadic Tuareg people, singer and guitarist Omara “Bombino” Moctar traveled from Niger to the Nashville studio run by Black Keys frontman Dan Auerbach and recorded the searing 2013 album Nomad. It kicks off with the anthemic “Amidinine,” which bridges West African “desert blues” and the pyrotechnics of Jimi Hendrix, whom Bombino discovered as a child living in exile with his family in Algeria. As he told Rolling Stone, “The freedom that Jimi expressed through his guitar sent me to another world, where I was also free.” You can hear that freedom in every note he plays.—J.D.

- Avril Lavigne, ‘My Happy Ending’ (2004) Following the spunky one-two punch of breakout hits “Complicated” and “Sk8ter Boi,” Avril Lavigne had something to prove on her sophomore effort, 2004’s Under My Skin. Though barely 20 years old, the Canadian pop-punk star had already seen her share of challenging relationships, channeling her disappointment into a singular line — “So much for my happy ending” — at the top of the album’s breakup ballad. She’s a co-writer on the song, with producer Butch Walker, and Lavigne’s lament is achingly felt in the bridge, “It’s nice to know we had it all/Thanks for watching as I fall/And letting me know we were done.” The success of “My Happy Ending” confirmed the opposite, as Lavigne’s star continued to rise.—Shirley Halperin
- Yungblud, ‘Hello Heaven, Hello’ (2025)

While he hadn’t yet turned 30 when his fourth album, Idols, came out in 2025, British agit-rocker Yungblud had already blazed a singular career path by the time of its release, and he used its opening cut to reintroduce himself to the world. The nine-minute, three-part rock opera, he told Rolling Stone, was inspired by him realizing the parallels between stadium rock and concert-hall classical; Yungblud added a dollop of 21st-century angst to the mix, cementing the song as his own. “Hello Heaven, Hello” veers from propulsive rock to swaggering post-glam to cavernous neo-power-balladry; it’s audacious and triumphant, with Yungblud’s tightly wound yawp sounding ready to conquer the world. —Maura Johnston

- Downtown Boys, ‘Monstro’ (2015) Providence, Rhode Island’s Downtown Boys combined refreshingly confrontational left-wing politics and a refreshingly confrontational punk attack on their excellent second album, Full Communism. The album’s peak cathartic moment was “Monstro,” a roaring critique of sexist, racist stereotypes and celebration of revolutionary power. With a blaring Lora Logic-style sax leading the charge, the song builds and builds until it combusts, as frontwoman Victoria Ruiz repeats the line “She’s brown! She’s smart!” like a battle cry. It’s political punk rock primed for the DSA era. —J.D.

- Moses Sumney, ‘Virile’ (2019) Moses Sumney is no stranger to challenging our expectations, whether he’s making your jaw drop with his ocean-deep, sky-high vocal range or creating spellbinding visual worlds to complement his otherworldly music. On “Virile,” a standout from his 2020 album, Græ, Sumney raises his glass to masculinity and smashes it on the ground. Sumney does rock music his way, alchemizing cavernous drums with spritely harp, industrial rock with classical music, heaven with hell. “Dear son,” he screeches to the stars, before slinking into his lower register, “We pick our own prisons.” “Virile” is evidence that we’re only confined to the boxes we lock ourselves into. —Jaeden Pinder

- Sleigh Bells, ‘Rill Rill’ (2010) A band birthed both in the belly of MySpace and peak-hipster Williamsburg, Sleigh Bells became a huge hit with blog-era tastemakers. This breakout track — off 2010’s Treats — sounds like your heart beating its way out of your chest, a tidal wave of guitars, booming drums, and electro sleaze, all showcasing Alexis Krauss’ almost too-sweet vocals. If you ever saw them perform live, you’ll know the feeling of all those amps buzzing in your chest as the crowd pogoed along. The track just sounds like 2010: languid and hopeful, a party before the world burns. —Brenna Ehrlich

- Alejandro Escovedo, ‘Castanets’ (2001) No one is better at merging the worlds of country-roots and punk than Alejandro Escovedo, and no song of his embodies his New York Dolls meets Austin roadhouse sound than “Castanets.” Escovedo storms and stomps his way through his deceptively nuanced tale of “a woman people don’t understand,” as he later explained. When George W. Bush was reported to have liked the song in 2005, Escovedo retired it from his set lists for several years, even though it was his most well-known tune. Then, more than two decades later, Escovedo deconstructed his cowpunk anthem with an entirely new arrangement and Spanglish lyrics on 2024’s “Castañuelas.”—Jonathan Bernstein
- King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard, ‘Rattlesnake’ (2017)

The marvelously prolific Australian psych-punk shredders King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard have released a slew of songs that could potentially be on this list, but the opening track from their 2017 exploration of alternate guitar tunings Flying Microtonal Banana has taken on a life of its own. Chugging guitars and huge gales — as well as a Vibraslap that echoes the titular serpent’s warning sound — give “Rattlesnake” an ominously windswept, while lead Gizzard Stu Mackenzie’s constant repetition “rattlesnake” (he says it 54 times on the album version, according to fans) and the microtonal tuning make it feel like a fever dream that won’t — and shouldn’t — end. —M.J.

- Red Clay Strays, ‘Wondering Why’ (2022) Though ostensibly a country band from Alabama, the Red Clay Strays sure can rock: Songs like “Ramblin’” and “Down South” have all the punch of Lynyrd Skynyrd. In the case of their breakout song, “Wondering Why,” however, they display more of a slow burn. There’s no big riff, no bombastic intro — just Elvis-adjacent frontman Brandon Coleman’s smoldering croon, which blazes near the song’s end as drummer John Hall plays an understated beat with a few choice cymbal hits. For the really ferocious version of “Wondering Why,” check out the band’s Live at the Ryman album.—Joseph Hudak

- Future Islands, ‘Seasons (Waiting on You)’ (2014) The idiosyncratic Baltimore indie band had a surprise hit with the high-drama synth-pop of “Seasons (Waiting on You),” a song about how time may pass but some people remain frustratingly the same. Singer Samuel T. Herring delivered his heartbroken lyrics with an uncanny emotional force, going from a forlorn croon to an overwrought rasp that was hard to shake once you heard it. His ungainly dance moves were unforgettable too; when the band performed on The Late Show With David Letterman, the host’s floored reaction helped seed the song’s viral success. —J.D.

- Blondshell, ‘Salad’ (2023) “Gonna get big,” Blondshell’s Sabrina Teitelbaum declares. She accomplishes all that and more on “Salad,” the deliciously dark centerpiece of her 2023 self-titled debut. It’s the indie-rock version of “Goodbye Earl,” as Teitelbaum sets out to get revenge on a guy for abusing her friend — specifically by poisoning his greens. She lays out her plan across thrashing, restless riffs, inspired by Hole’s “Doll Parts” and Nirvana’s “You Know You’re Right,” a move that proved she was carrying the furious torch of the Nineties into a new generation. “Look what you did/You’ll make a killer of a Jewish girl,” she sings. It was one of the first startlingly great Teitelbaum lines — and certainly not the last. —A.M.

- The Monkees, ‘Me and Magdalena’ (2016) The idea of a brilliant new Monkees album in 2016 seemed about as likely as the Archies making a major musical comeback. But for their 50th anniversary, Monkees superfan Adam Schlesinger recruited an incredible slate of songwriters, including Noel Gallagher, Paul Weller, and Rivers Cuomo, for the comeback LP Good Times! Dead Cab for Cutie’s Ben Gibbard contributed the gorgeous ballad “Me and Magdalena,” which Schlesinger arranged as a duet between Micky Dolenz and Michael Nesmith. Their voices blended as seamlessly as they did back in the 1960s, finally giving them a new classic they could play in concert alongside “I’m a Believer” and “Pleasant Valley Sunday.” —A.G.

- Mdou Moctar, ‘Afrique Victime’ (2021) Equally inspired by Eddie Van Halen as he is by the Tuareg guitarists of his native Niger, Mdou Moctar is one of the 21st century’s greatest guitarists — and his hypnotizing solo on the desert blues track “Afrique Victime” is a perfect example why. Across the song’s seven-minute run time, the tempo rises and rises as Moctar laments French colonialism’s eternal scar on Niger. He plays the song’s guitar solo as if he’s vehemently typing away on a computer, sliding back and forth and drumming along the strings, warping the instrument’s tones to mimic a wailing siren. “Afrique Victime”’ is frenetic yet liberating — it’s no wonder he’s often called the Hendrix of the Sahara. —J.P.

- Sum 41, ‘Fat Lip’ (2001) “Fat Lip” is so immaculate, you’d never know Sum 41 frontman Deryck Whibley cobbled it together from disparate parts: a monster riff, a howl-along chorus, a tender bridge, and, most daringly, a rap-rock verse with the pass-it-off stylings of the Beastie Boys and Run-D.M.C. By Whibley’s admission, the demo stunk, but producer Jerry Finn saw the vision. “Fat Lip” remains one of the great achievements of the early-aughts pop-punk boom: an undeniable hit that’s sneakily inventive in construction and execution; a brilliant loser anthem that’s defiant, deprecating and degenerate, funny and furious. Still, to this day, it’s guaranteed to get the pit going. —J. Blistein

- The Rolling Stones, ‘Whole Wide World’ (2023) At the start of the 2020s, Rolling Stones fans had resigned themselves to the idea that they were simply a touring band at that point. Fortunately, producer Andrew Watt didn’t share this viewpoint and managed to coax them into the studio for 2023’s revitalized Hackney Diamonds. The LP’s climax is “Whole Wide World,” where Mick Jagger sings about a broke-down Londoner convinced his best days are long behind him: “When the whole wide world’s against you/And that’s got you on the run/And you think the party’s over/But it’s only just, only just begun,” he sings. The song was also a tribute to the Stones themselves, who managed to extend the party longer than any rock band in history. —A.G.
- Electric Six, ‘Danger! High Voltage’ (2002)

All together now: “Fire in the disco! Fire in the Taco Bell!” (Yes, it rhymes with “gates of hell.”) “Danger! High Voltage” was an insanely catchy floor-filler in the indie-sleaze days of the early 2000s — if you were a drunk girl and this song came on in the scuzzy rock bar at 2 a.m., you were legally required to dance on a table and kick the DJ’s drinks over. Detroit conceptual mastermind Dick Valentine groans about the agonies and ecstasies of physical love for a global left-field hit. But he gets a big assist from his duet partner: Jack White, uncredited but unmistakable, wailing “danger, danger!” in his high-pitched sex yelp. —R.S.

- Jason Isbell and the 400 Unit, ‘Cumberland Gap’ (2017) Before his name became synonymous with the best in detail-rich Americana songwriting thanks to albums like his 2013 opus, Southeastern, Jason Isbell was one of the three singer-guitarists in this century’s top literate bar band, Drive-By Truckers. On this rocker from his 2017 LP, The Nashville Sound, Isbell showed how hard he could still bring it, singing about working-class angst and desperation in the heart of coal country over the roaring backing of his band the 400 Unit. “Maybe the Cumberland Gap just swallows you whole,” he wonders. That sense of fatalism is deep in his bones, but so is the dream of punching your way out. —J.D.

- At the Drive-In, ‘Arcarsenal’ (2000) At the Drive-In’s third album, Relationship of Command, truly felt like a band firing on all cylinders. Their sound was sharper, crisper, and more adrenaline-surged than ever — some of that a result of producer Ross Robinson finding ways to capture the musicians at their most heightened state. And the first song, “Arcarsenal,” offers the best introduction to the power coursing through the album, functioning as a forceful call to action to break from societal conformity. It’s also a solid example of Omar Rodríguez-López and Cedric Bixler-Zavala’s almost telepathic connection, with Bixler-Zavala howling out the lyrics (“I must have read a thousand faces”) to Rodríguez-López’s blistering riffs. —J.L.

- Louis XIV, ‘Finding Out True Love Is Blind’ (2005) Deliciously sexy and sleazy, this track epitomized why Louis XIV were once banned in Alabama. What other band can make “carrot juice” sound dirty? The standout on 2005’s The Best Little Secrets Are Kept, this song encapsulates a truly horny era replete with flat-ironed bangs, that first foray into skinny jeans, and a solid lacquering of eyeliner. The song may have an STD or two, but singer Jason Hill is an equal opportunity letch: smart girls, short girls, tough girls, girls of all races and creeds, he’s down to wind you up and make you crawl to him — even 20 years later. —B.E.

- Deerhunter, ‘Desire Lines’ (2010) On their space-rock epiphany “Desire Lines,” the Atlanta band Deerhunter found a happy place somewhere between moody Velvet Underground drone poetry and languid, stretched out, eat-a-peach transcendence. The peak moment on their great LP Halcyon Digest, the song begins as a hesitant reflection on twentysomething coming-of-age ambivalences, then lifts off into a mind-meld monster jam between guitarists Lockett Pundt and Bradford Cox, who make like shoegaze ninjas for three dazzling minutes. It’s a modern psychedelic bounty that brilliantly undercut trippy escapism with real-life ambivalence. —J.D.

- Sturgill Simpson, ‘Call to Arms’ (2016) After the release of his breakthrough album, Metamodern Sounds in Country Music, it was clear that Sturgill Simpson was in a category all his own, far beyond just the bounds of traditional country. He cemented that on 2016’s A Sailor’s Guide to Earth, which ends with the furious “Call to Arms,” where Simpson, alongside a wailing horn section, bemoans our modern discontents. “They serve up distractions and we eat ‘em with fries, until the bombs fall out of our fucking skies,” he sings. When Simpson appeared on Saturday Night Live, he finished the song with the ultimate rock star move: smashing his guitar.—Marissa R. Moss
- Ought, ‘Beautiful Blue Sky’ (2015)

The Montreal post-punk rebels Ought racked up a string of cerebral records in the 2010s, eventually evolving into the new band Cola, which put out one of 2026’s finest rock statements with Cost of Living Adjustment. “Beautiful Blue Sky” is a life-affirming staccato guitar groove, building under Tim Darcey’s acerbically witty voice, as he narrates another boring no

items.title: Dancing With the Stars Recap: The Boy Is Nine
items.description: Dancing With the Stars continues to be a fever dream of the highest order. Where else can you turn on the television and get an Argentine tango set to “Thong Song”; an adult human saying with her full chest, “Turning your sister into your lover for one night”
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Dancing With the Stars continues to be a fever dream of the highest order. Where else can you turn on the television and get an Argentine tango set to “Thong Song”; an adult human saying with her full chest, “Turning your sister into your lover for one night” in the first ten minutes of the broadcast; and also Sheryl Crow? Nowhere, okay. God bless America, and God bless Dancing With the Stars.

It’s “Grammy Night” and also the quarterfinals — we’re really getting so close to crowning a new Len Goodman Mirrorball Champion. Everyone’s dancing like it, too. I mean, did you see that opening pro number to “Just Keep Watching”? It’s one of the best performances of the season. Also, that bumper with Sharna and Brandon, in which they start in a lift position and he throws her up from there? I shrieked. Incredible. As the season hurtles toward its end, people are leaving it all on the ballroom floor, including — especially — the seven couples still in the competition. All of whom, by the way, have to learn two dances this week thanks to the Dance-Off competition later in the evening. But first, our regularly scheduled routines.
Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach
Argentine Tango // “Crazy in Love,” by Beyoncé

Since the beginning, Daniella has wanted to highlight, not shy away from, showing off Ezra’s prosthetic, and she goes into the Argentine tango with the same mission. The sharp kicks and flicks of the Argentine tango are, admittedly, the first time I was genuinely worried there might be a mishap out on the dance floor. There is not! But Ezra does seem to have a lot of balance issues in this routine, and he seems less sturdy a partner than he has been in the past. But who can really concentrate on this routine when this is the moment Carrie Ann decides to make the “sister/lover” comment that will be burned into our brains for the rest of eternity?
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 9
Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov
Paso Doble // “Bring Me to Life,” by Evanescence

You know when the guy is doing a no-shirt paso, it’s going to be serious. I’ve been waiting to see Amber take on this style because it feels really suited to her strengths — the drama, the power, the shaping. (Her arms! Her hands!) Amber and Pasha don’t disappoint. Those knee spins alone should have earned this an automatic perfect score. Both Carrie Ann and Derek marvel at Amber’s ability to have resistance and tension but do it so gracefully. And yet still, these two aren’t handing out tens. What does this woman have to do to get a perfect score around here?
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 10
Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas
Argentine Tango // “Thong Song,” by Sisqó

I’ve never been so concerned about rib health in my life. First Julia, now Maura. Maura looks like she is in so much pain every time Mark lifts her in rehearsal, which is a lot — this is Argentine tango, after all. But her injury doesn’t seem to have any effect on her performance — that final lift in which she’s upside down for so long? Flawless. This style, which features a lot of time in hold, does wonders for Maura. She gets to remind us of her great lines, her poise, and precision. She also has a sparkly thong coming out of her costume, and that kind of commitment to the bit should earn her 11s at least. It’s the best Argentine tango of the three we get tonight.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 9
Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy
Jazz // “All for You,” by Janet Jackson

Jenna Dewan’s career began with Janet Jackson — in her videos and then on her All for You Tour — so I’m glad we’re finally getting to see Jenna celebrate that. Janet even calls in! DWTS has so much cachet at the moment — we’re getting video messages from Janet freaking Jackson? Obviously, Jenna crushes this jazz. (Or, as Val notes, a jazz-funk.) She could’ve danced the whole thing solo, to be honest. I’m actually shocked this doesn’t earn tens across the board. Bruno does say she looked in her “comfort zone,” so maybe it was … just … too easy?
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 9
Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik
Tango // “Boom Boom Pow,” by Black Eyed Peas

My little sweeties are sweetie-ing again! It seems like Tatyana and Jan expect to get eliminated every week, so they are simply dancing with abandon. For the fun of it. And this performance is fun. Not to be dramatic, but Tatyana staring directly into the camera to lip-sync a portion of this did alter my DNA. The judges love this routine, praising Tatyana’s power and control and her ability to always draw us in. Their technique may not always look as sharp as some of the people on top of the leaderboard (Tatyana’s neck seemed extra tense this week — was it just the costume?), but they remain one of the most exciting couples to watch this season.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 9
Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold
Argentine Tango // “SexyBack,” by Justin Timberlake featuring Timbaland

Listen, I love Connor and Rylee, but this dance was not it. His biggest critique last week was that he needed to look more like a leading man. This week, he still doesn’t fully sell it. He is a sturdy partner for Rylee to do an insane amount of tricks and lifts throughout, but he is lacking finesse here. Where are all my Argentine tango kicks and flicks? The footwork is a little too stodgy for me, but the judges love the power and control, and they are our lords and commanders, as we know.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 9
Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson
Salsa // “Die With a Smile,” by Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars

Please give a raise to the editor who cut from Harry getting emotional about getting some closure and perspective on his childhood trauma of watching his family struggle while growing up in Costa Rica right into him doing some insane body rolls. This is the chaos we live for. With all seriousness, Harry really has worn his heart on his sleeve throughout this competition — he is insanely likable. But I don’t think that heart and emotion have always translated to these routines. This salsa is not their cleanest dance — it’s intricate and energetic, but at times it felt more chaotic than anything else. Derek points out that while Harry’s arms were incredible, his bottom half looked surprisingly “rigid.” They earn the best score of the night from the judges, but I’d easily put both Jenna and Val and Amber and Pasha over this routine.
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 9 // Bruno: 10

Honestly, I’m not a huge fan of the Dance-Offs. Couples are paired up and have to dance the same style to the same song (tonight, we’re getting all live performances from Brandy and Monica, Maren Morris, and Sheryl Crow, if you can believe it) side by side on the floor. The winner of each matchup will win two extra points to add to their score for the night. But the setup — while closer to actual ballroom competitions — makes it hard to really focus on what people are doing right (or wrong). Also, I get that DWTS is pairing up celebrities with similar backgrounds — the gold medalists, the actresses, the personalities — but the only fair way to really do this is by leaderboard points, no? Did everyone see Tatyana and Jan’s faces when Jenna and Val walked into the room? They immediately knew those two points were but a dream at that point. Harry and Jenna have the highest overall score of the season, so they have immunity from this mini-competition and automatically get their two extra points. Everyone else takes to the dance floor again.
Amber and Pasha versus Ezra and Daniella
Rumba // “The Boy Is Mine,” by Brandy and Monica

I may dislike the Dance-Off as a concept, but if it brings us performances like this, keep it coming. The Pashkovs and their Team USA partners said, Oh, you want us to compete against each other? That’s so cute. They turn this matchup into more of a team dance. By the end, they even switch partners so Amber can dip Daniella, while Ezra dips Pasha. It’s one of the best moments of the season.
Jenna and Val versus Tatyana and Jan
Cha-Cha // “The Middle,” by Zedd, Maren Morris, and Grey

At least no one is kidding themselves with what’s going on in this pairing. Both couples know that this is technique versus performance, and that’s exactly what we get. Jenna and Val dance the hell out of this cha-cha, and yet, my eye kept being drawn over to, as Bruno puts it, the sultriness of what Tatyana and Jan have going on. But maybe that’s just me!
Connor and Rylee versus Maura and Mark
Cha-Cha // “All I Wanna Do,” by Sheryl Crow

What I wouldn’t give for 20 full minutes of footage of Connor and Maura rehearsing together. A dream team. And the fact that they come out wearing the same fringe pants (just different colors)? The cherry on top. Maura and Mark have a leg up on technique, but I actually think what really does Connor and Rylee in is the bit of country line-dancing choreography they have in the middle of their routine. The judges were looking for pure cha-cha, and that’s not what was served up.

If you’ve been paying attention to scores tonight, the leaderboard is insanely close. Only nines and tens were given out (Derek gave every single routine a nine), and while the bonus points from the Dance-Offs move things around a little bit, this is really coming down to viewer votes.

It’s Jenna and Val who get the boot just shy of the semifinals. I’m actually not that shocked. It never seemed like people were going to hand the Mirrorball over to Jenna Dewan despite her consistently high scores and obvious technical prowess. She performed some great routines, but there was a bit of an emotional disconnect she never fully got past. Hey, the heart wants what the heart wants.

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Recap: Clash of the Dwarves
items.description: Uh-oh. Is it possible that Galadriel and Arondir have made a horrible mistake trusting Marnûkh and letting him lead them into the mountainside prison fortress of Gundabad? That’s always been a possibility, of course. Marnûkh has never seemed that trustworthy,
items.author: Keith Phipps
paragraphs: Uh-oh. Is it possible that Galadriel and Arondir have made a horrible mistake trusting Marnûkh and letting him lead them into the mountainside prison fortress of Gundabad? That’s always been a possibility, of course. Marnûkh has never seemed that trustworthy, and following him has been something of a desperation play from the start. But the early scenes of this episode seem to confirm they’ve been foolish to bet on Marnûkh’s sincerity. Once inside Gundabad with his “freshies,” Marnûkh announces himself as General Marnûkh and claims this has all been part of a plan to bring Galadriel and her Ring to Sauron, whom he expects is on his way. (And he is, having fed some fresh meat to The Beast, which sort of looks like a dragon but almost certainly isn’t a dragon because Tolkien dragons are much different creatures. We’re told it’s an eagle that’s been corrupted by Morgoth, which might make it to eagles what Orcs are to Elves. Maybe. It’s confusing.) Marnûkh sends Galadriel off to prison and takes Arondir, claiming he plans to question him about Rivendell’s defenses. Everything that unfolds before the credits seems pretty bleak for our Elf heroes.

They’re bleak in Khazad-dûm, too, where a debate rages about what to do now that news of Durin helping the Elves and sending Marnûkh to Rivendell has leaked and Sauron is amassing forces along the border. The Dwarf Lords demand Durin hand over the Dwarf Rings, which he refuses, but when he turns to Thráin for support, he finds his brother does not have his back. (Just how little Thráin has his back, he does not yet know.) And, to be fair, Thráin sounds reasonable when he says that the Dwarf Rings might be their best defense against Sauron. But Disa’s counterpoint that they risk madness by wearing them and that the Dwarves are tough enough to take on Sauron seems even more persuasive.

It also opens up the opportunity for Thráin to make his big move. If Durin III was wearing the Ring, and thus mad, when he reinstated Durin IV as heir, does that even count? There’s some legal ambiguity there, and Thráin exploits it. That leaves the crown up for grabs, and the proper heir can only be decided by the will of the Dwarf god Aulë. It’s trial by combat time, and Durin really has no choice but to rise to the challenge, he argues, despite Disa’s protests. And, in the end, even Disa comes around. If they’re going to hold on to what they’ve got, there’s only one path forward.

Of course, the Dwarves’ reluctance to take on Sauron is perfectly understandable. When the action shifts to Lindon, we see that the Elves have successfully fought off an Orc attack, but the victory has come at such a high cost that it doesn’t feel like victory at all. Even Gil-galad (Benjamin Walker), the Elves’ High King (ingaran, in Elvish), seems shaken, though he takes some reassurance from Círdan’s (Ben Daniels) insistence that hope might be their best weapon. But when Elrond arrives, after barely escaping an Orc attack, he doesn’t have much hope to offer.

He does come up with a plan, however, one that’s been cooking for a few episodes: They ought to reach out to Númenor, combine forces, and find a way for Elves and men to live together after they defeat Sauron. Even Círdan’s revelation that they’ve already tried only to receive a terse letter of refusal from Pharazôn doesn’t squelch Elrond’s enthusiasm. What Círdan reads as “drop dead,” Elrond interprets as pride. Their best plan of action is for Gil-galad to travel to Númenor and make a personal plea “king to king.” Elrond is also onboard when Círdan suggests Elrond accompany his king. (He was planning to go anyway, really.) Elrond’s brother Elros, after all, gave up his immortality to found Númenor. What better reminder of the bond between Elves and men could there be than an Elf than the twin brother who looks just like him?

But would they be so optimistic if they knew what was actually happening in Númenor? On what has to be the longest ride of Elendil’s life, he listens to Kemen reveal his secret origin as the son of a woman who “worked her trade at night” who was killed by Pharazôn after she informed him they had a son together. That hasn’t stopped Kemen, whom Pharazôn spared, from trying to win his dad’s approval, however. But as dedicated as he might be to the father who, in his eyes, spared him, Kemen doesn’t seem entirely unswayed by Elendil’s talk about finding “true freedom” by seeing Pharazôn for the monster he is and joining Elendil’s cause. Kemen doesn’t have long to mull this notion over, however, before Anarion and his men ambush the carriage and take him prisoner in the process of rescuing Elendil. It’s a stunning reversal of fortune for Kemen, and perhaps the first development to wipe the smirk off his face since season one.

Over at Gundabad, things don’t seem to be going gundagreat for Arondir, who’s seemingly headed to the deepest, darkest cell in the place. Until, that is, Marnûkh turns on the other Orcs and frees his Elf companion. This, it turns out, was part of the plan all along, even if Arondir is kind of pissed by the degree of abuse Marnûkh heaped on him in the name of retaining the ruse. They proceed with their plan to rescue Maitalle only to find an Elf corpse in her cell shortly before hearing the sound of approaching Orcs. Maybe this was a bad idea after all?

Hope presents itself in the unexpected form of a living Elf. And not just any Elf. It’s Celeborn, who discovers his legend does not precede him when he reels off his bona fides to Marnûkh and Arondir. He doesn’t even get a chance to tell them he’s Galadriel’s husband before they start to leave. Then Celeborn proves they need him to make their escape by demonstrating that he knows the Orcs’ routines and is their best shot at escaping.

Miles away, drama has begun to escalate at Khazad-dûm. Over drinks, Thráin attempts to enlist Disa into a couple of power plays. First, he says he’ll give up his claim on the throne in exchange for the Rings of Power Durin has hidden. Then he tries extortion, threatening to tell Durin that he has a history with his wife. To circumvent this, Disa confesses to Durin, telling him that once, before they were married and while they were fighting, she hooked up with Thráin. And, honestly, Durin seems pretty cool and sensitive about this. (He also, rightly, sees Sauron’s influence as a real possibility.) But when Gamli brings up that he saw his mother and uncle alone just before the brothers’ scheduled fight, Durin sees red. Losing his head, he flies into rage, allowing Thráin to get the better of him. As the crowd chants Thráin’s name, it looks like the reign of Durin IV has come to a premature end.

While this unfolds, Sauron is flying high, literally. Mounted on the Beast, he soars toward Gundabad while Marnûkh, Arondir, and Celeborn (who quickly establishes himself as a crucial part of their plan) attempt to make their escape. Without knowing the identity of the third member of Marnûkh and Arondir’s party, Celeborn strongly advises them to leave without her, then starts to make an exit himself before heading back after Marnûkh mentions Galadriel’s name. Within moments, the couple has reunited, and both seem too shocked to know what to do or say. But they don’t have much time to process their feelings before Sauron shows up, demanding that Galadriel and Marnûkh be taken alive.

As Galadriel and the others attempt to make their way to the roof, it, once again, appears as if Marnûkh is on the verge of switching sides before he again proves his loyalty to his new friends (if that’s the right word) by releasing all the nearby prisoners and causing all hell to break loose. They barely make it to the top alive, then have to fight off an Orc horde for the right moment to make their escape via Landroval, which the Great Eagle Galadriel summons. In a touching moment, Arondir heroically saves Marnûkh’s life despite their past troubles. But the moment doesn’t last.

When a Nazgnagôl arrives, he wastes no time before killing Marnûkh. Then, curiously, the Nazgnagôl warns Arondir to leave rather than attacking him before taking off his mask. It’s Theo, now fully Nazgûled up. Despite this, Arondir seems to be on the verge of convincing him to abandon Sauron and remove the Ring that gives him power but leaves him in Sauron’s control. That ends, however, with Sauron’s arrival. At his master’s command, Theo kills Arondir while Galadriel and Celeborn look on in horror before Celeborn forces them both to dive off the roof and into Landroval’s clutches. Then Sauron and Theo leave Arondir’s body on the roof.

That’s … actually pretty shocking. Arondir has been a major character from the start. And though the departure of Nazanin Boniadi at the end of the first season brought Arondir’s romance with Bronwyn to a premature end, he still had a lot to do in the second season (and, to this point, in the third).
