But maybe it shouldn’t come as a surprise. We’ve reached a point in the story when it would seem that anyone whose fate isn’t explicitly laid out in Tolkien’s text might not be safe. (RIP Eärien. Everyone else, from Kemen to Largo Brandyfoot, should probably watch their backs.)

We’ve also reached the point in the season when tension has reached a point unlikely to let up until the season’s end. Are Durin and his family outcasts now? Does Elrond know what he and Gil-Galad are in for when they reach Númenor? Is Theo — who’s increasingly looking like the show’s Anakin Skywalker — completely beyond redemption now, or is there still good in him? With the possible exception of what Gandalf is up to in Rhûn, a plot that hasn’t quite caught fire yet, all the story lines remain compelling, too, which hasn’t always been the case with The Rings of Power. Halfway through, this looks like the series’ best season to date. Let’s see if that’s still true at the end of the second half.

• RIP Marnûkh, too? Where it looked at first as if he would serve as a kind of Orcish analog of Gollum, he revealed hidden depths with each episode. He taught us all that Orcs, too, have poems in their hearts. Hopefully, he has an afterlife filled with grubs and all the other awful things he loved to eat.
• What is the vibe of Galadriel and Celeborn’s reunion? It’s hard to discern. Maybe it’s impossible to get what’s going on there if you’re not an Elf.

• Maybe the distinction between the Nazgnagôl and the Nazgûl we know from Tolkien is a matter of intensity. The Nazgnagôl possess some magical powers, but they’re also recognizably human when they remove their masks. Also, if Theo is typical, they’re under Sauron’s influence but not yet wholly in his thrall. There’s some free will left, even if it’s dwindling.

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Recap: The Long Walk
items.description: If you’ve spent the past two episodes wondering what Gandalf was up to, wonder no more. The opening of this third episode of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power’s third season puts the focus on Rhûn, the desert in the east of Middle-earth. This is the la
items.author: Keith Phipps
paragraphs: If you’ve spent the past two episodes wondering what Gandalf was up to, wonder no more. The opening of this third episode of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power’s third season puts the focus on Rhûn, the desert in the east of Middle-earth. This is the last major Rings of Power setting to debut this season, so let’s do one final bit of catching up.

- This one’s actually pretty simple: As the second season drew to a close, the Wizard Previously Known as the Stranger, now known as Gandalf (Daniel Weyman), did battle with the Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) in the valley occupied by the Stoors, a halfling group who’ve long called the region their home. By the time the battle is over, however, they’ve been turned into nomads, their valley having been destroyed after Gandalf refused to become an ally to the Dark Wizard and take on Sauron. On their way out, accompanied by Nori (Markella Kavenagh) and Poppy (Megan Richards), they gave Gandalf his name, a corruption of “Grand Elf.”
- Also, Gandalf has been hanging out with Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear), a bright spirit in a dark world who seems to have some wisdom to impart.

So what’s going on in Rhûn? Nothing good, it would seem. The Dark Wizard remains in control, and, if anything, his following has expanded in the five-year gap between seasons despite his inability to use his magic to accomplish what seems like ought to be a relatively simple task: growing a flower that used to be plentiful in Rhûn. “Once I have the Ring, everything will be as it once was,” he says to one acolyte, though it seems like he’s really speaking to himself.

Not all of his followers are as dedicated as he believes, however. In addition to Gandalf and Tom Bombadil having infiltrated his acolytes’ ranks, Khamûl, the returning Gaudrim warrior — now a Nazgnagôl — tells the Dark Wizard that he’ll be taking the Dark Wizard’s throne, thank you very much. The ensuing confrontation ends in something like a draw. Khamûl doesn’t give up his Ring, but neither does the Dark Wizard surrender power. To save face, the Dark Wizard tells his followers that Khamûl has returned as an emissary to reveal that Sauron has accepted a proposal that Rhûn and Mordor become allies. He’ll be back soon, Khamûl, with his legions; then they’ll all team up to take on Middle-earth. The Dark Wizard survives for now, but the “Hail Sauron!” chants don’t bode well for the future, nor does Khamûl’s cryptic threat that he might lose his following if “they were to learn what became of your partner.” Hmm …

All this worries Gandalf quite a bit. (Tom Bombadil not so much.) But he’s not exactly powerless. Outside, he takes out a Dark Wizard henchman without even realizing it, shortly before reviving an oliphaunt and using magic to restore its natural, gentle personality and helping to remove its battle armor. There’s nothing dark about him or his use of magic, it would seem.

The previous episode ended with Pharazôn preparing to send Kemen to attack the Havens of the Faithful on the west coast of Númenor. Here we learn that Númenor isn’t exactly defenseless thanks in part to Anarion (Andrew Richardson), Isildur and Eärien’s brother, whom we meet for the first time drilling a bunch of heavily armed troops. After the exercise ends, his father, Elendil, takes him aside to share news from Eärien, whose death they don’t yet know about, that there is a traitor in their midst. Anarion can’t believe it, but Elendil knows it to be true and knows the turncoat has plans to hand over a map of the havens at a secret meeting. Obviously, this must be thwarted, but at this point Elendil only trusts himself and Anarion, so they make plans to do the thwarting themselves.

It looks like if the Middle-earth bad guys are to be defeated, it’s going to be the responsibility of only a handful of people because, just as the Faithful’s fate rests on the success of Elendil and Anarion, it’s only the small party of Galadriel, Arondir, and Marnûkhh charged with traveling to Gundabad and keeping the Elven-smith Maitalle from falling into Sauron’s hands. For the Elves, this is not a happy outing, but Marnûkh seems to be having a grand time, chattering away about piss as thick as tree sap and (maybe) joking about how he likes to eat small children. “We eat all ages,” he then clarifies, and it’s not certain if this is a joke either.

After the trio comes upon a group of fallen soldiers — both Orcs and Elves — Marnûkh advises them to veer off the trail in order to avoid Sauron’s legions, who are scheduled to attack the nearby hills with trebuchets. Arondir and Galadriel aren’t sure if this is a trap, but they don’t have a lot of other options, so they follow Marnûkh’s lead (but make him go first). Soon it becomes clear that even Sauron doesn’t know whose side Marnûkh is on. After getting word of his location from a pair of Nazgûl — by way of a bird turned into a dreadful crow by dark magic — an Orc henchman offers some possibilities: Maybe Marnûkh wants them to follow him? Maybe he’s in it for himself? “I want to know more about this Orc,” Sauron tells him. Everyone does, really.

In Rhûn, Gandalf and Tom Bombadil seem quite aware of how overmatched they are, but Gandalf has a plan. They don’t need to take out the Dark Wizard and Sauron’s forces. If they can just take down the Dark Wizard and break the spell he holds over his followers, the whole house of cards might collapse. But Tom Bombadil’s not so sure. Or, more precisely, Tom Bombadil has some thoughts that he’ll only share via frustratingly cryptic statements like “Mayhap you’re not meant to defeat it at all.” This, understandably, frustrates Gandalf, leading Tom Bombadil to suggest this might be a good time for him to return to the Withywindle.

Gandalf begs him to share one hint about how to defeat their enemies before he leaves. It arrives in the form of a song. Sort of. If this is really a hint, Gandalf can’t figure it out and leaves to fetch the rabbit Tom Bombadil has requested. In the process, he stumbles on — or is led to — a flame he recognizes as the Secret Fire, who provides some backstory with a side helping of advice. Gandalf was one of five servants sent to save Middle-earth. Also, the Dark Wizard used to be called “Pallando.” Whether the Dark Wizard/Pallando was one of the aforementioned five remains unclear, but we do learn that the Dark Wizard first traveled to Rhûn with a partner he then murdered, which is how Rhûn became the wasteland it is now. That being said, the Secret Fire continues — Gandalf is meant to save the Dark Wizard, not defeat him, and thus prevent the impending Rhûn-Sauron team-up. Knocked out (literally) by this information, Gandalf awakens and returns to Tom Bombadil’s home to discover that his host wasn’t kidding when he said he planned to vamoose. With work to do and no good reason to hang around, Gandalf decides to do the same.

Shortly after a helpful Orc informs Sauron that Marnûkh was a torture master who fought at Eregion, information that makes him want to know more, the episode returns to Marnûkh, Galadriel, and Anarion’s journey. As they make progress, the Elves are surprised to learn that Marnûkh likes to compose poems, including one about a fallen comrade whose body they found — and even more surprised to learn he’s pretty good at it. But they only have a moment to consider his artistic merits before a threat arrives in the form of the Nazgnagôl, one they’re able to fend off by hiding as Galadriel uses her Elven ways to summon a swarm of butterflies.

Later that night, the Elves question whether or not their companion intentionally led them into a trap. Where, for starters, was that promised trebuchet attack? The answer remains unclear as the antipathy between Marnûkh and Arondir deepens. When Marnûkh learns that his late master, Adar, was responsible for the death of someone Arondir loved (Bronwyn back in the first season, in case you’d forgotten), the two almost come to blows. Later, Arondir suggests to Galadriel that they might be on a wild goose chase that will bring them to a bad end. Galadriel, however, thinks that grief has clouded his judgment and that it would be best if they parted ways and that Arondir go back to his original plan of returning to Pelargir and checking in on Theo. Whether he’s trying to betray them or not, one thing is clear: Marnûkh can be a big jerk.

Across the sea on Númenor, Anarion confesses to his father that he has a bad feeling about their plan as they lay in wait for the traitor to appear and betray them to Pharazôn. It’s soon revealed that Anarion was right to feel ill at ease. There is no traitor and no map; it’s all been a trap set by Kemen to lure him out in the open and take him prisoner. As they exchange words, Kemen breaks the news of Eärien’s death to Elendil in the least sensitive way possible. But all is not lost. Despite Elendil’s orders to flee, Anarion has stuck around and manages to single-handedly take out Kemen’s men. Most of them, anyway. It’s not enough to prevent the survivors from shoving Elendil into a carriage and whisking him away, which might be all that matters.

The episode ends with a string of incidents intensifying the drama around the search for Maitalle. In a truly horrifying scene, Sauron tortures a nice Elf couple into supplying some additional information on Marnûkh via poison and the false promise of an antidote. Before dying, they give him enough to go on to put him on Marnûkh’s scent. He then tells his henchman to “saddle the beast,” an order followed by a glimpse of what appears to be a dragon (?). He’s headed to Gundabad, but Galadriel and Marnûkh are already there, where they’re soon joined by Arondir, who’s come to trust Marnûkh after witnessing the trebuchet attack he thought the Orc had made up. It looks like these opposing forces will soon converge, and it probably won’t be a peaceful meeting when they do.

This season’s third episode alternates between ratcheting up the tension and piling on the lore. It’s fairly successful at both tasks, but it’s getting hard to keep track of all the legendary wizards from days gone by and who betrayed whom. (Not impossible. It just takes some work.) Regardless, the Gandalf-focused scenes are the season’s least lively to date. It’s also not clear who gave Elendil bad intel about a traitor in the Havens. This was alleged to come from Eärien, so it would make sense for Kemen to have supplied it, but how would he know what methods she used? Maybe we’ll find out soon. And does every episode have to attempt to up the ante with increasingly grim reminders of just how evil Sauron is? Regardless, there’s quite a bit of intrigue around every storyline, and we haven’t even caught up with the Harfoots yet. Surely they also have some role to play, although the series has yet to reveal exactly what that will be or where it will occur.

• Is this the last we’ll see of Tom Bombadil? That’s unclear, which makes it a little too soon to do a postmortem. But this episode keeps with Tom Bombadil’s appearance in the previous season. It’s an interesting characterization, and Rory Kinnear has a lot of fun playing a beatific, gnomic, sort-of mentor to Gandalf. But this Tom Bombadil doesn’t really seem to have that much in common with the Tom Bombadil we meet in The Lord of the Rings.
• Based on the first episode, it seemed like we would have seen more of Celeborn by now, in flashback if not in the current timeline.
• That is a big hill that Galadriel & Co. will have to climb.

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Recap: Somewhere Beyond the Sea
items.description: How big is the scope of Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power? Not only did we get a fleeting glimpse of Gandalf — a major character, to say the least — in the previous episode, but we didn’t even get a scene set in Númenor, one of the show’s major locations.
items.author: Keith Phipps
paragraphs: How big is the scope of Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power? Not only did we get a fleeting glimpse of Gandalf — a major character, to say the least — in the previous episode, but we didn’t even get a scene set in Númenor, one of the show’s major locations. Gandalf is completely MIA this episode, but Númenor plays a major role. So, as with the previous episode, here’s a quick catch-up with what had been going on in that faraway island kingdom.

- In season two, Ar-Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), with the help of Lord Belzagar (Will Keen), assumed power after ousting his cousin Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson), who was blinded when Mount Doom erupted. Míriel’s blindness made some uneasy, as did her possession of a Palantir, the existence of which was revealed by Eärien (Ema Horvath). Also, Pharazôn touched a giant eagle during Míriel’s coronation, which some Númenoreans interpreted as an omen in favor of his rule, greasing his ascent.

- But not everyone is down on Míriel. Eärien and Islidor’s father, Elendil (Lloyd Owen), for one, is on her side. This does not sit well with the new leadership, who wants to throw Elendil into the ocean to undergo a Trial by Abyss in which, if guilty, he’ll be eaten by a sea monster. When Míriel submits to the trial instead, the sea monster spares her. This hardens the beliefs of a pro-Míriel group known as “the Faithful,” whom the Pharazôn regime regards as enemies of the state after falsely accusing Míriel of being aligned with Sauron.
- Her loyalties divided, Eärien ultimately decides to help her father escape, but Míriel remains behind.

Five years later, Númenor appears to have adapted to the regime change and even embraced Pharazôn as their leader, based on the cheering Númenorians that greet him as he parades through the streets. (That he’s freely throwing coins to the crowd probably doesn’t hurt.) The place seems to be thriving, and Pharazôn can boast of building “the most powerful armada the age has known,” which he soon plans to put to use in fighting Sauron. (Belzagar, who seems to be enjoying the decadence his power and wealth afford him, would rather not, but Pharazôn remains determined.) But there are signs of discontent. In fact, signs of discontent don’t get more obvious than the assassination attempt Pharazôn faces in the episode’s opening scene, one staged by Isildur (Maxim Baldry) and a companion named Haleth (Karl Queensborough) posing as a shepherd. This ends with Belzagar’s companion taking an arrow to the chest, Pharazôn wounded, and one of the would-be assassins in chains.

Later, Belzagar blames the Faithful, whom we learn have helped Míriel escape from Pharazôn’s clutches. But Pharazôn doesn’t think Míriel, who abhors murder, would stoop to using assassins. Either way, Pharazôn has another problem. Someone known only as the “Man with the White Flame” is assembling an army, which Belzagar posits as yet another reason not to pursue Sauron at this time. Maybe there’s someone in their midst conspiring against them? With a hint of glee, Pharazôn uses this possibility as an excuse to torture their captive in the hopes of revealing the traitor.

The traitor, it turns out, is quite close at hand, as in just a few rooms away. Where Eärien previously wavered, she’s now firmly aligned with the Faithful, as revealed when she whispers her allegiance to Haleth, whom Pharazôn’s men have been torturing, when they get a moment alone. This actually doesn’t come as a surprise to him. He’s aware of her loyalties and grateful for her work and now would like only a release from the pain. To this end, Eärien tells the soldiers she has a name — her fiercely anti-Faithful servant — and then tells them to kill Haleth.

At the servant’s execution, Belzagar tells Eärien that there’s soon to be some kind of action against the Faithful in the West, a revelation that Eärien can’t know will soon seal her fate. Later, while still racked with guilt about her actions, she brings this information to Isildur, who suggests she consider fleeing. When she accompanies him to the Faithful’s hideout at the Bay of Elros, it appears at first as if she’s taken this advice to heart. There, Míriel talks to her followers, whom she’s helping escape to the even safer Havens on the West Coast.

Míriel’s not too happy about the assassination attempt, correctly surmising that this will escalate Pharazôn’s hostilities and endanger Elendil in the Havens. Because Elendil is too far away to reach in a timely fashion — every once in a while, Rings of Power does seem to care about how long it takes to get from point A to point B — they seemingly don’t have many options. Until, that is, Isildur suggests using the Palantir, which Eärien believes she can access despite it being locked up.

Meanwhile, Sauron oversees a much smaller-scale power struggle in Mordor as Theo and one of his companions struggle to be the sole survivor and claim the Ring of Power Sauron has offered. But upon spotting the marks on Theo’s arms, marks he obtained by handling that mysterious, blood-fueled sword, Sauron decides the fight in Theo’s favor by killing Theo’s opponent. When Sauron asks how he came by the sword, Theo replies that the father he never knew, and whose fate remains unknown, left it for him. To this, Theo receives an unexpected reply: “Would you like to meet him now?” But when an Orc arrives with the news that Marnûkh has surrendered to the Dwarves, Sauron gets a little sidetracked.

As unwelcome as this news may be for Sauron, Marnûkh’s surrender has created a whole new set of complications for the Dwarves. Marnûkh tells them he needs to share some secrets with Galadriel, and only Galadriel. So what’s going on? Is this a trap set by Sauron? And if it’s not, do they really want to piss Sauron off by openly siding with the Elves? In the interest of doing what’s right, Disa suggests they send for Elrond, who quickly arrives to take Marnûkh off their hands, but shoots Durin a look that suggests he knows this may open up a whole new set of problems.

He’s right, too. Before long, a pair of Nazgnagôl show up at Khazad-dûm demanding Durin give up Marnûkh. After Durin refuses, one of them begins unreeling a seemingly hypnotic promise of doom involving Durin being dragged away to “the houses of lamentation.” This seems to freak Durin out until Thraîn announces his arrival with a belch and curses them out by saying their threats are tantamount to a declaration of war. What a hero! But what’s the strange expression on Thraîn’s face as his brother hugs him? Before the episode ends, its meaning will become all too clear. In the woods, Thraîn confers with the Nazgnagôls (Nazgnagôlim?), telling them, “The trap is set; I just need Durin to fall into it.” He then reveals that Marnûkhis is in Rivendell, prompting them to head off at top speed.

So what exactly does Marnûkh know that might be so dangerous? Upon reaching Galadriel, accompanied by Elrond and Arondir, he spills the news that Sauron is working on the One Ring, news that makes Galadriel and the others extremely wary. A firm believer in Orc independence, Marnûkh is motivated by his father’s story of Galadriel being willing to form an alliance with the Orcs, whom he (rightly) suspects will become cannon fodder in Sauron’s war. Marnûkh also knows that Sauron’s inability to forge that ring has something to do with the pure Elven rings crafted without his involvement.

Marnûkh has one more ace to play, too: He knows that Celebrimbor’s assistant Maitalle, the “last of the Elven-smiths,” is still alive, having stashed her in the Fortress of Gundabad, a remote prison where “no Elf would dare follow.” The Elves then debate whether they can trust their new Orc ally, particularly since they’re already in a tough spot that could turn the tide in Sauron’s favor. So they come up with a two-part plan: Elrond will go to Númenor and seek help there while Arondir and Galadriel will head north in search of Maitalle.

Over in Mordor, Sauron continues his attempt to seduce Theo by introducing him to the unseen world of the dead that can be accessed via necromancy. Only the wise can communicate with this world, and even they need some help to talk to the dead, in this case the (literal) tongue of an Orc, which Theo removes for his new friend. In return, he’s able to witness Sauron communicating with something by using the Black Speech. “Your father’s name was Fäldred, son of Hammethreg,” Sauron tells him. What’s more, Fäldred is there and ready to take questions.

Fäldred (or “Fäldred”) then reveals that he belonged to a house that served as one of the “sworn servants of Mordor” and that members of that house have “certain powers” they pass down to their descendants. This, Sauron tells him, is why he was drawn to the hilt that marked him. It’s also why Theo’s mother murdered his father. Is this true? Unable to interpret the Black Speech, Theo has only Sauron’s word to go on. He’s eager to reject it, calling Sauron “evil.” “The wise know there is no such thing. There is only power. Power to control or be controlled by another,” Sauron retorts. (For the record, that’s not a denial that he’s lying.) Perhaps Theo would feel better if he had a Ring of Power on his hand?

As Elrond makes plans to head to Númenor, we learn that Kemen is there already and wants to know when his father plans to launch his attack. But Pharazôn has another item ahead of it on his to-do list. He’d like Kemen to defeat the Faithful in the west and, in return, Pharazôn will name Kemen his heir. But Kemen won’t have to travel at all to encounter drama. Though Eärien (who did not flee) succeeds in stealing the key that will give Isildur access to the Palantir (allowing him to warn Elendil), she’s exposed as a traitor in a private meeting with Pharazôn, Kemen, and Belzagar. Pharazôn sees a future in which she spills her secrets and works as a double agent. Eärien sees no future at all and throws herself off the nearest balcony. And on that shocking note, the episode ends.

Did anyone see that coming? Eärien’s a character created for the series who’s not in the source material, but she’s been a major presence in the Númenor sections. It’s unclear what will happen next without her presence in the palace, but it does seem like the Pharazôn-versus–the Faithful drama is escalating quickly. Middle-earth is a big world, but it’s getting smaller in some respects now that Elrond is possibly on his way to Númenor. It’s unclear what will happen when (or if) he arrives, but his presence seems likely to make the series feel more tightly knit as well. The Númenor material has been compelling, but it’s also sometimes felt like it’s part of another, more Game of Thrones–y fantasy series.

It also seems like we’re pretty deep into this season’s story lines just two episodes in. Of course, The Rings of Power has always felt pretty fast-paced. The episodes aren’t short — these first two have both pushed past the 60-minute mark — but the seasons are, which means a lot of narrative has to be packed into a mere eight episodes. That might help explain why Thraîn has already been revealed as a double agent not long after being introduced. It might also explain why major characters have barely been seen when they’ve been seen at all. Will we learn what Gandalf has been doing next episode? Stay tuned.
• Unless I’m missing something, the still-to-be-seen Maitalle is also original to this series.
• “The enemy relies on force. Let us trust in fellowship.” Every once in a while, The Rings of Power strains a little too hard to create echoes of The Lord of the Rings.

• The people love Pharazôn, a demagogue on the verge of starting a war, who wants to smash his political opposition using extralegal means, has placed his questionably competent son in a position of power, and who is clearly using his political office to line his own pockets. Is this commentary?

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Premiere Recap: 5 Years Later
items.description: Welcome back to the prequel series that spans the breadth of Middle-earth and proves that whole seasons can be spun out of another book’s appendices, provided they’re the work of an author whose head contained centuries of alternate history. It’s been over two
items.author: Keith Phipps
paragraphs: Welcome back to the prequel series that spans the breadth of Middle-earth and proves that whole seasons can be spun out of another book’s appendices, provided they’re the work of an author whose head contained centuries of alternate history. It’s been over two years since the premiere of “Shadow and Flame,” the second-season finale of Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, but even more time has passed in the series’ timeline. And if you thought things might have settled down in the time between then and now, well, think again. There’s trouble everywhere, and it doesn’t look likely to go away anytime soon.
A quick refresher on what you need to remember about where the show left off:

- Durin IV (Owain Arthur) is now King Durin IV after Durin III (Peter Mullan) sacrificed himself fighting the Balrog, which had been shaken loose by the overmining spurred by Durin III using a ring of power. Durin’s not an only child. In fact, he’s not even the oldest of Durin III’s sons. That would be Thrain. Will this create a succession crisis? Maybe. But even if there isn’t, the Dwarves who paid a lot of money to Durin III on the promise of getting Rings of their own aren’t going to be happy.
- Kemen (Leon Wadham), with a smirk on his face, has claimed Pelargir as a military outpost of Númenor, inspiring resentment from those he’s subjugated, including Theo.

- Sauron (Charlie Vickers) has the nine Rings of Power forged for Man and would very much like to acquire the Dwarves’ and Elves’ Rings, too, in addition to forging the One Ring to rule them all. The first problem: The Elves have found a nice valley in which to build the sanctuary soon to be known as Rivendell. The second problem: Sauron killed Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) and destroyed the documents explaining how all this magic works. Oops.
- Also, The Stranger is The Stranger no more. He’s now known as Gandalf (Daniel Weyman). (But he doesn’t play much of a role in the season premiere.)

Now, back to the present, where, as the episode opens, Galadriel’s voice-over explains that the Elves and Sauron have been fighting for five years and that Sauron is, unfortunately, doing pretty well. But the Elves still hold Lindon and Rivendell, and that’s not nothing. The war has two wild cards in the “mighty” island kingdom of Númenor to the west and the eastern desert land of Rhûn. And as for Mordor? There’s some pretty dark stuff happening there.

Specifically, Sauron is using Orcs as guinea pigs in his attempt to create The One Ring, and so far the result has been a lot of toasted Orcs. “All creation requires sacrifice,” Sauron says, but it’s easier to say that when you’re not the one being sacrificed. Though Sauron holds out some hope that Celebrimbor’s secrets might, or an Elven-smith who worked with him might, be found, an assertive Orc named Marnûkh (Adam Young) suggests that this situation is hopeless. Nonetheless, Sauron insists that the answer can be found somewhere and that the Orc who finds them will be, in Marnûkh’s phrasing, “the Orc who won the war.” Correcting him, Sauron says he’d be the “Orc who won all wars,” which seems to inspire Marnûkh to do his best to please his master.

Post-credits, it’s time to roll the clock way back to thousands of years ago in the First Age, where a battle rages between Orcs and Elves. History, it seems, repeats itself even here. In this case, a particularly dashing, armor-clad Elf who we’ll, before long, learn is named Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) takes out a particularly ugly Orc at the tail end of a battle that will inspire a celebration later that night. For some reason or another, Celeborn decides to wander off into the woods, where he meets Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), who’s decided to spend the evening sparring on her own rather than dancing with the others.

Intrigued, Galadriel asks her new acquaintance his name, which he then says he’ll only give up if she can “touch flesh” when they spar. They fight to a virtual (but chemistry-charged) draw, after which they seem to fall instantly in love after exchanging names. (Is this unusual for Elves? Unclear.) Before long, they’re kissing, then engaged to be married. But we know this won’t exactly be a happy ending, or at least have some rough spots. In the present timeline, Celeborn is lost, and Galadriel acts as if she’s unsure if she’ll ever see him again.

Also, the present kind of sucks for Galadriel for other reasons, too. When we return to the current moment, we find her mid-battle fighting Orcs alongside Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova). Though the Orcs start to retreat, Galadriel, thanks to some help from her Ring, knows their troubles aren’t yet over and prepares her troops for a second wave of attack. When it comes, their enemies are human, and Arondir in particular seems disturbed by this, particularly after killing a boy soldier who’s a dead ringer for Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin). But the party has bigger problems than guilt when, holy crap, a Nazgûl — or, as the series seems to prefer without clarifying any difference, a “Nazgnagôl” — shows up. (Celeborn is not the only one making a premiere appearance this episode, it turns out.) Also, he really wants Galadriel’s Ring. They fight. Galadriel escapes. But the Nazgnagôl seems disturbingly unfazed by this development.

They say it’s lonely at the top, but Sauron has found some companionship in the form of Celebrimbor’s ghost, which he may or may not be hallucinating. It doesn’t really matter. Real or not, Celebrimbor is there to remind him that Sauron doesn’t know his secrets and that, unlike the Rings made for Men and Dwarves, he’ll never gain control of the Elven Rings because he didn’t help make them. Celebrimbor is also there to psychoanalyze Sauron a bit, telling him that the “machinery of your soul is missing a piece, the one that allows for true bond, a true union with another person, so instead of connection, you seek control.” This probing of what makes Sauron tick seems like an odd, not particularly Tolkien-esque choice, but it might also be the inevitable result of the series’ decision to depict Sauron as a human being with all the doubts and neuroses that come with that rather than a cold, distant, unknowable embodiment of evil.

Sauron does get some good news to offset all this taunting, however. Five of the Dark Wizard’s Gaudrim warriors show up to say that their master has accepted an alliance between Mordor and Rhûn. But Sauron has another idea in mind: What if they turned on the Dark Wizard, an outsider who’s taken over their homeland (and not been very nice about it)? And what if he helped them by giving them a Ring of Power. But just one. After killing two of them, he lets the survivors fight for the privilege of becoming the next Nazgnagôl. They do, of course, and later we witness how Sauron makes a man into a Nazgnagôl. (It’s painful.) In the end, the victor emerges with a new title to match his now immortal (?) body: Khamûl, the Fairest of the Nine (Zubin Varla).

At least things are peaceful back in Rivendell, where the Elves regroup after the Orc battle. Upon their arrival, Elrond (Robert Aramayo) immediately begins to tend to the wounded as Galadriel looks on wistfully at all the happy reunions, undoubtedly reminders that she has no one with whom to reunite. Well, there’s Elrond, but he’s more of a business partner. Together, they try to make plans for next steps. Elrond prefers to stay safe in Rivendell. Galadriel wants to seek out allies. Maybe Númenor? The meeting ends with no decision made, but Galadriel’s sense that Sauron is somehow watching her — a feeling reinforced by a nightmare — suggests that she won’t be content in staying put. Disturbed, she heads out into the night where she meets Arondir and they exchange the “secret pains” keeping them up at night. She advises Arondir to go to Pelargir and try to make things better (or at the very least, ease his conscience). As for her secret pain, it’s “loneliness,” which makes sense for someone whose husband has disappeared, who knows where, for who knows how long.

Our first glimpse of Pelargrir suggests that Arondir is much needed there, and that even he might not be enough. Kemen has forced the locals, including Theo, to chop down the surrounding forest in the service of building an armada. He’s dismissive of the “vile land” he’s overseeing and of Mordor’s offer of an alliance, which he tosses away like garbage. This will likely turn out to be a big mistake. Theo picks it up shortly before being whipped for his insolence. The consequences of this coincidence will arrive at the end of the episode when Theo and others show up in Mordor only to discover that Sauron (a) has a Ring to share but (b) is only interested in bestowing it upon one of them. We don’t see the outcome of this fight, but it sure looks like Theo wants it more than the others.

What, you might be wondering at this point, is going on at Khazad-dûm and with Gandalf? The answers to the first question dominate the rest of the episode, while the second question is mostly punted to an upcoming installment. Though the Dwarves are officially neutral in the war between Elves and Sauron, Durin has been supplying the Elves with weapons, in no small part due to his friendship with Elrond. They haven’t seen each other in a while, however. When Durin mentions that his two children are now teenagers, Elrond seems shocked, leading to a discussion of how differently they perceive time and a promise from Elrond to be more attentive (despite fighting a war).

But the meat of their conversation concerns Durin and the imminent arrival of his brother Thraîn. After they part, Durin enters a chaotic scene tied to that arrival. Gamli (Lee Braithwaite) attempts to perfect his ram’s horn-blowing skills to the annoyance of everyone, especially his sister, Gerda (Amber Mendez-Martin). Despite the yelling, it’s a cozy domestic scene. No matter what’s about to happen, at least Durin has Disa (Sophia Nomvete) and his kids, though he’d like to have good relations with Thráin, the only other surviving member of his family.

At the welcoming ceremony, Gamli nails the horn part as Disa and Durin greet their distinguished visitors, including a female Dwarf with a “marvelous beard” (which is apparently something of a rarity, despite the lore established by Tolkien). It all goes well until it becomes clear that Thráin is not going to show. Or, more specifically, he plans to arrive on his own schedule because he’s too busy partying with some old friends in one of Khazad-dûm’s subterranean inns. When asked, Thráin (Eddie Marsan) suggests that Durin join him and his friends. Immediately sensing this is a power play, Disa orders all inns be shut down but enough ale be brought to the Great Hall to turn it into party central.

Any fear that Thráin won’t acknowledge Durin as the king vanishes when Thráin kneels before his brother, but it doesn’t take long for the squabbling to begin. The other Dwarven leaders want the Rings promised to them by Durin III. That’s a non-starter. Disa tells them they’ll be compensated, but the Rings, already hidden, will soon be destroyed. This, predictably, does not go over well. Less predictably, Thráin takes Durin’s side on this issue. But Thráin’s support isn’t unconditional. He wants to know the details of his father’s death, rightly sensing it was no simple “mining accident.” Whatever their issues, there seems to be genuine warmth between the brothers as Durin discusses their father’s death and the feelings it inspired.

But, uh-oh, it’s a little more complicated. Alone with Disa, Thráin refers to her as an “old flame.” Disa pushes back at this description, but there’s clearly something from their shared past she’d prefer to stay buried, and Gamli’s unexpected arrival startles her. (He’s clearly confused by what he sees, too.) If that weren’t bad enough, Thráin catches Durin supplying the Elves with weapons. Durin immediately jumps to the worst conclusion, that Thráin is after his throne, and they fight — a fight interrupted by an unexpected visitor: Marnûkh, who tells them he “has knowledge that could save Middle-earth.” What does that mean? And whose side is he really on? Those are big TBDs that look like they’ll play a major role in this season.

Before the episode ends, he also gets a glimpse at another field of play. After witnessing Marnûkh’s actions via a Ring of Power, Círdan (Ben Daniels) makes a reference to Gandalf playing a role in protecting Rhûn. And with that, we’re at the end of an episode that serves as a promising beginning to what should be an action-packed season. In some ways, it feels like this is the season for which the first two seasons have been setting the stage, one with clear battle lines drawn in a struggle for the Rings of Power, the objects that give the series its title. We get a chance to see what old, familiar characters have been up to while meeting some new ones in the process.

The question hanging over it, however, is whether these clear lines will make The Rings of Power more or less compelling. Will Sauron be as dynamic ruling from Mordor rather than walking among the other characters? (Assuming that’s what will happen.) If the struggle for Theo’s soul is done — a big if — will that character now just be firmly in the “evil” column? We’ll find out over the course of the next seven episodes.

What remains clear is that the series’ visuals continue to benefit from a no-expenses-spared approach and the creative team — this episode was written by showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay and directed by series regular Charlotte Brändström — appears to be as confident in their vision as ever, even if the first two seasons have failed to make Rings of Power the biggest show in the world, as seems to have been Amazon’s hope. Instead, it remains an intriguing expansion of Tolkien’s world filled with remarkable visuals, some standout performances, and a sense that it could really catch fire at some point. Maybe this is the season. Without a Ring of Power capable of looking into the future, we’ll have to wait to find out.

• One of the most striking elements of the flashback scene is how much younger Galadriel seems. That has everything to do with Morfydd Clark’s performance. She looks the same, but Clark plays her as someone who’s yet to have the weight of many years on her shoulders.
• Jamie Campbell-Bower should make an excellent addition to the cast, but he was so creepy on Stranger Things that it might take an episode or two for Celeborn to seem trustworthy.
• A lingering question: Middle-earth is vast. How are characters crisscrossing it so quickly?

• Presumably still to come: What’s up with Gandalf? (Whom we only see briefly.) What’s going on in Númenor? (Presumably nothing good since Kemen is still calling the shots in Pelargir.) What about Poppy and Nori and the other halflings? Well, that answer might be a long time coming, if we get one at all.

items.title: Skydance Succession: As David Ellison Sets His Team, Heads Are Rolling as Hollywood Finds Out Who’s Really in Charge
items.description: Of all the things keeping David Ellison up at night, the countdown to 2028 may be the most pressing. At least that’s what many media observers and Hollywood insiders believe. Ellison’s anxiety, they say, isn’t fueled by the forthcoming presidential election or
items.author: Matt Donnelly
paragraphs: Of all the things keeping David Ellison up at night, the countdown to 2028 may be the most pressing. At least that’s what many media observers and Hollywood insiders believe. Ellison’s anxiety, they say, isn’t fueled by the forthcoming presidential election or the Olympic Games that will descend on Los Angeles, where Ellison now owns two iconic studio lots. Instead, his agita is arising from the 8 movies he still needs to acquire or produce in 2028 to reach the magic number of 30 — that’s the benchmark Skydance pledged to meet annually in order to close the $111 billion acquisition that made his company a content behemoth.

Between Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures, 22 films have been dated for 2028 so far. A large number of those — like “Gremlins 3,” Baz Luhrmann’s rumored Joan of Arc biopic and an untitled movie from the Duffer brothers — have yet to start production. And, of course, Hollywood is keeping a close watch on how the new regime handles the urgent task of closing deals with Margot Robbie and Greta Gerwig for a “Barbie” follow-up.

Despite Skydance’s other pledge — to streamline costs via cutting-edge technology — feature films remain one of the most expensive gambles in the business (and that’s if audiences respond). The challenge before Ellison and his team is to churn out hits fast — not just to prove their hotly debated merger will be viable in the long run but to generate the cash needed to pay down the combined company’s staggering $80 billion debt.

Five weeks in, if Team Ellison is losing sleep about the operational challenges ahead, it’s not letting that on to the media. “People are viewing our $30 billion-plus content spend as an expense, but content is our asset,” Skydance chief financial officer Dennis Cinelli told Variety, speaking ahead of the company’s third-quarter earnings report. “Whether it’s for our theatrical or TV business, both of our streaming platforms, third-party sales, the networks portfolio — we’re investing in content because it has proved tremendously valuable. We’re confident we can drive growth and increase profitability and cash flow.”

On Nov. 9, as Skydance unveiled its first quarterly earnings report as a combined company, leadership said a big push will come in early 2027 to offer consumers a bundle of the streaming services now under the Skydance roof: HBO Max and Paramount+. The price will come at a competitive discount designed to allow Skydance to gain market share among subscribers, one source says. Skydance plans to offer a fully integrated service that puts both brands on a single platform — which will make it easier for the company to keep viewers moving around its streaming universe — by 2029. There is much speculation that the company will eventually retire the Paramount+ moniker, given that HBO is the more powerful consumer brand.

Meanwhile, Skydance is touting the power of its portfolio: A combined 205-million streaming subscribers in more than 100 global territories, a library of roughly 15,000 films and more than 100,000 hours of TV series. Hollywood’s new colossus has a content library larger than its studio rivals’ by a significant factor, even if its stewards change, as James Gunn and Peter Safran found out the hard way this week. (The DC Studios chiefs made it just five weeks into the Skydance regime before Ellison announced on earnings day that he would replace the pair with producer Jeremy Latcham, an early architect of Marvel Studios.) Superman, Batman and many other characters in the Skydance vault represent a treasure trove of the kind of IP that can yield new adaptations and spinoffs for decades. The chance to buy Warner Bros.’ vault was so attractive that last year even Netflix, the leader in global streaming, was driven to give up its build-not-buy philosophy regarding big acquisitions to chase Warner Bros. and HBO — until Ellison stuck his foot in the door and refused to leave without a deal.

Streaming is the engine of the future for Skydance. But in the short term, the company’s fate will be determined by that of its linear cable channels. With the merger, Skydance hasn’t just doubled down on this sector — it has tripled down; Skydance has by far the industry’s collection of linear cable channels. Its TV portfolio is anchored by CBS and spans some 55 cable networks, including CNN, TNT, TBS, Cartoon Network, TCM, Nickelodeon, Comedy Central, BET, Discovery, TLC, Food Network and HGTV.

But the traditional business of cable television is deteriorating; subscribers are slowly but surely giving up on linear cable services in favor of streaming platforms. The erosion of once-reliable cable TV profits has bedeviled Hollywood’s majors for more than a decade and has been a catalyst for the latest round of merger mania.

As was the case for Paramount and WBD when they were separate companies, the enlarged Skydance remains heavily dependent on linear TV for cash flow and profits — and the cable and satellite biz remains a steadily melting iceberg. In the second quarter of this year, for example, Paramount’s TV business revenue slid 9% to $3.1 billion, but the segment still delivered all of the company’s adjusted $1.1 billion earnings for the quarter.

Skydance’s ability to meet its post-merger financial targets hinges on whether the TV business crumbles faster than Ellison and his financial engineers have projected, and whether streaming sees commensurate growth to make up for it. That’s a lot to leave to fate.

Here’s the quandary: Skydance must slash costs while investing in content and paying down its immense $80 billion in net debt. The numbers may not add up. “[W]e are concerned more aggressive cost-cutting measures in TV media could leave the segment vulnerable to a faster-than-expected rate of revenue declines,” MoffettNathanson analyst Robert Fishman wrote in an Oct. 23 research note.

Industry veterans have watched the creation of Skydance with wonderment. More so than Disney’s acquisition of 21st Century Fox, the union of Paramount and Warner Bros. feels like a milestone transition for the motion picture business that emerged in the 1910s and ’20s around silent films. Both iconic studios were foundational brand names for entertainment back then, and there is great hope among the many industry insiders who have worked across both that those proud logos and studio lots will endure for another century.

After finally closing the WBD acquisition, Skydance leadership opened themselves up to a media firing squad on the Paramount lot in early October. Ellison and team addressed burning questions about real estate, cash flow, layoffs and more. Yet inside the company, rank-and-file employees across both operations feel left in the dark. Conversations with staffers in many corners of the Skydance business yielded a feeling of “radio silence,” as one person put it, from the top as pink slips loom and anxiety around greenlights and general spending persists. On balance, another source inside the company deadpanned: “It’s been about a month” since the two entertainment giants combined (Skydance had no comment on the matter).

Who can blame them, as the town places bets on whether Ellison will have the cash to pay back his lenders. Skydance’s interest expenses are expected to be more than $6 billion next year. According to financial projections, the company intends to reduce that debt load from a figure that is seven times larger than its adjusted annual earnings to a number that is three times larger than adjusted net earnings, which is a more typical debt ratio for large companies.

If that model doesn’t hold, Ellison will need to find additional sources of capital. Will his father, billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, whose Ellison Family trust committed $14 billion in equity financing for the WBD takeover, be willing to pump even more money into his son’s gambit to create one of Hollywood’s biggest conglomerates? That remains to be seen. There have also been rumors that David is hunting for more big-money backers to keep Skydance afloat — including Elon Musk. Cinelli told Variety that Skydance is not seeking any additional capital at this time. (Skydance and Musk declined to comment on the tech mogul’s possible involvement.)

Skydance’s pledged $30 billion annual spend on new content towers over those of rivals Netflix ($20 billion annually) and Disney ($24 billion in 2026), but investment and prayer alone will not make a meaningful dent in the company’s tremendous liabilities. To that end, bloodletting will come in the form of layoffs (expected by the end of the year and extending into the first quarter of 2027) and ruthless efficiency targets.

Insiders at Skydance say cost savings from the company’s acquisition of Paramount Global will blow past an anticipated $2 billion in cuts and approach $3 billion. That’s after only a year in control of the former Shari Redstone empire. Fat-trimming opportunities from the inherited Warner Bros. Discovery books also abound, three sources say. A recent team meeting on the Warner Bros. lot revealed that Skydance will be looking closely at its financial commitments to sporting events like the Olympics.

Unexpected (and eyebrow-raising) expenses have been discovered, like trifling luxury costs that amount to “tens of millions” of dollars, per two sources, on hospitality splurges like dining, travel and gifts. The former WBD regime spent in ways big and small — like stacks of receipts for sandwiches and green juices from the gourmet grocery store Erewhon. There will also be “millions” saved by combining or reducing spends on outside vendors, studio services, redundant marketing budgets and more (one source even suggests press junkets will be revamped. Sorry, journalists: No more sushi at the Four Seasons.

And Ellison’s executive table prides itself on its strong, effective characters. Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, a respected operator and the former CEO of Mattel, has claimed daily operations as his purview. President Andy Gordon and CFO Cinelli will mind people and the purse, respectively. HBO golden child Casey Bloys sits atop the entire streaming operation with JB Perrette. Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein are now at the molten core of the movie business, controlling both Paramount, WB and DC Studios. Former CBS chief George Cheeks now runs all of linear TV, cable nets, news, sports and three production studios. And what about David?

“There’s a lot of talk about David Ellison. Not since Walt Disney have you had an owner-operator running a major Hollywood company,” says Cinelli. “David is uniquely well-positioned to lead. He’s someone who loves the creative aspect of the business, and wants to spend his time making films and shows with passion. But he also grew up in Silicon Valley. His mentors and most valuable lessons come from that place, and that’s exactly what Skydance needs to succeed in the future.”
As any Hollywood executive knows, all the strength in the world cannot account for the exercise in pain that is managing creative budgets. Take the juicy fallout around “Barbie 2” as a case study.

As Ellison toiled for almost a year to win WBD, that company was stuck in tense negotiations for a sequel to Warner Bros.’ highest-grossing movie ever: “Barbie.” Director Gerwig and co-screenwriter Noah Baumbach dangled a concept for a sequel in front of now-axed WB film chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy. They would not, however, allow a new movie into development until new deals were struck for themselves, producer-star Robbie and her A-list Ken doll Ryan Gosling that reflected the runaway success of the first film. So the negotiations, led by the creative team’s all-powerful CAA agent Bryan Lourd, broke down.

The creatives were demanding equal pay, which one person familiar with the deal pegs at around $25 million each for Gerwig, Robbie and Gosling (Baumbach would share in the writing fee with Gerwig, and he conveniently received a new overall deal at Warners while the “Barbie” negotiations were churning). Team “Barbie” also requested increased pieces of the back end, at which point then-WBD CEO David Zaslav balked — shutting down the talks as the studio’s licensing rights to the famous toy faced a year-end deadline for renewal.

Ellison, Keisz and Lourd are keen to make the “Barbie 2” deal happen by the end of the year, two sources say, and Kreiz is obviously close to the property as Mattel’s former chief executive. But for a company with an $80 billion debt tab, how does a decreased profit margin make sense?

In the view of former Warner Bros. CEO Barry Meyer, the key thing that the new owners need to remember is to invest in creativity. At the end of the day, it’s all about the movies and shows. “Creating value with the content is very, very important. Distribution is usually a lot more commoditized than content,” says Meyer, who spent 41 years at Warner Bros., capped by a 14-year run as CEO. “Content is creative. Content is unique. Streaming is how you get it there, but the content is where the value is.”
Todd Spangler and Jennifer Maas contributed to this report.

items.title: ‘Adults’ Renewed for Season 3 at FX
items.description: “Adults” has been renewed for Season 3 at FX and Hulu, Variety has learned.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: “Adults” has been renewed for Season 3 at FX and Hulu, Variety has learned.

The third season of the ensemble comedy will consist of 16 episodes, which is double the eight episodes the show aired for both its first and second seasons. In addition, creators Ben Kronengold and Rebecca Shaw have also set a new overall deal with FX Productions.

“We started working with FX over six years ago, back when Paul Baker was but a twinkle in all of our eyes,” said Kronengold and Shaw. “In the years since, John [Landgraf] and the rest of the team have taught us everything we know about how to lead, produce, and tell stories that make people feel like part of a community. They’ve become family, and we’re so glad to make it official — and to start yelling at them like we do our parents.”

“Adults” stars Malik Elassal, Lucy Freyer, Jack Innanen, Amita Rao, and Owen Thiele. Per the official logline, the show is “about a group of twenty-somethings in New York leaning on each other to navigate love, work, friendship and family. Samir (Elassal), Billie (Freyer), Paul Baker (Innanen), Issa (Rao) and Anton (Thiele) are five friends crashing together in Samir’s childhood home.”

Kronengold and Shaw are executive producers and showrunners on the series in addition to creating it. Nick Kroll, Sarah Naftalis, Jonathan Krisel, Alicia Van Couvering, and Rob Rosell also executive produce. FX Productions is the studio.

“Ben and Rebecca have elevated ‘Adults’ in every way, earning critical praise and a legion of devoted fans who have embraced the friend group as their own,” said Nick Grad, president of FX Entertainment. “’Adults’ showed significant growth in its sophomore year and we’ve seen the show inspire everything from memes to Halloween costumes, so the decision was easy – more episodes and a new deal at FX for Ben and Rebecca!”

Per FX, Season 2 was up 60% in viewership over Season 1 on Hulu and Disney+ globally through its first five weeks, while international viewership was up 100%. FX did not provide specific viewership numbers, however.

“Adults” has been well-received by critics and audiences since its original launch in 2025, with FX also releasing the standalone special “Marathon Day” in July 2026 ahead of the debut of Season 2. The show currently has an 88% critical approval rating across both seasons on Rotten Tomatoes. In her review of Season 2 for Variety, Alison Herman wrote, “‘Adults’ finally has its own momentum, largely generated by a cast whose rapport obviates the need for any sweeping statements about their generation.”

items.title: Kate Berlant and John Early to Host Film Independent Spirit Awards
items.description: Kate Berlant and John Early, two of comedy’s most gloriously unpredictable performers, will co-host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards.
items.author: Clayton Davis
paragraphs: Kate Berlant and John Early, two of comedy’s most gloriously unpredictable performers, will co-host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards.

The 42nd annual celebration of the best in independent film and television takes place Saturday, March 6, 2027, at the Hollywood Palladium, eight days before the 99th Academy Awards on March 14. The date marks a later slot on the calendar and a return to Saturday after this past year’s Sunday, Feb. 15 ceremony, which was hosted by “Saturday Night Live” alum Ego Nwodim.

“If there’s one thing we don’t need, it’s another predictable awards show,” says Film Independent President Juan Devis. “Kate and John are two of the funniest, strangest and most brilliantly unpredictable performers working today. They embody everything we love about independent storytelling: originality, fearlessness and a healthy disregard for convention. We’re excited to shake things up, break a few rules and have some fun along the way.”
The hosts are ready for the assignment.
“We’ve always been obsessed with awards shows, and we’re so honored we get to host the coolest one. Tune in to see if we choke under pressure!” Berlant and Early say in a joint statement.

Berlant and Early join a roster of past Spirit Awards hosts that includes Nwodim, Aidy Bryant, Hasan Minhaj, Megan Mullally and Nick Offerman, Aubrey Plaza, Nick Kroll and John Mulaney, Kate McKinnon and Kumail Nanjiani, Fred Armisen and Kristen Bell, Andy Samberg and John Waters.

Friends and creative collaborators for more than a decade, Berlant and Early have built a devoted following on a distinctive brand of absurdist comedy that blends sharp social satire, improvisation and performances that rarely go where you expect. Their joint work includes the acclaimed sketch series “555” and the Emmy-nominated Peacock comedy special “Would It Kill You to Laugh?,” which took familiar comedic conventions and twisted them into something entirely their own.

Individually, both have carved out celebrated careers across film, television and live comedy. Berlant’s film credits include “Sorry to Bother You,” “Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood” and “Don’t Worry Darling,” and she has appeared in FX’s comedy-drama series “The Bear.” She also earned acclaim for her one-woman show “Kate” and her comedy specials “Cinnamon in the Wind” and “Parmesan.”

Early is best known for his breakout performance in the dark comedy series “Search Party,” which ran on TBS before moving to HBO Max, as well as his stand-up special “Now More Than Ever.” He recently made his feature directorial debut with “Maddie’s Secret,” which also features Berlant.
This year’s ceremony adds two new categories, best international first feature and the Digital Creator Award, expanding the show’s reach across platforms.

Filmmaker Roman Coppola will also bring his artistic vision to the show in the newly created role of creative consultant.The Nominee Brunch, the annual gathering that honors all nominees and features the presentation of the Emerging Filmmaker Awards, returns to The London West Hollywood on Saturday, Jan. 9, 2027.
Nominations for the 42nd Spirit Awards will be announced Dec. 2.

items.title: Druski Brings ‘SNL’ 5.6 Million Viewers, Its Biggest Audience in Two Years
items.description: The Nov. 7 episode of “Saturday Night Live,” hosted by internet comedian Druski with the Strokes as musical guest, brought a strong 5.6 million viewers to NBC.
items.author: Selome Hailu
paragraphs: The Nov. 7 episode of “Saturday Night Live,” hosted by internet comedian Druski with the Strokes as musical guest, brought a strong 5.6 million viewers to NBC.

Not only does that total outpace the 5.2 million viewers achieved by the Halloween episode headlined by Inde Navarrette and Gracie Abrams, which set the previous Season 52 record, but it marks the most viewers “SNL” has seen in two years.

The most recent episode to outrank Druski’s was during the landmark 50th season, when John Mulaney and Chappell Roan boosted the show to 6.6 million viewers on Nov. 2, 2024. Druski’s episode also scored the highest rating among the adults age 18-49 demographic since Mulaney’s in 2024. And among viewers age 18-34 in particular, last week’s show achieved the best rating in more than four years, since Elon Musk hosted on May 8, 2021, with Miley Cyrus as musical guest. On Peacock, Druski hosted the most-watched episode ever, and it garnered 424 million video views across YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and X, the best social performance since Ariana Grande hosted with Cher as musical guest ahead of Christmas 2025.

Given that Mulaney is returning to “SNL” this Saturday, joined by musical guest Phoebe Bridgers, it seems possible that the late-night sketch show will outdo itself for the third week in a row. It’s clear that the recent prioritization of the Gen Z audience by the “SNL” talent team — evidenced by the booking of Navarrette, Druski and Mulaney, who all draw in younger viewers — is paying off.

items.title: FKA Twigs Becomes Josephine Baker: Inside the Lavish, Globe-Spanning Biopic from Maimouna Doucouré and Studiocanal (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: On a crisp October afternoon in the Bois de Vincennes, on the outskirts of Paris, FKA twigs is transported back to 1950s America. Wearing a cream-colored pinstriped coat, a dark beret and black leather gloves, the British singer and dancer has been up since th
items.author: Elsa Keslassy
paragraphs: On a crisp October afternoon in the Bois de Vincennes, on the outskirts of Paris, FKA twigs is transported back to 1950s America. Wearing a cream-colored pinstriped coat, a dark beret and black leather gloves, the British singer and dancer has been up since the early hours, with a 4 a.m. pickup for hair and makeup to transform into Josephine Baker, the legendary entertainer and civil rights activist.

Standing opposite her is Oscar-nominated actor Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor, who plays Baker’s mother. The two are filming a tense confrontation at a cemetery, a scene that cuts to the heart of Maïmouna Doucouré’s ambitious biopic.
Between takes, FKA twigs stays in character, looking pensive and emotional. The atmosphere on set is studious and distinctly international, with cast and crew switching between English and French.

And while the cemetery scene unfolding that afternoon is intimate, other sequences have the scale and flamboyance of a classic Hollywood production, notably those recreating the legendary Folies Bergère cabaret in Paris, where Baker became a sensation in the 1920s. The sprawling production has enlisted some 2,400 extras.

Yet behind the lavish costumes, musical performances and sweeping historical canvas, “Josephine Baker” is ultimately a portrait of a woman whose extraordinary public life was shaped by private wounds.

“What’s most important to me is not simply portraying Josephine as this powerful woman, this icon who was inducted into the Panthéon. We already know that side of her. I want to tell the story of the woman behind the icon,” says Doucouré, the Sundance-winning filmmaker behind “Cuties” and “Hawa,” speaking during lunch with the crew.

“I want to explore her wounds, her vulnerability, her flaws, the things that shaped her and the extraordinary resilience she developed,” she says. “I think her strength becomes even more extraordinary when you understand where it comes from.”

Rather than delivering a conventional biopic, Doucouré has built the narrative around Baker’s return to the United States in 1951, when the celebrated performer, who had found fame and freedom in France, confronted the racial segregation she had fled decades earlier. The film moves between that pivotal period and flashbacks to Baker’s childhood in St. Louis, her meteoric rise in 1920s Paris, her work with the French Resistance during World War II and her later years.

The prestige project marks a considerable leap in scale for Doucouré and ranks among the most ambitious French-produced biopics in years. Studiocanal is co-producing with Bien ou Bien Productions, Doucouré and her partner Zangro’s banner, as well as financing and handling international sales.

Finding the actress who could convey both Baker’s strength and vulnerability proved particularly challenging, even though FKA twigs was among the first performers Doucouré saw during the London leg of her casting search.

Doucouré traveled from London to New York and Los Angeles, auditioning major stars and emerging performers alike. She insisted on seeing candidates perform, regardless of their fame. Each audition included singing, dancing and a demanding dramatic scene.

“I met some incredibly talented actresses, but I couldn’t cast someone just because she was famous or even because I admired her work. I needed to see something very specific, to see Josephine come alive in front of me.”
It happened when FKA twigs showed up. “You could tell she was nervous. You could feel how much it meant to her,” Doucouré recalls.
“I literally started crying because suddenly I was seeing Josephine Baker. I completely forgot that I had written the scene. I forgot that I was sitting in an audition room.”
Although she continued auditioning actresses, Doucouré couldn’t shake the impression FKA twigs had made. “I kept thinking, ‘I found her.’”

The British artist, whose screen credits include “Honey Boy,” “The Crow” and A24’s “Mother Mary,” had never carried a feature of this magnitude. The role demands acting, singing and dancing, with FKA twigs portraying Baker across several decades, performing her songs and speaking French, which she didn’t previously know.

“She also had to learn to speak French in a very short amount of time and master different American accents, even though she’s British,” Doucouré says. “You can’t simply switch from one accent to another. You have to show that evolution naturally.”
Capturing Baker’s distinctive stage presence without merely imitating her was another challenge.

“FKA twigs is an extraordinary performer, but she has her own way of moving, her own musical identity. And Josephine had such a unique physical language. The challenge wasn’t just to reproduce her movements or her voice. It was to understand what made her performances so singular and then make them feel alive rather than imitated,” says Doucouré.
Doucouré was determined to showcase FKA twigs’ talents without turning the film into a conventional musical.
“I didn’t want to make a film about Josephine Baker without showing her dancing and singing. Come on, it’s Josephine Baker! And I have FKA twigs. Of course, I’m going to make her dance and sing!”

Bringing Baker’s life to the big screen was a formidable undertaking long before FKA twigs came aboard. Zangro says at least 16 production companies had previously attempted it, while Baker herself (who died in 1975) had tried to develop a film about her life as far back as 1968.

“The project had been circulating at Canal+ for more than 10 years,” Zangro says. “At the beginning, Maïmouna and I thought we might be a little smarter than everybody else, but we very quickly realized what we’d gotten ourselves into. It was Everest.”
The film spent four years in development, with repeated rewrites, production delays and mounting financial challenges. Baker’s extraordinary life made it difficult to determine what to include.
“At first, I wanted to tell absolutely everything,” Doucouré says. “This woman lived 400 years!”

“She was a pilot. She survived plane crashes. She served during World War II. She was a secret agent. She fought for civil rights. She knew Martin Luther King. She tried to save her château,” says Zangro. “When you read Josephine Baker’s biography, you almost feel like you haven’t lived your own life.”
The breakthrough came when the filmmakers decided to anchor the narrative in one pivotal chapter rather than attempt to chronicle everything.

Doucouré, who co-wrote the screenplay with Olivier Lorelle (“Days of Glory”), spent years researching Baker and working closely with her family. The project has the blessing of her sons Jean-Claude Bouillon Baker and Brian Bouillon Baker, as well as the Rainbow Tribe of children she adopted.
“There are books, of course, but sometimes those books contradict one another. Who better to tell me about Josephine Baker than her own children?” Doucouré says.
Although much of “Josephine Baker” takes place in America, the production is shooting entirely in Europe, with filming in France and Sofia, Bulgaria wrapping this week.
The cast also includes Giuseppe Maggio, Grégory Montel, Benjamin Millepied, Féodor Atkine, Alex Lutz and Harmony Raine Riley.

The movie is aiming for a broad international rollout. Studiocanal will distribute across its own territories, including France, the U.K., Germany, Italy, Benelux, Poland, Australia and New Zealand, and is handling worldwide sales.
“It’s not a French film made for the international market. It’s an international film in every respect, from the cast to the locations and languages,” Zangro says.
Bringing that world to life, however, has required some creative solutions, not least because the film couldn’t afford to shoot in the United States.

“The United States has become too expensive for filming,” Zangro says. “So we’re doing what the Americans themselves are doing. We’re going to Sofia, Bulgaria, where there are backlots where we can recreate Harlem and Broadway.”

The filmmakers have also transformed a parking lot in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis into a street in 1918 St. Louis, complete with brick and stone buildings. Production designer Stéphane Rosenbaum, whose credits include “Moulin,” has had to conjure up everything from roaring twenties Paris to 1950s Miami, where a hotel suite was recreated with LED screens providing the exterior views.
“I looked at a lot of photographs for inspiration,” Rosenbaum says. “But we’re not making a documentary, so we also had to invent a visual universe.”
Costume designer Emmanuelle Youchnovski, whose credits include “The Substance” and “Dalida,” has been equally uncompromising.
“We decided to make absolutely everything rather than rent costumes,” she says. “We made the hats, the shoes, even the buttons.”

The production tapped artisans who work with Chanel for buttons and ornaments, commissioned embroidery from workshops in India and enlisted Faubourg 22-11, an atelier associated with Schiaparelli that worked on the famous yellow coat in “The Substance.”
Among the biggest challenges was Baker’s iconic banana skirt, which Youchnovski had to adapt to FKA twigs’ athletic dancer’s physique.
“The banana skirt was a real challenge,” she says. “We made a banana skirt. We didn’t reinvent the wheel. But we approached it a little differently.”
For Doucouré, the costume is also a reminder of Baker’s complicated relationship with the racial stereotypes of her time.

“Of course, you can’t separate the banana skirt from the colonial stereotypes of that time. But what fascinates me is what Josephine did within those constraints. She found ways to play with those stereotypes and sometimes even turn them to her advantage. That’s where I find her so fascinating.”
Baker was also a trendsetter who challenged prevailing beauty standards.
“We’re talking about the colonial era, and white women were trying to look like Josephine Baker,” Doucouré says.

Youchnovski has traced Baker’s evolution from a mischievous young performer to an international star and, later, a more modest figure, using tailored jackets and exaggerated accessories to reflect her willingness to play with masculine and feminine codes.
“The actress absorbs the character and magnifies her. And that’s exactly what FKA twigs is doing. It’s extraordinary,” Youchnovski says.

For Doucouré, Baker’s legacy extends far beyond entertainment. The woman who challenged segregation, fought fascism and built a multiracial family remains a powerful figure amid renewed political and racial divisions.
Doucouré says she has debated whether Baker should be considered a feminist with one of her sons.
“He always tells me, ‘Stop saying my mother was a feminist. Feminism didn’t exist. My mother was a humanist.’”

“And I tell him, ‘Yes, but even if she didn’t necessarily define herself through the labels we use today, your mother challenged so many of the limits imposed on women at the time. To me, that’s deeply feminist.’”
The filmmaker sees a direct connection between Baker’s struggles and the present.

“You look back at history and think, ‘How could people have allowed these things to happen?’ And then you realize that future generations may look back at our own time and ask exactly the same question.”
As filming draws to a close, Doucouré says she likes to imagine Baker herself watching over the production.
“I grew up with the belief that the spirits of our ancestors watch over us. Whether that’s true or not, I don’t know. But I like to believe that Josephine’s spirit is with us.”
