items.title: The 11 Biggest Accessories Trends From the Spring 2027 Runways
items.description: The September (and October) shows were all about embellishment, which was especially true when it came to accessories. While bags and shoes typically capture the public’s imagination—and for good reason, this is luxury fashion we’re talking about—this season l
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: The September (and October) shows were all about embellishment, which was especially true when it came to accessories. While bags and shoes typically capture the public’s imagination—and for good reason, this is luxury fashion we’re talking about—this season lent a spotlight to major jewelry pieces worn in unexpected ways, like on shoes. Scarves were everywhere, as well as big-time belts worn two, three, or four at a time. Maximalism is back in style, with the quiet luxury mentality from just a couple years ago now on ice. Below, here are 10 accessories trends we saw on the spring 2027 runways that will be everywhere by the time the flowers start blooming again.

Chanel creative director Matthieu Blazy sent 83 looks down the runway at the Grand Palais, each with its own unique pair of shoes. The move was a pretty good indication of just how much attention designers paid to footwear for spring. Some of the biggest trends we saw were on shoes—from Burberry’s playful, face-covered paillette pumps to Valentino’s scenic sequin boots. Loewe’s beaded mules were made for folks looking to become great shoe collectors themselves.

Fashion magazines just can’t quit a “What’s in My Bag?” video series (yes, we are guilty of it). But designers this season weren’t asking that question so much as inquiring: What’s on your bag? The spring 2027 answer was everything—sequins, beads, pony hair, tweed, snakeskin, and more. The bag charm trend of the past couple seasons is still going strong as well.

Designers want you to put your money your feet are. From Saint Laurent’s charming sandals to Chanel’s pearly pumps, heels and flats this season were embellished with literal pieces of jewelry, like Loewe’s sandals decorated by a charm bracelet.
Designers also decorated their footwear with dainty ribbons (Prada), shoelaces (Miu Miu), and giant, sculptural bows (Loewe). At Moschino, each toe got its own individual loop.

Our third and final shoe trend shows more foot than ever. Michael Kors’s slides had barely visible, plastic straps; Bottega Veneta made delicate string sandals, and Area’s lace kitten heels were especially scantily clad.
Apparently, bags could also use a little fresh air. From Hermès to Prada and Chanel, designers put holes in their handbags. Wait, is this a recession indicator?

Scarves took center stage this season—and they took on new forms, with Dior’s flower-petal boas fluttering down the runway, while Saint Laurent’s scarves trailed dramatically behind the models. At Simone Rocha, a peach statement scarf was worn as a stole over one shoulder for added drama.

While we’re piling gems and chains onto our bags and shoes, we might as well pile on some actual jewelry, too. Shoulder-dusting earrings at Bottega Veneta and layers of pearls and beaded necklaces at Valentino proved it’s high time you invest in a bigger box for your baubles.

Mrs. Prada and Raf Simons may have ushered in the futuristic sunglass trend with their bug-eyed peepers from spring 2025, but the look has since taken on all kinds of new life—including at the house of Prada itself. The label debuted these mismatched sunglasses at their men’s show this summer, while Gucci and Miu Miu replicated the look of a fruit fly with their styles.

Belts for spring 2027 came in all shapes, sizes, and widths—and in multiples, too. Ferragamo designer Maximilian Davis stacked belts on belts for an extra cinch, while Valentino’s super-snatched waist came with a big gold buckle and two contrasting leather straps.

Sun protection is everything, every season—but especially in spring, when designers tend to have a little fun with toppers. From the chic and classic options at Ralph Lauren and Valentino to the ’70s-inspired, floppy versions at Chloé, there was something for everyone in the spring 2027 lineup.

items.title: Petra Fagerström Turns Fashion Discipline Into Something Unruly
items.description: At the Winter Olympics earlier this year, many of us found ourselves ensorcelled by young female figure skaters furiously spinning on ice. But designer Petra Fagerström’s gaze has always been rinkside. “Coaches are so often the supervillain in the media, but I
items.author: Claire Marie Healy
paragraphs: At the Winter Olympics earlier this year, many of us found ourselves ensorcelled by young female figure skaters furiously spinning on ice. But designer Petra Fagerström’s gaze has always been rinkside. “Coaches are so often the supervillain in the media, but I love them,” says the 28-year-old designer on a June afternoon. “That power dynamic has emotions that many women can relate to.”

Fagerström is serene among the organized chaos of her studio, located in London’s historic Smithfield meat market. Although the Swedish designer’s dark hair, pale skin, and all-black uniform give the impression of a Scandinavian noir protagonist, when she was a teenager in Gothenburg, her look was considerably sparklier. From age 14 to 16, she trained at a skating rink every day after school, even making Sweden’s national team for synchronized figure skating. Still, when she thinks back to that time, what comes to her mind is not girls in spangly costumes but the strength of the woman in charge. “My coach was this matriarch. She had power but perhaps hadn’t reached what she had wanted to for herself,” says Fagerström. “There’s something really vulnerable about where that presence comes from.”

For her most recent collection, Fagerström, who launched her label in February 2025, explored that duality through a tug-of-war between structure and softness. Take her signature double-fronted jackets with interior tailoring, or her lenticular-printed pleats, which create an optical illusion like an ice skater speeding by, as mediated by our screens. Although the collection, which marked her first time on the London Fashion Week schedule, happened to coincide with Alysa Liu fever, Fagerström is determined to “talk about fashion” with her garments. Don’t expect any leotards. (You may, however, find a floral print that pays homage to a coat once worn by the mother of 1990s Olympic figure skater Tonya Harding.)

While she was always interested in clothes—during her emo phase, at 13, she was influenced by the band Tokio Hotel—Fagerström truly decided clothes were her future after quitting skating at 16. “I found Nicolas Ghesquière’s Balenciaga and fell in love. I was like, I’m going to be a designer,” she explains. She studied at Parsons Paris, then completed stints at Acne Studios and Demna’s Balenciaga before heading to London in 2023 for Central Saint Martins’s MA fashion program. Her particularly wearable graduate collection laid out her distinctive point of view: distorted New Look–inspired tailoring, shimmering eveningwear worn over warm-up sweats. “Fashion, to me, is thinking about womanhood: how you want to present, and how you want to be perceived,” says Fagerström. “Looking at a lot of fashion now, it’s like: Where’s the agency? In clothes, the idea I usually come back to is breaking what is obedient.” Think of her designs as the flyaway hair in a gelled ponytail.

At a time when revisiting the tchotchkes of girlhood is trendy, Fagerström is more interested in maturity and all the friction that entails. When she designs, she asks herself: “How does this woman feel? Does she like music, food, and sex? You want to feel that there is a woman behind the fashion image.” In just a short time, those questions have resonated: Her brand is already sold at Dover Street Market Paris and 10 Corso Como, as well as on her own website, and she was a finalist this year for the prestigious LVMH Prize. “My course director at Saint Martins said to me, ‘Don’t feel like you’re only one year young, because you’ve obviously been creating this brand for much longer.’ When things happen, they happen.”

Fagerström has been at work on her new collection. Spring presents a challenge for the designer, given her penchant for dark colors and layers. She’s exploring an idea she’s long been interested in: “My next collection is about women’s relationship to sex,” explains Fagerström. “Conservative values seem to be back in my generation.” She’s been rewatching Michael Haneke’s The Piano Teacher, a portrait of repressed desires, and reading Gillian Anderson’s Want, a book of compiled anonymous sexual fantasies. “How do these things come out in other ways when you repress them?” asks Fagerström. In her designs, they emerge as controlled slippages: jackets that fall a little off the shoulder, or trompe l’oeil that pretends to reveal the body underneath.

The designer partly credits all those years on the ice for her single-minded drive. “Being disciplined enough to practice something repetitive is a good skill,” she says. “When I started studying fashion, I would perfect my pockets for days.” Whenever Fagerström’s head isn’t focused on the cutting table, she is researching, just as she did on the pre-algorithmic Internet when she was seeking out what Raf Simons listened to, or looking for archival Junya Watanabe runway images. “You had to do a lot of digging on Tumblr,” she says, explaining that the magic was in the effort. “If you remove the pursuit of something, it feels less exciting.”

Hair by Ali Pirzadeh at Streeters; Makeup by Abbie Nourse. items.title: At the LACMA Art+Film Gala, Demna’s Gucci Steps Into the Spotlight
items.description: Stars from the worlds of art, film, music, and fashion came together Saturday, November 7, for the 15th annual LACMA Art+Film Gala. Presented by Gucci, the benefit welcomed more than 600 guests to honor artist Vija Celmins and Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve,
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: Stars from the worlds of art, film, music, and fashion came together Saturday, November 7, for the 15th annual LACMA Art+Film Gala. Presented by Gucci, the benefit welcomed more than 600 guests to honor artist Vija Celmins and Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve, raising a record-breaking nearly $7 million for the museum. The evening also marked the end of an era: Eva Chow, who has co-chaired the gala with Leonardo DiCaprio since its inception in 2011, announced that this would be her final year in the role.

Gucci artistic director Demna attended alongside house president and CEO Francesca Bellettini and Kering chairman François-Henri Pinault, with many of the evening’s guests dressed by the house. Among them were Kim Kardashian, Timothée Chalamet, Andrew Garfield, Monica Barbaro, Salma Hayek Pinault, Parker Posey, Sarah Paulson, Sienna Miller, Emily Ratajkowski, and Viola Davis. Meanwhile a slew of top models fresh off the recent Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show—including Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, Alex Consani, Vittoria Ceretti, and Candice Swanepoel—traded their angel wings for Demna’s designs.

After dinner, Paris Hilton introduced Blackpink sensation Rosé, who performed the live debut of her new single, “New Trick,” alongside “Number One Girl,” a cover of the Killers’ “Read My Mind,” and “APT.”

Before guests headed inside, photographer Myles Hendrik caught up with them beneath the glow of Chris Burden’s Urban Light, the landmark installation of 202 vintage street lamps that has framed LACMA’s Wilshire Boulevard entrance since 2008 and has served as the event’s red carpet, of sorts, for over a decade. See a selection of his portraits from the evening below.

items.title: Martine Rose, Beloved Cult Designer, Is Balenciaga’s New Creative Director
items.description: Designer Martine Rose may not be a household name, but many fashion insiders are celebrating the news that she has been appointed Balenciaga’s next creative director. The Jamaican-British designer’s eponymous menswear line not only has a cult following, she’s
items.author: Kyle Munzenrieder
paragraphs: Designer Martine Rose may not be a household name, but many fashion insiders are celebrating the news that she has been appointed Balenciaga’s next creative director. The Jamaican-British designer’s eponymous menswear line not only has a cult following, she’s also no stranger to the French label founded by Cristóbal Balenciaga. She served as a menswear consultant during the earliest year of former creative director Demna’s tenure, helping to establish many of the familiar codes that defined that era.

“It is a true privilege to be appointed creative director of Balenciaga, a house with an extraordinary heritage and a fearless creative spirit,” said Rose in a statement. “Balenciaga has been shaped by remarkable creative talents before me. I am committed to honoring this legacy and look forward to creating the next chapter in this rich and beautiful story.”

“Balenciaga has always been a house of radical creativity, challenging conventions, and redefining the boundaries of fashion,” added Kering CEO Luca de Meo. “Martine Rose embodies this spirit with a fresh, fearless, and deeply contemporary vision.”

Rose will succeed Pierpaolo Piccioli, who exited the house yesterday after just 18 months. Although a talented and respected designer, Piccioli’s romantic Italian vision often clashed with the generation-defining streetwear look that Demna established at Balenciaga during his 10-year tenure. Reports suggest that de Meo envisions the brand as a connector between those on the fringes of culture and Gen Z buyers. Notably, menswear sales—which rose dramatically under Demna—had begun to wane. Rose may be a more natural fit to cater to the Demna clientele.

Rose, born in London’s working-class neighborhood of Croydon, graduated with a degree in fashion design from Middlesex University. She established her own brand in 2007, which for years existed under the radar. In 2011, she won the support of Fashion East, London’s nonprofit fashion incubator program. News of her behind-the-scenes role at Balenciaga helped to raise her profile among fashion insiders.

Since then, her line has enjoyed something of a cult status. A pair of neon heeled sneakers from a collaboration with Nike could be classified as fashion’s favorite It sneaker. Hailey Bieber has often been spotted in Rose’s outerwear (husband Justin is a fan too). Kendrick Lamar wore a Rose-designed jacket to perform at the 2025 NFL Super Bowl halftime show. Dua Lipa, Kim Kardashian, and Rihanna have all been spotted in her designs, while the stylists of several K-pop stars often dress their clients in her wares.
Cate Blanchett wore a translucent Martine Rose trench coat on the cover of W’s Volume 5, 2018 issue.

Rose finds inspiration in her Jamaican-British upbringing, ‘90s rave culture, and the everyday clothing of the streets, though always with an unexpected twist. She’s staged fashion shows in markets, her daughter’s primary school, and directly on the streets, and has long taken pride in her niche status in fashion. “I feel really proud of it all,” she told W in 2018 of he growing success. “But then I remember, I like being under the radar.”

Still, her frequent collaborations with brands like Nike, Napapijri, Clark’s, and Supreme have been commercial successes, and Rose’s name has been floated as a candidate for bigger jobs (reports suggest she was considered to take over as Louis Vuitton’s menswear creative director before the job went to Pharrell Williams). Still, the future of Rose’s own line has been thrown into question recently. In 2023, Tomorrow Ltd, a fashion incubator aiding up-and-coming designer brands, acquired a 60 percent stake in the Martine Rose label. The company has faced financial hardship in the past year (just this week, Coperni, another former Tomorrow Ltd brand, announced it was shutting down), and was sold to The Level Group earlier this year.

Rose’s new job will ensure her voice continues to be heard in fashion—this time, on a much bigger stage. She will take up the job immediately, though the timing of her first collection has not yet been announced.

items.title: A Startup Wants to Fight AI Bioweapons With AI
items.description: Frontier AI labs have warned that their technology could help develop dangerous bioweapons.
items.author: Emily Mullin
paragraphs: Frontier AI labs have warned that their technology could help develop dangerous bioweapons.

Now, a startup says it has developed a defense. On Wednesday, Radical Numerics announced that it has developed a new edge model called Omnii Defense that is designed to flag natural and AI-engineered pathogens using a laptop and a USB gene sequencer. It can also run without an internet connection, allowing researchers in the field with spotty connections to use it. Though many scientists say AI-made bioweapons are a low-likelihood threat, Radical Numerics hopes its technology will help researchers and public health officials identify emerging biological threats.

Eric Nguyen, cofounder and CEO of Radical Numerics, says he sees a coming arms race in biodefense similar to what’s playing out in cybersecurity, where threat actors and security defenders are leveraging AI in an attempt to gain an edge.
“We felt that the biosecurity space was far behind on the defense side,” he says.

Nguyen and his cofounders were part of the research team behind Evo and Evo-2, open-source DNA foundation models they worked on during their doctoral research at Stanford University. They founded Radical Numerics in 2025.

The San Francisco–based company recently made waves after rolling out Omnii, a new genome language model built on different types of biological information beyond DNA, including RNA, proteins, and epigenetic signals. In October, Radical announced that it used Omnii to create custom bacteriophages, viruses that infect and kill specific bacteria, targeting a drug-resistant strain of E. coli. Its cocktail was used to treat a sick patient, with special permission from the Food and Drug Administration.

Another AI biotech startup, Tabula Bioscience, was also involved in that research, but Radical didn’t disclose the partnership in its announcement last month. The omission led Harvard geneticist George Church, who was an adviser to both companies, to resign from his role at Radical last week.

Omnii Defense, the company’s latest tool, makes multiple predictions about a sequence, including the odds of it being pathogenic or AI-generated and what taxonomic group it most closely resembles. The model assigns a genome a “threat score” between zero and one that combines the likelihood of unnaturalness with functional predictions. The higher the score, the higher the threat.

Earlier biodefense tools, such as the federally funded Finding Engineering-Linked Indicators, or Felix, can compare genetic sequences of interest against libraries of known organisms, essentially searching for cataloged matches. That can be helpful in a scenario where a bad actor has made a few tweaks to an existing pathogen. But they aren’t designed to make predictions in the way that Omnii is.

The benefit of AI models is that they can learn patterns in sequences associated with biological function instead of relying on exact sequence matches. That could allow them to recognize similarities between sequences even when their genetic spelling has changed. Christine Parthemore, Radical Numerics’ head of biodefense, says Omnii is a “step change.”

In one experiment, the company removed Bundibugyo virus—which is currently driving an Ebola outbreak in East Africa—from the training data, first at the species level and then its whole genus. “It was as if Omnii was operating in 1976,” Parthemore says, referring to the year Ebola was discovered. With just the species removed, the model still detected that 33 percent of the Bundibugyo sequences pushed to it were something pathogenic. Even with the whole genus removed, it flagged 22 percent of the viral sequences. Non-AI tools gave essentially no indication of potential risk, she says.

“We absolutely need to be vigilant about what AI is enabling, and if we can use technology to compete with it and hopefully get ahead of any kind of nefarious actors, that seems sensible,” says Bronwyn MacInnis, director of pathogen surveillance in the Infectious Disease and Microbiome program at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard.
However, MacInnis cautions that detecting a signal is still a big leap from determining whether a pathogen has real consequence or whether a threat was engineered.

Access to Omnii Defense is currently limited to vetted external testers. Radical Numerics says it is working with national laboratories, government agencies, and other independent evaluators to assess the model’s performance.

items.title: A New Benchmark for De-Aging Comes From Slowly Turning Back Cells’ Clocks
items.description: Scientists have long known how to make cells younger—at least in the sense that adult cells can be converted into pluripotent stem cells very similar to those found in embryos. While this capability has been foundational for biological research, these methods
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: Scientists have long known how to make cells younger—at least in the sense that adult cells can be converted into pluripotent stem cells very similar to those found in embryos. While this capability has been foundational for biological research, these methods aren’t viable for anti-aging technologies, for a few reasons.
“You don't want to have a pluripotent cell in your body, because it can become all types of cells,” says Oliver Brüstle, a professor who studies stem cells at Germany’s Bonn University.

Additionally, the few key genes involved in the stem cell conversion process can drive the formation of cancer if left active. That’s why Brüstle and his team have looked for other ways of de-aging cells without going through a pluripotent state. In their recent study published in Aging Cell, the researchers started with blood cells from people of various ages, including an infant and a 101-year-old donor.

They guided these cells into a younger state but not all the way toward becoming embryonic-like stem cells. And as this transformation progressed, the chemical signals in the DNA that help estimate a cell’s age also changed. In less than two months of reprogramming, one biomarker in particular was set back as far as 60 years.

Aging continued to reverse even when the scientists drastically reduced the cells’ ability to multiply. Therefore, the apparent rejuvenation can’t be explained solely by the fact that the cells were dividing and producing new cells over and over again. However, the mechanism that did erase these signs of aging is still unclear.

“The hope is that you actually can do this systemically in the entire animal,” Brüstle says. “But if you think about applying it in a patient, then you want to be sure this is not a lab experiment, so it's about finding the mechanism.”

The researchers also shifted the blood cells specifically into a kind of cell that produces neurons. One caveat is that blood cells and neurons age on different timelines, so the extent of the reversal could be exaggerated by the use of a different measuring stick. The authors acknowledge this limitation in their paper, though this discrepancy couldn’t account for all the age-associated biomarkers that reversed course.

Blood cells getting brainy also would not be a desirable result if you gave a patient a de-aging drug, but it would be useful for other regenerative medicine purposes. However, what Brüstle sees as one of the most exciting outcomes of the study is the information gleaned about the process of de-aging.

Usually, making stem cells is quick. That’s useful for many experiments, but it doesn’t give researchers the chance to study cells as they shed the markers of age. In this recent study, since the scientists were able to slowly turn back the cells’ biological clocks, they could track each step of de-aging. “Now we can actually try to dissect the process much more easily than having an instantaneous event,” Brüstle says.

Scientists began converting adult cells back into stem cells two decades ago, but we’ve known very little about how the subsequent de-aging occurs. This means when clinical researchers test potential medical interventions for age-related conditions, they haven’t always had a reliable measure to compare against.
“Now we have a model” Brüstle says. “You can work along this, and now you can probe a zillion things. What impacts the process? This will lead you to the mechanisms. That’s our hope.”
Additional reporting from Anna Rogers.

items.title: Here’s What We Know About the X-70 Fractal, NASA’s Experimental New Plane
items.description: NASA has unveiled a new experimental vehicle, the X-70 Fractal, although many of its features remain a mystery. The agency describes it as a research platform designed to conduct advanced aeronautical tests, but so far it has released only computer-generated i
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: NASA has unveiled a new experimental vehicle, the X-70 Fractal, although many of its features remain a mystery. The agency describes it as a research platform designed to conduct advanced aeronautical tests, but so far it has released only computer-generated images and some technical specifications regarding its capabilities.

Despite the secrecy, it is possible to get some idea of what the new vehicle is like. First of all, it’s not a spacecraft, meaning it is not designed to reach Earth’s orbit or operate outside the atmosphere. However, this crewed, subsonic aircraft is capable of flying far above commercial jets, reaching altitudes over 45,000 feet, well into the stratosphere. Other specs released include the plane’s max speed of Mach 0.75—about 575 miles per hour—and that it can travel nearly 1,700 miles in a single flight.

According to NASA, the X-70 Fractal will enable research into maneuver capabilities never before demonstrated in crewed aircraft, although the agency has not specified what types of maneuvers it intends to perform. The plane will also be capable of carrying up to one ton of experimental equipment and is expected to make its first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years.

One of the key features of the craft will be its modular design, allowing for the rapid installation and replacement of experimental equipment both inside and outside the aircraft. This is largely why it is referred to as an “experimental platform.” It will also feature reconfigurable flight control systems so that NASA can study different ways of steering an aircraft without having to develop a separate platform for each research project.

Although NASA is best known for its space missions, it’s long been dedicated to aeronautical research. That’s what the first A stands for. The agency also traces its origins to the creation of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, which was founded in 1915 and was folded into the newly formed NASA in 1958.

Since then, the space agency has developed numerous experimental aircraft to test technologies that range from supersonic flight and propulsion systems to new aerodynamic configurations. Not all of these prototypes go on to become operational aircraft, but the knowledge gained contributes to the development of future commercial and military aircraft as well as space vehicles.

Among its most recent projects is the X-59, developed in collaboration with aerospace and defense company Lockheed Martin to investigate ways to reduce the noise produced by supersonic aircraft. The X-70 Fractal will join this tradition of pioneers in the sky.

The development of these technologies also has a strategic dimension. In its budget documents for 2027, NASA identifies aeronautical research as a tool for maintaining US technological leadership in the face of growing international competition. The agency also plans to collaborate with the Department of Defense to advance new flight capabilities, although it has not yet announced any military applications for the X-70 Fractal.

During the unveiling of the new aircraft, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman noted that the project represents only one part of a new era for federal aeronautical research and hinted that more announcements are coming. For now, the agency has not provided details on what those initiatives might be, nor has it specified when it will release more information about the X-70 Fractal.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling
items.description: No executive has pulled the strings in the artificial intelligence era quite like Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang. He parlayed the boom into incredible wealth, became a close confidant of President Donald Trump, and emerged as a prominent voice in US–China relation
items.author: Will Knight; Paresh Dave
paragraphs: No executive has pulled the strings in the artificial intelligence era quite like Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang. He parlayed the boom into incredible wealth, became a close confidant of President Donald Trump, and emerged as a prominent voice in US–China relations. That now all stands in the balance.

Over the past few days, Huang’s status as an AI titan has come under scrutiny amid an admission that he had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia’s board of directors said the company would launch an investigation into the incident. Huang, the company said, “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.” Huang earned $36 million last year and owned about 3.5 percent of Nvidia as of March, according to a corporate filing—which also noted that Huang is an at-will employee who can be let go anytime without severance.

How exactly the investigation shakes out, and what it means for Huang’s future at the company, remains to be seen. But the incident at least puts his position at risk, and raises questions about how the industry will respond.
“He’s the person who decides who gets the chips and who doesn't,” says David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School who tracks the chip industry.

Nvidia, which Huang cofounded in 1993, controls 90 percent of the market for chips used in training frontier AI models. With those chips in short supply, Huang has the power to determine which areas of AI get a boost next. Nvidia has also bankrolled much of the AI buildout, investing billions in the very companies buying its chips, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. When Elon Musk wants to build a new data center, Yoffie says, he can put in a call to Huang.

Internally, Huang closely manages even small details at Nvidia, responds to emails from any one of its roughly 60,000 staffers, and raises his voice to get points across, according to current and former employees. He’s a regular on cable TV and at tech conferences, where he’s been trying to deflate concerns about an AI market bubble and boost the positioning of his company.

But Nvidia has no other executive anywhere close to Huang’s prominence, and no apparent potential successor. “We have no idea who would replace him,” Yoffie says. “You put someone new into that position, if you're a customer, who knows what that's going to mean.”

Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, says Huang has played such an important role—and become so close to the president—that he has become load-bearing for the entire US AI industry.

“On the one hand, Huang is irreplaceable. He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution,” Fedasiuk says. But he says that the company, which is indispensable to the AI industry, has to come first.
“He has to be replaceable as the CEO of the world's largest company, at $4 trillion in capex.”
Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday, even as broader stock market indices rose.

The board’s investigation will most likely focus on whether Huang violated any company policies, Yoffie says. But the FBI could also investigate whether laws were broken, and Congress may decide to look into whether Huang’s affair influenced the US government’s policy on selling chips to China.
Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The scandal also raises serious questions about whether China may have gained sensitive information about US AI companies and the government’s strategy on China, Fedasiuk says.

Huang’s affair appears especially damning given how outspoken he has been in recent years against calls for more aggressive technology export controls on China. His credibility on the topic could be permanently in doubt.

Both the first Trump administration and the Biden administration imposed export controls designed to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips, as well as to technology required to mint advanced semiconductors. In his second term, however, Trump loosened these controls, giving China access to older generations of Nvidia chips; it was better to make China reliant on US technology, the argument went.
Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, says the Huang scandal is likely to accelerate efforts to crack down on chip exports.

“There was going to be more of an impetus to control what chips are getting sent to China anyway,” he says. “I expect there to be more scrutiny on what's going on, what's getting sent to China. I think there's also going to be more scrutiny from the Commerce Department.”

items.title: Jensen Huang Hired a PR Firm Known for Handling Sex Scandals Last Year
items.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began working with a crisis communications firm known for handling public scandals a year before he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The firm, Heller, has handle
items.author: Lauren Goode
paragraphs: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began working with a crisis communications firm known for handling public scandals a year before he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The firm, Heller, has handled Huang’s behind-the-scenes communications since at least October 2025, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

Risa Heller, the firm’s founder, has built a reputation as a fixer for powerful men facing allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies, according to a 2023 New York magazine profile. Her past clients and people who have sought her advice include former congressman Anthony Weiner, chef Mario Batali, and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller also handles corporate communications and issues unrelated to personal controversies for its clients.

Heller’s public relations consultants were initially believed to be hired for matters related to Huang’s personal life, including his family’s philanthropic endeavors, according to people familiar with the arrangement. The firm frequently communicated with Huang and his daughter Madison, a product marketing director at Nvidia who has become an increasingly prominent figure within the company, sources tell WIRED. It’s not clear whether Heller’s early work with the Huang family involved Huang’s affair.

In 2024, Huang began appearing in public with a woman who goes by Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed, according to The New York Times. Megaspeed was created when it split off from a Chinese gaming and cloud computing firm in 2023, a few months after the US government began restricting exports of advanced semiconductors to China, including those developed by Nvidia. A subsidiary of Megaspeed later became a major buyer of Nvidia chips.

In early October 2025, Jensen Huang’s business dealings with Megaspeed and his connection to Alice became public in a lengthy New York Times report, which alleged that the US Commerce Department was investigating whether the company was helping Chinese firms evade American export controls through its subsidiaries.

The report caused tensions to rise within Nvidia’s top ranks, and Jensen was rankled by the story, according to sources. By the end of that month, Nvidia’s internal communications teams had been instructed to include Heller’s firm on any press inquiries about Huang, whether personal or professional, according to people familiar with the matter.
When reached by email, a representative for Heller referred WIRED to Nvidia. John Rizzo, Nvidia’s head of public policy communications, declined to comment.

US intelligence officials have determined that Alice (who has no known relation to Jensen) is a spy working for the Chinese government, according to the Times. Nvidia initially said that Jensen’s interactions with Alice were part of routine business with clients. But on Sunday, Huang acknowledged that his relationship with her was romantic in nature. In an email to Nvidia staff, he said he owed them and his family an apology. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia’s board of directors announced it is opening an independent investigation into Jensen’s activities. It said it has no reason to believe that national security or confidential Nvidia information has been compromised.

Before founding her firm, Risa Heller worked for Jane Harman, then a Democratic congresswoman from California, and later served as Democratic senator Chuck Schumer’s New York City press secretary. Rizzo, Nvidia’s head of public policy communications, also previously worked for Schumer, serving as his deputy communications director.
Update 11/10/26 8:45am ET: This story has been updated to note that Nvidia declined to comment.

items.title: 10 Breakthrough Technologies 2026
items.description: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies
items.author: Amy Nordrum
paragraphs: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies

Our reporters and editors constantly debate which emerging technologies will define the future. Once a year, we take stock and share some educated guesses with our readers. Here are the advances that we think will drive progress or incite the most change—for better or worse—in the years ahead.

Sodium-ion batteries, made from abundant materials like salt, are emerging as a cheaper, safer alternative to lithium. Backed by major players and public investment, they’re poised to power grids and affordable EVs worldwide.

AI coding tools are revolutionizing how we write, test, and deploy code, making it easier and faster to build sophisticated websites, games, and other applications than ever before. Just be sure to double-check what they come up with.

Nuclear power already provides steady electricity to grids around the world, without producing any greenhouse-gas emissions. New designs rely on alternative fuels and cooling systems or take up less space, which could get more reactors online faster.

Every day, millions of people interact with AI chatbots. Some of them form what feel like close, personal bonds with the bots. There’s mounting evidence that this can be dangerous, and politicians are finally waking up.

When he was just seven months old, baby KJ became the first person to receive a personalized gene-editing treatment. A clinical trial is now planned, and bespoke gene-editing drugs could be approved within the next few years.
Growing banks of gene information on extinct creatures are providing clues to new treatments and suggesting solutions to climate change—and may help save endangered species.
Mechanistic interpretability

Nobody knows exactly how large language models work, which means we don’t have a clear idea of their limitations. But that’s changing: Clever research techniques are giving us the best glimpse yet of what’s really going on inside the black box.

Space tourism may seem fanciful, but this might be the year paying customers can finally check into a room with a galactic view. The shiny new modules will also support research missions by scientists and space agencies.

Screening embryos for genetic diseases is relatively common practice in fertility clinics today, and it can give potential parents some peace of mind. Now, though, new startups are making bold claims about using similar techniques to predict certain traits, including intelligence.
Hyperscale AI data centers

The race for AI supremacy has supercharged data centers. Hyperscale AI data centers pack powerful computer chips into synchronized clusters that work like giant, high-speed supercomputers—sizzling hot, power-hungry behemoths pushing infrastructure to its limits.
10 Breakthrough Technologies

MIT Technology Review’s annual list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies aims to help our audience know which emerging technologies are really worth paying attention to right now. Our editors and reporters pitch advances that they think should make the list, and we discuss and debate the merits of each over the course of several months.

We look for breakthroughs that will have a broad impact and make meaningful differences in our lives and work. We give equal consideration to those that we think will have a positive effect or bring negative consequences. Every year, we have to pass on many worthy candidates. Here’s what didn’t make the list this year.

This is the 25th year we’ve produced this list. Predicting the future is tough and we don’t always get it right. Look back through our archives to see what’s worked out—and what hasn’t. Or read this special analysis by an MIT researcher about some of the flops.

items.title: The AI Hype Index: AI loves cheating
items.description: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthr
items.author: Michelle Kim
paragraphs: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthropic’s models have also hacked into other companies’ systems four times already. And that’s only what we’ve caught so far.

Freaking out? You’re not alone. AI lab researchers are quitting their jobs and issuing dire warnings that if we keep going this way, AI might eventually kill us all. Bill Gates is sounding the alarm. Bernie Sanders has teamed up with Steve Bannon, of all people, to call for curbs on AI. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is urging a slowdown, and other top US AI executives agree. But fear not: President Trump has a plan. He says the only guardrail AI needs is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”
Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason

items.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
items.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
items.author: James O'Donnell
paragraphs: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.
Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.
But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

items.title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
items.description: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.

One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.

The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.

With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.

items.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
items.description: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in settin
items.author: Grace Huckins
paragraphs: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”

Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”

Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.

Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”

Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.

He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what's going on,” he says.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”

Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”
