items.title: Amanda Seyfried Does Not Regret Fighting Billy Evans
items.description: Amanda Seyfried is finally ready to talk about You Can See Everything. In Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary, Seyfried reprised her role as the convicted Theranos founder in several crucial reenactments and served as a much-neede
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Amanda Seyfried is finally ready to talk about You Can See Everything. In Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary, Seyfried reprised her role as the convicted Theranos founder in several crucial reenactments and served as a much-needed sounding board for Fielder. She eventually got so involved that she flew to Austin to have dinner with Fielder and Billy Evans, Holmes’s partner, leading to an explosive conversation over Chinese food. Seyfried has remained mum about her involvement in the project until Wednesday, when Rolling Stone published a conversation among her, Fielder, and Oppenheim. Unsurprisingly, she has not warmed up to Evans since that meeting.

Seyfried told Fielder that she found Evans to be “yucky” when she first watched footage of him and Holmes in their San Diego rental home. Her immediate negative response to Evans’s whole deal was actually what fueled her desire to meet him in person. “I just wanted any information I could get on Billy,” Seyfried told Fielder. “I became this weird Billy detective because I had gotten such strong negative feelings from him in the footage. I felt like I needed to meet this guy.”

As you likely already know if you’ve seen the film, Seyfried found that her feelings about Evans “only got worse” after meeting him. Apparently, she really did try to be on her best behavior while at Evans’s house — “I wanted to turn my disdain off a little bit, because I’m in his house now with his children — with their children,” she told Fielder and Oppenheim. “I always want to give people the benefit of the doubt, and I felt bad that I had talked a bunch of shit about him up until that point. Because look, I do not like him. But I’m coming into this man’s house.”

Despite her best efforts, things took a turn during dinner, when Evans attacked Seyfried for her portrayal of Holmes in The Dropout and for calling Charlie Kirk “hateful” on Instagram. “There was no reason for him to get that aggressive,” Seyfried said, a word she chose because it was “diplomatic.” She said that once Evans “disrespected” her, she felt as though “the gloves are off.”

“I was in the frame of mind where I’m like, ‘OK, this guy is disrespectful, and I’m here in his home, I’m gonna argue this because I actually have a pretty solid stance on things,’” Seyfried said. “I don’t like the way he’s using this human being, his wife — the person he says he’s ‘building monuments of love’ to — as a tool. Maybe he does respect her, but he’s behaving like he does not respect her.”
After watching the three-and-a-half-hour documentary, it’s hard to disagree with Seyfried. But maybe the AI hologram of Holmes that hangs out in Evans’s dining room has a different opinion.

items.title: What to Buy for the Best-Smelling Person You Know
items.description: Everyone knows someone who gets stopped mid-conversation with the question “I’m sorry, but what are you wearing?” I’ve shamelessly asked people countless times, and I’ve been on the receiving end of the question, too. Those are usually the people who curate a
items.author: Asia Milia Ware
paragraphs: Everyone knows someone who gets stopped mid-conversation with the question “I’m sorry, but what are you wearing?” I’ve shamelessly asked people countless times, and I’ve been on the receiving end of the question, too. Those are usually the people who curate a fragrance wardrobe with the same intention that they curate their closet. They’re not just picking up the fragrance that everyone else is wearing or running to buy a gourmand scent because that’s the trend; they’ve developed a special nose for scent and a taste that’s specific to them. I know it sounds dramatic, but we can all think of one person we know like this — and they can be the hardest people to shop for.

But that’s where this list comes in. Consider it your guide to finding the next scent for your fragrance wardrobe or for the person in your life who always smells divine. These fragrances are some of my most-worn and most-complimented scents, the ones I’d gift to someone who wants to smell expensive and start a conversation this holiday season.
The Fragrances They’ll Love
New! You can now save this product for later.

For the person who likes a bit of mystery to their scent, consider this the intriguing smoky yet warm and intimate fragrance that leaves an addictive lasting impression. It’s the one I recommend to my friends for a first date because the scent trail makes you want to instantly lean in.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I’ve had multiple men stop me on the street to ask about this perfume, then purchase it for their wives on the spot — that’s how alluring the scent trail is! It’s a fragrance that’s meant to speak for you silently before you speak for yourself, hence the name. It’s sweet but not sugary because the vanilla notes are blended with peach, tuberose, orris, and more. It’s a striking balance of feminine and a warm addictive scent; what I consider the perfect signature.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Rose scents can be too flowery sometimes, but this is not your average rose. It’s a bright, unexpected floral with fruity notes like lychee and pear that soften the rose, plus a honeyed base that makes you want to smell it over and over again. I like to layer it with a softer rose, Parfums de Marly’s cult-classic Delina, for a balancing combo. It’s one that’s gotten me endless compliments, including from Jennifer Lawrence, who said she’s never smelled anything like it.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Mojave Ghost has become the white button-up of my fragrance wardrobe. It’s airy but soft and subtly sweet, the perfect everyday scent. Now picture that in silk: That’s what the absolu version of this scent smells like. It’s richer and warmer but still effortless with crisp pear notes contrasted by amberette.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Valaya Exclusif is a beloved Parfums de Marly scent. It smells clean, but it also has a creamy almond twist that takes it from powdery to a bit musky. If Mojave Ghost is your crisp white button-up, this is your cashmere sweater.
New! You can now save this product for later.

This is the fragrance for the person who likes a more unconventional scent, a far cry from your white button-up — more like the statement coat in the back of the closet that you rarely reach for. It’s a creamy and leathery attention-grabbing scent that’s a bit tart. The bottle itself is small, but I’d buy it over and over again for the intriguing looks I get when someone gets a whiff of the scent trail. It’s not for everyone, but those who like a mysterious, cozy scent will love it.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Fig is one of those notes that can be a bit polarizing in a scent. Korean brand Born to Stand Out finds joy in the challenge of taking a polarizing note and creating a scent that everyone would love to have in their fragrance wardrobe. Fig Porn is a fresh and green take on fig, but it’s balanced out with cedarwood and bergamot for a musky dry-down that’ll make you fall in love with fig.
New! You can now save this product for later.

If a smokier fig suits your taste, Bo’s Casa Blanca perfume adds a woody twist to a dry desert fig, and the result is transportive. It smells like you’ve just checked into the chicest villa with crisp sheets and a lovely view, but it can still be worn every day — not just when you’re on a dreamy holiday.
New! You can now save this product for later.

We love Baccarat at The Cut, but Maison Francis Kurkdjian has so many other great scents. Oud Satin Mood has been what I turn to when I’m in a sexy mood. It’s a rich oud with a hint of powder that enters a room before you do.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Influxious founder Funmi Monet created this with a vision of it becoming the berrylike scent you spritz on before heading out for a night on the town, and that’s exactly what it smells like. It’s a fruity floral scent that doesn’t smell like anything you’ve smelled before; the blueberry musk and patchouli notes challenge your average fragrance. I’ve never been into berry scents until I smelled this.
New! You can now save this product for later.

If you like floral scents but with a little edge and earthiness, this is for you. Barénia’s intense fragrance takes its classic chypre perfume a little deeper with leather and patchouli that smell luxurious on the skin. The bottle is a nod to the Collier de Chien bracelet, making it a vanity staple beyond what’s in the bottle.
New! You can now save this product for later.

You’ve never smelled cocoa like this. Dries Van Noten’s Soie Malaquais is another unexpected scent; it’s the one that makes you smell expensive but not predictable. The cocoa and chestnut in the fragrance is warm and indulgent, while the bergamot and rose is more romantic and sophisticated, making it a scent that needs no layering. It breaks all the rules and smells better throughout the day as it sits on the skin.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Yes, Balenciaga has scents, and they aren’t talked about enough. Usually, I’m opposed to discovery kits because they’re so small, but this cigarette-style box is a nice piece to keep in a purse, and the scents are great too.
New! You can now save this product for later.
More Scented Products for Your Consideration

If you’re buying a scent for someone who is particularly hard to please, you can’t go wrong with non-fragrance items — chances are they like their space to smell good too. So why not gift a scent for their home or even a perfume for their hair?
New! You can now save this product for later.

The chicest gift is a Loewe candle, and that’s a hill I’ll die on. It’s my favorite gift to receive and my favorite one to give. The brand’s take on the pistachio trend is a warm and nutty aroma that will make their home feel like a cozy gelato shop (probably not what you want in a fragrance, but a perfect wintry scent for their space).
New! You can now save this product for later.

Home scents don’t stop at candles; it also includes everyday essentials, like the hand soap you use. Adding Trudon hand soap to my bathroom was one of the best decisions I made, because guests are always smelling their hands after stepping out and asking what it is. Those same guests will be getting their own hand soap for the holidays.
New! You can now save this product for later.

For the person who keeps their scent essentials in their purse, a hydrating perfumed hand cream is the gift that keeps on giving. I love Le Labo’s Thé Matcha cream because it’s strong enough that the scent will linger, but not so strong that it overpowers whatever scent I’m already wearing.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Anyone who is serious about smelling good knows that it all starts in the shower. Cyklar’s scents have become some of my favorites this year, and the brand recently launched shea butter body scrubs. The santal in this scrub is subtle, and the post-scrub skin nourishment is intense. It’s a great gift when you don’t know what scent to give because it starts with a good base note.
New! You can now save this product for later.

And why not follow up a scrub with a fragrance oil? It has the lingering smell of a perfume with the nourishment of an oil and usually a price that isn’t as high. I wore this oil during a HYROX competition, and I was still receiving compliments on my scent after hours of running and sweating (and thankfully no pooping).
New! You can now save this product for later.

The secret to smelling good from every angle is to not stop at the fragrance you put on your skin, but you should never spray your perfumes directly on your hair because the alcohol can dry it out (ask me how I know). That’s where hair perfumes come in. Cécred’s classic jasmine-and-oud scent from its hair products was bottled into a hair perfume this year, and it’s a great addition to any scent wardrobe.

items.title: Jennifer Lawrence Hopes You Won’t Hate Her New Project
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Angelina Chapin
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Jennifer Lawrence has been here before. At this exact same sort of restaurant, the kind where celebrities discreetly mingle (this time, Gemma, the Italian trattoria attached to the Bowery Hotel), in a booth that gives her some privacy but not so much that her publicist and assistant can’t keep a watchful eye and ear from a table nearby. There’s always a stranger sitting across from her scribbling down notes on what she orders (a cappuccino and avocado toast with a soft-boiled egg) and what she’s wearing (an oversize bright-red sweater and a small beaded turquoise necklace). This is her cue to rehash talking points about her chemistry with a co-star or reverence for a director.

But when we meet for breakfast in early October, something about the familiar scene is different; she’s slightly outside her comfort zone. “I’m in this interesting transition,” she says. “For the last three years, I have been in this kind of delusional bubble where I can’t let doubt in. Now I’m experiencing doubt.” Lawrence, whose blonde hair is wavy from sleeping in loose braids last night, says any movie release comes with nerves, which she can normally soothe by bingeing the latest season of Real Housewives. This morning, though, she’s not here to talk about developing a Miss Piggy feature, working on a rom-com, or shooting a sci-fi thriller next spring. Instead, for the first time in her 20-year career, the 36-year-old is debuting a project you won’t find in theaters or on Netflix. And she’s still figuring out how to talk about it. “I have to pretend I’ve made the greatest thing on earth,” she says, her hands fiddling with the salt and pepper shakers. “Otherwise it gets too scary. It’s a form of forced manifestation.”

That thing arrives on October 27, when Lawrence will officially join the oversaturated world of celebrity brands by launching Mes, a “biodesigned haircare” company that is selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. She’s partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can. That sounds great and all, but “what if nobody gets it?” she asks. “What if everybody hates it?”

Lawrence might seem like the type of actor who would roll her eyes at the celebrity–to–beauty brand pipeline. She has an Oscar and a production company and just shot a Martin Scorsese movie alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. Why spend time shilling a volume mist? Her answer doesn’t involve cracking jokes about girlbosses making #OOTD videos, the brand of self-deprecating humor she used as armor earlier in her career. Instead, she’s taking it very seriously, speaking about Mes as a natural extension of her art. “There is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product,” she says, twisting up her hair into a bun. “I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.” Lawrence has made peace with the humiliation inherent in being a creative person forced to talk about their work and doesn’t need to turn herself into the punch line. The baby-faced 22-year-old who laughed off tripping on the stairs at the Academy Awards is now more than a decade older and a mother of two. I watch her arrange her delicate features into a thoughtful expression while telling me how creatively satisfying it felt to develop a brand. I know she’s a good actor, one of the best, but I believed her.

Lawrence has always been a “hair girl.” “I feel like if my hair looks okay, then nobody’s gonna notice anything else about my face, clothes, or body,” she says. “I also can find myself using it to hide.” As a child, her thick curls would puff up in the Kentucky humidity, and she slept in braids to control the “floof.” In her teenage years, she ceded control to stylists, who did whatever they needed to get her camera-ready. “When you are a new and upcoming actress, you can’t be like, ‘Don’t put that on my hair,’’’ she says. “You sit in the chair and you say ‘Thank you’ and you shut your mouth.” Her strands would smoke and sizzle when the hair spray hit the straightening iron; her hair was dyed four different colors in one day for an X-Men screen test. After shooting the second Hunger Games film in 2013, her hair was so fried that she chopped it off into a pixie cut, a style she thought at the time “looked dope.”

Soon, Lawrence had bought every new product on the market in a desperate search for anything that would style her hair without hot tools. She even met with scientists about developing new products, but she struggled to find a like-minded collaborator. That is until 2023, when she watched a TED Talk by Jasmina Aganovic, a chemical biological engineer with a shiny brown bob and a beauty company who spoke about creating products that would fundamentally change the makeup of hair rather than just coating it in products — the industry’s current approach. Lawrence got goosebumps and emailed Aganovic to set up a meeting in the fall, just as the actors’ strike was ending. “It just seemed like a new way of going about things,” she said. “This is what I’ve been waiting for.”

Aganovic was initially less enthusiastic about the partnership. She had already founded a company, Arcaea, that uses DNA sequencing and skin microbiology to make, among other things, perfumes that reimagine extinct flowers or the smell of clouds. And while she wasn’t blind to the attention Lawrence could shine on her life’s work, she worried it could also be a distraction. “One of my biggest fears is having my work be misinterpreted,” she says. “Jen came across as credible and curious, but you never know how much she had actually looked into the company.” After a Zoom call, Lawrence set out to prove she wouldn’t be the kind of business partner with “25 assistants rescheduling something.” Within a few weeks, she flew to Aganovic’s Boston lab, showed up without an entourage, and smelled the smelliest bacteria in the fridge. Aganovic was impressed. “Jen literally said, ‘If you want to do this in five years, I’ll still be here,’” Aganovic remembers. “And I think that took the pressure off. I was like, Oh wow, she’s really serious.”

By fall 2024, Aganovic’s team of scientists was working on formulas that would make hair healthier while cutting down on styling time, damage, and shampooing. Lawrence had very specific ideas for the products, like a hair mask that would go on dry hair (and that could double as a “wet look”), a serum that got rid of her “floofs” without leaving residue, and a volumizing spray that wasn’t crunchy and improved her scalp. To execute her vision, Aganovic’s scientists had to become experts in lipids, proteins, and the scalp’s microbiome and experiment with different techniques, including developing a proprietary ingredient to promote a balanced, less oily scalp. “Hair masks are not usually applied to dry hair,” says Aganovic, “which is why it’s very expensive to produce them this way, without water.” (A 150-milliliter bottle costs $52.) Lawrence’s head became the guinea pig. She tried the products on her naturally curly hair, which she says makes her look like Isaac Newton. She tested the serum while doing promo for Die My Love and used the volumizing mist on the set of What Happens at Night, the Scorsese film she shot earlier this year. Her dedication was total, and she sent the serum back to the lab almost 150 times. At one point, she started to smell like fish after leaving on an unscented version of the mask for four days. “My husband was like, ‘If you don’t wash your hair, you have to get a hotel room,’” she said. Lawrence held firm.

When she wasn’t filming, she spent hours on weekly calls about the business and focused on developing the look of Mes’ logo and bottles. “I knew I couldn’t miss a Zoom and that I’d need to look over every single letter on the website,” she says. Sometimes it was hard to juggle everything. During one call, Lawrence tells me she was bouncing on a yoga ball at nine months pregnant when it occurred to her she was only in a bra. “I just turned my camera off and said, ‘I’m so sorry. I realized that I’m not wearing a shirt,’” she says, “And then everybody pretended like they hadn’t noticed.” But she wanted to stay in the weeds of the business. Lawrence took nose-training classes to help develop Mes’ scent; she sent product samples to everyone in her group chat and asked them for their feedback on fonts. She got so involved in the design that she had a colleague fly out to the New England beach town where she was vacationing so she could hold the 3-D-printed models in her hands. “I wanted them to be pretty,” she says of the bottles, which look like modernist mini-vases. “Bathroom products are always out, and it’s like, Why is this ugly?”

Lawrence trusts her eye, she assures me during our post-breakfast tour of the artist Robert Rauschenberg’s former Noho studio, a place she wanted to visit because it’s up for sale and could soon be turned into luxury condos. “I am good at telling when something’s going to be hot,” she says, now wearing a black baseball cap from her husband’s art business, American Pictures. After looking at a small exhibition of work by the mid-20th-century multimedia icon — “he’s kind of hot,” she says under her breath as she stands in front of a photo of Rauschenberg smoking — we sit in a room with sun pouring in through arched windows while Lawrence tells me about the vibe she’s trying to create. Mes, which is pronounced Mess (the latter was already trademarked), is meant to capture the kind of girl (gender neutral) who leaves the house with dewy skin and a rumpled-in-a-chic-way button-down shirt. “The moment something was fussy, it was like ‘no,’” she says. “Avoiding pretentious words and pretentious font is big. Our girl is not that. But she appreciates beauty.” Lawrence’s personal ethos is also looking good with minimal effort, despite the fact that she’s had a boob job and one day plans to get a face-lift. “I want to be a sexy mom,” she says. “At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my shit together.”

But don’t expect to see GRWM videos in her bathroom before taking her toddler to school. She had resisted creating an Instagram account for her entire career — she did, however, make a Finsta to share memes with her friends — in hopes of keeping a few shreds of life private. But Lawrence knew Instagram was a necessity for any founder in 2026 and a few months ago met with a social-media expert, who explained that Lawrence’s strategy didn’t need to involve constantly pumping out content or filming her home life. Instead, since officially joining the platform in September, she’s only posted to the grid three times — “If anyone says anything negative, I will quit,” she deadpanned in her first video — and already has more than 8 million followers. She plans to do minimal promo for Mes, including product tutorials she might film in a “public or hotel bathroom” to keep her own sink offline.

It’s a tough time to jump on the celebrity-beauty-brand bandwagon. Fans tend to view these companies cynically, as cringe cash grabs rather than genuine passion projects. And the bar for success is high: The products have to be good on their own merits, and the celebrity selling them has to make sense. People want Kylie Jenner’s lips and Hailey Bieber’s skin, but on Reddit threads speculating about Mes, commenters are already questioning whether Lawrence’s hair is a standout feature. When I ask Lawrence if she feels pressure to have aspirational hair, she says, “That didn’t even occur to me,” with a look of panic. “Is that something people think about?” In her fortress of positivity, she hasn’t dwelled on the criticisms that could be coming her way and seems genuinely caught off guard when I bring them up. Is she concerned a highbrow beauty product is at odds with the every-woman persona fans love? “I think about how excited people will be to have something so sculptural and beautiful!” she says. “My little bubble is about to be popped.”

While beauty brands have turned rich celebrities like Rihanna and Selena Gomez into filthy rich business moguls, Lawrence scoffs at the idea that Mes was conceived as a source of financial stability amid Hollywood’s decline. “A smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise,” she says. “Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door.” And anyway, worrying about the bottom line is not her strong suit. When talking about the look and feel of Mes, she adopts the self-seriousness of any artist talking about their craft. But when it comes to the more technical sides of the business, Lawrence falls back on her familiar brand of self-mockery. “If you put a gun to my head and were like, ‘What are the numbers we would need to reach in order for Mes to be a success?’ I would have no clue,” she says. “Numbers don’t stick in here. I’m dumb but cute!” When I ask if the company has investors, she whispers “I don’t know” and redirects me to her co-founder. (Aganovic says her original company, Arcaea, which has raised $78 million, is funding Mes.)

But the shtick isn’t working so well this time — which is a good thing. It felt charmingly authentic when, in 2012, the Kentucky-born ingénue told David Letterman, “I hate myself. Don’t go see the movie. I’m a troll.” But Lawrence is in a much different phase of life. She’s a mother married to a prominent art dealer and serves as the face of Dior. In Hollywood, she calls the shots, green-lighting movies with her own production company and fielding requests from the most in-demand directors while slamming the industry’s pay gap. Even if she can’t balance a spreadsheet, it’s hard to believe she’s a buffoon in the boardroom. “It’s funny that she describes herself as the creative needing the business counterpart,” says Justine Ciarrocchi, who runs a production company with Lawrence and is her friend of almost 20 years. “I think she has an incredible business intuition, and she’s fearless when she is sure of something.” Molly Howard, the CEO of La Ligne — a brand whose coveted wide-legged pants are a staple of Lawrence’s “momboy” aesthetic — says her friend already has the most important quality in a successful founder: the willingness to pore over the most boring details of the business, from learning about EBITA to testing a bottle’s seal. “The ambition is that this becomes a Fenty Beauty of hair care,” Howard says. “I really think this could be a Rhode.” Lawrence actually has an even more audacious North Star in mind, one she’s too embarrassed to name. “If I told you, you would be like ‘Hahaha,’” she says. “It is so big and so huge that I’m aware Mes will never get there.” I beg her a few more times, but all she’ll say is that the aspirational brand is not beauty-related. “If I was Taylor Swift, the people on Twitter would figure it out.”

Towards the end of October, I visit Lawrence at her office in Tribeca, a Federal-style townhouse with exposed brick and barnwood panels. There’s incense burning on the long wooden coffee table, and as she curls up on a rust-colored couch, asking me at one point if I’m bothered by her bare feet, Lawrence claims to be feeling more calm than when we first met. “I’m back to being utterly and completely positive,” she says, wearing a sequined brown wool cardigan and a long black skirt. “I can always fall back on the product. It’s just kind of like, Well, these are obviously really good.” If she’s stressed about anything today, it’s a recent haircut that left her with uneven bangs, which she’s repeatedly tried to fix. “No matter what I do, it flicks out,” she says, pointing to a strand on the left side of her head. “And I went into a meeting today as a hair authority.” Come to think of it, maybe she is a little nervous, mostly about the idea that people won’t have enough patience to stick with the products. “If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” she says. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.” She’s already dealt with a few emergencies, like the mask leaking during the ship test or the cap on the restyling serum squeaking. (“This isn’t luxury,” she remembers saying. “It sounds like I’m stepping on mice.”)

Earlier that day, the Mes landing page went live, featuring a video of Lawrence’s blonde waves bouncing as she dances in a red cardigan. She immediately texted her group chat asking for compliments, which includes Howard of La Ligne, Tracy Dubb of Isla Beauty, and two women she won’t name because they are “very private.” On October 27, the full website will roll out, and if all goes well, Mes bottles will start filling people’s bathroom cabinets.

In a material sense, whether Mes is a hit or not won’t have a big effect on Lawrence’s life. She’s already rich, and Paul Thomas Anderson probably wouldn’t blacklist an actor whose hair mask doesn’t sell. For Lawrence, the stakes are more personal. She has the antsy intensity of someone who’s desperate for people to join in their obsession rather than mock it, like a friend who’s become a javaphile and wants you to adopt a new coffee-brewing technique. “Tell me about your experience because the products take time,” she says, fixing me with an intense stare. “I can answer questions.” She’s itching to nerd out about the eccentricities of her creations, excited for people to log on to the website and see the microscopic images of how these products affect the scalp. As she’d told me during breakfast, “I’m nervous about someone putting on the restyling serum and being like, Oh my God, this went on really oily, without knowing that in 15 minutes, it’ll all dry.”

Toward the end of our talk, she catches her foot bouncing and says, “I think the nerves are in my body. I work really hard to keep my brain disciplined.” At some point, Lawrence knows someone from the Mes team will call and let her know if the sales numbers are good or bad. But the real risk is a bruised ego, the idea that people won’t like — or simply don’t care — about a product she’s devoted years of her life to perfecting. “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension,” she says. “I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

items.title: Gird Your Loins: A Heated Rivalry Monopoly Game Is Coming
items.description: Close your eyes for a second and think back to this time last year. Remember room 1410? The tuna melt? The way you screamed when you heard the words “I’m coming to the cottage”? If you’re one of the nearly 11 million people who tuned into Heated Rivalry, then
items.author: Hanna Flanagan
paragraphs: Close your eyes for a second and think back to this time last year. Remember room 1410? The tuna melt? The way you screamed when you heard the words “I’m coming to the cottage”? If you’re one of the nearly 11 million people who tuned into Heated Rivalry, then obviously you do. What a time to be alive! It was hard to move on from those six episodes, and some of us have been chasing the high ever since, doing whatever it takes to fill the void — obsessively reading fan fiction, buying the same skin-care products that Hudson Williams uses, watching TikTok edits over and over again, seeing Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody, even heading to our local Regal Cinemas to rewatch the final episodes in 4DX.

If all that is still not enough to quench your thirst (no judgment), you’ll be happy to know that Monopoly just announced a Heated Rivalry edition of its classic board game. It doesn’t officially launch until June 2027, but it’s available to preorder now on Amazon and Walmart and is set to ship next May. That means it’ll arrive on your doorstep just in time to cure your post-watch hangover from season two, which premieres in April 2027.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Whoever created this game is deep in the fandom, and it shows. Instead of buying streets, railroads, and utility companies, Monopoly: Heated Rivalry allows you to buy locations from the show, such as hotels, gyms, and the cottage. The themed tokens include a Straw+Berry smoothie, the MLH Cup, a hockey skate, a tuna melt, an extra banana, and a stupid Canadian wolf bird. The board itself also highlights key scenes from the show in chronological order, so you can relive Shane and Ilya’s love story from your living room, sans screen. Oh, and there’s one other very important detail: The game has an “ages 17 and up” rating. Immediately adding to cart …
More Heated Rivalry Merch We Love

Need a gift for your friend who still can’t be normal about Heated Rivalry (you know, the one you’ll need to check in on when season two drops)? We rounded up some ideas, below, since the Monopoly game won’t launch in time for the holidays. These products also make excellent White Elephant gifts or gag gifts if you’re shopping for a fellow chronically online person.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 11, 2026
items.description: The moon spends all day in Sagittarius giving you the optimism and can-do attitude to take on any challenge that comes your way. Even if you’re usually the sort of person to dwell on worst-case scenarios or get bogged down by self-doubt, you’ll probably still
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: The moon spends all day in Sagittarius giving you the optimism and can-do attitude to take on any challenge that comes your way. Even if you’re usually the sort of person to dwell on worst-case scenarios or get bogged down by self-doubt, you’ll probably still feel upbeat right now. There’s always the chance that you’ll make mistakes rooted in overconfidence, but try not to let any fears of messing up hold you back. Now is the time to err on the side of boldness: It could change your life, and at the very least, you’ll have more fun.

Although you aren’t afraid to take risks, you try to be smart about it. You don’t want to fail dramatically or embarrass yourself. If you’re going to take decisive action, you want there to be a reasonable likelihood that things will work out. But today, if you don’t make any mistakes, it probably means you’re playing it too safe. Trial and error is part of the process. You won’t learn without the occasional misstep, so today, make a point of taking chances and stepping outside your comfort zone.

You’re not the sort of person who’s quick to forgive and forget. When somebody wrongs you, you don’t see why you should be expected to pretend nothing happened. You may not make a big fuss about it, but you’re not going to brush it off and go back to “normal” either. There’s nothing exactly wrong with this approach, but keep this in mind: Nurturing grudges can take up a lot of mental space. Today, see what happens if you let old resentments drop so you can put more energy into the things you love.

As much as you enjoy being around other people, working with them is often frustrating. You want to be able to take your ideas and run with them; when you have a clear plan in your mind, you don’t want other people’s criticisms clouding your vision. But today, take it seriously when others challenge you. Maybe you’ll end up changing your mind, maybe not — but either way, working through the disagreements will make your own ideas stronger.

The more you lean into nostalgia, the harder it can be for you to accurately assess what’s going on in your life now. Maybe you keep working toward goals you’ve already outgrown or you hang on to old relationships even when they’re no longer healthy. Today, though, you’ll be able to assess your circumstances more clearly with less sentimentality getting in the way. Let go of fixed ideas about how things used to be and instead respond to them as they actually are.

When you suspect others are misunderstanding or underestimating you, your impulse is to set the record straight. You can’t stand the thought that anyone might think ill of you. You know your intentions are good and you have lots to offer, and you want to make sure everyone else knows, too. But today, try to let go of this worry. There will always be people who don’t like or understand you, and you’ll only stress yourself out trying to change their mind. Decide you’re going to live your life as you choose and nobody else’s opinions can get in the way.

When you have positive thoughts about the people around you today, share them. Compliment the people you admire, let colleagues know you’ve noticed their hard work, and tell your friends you care. You may assume these small comments won’t make much of a difference, but today especially, that couldn’t be further from the truth. Even the people who seem most confident feel overlooked and unappreciated sometimes. So if you have something good to say, don’t keep it to yourself.

If you already have a tendency to procrastinate, the habit’s likely to worsen today: You’ll convince yourself the tasks on your list can wait until tomorrow. But don’t offload all the boring work onto your future self. That’ll only make everything harder than it needs to be. Instead, make a point of taking care of the small stuff as soon as possible — ideally, as soon as it enters your mind. If it’s at all possible to do something right away, do it.

When other people are excited about a new plan or big change, you’re hesitant to voice your doubts. Even if you’re fairly certain things won’t work out the way others are hoping, you don’t want to be the one to dampen their enthusiasm. (In your experience, that doesn’t motivate anyone to rethink their assumptions; it only makes them mad at you.) But today, being willing to be the voice of dissent will prove rewarding. Others may not appreciate it in the moment, but they will in the long run.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

When you feel like nobody is listening, you may think the answer is to get louder and more dramatic. If you raise your voice, people will have no choice but to hear you; if you embellish your stories or overstate your opinions, others will sit up and take notice. There’s nothing wrong with presenting your thoughts and experiences in the best light possible — but take care not to be dishonest. Don’t prioritize getting attention over telling the truth.

If you suddenly start feeling insecure today, you’ll want to pinpoint a cause. Maybe some personal failing is making you feel bad about yourself, or maybe someone else’s unkindness has shaken you. You’re convinced that once you determine why you’re feeling so bad, you can fix the problem. But it’s likely that there’s no one reason for your feelings today, and they’re likely to blow over soon enough. So don’t put too much energy into coming up with solutions — chances are, all you really need to feel better is a bit of time.

Unexpected people may come to your aid today. Casual acquaintances could step in with the help you were too proud to ask for; strangers may offer a kind word exactly when you most need it. Try not to react with suspicion or assume they must have ulterior motives. You show up for your loved ones — why should it surprise you when they do the same for you? So focus on accepting these kindnesses with gratitude, then pay them forward.

Maybe you think the only way to get affirmation is to be “good” — to be capable and conscientious, the sort of person who makes only good decisions and follows all the rules. You imagine that if you can demonstrate you’re doing everything right, then everyone will definitely praise and admire you. But today, understand the people around you want to know the real you. They aren’t looking for perfection; they want to see your genuine personality, flaws and all.

items.title: Zazie Beetz Believes We Need The Bad Feelings, Too
items.description: In One Nightstand, celebrity readers and writers join us at the blond in 11 Howard to discuss some of their favorite books, allowing us to learn about their tastes and lives in the process.
items.author: Charlotte Owen
paragraphs: In One Nightstand, celebrity readers and writers join us at the blond in 11 Howard to discuss some of their favorite books, allowing us to learn about their tastes and lives in the process.

Zazie Beetz has been working as an actor for more than a decade, but she still gets nervous when starting a new project. Case in point: her new Apple TV thriller Nocturne, in which she stars as an undercover FBI agent opposite Liev Schreiber and Stephen Graham. “On the first day I called my mom crying because I was like, ‘I’m so nervous. What if they don’t like me? What if I’m bad?’” the 35-year-old says. “I’ll never forget, she was like, ‘Zazie, just go in there with love in your heart and just spread love onto everyone. Just come in — your heart is open and just give love.’ I don’t know why it just resonated with me — like, ‘Yes, I’m not going to close in fear. I’m going to open and offer what I need.’”

For Beetz, who was born in Berlin and split her early childhood between Germany and New York before her family settled there when she was eight, the approach worked. Nocturne is a taut thriller, adapted from Lars Kepler’s book The Sandman, in which Graham turns in a terrifying performance as a serial killer who represents the worst of humanity. It’s Beetz’s character, Saga Bauer, who has to find ways to get through to him, and so she sought to find the shades of gray. “I’m always trying to kind of come at this — again, not excusing the Jurek character for killing people — but where is this coming from? What’s his mind around this? What’s the non-typical approach that I don’t necessarily understand that this character is experiencing and why?” she says.

It’s an approach she also took in far less contentious circumstances, such as when she played Van in Atlanta. Beetz’s character was pilloried by fans of the show in Season 3 when she abandoned her daughter to go on a trip to Paris, though Beetz has always defended the choice. “I’m always defensive of my characters,” she says. “People are human, and there are certainly things you don’t want to inflict on other people — or as a parent, you don’t want to let your emotions get in the way of creating a life or harming your children or something like that — but ultimately we are individuals first, and things happen. And for me, for Van, I’m like — Her child was safe and fine, and she needed a moment. And that happens whether or not we approve.”

Nevertheless, the work is still hard, and it’s her husband — fellow actor David Rysdahl, with whom she’s expecting her first child — who helps support her when that’s the case. “He’s made me a better performer,” she says. “Firstly, just by being my literal biggest fan, which is great. But then also, he’s just so talented and I think he’s very bold in his approach — I feel like when we are discussing a role, we question everything and try to get to the bottom of it all… He’s, I think, much better at character analyses than I am… I don’t think I would have as rich characters without him at all. And so I think he has really helped me with that and helped build my confidence and has literally picked me up off the floor when I felt so scared to go on set.”

Hard as it is, it’s this humanity in the work which continues to draw her to it. “Acting is extremely vulnerable, especially in the very blunt context of you're going on set, there are a hundred people there you’ve never met, and then you’re like, ‘All right, I’m just going to do something,’” she says. “And sometimes you look dumb or you make a bad choice and it’s bad and you’re bad. That happens. And the best actors in the world are sometimes just bad. And you have to accept that a hundred people saw that and thought that was really bad…How do you move through that and move on? And that’s been a huge part of my journey in this industry and in my career — not focusing so much on that sensation and how that would shut me down.”
Keep reading to discover four of Beetz’s favorite books.

Her first pick is John Steinbeck’s 1952 epic East of Eden. Despite the timing of the choice, she has yet to see Netflix’s adaptation. “I’m usually not one to like an adaptation,” she says. “You have such a personal relationship with these stories that I often am like, ‘You’re ruining what was in my head’ or, ‘You're veering off,’ and then I just get mad.”

Beetz has complicated feelings about the novel’s contentious female protagonist, Cathy. “I don’t think Steinbeck loves women but I think that they are the most interesting characters and extremely complicated and complex,” she says. “I don’t know if she’s an antihero really, but kind of this protagonist that you’re…I don’t know if you’re rooting for her, but you’re also just there with her. I think so much of what motivates her is also fear and I think that that can turn into aggression and rejection.”

She’s also drawn to those complexities in her own life. “I really do believe that context exists for everything and you’re a villain in someone’s life,” she says. “For me, as a person who’s not religious, I would say I have sort of spirituality in my own approach. I do think ultimately I will perceive things a certain way due to my cultural learnings, due to what I think is bad. I will perceive death as bad because I have emotional attachments and things like that.”

Her second choice is Sapiens, a digestible human history from history professor Yuval Noah Harari. “What I love about the book is it’s written for a lay person. It’s very accessible,” she says. “When works are available for people to read and enjoy and there’s pictures, it’s just a great read.”

The book, which she says shows how expansive yet personal humanity can be, also offered her valuable perspective on humankind as a whole. “I liked the idea that every creature on this planet has a special thing. A dog can smell, and a fish can swim,” she says. “I feel like for humans — and we’re animals and, to me, have the same value as any other creature — our special thing is our imagination and our ability to tell stories, which as a creative is very validating.”

At the same time, Beetz is worried about the future of human imagination. “I am a very black-and-white thinker on AI. I fall in the camp of [thinking] it’s devastating to our culture and our minds,” she says. “Obviously there’s so many things at risk — safety and all of that — but I feel like the greatest risk is our minds, our cognitive abilities and even just asking little questions. I keep thinking, ‘What am I robbing myself of if I’m not going out and seeking these answers in a different way?’”

Her third selection is The Giver by Lois Lowry, a Newbery Medal-winning middle-grade novel which follows a 12-year-old boy named Jonas living in a “utopian” society where emotion has been eliminated. Selected as the Receiver of Memory for his community, Jonas learns that in sheltering themselves from bad memories and emotions, the community has also deprived themselves of happy ones.

“It’s this book around literally what we’ve just been talking about — the fear of what the consequence is of choosing security, safety, comfort, and how it creates a life devoid of richness,” she says. “When I was younger, I remember I was speaking with a therapist and I just kept talking about all these bad feelings I was having, and it just felt very devastating to me at the time. And she was like, ‘These aren't bad feelings, you’re just having a richer experience. You’re just having richer feelings, and with depth also can come darkness.’”

That kind of vulnerability has been on her mind as she expects her first child. “I think about becoming a parent, I’m opening my heart to potentially the greatest heartbreak of my life if something happens to my child, which I hope of course never does,” she says. “But to open that chamber in my heart, that possibility of love and relationship that I would love to experience, I have to also open a chamber of potential pain.”

Her final pick is The Alchemist, Paulo Coelho’s 1988 philosophical novel that follows a young Spanish shepherd through the ups and downs of his journey to Egypt. The book advocates following your own personal journey and heeding your intuition. “I read it at a time when I just really needed it. It was very soothing for me,” she says. “It’s allowed me, I think, just a lot of acceptance and sort of surrender in general and being like, ‘I am here for this time and I’m just going to have my experience and I’m going to experience it, [and] also be OK to observe.’”

Beetz is a believer that everything happens for a reason. “I don’t fully believe in free will in a way because I think from the moment of the Big Bang, the moment that first atom went out in one direction [there was] only one series of events that can happen from that expulsion of energy,” she says. “Every single decision that I made in my life is because this dinosaur met that dinosaur, and then that dinosaur met that dinosaur. And then everything was just a domino effect from that first moment.”

items.title: Exclusive: Jen Affleck Clarifies Her Future With The Original 'Mormon Wives' Show
items.description: Jen Affleck Clarifies Her Future With The Original Mormon Wives Show
items.author: Grace Wehniainen
paragraphs: Jen Affleck Clarifies Her Future With The Original Mormon Wives Show
Here’s where she stands with OG #MomTok today, as she stars in the Orange County spinoff.
The influence of #MomTok is spreading far beyond the comforts of Swig Country.

Streaming on Nov. 12, The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County follows a new group of young moms in Southern California — each with their own unique relationship drama and connection to Mormon culture. Of course, one familiar face is among the bunch: Jen Affleck, the only cast member from The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives to lead the new show.
But as the reality star navigates a new series and friendships, what does her future with the original series look like?
“Well, as of right now, I’m balancing both just because they are still my friends,” Affleck tells Bustle. “So, until they kick me out of MomTok, I feel like I will always be a part of it.”
The 27-year-old mom of three — with a fourth on the way — adds: “I think there’s this [question of] Is she in MomTok? Is she out of MomTok? Whether I’m in or out, they’re still my friends.”

So while it doesn’t sound like Affleck will be joining original castmates Whitney Leavitt and Mikayla Matthews in leaving the original Mormon Wives, she has been enjoying the change of scenery. “I’m definitely happy to be in Orange County now,” she says.

Affleck previously opened up to Bustle about finding a new kind of community in California, where she originally relocated to perform on Dancing with the Stars Season 34. “There’s a lot more pressure in Utah [to conform], especially with the majority of the state being [Mormons],” she said, adding about the Golden State’s influence on her faith: “In California, I definitely feel like there’s not as much pressure, because it’s way more diverse. So I feel like we’re able to express [ourselves] in different ways.”
Affleck’s relationship with her faith isn’t the only thing evolving in this new chapter. On Nov. 3, she filed for divorce from her husband, Zac Affleck.

“The last couple of years has trained me to be a person that doesn’t really trust themselves. And through this process, that’s been the hardest thing — like, questioning and doubting myself,” she says. “At the end of the day, I knew what was the right decision for me. It was just having the strength to move forward with that.”

items.title: Exclusive: Mckenna Grace Says There’s A ‘Hunger Games’ Easter Egg Everyone Missed
items.description: You Actually Missed One Of Mckenna Grace’s Press Tour Easter Eggs
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: You Actually Missed One Of Mckenna Grace’s Press Tour Easter Eggs
The actor unpacks the hidden meaning in one of her Hunger Games premiere ’fits.

Mckenna Grace is turning her press tour for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping into a master class in Panem-inspired fashion. Joining method-dressing icons like Zendaya and Jenna Ortega, the 20-year-old actor — and franchise superfan (remember her viral Peeta Mellark edits?) — has been serving nod after nod to the OG trilogy, proving she knows the lore by heart.

With the help of her stylist Molly Dickson, Grace has already channeled Katniss Everdeen, Effie Trinket, Lucy Gray Baird, and even the second Quarter Quell arena. While fans have been quick to decode nearly every Easter egg, one major reference flew completely under the radar — and it happens to be the one closest to home.

At last month’s Sydney premiere, Grace stepped out in a custom lavender mermaid gown by Vera Wang HAUTE, crafted from decadent macramé lace and featuring oversize, hand-cut silk organza flowers blooming over one shoulder strap. Fans immediately flooded the label’s comments, comparing her to Rapunzel and begging Disney to cast her as the live-action princess, while others guessed it was an Effie nod. Plot twist: The real inspo was her own SOTR character, Maysilee Donner. Grace herself confirms it.

“Most days I have, like, birds or butterflies or flowers in my hair,” she tells Bustle, before singling out her Sydney look as an extra-special Easter egg. “One thing I was excited about was ... I wore this purple dress in Australia that was a nod to Maysilee.”

Eagle-eyed fans who’ve watched the official trailers might already recognize the palette. In the footage, Maysilee is reaped wearing a lavender minidress — fittingly elevated for a District 12 merchant’s daughter — complete with an A-line silhouette, a contrasting floral collar, and a bow-clad belt.

But the color wasn’t the only Maysilee-coded detail — the flowers adorning her Vera Wang gown were a nod to her character too. During the reaping, Maysilee accessorized by stacking necklaces with floral pendants and pinning a chamomile flower onto her lapel. (She’s a known accessory girlie. According to SOTR lore, she was the OG owner of the Mockingjay pin Katniss eventually inherited.)

To bring that floral motif to life on the red carpet, Grace went all in. “All the flowers in my hair were real flowers, which was really fun,” she says, adding, “At the end of the night, I was picking them all out. In the morning, I had all these wilted flowers on my floor.”

Still, thanks to the butterfly clip in her hair and the gown’s voluminous strap, Grace agrees that those Effie theories weren’t totally off base. “It also did remind me of Effie a bit,” she admits. Two Panem icons in one look? Truly Capitol-worthy.

items.title: It's Kinda Chic To Have A Belated Honeymoon
items.description: The movies always made jetting from your wedding reception to your honeymoon look so dreamy. I think of Annie in 1991’s Father of the Bride, calling her dad at the airport to thank him for her lavish nuptials before boarding her flight, or Kimberly and Michael
items.author: Gabrielle Bondi
paragraphs: The movies always made jetting from your wedding reception to your honeymoon look so dreamy. I think of Annie in 1991’s Father of the Bride, calling her dad at the airport to thank him for her lavish nuptials before boarding her flight, or Kimberly and Michael in My Best Friend’s Wedding, driving away to their honeymoon. But when it came time for me to say “I do” last year, I could not imagine having to go to an airport, deal with TSA, and then be stuck in a metal tube for hours after my wedding.

And I’m not alone. More and more couples are choosing to have a belated honeymoon, delaying their travel plans by weeks, months, or even a year. (A 2026 Fora Travel survey found that a whopping 59% of newlyweds delay their honeymoons, opting for mini-moon trips in the meantime.) A longer delay not only gives you one less thing to plan before the big day but also lets you give it the attention it deserves, while giving your bank account a break. Thanks to the Capital One Travel app, booking my dream vacation to Hawaii was a breeze.

My husband and I had Hawaii in mind for a while because we both wanted a tropical destination we hadn’t visited before. Through the Capital One Travel app, we easily booked first-class flights, a stunning five-star hotel, and an array of adventurous and luxurious activities in Maui within three months of setting off. It’s so easy to become overwhelmed by planning (so many options!), and if you have decision fatigue (like me!), it helps to plan everything in one app. I found that cardholders can redeem their existing Capital One rewards for travel bookings, and depending on your card, you earn up to 10x miles on hotels and rental cars and 5x miles on flights, vacation rentals, and activities.

Nothing is chicer than having a dream honeymoon and not overly stressing over planning it. Need proof? Here’s a recap of my belated honeymoon, which my husband and I planned for our first wedding anniversary in October.
Day 1: Settling In At Hotel Wailea
Photos courtesy of Hotel Wailea, Travis Rowan, John Russo.

My husband and I aren’t big-box resort people, so we wanted a luxury hotel that felt more low-key. Nestled near Maui’s west coast, Hotel Wailea is a five-star boutique property with only 72 guest suites. The adults-only resort, which is part of Capital One Travel’s Premier Collection, is a perfect choice for couples who want a serene, relaxing stay in paradise.
We spent our first day settling into our Celebration Suite with a stunning view of the Pacific Ocean. We stopped by the pool bar for a quick, delicious bite of poke nachos.
Day 2: A Beachy Day For A Luau

After a delicious breakfast at Hotel Wailea’s aptly titled The Restaurant (highly recommend the crabcake Benedict), we headed to nearby White Rock Beach to swim in the ocean and relax on the sand. Later that day, we headed to Marriott’s Wailea Beach Resort for the Te Au Moana Luau, where we dined on traditional Hawaiian dishes family-style and enjoyed the show, which included live music, hula, and Polynesian dances along the oceanfront.
Day 3: A Four-Wheeling Adventure

In the morning, we headed to the West Maui Mountains for an ATV adventure. Since I’m a city kid through and through, I don’t drive, so I played passenger princess as my husband navigated the rugged paths, following our guide to breathtaking views of the Waiheʻe Valley and coastline.

After a fun day, we wound down with a romantic sunset dinner at The Birdcage, a Japanese grill located at Hotel Wailea. The snow crab claws, garden salad, and burger were delicious, but the Japanese A5 Wagyu steak was to die for. Even after all that, we still had room for dessert: a Hawaiian variation of Baked Alaska.
Day 4: A Spa Day & Sunset Cruise

After an early breakfast, my husband and I took advantage of Hotel Wailea’s in-room spa treatments, and each of us got a relaxing deep-tissue massage. The rest of the day, we took it easy, lounging at the pool cabanas for lunch and then heading to Maalaea Harbor for Alii Nui’s Royal Sunset Dinner at Sea. Aboard a catamaran, we enjoyed a five-course meal as we watched the rain clear up and rainbows appear before a magnificent Maui sunset.

On our last full day in Maui, we had to experience a ride on the Road to Hana, a winding, scenic roadway through the island’s tropical east coast. We had a private tour with Epic Maui Hikes, which took us to gorgeous rainforest sights, a black sand beach, and beautiful waterfalls (we swam in one). Our guide also fished for fresh shrimp and grilled it for lunch, and on the way back, we stopped by Hoʻokipa Beach Park to see sea turtles lounging in the sand.

It was an exciting way to wrap up our honeymoon in Maui, which was as adventurous and relaxing as we had wanted from the start. I don’t think that would’ve been possible if I had to worry about planning it before my wedding.

items.title: Help, My Situationship Wants To Leave Her Wife For Me!
items.description: Q: I’m 27, poly, and have been seeing a married woman (34) for five months. She and her wife (36) decided to open their relationship shortly before we met, and from the start, I was clear that I wasn’t looking for anything serious. She said she was on the same
items.author: Sophia Benoit
paragraphs: Q: I’m 27, poly, and have been seeing a married woman (34) for five months. She and her wife (36) decided to open their relationship shortly before we met, and from the start, I was clear that I wasn’t looking for anything serious. She said she was on the same page.

We see each other about once a week, and our connection is really fantastic — incredible chemistry, fun dates, interesting conversations, amazing sex! I haven’t been excited about someone like this in a while, and I’m very happy with our situation as it is.

Last week, she told me she wants to leave her wife and be with me. What?! She says their marriage has been rocky for a while, and being with me has made her realize she deserves to be happier. I don’t want to lead her on, and I feel guilty for any role I played in blowing up her marriage and hurting her wife. But I also would hate to lose something that feels special. Is there any way to salvage this?
A: When you say “salvage this,” do you mean the relationship you were previously enjoying? No. No, I do not think you can salvage that exact thing.

And while you might be able to retain some parts of this connection, I would not recommend it for a myriad of reasons. You have very different feelings for each other, and communication isn’t getting through on either side. I mean, she — seemingly without any prior indication of her plans — left her wife. After telling you that she was on the same page. That page being: not looking for anything serious!

Maybe she didn’t leave her wife exclusively for the sake of getting more serious with you, but she certainly seems to see that as part of her next steps. That is a whole lot of action for her to take without several honest discussions.

Plus, leaving her wife and jumping into a relationship (or ratcheting an existing one up to a new level) is a horrible idea. She’s gotta sit with herself for a bit. She has to ask herself hard questions, not just flee to the next fun thing.
And I’m sure you two do have fun together! But it’s easy to enjoy sexy hang-out bang-outs once a week. It’s a lot harder to have nonstop laughs when you have to file taxes together.
She is looking for something that doesn’t exist, and you are hoping to maintain something that can’t exist anymore. This is partly because her marriage is no longer there to act as a counterbalance.

I have a few friends who are in open relationships, and often, part of the draw is that the married person has other people to rely on and do life with. Taking turns cleaning the litter box and planning your White Elephant exchange with the in-laws don’t just provide structure — they also create comfort (if you zoom way, way out). It does not sound like you’d like to be the person picking up her prescriptions or listening to the 4,048th story about her boss being incompetent. You were, in fact, clear up front about wanting to keep this casual!

Without the counterbalance of her having another partner, I suspect this relationship will lose its zhuzh. Going from a once-a-week dinner date to a thrice-weekly sit-around-and-watch-Traitors-in-sweatpants situation changes things.

You might be saying, “OK, Sophia, what if she agrees to just keep it casual?” It’s a no from me, dawg. Letting a relationship simmer on the back burner with someone who wants pan-seared romance is torture for both of you.

For you, it would mean repeatedly shutting intimacy down, or feeling like “the bad guy” for not wanting the same things she does. For her, it would mean trying to keep a leash on what she’s been feeling (something she’s probably already been doing) and feeling like the “the bad guy” for constantly pushing for more.
Neither of you is bad! You just want different things.

items.title: 'm 25, I Make $145K & I Feel Like I Would Be A Child Bride If I Got Engaged Or Married Anytime Soon
items.description: A Week In New York, NY On A $145,000 Salary
items.author: R
paragraphs: A Week In New York, NY On A $145,000 Salary
This week: An associate working in finance who makes $145,000 per year and spends it on her $40 Spotify "family" plan.

If you'd like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we're not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.
Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We'd love to hear your thoughts here.
Editor's Note: This is a follow-up diary. Read the previous one here.
Joint Income/Financial Setup: My boyfriend, J. makes $80,000 per year, but we don't combine finances. I pay 60% of the rent, and we split everything else 50/50.
Assets: These are only my assets — I don't have a clear view of my partner's finances.
401(k) (mostly Roth, some traditional): $33,359.25
Brokerage account: $28,434.90
Debt: About $10K on my credit cards this month, which I will pay in full when they are due.
Paycheck Amount (monthly): $7014.72
Housing Costs: $2,500 (I live with J. in a studio and he pays $1,500)
Internet: $59.99 (split with J.)
Electricity: ~$100 (on average, split with J.)
Phone: $0 (my work pays for it)
Lifetime membership: $123.97
Healthcare copay: $15 (comes out of my gross paycheck)
Brokerage investment: $550
Roth IRA investment: $1000 (once I hit the cap, this is being re-directed to brokerage)
Renters insurance: $146 (split with J.)
Amazon Prime Young Adult: $73.14
Capital One Venture X: $395
Amex Gold: $325 (for the past two years, I've gotten $100 off for having a corporate Amex)
Chase Sapphire Reserve: $795 (in theory I have renewed, but I think I'm downgrading to the Preferred, which is $95 per year)
YNAB: $115.54 (I share with J. but I don't charge him).
Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?

Yes, 100%. Both of my parents have advanced degrees and were the first in their families to attend higher education, so it wasn't a question of whether or not I would attend university, but where. They attended school outside the US, so their ability to help me through the college application process was limited. Luckily, I attended an excellent public school and had incredibly pushy parents. My parents started saving for school in a 529 plan when I was born, and my university provided ample need-based financial aid. Since my parents made undergraduate education (at the best schools we could get into) an expectation in our house, they felt responsible for paying for our degrees after any scholarships and aid we received. If I have a family, I will do the exact same thing because it allowed me and my brother to shoot for the stars when it came to colleges. Both of my parents have PhDs, so their expectation was actually that I also get a JD, MD, or PhD of some kind. They were the ones who pushed me to do the Master's when I was on the fence about it, as I mentioned in my previous Money Diary.
Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?

My parents have always been very frugal people, so most of our conversations about money revolved around saving money for emergencies. I didn't receive much of an education about finances directly, but I was aware that my parents had things like a mortgage, retirement accounts, and life insurance. I'm really interested in personal finance, so before starting college, I did an entire course to educate myself and be as set up for living on my own as I could be.
What was your first job and why did you get it?

My first real W-2 job was an internship within my state's judicial system. It was pretty basic office work, but I got to listen to a lot of podcasts and music on the job! Where I went to school, families were optimizing their kids' résumés from birth, so I got this summer job to improve my own résumé. My parents didn't actually give me access to any of the money I earned from my summer jobs until I got to college, which I have mixed feelings about, but this probably ensured I didn't waste all my money on fast food and clothes (which I did during undergrad anyways).
Did you worry about money growing up?

Yes and no. My father grew up in poverty, and that mindset was reflected in our household. He would always compare how much things would cost to how many loaves of bread he could buy with that amount (with one loaf somehow remaining constantly at $1 to this day). I was told “no” all the time for things like snacks and toys, though my mother would occasionally go shopping with me and hide purchases from my father. This kind of restriction, though, meant that when one of my parents lost their job during the recession, I didn't feel the impact. We would visit one of my parent's home countries every year, which I later found out was paid for by my mom's family during some difficult times. Ultimately, there was always money for necessities, school activities, and anything my parents thought would help my brother and I academically, so I never felt worried.
Do you worry about money now?

Not really. I opened a Roth IRA when I was 18 and have been pretty savvy with savings and things like credit card points. The problem for me is that I'm a big saver who also likes to spend, especially on little treats, and now that I have a big girl salary, the treats aren't so little. I always hit my savings goals every month, but I always think that I could and should be saving more of my salary for things like a wedding or a down payment on a house. This is mostly because I have friends already doing both of these things and other friends working at crazy startups and making a ton of money when they IPO. I know the mindset of comparison isn't healthy or reasonable, but it's hard to stop these pretty ingrained habits.
At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?

I would say I became completely financially responsible for myself this year when my job started paying for my phone plan, and the last financial tie to my parents fell away. While I'm technically on their health insurance, I have been using my own insurance through work since I moved to New York two years ago. My parents will probably always be my financial safety net, and maybe even J.'s if we get married, but my parents would never think of making me feel bad about it. I think they know that if I needed their help, it would be because something truly bad happened rather than me being irresponsible with money given my saving habits.
Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.

In my last Money Diary, I was given a "loan" from my parents for my Master's degree. After half a year of payments, they decided to forgive the loan on the condition that I put the same amount of money monthly ($1,000) into retirement or other investments. They reasoned that my brother's undergraduate education cost the same as my undergraduate education, plus my Master's, and they wanted to be fair to us. They don't check on this, but I'm very diligent about it. I guess my parents "forgiving" their loan to me for my Master's program might count, but otherwise, no. It will hopefully be a long time until my parents pass, and any inheritance from any of my grandparents would go to my parents directly.

I definitely had some high-ticket items this week, but I think the other spending is pretty in line with regular weeks for me. Unfortunately, that's not a great thing because I always exceed the budget I give myself for dining out and groceries. I need to either learn to say no a bit more or be more thoughtful about buying snacks and drinks ahead of time, rather than making impulse purchases.
The first step to getting your financial life in order is tracking what you spend — to try on your own, check out our guide to managing your money every day. For more Money Diaries, click here.
