items.title: Why ‘patient influencers’ should come with a health warning | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Emily Miller was a 20-year-old university student in the UK when, shortly after a COVID-19 infection, she started having sensations that mirrored a heart attack. Other bewildering symptoms followed – dizziness, fainting, and uncontrollable muscle spasms. ‘By t
items.author: Zoe Cunniffe
paragraphs: Emily Miller was a 20-year-old university student in the UK when, shortly after a COVID-19 infection, she started having sensations that mirrored a heart attack. Other bewildering symptoms followed – dizziness, fainting, and uncontrollable muscle spasms. ‘By the time my classes ended I felt drunk, disoriented and my ears would ring,’ Miller wrote in a pinned post on her Instagram page, @thatgirlwithlongcovid_. ‘I couldn’t remember getting home from class.’

Miller is a ‘patient influencer’ – one of a growing number of people who share vivid accounts of their health experiences on social media. She first started posting about life with long COVID because her experience was incredibly isolating while her peers were still partying and going to classes like normal, and she hoped posting online would connect her with other young people in the same situation. Today, she has a small but engaged community of about 4,000 followers on Instagram and 3,000 on TikTok. Miller shares intimate details of life with long COVID, such as photo timelines outlining the onset of her symptoms and videos discussing everyday difficulties.

Patient influencers like Miller often build deeply personal bonds with their followers, many of whom live with the same condition. On a recent pair of Miller’s posts featuring the medical interventions that did and didn’t help her, followers have posted long comments detailing their own treatment experiences and thanking her for her advice.

As valuable as chronic illness content is for spreading awareness and building communities around stigmatised illnesses – maybe you too have found a sense of support and camaraderie from individuals whose experiences you identify with – there are also concerning aspects to this new trend. At the heart of it is the way social media serves up a distorted version of reality, drawing on selected content from patient influencers in ways that often don’t reflect the full range of chronic illness experiences people have in real life.

Patient influencers are often well meaning but can find themselves forced to choose between leaning into these narratives and losing engagement. ‘You’re not [posting] for followers or to get as many views as you possibly can,’ says Miller, ‘but you do want [your content] to be reaching the right people.’

Like Miller, Kaysie was in college when she first developed symptoms she couldn’t make sense of. Along with dizziness and sleepiness, Kaysie started falling down frequently. ‘It was super unclear exactly what the problem was,’ she says.

Hoping to alleviate her uncertainty, Kaysie turned to Reddit – another online environment where patient influencers share their stories and advice – where she saw her symptoms reflected in people’s posts about postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), an autonomic nervous system disorder that causes dizziness and fainting. Reading other people’s stories was comforting, giving Kaysie a framework to make sense of what was happening.

Diagnosis of a chronic illness can take years, particularly for conditions like POTS that aren’t well-understood, so it’s understandable why patients like Kaysie may be drawn to social media’s focus on diagnostic labels (a 2025 study led by the paediatrician Lindsey Daon analysed hundreds of chronic illness posts on Instagram and found that 87 per cent mentioned a specific diagnostic label). Yet this desire for the certainty of a diagnosis can lead to problems. Patient influencers with their own specific diagnosis often list the early signs of their illness that they originally overlooked – such as constant exhaustion, joint pain and dizziness. But symptoms like these can be associated with many different conditions, and followers who latch onto an influencer’s diagnosis often do so prematurely.
People become vigilant to body sensations that match their expectations, and filter out sensations that don’t

This is exactly what happened to Kaysie. Two years after being convinced by patient influencers that she had POTS, she was diagnosed by medical professionals with a different condition – narcolepsy. She learned that she was actually falling down because narcolepsy can cause cataplexy, a sudden, temporary loss of muscle control. ‘I definitely ended up on a weird path that wasn’t quite accurate,’ she says.

A related concern is that patient influencers can teach their followers to centre their own identities around a diagnostic label. ‘I’ve seen people that have ultimately felt a lot of grief because they really feel that they don’t have much left, other than their illness,’ says Sara Davin, a pain psychologist at the Cleveland Clinic.

Patient influencers could also be affecting their followers’ symptoms through a process called social transmission. Health researchers believe this phenomenon occurs because, when people develop expectations about what they should experience, they become vigilant to body sensations that match these expectations, and filter out sensations that don’t.

A 2023 study makes this process vivid. Participants observed someone else undergoing a virtual reality (VR) experience before undergoing it themselves. What participants didn’t know was that some of the people they observed were actors, who modelled the symptoms of cybersickness, a feeling of nausea and discomfort sometimes caused by VR.

Participants were told that the study was about online learning in VR, assessed through a series of memory-based questions, but the researchers’ real aim was to measure participants’ cybersickness. They found that those who viewed an apparently sick actor subsequently reported feeling more cybersickness symptoms themselves, compared with other participants who saw someone use the VR without getting sick. The study serves as a proof of concept confirming that seeing other people’s health experiences can shape our own.

Social media may be an especially fertile breeding ground for this kind of symptom transmission because of its ability to rapidly spread information across large populations. ‘In real life, you only have so much that you can actually observe,’ explains Winston Tan, lead author of the VR study. In contrast, he says that as soon as you go online, you can easily access thousands of people’s stories – and once you start engaging with them, the algorithm is more likely to keep feeding them to you, further heightening your expectations about having these experiences yourself.

None of this means that people’s health experiences should be dismissed just because they see themselves in patient influencer content – after all, the initial draw of the content is that it reflects what they’ve already been experiencing. In these cases, social transmission may be less about causing symptoms in people who were completely healthy and more about intensifying existing symptoms or adding new ones.

One of the most prominent social media-transmitted illnesses is the ‘TikTok tics’ of 2020-21, when neurologists began seeing increasing numbers of teenage patients with tics, or sudden, involuntary movements and sounds. Experts believe this trend was driven by the spread of videos from users with Tourette syndrome, and exacerbated by the anxiety of the COVID-19 pandemic (anxiety is thought to increase the social transmission of symptoms).
Repeated exposure to this highly medicalised content could prompt users to develop false beliefs

Unfortunately, social media algorithms tend to favour exactly those health-related posts that evoke fear and stress. Breonna Winfield (posting on Instagram as @healthywealthydivinesociety) coaches patient influencers and other content creators on how to build their followings. She explains that engagement is best when content is ‘drastic’ or ‘over the top’. She tells me about one particularly successful post that came from a client whose doctors repeatedly told her she just needed to lose weight – until, finally, the client learned that her symptoms were caused by a 30-pound fibroid lodged in her uterus. ‘People were shocked,’ Winfield says. ‘Personal stories that connect with their audience, those go the farthest.’

Daon’s study of Instagram posts backs up this idea. She found that posts featuring photos of invasive medical equipment tended to overperform, or receive more engagement, than other posts from the same account.

She warns that repeated exposure to this highly medicalised content could prompt users to develop false beliefs about the level of treatment their own condition requires. After all, research has shown that knowledge of other people’s personal experiences plays a key role in patients’ healthcare decision-making. Daon tells me she has even noticed patients asking for invasive treatments such as feeding tubes just because they’ve seen them online.

While this phenomenon may seem harmless in a world where doctors still need to prescribe treatments before patients can access them, research shows that patient requests have major influence over what physicians prescribe. (In one study, patients with sciatica symptoms who requested a strong narcotic were significantly more likely to receive one than those who didn’t – which is concerning, the study’s authors noted, because narcotic pain medications aren’t generally recommended for managing sciatica.)

Of course, most patient influencers want to help their followers, not hurt them – and when created with that intention, their content can be a source of comfort and patient education. Now that she has a confirmed diagnosis, Kaysie finds personal stories from Reddit much more useful than she used to. ‘You Google narcolepsy symptoms, and it’s always very general diagnostic information,’ she says. Reading about others’ experiences online has helped her figure out things that her doctor wouldn’t have known about, such as the fact that her cataplexy can be triggered by laughter.

Ella, a young woman who experiences chronic pain, says she finds social media useful for managing her symptoms even though she doesn’t have a specific diagnosis. ‘You don’t have to be diagnosed with something to treat yourself,’ she says. She’s also found ways to protect herself from the risks of harmful or misleading content by being more savvy online. She’s come across illness-related content that she found problematic at times – posts that seemed focused on stirring up emotions more than anything – but she’s noticed that avoiding engaging with this content has trained her algorithm to give her less of it. ‘I only interact with posts that are either educational, people being curious, or some kind of positive take,’ Ella explains. ‘I don’t want to just see people fight about things.’

Other ways to benefit from patient influencers while protecting yourself from the risks include deliberately seeking out people’s positive experiences (in the cybersickness study, researchers found that participants were actually less likely to experience cybersickness if they observed someone undergoing VR without these symptoms than if they didn’t observe anyone at all).
She wants her content to ease viewers’ anxieties, which means working against the algorithm’s desire for emotional stimulation

It’s also important to be wary of posts that centre on medical treatment, keeping in mind that one person’s need for a treatment does not mean everyone with the same condition will need it too. Other people’s experiences can be a valuable source of emotional support and lifestyle advice, but when it comes to the biomedical side of life with chronic illness, speaking to a doctor or finding reputable online sources is more reliable.

Meanwhile, even as the algorithm’s authority over social media content increases, there are still creators who refuse to tailor their content to its demands. ‘It’s important for me to be authentic,’ says Talia Cohen who as ‘Dr Talia PhD’ on Instagram provides chronic illness support to her 14,000-plus followers. ‘If I change myself for the algorithm, I won’t be attracting the people to my community who could really benefit.’

Cohen, who lives with chronic illness herself, wants her content to ease viewers’ anxieties, which means working against the algorithm’s desire for emotional stimulation. ‘I have a very calm tone,’ she says. ‘I don’t want to do anything that contributes to nervous system dysregulation when most people with chronic health conditions already struggle with that.’

Most of her posts are reassuring and involve either a video of her speaking or a line of text against a muted background. One from June contains a carousel of reminders that people with chronic illness may need, including sentiments such as ‘It’s allowed to be painful to think about what your body used to be able to do’ and ‘Compassion for yourself during flares is the best medicine there is.’

Refusing to conform to the algorithm doesn’t happen without consequences, of course, and Cohen has seen drops in engagement as the algorithm continues to shift its priorities. Still, she says: ‘My content will find the right people that it’s meant to find. Even if I’m helping just a few people, it’s worth it.’

items.title: How to help someone whose thinking seems delusional | Psyche Guides
items.description: isa licensed clinical psychologist and assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale University. She directs the Specialized Treatment Early in Psychosis (STEP) Learning Collaborative, Connecticut’s statewide learning healthcare system for young people experiencin
items.author: Laura Yoviene Sykes
paragraphs: isa licensed clinical psychologist and assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale University. She directs the Specialized Treatment Early in Psychosis (STEP) Learning Collaborative, Connecticut’s statewide learning healthcare system for young people experiencing recent-onset schizophrenia spectrum disorders, and leads family services for the STEP Clinic. Her work is also informed by her personal experience as a family member of someone who lived with a schizophrenia spectrum disorder.

isa licensed clinical psychologist and assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale University. She directs the Specialized Treatment Early in Psychosis (STEP) Learning Collaborative, Connecticut’s statewide learning healthcare system for young people experiencing recent-onset schizophrenia spectrum disorders, and leads family services for the STEP Clinic. Her work is also informed by her personal experience as a family member of someone who lived with a schizophrenia spectrum disorder.

A ‘delusion’ might sound like a belief that is obviously unreal. But if someone in your life is experiencing one, it will certainly feel real to them. In some cases, it might even seem plausible to you at first – especially when it draws on real experiences or common fears.
A delusion could look like:
a friend or partner feeling convinced that they’ve been sabotaged by their co-workers, and hyperfocusing on past conversations and emails;
a university student believing that social media posts and songs contain messages intended specifically for them, making it harder to focus on anything else; or
a family member saying they have been chosen for a special mission – that they are the only person who can expose a vast network of corruption.

If you have a loved one who has a concerning belief and who you think might show signs of delusional thinking, it’s normal to feel frightened for them, overwhelmed and unsure how to respond. You might wonder whether it’s best to question the belief, to just ignore it or to encourage the person to get help. Many people find themselves caught between two fears: the fear of saying too much and making things worse, and the fear of saying too little and overlooking a serious problem.

This Guide is for people in your situation. As a clinical psychologist, I’ve spent much of my career working with people who are experiencing delusions and other symptoms of psychosis, as well as with the loved ones who support them. My approach is informed by a framework called cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp), which emphasises curiosity, collaboration and reducing distress. I’ll draw on these experiences throughout this Guide. After saying a bit more about what delusions are, I’ll describe how to consider whether someone in your life is truly experiencing one – and if so, what you can do to help.
What mental health experts mean by ‘delusions’

In everyday language, people use the word ‘delusion’ loosely, but clinically it refers to a belief that remains fixed despite clear evidence to the contrary, and one that is not widely shared within a person’s cultural or social context. What matters is not just the content of the belief, but how a person experiences it.

Often, it’s not one unusual statement that alerts loved ones, but the growing certainty a person feels and the increasing distress and disruption to daily life. I’ve seen versions of this pattern many times. For example, parents might initially hear their university-age child say that a group of students in the library seemed to be watching them, or that cars of the same make or colour kept appearing around campus. The comments may sound a little odd, but still plausible enough that the parents brush them off. Over time, the student may become increasingly certain that the other students, the cars and other seemingly unrelated events are all connected and are evidence that someone is monitoring them. The parents might eventually find out that the young person has lost weight and has been avoiding the dining hall and other places because they no longer feel safe there.

Some people have a single delusional belief, while others have several, often with related themes. They may occur on their own, or alongside other symptoms of psychosis – such as hearing or perceiving things that other people don’t, or disorganised speech or behaviour. Delusions can also coincide with mood disorders, substance use or periods of extreme stress or sleep disruption. (They are also seen in medical conditions such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease, and can appear at any stage of life, but this Guide focuses primarily on adults and adolescents who have delusions in the context of mental health conditions.) For loved ones, it is usually less important to determine the exact cause than to notice that something has changed and that it’s affecting the person’s wellbeing.

You do not need to diagnose someone, nor convince them that their belief is wrong, in order to help. In fact, approaching them with curiosity and compassion, and focusing on staying connected, can help preserve the trust between you and make it easier for them to accept support.
It’s normal to feel unsure about how to respond to concerning beliefs. You don’t need to convince someone that their belief is wrong in order to help.
Look for the signs of a delusion. Not all unusual beliefs are delusions. Delusions are marked by strong conviction, frequency and intensity of interest, and negative impacts on the person’s life.
Prioritise your connection. Stay connected in ways that are not about the belief, such as through shared routines or talking about everyday things.
Express your curiosity. Show that you are trying to understand what they are experiencing, rather than simply judging or correcting their belief.
Validate their emotions. Tell them that you take their experience and feelings seriously, even if you don’t agree with their belief or interpretation of events.
Gently explore alternatives to their belief. After hearing them out, you might be able to raise other ways of seeing the situation and create a little more room for uncertainty and reflection.
Encourage support-seeking. Connect the idea of getting help from a therapist or doctor to goals that you and the person both agree on, such as feeling less stressed or staying connected to others.
Reach out for professional guidance. You can also seek assistance directly, whether the signs that concern you are moderate or growing more urgent.
Look for the signs of a delusion

Not all unusual or strongly held beliefs are delusions. For example, anxiety can lead to intense thoughts like ‘Something bad is going to happen’ or ‘People are judging me,’ but these tend to shift over time and respond to reassurance. Similarly, people who have experienced actual harm or discrimination might understandably be vigilant in certain situations. And cultural, ideological or religious beliefs that seem unfamiliar to you would not be considered clinical delusions if they are widely held and meaningful within a person’s cultural group.
To understand whether a belief is a delusion rather than a more common or understandable way of thinking, clinicians look at three core features:
Conviction: how strongly the belief is held, and whether the person can consider other explanations.
Frequency and intensity: how often the belief comes up and how much it occupies the person’s attention.
Impact: how much the belief is affecting a person’s emotions, behaviour and day-to-day life.

When you are concerned about a belief that someone has, it’s natural to focus on whether the belief is true. But a more helpful approach is to consider these key features. To start, you might ask yourself: What has changed, and how is this affecting them?
You might begin to notice patterns such as:
growing certainty or difficulty considering other explanations;
the belief coming up more often or taking up more mental space;
increased fear, anxiety or urgency;
changes in behaviour, such as avoiding certain situations, withdrawing socially or heightened alertness to possible threats; or
a negative impact on school, work or relationships.

Consider a relatively common scenario: someone becomes very interested in an online conspiracy theory. They bring it up from time to time and seem to believe parts of it strongly, but they also recognise that others see it differently and they acknowledge that it is a controversial interpretation. The belief is shared by a broader online community, does not dominate their attention and is not significantly affecting their daily life. The belief may seem unusual or concerning to you, but those features would make it less suggestive of a delusion.

In contrast, consider someone who becomes convinced that posts on social media or comments made on television are sending messages specifically to them. At first, they mention it occasionally, but over time, they become increasingly certain that the messages are intentional and meant to warn them. They spend hours looking for connections, have difficulty considering that the posts or broadcasts may be unrelated to them, and begin missing school or work because they feel the need to keep monitoring the messages. Here, the strong conviction, increasing preoccupation, and disruption to daily life would be indicative of a possible delusion and potentially a need for professional help.
It is also important to look at the broader picture. A concerning belief or potential delusion may occur alongside other experiences, such as:
hearing or perceiving things that others do not;
unusually elevated or irritable mood;
disorganised speech or behaviour;
changes in thinking or memory;

These signs can provide important context and strengthen the case for seeking direct guidance from a clinical professional. At the same time, none of these features allows you to diagnose someone yourself. The goal is not to decide with certainty that a person is having a delusion, but to recognise when a pattern is concerning enough to warrant a closer look or professional support.
Prioritise your connection
If someone is showing signs of delusional thinking, it is very difficult to make progress starting from a place of conflict. Good communication strategies work best when the relationship feels safe.

In practice, this means staying connected in ways that are not centred on the belief. Spending time together, continuing shared routines or talking about everyday things can help maintain a sense of normality and trust. In many ways, the relationship itself can be a foundation for change. If someone feels judged or corrected, they are more likely to become guarded. By contrast, if they feel understood and respected, they are more likely to stay engaged, reflect on their experience and accept support. The way you show up in everyday interactions could matter as much as what you say about the belief itself.

Staying connected can be challenging if you become part of the delusional belief yourself: for example, if the person is convinced that you cannot be trusted, that you are working against them, or even that you aren’t who you say you are. In these situations, if the person can tolerate your presence, try to preserve the relationship through ordinary activities or neutral topics. But if being around you seems to increase their fear, mistrust or agitation, it may be necessary to step back and ask another trusted person in their support network to take a more active role for a time. If you ever feel unsafe, prioritise your safety and get support (see the later step Reach Out for Professional Guidance).

One of the most important principles when talking with someone about a concerning belief is to approach them with curiosity and compassion rather than confront them. Although it is very understandable to want to challenge the belief directly – especially when it’s causing distress – in most cases, a direct challenge does not help. Because the belief feels real to the person, it can lead to defensiveness, pulling away or increased distress.
Curiosity communicates that you are trying to understand the person’s experience rather than judge or correct it. You could use open-ended questions such as:
‘Can you tell me more about what’s been happening?’
‘When did you first notice this?’
‘What has that been like for you?’

For example, if someone says they believe they are being watched, you might ask them to tell you what their experience has been like. They might say that they feel they can never relax, or that several events now seem connected. You could then ask how they have been making sense of the experience. They might respond: ‘I think someone is tracking me. I keep seeing the same kinds of cars, and people seem to show up wherever I go.’ Rather than immediately challenging that interpretation, you could stay curious, asking what feels most convincing, or most stressful, about the experience. You can also check in to make sure you are correctly understanding what they mean: ‘Am I getting that right?’ And, if not, then: ‘Thank you for clarifying. I want to understand what you’re going through.’ This kind of back-and-forth can help you understand how the person is interpreting what is happening, how strongly they hold the belief and how much distress or disruption it is causing.

It is common to feel hesitant about asking these kinds of questions. In practice, though, respectful curiosity often helps the person feel less alone. Focusing on these questions can also help you avoid defaulting to rapid-fire interrogation (‘Are you sure? What proof do you have?’), which can feel like a challenge rather than an attempt to help.

Even with the best intentions, most people feel a strong pull to correct or reassure someone who’s describing a delusion. This is sometimes called the ‘righting reflex’. You might feel compelled to say things like ‘That’s not happening’ or ‘You’re overthinking this.’ These responses might come from a place of care, but they are likely to backfire. If you’re feeling this way, it can help to notice that urge without acting on it right away. You might remind yourself that you do not have to settle the question of what is true at that moment. If the person feels frightened, confused, defensive or overwhelmed, the more useful first step is usually to try to understand what they are experiencing and respond to that.

A helpful way to think about this is that, while the belief may not be accurate, the emotion is always real. Acknowledging the emotional experience helps the person feel seen and understood. Sometimes it can help to gently connect how the other person is feeling to what they are experiencing in their day-to-day life: ‘It sounds like you’ve been really on edge, and that’s why it’s been hard to go out or be around people.’

There are ways to disclose that you don’t agree with the person’s belief or interpretation of a situation while still being supportive. For example, you might say: ‘I’m not interpreting the situation the same way, but I can see how real and upsetting this feels to you.’ This allows you to be supportive without colluding with the belief or setting aside your own perspective.

When someone feels understood, they are often less defensive and more able to stay in the conversation. This creates the conditions for trust, problem-solving and greater flexibility. It makes it easier to help them consider other ways of seeing their experience (without feeling confronted) and accept support when needed. We’ll turn to these things next.
Gently explore alternatives to their belief

As your conversations continue, one goal is to support greater flexibility over time. By flexibility, I mean helping the person become less certain that there is only one possible explanation for what they are experiencing, and more able to consider other possibilities. Typically, when flexibility increases, the beliefs also become less preoccupying and disruptive for the person who holds them.

When the person feels heard and the conversation is calm, you may be able to explore other possibilities. It can help to first ask permission: ‘Would it be OK if we thought through a few possibilities together?’
‘What do you think is the most likely explanation?’
‘Have there been times when it felt less certain?’
‘Have you considered any other possible explanations?’ (You could ask about the possibility that seemingly related events are a coincidence, for example.)

For example, if someone says: ‘I know those people were talking about me,’ you might ask: ‘What makes that feel like the most likely explanation?’ After listening (and reflecting and validating how they feel), you could follow with: ‘Is there any other way you could imagine that situation?’ They might say: ‘Maybe they were talking about something else, but I still think it was probably me.’ That may seem like a small change, but being able to hold even one alternative alongside the original belief can be meaningful.

Your aim is not to replace the belief with a new explanation or convince them they are wrong. Rather, it is to help create a little more room for uncertainty and reflection. A change in how someone relates to a belief often happens gradually. Rather than trying to resolve everything at once, it can help to think in terms of ‘planting seeds’ over time. A foundation of curiosity and validation usually needs to come first: the person is more likely to consider other possibilities when they feel heard, respected and less defensive. Moments of gentle reflection can build on that foundation and create space to begin to question the belief or consider alternatives.

This kind of exploration will be more useful in some situations than others. If someone is very distressed, highly certain of the belief or amid an acute episode of psychosis, they may have much more difficulty considering alternatives. In those moments, it is usually more helpful to stay calm, maintain connection through validation and help them access professional support rather than to keep pressing for a different interpretation.

If your concerns continue, it can help to raise the idea of seeking professional support, such as a therapist, primary care doctor or psychiatrist. Rather than focusing directly on the belief, connect the idea of seeking help to goals that you and the person both agree on, such as feeling less stressed, sleeping better, staying connected to others or getting back on track with school or work.

You might say, for example: ‘It seems like this experience has been really exhausting’ or ‘I can see how much this has been getting in the way of things you care about.’ From there, you can gently suggest support: ‘I wonder if talking with someone could help with some of that.’ Framing support in this way can feel more collaborative because it starts with the person’s own concerns and goals rather than asking them to agree that their belief is a symptom or accept a particular diagnosis.

If your loved one becomes upset or feels that you are dismissing their experience, it can help to step back from the suggestion of getting help and return first to validation. You might say: ‘I can see that this feels very stressful for you, and I don’t want you to feel like I’m dismissing what you’re going through.’ Once the person feels heard, you can leave the door open for a future conversation by adding something like: ‘If you ever want help figuring out how to make this feel less overwhelming, I’m here.’ When the person is not ready, you may need to return to the conversation at a later point.
Reach out for professional guidance

If you are worried about someone, you do not have to wait for the person to agree to seek help before reaching out for guidance yourself. You can contact a general practitioner or another primary care provider, a mental health professional, a specialised early-psychosis programme or a crisis service to describe what you are noticing and ask about next steps.

It can also be helpful to reach out to a professional for guidance about what you are noticing even when signs of possible delusional thinking are still relatively subtle. This might include various signs already discussed in this Guide, such as a loved one’s increasing distress or fear, withdrawal from others or beliefs seeming to interfere with daily life. Reaching out early can help clarify what is happening and provide support before the concerns escalate. (See the Links & Books section at the end of the Guide for examples of support-seeking resources.)

More urgent support may be needed if you notice a rapid decline in the person’s functioning, an inability to meet their basic needs, or extreme fear or agitation, or if you have concerns about safety. A local mobile crisis service may be able to provide timely assessment and support. If there is an immediate, life-threatening emergency, such as imminent harm to the person or someone else, contact local emergency services. Staying calm, giving the person space and speaking clearly can help reduce escalation while crisis support is being arranged.
In any of these situations, remember that you do not need to be certain about what is happening to take your concerns seriously or to reach out for guidance.
What recovery can look like

For someone who has experienced delusional thinking, recovery does not always mean that the delusion completely disappears. More often, the person becomes less preoccupied with the belief, feels less distress, experiences more flexibility and starts to function better in day-to-day life.

With support – which frequently includes therapy and medication – many people experience a meaningful improvement over time. For example, the student who felt certain that social media messages were directed at them might still occasionally have that thought, but it might feel less convincing and come up less often. They may be able to use social media again without becoming preoccupied and stay engaged in classes. Similarly, someone who felt they were being monitored may continue to have moments of doubt about whether that has happened – but they might stop avoiding places and no longer feel on edge the way they did before. The belief may still be there, but it no longer drives their behaviour or dominates their daily life.

Sometimes a delusional belief becomes less intense as stress decreases, sleep improves or the circumstances around it change. But when a belief is persistent, highly distressing or part of a mental health condition such as schizophrenia, another psychotic disorder or a mood disorder with psychotic features, professional treatment is often important. Some people with these conditions need support for a shorter period, while the majority benefit from ongoing care.

Families and loved ones are not expected to act as therapists or replace professional care. Rather, the tools in this Guide are meant to aid and empower you in how you communicate and stay connected, alongside appropriate professional support.
Why delusions feel so real

Every person’s brain relies on mental shortcuts to make sense of the world quickly. This helps us interpret situations and respond efficiently, but it can also lead to common thinking patterns such as jumping to conclusions, black-and-white thinking, and catastrophising. Most of the time, these patterns are flexible and can be reconsidered. Under certain conditions, however – including stress, sleep disruption or mental health conditions such as psychosis – these thinking patterns can become more intense.

When someone is vulnerable to or experiencing psychosis, for example, certain ways of thinking often become more pronounced. A person might draw strong conclusions from limited information, begin to see personal meaning in neutral events or focus on information that supports a belief while overlooking other possible explanations. These patterns can reinforce one another over time and contribute to the development of delusional beliefs.

From this perspective, delusions can be understood as the brain’s attempt to make sense of experiences that feel confusing, intense or overwhelming. The delusional belief that results feels like a clear and convincing conclusion based on what the person is noticing and interpreting, even if it does not match how others see the situation.

A common and related part of delusional thinking is a limited ability to recognise that a belief may be inaccurate or part of a mental health condition. This is often referred to as reduced insight. Importantly, this is not the person simply being stubborn or in denial. It reflects a change in how the brain processes and makes sense of experiences. From their perspective, their interpretation feels accurate and logical. They may genuinely feel that nothing is wrong with their belief, or that others are misunderstanding what is happening.

This helps explain why correction or reassurance often does not work. When someone is convinced of their experience, being told they are wrong can feel dismissive or confusing, and it might even lead them to become more certain in their belief. Reduced insight can also affect how someone thinks about getting help. If the experience feels real and accurate, seeking professional help may not make sense to them, at least not at first.

For families and loved ones, understanding this can help to reduce frustration and blame, and encourage a more compassionate, effective approach. With support and treatment, insight often improves, and someone may become better able to reflect on their experiences and consider alternatives to their belief.
If you’re looking for help

In the United States, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) offers a national directory to help find treatment, including early psychosis programmes and specialist care.
In the United Kingdom, the National Health Service (NHS) website provides information on psychosis, including guidance on accessing treatment.
In Australia, Medicare Mental Health is a government-supported service that helps people find mental health support, including early psychosis services.
If you want to learn more about delusions or psychosis

The bookBack to Life, Back to Normality, Volume 2 (2018), edited by Douglas Turkington and Helen Spencer, is an accessible, practical guide for families that explains psychosis through a CBT-informed lens. It includes real-life experiences alongside concrete strategies for supporting a loved one’s recovery.

I helped create a series of videos for families through the STEP Learning Collaborative, part of the Specialized Treatment Early in Psychosis programme. They offer practical, relationship-focused guidance, including communication strategies and role-play demonstrations of how to support individuals experiencing delusions and other symptoms of psychosis.

Voices of Lived Experience, another video series from the STEP Learning Collaborative, features first-person accounts from individuals who’ve experienced psychosis and their caregivers. They describe what these experiences feel like and what support was helpful.

On the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) website, you can find family-friendly resources, education programmes and support groups for those supporting a loved one who’s experiencing psychosis or other mental health concerns.

The LEAP approach is a practical communication framework based on listening, empathising, agreeing and partnering, designed for supporting someone who may not recognise they need help. To find out more, check out the TEDx talk ‘I’m Not Sick, I Don’t Need Help!’ (2017), given by the clinical psychologist Xavier Amador, and the LEAP Institute website.

Psychosis REACH (Recovery by Enabling Adult Carers at Home) is a form of evidence-based training for families that teaches CBT-informed communication and support strategies. You can learn more on the REACH website or by reading the Psyche Guide informed by this approach: ‘How to Support a Loved One Through Psychosis’ (2022) by Akansha Vaswani-Bye.

We work hard to bring you the most trustworthy, expert and up-to-date information on psychology and mental health in our Guides. You can learn more about how we ensure that they are a reliable source of information here. This Guide is provided as general information only. It is not a substitute for independent, professional medical or health advice tailored to your specific circumstances. If you are struggling with psychological difficulties, we encourage you to seek help from a professional source.

A ‘delusion’ might sound like a belief that is obviously unreal. But if someone in your life is experiencing one, it will certainly feel real to them. In some cases, it might even seem plausible to you at first – especially when it draws on real experiences or common fears.
A delusion could look like:
a friend or partner feeling convinced that they’ve been sabotaged by their co-workers, and hyperfocusing on past conversations and emails;
a university student believing that social media posts and songs contain messages intended specifically for them, making it harder to focus on anything else; or
a family member saying they have been chosen for a special mission – that they are the only person who can expose a vast network of corruption.

You might wonder whether it’s best to question the belief, to just ignore it or to encourage the person to get help. Many people find themselves caught between two fears: the fear of saying too much and making things worse, and the fear of saying too little and overlooking a serious problem.

This Guide is for people in your situation. As a clinical psychologist, I’ve spent much of my career working with people who are experiencing delusions and other symptoms of psychosis, as well as with the loved ones who support them. My approach is informed by a framework called cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp), which emphasises curiosity, collaboration and reducing distress. I’ll draw on these experiences throughout this Guide. After saying a bit more about what delusions are, I’ll describe how to consider whether someone in your life is truly experiencing one – and if so, what you can do to help.
What mental health experts mean by ‘delusions’

In everyday language, people use the word ‘delusion’ loosely, but clinically it refers to a belief that remains fixed despite clear evidence to the contrary, and one that is not widely shared within a person’s cultural or social context. What matters is not just the content of the belief, but how a person experiences it.

Often, it’s not one unusual statement that alerts loved ones, but the growing certainty a person feels and the increasing distress and disruption to daily life. I’ve seen versions of this pattern many times. For example, parents might initially hear their university-age child say that a group of students in the library seemed to be watching them, or that cars of the same make or colour kept appearing around campus. The comments may sound a little odd, but still plausible enough that the parents brush them off. Over time, the student may become increasingly certain that the other students, the cars and other seemingly unrelated events are all connected and are evidence that someone is monitoring them. The parents might eventually find out that the young person has lost weight and has been avoiding the dining hall and other places because they no longer feel safe there.

Some people have a single delusional belief, while others have several, often with related themes. They may occur on their own, or alongside other symptoms of psychosis – such as hearing or perceiving things that other people don’t, or disorganised speech or behaviour. Delusions can also coincide with mood disorders, substance use or periods of extreme stress or sleep disruption. (They are also seen in medical conditions such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease, and can appear at any stage of life, but this Guide focuses primarily on adults and adolescents who have delusions in the context of mental health conditions.) ‘Have there been times when it felt less certain?’
‘Have you considered any other possible explanations?’ (You could ask about the possibility that seemingly related events are a coincidence, for example.)

For example, if someone says: ‘I know those people were talking about me,’ you might ask: ‘What makes that feel like the most likely explanation?’ After listening (and reflecting and validating how they feel), you could follow with: ‘Is there any other way you could imagine that situation?’ They might say: ‘Maybe they were talking about something else, but I still think it was probably me.’ That may seem like a small change, but being able to hold even one alternative alongside the original belief can be meaningful.

Your aim is not to replace the belief with a new explanation or convince them they are wrong. Rather, it is to help create a little more room for uncertainty and reflection. A change in how someone relates to a belief often happens gradually. Rather than trying to resolve everything at once, it can help to think in terms of ‘planting seeds’ over time. A foundation of curiosity and validation usually needs to come first: the person is more likely to consider other possibilities when they feel heard, respected and less defensive. Moments of gentle reflection can build on that foundation and create space to begin to question the belief or consider alternatives.

This kind of exploration will be more useful in some situations than others. If someone is very distressed, highly certain of the belief or amid an acute episode of psychosis, they may have much more difficulty considering alternatives. In those moments, it is usually more helpful to stay calm, maintain connection through validation and help them access professional support rather than to keep pressing for a different interpretation.

If your concerns continue, it can help to raise the idea of seeking professional support, such as a therapist, primary care doctor or psychiatrist. Rather than focusing directly on the belief, connect the idea of seeking help to goals that you and the person both agree on, such as feeling less stressed, sleeping better, staying connected to others or getting back on track with school or work.

You might say, for example: ‘It seems like this experience has been really exhausting’ or ‘I can see how much this has been getting in the way of things you care about.’ From there, you can gently suggest support: ‘I wonder if talking with someone could help with some of that.’ Framing support in this way can feel more collaborative because it starts with the person’s own concerns and goals rather than asking them to agree that their belief is a symptom or accept a particular diagnosis.

If your loved one becomes upset or feels that you are dismissing their experience, it can help to step back from the suggestion of getting help and return first to validation. You might say: ‘I can see that this feels very stressful for you, and I don’t want you to feel like I’m dismissing what you’re going through.’ Once the person feels heard, you can leave the door open for a future conversation by adding something like: ‘If you ever want help figuring out how to make this feel less overwhelming, I’m here.’ When the person is not ready, you may need to return to the conversation at a later point.
Reach out for professional guidance

If you are worried about someone, you do not have to wait for the person to agree to seek help before reaching out for guidance yourself. You can contact a general practitioner or another primary care provider, a mental health professional, a specialised early-psychosis programme or a crisis service to describe what you are noticing and ask about next steps.

It can also be helpful to reach out to a professional for guidance about what you are noticing even when signs of possible delusional thinking are still relatively subtle. This might include various signs already discussed in this Guide, such as a loved one’s increasing distress or fear, withdrawal from others or beliefs seeming to interfere with daily life. Reaching out early can help clarify what is happening and provide support before the concerns escalate. (See the Links & Books section at the end of the Guide for examples of support-seeking resources.)

More urgent support may be needed if you notice a rapid decline in the person’s functioning, an inability to meet their basic needs, or extreme fear or agitation, or if you have concerns about safety. A local mobile crisis service may be able to provide timely assessment and support. If there is an immediate, life-threatening emergency, such as imminent harm to the person or someone else, contact local emergency services. Staying calm, giving the person space and speaking clearly can help reduce escalation while crisis support is being arranged.
In any of these situations, remember that you do not need to be certain about what is happening to take your concerns seriously or to reach out for guidance.
What recovery can look like

For someone who has experienced delusional thinking, recovery does not always mean that the delusion completely disappears. More often, the person becomes less preoccupied with the belief, feels less distress, experiences more flexibility and starts to function better in day-to-day life.

With support – which frequently includes therapy and medication – many people experience a meaningful improvement over time. For example, the student who felt certain that social media messages were directed at them might still occasionally have that thought, but it might feel less convincing and come up less often. They may be able to use social media again without becoming preoccupied and stay engaged in classes. Similarly, someone who felt they were being monitored may continue to have moments of doubt about whether that has happened – but they might stop avoiding places and no longer feel on edge the way they did before. The belief may still be there, but it no longer drives their behaviour or dominates their daily life.

Sometimes a delusional belief becomes less intense as stress decreases, sleep improves or the circumstances around it change. But when a belief is persistent, highly distressing or part of a mental health condition such as schizophrenia, another psychotic disorder or a mood disorder with psychotic features, professional treatment is often important. Some people with these conditions need support for a shorter period, while the majority benefit from ongoing care.

Families and loved ones are not expected to act as therapists or replace professional care. Rather, the tools in this Guide are meant to aid and empower you in how you communicate and stay connected, alongside appropriate professional support.
Why delusions feel so real

Every person’s brain relies on mental shortcuts to make sense of the world quickly. This helps us interpret situations and respond efficiently, but it can also lead to common thinking patterns such as jumping to conclusions, black-and-white thinking, and catastrophising. Most of the time, these patterns are flexible and can be reconsidered. Under certain conditions, however – including stress, sleep disruption or mental health conditions such as psychosis – these thinking patterns can become more intense.

When someone is vulnerable to or experiencing psychosis, for example, certain ways of thinking often become more pronounced. A person might draw strong conclusions from limited information, begin to see personal meaning in neutral events or focus on information that supports a belief while overlooking other possible explanations. These patterns can reinforce one another over time and contribute to the development of delusional beliefs.

From this perspective, delusions can be understood as the brain’s attempt to make sense of experiences that feel confusing, intense or overwhelming. The delusional belief that results feels like a clear and convincing conclusion based on what the person is noticing and interpreting, even if it does not match how others see the situation.

A common and related part of delusional thinking is a limited ability to recognise that a belief may be inaccurate or part of a mental health condition. This is often referred to as reduced insight. Importantly, this is not the person simply being stubborn or in denial. It reflects a change in how the brain processes and makes sense of experiences. From their perspective, their interpretation feels accurate and logical. They may genuinely feel that nothing is wrong with their belief, or that others are misunderstanding what is happening.

This helps explain why correction or reassurance often does not work. When someone is convinced of their experience, being told they are wrong can feel dismissive or confusing, and it might even lead them to become more certain in their belief. Reduced insight can also affect how someone thinks about getting help. If the experience feels real and accurate, seeking professional help may not make sense to them, at least not at first.

For families and loved ones, understanding this can help to reduce frustration and blame, and encourage a more compassionate, effective approach. With support and treatment, insight often improves, and someone may become better able to reflect on their experiences and consider alternatives to their belief.
If you’re looking for help

In the United States, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) offers a national directory to help find treatment, including early psychosis programmes and specialist care.
In the United Kingdom, the National Health Service (NHS) website provides information on psychosis, including guidance on accessing treatment.
In Australia, Medicare Mental Health is a government-supported service that helps people find mental health support, including early psychosis services.
If you want to learn more about delusions or psychosis

The bookBack to Life, Back to Normality, Volume 2 (2018), edited by Douglas Turkington and Helen Spencer, is an accessible, practical guide for families that explains psychosis through a CBT-informed lens. It includes real-life experiences alongside concrete strategies for supporting a loved one’s recovery.

I helped create a series of videos for families through the STEP Learning Collaborative, part of the Specialized Treatment Early in Psychosis programme. They offer practical, relationship-focused guidance, including communication strategies and role-play demonstrations of how to support individuals experiencing delusions and other symptoms of psychosis.

Voices of Lived Experience, another video series from the STEP Learning Collaborative, features first-person accounts from individuals who’ve experienced psychosis and their caregivers. They describe what these experiences feel like and what support was helpful.

On the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) website, you can find family-friendly resources, education programmes and support groups for those supporting a loved one who’s experiencing psychosis or other mental health concerns.

The LEAP approach is a practical communication framework based on listening, empathising, agreeing and partnering, designed for supporting someone who may not recognise they need help. To find out more, check out the TEDx talk ‘I’m Not Sick, I Don’t Need Help!’ (2017), given by the clinical psychologist Xavier Amador, and the LEAP Institute website.

Psychosis REACH (Recovery by Enabling Adult Carers at Home) is a form of evidence-based training for families that teaches CBT-informed communication and support strategies. You can learn more on the REACH website or by reading the Psyche Guide informed by this approach: ‘How to Support a Loved One Through Psychosis’ (2022) by Akansha Vaswani-Bye.

We work hard to bring you the most trustworthy, expert and up-to-date information on psychology and mental health in our Guides. You can learn more about how we ensure that they are a reliable source of information here. This Guide is provided as general information only. It is not a substitute for independent, professional medical or health advice tailored to your specific circumstances. If you are struggling with psychological difficulties, we encourage you to seek help from a professional source.

items.title: How does Roshi Joan Halifax make sense of her Buddhist life? | Aeon Essays

items.author: Ben Daitz
paragraphs: Six weeks after two open-heart surgeries in 12 days, Roshi Joan Halifax invited me for a visit. She was recovering, but feeling ‘weak as a kitten’. When I’d last seen her, three or four years earlier, her hair had been shorn in a Zen tonsure; now it hung in a lush, grey-streaked braid to the middle of her back. She was pale and short of breath.

As a physician and her friend, I was reluctant to press on with the interview, but she wanted to begin. She was staying with Wendy Lau, her close friend, an emergency physician and Zen priest whose home overlooks Upaya, the Zen centre Halifax established in 1990 in the foothills above Santa Fe in New Mexico. We sat on Lau’s back porch, drinking tea.

Halifax is a medical anthropologist, a Buddhist teacher and a caregiver to the dying, who has worked with the suffering of others for more than 50 years: in burn units and jail clinics, in remote Himalayan villages, at the bedsides of people for whom there was nothing left to cure. She learned that the qualities that drew her there could also pull her under, and more than once they did. When she found her way back, it was Buddhist practice that helped her remain steady enough to help.

Halifax had almost died. She had gone into the operating room at Stanford cheerful, she told me – upbeat, confident. Surgeons repaired her heart’s mitral valve. Coming out of anaesthesia, intubated, she was certain the tube was positioned incorrectly. She couldn’t speak, so she made writing motions until someone put a pen in her hand, and – stoned, half-conscious – she wrote glottis. Wendy Lau understood. They fixed it.

Then came what she called the worst 12 days of her life. The valve replacement was failing. Her blood pressure plunged; she bled internally; she had a dangerous arrhythmia, and had to be shocked to restore a normal heart rhythm. ‘Death is easier than this,’ she told Lau. She meant it. ‘I actually wanted to die,’ she said. ‘I just was so sick.’
She was still on a gurney from the latest resuscitative shock when the surgeon appeared in his scrubs and told her: ‘We have to take you back in.’
‘I had a moment of Yikes!’ she told me.

In the intensive care unit after the second operation, she awoke convinced she was hanging upside down against a wall of moss. A warmth enveloped her chest and expanded, and kept expanding, into utter bliss. Then a male voice said: ‘You’re not done with your work yet,’ and she found herself back against the moss-covered wall. The cycle began again. ‘My recognition was: this is death. It’s fine,’ Halifax said.

Halifax has spent much of her life crossing thresholds, sometimes knowingly and sometimes not, and in the process delivering a grittier, more hands-on and help-oriented form of Buddhism to the West. Now aged 84, facing her own mortality, she names the charnel grounds where she practised her art: refugee camps, prisons, cancer wards, war zones. To that list she adds one more. ‘My latest charnel ground was being hospitalised for this heart surgery,’ she said.

Halifax’s first encounter with illness had come 80 years earlier. Aged four, she woke one morning unable to see and partially paralysed on her left side. She remembers feeling her way along the wall into her parents’ bedroom. Later, when a doctor picked her up in his convertible, she knew the top was down only from the wind.

She spent much of the next couple of years in bed with polio, away from other children. ‘I discovered that I had a spiritual life, an inner life,’ she said. Even now, she can walk through a building in her mind, imagining its rooms and passages, ‘because that’s what I did when I was four.’

Her parents hired Lila Robinson, a local Black woman, to care for her, keep house and cook. The Halifaxes lived in Coral Gables in Florida, a restricted, all-white enclave where neither Jews nor African Americans were allowed to live. Robinson and her three daughters lived across the railroad tracks in West Coconut Grove, then known as ‘Coloured Town’, in what Halifax called a ‘concrete monster’ – one of the mould-filled, roach-infested semi-high-rises baking in the Florida heat. To Halifax, Robinson was ‘the most incredibly kind person in the world, a manifestation of unconditional love and brightness – the woman who raised me.’

As Halifax recovered, she sometimes rode with her father to pick up Robinson. The journey carried her between ‘two different universes’: one had a country club and an all-white school, and the other: understocked shops, tired cars, good music and warmth. She saw the gulf between the two but was not entirely convinced that hers was the better world. Looking back, she traced her attraction to places of suffering to that early collision of inequality and love.
‘You could be both contemplative and a social activist. I want to be like that’

At the H Sophie Newcomb women’s college of Tulane University in New Orleans, the disparity Halifax had registered as a child became something she could act on. It was 1960 and, with the civil rights movement gathering force around her, she joined protests and the fight for racial justice. ‘There was a whole cadre of us who felt that racism was abhorrent,’ she said.

Through that work, Halifax met Hodding Carter II, the progressive Southern newspaper editor who had established the Delta Democrat-Times in Greenville, Mississippi. Carter was going blind. ‘For a time, I became his kind of eyes and feet and hands,’ Halifax said – his assistant in civil rights activities. Carter and his wife supported her, but her activism put her at odds with Tulane. ‘I graduated early from Tulane with Tulane’s help, so to speak,’ she recalled. ‘They really wanted me out of the system.’

In 1963, she left for New York, where her civil rights work opened into a wider world of artists, musicians, filmmakers and political activists. There she met Alan Lomax, the folklorist and ethnomusicologist whose field recordings of folk, jazz and blues musicians had taken him around the world. His project studied music, dance and language across cultures. The work carried her from a huge computer in a university basement to field trips in Morocco, the Bahamas and rural Arkansas. ‘I was in anthropology heaven,’ she recalled. ‘I just wanted to learn everything about anthropology that I possibly could.’

Two years later, a different kind of encounter opened a path inward. Halifax heard the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh speak when he came to New York to urge an end to the bombing of his country through the calm of his Buddhist practice. Halifax was then ‘angry all the time’ – at the war, racism, the government and the suffering around her. She understood that ‘you could be both contemplative and a social activist. I want to be like that,’ she thought. But for almost a decade, she remained a ‘book Buddhist’, absorbing what she could from reading alone.

For now, her focus was anthropology. By 1968, she was in Paris, indexing ethnographic films at the Musée de l’Homme. There she met Germaine Dieterlen, a French anthropologist who had spent more than 20 years among the Dogon people of central Mali. Dieterlen told Halifax that the Dogon were midway through the Sigui, a seven-year cycle of ceremonies moving through 289 villages and held only once about every 60 years. Most Dogon would attend just one Segui in a lifetime. To Halifax, it was a rite of passage that ‘reconsecrated an entire culture’.

The attraction was also personal. Robinson’s family had roots in the Bahamas and, farther back, in Africa; her grandmother had been a slave. Halifax knew little more – not when the family had been taken, nor from where. ‘I really wanted to go to Africa,’ she told me, ‘to understand the cultural roots of this woman who had raised me.’

In early 1969, Halifax drove a VW bus, modified for desert driving, from Germany to Marseilles in France and on to a ship bound for Oran, on the Algerian coast. From there, she drove alone to Gao in Mali – including 1,600 miles of unpaved track across the western Sahara. There was no map. The route was marked by oil drums filled with rocks, like buoys set in an ocean of peach-coloured sand stretching to the horizon. She encountered only three transport trucks on the entire crossing; the drivers dug her out when she was stuck, and she rewarded them with oranges.

Three and a half weeks after setting out, she reached Gao, an ancient trading centre on the Niger River at the southern end of the Sahara. From there, she put the VW bus on a barge down the Niger, then drove on to the Bandiagara escarpment, a wall of sandstone cliffs extending more than 100 miles. ‘The Dogon villages were spectacular,’ she told me. ‘The ceremonies and incredible masks and dances were extraordinary. The ceremony began with elder women who had been alive and present in a previous Sigui cycle, 60 years before. These were powerful women, their torsos completely exposed, not big people, but very, very thin. Old, muscular women, marching out in front of all the men.’ She spent about five months interviewing Dogon spiritual leaders and photographing the Sigui with her Pentax. Among the Dogon, she found a cosmology in which death was a passage, one that bound the living to their ancestors.

In Bamako, Mali’s capital, she realised she had contracted hepatitis. ‘There was a war going on with Chad,’ she recalled, ‘and there were no hotel rooms, and I ended up sleeping in an iron bed in a whorehouse, listening both to the war and to people having sex, and I was so sick.’ She made her way to the train station. The manager saw how ill she was and arranged passage for her and a flatcar for the bus to Dakar. The US embassy and her parents helped her to fly to Miami for medical care. She doesn’t know what happened to the bus.

The hepatitis that sent Halifax home to Miami changed the direction of her work. The city had been remade while she was away. Hundreds of thousands of Cuban refugees had arrived after the revolution and, by 1969, the local healthcare system was overwhelmed – not only by the numbers but by the differences in culture. Mainstream medicine was often inaccessible or inadequate to Miami’s growing Latin American and Caribbean communities, and many people instead sought care from alternative, often unlicensed practitioners – a clínica, a storefront doctor’s office of uncertain legality, or a santero, a priest of the Afro-Cuban religion of Lukumí, or Santería.

Recuperating in her parents’ apartment on Key Biscayne, she met Emanuel ‘Manny’ Papper, a neighbour in the building and dean of the University of Miami School of Medicine. ‘That’s how I made it into the anthropology department at the medical school,’ Halifax said.

There, she joined the Miami Health Ecology Project, led by Hazel Weidman, a senior medical anthropologist in the University of Miami School of Medicine’s psychiatry department and a founder of the Society for Medical Anthropology. The project studied five ethnic communities surrounding Jackson Memorial Hospital – Bahamian, Cuban, Haitian, Puerto Rican and Southern Black – and asked what illness meant to the person who had it: what caused it, who could heal it, and what being made well would mean.
He believed Jose had been cursed, and recommended an exorcism. I called Halifax. She came immediately

Soon, Halifax was pursuing her PhD in medical anthropology and doing fieldwork in neighbourhoods, clinics and houses of worship. Because of her experience in Africa and the woman who had been her caregiver when she was first so sick, she was drawn to Dade County’s ‘co-cultures’. She began identifying healers, especially in Miami’s Cuban communities. In the cabildos – ‘cult houses’ devoted to different orishas (deities) – she watched ‘different qualities manifesting through the members who were possessed’.

‘It was just fascinating,’ she said. She became ‘a kind of cultural broker’, bringing Santería healers into the medical system at Jackson Memorial. That’s how I met her, in 1972, when, as a family medicine resident, I attended one of her lectures on the ceremonies, spells and healing traditions practised among South Florida’s Caribbean communities. Not long after, at the Dade County Jail clinic I’d helped start, a 20-year-old Cuban inmate named Jose – ‘normal’ when arrested for burglary the night before – sat staring and unresponsive in what appeared to be a catatonic trance. Needle tracks marked his hands and forearms. I wondered about schizophrenia or conversion hysteria. Ron, a former Navy medic and the clinic’s physician assistant, had apprenticed with a Santería priest. He believed Jose had been cursed, and recommended an exorcism. I called Halifax. She came immediately.

Ron pulled a beautiful king conch shell out of a grocery bag and smashed it into a hundred pieces on the floor. With a sharp piece of shell, he made a cut halfway up Jose’s forearm, blood oozing. With another piece of shell, he matched Jose’s cut on his own left forearm. Jose didn’t flinch, but Joan and I reached for each other’s hands and squeezed. Ron bound their arms together, palm-to-palm, with a red bandana, and spent the night in the clinic with Jose. The next morning, Jose began to speak.

He said he had used heroin since his early teens. After his mother threw him out and he consulted a Santería priest, he robbed a convenience store and returned to the family house to hide. A king conch stood beside the door; police waited in the bushes. To Jose, the shell embodied Elegua, the orisha of the crossroads, who had placed him under a curse. Only an exorcism could lift it.

Given permission by the warden, we all met the following morning in the jail laundry room, flanked by banks of industrial washers and dryers. I spoke and understood Spanish, but Ron’s incantations sounded like no language I had ever heard. I drew Jose’s blood, finding a vein despite his years of heroin use, and squirted it into a bowl. Jose’s hair and nails were clipped into other bowls and covered with red bandanas. Candles flickered in a semicircle; across the room, the glass door of a dryer gave back a distorted reflection of the ceremony. I could feel my pulse beating in my ears and shivers up my spine. At the end, Jose buried the red bandanas containing his hair and nail clippings in a grassy plot inside the jail’s security doors. The ceremony was deemed successful by all of us, most importantly, Jose. Looking back, I can hardly believe we exposed ourselves to one another’s blood – or that the warden had even allowed the ceremony.

When, over 50 years later, I asked Roshi Halifax, by now a Zen Buddhist priest, to reflect on the exorcism, she said: ‘By the time we first met, my life had been so intense and filled with challenges, this was just an interesting experience for me. It wasn’t a big deal. We were like characters in this strange drama. I felt a lot of compassion toward Jose. You could feel the pain in him, and I look at drug addiction as a way to cover pain; the whole thing was beautiful and bizarre. There was a suffering human being, and we did what he wanted and needed, and that was good.’

At Jackson, Halifax had encountered another kind of suffering as well. She worked in the burn unit and sat with dying patients, watching young clinicians confront an injury they could no longer cure. Many had entered medicine wanting to help, yet she felt conventional medical training was not grounded in compassion. ‘What does healing mean in our culture?’ she began asking herself. ‘What is the difference between healing and curing? … What is the relationship between compassion and equanimity? Can compassion be taught?’

Several months after the exorcism, at a meeting of the American Psychiatric Association in Dallas, Halifax met Stanislav Grof, a Czech psychiatrist who had pioneered LSD research and was studying its effects on patients dying of cancer at the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center. They were married five weeks later in a volcanic crater in Iceland. Halifax wore a black Icelandic dress and a peaked crown representing a glacier; the world religions scholar Huston Smith officiated, and the mythology scholar Joseph Campbell gave her away. She had taken 600 micrograms of Sandoz LSD – what she called a ‘single overwhelming dose’.

‘There I was – married. All of a sudden!’ she recalled. ‘I was kind of in an altered state.’ The ceremony was ‘so archetypal’, she said. ‘And, needless to say, our marriage was a little bit like that.’

After leaving Miami, Halifax joined Grof’s research with dying cancer patients in Baltimore. The study was funded by the National Institute of Mental Health, and every patient knew the treatment would include LSD. The work began with preparation, including meetings with family members; on the day of the LSD session, Halifax might remain with a patient from 7:30 am until midnight, through the experience and the crucial period of integration afterward.

Aged 30, Halifax thought she was already somewhat experienced in medical settings and in being with suffering and death. She later wrote that she ‘was not prepared’ for the work or for the depth of the relationships she developed with people who were dying. Most were in extreme suffering, seeking relief from pain and fear and, as Halifax put it, the possibility of a ‘gentle death’. Death came to seem to her less like medicine’s failure than ‘the final developmental stage in a person’s life’ – one that called for attention even when curing was no longer possible.
Being a woman gave her ‘the permission and latitude to ride straight into a catastrophic mental and physical state’

At the same time, Grof had become her LSD therapist. She believed the drug might enable her ‘to know my mind completely. Talk about hubris. Oh my God.’ Instead, frequent high doses dissolved her defences and left her mentally fragile. The marriage approached a breaking point even as she continued the work. ‘It took me to the brink,’ she said. ‘Not only were these cancer patients suffering, but I was about to join the list of casualties as I plunged into the depths of physical and mental confusion. But it was also incredibly inspiring.’

In 1973, amid Halifax’s personal crisis, she and Grof went to Esalen, the experimental community on the cliffs of Big Sur in California, where psychedelics mingled with Zen and other contemplative traditions. There, she designed and produced ‘Buddhism in Mind’, a month-long gathering of teachers and scholars. During the programme, she confided to Jack Kornfield, a young American Buddhist teacher recently returned from monastic training in Asia: ‘I feel like I really need a teacher.’ Kornfield suggested Seung Sahn: ‘There’s this crazy intense Korean person. He might be a good match for you.’ Halifax invited the Korean Zen master to the gathering. ‘He and I connected,’ she said.

Halifax and Grof divorced in 1975. By then, she was experiencing what she described as extreme confusion and anguish, with full-blown hallucinations. She found herself ‘deeply identified with the so-called psychotics I had worked with in Florida’ – the people she had once approached as an anthropologist and could no longer regard from outside. Looking back, she thought her gender had made the descent possible: little was expected of her, and a man in her position would have had a harder time falling that far. Being a woman, she wrote, gave her ‘the permission and latitude to ride straight into a catastrophic mental and physical state’. She was, she said, ‘assigned and resigned to “my fate”’.
Her own summary of those years ran to four items: ‘A failed marriage, a failed career, my mind disordered, reputation lost.’

She looked for help in two places. The first was anthropology: Indigenous cultures have people who go crazy, and some of them go on to heal themselves and become healers. So she left the laboratory for the field. She went to Mexico several times a year, not to study the Huichol but to study with them, and ask for their help. There she met an old man named Don José Matsúwa: ‘No right hand, no teeth, Don José was dexterous and sharp in ways of the mind,’ she wrote. ‘With him, through him, and with the help of peyote, my humour was unearthed.’ All this helped her write the book Shamanic Voices (1979), gathering the testimony of shamans across more than a dozen cultures – accounts of initiation, of visionary journeys, of the healer who has first been broken, then healed.

The second source of help was Buddhist practice. LSD had opened Halifax’s mind without giving her a way to steady it. Meditation did. She described the essence of the practice as finding ‘the iron pivot in the spine that does not move even in the midst of great suffering’. A Buddhist metaphor.

For the next 10 years, Halifax travelled and practised with Seung Sahn’s community in the United States and abroad. One day, he casually asked how she had been spending her time. Halifax recited her recent ‘“good” deeds’. He paused and, as she later wrote, ‘growled: “You are a bad bodhisattva!”’

She felt like she had been ‘struck by lightning’. In Mahayana Buddhism, a bodhisattva dedicates her life to relieving suffering. A bodhisattva’s commitment requires humility as well as compassion. When Halifax recited her ‘good deeds’, Seung Sahn heard that she was keeping score.
