So, we must find another way to explain why there are multiple distinct things. Doing so in terms of properties won’t cut it.

Instead of maintaining that different things merely have different properties, perhaps we ought to say that they are radically different in their essential attributes. What are ‘essential attributes’? Recall that, according to dualism, reality is bifurcated into mental substance with the essential attribute of thought, and physical substance with the essential attribute of extension. In other words, the mental and the physical have radically different essential attributes. But this raises a new question: why is mental substance not extended, and why is physical substance not thinking? The PSR demands an explanation. One might think that the nature of mental substance excludes being extended, and vice versa. But Spinoza objects that this violates the independence of substance, since it entails a mutual dependence of mental and physical substance to explain the fact that they exclude one another. Ultimately, Spinoza thinks there is no reason why substances would differ from each other and, since there is no reason, they do not differ. There is, then, just one substance, one thing, and this thing has all properties, and is both extended and thinking, because there is no reason that it should lack any properties or essential attributes.

A single thing with all properties and essential attributes fits the bill of both God and nature, hence Spinoza’s argument, that only one thing exists, is an argument for pantheism. But this can also be cast as an argument for panpsychism. The single existing substance is, according to Spinoza, both extended and thinking. Hence, thought is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of reality. There is, however, scope for debate about whether the fundamentality and ubiquity of thought amounts to panpsychism since there is reason to believe that not all thought is conscious thought, in Spinoza’s system. But, at the very least, mentality is a fundamental property of matter, for Spinoza, and many are happy to equate this with consciousness and, thus, categorise Spinoza as a panpsychist. The US philosopher Martin Lin, for example, writes: ‘Spinoza is a panpsychist. For him, mentality is a pervasive and fundamental feature of the natural world.’

This argument for panpsychism (and pantheism) results from leaving no stone unturned in the application of the PSR, and, in particular, from the demand to explain the idea that there are multiple distinct substances with different properties or attributes. Ultimately, Spinoza concludes that this demand cannot be met, which leads to the conclusion that there is a single fundamental substance with all properties and with both essential attributes of thought and extension. This conclusion can be cast in pantheist terms: to maintain that there exists just a single substance with all properties and attributes invites the identification of this substance with both God and nature. It can also be cast in panpsychist terms: the single fundamental substance is essentially a conscious, thinking thing. Hence consciousness is a fundamental property of reality.

Pursuing the demand for intelligibility leads to unexpected and thought-provoking places. If panpsychism doesn’t resonate with you, it’s worth asking if there truly is a reason for everything – if the world is ultimately intelligible after all. On the other hand, if you consider the PSR indispensable, panpsychism may seem inevitable.

But does this latter path offer a deeper sense of meaningful existence? I’m not so sure. In fact, uncertainty about ultimate meaning fuels the arts, which, at their most powerful, embrace and celebrate the unintelligibility and absurdity of life. On the other hand, it seems legitimate to criticise art when its meaning is too obvious, its message too on the nose. So, just as clear and unambiguous meaning is far from the supreme aesthetic goal, it’s not clear that rendering reality fully intelligible, providing the ‘meaning of life’, is a desirable or realistic aim for philosophy.

Dissatisfaction in life, a crisis in meaning, may originate when we can find no good reason for our personal and professional pursuits, and, analogously, philosophical dissatisfaction may stem from an inability to render the world intelligible. But it is far from clear that this sort of dissatisfaction can ever really be remedied by the provision of better reasons.
A messy, unintelligible world doesn’t preclude the construction of highly orderly philosophical edifices

A more prestigious or better-paid job may constitute a reason to get out of bed in the morning. But deep questions about value and meaning will remain untouched. The absurd is not so easily vanquished. Similarly, the promise of a philosophical system built on the PSR, such as Spinoza’s, may appeal to the extent that we want to ‘solve’ philosophy by providing an answer to any possible question. But we may equally take an explanation of everything as an explanation of nothing.

Instead of seeking perfect reasons for all our pursuits, perhaps we ought to just embrace what we do, whatever it may be, for what it is. As the French philosopher and writer Albert Camus reflected, solace for Sisyphus can only come from positively embracing his situation: ‘The struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.’

Perhaps it’s misguided to expect to render the world intelligible, and we ought instead to just enjoy the process of contemplating its messy unintelligible glory, of pushing our philosophical boulder up the mountain. One way of engaging with this contemplative project is in the development and exploration of systematic philosophical theories. A messy, unintelligible world doesn’t preclude the construction of highly orderly philosophical edifices. But it would be a mistake to think these capable, even in principle, of definitively dissolving life’s mysteries. Philosophical theories such as panpsychism are better thought of as providing new and enriching perspectives on these mysteries, and we should remain open to the possibility of their collapse and replacement.

By giving up the all-encompassing demand for intelligibility and, instead, conceiving of philosophy as providing different perspectives on our condition, we can better understand what it is to make progress in philosophy. Widespread philosophical disagreement should not be taken as evidence that philosophy is degenerate compared with, say, the natural sciences. Rather, we should celebrate the fact that opposing views such as dualism, physicalism and panpsychism exist to provide us with richly diverse perspectives on life’s most tantalising mysteries.

Can panpsychism make the world intelligible? I’m not sure that anything can, or that it even makes sense to pursue supreme reasons. But there is still plenty of joy to be had in the contemplation of panpsychism as a response to the deep mystery of consciousness, and I doubt we could ask any more of a philosophical theory.

items.title: The politics of masculinity at the end of the Roman republic | Aeon Essays
items.description: What does it mean to be a man? In the early 21st century, masculinity is contested and fraught with anxiety; influencers offer models of manliness involving fast cars, sexual conquests, and building up muscle. Before the rise of feminism, they suggest, in some
items.author: Catharine Edwards
paragraphs: What does it mean to be a man? In the early 21st century, masculinity is contested and fraught with anxiety; influencers offer models of manliness involving fast cars, sexual conquests, and building up muscle. Before the rise of feminism, they suggest, in some supposed Golden Age, everyone had a shared sense of what it meant to be a man – and being a man was unproblematically good. The Roman Empire, in their view, offers men today an inspirational example of power, hierarchy and achievement, which is why men think about it so much – unlike women, who are too immersed in their feelings…

Manliness certainly was celebrated in the works of Cicero, republican Rome’s most eloquent statesman. In the mid-1st century BCE, his persuasive powers in the law courts and the senate were second to none; his speeches went on to inspire would-be orators well into the 20th century. He is often seen as the very embodiment of the Roman republic. The political world in which he flourished was a self-consciously masculine one; to be accused of acting like a woman was, for a Roman man, a grievous insult. Yet in Cicero’s writing we can find other strains too.

For Roman men, anything labelled feminine was necessarily to be avoided, something to be ashamed of. But what exactly did it mean to act like a man? Ancient Rome in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE saw the rise of a succession of military leaders who were promoted as masculine role models. The great general Marius won a series of victories in Spain, North Africa and on Italy’s northern frontier. For several years in a row, he was elected consul, one of Rome’s two chief executive officers. Unlike many other Roman politicians, he didn’t have an aristocratic background. One Roman writer imagines Marius fending off accusations that he was coarse in his manners:
elegance is becoming to women but toil to men. All virtuous men ought to have more fame than riches. Arms, not fine trappings, bring glory.
– from The War Against Jugurtha by Sallust
(All translations are adapted from the Loeb Classical Library.)
Here was a model of manliness forged on the battlefield.

Given the military might of ancient Rome, it is surely unsurprising that Romans often associated masculinity with courage in battle. The word virtus, a term cognate with the Roman vir (meaning man as opposed to woman), clearly means ‘courage in war’ when it is first recorded in the mid-5th century BCE. Courage in battle could be taken as the foremost manifestation of Roman masculinity. The historian Sallust, writing in the 40s BCE, praises earlier generations of Romans for their pre-eminent manliness in war: ‘whenever their virtus repelled dangers, they rendered aid to their allies and friends.’ And yet, while Rome continued to boast ever more notable military successes in the middle and later republic (from the 3rd to the 1st century BCE), the battlefield was by no means the only arena in which Roman masculinity might be put to the test.

When Cicero was 16, like others of his social standing, his transition to adulthood was marked by a special ceremony, most likely at the feast of the Liberalia in 90 BCE. This was the moment when he first put on the toga of manhood, a cumbersome length of woollen fabric worn by Roman citizen men, a garment associated with civilian as opposed to military life. Years later, as consul in 63 BCE, Cicero played a leading role in uncovering and suppressing a conspiracy against the Roman state, and boasted that this was a victory won by ‘citizens in togas’. It was his speeches that had convinced his fellow senators and the Roman people of the dangers posed by Catiline’s conspiracy, leading to decisive action against those involved. Cicero had used his voice as consul to save Rome, he declared in a speech a few years later. Throughout his life, he insisted his victory was comparable to those of Rome’s greatest generals. Masculine achievements weren’t confined to the battlefield; rhetoric and oratory could also conquer.

By the time he secured the consulship, Cicero was regarded as Rome’s top orator. Public speaking was highly prized by members of Rome’s governing elite. Its end result mattered hugely – winning over one’s listeners. But the way Rome’s politicians spoke and even how they dressed could also serve to demonstrate their manliness. Codes of civilian masculinity governed behaviour in public spaces such as the Forum, the law-courts and the senate. Markers of manliness in this sphere were subject to relentless public scrutiny. As the later expert on oratory Quintilian put it, the orator’s dress needs to be ‘resplendent and manly: for when it comes to one’s toga and shoes and hair, excessive care as well as negligence are equally blameable’. The toga, for instance, must be correctly draped; he notes a little later, ‘throwing back the fold from its bottom onto the right shoulder is foppish and effeminate’.

Orators were alert to the niceties of their own – and one another’s – masculine self-fashioning. In the cacophonous world of the Roman republic, politicians, advocates and those aspiring to a public role exchanged no-holds-barred insults. Often, they cast aspersions on one another’s masculinity, with disparaging comments on an opponent’s way of speaking, his gestures, the way he wore his toga – as well as his sexual behaviour. Orators would be praised for speaking in a ‘manly’ way. And they were robustly attacked for any ‘effeminate’ deviations in their style and manner of speech. Some orators favoured a more elaborate style fashionable in the long-established rhetorical schools of the eastern Mediterranean, the zone the Romans called Asia. Contrasts were drawn between ‘Asian’ style and the plainer style associated with Athenian rhetorical tradition. The Asian style was regularly denigrated as ‘effeminate’. Yet too ‘unpolished’ a style could seem old-fashioned, even coarse. Moderation was itself celebrated as a quintessentially masculine quality. But where to draw the line?
Quintilian criticised rhetoric teachers who encourage their students to show off

In the late republic, attempts were made to codify guidance to aspiring orators. An anonymous treatise on rhetoric addressed To Herennius promises to help its reader present himself as a proper man through training in public speech. The author advises, for instance, against any sharp exclamation that ‘injures the voice and likewise jars the hearer, for it has about it something ignoble, suited rather to feminine outcry than to manly dignity in speaking.’ In On the Orator, Cicero has a character emphasise the importance of appropriate gestures in seeking to arouse particular emotions in one’s listeners: ‘all these emotions must be accompanied by gesture – … with this vigorous manly throwing out of the chest, borrowed not from the stage and the theatrical profession but from the parade ground or even from wrestling.’ The theatre had morally dubious associations; actors were often branded effeminate. Performer though he was, an orator would do well to cultivate a more military aura and disguise the degree to which his art drew on dramatic technique.

Writing a century after Cicero, Quintilian was a huge admirer of his work, regarding him as the ideal model for the aspiring public speaker. In Quintilian’s wide-ranging treatise on the education of the ideal orator, sound ethical character but also manliness are presented as essential qualifications: ‘I am training the consummate orator, a figure whose existence is predicated on his being a good man [vir bonus].’ Quintilian expresses his disapproval of speeches composed merely for display, a widespread practice in his day, criticising teachers of rhetoric who encourage their students to show off:

The teachers, I feel bound to say, have been guilty of the same offence as slave dealers who castrate boys to increase their attractions. As those dealers think there is no beauty in strength or in a muscular arm, and certainly not in a beard and the other natural endowments of the male, and so take what might, if left alone, have developed into sturdiness and soften its supposed hardness – so do we cover up the manly form of eloquence and the power of lean and vigorous speech with a delicate veneer of style, and think effectiveness of no importance, so long as everything is smooth and polished.

This simile – shocking in multiple ways to a modern reader – aligns the recommended mode of speech with the embodiment characteristic of the free, adult, bodily intact male. Indeed, the right kind of speech makes clear the laudable moral character and manliness of the speaker: ‘I decline to regard as eloquence in any sense something which shows no trace at all of a normal male, let alone of a man of weight and integrity,’ Quintilian continues.

But there was of course a paradox in all this effort focused on generating an impression of authentic masculinity, a paradox apparent in the advice in To Herennius to ‘make everything seem straight from the heart’. The artifice required to generate authentic-seeming masculinity was all too evident. We can see this as a symptom of the ongoing challenge of justifying male supremacy, through assertions of the ‘natural’ superiority of men to women (and indeed of free men to enslaved ones). What exactly was ‘masculine’ rhetorical style? Opinions could differ significantly. But masculinity itself was always a positive term. And giving effective speeches in Rome’s public spaces was an ideal way to communicate one’s specifically masculine virtue.

What happened, though, when a member of Rome’s elite, once renowned for his eloquence, found himself cut off from the Forum and the senate? Cicero’s role in the punishment of those who had conspired with Catiline was controversial; Roman citizens had been executed without trial – a breach of the rights of the Roman people. In 58 BCE, following the manoeuvrings of his political enemy Clodius, Cicero was unceremoniously exiled. He languished far from Rome for 16 months, often fearing for his life, separated from family and friends – but also from access to the public arena where he’d held his own for so long. His letters home are full of lamentation. To his old friend Atticus, Cicero communicates his utter misery and despair. He often wishes he were dead. Reflecting on his losses felt like tearing open a wound: ‘I mourn the loss not only of the things and persons that were mine but of my very self. What am I now?’

Cicero was criticised by his contemporaries (and by later commentators) for his emotional reaction to exile. Should he have adopted a Stoic stiff upper lip, perhaps? To have been unaffected by this experience would have been inhuman rather than manly, he asserts in a speech given after his return in 57 BCE:

I could not now describe my action as praiseworthy or say that I was the source of any benefit to the republic, if I had but abandoned, for the republic’s sake, what I felt no pang at losing; I should hold that such mental apathy, like the physical apathy which does not feel the sting of fire, was brute insensibility rather than bravery [virtus].
In his own way, he claimed, even his retreat into exile, and even his frequent complaints, had shown bravery – manliness.
Cicero, eloquent exponent of Roman republican values, struggled to articulate his political disappointment

Back in Rome, however, Cicero remained anxious. Generals in command of large armies – Julius Caesar, above all – asserted their dominance over the state. Rome’s senate felt increasingly powerless. ‘The republic is an empty husk,’ Cicero lamented in a letter to Atticus in 54 BCE. Another celebrated general, Pompey, eventually led the challenge to bring Caesar under control. Yet, even if this was an attempt to shore up traditional modes of government where the senate exercised greatest authority, it ended in failure – and there were also doubts about Pompey’s intentions. Was he too, perhaps, aiming at one-man rule? Following a bitter civil war lasting from 49 to 45 BCE, a victorious Julius Caesar ruled the Roman world as dictator. Cicero, Rome’s foremost orator and long at the centre of its political life, was in despair. Throughout his career, he had championed a traditional political order in which Rome’s elite competed against one another in elections and took collective decisions in the senate. This was above all a culture of robust debate, in which persuasive speech played a critical role. But now the Forum was silent. In the senate, no one dared speak against Caesar.

Cicero, most eloquent exponent of Roman republican values, struggled to articulate his profound political disappointment. This was an experience compounded by devastating personal bereavement. In 45 BCE, shortly after giving birth to a little boy, Cicero’s daughter Tullia died. He was knocked sideways. Friends wrote letters of consolation. A long letter from one, Servius Sulpicius Rufus, observed that at least Tullia, dying when she did, avoided witnessing the end of the republic. In an equally lengthy reply, Cicero acknowledged his friend’s kindness – but disputed the claim that any comfort might be found in the timing of Tullia’s death. He contrasted his own situation with that of earlier Roman public figures, who had managed to avoid giving in to personal griefs by devoting themselves to public service: ‘the high standing they derived from public life soothed their mourning’. In current political circumstances, Cicero no longer had a part in public life. He couldn’t bear even the sight of the senate – the scene of his former triumphs. In these wretched political times, it was Tullia who had been Cicero’s one source of comfort. She was ‘a haven of refuge and repose, one in whose conversation and sweet ways I put aside all cares and sorrows.’ And now she was gone.

The collapse of the Roman state in its traditional form was something Cicero had been lamenting, at least on and off, for some years. He often used the language of death, bereavement and mourning in relation to the political situation. ‘For a long time it has been my part to mourn our liberties,’ he wrote to his old friend Atticus. Just a short while before Tullia’s death, he wrote to another friend: ‘I have already grieved for the state more deeply and longer than any mother for her only child.’ It is impossible to disentangle Cicero’s devastation at the loss of his daughter from his feelings of loss at the drastic transformation of Rome’s political landscape. The one loss intensified his grief at the other. And as Cicero’s words comparing himself to a bereaved mother suggest, he experienced both the loss and the intense grief it provoked as profoundly emasculating. He could no longer be the man he once was.

And yet perhaps another sphere of activity might offer scope for a new kind of self-actualisation, a new way for a man of Cicero’s extraordinary talents to win fame through service to the state and his fellow Romans. Even before Tullia’s death, Cicero had been increasingly immersing himself in philosophy. In 46 BCE, he had written to Sulpicius of his retreat from public-speaking: ‘seeing there is no further place in the Senate House or Forum for the craft which I have studied, I have devoted all my time and attention to philosophy.’ In changed political circumstances, with the dictator Caesar as Rome’s sole ruler, philosophy felt like a kind of salvation.

Cicero’s focus in his writings of these years was on a range of mainly ethical issues, particularly the nature of virtus – now taken in a sense much closer to the English term ‘virtue’ or ‘moral excellence’. A particular concern was the management of emotions in the pursuit of spiritual wellbeing. This was an issue of pressing personal significance to Cicero following his family bereavement but also of broader relevance to those who mourned the political changes in Rome.
It is about what it means to be a man and how manhood can be forged in – and by – challenging circumstances

Cicero (and other Roman writers), influenced by Greek philosophical explorations of virtue, might sometimes attribute to women virtue of a more generalised kind. But the Latin term virtus never completely lost its association with masculinity. Noting the word’s derivation, Cicero observes in his treatise on the management of emotions, the Tusculan Disputations:
the proper virtue of a man is above all courage, whose particular functions are contempt for death and pain. We must exercise these qualities if we wish to be virtuous, indeed if we wish to be men.

Closely concerned with philosophical approaches to dealing with grief and the fear of death, this treatise is also about what it means to be a man and how manhood can be forged in – and by – challenging circumstances. ‘For surely virtue [virtus] gives sufficient to make us live bravely; if bravely, sufficient too to make us high-souled and in fact never appalled by any event and always undefeated,’ he asserts. Similar concerns surface in other works he wrote around this time: in On Ends, he stresses the importance of self-control – which he defines as avoiding behaviour that’s ‘unmanly’ – parum virile.

Cicero’s philosophical writings were themselves an act of public service, he insisted. Through setting out philosophical ideas in Latin, he was offering a way for his fellow citizens to encounter the highest kind of learning. It was a particular comfort for Cicero in a time of deep political crisis, he declared, that this moment might see the birth of philosophy in Latin.

Cicero did return, albeit briefly, to the public arena in the last year of his life. Following Caesar’s assassination, his erstwhile deputy Mark Antony manoeuvred to take over Caesar’s following and resources. Cicero thought he too was aiming at dictatorship, and gave a series of speeches, attempting to rally his fellow senators behind the ‘liberators’ and against Antony. These speeches, known as the Philippics, were a dazzling return to form.

In the second Philippic, Cicero insisted at length and in colourful detail on the ways in which Antony was a slave to bodily pleasures – a man with no capacity for self-control. Cicero dredged up a story from years previously alleging Antony had had a homosexual affair with another Roman elite man, Curio, a relationship in which Antony willingly played a ‘passive’ role: ‘No slave boy bought to satisfy lust was ever so completely in his master’s power as you were in Curio’s,’ he fulminated. The lust here is implicitly Curio’s, not Antony’s – but this willingness to subordinate himself revealed Antony’s ‘slavish’ disposition. Such sexual ‘passivity’ in an elite male – taking what was seen as a ‘feminine’, receptive sexual role – was deeply shocking for Romans. It is notable that in his swansong Cicero does his utmost to paint Antony as a man of ‘unmanly’ sexual habits, addicted to pleasure and with no sense of masculine moderation. Cicero, ever the rhetorician out to win the argument, was quite prepared to exploit his audience’s masculinist prejudices to demean an enemy.

With these speeches, Cicero managed to rally his fellow senators, at least for a time, but, in the end, the power of those who commanded the legions was unstoppable. In 43 BCE, Antony eventually joined forces with Julius Caesar’s great-nephew and heir, Octavian. They rapidly gained control of the Roman Empire – and engineered the deaths of prominent opponents, among them Cicero. When a posse of legionaries finally caught up with him, Cicero is said to have offered them his neck, meeting his end with great bravery.

Military might prevailed for the time being, underpinning the regime of Rome’s emperors which was established a few years after Cicero’s death. Yet long after the Roman empire had fallen, his writings and reflections on the nature of educated masculinity would continue to influence European elites. While masculinity in Cicero’s world – and that of many of his later readers – is always a positive term, it’s also clear that its precise significance was just as contested then, albeit in different ways, and within different limits, as it is in the early 21st century. And just occasionally Cicero himself reveals the conscious effort involved in putting on a performance of authentic manliness.

items.title: AnOther Loves: Nova Check for November
items.description: Burberry keeps its most recognisable code in check this season – the pattern has long been associated with British weather after all
items.author: George Pistachio
paragraphs: Burberry keeps its most recognisable code in check this season – the pattern has long been associated with British weather after all

It’s autumn, when dressing in brown is an excellent idea. The leaves go tobacco, the parks turn olive and beige. Conveniently, Burberry has already put most of those colours into a rather famous check. For the new season, bowling bags, buckets and totes come in these autumnal shades. It is difficult to think of another pattern so immediately associated with British weather, which makes sense – the Burberry check began life in the 1920s lining raincoats. Among its later incarnations is Nova Check, a beige, black, red and white grid, ubiquitous around the turn of the millennium. Back in 1967, a buyer in Burberry’s Paris store, preparing a presentation for the British ambassador, pulled the check from a coat and used it to wrap luggage and cover an umbrella: the idea of making a bag in it was never very far away. Since arriving at Burberry in 2022, Bradford-born creative director Daniel Lee has set about reimagining the motif – with twists: the check has been turned on the bias, blown up, recoloured and worked into everything from kilts and bikinis to bags.
Burberry’s check bags are available to shop here

items.title: Chiwetel Ejiofor: “Characters Have to Take Over a Part of Your Psychology”
items.description: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:
items.author: Hannah Lack
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:

On the sprawling Vancouver set of Kane Parsons’ liminal horror Backrooms, crew members regularly found themselves lost amid the 30,000-sq-ft puzzle of queasy fluorescent lighting and jaundiced wall-to-wall carpet. Maps were distributed each morning but even so, rescue missions were launched for those who’d taken a wrong turn. The A24-produced phenomenon, sprung from a 4chan image taken in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, via Parsons’ uncanny web series (it has hooked more than 224 million views to date), conjures an infinity loop of interchangeable, dread-submerged rooms that replicate and curdle memories like a malfunctioning photocopy machine.

It’s hard to imagine anyone better suited to interpreting Parsons’ mind-bending vision than Chiwetel Ejiofor, an actor feted for the kind of magnetic, deep-waters presence that keeps an audience tethered to his side whether he’s immersed in dystopian futures, comic-book universes or two centuries in the past. As Backrooms’ tragic villain Clark – the divorced owner of a cut-price 90s furniture store – a lifetime of disappointments ripple beneath the surface as he tumbles into the Escher-like underworld lurking in his store’s basement, his questionable decisions and self-delusion so messily human it’s as unsettling as the disorienting maze of drywall conjured by his fraying psyche.

The prodigious 21-year-old Parsons has said Ejiofor was the only actor he envisaged for the role – just as seasoned artist and filmmaker Steve McQueen could accept no one else to channel the quiet gravitas of Solomon Northup, the freeman forced into slavery played by Ejiofor in his unflinching 2013 masterpiece 12 Years a Slave. For two decades and more than 60 films (a couple of which he also wrote and directed, both centering on father-son dynamics), Ejiofor has excavated his life and emotions to play roles that contain multiplicities: conflicted radical militants, drag queens in thigh-high PVC boots, unravelling Los Angeles detectives, aliens from a dying planet, wayward heroin smugglers, and wry sorcerers – the latter a Marvel spectacle played by Ejiofor with Shakespearean undertones. That was perhaps only natural given Ejiofor’s award-heavy background on the London stage, where he has mastered Shakespeare, Chekhov, Ibsen and Césaire over the years. As a young teenager growing up in West Norwood, he remembers covering his bedroom walls with handwritten lines from Macbeth or Measure for Measure the way other kids might scrawl their favourite band’s lyrics.

Ejiofor was born to Nigerian parents who had escaped the Biafran war – his mother was a pharmacist, his father a successful musician and a doctor. At the age of 11, he survived the kind of unconscionable trauma that divides a life into before and after; during a family trip back to Nigeria, a car accident killed his father and hospitalised Ejiofor for 10 weeks, leaving a scar still visible on his forehead. His indefatigable mother went on to raise him and his three siblings singlehanded. Ejiofor’s discovery of acting aged 13 in his Dulwich school plays, brought what he describes as “a calming of the spirit”. By 18 he was playing Othello, by 19 he was on set with Steven Spielberg, and at 25, had the breakout lead in Stephen Frears’ Oscar-nominated Dirty Pretty Things, playing an undocumented immigrant confronting nocturnal London’s darkest secrets during night shifts at a seedy hotel. Today, on a busy Saturday morning in Soho, we meet the now 49-year-old at a considerably more pleasant hotel to discuss Backrooms’ looming tech-age anxieties, Ejiofor’s own psychological loops and thought patterns, the early obsessions that shaped him, and his forthcoming roles: as a ruthless tyrant in Gina Prince-Bythewood’s mythological fantasy Children of Blood and Bone and an ex-con turned priest opposite Scarlett Johansson in Mike Flanagan’s Exorcist adaptation.

HANNAH LACK: Horror films are said to reflect the fears of our times – the 50s atomic age in Invasion of the Body Snatchers, nature striking back in Jaws... What do you think Backrooms is saying about our current anxieties?

CHIWETEL EJIOFOR: I feel like it has a lot to say about our relationship to technology. My character Clark and his relationship to the Backrooms is so much about what brings you comfort in what might seem the blandness of the technological age. In the face of the complexities and difficulties of existing, the technological age offers all this comfort, simplicity, uniformity. And increasingly with generative AI, this idea of something having all the answers – being able to switch off from the much messier, unknowable, difficult business of being a human being: just turn to the machine for the answers to guide you through the process. That can be comforting, but the flip side is that it is completely horrifying.
HL: Were you familiar with the series before you met Kane Parsons? If I’d said ‘creepypasta’ to you...

CE: I would have guessed some sort of fusilli. Never heard of it. So I was astounded how big it was, how many people online had seen these shorts. But when I watched it, I completely understood why people had gone down that rabbit hole. Kane’s take on it was extraordinary in its scope and the developed science fiction aspects of it, and the capacity to involve and terrify an audience – not only with the fear factor, but psychologically to really put yourself in different worlds. His ability to surprise with some of the stuff he was achieving in Blender – you’re just not expecting the directions it goes in visually, which is so rare. And these concepts are severely pressure-tested by YouTube, an open platform where people are not shy about telling you what they think in the comments section – or they’ll just ignore you. Kane’s handle on the world was so complete at the point when I spoke to him. And he was really challenging himself to get underneath these characters in a rich way.
HL: Clark is so messily human, I found myself feeling a lot of sympathy for him despite some questionable decisions. What was your point of connection with Clark?

CE: I actually found Clark quite easy to relate to. I don’t know what that says about me! But his honesty and frankness and ways of looking at his place in life and evading his own culpability – that was relatable. The way we tell stories to ourselves about why we are who we are, and why we are where we are – it’s very human in the self-delusional aspects of it.
HL: So if you were in Backrooms, what loops do you think you’d find yourself in?

CE: Well all of us, as we travel through life, have relationships, friendships, that we tell ourselves the narrative of. And I think often we try to come out of those as the hero, which may be healthy to some degree. But how many of those stories would bear cross-examination? In the end, that is just part of the experience. Unfortunately, you’re never going to get through life completely clean. There will be things you could have done better, things that could have gone worse. So with Clark, the dynamics would be wildly different, but the capacity for self-delusion – I have that as much as anybody else.
HL: You’ve spoken in the past about being a perfectionist. How have you navigated that as an actor, because I imagine part of the process is trying things that aren’t necessarily going to work...

CE: Yeah, and I don’t think I’ve moved beyond perfectionism as much as I would have liked. Once you have that in you, it’s always going to slightly define your approach. I still approach roles with the idea that there is a correct way to play it, and my job is to find the correct way. And whether it succeeds or fails is based on how successfully I’ve achieved that. I don’t know if that’s healthy, but it’s the way my mind works. A lot of actors would say there isn’t a correct way of approaching artistic work. Which I do understand intellectually – I just don’t believe it emotionally. I sort of feel like there is the correct way, and it needs to be uncovered. But no matter how much you prep beforehand, the character teaches you so much in the playing of them – it’s always in the last week of shooting that you know the most about them.
HL: So when you know you’re going to play, say, King Saran in Children of Blood and Bone, where does the process of building him start?

CE: I think characters have to take over a part of your psychology. It’s the only way. It’s: where do I as an individual meet this other individual? Because whatever I end up doing is going to be a hybrid of the two of us.

It’s great when there’s time for that process to happen – in this case, it was a few months of allowing this character to sit in my psyche and Zooming with Gina (Prince-Bythewood). There are such complex family dynamics at play in this film, so I was keen on getting into that room as soon as the family unit was cast, to find the through lines for these relationships. The combination of Gina and shooting in South Africa was irresistible – in that area of Cape Town and beyond, the vistas are completely magical and give the film such a rich density, complexity, and there’s a human quality that is beautiful and deep. I love Gina’s detail and capacity to ground big stories. Early on she showed me all the artwork, the drawings they were working with. She didn’t need to convince me; I was already in – and the books are extraordinary.
HL: I read in your sister’s memoir that as kids your mother would give you books to read and report back on each week – did acting start with a love of language?

CE: It was English literature classes at school, being introduced to humanistic poetry and stories that weren’t about plot, but really intimate thought patterns, about the overall experience of living for its own sake. When you’re first exposed to Shakespeare, there’s the plot of Henry IV Part One – he does this and that – but the real point is, what does he think about life? That really captured my imagination as a young teenager. I ended up going to the theatre to try to get to the root of it. And that led to deciding to get on stage and inhabit it.
HL: What was the first role where something clicked for you?

CE: It was doing Measure for Measure when I was maybe 13, playing Angelo. I felt like I had gotten underneath this character. It wasn’t a choice after that. It was way beyond that. It was what I was thinking about when I’d wake up and all through the day. Everything else was in the margins for the main event, which was theatre at school. Then that extended into holidays with the National Youth Theatre or the Dulwich Youth Theatre – it just became part of my personality, that was it.
HL: Your late dad was a doctor but also a musician, do you think he opened a creative door for you when you were very young?

CE: I don’t know. I hadn’t really thought about art until I experienced it firsthand. And when that happened it was as if I didn’t think anybody else had ever travelled this route before. It was like I was the first to discover this code for living that no one else knew about. Art was this way of self-expression, but with this caveat that you didn’t have to expose yourself too much. You could be somebody else and still express yourself. The hybrid of two things – reading the text and you as an individual talking about your experiences – could create something even more compelling. And for me, within that there was a calming of the spirit. I found a way of communicating with people, not having to use my own words but still representing myself profoundly. I knew I would do this for the rest of my life. There was no doubt. Later, working on Joe Penhall’s play Blue/Orange, I was the younger of the group, 23 or so, and that was also a strong entry point into what the profession could be, dealing with these contemporary issues surrounding mental health.
“I wake up in a panic because I know at 7:30pm the show’s on. There’s no way I can have a normal day” – Chitewel Ejiofor
HL: Stephen Frears saw you in that play and cast you in Dirty Pretty Things, right? That was a big moment.

CE: Dirty Pretty Things was so ahead of its time in many ways, detailing a London that later on people would talk about more frequently, but at the time was as hidden culturally and in the media as it was in the narrative. I fell in love with film on that job. It was the extraordinary precision of Stephen Frears, but also Chris Menges as a cinematographer; understanding the poetry of filmmaking, the truthfulness that can be communicated, the silence of moments, and what drama can mean in film being very different to theatre. I’d always assumed I wasn’t a film actor. That film changed my perspective.
HL: Why had you assumed you weren’t a film actor? Is there a different energy required for film?

CE: I mean, there are people who can wake up in the morning and have a completely normal day and then go down to the theatre at 5:30pm, have a bite to eat and get ready for curtain up at 7:30pm. I’ve never been able to do that. I wake up in a panic because I know at 7:30pm the show’s on. There’s no way I can have a normal day. I remember in the play Everyman, my entrance was from the top of the Olivier Theatre on wires coming down onto the stage. I would be getting into a harness, watching the audience coming in like ants – they were so small beneath me. I had a harness on, but my hand was holding onto the rail and every night, I had to have my hand coaxed away from the rail by one of the stage team: “The show’s going up now, Chiwetel. You can let go now...” Once I landed, the business of doing the show felt much easier. But no, the rhythm of film and theatre is the same in that you live with the character all of the time until the show or the film is complete.

HL: You’ve worked with many incredible directors – Alfonso Cuarón, Spike Lee, Ridley Scott – and Steve McQueen, who brought you an Oscar nomination for 12 Years a Slave. He was absolutely clear he wanted you for the role of Solomon Northup – did he tell you what convinced him?

CE: Yeah, I mean he did. He would say that there was a quality of inherent integrity or something trustworthy about Solomon – that you felt you could be in his company and there were no sides to him. Not that he was naive or guileless, just that he was open, and so the audience could go on the journey with him and be carried by his experiences. I think for Steve it was around that – not charisma exactly, but an integrity or trustworthiness that he at least believes I exude – whether he thinks I actually have that, I don’t know!
HL: What did you take away from that set that you hadn’t discovered before?

CE: Steve would often talk about “catching butterflies” – the idea that you can set up an environment where something magical can happen. It could just be a question, or something completely unexpected that an actor who is immersed in a moment can produce, which could never be produced anywhere else. There’s a horrifying, extraordinarily powerful scene, the flaying of Patsey, Lupita Nyong’o’s character, where the camera movement, actors, the creation of that space, how the camera flowed in a sequence was mostly in one take. But as performers, we weren’t adhering to specific marks. It was everybody being open to where the scene would go.
HL: Did you take that idea of catching butterflies to your own sets? You’ve directed twice now, with The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind and Rob Peace...

CE: If you’re an actor-director, your relationship to performance is very different. What I get excited about is the silent communication between actors. I didn’t need language that much because I was already communicating so much about tone and style by the way I was acting in the scene, which other actors pick up on quickly. I was looking at stories, writing a little bit, kicking the tyres around directing. But when I read The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind, I could see it as I was reading. It was thematically aligning with so many things I had been searching for in ways I didn’t even know that I had been. Not just as a creative, but as a person – it was a story that meant so much to me, on so many different levels.
HL: You wrote both films as well. Have you always written, did you keep a diary as a kid?

CE: Yeah journals, diaries, all of that. Mostly day-to-day stuff and then during teenage years – actually not just teenage, into the turbulent 20s – it was a way of processing the world around me, trying to make sense of it. When I look back at the things I wrote, it’s fascinating because it does help identify patterns in behaviour, thought patterns. I think it helped me rationalise, compartmentalise the world that I was experiencing and some of the complicated emotions I was having.
HL: There’s a line in Rob Peace where he says he needed to “control the chaos”...
CE: Yeah exactly. It takes your feelings out of the chaotic world and creates something almost tangible, something that can hold it.
HL: I read that you’re a bit of a hoarder; what have you kept from your film roles?

CE: You know, since I mentioned that, it turns out there’s a hoarding community out there. There are support groups; there’s help if you need it. It has actually made me feel a bit better – declaring it has somehow alleviated some of the burden for me. But the thing is, it doesn’t have to be anything that holds value. That wouldn’t be a problem – a nice keepsake from a set or something with sentimental value – great! But it’s the stuff that doesn’t mean anything and I can’t explain why I’ve kept it; I just can’t get rid of it. It’s an ongoing challenge.
HL: Is it good then to find yourself often in hotel rooms without a lot of stuff?

CE: Where everything is out of sight? Yeah – but actually I found very early that living out of a suitcase and the constant travel didn’t agree with me. One of the reasons I started sailing was because I found that if I was in a new city and I could see that city from the water, it contained it. So that’s what I would do: land somewhere and immediately figure out how to get onto the water so I could see the city from a distance. And also, as a Cancerian – not that that’s really my thing – but I think I engage with water in a way that feels very grounded to me. Looking back at Vancouver or Los Angeles from the water allowed me to connect to the city in a different way. I don’t sail as much now, sadly, but when I can, I get on a houseboat and chase that feeling a little.
HL: You’ve been shooting a new adaptation of The Exorcist with Mike Flanagan. The original was famously cursed on set... has anything unusual been happening on this one?

CE: So far, so good. It’s one day at a time (laughs). But actually, it is always in the back of your mind because it’s dancing with certain... elements. I don’t know if I’m very superstitious, but if you’re doing The Exorcist, you lean into it a little more. I loved the original, the filmmaking is extraordinary and the last half of the film is so terrifying, but also so watchable, the characters and the depth of feeling you have for everybody in that house by the end is remarkable. Having worked with Mike on Life of Chuck, it was exciting to jump into the world with him. All I can say about it is, he’s created something so rich on so many levels – I can’t wait for people to see it.
HL: What’s the one film you’ve watched the most?
CE: Probably The Abyss – I actually love that film.
HL: Last question – what’s something thing you’d like to pass along to your daughter that you inherited from your parents?
CE: Well, my mother has always had a certain tenacity and an engagement with life that is electric. That’s what I’d pass on – but you know, I feel like my daughter has that already.

Photography OLIVER HADLEE PEARCH. Styling RAPHAEL HIRSCH. Grooming MATT MULHALL at Streeters. Set design ANDREW TOMLINSON at Streeters. Casting GREG KRELENSTEIN at GK-LD and Management Artists. Digital tech BELLA SPORLE. Photographic assistants ALBI GUALTIERI, THOMAS LOMBARD and STEFAN TURNER-POWELL styling assistants STORM FOSTER and ART O NEIL. Tailor JO O’CONNOR. Make-up assistant JO MEROLA. Production MIMI LOMAX at Partner Films. Production. Assistants THEA LEVINE and CELESTE MANDERS
This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man, which is on sale from 5 November 2026

items.title: Death and Entrances
items.description: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
items.author: Susannah Frankel
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
Among the earliest and most famous depictions of a female nude is the Venus of Willendorf.

There are many Venuses, a broad – and obviously retrospective – nomenclature for figurines originating from the Upper Palaeolithic period, dating back 10,000 to 40,000 years. The Venus of Willendorf is carved in oolitic limestone. Standing a mere 11.1 centimetres tall, she is reputedly 30,000 years old. She has swollen breasts and a protuberant belly, both suggestive of pregnancy. Many thousands of words have been written about her. Is she, in fact, pregnant? Is she an ancient fertility doll, designed to be held in the hand of prospective or birthing mothers? Is she not pregnant at all but a symbol of beauty as it was perceived at that time? Also conjecture: the perspective of this Venus and more than a few of her Venus sisters, the fact that she has no facial features, or indeed feet, has led some to surmise that her creator was female – she is a self-portrait. Of course, nothing is proven. The issues this little Venus’s provenance raises, though, seem pertinent now for Harley Weir, whose exploration of the female form – and just the female – including her own, has led to some of the most striking and evocative imagery of the past decade.

In the history of art, depictions of pregnant women are few and far between. They are predominantly seen through the eyes of male artists. Their bodies are either hidden – through the medieval and Renaissance periods it was the fashion for women to wear voluminous clothing – or idealised. The Madonna is the most prevalent of all pregnant females in art history – the mother of all art historical clichés? – and her baby’s conception was immaculate. In myriad portrayals, myriad Annunciations, that purity is signified by the presence of a white dove. Of that same era, for many years critics speculated that the female figure in Jan van Eyck’s The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) was pregnant. Emblems of fertility – a carving of Saint Margaret of Antioch on a chair by the bed, ripe oranges, a symbol of prosperity but also fecundity, on the windowsill – are present in the painting’s background. The fullness of her famous green dress has since been attributed to the extravagance of its fabrication, however. Three-dimensional laser scans of Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa (1503–17) captured some 20 years ago now are not so easily dismissed. A fine gauze veil – or guarnello – seen over her dress, until that point hidden by aged varnish on the painting’s surface, is typical of those worn by soon-to-be or new mothers of that time. Representation of pregnant nudes in classical painting, meanwhile, are likely negative. Titian’s masterpiece Diana and Callisto (1556–59), which hangs in the National Gallery in London, is the best known. Nymph Callisto’s shaming, the revelation of her naked, pregnant body and subsequent fall from chastity, is subject to the goddess Diana’s fierce disapproval. Raped by Jupiter, Callisto was later transformed into a bear by that god’s wife, Juno. Or so the story goes.

A few centuries on, and modern artists from Gustav Klimt to Pablo Picasso and Lucian Freud painted (and sculpted) pregnant women, but always – inevitably – from a distance. Klimt’s Hope paintings, dated 1903 and 1907–08, of his favourite model Herma were executed against her better judgment, and the earlier rendition, portraying her naked surrounded by mythical monsters, caused a scandal. Picasso’s 1950 sculpture La Femme Enceinte was inspired by his partner at the time, Françoise Gilot, who had recently given birth to their second child, Paloma; he used ceramic bowls and pitchers to create the figure’s rounded breasts and stomach. Freud’s portraits of pregnant women, some carrying his own children, were forensic in their attention to detail: the subject as specimen.

It wasn’t until the last century that female artists’ representations of pregnancy began to enter the gallery setting. Paula Modersohn-Becker’s nude self-portrait of an imaginary pregnancy in 1906, Alice Neel’s paintings of pregnant women, clothed and nude, in the Sixties and Seventies and Chantal Joffe’s pregnant self-portraits are impassioned in their bid for reclamation, showing not only pregnancy’s beauty and power but also its complexity. For the first time, there is a sense of women’s alienation from their own bodies antepartum, for their feelings of intense love alongside, and never unreasonably, fear.

Harley Weir is no stranger to the self-portrait. Her 2022 Beauty Papers monograph, dedicated to “all the dolls in the world”, is an unflinchingly visceral – at times grotesque – representation of the tropes of femininity and the preconceptions those raise. Four years on, and ten weeks pregnant, Weir began to regularly take pictures of herself naked or near-naked in the relative privacy of her bedroom. At 32 weeks a further, more studied series was taken, including portraits of Weir, now helped by John Kelleher, her husband and the father of the baby, and of a body double wearing a pregnancy belly and Harley Weir mask. With styling by her friend and longtime collaborator Georgia Pendlebury, these images serve as Weir’s visual response to her physical and emotional transition at a time that may be as challenging as it is joyful. And intimate, but: “The real private self isn’t this though,” she says. “It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait.”
SUSANNAH FRANKEL Do you know the Venus of Willendorf? She’s got no feet. People think a woman may have made her.

HARLEY WEIR Because she’s looking down at her body? I’ve been documenting my pregnancy from week ten and there are a lot of looking-down pictures and also looking up in the mirror. When you’re pregnant there are so many blind spots. My husband helped take many of the pictures for that reason. The series is called Death and Entrances because, from what I’ve read, it’s like an ego death. You’re giving birth but you’re also dying, you change. I felt, physically in this story, as if I was wearing a disguise.

That’s something I think connects back to the Venus of Willendorf, this idea of a woman looking down at a body that is powerful, but also unfamiliar. During pregnancy, your body becomes the most visible thing about you, but at the same time it can feel like it no longer belongs. Here, I don’t have my usual breasts, I don’t have my usual stomach. I felt almost free from the shame of being nude because the bump isn’t me or us.

SF The physical state of pregnancy is extreme. We are taught from an early age to control our bodies and our body image. When you’re pregnant, you surrender that control. Perhaps your body is preparing you for becoming a mother, because once that happens your life is not your own in the same way.

HW Yes, it feels like that. It feels good. I’ve always been self-conscious about my breasts because they were so small. Now they are engorged and full of stretchmarks, but I don’t care who sees them. They’ve become functional objects. And there’s a safety in that. I feel much more at ease. I love being this blob that will bring purpose to someone new and it in turn gives my body purpose, a reason for its irregular shapes that before felt like deformities.
SF Is there any fear involved?

HW There was a lot more at the beginning. But I’m still at the stage where you don’t really know what’s about to hit. I’m in the phase where I feel this is the baby, it’s this bump. But no, the baby is going to come out and rock my world.
SF Have you looked at the way pregnant women are represented in art?
HW I haven’t seen much pregnant art – especially from the past. There’s the Virgin Mary, but we rarely see her pregnant. She didn’t even have sex. The virgin and the mother.
SF There’s that – the Christian ideal – but also some quite violent portrayals.

HW I have to say I can’t think of one classical painting where you see a pregnant woman. Klimt maybe. My mother talks a lot about how, even when she was younger, you had to cover the bump up, you couldn’t show it freely. I feel now we’re having a renaissance for mothers. The mother is more celebrated. I didn’t feel secure enough to be having a kid until now. And I’m getting on. I’ll be 38 when it comes out.
SF People called me a geriatric mother. I was 37.
HW But they’ve changed it now.

HW I would have been, but they stopped using that term recently, which is great. I do think this is an amazing moment for mothers. On Instagram there are so many inspirational women sharing their motherhood stories. Once you get pregnant your algorithm knows and they’re everywhere. So many cool mothers online, which I feel is something you wouldn’t have seen in the early Noughties. Mothers were dismissed or hidden. There was the fear of overpopulation and that having children was bad for the environment,

I used to hear that a lot. Now in the west fewer people are having babies, pregnancy is a positive thing again. It goes in cycles, I suppose. I’ve just finished reading Born [The Untold History of Humanity by Lucy Inglis]. It’s fascinating how attitudes shift. During the Roman Empire, people would kill unwanted babies, by “exposure” – especially girls.
SF In China and Japan they are now rolling out financial incentives to persuade people to have babies.
HW Exactly. First China wasn’t allowing more than one baby. Now there aren’t enough. For now, it feels like we’re in a baby-positive cycle.
SF The death part of the equation is the old you saying goodbye to your old life.

HW And saying hello to the mystery of what is about to begin. I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed.

SF You’ve photographed yourself before. How much of that process is about showing yourself to the world and how much is it about introspection, working out what, in this case, your pregnancy means for you?
“I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed” – Harley Weir

HW My life is already very bump-forward. Wherever I go, it’s the focal point of conversation. It’s hard not to be obsessed by the pregnancy. At one point people argued that because the baby takes so much nutrition, the mother’s brain shrinks by 20 per cent. Now they are calling it rewiring. I’m rewiring. And my way of coping with things is photography – it’s like therapy. It’s a way for me to work out those ideas and also to detach from them. I was thinking how I’m kissing goodbye to this flat-chested girl and becoming a woman. The pregnancy at this stage is visual, the changes are reflected in the mirror. Every Wednesday I read my update that tells me how big the baby is.
SF How big is your baby now?
HW Honeydew melon. You know, it’s so silly. Apparently, there’s a dog one too.

SF How interested are you in the relationship between us as voyeurs and you as the subject? I looked at Beauty Papers. That’s overtly sexual, about fetishising women. This is almost more like you fetishising your own pregnant body.

HW I do think there’s something in the fact that I’m still a sexual being. In old tropes you become a mother and your sexiness was stripped from you. Almost as some kind gesture of respect that we never asked for. That’s what is interesting about fashion. It’s been a way to explore the female – that’s what I do. There are also many personal secrets tucked away inside the images, where they often look overly sexual – rarely my first thought, if thought about at all. There’s an undercurrent of personal meaning. Some images in the story are overlaid with pictures from my dad’s favourite beach. That’s seaweed. Mother earthing. My dad has Benson’s disease, so he’s not able to communicate any more. But I still want to include him in my life in ways that I can. It’s sad when I think of how good he would have been as a grandfather.
SF This story is so intensely autobiographical. Do you think all of your work is?

HW It is. I graduated from art school in 2010. I loved emotive art and started as a painter, which seemed to be the most primitive and uninteresting trade at the time. There was a bit of a backlash against people like Tracey Emin – who wore their heart on their sleeve. People whose work was too autobiographical, too self-involved. I loved her diary works and felt a kinship to them but my era was having a conceptual moment that I didn’t fit in with. I will always be an artist first but fashion allowed me to continue to use emotive language more freely and the impulse has never left me. There’s a picture of me with a pushchair on fire. I wanted to express the fear of being a bad mother. That’s my neighbour’s shed. It’s like a doll’s house. The dream gone wrong.
SF Very few artists have represented fear in pregnancy. Probably because they are mostly men, so maybe it’s not their place to look at that.
HW Yes, that was nice. They left it for us.
SF But being pregnant can be really frightening at times.

HW Part of the story I wanted to show was my thoughts of, oh God, am I going to be a bad mother? Am I going to drop the baby? Am I not going to love the baby? Am I going to have postpartum depression? What’s amazing is that there is so much information about those things now and people talk about it all the time.
SF That anxiety goes on for ever, I think. Did working with a body double in a mask feel strange to you?

HW So strange. Every time I look in the mirror now, I see the mask. It’s terrifying. When you ordinarily look in the mirror you see what you want to see. You think you look good or you think you look terrible. It doesn’t matter what you actually look like. I asked Chaïm, who made the mask, to get all the bits and bobs in there. Go hard on the skin blemishes. I knew they were there but when you actually see them looking back at you, it’s quite grotesque. My face like a piece of meat, you really see it that way. When I show the photos to people, they can’t understand that it’s not me in those pictures.
SF Did you do it for purely practical reasons?

HW Not only. There is something very laborious about taking a self-portrait, the tripod, the focusing etc, but I also wanted to divide myself – the divided self. She was supposed to be the idealised version of me, unstretched and glossy. It’s a shame we didn’t have more time with Anna, who wore the suffocating mask along with the fake bump and wig. There was so much more fun to be had.
SF The image with the snake is referencing Avedon’s Nastassja Kinski and the Serpent [1981]?
HW Yes. I thought that was funny. It’s my “pregnancy picture”.
SF You know the thematic of this issue of the magazine is cliché?

HW So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask.
That’s a real snake crushing me in the picture. I put make-up on in that one too, to cover the pigmentation on my face, to be the idealised pregnant woman for her pregnancy shoot.
SF And there’s an apple in another image. Eve’s apple.

HW Yes. Purity lost. And for taking the apple we must suffer in childbirth. But I actually feel purer than ever. There’s something in the body becoming so functional, it’s before shame. The instinctiveness and the nakedness of breastfeeding, for example, feels like that moment before the apple when there was no shame attached to the naked body. There’s one really disturbing breastfeeding image, the masked me breastfeeding me, the idea of a mother still needing a mother. There’s also me breastfeeding from John. Which takes the breast even further away from the sexual, because he doesn’t have one. It’s about becoming dependent on each other in a new way as a family and recognising that we all need to be nurtured.

SF You are photographing something that is transient, and by photographing it you’re fixing it in time. I suppose that is what photography is more generally, but it feels somehow more pronounced in this context.

HW The permanence is scary sometimes. I only thought about showing my child these images today. I thought maybe the baby never sees these. It’s very different because it’s still inside me. Baby out, different.
SF Do you think about that often, with explicit imagery?
HW I think about it all the time, but I try to be free. I don’t always get it right and people correct me. I like that conversation though.
SF Do people ever talk about your nudes, or look at your nudes, in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable?

HW It’s hard to put yourself out there and be judged. The real private self isn’t this though. It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait. Looking back, I realised I was trying to seem approachable, not too attractive or too sexy. But I’m obviously aware of the camera and that annoys me. I wanted to catch myself in a real state, but because I’m the one taking the photograph, that’s almost impossible. Some pictures are ugly because I felt I should include them, so I wouldn’t seem vain, which is probably the vainest thing you can do. In one I’m standing nicely, in another I’m slumped and badly postured. Sometimes I feel I can be quite vulgar. That’s part of me, letting people see a little too much. Not necessarily deliberately.

“So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask” – Harley Weir
SF And you don’t lie awake at night thinking about that.

HW Sometimes. You don’t want to read the comments too much. I don’t put much on Instagram for that reason. I would say that I have some boundaries, but the idea of vulgarity is something I subconsciously play with a lot. Or at least it seems my tolerance is higher than most. There is me covered in milk with my legs up. It reeked, because it came from France in a heatwave with Leana the make-up artist. I was trying to photograph what the baby would see coming to get the milk. Unfortunately, I didn’t get a linea nigra, the dark line that can appear when pregnant, apparently as an arrow to direct a new born to the breast.
SF There’s also the cliché of the earth mother, and that huge power, but equal to that is vulnerability.

HW Since I’ve become obviously pregnant, when I’m not with John, I don’t like walking around at nighttime. I want to be with my husband. I know most people are not thinking bad thoughts, but I feel vulnerable. There’s something of the mother earth in the photo of me feeding the fawn. This instinct to nurture, but also suggestive of how exposed motherhood can make you feel. I read that, in England, they used to use puppies to keep the milk supply going if your baby was away from you, fawns or pigs in other countries. And if your milk wasn’t working, they would bring round a donkey or a goat for the baby to suckle from.
SF Some of your self-portrait imagery displays a complete lack of vanity.

HW Art and fashion both rank quite high in the thoughts of the self. Oddly with fashion, being the voyeur that I am, possibly the less self-absorbing of the two. It’s so much about the other. It’s rare to see the photographer. We’re like ghosts haunting the image but we are never really there. I often photograph some of the most attractive people in the world and then sit with retouching comments to make them look even more attractive. So it’s hard to think, damn I look hot here, because in my mind, by comparison, I look like a gremlin. Me looking vain as hell to the public is probably me thinking I look real and unfiltered. It’s hard to be objective when it’s me in front of the lens but I like to think I show both sides. Perfection isn’t interesting.
