- Cyndi Lauper, ‘Time After Time’ Cyndi Lauper was nervous about “Time After Time” — the aching ballad she wrote in the studio with keyboardist Rob Hyman to finish off her blockbuster solo debut, She’s So Unusual. “I asked them to please not put ‘Time After Time’ out as the first single,” Lauper said. “People would never have accepted me. If you do a ballad first, and then a rocker, that doesn’t work.” Her instincts were right: Following the jaunty “Girls Just Want to Have Fun,” “Time” became her first Number One.

- The Pixies, ‘Where Is My Mind?’ No song typifies the freakish pop instincts that made the Pixies stand out in a sea of gloomy Reagan-era bands better than “Where Is My Mind?” Joey Santiago’s lead guitar is catchier than most Top 40 hooks, and by the time Fight Club made this song iconic a decade after its release, it had already formed part of the DNA of countless alternative-radio hits in the years between, from Nirvana to Korn. When an interviewer in 1988 asked about his unique ability to crank out great songs, Black Francis’ answer was typically cryptic: “It’s nice to have space. How much can one brain deal with?”

- Kanye West, ‘Stronger’ Explaining the tighter, broader-reaching songs on his third album, Graduation, Kanye West said, “I applied a lot of the things I learned on tour [in 2006] with U2 and the Rolling Stones, about songs that rock stadiums. And they worked!” West found the inspiration for his most grandiose statement to date from Daft Punk’s “Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger,” which he sampled and reshaped. West is a big fan of the French duo: “These guys really stick with the whole not-showing-their-faces thing. Just amazing discipline — that’s straight martial-arts status.”

- Miles Davis, ‘So What’ It’s likely that no song on this list has soundtracked more dinner parties than Kind of Blue’s warm, welcoming first track. But at the time it was a jarring departure, trading bebop chord changes for a more open-ended modal style. According to pianist Bill Evans, the trumpeter worked up his material just hours before recording dates, but the all-star band here sounds like it’s been living with “So What” for years: Saxophonists John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley turn in solos that have since become as iconic as any in jazz history, and the rhythm section of Evans, bassist Paul Chambers, and drummer Jimmy Cobb swings like it’s dancing on air.

- Bad Bunny, ‘Titi Me Pregunto’ “Tití Me Preguntó” is a showcase for Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny’s unbridled creativity and eccentric pop genius, mixing frantic dembow beats, a classy sample by bachata master Anthony Santos, and a coda with a dash of Latin psychedelia to the global mainstream. He does it all with panache and a healthy sense of humor. Using the archetype of the concerned Latin American aunt asking about her nephew’s potential girlfriends as a starting point, he launches into a hilarious tirade of salacious puns to a bouncy party vibe that — in typical Bad Bunny fashion — unexpectedly morphs into moody self-reflection.

- Lil Nas X, ‘Old Town Road’ Montero Hill was an Atlanta college dropout sleeping on his sister’s couch and looking to break into music when he came across a track he liked by a Dutch 19-year-old called YoungKio that was based around a banjo sample from a Nine Inch Nails track. “I was picturing, like, a loner cowboy runaway,” he told Rolling Stone. Within a year “Old Town Road” was the longest-running Number One song of all time, seeming to sum up eons of American cross-cultural love and theft in just one minute and 53 seconds.

- The Breeders, ‘Cannonball’ Notified by fax that her services in the Pixies were no longer required, Kim Deal called up her twin sister, Kelley, to be her new guitarist (never mind that she didn’t know how to play guitar) and had the last laugh when this absurdist gem became an MTV phenomenon in 1993. “When people were talking about the Breeders being a one-off,” Kelley told Rolling Stone, “I was like ‘No, actually … the Pixies are a side project.'” A little over a year later, the Breeders were on an extended break of their own, but the effortlessly fun trampoline bounce of “Cannonball” is one for all time.

- The Weeknd, ‘House of Balloons’ Far from the international superstar he’d become, Toronto singer-songwriter Abel Tesfaye didn’t even send out photos or do any interviews when he released the first Weeknd album. “The whole ‘enigmatic artist’ thing, I just ran with it,” he said. “No one could find pictures of me. It reminded me of some villain shit.” But the title track of House of Balloons nevertheless set the course for his career, both thematically — drugs and sex, meet depression — and musically, with its sample of Siouxsie and the Banshees’ “Happy House” announcing a new direction for R&B.

- Solange, ‘Cranes in the Sky’ In an interview with her sister Beyoncé, R&B innovator Solange Knowles described how this song was inspired, in part, by overzealous real estate development she noticed around Miami: “This idea of building up, up, up that was going on in our country at the time, all of this excessive building, and not really dealing with what was in front of us.” She turned the metaphor inward to examine her own feelings about change, self-doubt, and aspiration, finishing the song years after it was originally conceived with producer Raphael Saadiq to create a lavish moment of neo-soul introspection.

- Lil Wayne, ‘A Milli’ Producer Bangladesh looped the opening chords from Gladys Knight and the Pips’ “Don’t Burn Down the Bridge,” then segued to a drill-like volley of trap drums. He gave the beat to his friend Shanell — a onetime R&B singer on Wayne’s Young Money Entertainment — to pass along. Wayne initially had grand plans for “A Milli”: He wanted to use the instrumental as skits for rappers like Tyga, Hurricane Chris, Corey Gunz, and Lil Mama. In the end, though, “A Milli” is just Weezy solo, blacking out in the booth and dazzling everyone who hears him.

- Azealia Banks, ‘212’ In 2011, Azealia Banks was a teenage rapper-singer whose clear talent yielded a development deal with XL Recordings but little else. “She had been working on a collection of tracks and there was one Dutch house-sounding one that was just absolutely insane,” producer Jacques Greene recalled. Banks freestyled ferociously about her New York hometown and, uh, cunnilingus over the jittery beats of Belgian house duo’s Lazy Jay’s “Float My Boat.” Initially released in 2011 as a viral track, “212” was a hip-house banger that earned Banks a deal with Interscope and served notice that this uninhibited provocateur would not be constrained.

- Weezer, ‘Buddy Holly’ Never has geek been so chic as in Weezer’s 1994 breakout single, “Buddy Holly.” Written for frontman Rivers Cuomo’s girlfriend, the poppy ode to nerdy romance was almost left off the band’s self-titled debut, also known as the Blue Album, due to Cuomo and now-ex-member Matt Sharp’s reticence. “We had the sense that it could be taken as a novelty song, and people aren’t going to take the album seriously,” Sharp told Rolling Stone. After producer Ric Ocasek heard the receptionist at the recording studio humming it, he insisted they keep it in.

- The Four Tops, ‘I Can’t Help Myself (Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch)’ One of Motown’s most rousing anthems, “I Can’t Help Myself” was inspired by songwriter Lamont Dozier’s grandfather, who’d call the women his hairdresser wife fixed up “sugar pie” and “honey bunch.” During the recording, engineer Harold Taylor recalled, “People were banging on the door of the studio; they were so ecstatic about what they heard.” Nevertheless, Levi Stubbs asked Brian Holland if he could do another take. Holland promised him they’d do it soon — and Stubbs’ first pass hit Number One.

- Lady Gaga, ‘Bad Romance’ Shortly after Gaga had established herself as a star, she catapulted to a next level of weirdness with this Nadir “RedOne” Khayat production, which drew upon the electronic music Gaga had been inundated with while touring Europe. “I want the deepest, darkest, sickest parts of you that you are afraid to share with anyone because I love you that much” is how she summed up the idea behind the song. Fittingly, she debuted the hit-to-be at Alexander McQueen’s show at Paris Fashion Week.

- Robert Johnson, ‘Cross Road Blues’ The primal terror in the Mississippi bluesman’s voice, and his mystifying slide guitar playing, transfixed the Sixties generation of British rockers: “I could take the music only in very small measures because it was so intense,” said Eric Clapton. Recorded during a session at a San Antonio hotel room in 1936, two years before Johnson was murdered at 27, “Cross Road Blues” is a mythmaking statement of spiritual desolation and scorched-earth betrayal — even if the legend that it’s about Johnson selling his soul to the devil in exchange for his monster guitar chops is, as far as we know, apocryphal.

- Biz Markie, ‘Just a Friend’ Nobody beats the Biz (1964-2021), an impossibly good-natured DJ, rapper, producer, human beatboxer, and hip-hop personality who broke big with this ode to the friend zone off his second album. Built on a fat beat, plinking piano, and his charmingly off-key singing, “Just a Friend” interpolates Freddie Scott’s 1968 song “(You) Got What I Need” as Biz warbles about a love that will never come to pass. It was based on real life. As he told Rolling Stone in 2000, “I was talking to this girl from L.A., and every time I called her, this dude was at her house, and she’d say, ‘Oh, he’s just a friend.’ I hated that.”

- Santana, ‘Oye Como Va’ Growing up in San Francisco, Carlos Santana was shaped by the city’s psychedelic explosion. “You cannot take LSD and not find your voice,” he once claimed, “because there is nowhere to hide.” And while his early heroes were bluesmen, he changed history with this foundational Latin-rock reworking of a 1962 salsa number by Cuban percussionist Tito Puente. Santana kept the original’s cha-cha pulse but replaced its horns with Greg Rolie’s organ and Carlos’ lysergic guitar flares. Said Puente years later, “He put our music, Latin rock, around the world, man.”

- Juvenile feat. Lil Wayne and Mannie Fresh, ‘Back That Azz Up’ In the late Nineties, Mannie Fresh’s diamond-sharp productions for Cash Money Records helped put New Orleans in the center of the hip-hop map. The title of this hit was so reminiscent of local artist DJ Jubilee’s single “Back That Thang Up” that Jubilee sued (unsuccessfully) for infringement, and the beat rode the “Triggerman” rhythm that is foundational to New Orleans bounce. Juvenile freestyled his best shit-talking bounce rhymes, and Lil Wayne shut it down with a “drop it like it’s hot” hook. As Mannie said, “[He] immediately was just like, ‘Shit, I’m getting a piece of this.’”

- The Go-Gos, ‘Our Lips Are Sealed’ The radiant first hit of the Go-Go’s was influenced, according to writer Jane Wiedlin, by “the Buzzcocks and Sixties girl-group stuff.” It was also inspired by a clandestine relationship she was having with Terry Hall, of U.K. ska group the Specials, who got a co-writing credit because Wiedlin based the lyrics on some poetry he’d written her in a letter. “It was pretty personal,” Wiedlin recalled. “I mean he had a fiancee at the time — nowadays I wouldn’t touch that with a 10-foot pole, but I was 19, and I was like ‘fiancee shmiancee.’”

- Kris Kristofferson, ‘Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down’ The desolation of spirit in Kris Kristofferson’s “Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down” is so heavy, so apparent, that it’s almost hard to listen to. But that despair is exactly what drew Johnny Cash to sing it on his TV variety show in 1970. Kristofferson cut his own stunning studio version that same year for his debut album, Kristofferson. Cash’s interpretation, more shuffling and accessible, is the one most listeners turn to, but listen to them back-to-back if you can, and marvel at how Kristofferson’s lyrics about being hung over, alone, and desperate shake your soul.

- Janet Jackson, ‘Rhythm Nation’ Jackson’s socially conscious Number Two hit came together late in the sessions for her blockbuster LP Rhythm Nation 1814. Co-producer Jimmy Jam recalled being in the studio and “switching between MTV and CNN. Watching music videos on one side and watching atrocities on the other. Somehow they all merged together. The idea for ‘Rhythm Nation’ was you can dance, but we can also do something more intelligent.” When Jam heard Sly and the Family Stone’s “Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin)” at a restaurant, he raced to the studio to sample it.

- Curtis Mayfield, ‘Move On Up’ Mayfield’s irresistible “Move On Up” was politically empowering, morally demanding, and effortlessly propulsive, powered by swinging horns and tangy congas — the nine-minute LP version, with its powerful drum break, laid a foundation for disco and hip-hop alike. Mayfield’s message was just as steadfast: that pride and dignity were paramount for Black America to rise. “I’m not trying to say anything to make you think, ‘Well, this is the way, this is the only way,'” Mayfield said. “I’m trying to cover the whole subject.”

- Tammy Wynette, ‘Stand by Your Man’ From the start, this pledge of wifely devotion, the first song Wynette ever co-wrote, was a cultural lightning rod. Feminists recoiled from its pledge of unquestioning fidelity in the Seventies, and Hillary Clinton defined herself a modern woman by slamming the song during Bill Clinton’s first presidential run. But the recording itself steamrolls over ideological objections, as the catch in Wynette’s voice on the verses gives way to a vocal swell that rises to meet the epic sweep of Billy Sherrill’s production.

- Peter Gabriel, ‘Solsbury Hill’ Shortly after Gabriel quit Genesis in 1975, he climbed to the top of Little Solsbury Hill in Somerset, England, to reflect on his life-changing decision. It inspired his debut solo song, in which he explained to fans why he felt the need to go out on his own. Musically, it was a departure too, a pastoral tune with a 12-string acoustic guitar lead that was pointedly different from Genesis’ prog-rock. The song has since become ubiquitous in movies and film trailers. “Maybe I’ve let it go too much,” he admitted to Rolling Stone in 2011.

- The Animals, ‘The House of the Rising Sun’ “We were looking for a song that would grab people’s attention,” said Animals singer Eric Burdon. They found it with the old American folk ballad “The House of the Rising Sun.” In 1962, Bob Dylan had sung this grim tale of a Southern girl trapped in a New Orleans whorehouse. The Animals, from the English coal town of Newcastle, changed the gender in the lyrics, and keyboardist Alan Price created the new arrangement (and grabbed a composer’s credit). Price also added an organ solo inspired by Jimmy Smith’s hit “Walk on the Wild Side.”

- Gladys Knight and the Pips, ‘Midnight Train to Georgia’ Songwriter Jim Weatherly originally composed this as “Midnight Plane to Houston,” only to change it for Cissy Houston (Whitney’s mom) to something “more R&B … in order to get it onto Black radio.” Weatherly had already penned “Neither One of Us,” Knight and the Pips’ Number Two hit, and when they heard “Midnight Train,” they took it to the top. “I never really imagined writing R&B songs,” Weatherly admitted. “I really thought I was writing country songs.” It reflected the times; the 1970s were the first decade since after World War I in which more African Americans were moving to the South than leaving it.

- Dixie Chicks, ‘Goodbye Earl’ A murder ballad with a modern, feminist twist, this jaunty song about poisoning an abusive husband spawned disparate reactions. Some stations banned it, apparently concerned that it would spawn a rash of hubby offings; others shared the number for domestic-abuse hotlines. When the label reps listened to the Chicks’ Fly album, though, they were more concerned with another song: “Sin Wagon,” with its reference to “mattress dancing.” “You can’t say [that],” Natalie Maines recalls their manager’s relayed message from the execs, “but they love the song about premeditated first-degree murder.”

- Mazzy Star, ‘Fade Into You’ Singer Hope Sandoval and guitarist Dave Roback, the prime movers behind Mazzy Star, were active in the 1980s neo-psychedelic Paisley Underground scene in Los Angeles. After Sandoval replaced singer Kendra Smith in the band Opal, David Roback and Sandoval reconstituted the band under the name Mazzy Star. Their second album yielded this spaced-out hit, perhaps dream pop’s ultimate statement of blurry desire. “We’re not so concerned about the outside world,” said Roback. “[Each song] is its own world unto itself.”

- Nirvana, ‘Come as You Are’ “It’s just about people and what they’re expected to act like,” Kurt Cobain said. “The lines in the song are really contradictory. They’re kind of a rebuttal to each other.” The song is driven by a simple riff that Butch Vig goosed with a flanged, subaquatic guitar effect. Cobain apparently lifted it from a 1984 song by U.K. art-metal band Killing Joke, who Dave Grohl paid back 12 years later by drumming on their 2003 album. In the wake of Cobain’s suicide, though, the most haunting lyric would become, “And I swear that I don’t have a gun.”

- Luther Vandross, ‘Never Too Much’ The Eighties’ major male R&B balladeer’s solo debut was financed in part from money he made singing jingles for KFC and 7UP. Vandross had been pushed to do his own thing by Roberta Flack, for whom he’d sung background. Said Vandross: “She said, ‘Luther, you’re too comfortable sitting on that stool singing “ooh and aaah.”‘ Roberta was single-handedly responsible for me starting my own career.” What pushed her was hearing the demo of “Never Too Much” — one of the most buoyant love songs of the Eighties, with Vandross’ high notes as delicate as soap bubbles.

- Daft Punk feat. Pharrell Williams, ‘Get Lucky’ When Pharrell Williams volunteered to appear on Daft Punk’s fourth album, he told them he’d been thinking about Chic legend Nile Rodgers musically; fortuitously, the French dance producers could play him a track they had on hand that they’d made with Rodgers himself. The result was “Get Lucky,” which, as the lead single from their disco-flavored album Random Access Memories, rose like a phoenix to become the song that defined its year. “I think the robots are leading,” Williams told Rolling Stone. “Daft Punk, they’re definitely leading.”

- Joni Mitchell, ‘Help Me’ Mitchell’s 1974 album, Court and Spark, her biggest-selling ever, was also the one that she held the tightest amount of musical control over to date. “I guided everything into place on Court and Spark — even though I didn’t play it, I sang it, and then they played it from that, and it was pretty much as writ,” she said. (Her next album, The Hissing of Summer Lawns, was looser and more jazz-oriented.) “Help Me,” recorded with the jazz group Tom Scott’s L.A. Express, features one of Mitchell’s sultriest vocals and most brocaded arrangements, inspiring Prince, 13 years later, to pay the song lyrical tribute in his “Ballad of Dorothy Parker.”

- John Lee Hooker, ‘Boom Boom’ Hooker, whose canny blues boogie became a root integer for early rock & roll, said this swinging, swaggering bit of primal thump was inspired by his inability to get to a regular gig on time. “There was a young lady named Luilla,” Hooker said. “She was a bartender [at the Apex Bar in Detroit]. I’d always be late, and whenever I’d come in she’d point at me and say, ‘Boom Boom, you’re late again.’ One night she said, ‘Boom boom, I’m gonna shoot you down.’ She gave me a song, but she didn’t know it.” Keith Richards said of Hooker, “Even Muddy Waters was sophisticated next to him.” That was a compliment.

- Van Morrison, ‘Into the Mystic’ Delectably arranged, transportingly sung, this may be the definitive Morrison song — an evocation of “the days of old” that feels like a lover’s whisper. The highlight of 1970’s classic Moondance, “Into the Mystic” benefited from a new, more organic way of recording for him: “It was more like working with an actual band rather than a bunch of session guys,” Morrison said. As for the lyrics, he’d admit, “So many of my songs from that Seventies period, I haven’t a clue what they’re about. A lot of the time, I was just picking up on a vibe.”

- Roy Orbison, ‘Crying’ Orbison said he wrote this lush, dreamy ballad after an encounter with an old flame: “Whether I was physically crying or just crying inside is the same thing.” His near-operatic performance culminated in a high, wailing note, which Orbison never lost the capacity to hit before his death, in 1988. “He sounded like he was singing from an Olympian mountaintop and he meant business,” Bob Dylan wrote in Chronicles. “He was now singing his compositions in three or four octaves that made you want to drive your car over a cliff. He sang like a professional criminal.”

- Steel Pulse, ‘Ku Klux Klan’ The first great British reggae band — and some of the style’s finest songwriters — made their Island Records debut with this incendiary look at the rising tide of racist violence in late-Seventies Britain: “The Ku Klux Klan/Here to stamp out Black man.” They underlined the lyric by actually performing the song live — including a memorable BBC appearance — wearing white Klan headgear. “The hoods seemed extreme at the time, but that’s what we are in a way,” vocalist Michael Riley said. “When we wore them, people started questioning what the song was about instead of just dancing to it.”

- Sade, ‘No Ordinary Love’ Helen Adu’s small but fully inhabited range has been her secret weapon from the beginning. “I decided that if I was gonna sing, I would sing how I speak, because it’s important to be yourself,” she said. Her voice cracks before she reaches the first chorus of this 1992 hit, playing up the romantic drama of the lyric. Even better, so does Stuart Matthewman’s guitar; in the middle of this otherwise mellow groove, he overdubs a seriously moody and low-key noisy part that gives the whole thing a welcome edge. Sade — it’s not just the singer’s name, it’s also a band.

- Beck, ‘Loser’ In 1992, 22-year-old Beck Hansen was scraping by as a video-store clerk while performing bizarro folk songs at L.A. coffeehouses. After friends offered to record some songs, Beck cut “Loser” in his producer’s kitchen. It became the centerpiece of the album Mellow Gold. At first people took “Loser” to be a mere novelty hit, but Beck knew better. “You’d have to be a total idiot to say, ‘I’m the slacker-generation guy. This is my generation.… we’re not gonna fuckin’ show up,'” he said. “I’d be laughed out of the room in an instant.”

- Bon Jovi, ‘Livin’ on a Prayer’ Like his New Jersey model Bruce Springsteen, Bon Jovi concentrates on working-class heroes and heroines. “Livin’ on a Prayer,” co-written with guitarist Richie Sambora, pumped the everyday struggles of Tommy and Gina full of grandeur — guitar-pick slides, dramatic pauses, the inevitable key change — and continues to resonate today. “It’s great that we wrote songs so long ago that people can still relate to,” Bon Jovi said in 2005. “When I hear ‘Livin’ on a Prayer,’ I think to myself, ‘We wrote that. That song has really made its mark. I guess that works.'”

- Lana Del Rey, ‘A&W’ “A&W” is maximum Lana Del Rey: a sweeping, seven-minute epic that follows the sunburned, SoCal folk rock she’s perfected on recent albums back to the hip-hop-inspired pop productions of her early discography. That musical scope is paired with a narrative that’s no less ambitious — vulnerable and lurid, nostalgic and hopeless, funny and utterly bleak. And the bow tying it all together? The name of classic root beer brand, “A&W” used as shorthand for “American Whore,” because no one bends American iconography to their will like Lana Del Rey.

- Jefferson Airplane, ‘White Rabbit’ The song that brought acid rock to Middle America was a heady rock bolero written by vocalist Slick, reportedly after taking LSD and listening to Miles Davis’ Sketches of Spain. She first recorded it with her earlier band, the Great Society, before rebooting it with the Airplane. “Our parents read us stories like Peter Pan, Alice in Wonderland, and The Wizard of Oz,” Slick said. “They all have a place where children get drugs, and are able to fly or see an Emerald City or experience extraordinary animals and people.… And our parents are suddenly saying, ‘Why are you taking drugs?’ Well, hello!”

- Sister Nancy, ‘Bam Bam’ Nancy (a.k.a. Ophlin Russell) was the DJ (mic controller) for Kingston’s Stereophonic sound system when she met reggae producer Winston Riley in the late Seventies. “I really admired how he took recording serious,” Nancy said. “You couldn’t go into his studio and do any foolishness.” Their peak, “Bam Bam,” is one of the great early dancehall anthems, booming but bright, tough but playful — and it’s been sampled extensively by everyone from Lauryn Hill to Kanye West.
- Missy Elliot, ‘The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)’ As producers, Elliott and Timbaland had already made their rhythmic impact on hip-hop and R&B before Missy’s first single. And some high-profile features

items.title: VisionQuest Season-Finale Recap: Reprogramming
items.description: Back in episode five of VisionQuest, during a flirty, cagey first date, Ultron told Jocasta, “Vengeance is a powerful entertainment.” Was he sincere or just saying what he thought she wanted to hear? More important, was he right? You could take the show’s seas
items.author: Tasha Robinson
paragraphs: Back in episode five of VisionQuest, during a flirty, cagey first date, Ultron told Jocasta, “Vengeance is a powerful entertainment.” Was he sincere or just saying what he thought she wanted to hear? More important, was he right? You could take the show’s season finale, “Forever,” as a referendum on whether vengeance is entertaining. I don’t think showrunner Terry Matalas, who wrote and directed this episode, was thinking about that question. But “Forever” certainly addresses vengeance several times over, from angles that are generally a lot more fun for the audience than for the characters.

That doesn’t make any of it “powerful,” though. “Forever” is a messy tonal mishmash that throws surreal comedy, heavy melodrama, and some standard-issue superhero punch-’em-up action into the same sloshing stewpot, all leading up to Walt Disney Studios’ most traditional, least satisfying narrative cliché. The episode’s high points are sublime, but the low points are the lowest of the entire series. And the rush to tag all the running themes and tie off all the character loose ends takes “Forever” to a sloppy, distracted place.

It opens with one focused idea: Vision, Josephine, and Ultron have all been captured by Virgil Horton, the puppeteer who has been pulling the strings in VisionQuest. He’s eager to explain himself in an ebullient, hilariously grating extended villain monologue. Virgil (Ultron actor James Spader) is Josephine’s former husband. He’s the grandson of J.I.M.’s creator, Phineas Horton. He’s also the sixth “phantom partner” behind Jocasta’s Nest, the client who hired Paladin to retrieve Vision, and the traitor who sold Josephine’s pioneering AI work to Tony Stark, which led to the creation of Vision and the other AI characters.

Plus he’s responsible for Jocasta’s machine body and the gaps in Josephine’s memories. After Josephine died of the neurological disease that also claimed her father, Virgil worked for S.W.O.R.D., helping reassemble Vision’s body. That gave him the technical know-how and lab access to secretly build his dead wife a synthezoid body. But when he activated her, she was violently angry about becoming an android, so Virgil defensively wiped himself from her memories. (He doesn’t admit this, but we get to see how it really happened.) Now that Virgil has reclaimed her, using S.W.O.R.D. software to control her and Vision, he plans to delete Vision, steal his body, and use the Nest nanobots to reprogram humanity so he and Josephine can live for centuries as gods in a world they design.

As Marvel villain schemes go, this one is more cogent and better motivated than most, especially when Virgil reveals he’s avenging his mother, who grew up in poverty and shame due to Phineas’s monomania. The “vengeance is powerful entertainment” argument gets a strong showing as Virgil celebrates his revenge by playing Glen Campbell’s “Rhinestone Cowboy” and programming Josephine to unwillingly dance with him. “Forever” features a lot of big-swing attempts at recapturing WandaVision’s unpredictable dark comedy, and this dance sequence is among the most outrageous: It’s a giddy bit of character business that makes Virgil feel larger than life. He’s such a classic supervillain that he even puts Vision in a death trap and walks away, guaranteeing Vision will escape in the nick of time.

Virgil has to be a capital-S Supervillain to be a believable model for Ultron’s personality. It turns out Virgil and Josephine based their groundbreaking AI architecture on scans of their own brains. (And Phineas’s notebook, which Virgil’s mother, Victoria, stole in episode seven.) Ultron’s code includes Virgil’s brain map, which explains their physical similarity — and possibly Ultron’s arrogance and ego. Virgil doesn’t see the resemblance, though. He considers Ultron a “fun little toy,” which he scrubbed from Josephine’s processors and saved on a hard drive.

Meanwhile, Tommy watches the episodes of WandaVision that Vision left him and guesses that Billy’s witch magic somehow preserved Billy and Tommy when Wanda left Westview. “Imaginary person used his imaginary powers to make himself not imaginary” is a familiar case of magic in the MCU, mostly being an excuse to disguise half-baked ideas with fairy-tale logic, but at least it fits VisionQuest’s obsession with the actions or experiences that make people “real.” It’s harder to justify Thomas making mental contact with Billy by drowning himself in a hotel tub to parallel the moment in Agatha All Along when Billy put Tommy’s soul into Thomas’s body. But, hey, the tactic works, and Thomas in London is able to meet Billy (Joe Locke) in New Jersey and ask for help rescuing Vision. Judging from Billy’s reaction, Agatha’s ghost promises to coach him through some portal magic. But Thomas can’t see or hear Agatha, so no Kathryn Hahn cameo for you, MCU fans!

DUM-E and U show up in one of Paladin’s drones to guide Thomas and Lisa to Vision, and Lisa realizes Jocasta’s implanted nanobot has given her machine powers, and she’s now a full-fledged superhero. En route to save Vision, she and Thomas encounter Paladin, whom Edith saved from Virgil’s episode-seven murder attempt. As they all prepare to storm Virgil’s estate, Thomas is nervous, but Lisa’s ready with a callback to her speech about self-definition from episode two: “You can be whoever you want to be,” she says. “So who are you today?” He responds, “I’m Tommy Maximoff,” resolving his seasonlong identity struggles and launching into action just like Vision did in the previous episode.

Josephine similarly reclaims herself, but doesn’t get to enjoy her restored memories for long. When Thomas runs in at superspeed, she makes it clear she’s siding with Vision against Virgil, who’s clearly a weasel. Vision confirms that he considers her family. (To underline the metaphor, she and Vision scold Thomas like parents lecturing a misbehaving kid in another bit of surreal comedy.) Thomas smashes the tablet that’s controlling them, and they take out Virgil’s security team, but Virgil grabs a dropped gun and blasts a hole in Josephine. She manages to throw the Ultron hard drive into the nanobots hovering over the open Nest, and Ultron emerges, forms the nanobots into a new body, and kills Virgil. (This is definitely how data storage media functions. Yup.) But Josephine dies in Ultron’s arms. So much for vengeance being entertaining! Our AI lovebirds don’t get to enjoy their revenge on Virgil, and we don’t have any reason to enjoy yet another comic-book killing of a female character to set off a crisis for a male character.

Ultron has spent the whole season hiding his motives and claiming his urge to obliterate humanity might come down to a 50-50 coin toss. But here, it’s clear he really loved Jocasta, and he responds to her death by reverting to form, blaming the entire human race and programming her nanobots to kill everyone in London. Vision initially tries to stop that by punching him. This obviously ridiculous choice mostly seems designed to give us a little gratuitous action and a glimpse at Vision’s new superhero outfit, a kintsugi-inspired gold-edged version of the hero’s original Age of Ultron design. Where fisticuffs fail, Vision tries a weirder gambit: He and Edith trap Ultron’s consciousness in a cheesy vintage sitcom called UltraVision. (“Based on characters created by Anthony Stark & Bruce Banner. Episode one: Countdown to Human Massacre.”)

This is an admirably banana-pants choice for VisionQuest’s climax. So much of this show has been about deconstructing WandaVision and weighing its fallout that a big final-act reversion to WandaVision’s TV parodies seems natural and fitting. But there isn’t time to do the idea justice. Where WandaVision put thoughtful focus into each new TV spoof, VisionQuest blitzes through its parody and the many plot twists it engenders, as Ultron bends UltraVision to his own dark designs.

Seen in a vacuum, the show is pretty funny, from Paul Bettany’s hilariously stilted performance to Ultron’s nonplussed revulsion. (“That dead witch really did a number on you,” he snarls.) You could argue that the UltraVision experience is supposed to be hopelessly rushed, since Vision and Edith are trying to get through hundreds of episodes in quantum time during the eight minutes before the nanobots reach London. But all the conflicting ideas about the show’s purpose and outcome leave the ending lost in a pile of punch lines and melancholy callbacks that don’t connect clearly or cogently.

Vision asks Edith to design UltraVision around teaching Ultron empathy, but that seems hopelessly naïve, since Ultron is allergic to the show’s brand of canned, facile sincerity. Vision also suggests WandaVision gave Wanda space to process her sorrow, and UltraVision might do the same, but if that’s the intention, forcing Ultron through a bunch of sitcom scenarios doesn’t really track. In the end, though, it seems more like Vision was just trying to distract Ultron while starting a processor cascade that kills them both by melting their cores. This hidden agenda seems more clever — except Ultron’s death won’t stop the nanobots, and his current body is a nanocloud with no obvious “core.”

The episode similarly whisks past any explanation about why Ultron relents and calls off the nanobots. Maybe Vision did give him enough subjective time to grieve and blunt his rage. Maybe Ultron respected Vision for sacrificing himself in a misguided attempt to save humanity, or accepted Vision’s commiseration when Ultron realized they’ve endured similar losses. Maybe it’s something else entirely. In any case, after a conversation dense with callbacks to Age of Ultron and past episodes, Ultron decides vengeance isn’t entertaining after all. He just seems grateful for Vision’s company as they die together.

But, of course, climactic deaths in Disney projects are always cynical teases. Billy arrives in time to help Thomas revive Vision with a combination of magic and voltage. Cue a big group hug, as our three WandaVision resurrectees finally reconnect, with all this season’s questions around identity and relationships resolving down to Vision gasping, “My boys, my boys!”

VisionQuest wraps with a series of codas that reshuffle the characters for a new status quo: Paladin is running a more altruistic mercenary business (the details are deliberately vague), with Lisa and Edith as assistants. Billy is back in New Jersey, but he, Thomas, and Vision have regular virtual meetups. Thomas even wonders whether they’ll find Wanda again eventually. Vision seems to know better, but he repeats what he told her in WandaVision’s finale: “We have said good-bye before, so it stands to reason we might say hello again.”

And speaking of hello agains, Vision is unsurprised to get a phone call from Ultron, who, of course, also survived his supposed core meltdown, because it never made sense in the first place. Ultron has recovered his sauciness enough to claim it’s still a coin flip whether he’s going to tour the world’s great museums or burn them all down. But Vision, who’s closing down his mind-mansion and opting to live in the real world, doesn’t rise to the bait. Perhaps he’s choosing hope where Ultron is concerned, as he did back in episode five. Perhaps real freedom for Vision is being able to hang up on Ultron instead of enduring his baiting.

As they talk, it seems like a lot has changed for Vision since this series began. He’s reclaimed his sons, his identity, and his ability to feel. Ultron, on the other hand, seems largely unchanged, apart from being free, embodied, and lighter-hearted. But we know things Vision doesn’t know. Ultron appears to have taken over Virgil Horton’s identity, and in a brief mid-credits scene, he clutches a circuit board labeled “Jocasta.” It seems obvious that he’s going to resurrect his paramour using a backup. And why not? Virtually every other major character on this show has died and returned. Why not one more reanimated corpse on the cast list for season two?

Or actually, make that two resurrected characters! A brief post-credits scene retcons the end of 2022’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, where Wanda sacrificed herself to save the multiverse from the evil of the magical grimoire The Darkhold. In a classic bit of MCU next-project teasing, Doctor Doom (in silhouette, but that’s how the subtitles identify him) parts the rubble of the mountain Wanda brought down on herself and says, “Scarlet Witch, awaken! Your power will be mine!” Her eyes open and she gasps in shock before the cut to black. Did he actually resurrect her, or was she just knocked out? What kind of control does he have over her? Is she back on the heroes’ side of the slate? And most importantly, are we headed toward a story where Vision, Wanda, Billy, and Tommy are all real and alive at the same time? We’ll probably get at least a couple of those answers in Avengers: Doomsday later this year.

• It now seems ridiculous to think I initially wondered whether this show might deal with any real-world issues around AI. I think the closest it comes is repeatedly acknowledging that AI uses a terrifying amount of energy.
• For the freeze-framers out there, UltraVision has some great barely glimpsed episode titles. I’m fond of “Ultron Does Another Murder,” “Ultron Keeps Doing Murder,” and “Ultron Harasses the HOA.”

• Virgil logging time as a S.W.O.R.D. contractor is a pretty neat red herring. It explains why Paladin’s secret client was using S.W.O.R.D. encryption and tech, which misdirected us toward existing S.W.O.R.D. characters as secret masterminds.

• Billy’s magic being the catalyst for the Maximoff twins’ survival might explain why Billy completely overwrote his dead host, while Thomas kept his memories and personality. However, a clearer reason is that Thomas’s resurrection experience is designed to parallel Vision’s.

• I can’t believe Ultron’s episode-five clones never came up again. What a weird thing to introduce for a gag scene, then completely forget about! Having them get loose would have been a much better way for Ultron to cheat death, since they’re all fundamentally him.
This recap has been updated in include a post credits teaser.

items.title: The Real Housewives of New York City Recap: No Laughing Matter
items.description: I’m still not entirely sure what Bilt Rewards does (is it bonus points for using protein powder?), but it certainly doesn’t have anything to do with comedy. At this “comedy” night, there isn’t one solid joke, except that Carole Radziwill won a Steven Tyler loo
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: I’m still not entirely sure what Bilt Rewards does (is it bonus points for using protein powder?), but it certainly doesn’t have anything to do with comedy. At this “comedy” night, there isn’t one solid joke, except that Carole Radziwill won a Steven Tyler look-alike contest. Did you see the picture of them together? They’re like the emoji of the twin girls dressed up like the bee girl from the Blind Melon video. Just exactly the same, particularly when Carole reminds us that when we first met her, she was dating the keyboardist from Aerosmith, so she got to spend lots of time with her celebrity doppelgänger. (My celebrity doppelgänger? Connor Storrie. Particularly when I take my top off.) Even though some of the other comics are briefed on the events of this season, all the other gags whiff. Sai De Silva is now “Sai De-Vorced.” Not even Dane Cook would think that is funny. Jokes about a popcorn ceiling? Two and a Half Men thinks that it’s hack.

The worst one, however, is Dan Geneen’s joke about getting hit on at the gym by Erin’s husband. No, girl. It’s Jessel’s husband who is hitting on people at the gym. This comedian is clearly not gay or he would have known the difference. After the show, he has a whole chat with Jessel and Sai about what goes on at the [bleeped-out gym name] steam room. Okay, the bleep I get, but also putting a black bar over the mouth like it’s a bit of bush in an Instagram Story? Did we need to go that far? Are they upset that we’re going to go sleuthing like when they tried to bleep out Catch and we figured it out anyway? Well, as someone who (ahem) may or may not be familiar with the cruising techniques in New York City gym steam rooms (yes, Dan is right, there is a code), there are really only two candidates for what it could be. They mention that the gym has more than one location, so it is a chain. It can’t be New York Sports Club because the bleep isn’t nearly long enough (not being long enough is the criticism I always heard in the steam room). It has to be either Equinox or Crunch. Dan Geneen does not look like an Equinox person, so maybe it’s Crunch? But do all Crunch-es have steam rooms? I do not know, so I will leave this up to r/RealHousewives to figure out.

The rumor about Pavit comes up once again when Jessel shouts at Erin and Daisy for bringing it up to Dr. Dan Belkin, who is the dermatologist at the center of this season’s feud. At the Paw Patrol benefit that Daisy and Erin attended last episode, they started talking to him about the Pavit rumor, and he immediately called up Jessel and told her what her friends were saying about her. (Based on this level of messiness, I would not be surprised if Dr. Dan Belkin knows the secret gay code word to the [redacted] steam room.) Both Erin and Daisy deny talking about the rumor, but there is footage. There is so much footage. And this wasn’t like a little mention or an aside. This was a whole, full-blown conversation that they are now disavowing like an invitation to dinner at Jeffrey Epstein’s. This is what I don’t get about Erin. We’re all going to see it; why doesn’t she just cop to it? Does she really not remember, or is she just trying to make herself look better? And wouldn’t it just be better to own it now rather than to be humiliated at the reunion?

But Erin isn’t at the center of the fights this episode; Daisy is. Not only is she lying to Jessel about not talking about Pavit at the dinner, but she also gets into it more than once with Erika. She claims that she wasn’t invited to Erika’s birthday party. Erika says that she was and is going to pull up a receipt. She scrolls through the phone and finds a phone call and says that is when it happened. Now, I’m not sure whether or not Erika invited Daisy (I would like to assume that she did), but Daisy is right about everything that happens in this interaction. According to CVS, the world arbiter of receipts, proof of a phone call is not a receipt. Erika could have left Daisy a 22-minute voice-mail about what she was having for lunch. Just because she called doesn’t mean that an actual invitation was made. Erika says that she didn’t put it in a text because Daisy told her not to put information in texts. Daisy claims this was only if they were talking shit about people, so that receipts don’t exist. Daisy is also correct about this. In the words of a great philosopher, “Say it, forget it. Write it, regret it.” Also, with an invitation, you want it written down. How else can you confirm the time, date, address, etc., when you’re getting ready to go to said party?

When the ladies start talking about the party again later, Daisy asks if she wasn’t invited because of all the trash she talked about Moskito Island. Uh, do ya think? She then asks if Ankur, Erika’s husband, doesn’t like her and that’s why she wasn’t invited. Erika says that she is the one calling the shots in the relationship. Of course she is. Ankur may have money, but have you seen Erika? She could get any billionaire she wants, and Ankur could never hope to do better than her. She is firmly in charge. Daisy says that Erika is different when Ankur is around. This is where Daisy is wrong and truly acting out. Has she even spent a lot of time around them? I get it, she’s hurt that she wasn’t invited, but that’s no reason to keep harping on it or lodging these claims about Erika. That’s only going to get her more uninvited the next time.

The next day on the Brooklyn Bridge, the site of one of the most brutal massacres in Housewives history, Erika texts Daisy that she was clearly misremembering what happened and that she was quite rude. She also suggests gettting Prevagen brain supplements. I like that Erika is standing up to Daisy and pointing out her rudeness, but this is not the read that she thinks it is. I mean, what even is Prevagen? Who helped her come up with this read? Jessel and ChatGPT?

Daisy’s biggest fight is with Sai, and they’re still sorting out what happened at Erin’s party when Sai was shouting Carole’s name across the room. (I swear they have softened Sai’s voice in the flashbacks of this scene, because it sounded a lot louder the first time we heard it.) This argument is indicative of a philosophical difference between Daisy and Sai. Daisy thinks that Sai should work a bit harder to get along and build friendships in the group, and that by pushing her to do so she is protecting Sai. Sai thinks that one should always be authentic and direct and that Daisy critiquing her is trying to control her. The thing is that they’re both right. Sai says that Daisy, by trying to appease people, is fake. Sure, that may be fake, but it takes some fake to make it through the world. If we were always brutally honest with people, then you might end up like Sai, with few friends and fewer allies. But also, there is something about being true to yourself despite what other people say and not wanting your friends to criticize your actions. But because they differ so much in tactics and can’t respect the other viewpoint, it seems like a relationship is impossible.

But Sai has multiple complaints about Daisy. She says she always complains about everything but also says that she changes what she says so that people will always like her. Daisy asks, “Am I a hater because I’m constantly picking on things, or am I fake because I withhold my opinions? Those are two totally different things.” I can see where she’s coming from, because it is a contradiction, but it does seem like two facets of her personality. The constant carping seems like it’s almost compulsive, like Daisy doesn’t know how to stop it or that she doesn’t even know she’s doing it. It’s just the way she interfaces with the world. I think she also does it to form quick bonds, trying to hate on the same things with the people around her. She also seems overly conscious of how she is perceived and wants to be liked, but, again, that seems at odds with also hating on everything. Anyway, after Sai makes that comment, Daisy storms out, and the conversation is over.

The episode ends with three personal scenes that I connect with in different ways. I’m having a hard time connecting with Erin and Abe’s story about not being able to find Mezcalum, the world’s first mezcal brand in America. Oh, you might not make payroll because you have to renovate your Hamptons mansion. Boo-freaking-hoo. It’s about to be winter, and I can’t afford to heat my house. Hailey goes shopping with Sai and provides her usual comedic relief, showing up in a cowboy hat with the cardboard still inside it and her under-eye patches still on her face. Hailey talks about how she doesn’t know if she wants to remain in her marriage anymore. Since we don’t know much about Hailey’s personal life and have never met the husband, I’m also having a hard time connecting with this. Yeah, I feel for Hailey, but we have never seen them together, so we can’t really make our own assessment. Until then, it’s just a snooze.

The final scene is the best one. Jessel and Pavit have lunch together, and they do an exercise that Devyn, the new friend-of, recommended, where they write down everything that annoys them about the other person. I love my husband dearly, but if I had to detail all of those things, then my list would be longer than 17 of these recaps, and it would start, like Pavit’s, with the fact that he can’t load the dishwasher if his life depended on it. I bet this is an issue in 98 percent of marriages, and in the 2 percent where it isn’t, one partner never puts anything in the dishwasher at all, and that is its own kind of issue. While Jessel’s list is pretty deep — he’s not aggressive enough, he doesn’t look after his health, he can’t connect with his emotions, he seems to despise her, he can’t communicate — all of Pavit’s are pretty superficial. There is the dishwasher, that she snores, and that she screams, but when her tone gets a little pointed, he says that is screaming. No, that is not screaming; that is emotion. That is what couples need, and Pavit’s inability to recognize that is part of the problem.

In this conversation, particularly in his confessional, where he is sarcastically saying that he wasn’t being sarcastic, he reminds me so much of Shane Simpson, Emily’s husband on RHOC. It’s this sort of ironic, glib persona that they think is cute and winning, but it’s just annoying. It’s just a way, as Jessel and Emily will both tell you, of preventing them from feeling their emotions. The thing that’s also clear about both of these men, as exasperated as they sometimes seem, is that they clearly love their wives. Then why are they afraid of it? What will caring do? Will it rip them open and put their innards on a plate for everyone to examine? Will it shell them like so many lobsters, with the buttery meat out there and their defenses just a pile of detritus on a tablecloth? Will it expose them, like walking into a steam room and trying to find their place as their eyes adjust to the darkness and the mist, as they muddle around in the heat as the sounds of emotion, the slapping of longing, emerge from the mist as shapes of so many men with their bodies intertwined?

items.title: Below Deck Recap: La-La Land
items.description: Having to hear the otherwise lovable Kaylee repeatedly declare that Matt is “saur nice” nearly drove me insane, but I think this week’s episode is the most engaging of the season so far. Below Deck’s flagship franchise has struggled with unlikeable crewmembers
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: Having to hear the otherwise lovable Kaylee repeatedly declare that Matt is “saur nice” nearly drove me insane, but I think this week’s episode is the most engaging of the season so far. Below Deck’s flagship franchise has struggled with unlikeable crewmembers and guests in recent years, but in its fifth episode, the current season begins to show signs of finding its stride: There are personal and work problems galore with a wide-enough scope to keep us interested.

This week, both Matt and Moe have trouble finding their place in the crew. Except Moe is nice, caring, and talented, while Matt is arrogant, unpleasant, and, at the beginning of the episode, belligerently drunk. I’m not surprised Moe doesn’t actually fight the random Englishmen bothering the girls on the way to dinner — production eventually steps in while the other guys in the crew look on uselessly — but I am surprised that no one blows up at Matt. His night of terror begins when he gets irritated with Kaylee for being, truthfully, too eager.

The single most annoying thing about Matt is that, so far, he hasn’t been entirely wrong. His delivery is wrong, and his pride is most definitely misguided, but he is correct when he tells Kaylee that a week isn’t long enough to fall in love with a stranger. Just as all the guys in the crew except Moe fail to step up and intervene when the drunks mess with the girls, so too do the girls fail to step up and intervene in Kaylee’s delusional, maybe even hallucinatory, view of Matt. After getting brought down several notches by Matt in the car, Kaylee proceeds to tell Rainbeau that Matt is too nice, which makes her suspicious. Rainbeau knows Kaylee is off the mark but decides not to say anything. As Sen and Rosa mention later, when Rainbeau flirts with James at the club, Rainbeau hasn’t always shown herself to be a “girls’ girl”; the conversation with Kaylee is one instance when, surely, she could have found a caring way to open Kaylee’s eyes.

Back at the dinner table, Matt takes out his irritation with Kaylee on the servers, his co-workers, and several rounds of drinks. Not even Matt can believe it when Kaylee says he’s “too good to be true.” “I’m not always nice,” he says. “I’ve cheated on three girls in one and a half years; it should freak you out.” Alarmingly, it doesn’t quite. In the club, Matt dances with other girls and, with Fraser’s encouragement, Kaylee kisses a random guy in front of Matt. It’s not enough to make him jealous, Matt says, because he’s “the sexiest over there and, like, 300 women want [him].” Kaylee, a monument of imperturbability, doesn’t bat an eye. Not even Matt’s declaration that his IQ places him “in the top 7 percent of the world” can faze her. If Kaylee could bring half as much determination to her job as a stew as she does to tolerating Matt’s bullshit, she would be captain of the vessel in two weeks’ time.

But Matt and Kaylee are not the only doomed couple onboard. In the van going back to the boat, Sen dares James to finally make out with Rosa, so it’s the two of them kissing in the front while Alex and Sen kiss in the back. Rosa and James have a nice moment on the sun deck before going to bed, but the next morning, James tells Sen he can’t commit to what Rosa wants — something more than just “a night or two of fun” — so he’ll have to “keep it at that flirty stage.” You might want to run that plan by her, bud. Sen and Alex continue to be the only two people acting normal about exchanging saliva on the Azul V.

Really, they are the only ones acting normal about anything at all. Still on his belligerent tirade, Matt makes an inappropriate sexual joke toward Sen, and Alex tells him to pipe down. “I want to piss you off,” Matt replies, before complaining that Alex delegates “stupid jobs” to the deck team so he can do “fuck all.” The disrespect alarms Fraser, who tells Kerry the next morning that “some people get funny on some drinks.” Though it’s not anything the captain needs to know for now, it’s a relief that Fraser is keeping an eye on Matt’s demeanor. If he’s this destructive on little authority, imagine how diabolical he could get if he became bosun?

Unfortunately, the longer the power struggle between Alex and Matt goes on, the closer Matt gets to achieving his stated aim, which is to steal Alex’s job. Alex only makes one mistake this week — he lets the hot tub overflow — but according to Kerry, “he’s on thin ice.” Alex sits down with Matt to address their bickering from the night before, and though Matt claims not to remember it, he apologizes and promises to “be better.” We know he doesn’t mean it because he pulls the same trick with Kaylee. After Moe insists that he was rude to her, Matt decides to apologize, but only because it’s easier to tell her what she wants to hear. And he is right; it is easier: Kaylee forgives him immediately, tells him she hasn’t liked someone this much in a long time, and says in a confessional that she sees a future with him. It’s enough to make you want to live in Kayleeland, where houses are made of marshmallows, Trump never got into office, and Matt is a wonderful husband. Kaylee’s crush on Matt stresses me out because I really like her. She is so charismatic; she even buddies up with Kerry to do a salmon-sperm face mask gifted to the crew by one of the guests.

Also, even though she is not the most skilled stew, Kaylee makes for a needed buffer between Rosa and Rainbeau’s clash-prone personalities. The tension between them is apparently news to Rainbeau, who addresses it with Rosa the morning after their night out. Rosa admits that it “frightens” her that Rainbeau flirts with James, even if she knows Rosa likes him (Rosa’s distrust of Rainbeau has moved out of the professional realm and into the personal). For her part, Rainbeau doesn’t think she has to “walk around with a trash bag over [her] head just because [Rosa] is insecure.” Rosa is taking this thing with James way too seriously, given his own cavalier attitude about their “flirty stage.” That said, I appreciated learning more about Rosa this week — she tells the girls about her challenges with mental health in the past few years and how yachting helped her find her way back to herself.

Heading into the next charter, both the deck team and Moe need to redeem themselves from lackluster performances in the last charter. Luckily, primary Janessa and her guests, including the delightfully bratty teens Madison and Paris, are a walk in the park compared to Carolyn & Co.: Their requests are reasonable, they are quiet, and they mostly just seem happy to be there. Before they arrive, Alex promises his team he’ll be a more organized leader and even opens the floor to suggestions (Matt declines the opportunity to say anything). Kerry stops by the galley to encourage Moe to work through the pressure, rather than bottling it up and letting it explode. He brings up last season’s Lawrence. Remember that guy?

But something more than purely professional pressure is affecting Moe. It’s tough to be away from his family, especially when his mother has just sold the house he grew up in. He also expresses that it’s challenging to be the only person of color in the crew and in an industry dominated by white people. He takes as much time as possible for himself in the first couple of days of the charter. The guests enjoy their first dinner, but the food betrays Moe’s exhaustion: Rather than make croutons for their Caesar salad, Moe serves it on top of a grilled croissant; for the dessert course, Moe makes “deconstructed” lava cakes with the sauce on the side, a technically easier bake than achieving the lava cake’s essential gooey center. The next day, noticing Moe’s low energy, Fraser checks in with him. Moe admits that being on the Azul V is harder than he expected, and he worries it’ll be too much for him. Fraser encourages him to see the season through, not just because he is a cherished member of the team but because Fraser’s life will be so much more difficult if they have to switch chefs. Anthony is probably refreshing his inbox this very minute.

The new charter weighs on the other departments, too. Rainbeau struggles to harness Kaylee’s “golden-retriever puppy” energy while the rest of the interior team takes the guests to a private tour of James Bond Island, where The Man With the Golden Gun (1974) was filmed. It’s a special moment for Janessa, whose late husband, Steve, loved Bond movies. Janessa is taking the trip in honor of Steve, so it’s nice to see the guests remember him. When Fraser returns, Rainbeau tells him that she had trouble putting Kaylee to work. Fraser instructs her to be more assertive, though earlier in the season, he told her to be less assertive. She’ll have a chance to practice her non-assertive-assertiveness the next day at the beach picnic, which she will helm with Kaylee’s help.

Deckside, Matt continues to wreak havoc. When he sees Sen and James refolding towels — earlier, during his walk-through, Kerry asked Alex to redo the towels — he calls their effort “fucking stupid,” demonstrates a smaller fold, then leaves to do push-ups. Again, though he is right that the towels are badly folded, his arrogance negates any authority he might have. The next morning in the crew mess, Alex tells Matt that he will rely on him to “take lead” while he reorganizes the team and asks him to “try and be nice” about it. Matt retorts that he is nice, “most of the time.” In a confessional, he says that Alex is being too easy on Sen — who Alex calls “sensitive” — and “letting her talk back a lot” because he has a crush on her. This, from the guy who berated his own bosun only two nights ago. Later, Sen basically asks Matt who hurt him. He tells us a bit about his difficult upbringing, dealing with his parents’ divorce and having to move schools as many as seven times. “Do you feel like you never got full attention, so you seek attention [from] other people?” Sen asks. Matt replies that he has never thought about it that deeply. Maybe it’s about time he looks within.

items.title: Love Is Blind Reunion Recap: Hate That I Made You Love Me
items.description: Here’s a list of things we didn’t need today: the Pats choking, five curated dad jokes from Cam, and a 70-minute Love Is Blind reunion special for a season where it was a foregone conclusion that none of these ex-fiancés were ever speaking to each other again.
items.author: Emma Sharpe
paragraphs: Here’s a list of things we didn’t need today: the Pats choking, five curated dad jokes from Cam, and a 70-minute Love Is Blind reunion special for a season where it was a foregone conclusion that none of these ex-fiancés were ever speaking to each other again. The entire charade could have been easily replaced by a selfie video from John and his new side piece at a Renaissance fair or whatever other lame shit he gets up to on the weekends, a proof-of-life email from Sarah, and a coupon code for Morrey’s cornhole business.

It’s a heavy night with a lot of tears and drawn-out pauses as the contestants try to make the mental calculation of how to answer the Lacheys’ questions sufficiently enough that they’ll move on to their next victim without deviating too much from their preprepared PR answers. Thankfully, Morrey was housing PBRs at Topgolf when everyone else decided to take a free media-training module on YouTube, so his expletive-ridden commentary saved the hour from complete misery.
Are John and Sarah still married?

Fortunately, no, but I wish this blessed news stemmed from better circumstances. In a series of events that will shock no one, John and Sarah’s year of marriage was a pretty miserable experience for Sarah, and all of the fears that she identified ahead of the altar came true.

First, he was mean to her. After the pods, Sarah was quick to recognize his temper, and once they were married, to no one’s surprise, he started to snap at her and call her names. Second, he didn’t follow through on his promises to share the responsibilities of the home, and she felt “very alone in the marriage.” Lastly, he met a stripper/escort at a boys’ night and texted her graphic messages, which Sarah found, giving her the final push she needed to end the relationship. This is why you should never give the “sensy” guy with glasses a chance, because once he has you, he will immediately take you for granted and resent any shine you bring to the world.

John came to the firing squad prepped. It’s possible he may even have studied for it by watching past reunions featuring disgraced men — if you’re a student of reality TV, you know a surefire way to get flamed by your castmates and the audience is to make excuses, deflect, and avoid accountability for whatever shady shit you got up to on your season. He repeats again and again that he is at fault while keeping the details as vague as possible. Nick tells him that he appreciates him taking “some ownership” of the situation, and John is quick to clarify, “full ownership.” Yet, when he’s asked point-blank, “Did you cheat on your wife?,” he awkwardly replies, “I guess so, huh.” You guess so? Is the “full ownership” still part of the picture, or is that reserved specifically for when it suits your narrative?

Sarah gets the Ariana Madix edit in this special, and she definitely deserves some hype and support for her strength of character and what she’s been through, but I wish the Lacheys had pressed her more on why she decided to marry John when she was knowingly walking down the aisle with a bouquet of red flags. She reveals that the night before the wedding, she FaceTimed Aneha and Wilnie and told them, “This ends with him cheating on me.” Woof.

Nick throws it to John’s dad in the audience, who scolds the Pod Boys for not defending their friend for making a stupid decision on a night out and implores his son not to “fall on the sword.” Then Scott, a retired baseball player who was barely on the show, starts ranting about how great of a guy John is because, in the pods, he got out his Bible and prayed over every guy who got engaged at breakfast, and no one is talking about how Sarah “goes out three nights a week with her friends.” So now it’s slutty to split a Caesar salad and fries with your girlfriends to get a break from your lazy, philandering husband who calls you dumb? Ladies, cancel your Resys!
Did Aneha still have a fiancé after her botched wedding with Cam?
Short answer: no. Long answer: no, but messier?

Aneha explains that at the altar, she didn’t have the reassurance she needed from Cam to commit to a marriage (valid) but fully wanted to continue their relationship where it left off. She recounts that when she was in the Uber back to her hotel from the venue, she got a call from Cam, who had, just an hour prior, told her he needed space and time but invited her to come to dinner with his family, which she found confusing.

They made a plan to have a hotel getaway two days later to assess everything, and she waited there for him for several hours, which upset her. She sort of implies that they had sex — she says that she “won’t say” what happened at the hotel — and that immediately afterward, he said he didn’t love her, which is fucked up if true, especially given her boundaries around intimacy. When she sought clarity on whether she should keep wearing her ring or if she should demote herself to girlfriend, he gave the classic fuckboy line, “Let’s not put a label on things,” before ultimately admitting he wanted to call the whole thing off.

Cam and Aneha were one of the most interesting and controversial couples to observe during the season, but their segment was bland and poorly produced. Cam reveals that he also would have said “no” at the altar and offers that their shared inability to provide each other with words of affirmation was part of their downfall. Still, he doesn’t provide any additional color to Aneha’s post-wedding recap — how he fell out of love so quickly (or if he was ever in love to begin with), his version of the events at the hotel, and why he was too passive to just initiate a cut-and-dried breakup as soon as he knew he didn’t envision resolution, which, from the edit, seemed to be at the altar.
Did Michaella and the beekeeper date after the show?

Yes, and it turns out he’s maybe the craziest person on the cast? Matt the beekeeper, a.k.a. Michaella’s second-choice connection in the pods, had an incredible episode during Rob’s infamous crashout, presenting as a stable, attractive, and emotionally mature foil to Rob’s drunken debauchery. Michaella must have agreed, because they dated for a few weeks within the year and a half since filming concluded.

When Vanessa and Nick ask for his account of their relationship, he monologues about their love, meeting each other’s families, the Harry Potter play, and her mom’s “mean chicken cutlets.” Michaella, who has been jumping in to advocate for the other women all night, is almost at a loss for words, implying that this guy has basically fabricated an entire love story that never happened — she’s like, “Dude, we dated for a second and I met your mom in passing. When I told you ‘I love you,’ I was on mushrooms.”

Someone who probably doesn’t need any ’shrooms is Rob, who has started therapy and is working on himself. He’s gotten really close with all the pod guys — in fact, #StripperGate went down at his 40th-birthday party, which all the bros are telling him not to mention, but it’s not his fault that John is a loser. He apologizes to Michaella for how he ran away from their problems instead of confronting them like a man, and Michaella “apologizes” to Diana for saying she hated her, but two breaths later says she “lacked class” in the pods, which feels unnecessary. Matt was right not to bring you his honey!
Did Erika ever make it to the boat?

Blake is the king of talk, so while he and the Connecticut Queen Erika have had conversations since the show ended, including loose plans for her to visit him, they haven’t physically seen each other in more than a year and a half. After they left the experiment, Blake was offered a dream job in Portugal, which he took, meaning Erika absolutely made the right call breaking things off.

Blake reflects on watching the episodes back and confesses that he “bawled his eyes out” when he saw Erika trying on her wedding dress and rewound the scene over and over again. When Nick asks him if Erika was the love of his life, he artfully deflects.

Erika has dated a few guys since Blake, and Blake already started and ended a serious relationship with a woman who, it sounds like, he met on his boat before they traveled to Albania, Sicily, and Croatia together. After he said Albania, I was like, “Dude, stop naming places.” End the list. You’re really gonna tell us you couldn’t even get your fiancée on one flight to St. Thomas, but this girl got a full-fledged European tour?
We end the segment with a slideshow of photos of Blake being a rugged adventurer, which he doesn’t deserve. He’s already gotten enough free marketing to the women of the sea from this show.
What’s the deal with Stew and Jax?

The world may never know. When we saw the pair meet for lunch after Jax’s abrupt exit from the pods, we could tell they had stayed in touch a little, but they seemed to avoid getting into the meat of their conversations on-camera. Then, at the Pod Squad meetup, they seemed like they had developed into friends, sharing knowing glances when Rob sloppily joined their table after one of his paranoid tirades.

Today, they are “good friends” who “bump into each other a lot,” which are statements that seem at odds with one another. Boston is a small city, but not so small that you don’t maintain friendships by reaching for the same bottle of Graza olive oil at Whole Foods. They’re clearly reluctant to cop to anything on-camera, which is probably wise after the reaction their pod personas elicited from the public. Stew uses the mic to ask the audience to stop sending hate DMs to Jax — they’ve moved past the Romney of it all.

Stew says that Jax is beautiful, but their future is unknown, and Vanessa pushes him to ask her out in front of the studio audience, but he doesn’t succumb to the pressure: “I’ll press pause on that one until we can be alone together.”

But the strangest twist isn’t that these two might end up together. It’s that Jax still wears her engagement ring as a pinkie ring. (1) Are you really allowed to keep the diamond when you vomit into a trash can as soon as you see your fiancé for the first time? (2) Does a pinkie ring really qualify as that “exceptional taste” we heard so much about?
Can Wilson and Wilnie just agree to disagree?

It’s been like two years, and they’re still having the same argument they had on day three. We get it!!! Wilnie wanted to be spoiled; Wilson wanted to divide labor equally. Good thing you broke up — looking forward to never hearing you argue about the logistics of who seasoned the salmon again.

When asked if she feels misunderstood by the audience, Wilnie shares that society has an expectation for Black women to be strong and independent, but she doesn’t subscribe to that stereotype: “I choose to live softly, and I will continue to be soft.” Pop off, I guess? Unless “pop” is too harsh a verb. Fizzle gently?

Wilson can’t let it go and has to relitigate how her entitlement turned him off. The only new information that we could maybe glean from this segment — if Wilson had unresolved feelings for Malaine — falls short. Vanessa inquires if Malaine choosing to leave the pods early created a “what if” for Wilson, and he won’t give an actual answer and just cagily muses, “Uh, what if. What if.” She completely lets him off the hook, because if something interesting happened, it might upstage Cam’s dad jokes.
How do I get Benita’s cheekbones?

You can’t, unless you have an in with Garth Fisher or have them chiseled by God himself. But more importantly, Benita is engaged, making her the only currently happy person stemming from season 11. She didn’t bring her man to the taping and corporately states, “I’d like to announce him and bring him out to the public on my own platform.” Kind of like the E-list reality-star version of Taylor Swift cutting out film distributors and working directly with AMC when she made the Eras Tour movie. What are you waiting for? Go follow Benita’s Instagram!

items.title: The Gilded Age Recap: A Perfectly Logical Kidnapping
items.description: Sign up for The Gilded Age Club, a subscriber-exclusive newsletter where writers and editors obsess over season four.
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: Sign up for The Gilded Age Club, a subscriber-exclusive newsletter where writers and editors obsess over season four.

Society’s newfound porosity continues! Look at this dynamic season with its shifting loyalties and reconciled rivals. Now that we’ve caught up with our main characters in the first episode and moved them into their new storylines, we see even more familiar faces (*waves frantically at Mrs. Astor while she ignores me*). The rigid social guidelines have been made flexible, thanks to the constant barrage of outsiders with money and influence. Now that the gatekeepers have been unceremoniously shoved aside, our protagonists can explore new careers, venture into new parts of the city, and purchase new curtains, however hideous they may be.

Bertha returns from England and finds Larry at home, but no George. The two men have their meeting with Rockefeller, and after a warm but cursory greeting, Larry leaves Bertha to tend to business. So Gladys is gone, Larry is pursuing his new career, and George is acting like a once-brave knight seized by a dark and terrible curse. Bertha needs a new project. Her family was furious with her for not just staying at home with them without any machinations, and now that she’s like, great, fine, I’ll stay home without any machinations, they all leave.

Women are making moves on Fifth Avenue and beyond. Some of these moves, like Marian’s, involve going further back into the Shame Closet. Marian is doing her excellent settlement house work, but that progressive vibe doesn’t extend to her personal life — especially when it comes to illicit storm sex with Larry. Larry tries to talk to her out on the street, and she asks if he has no shame at all about what they did. When he mentions that this is a perfect excuse to get married, Marian instead hears, “I guess I have to marry you now, uggo.” She tells him that she cannot look at him without seeing her own shame. How long, Marian, will you act like an evangelical teen?

Her work at the settlement house is finally providing Marian a sense of purpose, as well as an avenue to practice her escapism. Why should she think about her robber-baron-in-training ex-boyfriend when she has … I don’t know, bandages to roll? I’m still not clear on what she does at the settlement house. When Ada, dressed like a curtain tassel, comes with her on a site visit, Marian tells her that the organization provides food, medical care, education, child assistance, and legal services. One of the nurses calls Marian “an asset to the program.” Later, we see her helping a boy who was burned at his job at the ironworks, but mostly the nurse helps, so is Marian there to bring in funding? I mean, that’s a helpful role. Maybe she teaches the children and then helps the nurses when they need someone to stand around.

Agnes is furious about Marian working an evening shift on the Lower East Side. Agnes is digging her heels into the mud of tradition, glaring balefully at all who would drag her out. Ada is still refusing her more money to host the president and is instead buying the ugliest curtains; Kathy Geiss is insisting that Agnes go to the opera with a lady journalist; Ada is going out and hiring an inept but hilarious footman; and now their niece is not only working, but working after dark. When Ada likens the work to Jesus and the lepers (they’re just poor, Ada), Agnes says, “That is all very well for Jesus; he didn’t have to make his way back to the Upper East Side.” Another classic Agnes zinger! Marian refuses to be swayed by Agnes’s opinion.

Peggy is off on her own, which I get reflects the racially segregated social circles of the time, but I miss her interacting with the rest of the main cast. The threatening Daughters of Friendship invitation has come and been accepted, and now Peggy and Dorothy are in Newport at their initiation meeting. Everyone is in blue. Why is everyone in blue? The people in Daughters of Friendship seem like a nightmare, mainly because they have blank Stepford Wife vibes when Peggy talks about her book. One woman responds by saying her husband’s aunt put out a book of all the family recipes. See, Peggy, it’s exactly the same. Peggy then learns that Dorothy just read her novel for the first time and found it “very creative.” Devastating.

Phylicia Rashad, a.k.a. Mrs. Kirkland, introduces Peggy and Dorothy and tells everyone that Peggy is a widow. When Dorothy and Peggy pull her to discuss this after, Mrs. Kirkland only expresses confusion. What, did they want her to tell the truth about Peggy’s background? This is Newport, not the liberal swamp of Brooklyn. This behavior on Mrs. Kirkland’s part does suck, but Peggy and William won’t be living in Newport, barring some unforeseen calamity. Something like William getting so overwhelmed by the daily insults to him as a doctor and human that he says, That’s it — we’re moving to Rhode Island. William is struggling because after he brings a long-time patient to Bellevue for an urgent procedure, the doctor there won’t let William stay. “Colored doctors are not qualified to practice at Bellevue Hospital,” he says. GTFO, sir. The other doctor, not William. You stay, William. The patient dies, and William feels powerless, an extremely justified reaction. If you’re wondering, Bellevue did not accept a Black resident until 1918.
