And what the hell, let’s also mention Dr. May Edward Chinn, the first Black woman to graduate from Bellevue’s medical college in 1926. You’re so impressive, Dr. Vincent and Dr. Chinn.

I know that you’re like, But what of the opera this season? No worries, I got you. The journalist who interviews Agnes (BONNIE MILLIGAN, I see you) is going to write an article about Agnes at the Met, so now Agnes has to go to the opera house that caused such a furor in previous seasons. Mrs. Astor’s opera house has quickly gone down the tubes, so there isn’t another prestigious option in town. And, fortunately for those of us who like to see a large part of the cast mingle, so many people are there!

Mrs. Astor is in attendance, a shock. Bertha is there, wearing a dress that has been the cause of death for multiple birds. Mrs. Astor gives Bertha some advice as to absent husbands. This advice boils down to “Come up with a more believable excuse.” Carrie Astor is also at the opera, which makes me so happy, as are Enid and Oscar and Larry. The opera is a great place to pass along scuttlebutt. Enid, hoping to lord it over Bertha, tells her about Agnes hosting the president at her house and that there probably isn’t room for Bertha to come. Bertha stares, stunned. Will we get Bertha in Her Former Glory? Will this presidential dinner competition bring back her edge? Something has to happen, because I can’t handle this sad version of the Rich People Low-Key Fight Each Other show. Return to your machinations, Bertha! Steal the presidential luncheon!

Oscar and Enid are moving forward with their salon, which I, for one, am very excited to see. Their first guest of honor is William Merritt Chase, who later founded the school that became the Parsons School of Design. This is a school so famous that I, decidedly not an Art Person, have heard of it. The Fricks are thrilled to hear about the salon, which is a real get for Oscar and Enid. What is their couple name? Encar. Osnid. Probably Osnid. Osnid continues to have the greatest potential for fun on this show, and as Senator Palpatine says, we will watch your career with great interest, Osnid.

Larry is lured away from whatever opera is being performed (we never learn which it is! Consider me irked!) by a friend who wants him to invest in a more entertaining medium. This medium hilariously turns out to be operetta. “No, no, no one wants that stuffy old opera business anymore. We must turn to the future and the far different operetta format.” Amazing. They’re trying to bring Gilbert and Sullivan to America — specifically, The Pirates of Penzance. I mean, that’s a good one. At least it’s not The Mikado, because then we would have to have a whole discussion about how to ethically do that show.

And what of our curse-burdened knight? George’s Pinkerton detectives located his would-be assassin in a tenement, and we learn that it is Anne Morris’s son, Will. Do you remember Anne Morris? George Russell ruined her family in season one after her husband tried to go after George’s railroad station. Then her husband killed himself, and Anne swore revenge. Wow, Anne Morris, what a throwback. She also went to Bertha and begged her for help, and Bertha scornfully rejected her. I love a character growth moment, and we see that here through a parallel. After George and his detectives kidnap Will, Anne stops Bertha outside her house and pleads with her to intercede. This time, despite having seriously less clout in her family, Bertha listens. Anne tells her that if she loses her husband and her son, she won’t survive it. We are now encountering a Bertha who is much less assured of her place in the family, and of their own survival. Will almost killed George, and Gladys almost died in childbirth. We don’t see her agree, but she will talk to George about Will.

George is losing it, and we get more of a window into why in his confrontation with Will. His meeting with Rockefeller goes poorly, with Rockefeller intent on gouging Russell Industries. Larry tries to be conciliatory, and George ferociously turns on him after the meeting. “You know nothing, Larry Snow,” he says. When Bertha comes to see him at his office (pre–Anne Morris encounter), she asks him to come home, telling him he looks tired. George accuses her of looking for a weakness to “lure” him back. Dude. But then, when she tries to leave, he pulls her into a makeout session that some damn assistant interrupts. Come on, man.

When she returns the next day to discuss Will’s kidnapping, Bertha is upset that George didn’t tell her he found his attacker. George, you what? I know you’re mad at her and also everybody, but damn. Not to defend Henry Frick, but George is handling this very differently than Frick did when Sasha Berkman tried to kill him. He says if he turned Will over to the police, he would be hanged. Do you know that, sir? Berkman got 21 years in prison. George doesn’t seem moved by Bertha’s intercession.

Later, we find where they have been keeping Will: in a room at the end of a dirty warehouse tunnel. We also find out that George is drinking laudanum. For those not in the know, laudanum is rebranded opium. It’s not great. This is not great for George. Did he get addicted to opium after his surgery, and now he’s barging around being an asshole to everyone? Maybe! Now he just has to decide whether he’s murdering Will Morris. Anne is there too for some reason. It’s really unclear why. Did he want to punish her too? Did she ferret out the location off-camera, and now they’re making her watch her son’s murder because everyone in this dirty tunnel room is terrible?

George holds a gun to Will’s stomach, and talks about getting shot there himself, being conscious on the operating table and realizing his life was nothing. It’s really a toss-up as to whether he’ll shoot Will. I could not decide. He finally shoots off to the side, and I was like 75 percent sure he shot Anne instead, which would be fully insane. Can you imagine?! But somehow, his unfocused random shot didn’t hit any of the many people there, and Will and Anne run off, with Anne promising they’ll never set foot in New York again.

Returning home, all the edges of George’s vision are fuzzy. That’s not great. He goes to see Bertha and tells her he let Will go. When Bertha asks him what is going on with him and their relationship, George tells her that he doesn’t know how to answer that. He has no sense of direction. Bertha needs him to make a decision, because she can’t continue in this half-life, but she wants them to be husband and wife again. Excellent. Let’s keep making these moves, show. Will George and Bertha reemerge as the power couple, or will George continue down this flushing toilet of laudanum and despair? Time will tell.
Gossip Items for Mrs. Astor’s Next Ball

• Do you think if one person didn’t get the memo about wearing blue to the Daughters of Friendship meeting, they would be told to immediately leave, or just shamed into standing alone in the corner the whole time?
• Is Ada dressing like a tassel in honor of her new curtains? Discuss.
• Speaking of salons, has everyone seen the Renoir Sucks at Painting video that’s been circulating? It is compelling.
➼ How will the Russells get out of this one?
We know you have thoughts. Comment your response below for a chance to be featured in The Gilded Age Club newsletter.

items.title: Next Gen 2026: 35 Rising Hollywood Executives Under 35
items.description: Nobody ever said that Hollywood careers come easy. But right now, with consolidation and layoffs decimating the middle rungs of entertainment’s steep corporate ladder and studio remits changing with each earnings report, dream jobs have never been more difficu
items.author: Winston Cho; Aaron Couch; Caitlin Huston; Mia Galuppo; Ryan Gajewski; Katie Kilkenny; Borys Kit; Lacey Rose
paragraphs: Nobody ever said that Hollywood careers come easy. But right now, with consolidation and layoffs decimating the middle rungs of entertainment’s steep corporate ladder and studio remits changing with each earnings report, dream jobs have never been more difficult to land, much less retain.

Such trends aren’t slowing the ascent of THR’s Next Gen class of 2026, who join such illustrious alumni as Donna Langley, Ari Emanuel, Kevin Feige and Peter Rice. In fact, this group is too busy forging new paths through the chaos — whether that’s bringing Gen Z back to cinemas (as indie producer Christian Vazquez did with both Primetime and You Can See Everything) or fortifying the streaming ecosystem amid endless churn (see Claudia Shin and Louie Hayes, behind the Apple TV Emmy darling Widow’s Bay and the Prime Video breakout Sterling Point, respectively.)
Meet the 35 executives and reps, each of them 35 years old or younger, who should be atop your call list, if they aren’t already.

- Alyssa Altman, 35 RK Films, senior vp LOGLINE Championing rom-coms like Anyone But You and Netflix’s upcoming 13 Going on 30 update. THE ARC Altman got a unique view of the industry when she would join her father, Steve, who rented out lighting, camera and grip equipment: “I grew up doing my homework in grip trucks, and I just loved being on set.” Her dad’s rom-com adoration rubbed off during their weekly trips to the movies, where films like Love Actually made an early impression. Altman studied journalism at Emerson but caught the producing bug while moonlighting on college TV projects. After time at Gersh, she became then-Universal exec Jeff Kirschenbaum’s assistant and followed him to RK Films. While the company focused on bigger IP plays, she endorsed the script for Anyone But You (“That was my baby”), Sony’s Sydney Sweeney-Glen Powell feature that became a rare theatrical comedy hit. Up next: Amazon MGM’s tennis rom-com Love Love and Netflix’s Millie Bobby Brown-led Just Picture It. PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Andy Cohen. My favorite way to de-stress after a long day is to watch and listen to the soothing sound of people fighting on Bravo.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “The fact that movies geared towards women do great theatrically. Every time it happens, people act like it’s an anomaly. Women are starved for content and it’s not a coincidence.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “When I was an assistant at Universal, we set up a screening for an A-list star who specifically requested popcorn from the Universal Studios theme park. I had to sneak into the park through the back lot and bring it back before he arrived.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Sally Albright from When Harry Met Sally. She isn’t afraid to speak her mind, is a hopeless romantic, and has strong opinions on how she orders her food.”

- Jenna Berger, 35 Marvel Studios, director of production development LOGLINE Berger is serving as co-producer, and Kevin Feige’s right hand, on Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars. ’Nuff said. THE ARC An L.A. native with industry parents, Berger grew up wanting to make movies. “I had this theory that everybody who didn’t want to make movies was lying to themselves and secretly did,” she says. So, shortly after graduating from University of Pennsylvania with a double major in English and film, she landed a gig at The Mark Gordon Co. Still, it was Marvel that was making some of her favorite films — she saw Spider-Man: Homecoming four times in the theater — but the company felt impenetrable … until it wasn’t. In 2019, Berger scored a position, rising to junior exec before finding herself the solo exec on the Marvel TV series Ms. Marvel, where she earned a supervising producer credit and honed her creative leadership, talent development and production expertise. “It was the best crash course in figuring out how this company worked and making something worthy of the Marvel name,” she says. The higher-ups took note, which is why Berger now oversees some of the studio’s most ambitious films. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Kermit the Frog. Because my job is to bring amazingly talented people together to make something special amid total chaos … which sometimes means convincing everyone the show must go on before the set falls down around us.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “David Heyman. To get to work on Bond and Harry Potter?! A dream. Would love to trade places for a day … or forever.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Having a sneeze attack while leaving a voicemail for Aaron Sorkin on behalf of my boss.”

- Natalie Berkus, 35 LuckyChap, senior vp TV LOGLINE Developing (and producing) your future TV obsessions, including Andrew Garfield’sWild Things. THE ARC Rather than follow her agent dad and comedy writer mom into the business, Berkus arrived at University of Michigan eager to be a lawyer. “Then I rushed the law fraternity and didn’t get in,” she says. “I mean, I whiffed it and was like, ‘Shit, now what do I do?’ ” The answer, it turns out, was to parlay her love of TV into a series of PA gigs on shows like The Mindy Project before talking her way into a job as the writers assistant on Girls and, later, with Lena Dunham and Jenni Konner’s company. From there, she logged six years at Imagine Entertainment, where she was intimately involved in a slate that included The ’Burbs and the upcoming Siegfried and Roy series starring Garfield and Jude Law for Apple TV. But LuckyChap came calling a year ago, and the L.A. native and new mom to daughter Roonie jumped at the opportunity to work at the Margot Robbie-led hit factory. In that time, she has built a roster of 10 to 15 projects, including a Life Is Strange series for Amazon Prime Video. Still, Berkus doesn’t take herself too seriously. “If I had to brand myself, I’d say I like to bring a levity to this business,” she says, “because I think sometimes, especially now, things can get really stressful and we lose sight of the fact that ultimately this is just one big party.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Nina Rosenstein, who does all of the HBO comedy specials. We’ve never met, but Nina, girl, if you’re reading this, let’s link and get our Freaky Friday moment started!” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “That having unapproachable girlboss ‘I’m smarter than you’ energy is cool. It’s not, it’s lame! Normalize the quiet power in validating others and having a fun vibe.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Nowhere are you crazy!! No more of these!!”

- Mandi Brooksbank, 34 Netflix, senior manager, business affairs, scripted series LOGLINE Helps mold Netflix’s scripted slate, brokering deals with top talent like Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media. THE ARC As a kid in Reno, Nevada, Brooksbank figured she was destined for Broadway. While most her age were on the playground, she was busy with casino shows, doing dinner theater (and playing the harp) in vintage Hollywood glam. “It was entertainment or bust,” she recalls with a laugh. Later, she’d speedrun undergrad at USC and law school at Southwestern, finishing both in five years. Since then, she’s built a Hollywood résumé that includes stints at CAA, Donaldson Callif Perez and eOne. Now in her fifth year at Netflix, Brooksbank helps steer the streamer’s scripted series unit, striking deal after deal with TV’s biggest names. It’s a high volume affair, with Brooksbank managing a slate that includes The Altruists, Ransom Canyon and Sirens, among many others. “I’m the third child in a family of six,” she says of her negotiating chops. “They all have big personalities, so they prepared me well for Hollywood.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Miss Piggy.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Women directors’ second and third films. We talk about breaking through, but what about career longevity?” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “When I was considering law school, Patti Felker encouraged me to see being a woman as an advantage in negotiations, particularly the ability to read people, adapt and adjust your approach to the person across the table without losing sight of what you’re there to accomplish.”

- Barry Buren, 35 CAA, TV talent agent LOGLINE Makes deals for A-listers including Pedro Pascal, Matthew Rhys, Steven Yeun and Eddie Redmayne. THE ARC Hollywood has Orlando’s Central Florida Talent agency to thank for putting Buren on his path. After the New Jersey native graduated a semester early from nearby Rollins College, he picked up a gig at the model/talent agency to stay near friends who were still in school. Though he imagined he might become an engineer someday, he accepted an L.A.-based relative’s offer to live with her while giving Hollywood a try. As luck would have it, agenting stuck, and after a stint at Gersh, the avid golfer joined CAA in 2014. Today, the married rep is entrusted by actors including Josh Hartnett, Charlie Hunnam and Hannah Waddingham. Earlier this fall, client (and double Emmy winner) Rhys gave Buren a shout-out from the Emmy stage. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Serving coffee to people in an order determined by seniority and annual earnings. It was my first introduction to the Hollywood hierarchy, and I learned very quickly that even caffeine has a pecking order.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Being on a call with 15 people to schedule another call with 15 people, only to discover that the one person who actually needed to be there wasn’t invited.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Lorne Michaels. To have spent five decades at the intersection of comedy, culture, and discovering talent is pretty remarkable.”

- Winnie Carrillo Montiel, 35 Amazon MGM, film executive, production & development LOGLINE Oversees films that range from bro-y actioners (The Wrecking Crew) to weepy love stories (Honeymoon With Harry). THE ARC Carrillo Montiel’s career in entertainment began with a clerical error. As an Emerson undergrad, she was mistakenly admitted as a screenwriting major instead of the literature and publishing program she had applied to. She ended up staying the course, eventually doubling down by attending graduate school at USC’s famed Peter Stark Producing Program. While there, she landed a temp job in MGM’s film group, which she did by day, leaving classes for night. Ultimately, it was the studio’s then-president Jonathan Glickman who helped push through the Guatemala City native’s visa sponsorship to land her her first full-time Hollywood gig. “He just made me promise that I wouldn’t get my green card and leave,” she remembers. “This was almost a decade ago and I’m still here. So, I really kept my promise.” Carrillo Montiel has since survived several regime changes, not to mention an acquisition, to land at her current spot on Amazon MGM’s film team, where she has overseen such films as The Sheep Detectives and an upcoming slate with projects from Dan Fogelman (Honeymoon) and Michael Showalter (a Serendipity reimagining). One of her proudest accomplishments is shepherding Angel Manuel Soto’sThe Wrecking Crew, explaining, “Latinos are often put in a very specific box, and we are only hired to tell Latino-specific stories. I’m always looking for opportunities to elevate talent that I think are just great filmmakers.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Unlimited budgets.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “I was advised to look for an American husband as I was told it would be impossible for me to earn a work visa in this industry.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Cold calling very specific animal experts in Russia and Brazil to attempt to track down recent sightings of extremely large species of bears and snakes.”

- Margaret Clark, 32 20th Television, director of development LOGLINE Manages a roster of overall deals (Liz Meriwether, Drew Goddard) and development projects, including the Hulu hit Furious. THE ARC Technically speaking, Clark was discovered at the Panera on South Beverly Drive. At least, that’s where a guy from APA overheard her during an informational coffee with a fellow University of Virginia alum and offered to pass along her résumé to his agency mailroom. She was hired the following week. “I treated it like my grad school,” Clark says of her agency stint. By late 2017, the Virginia native and onetime theater kid had jumped to 20th Television, where she eventually found her way to Dana Walden’s desk for three pivotal years. In that time, she gained both a high-level education and a top-tier mentor. These days, Clark’s back on the 20th team, punching above her weight as she manages a slate of projects and the studio’s IP pipeline. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Jennifer Lopez in The Wedding Planner.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Buying a single old-fashioned donut for the CEO on Friday mornings. It had to be from Winchell’s. I wasn’t his assistant.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “The National Theater in London. Or the ABC Riverside Starbucks.”

- Sarah Colvin, 30 Neon, senior vp acquisitions LOGLINE Keeps Neon supplied with art house favorites and horror standouts, including The Secret Agent, Leviticus and All of a Sudden. THE ARC Colvin spends a good chunk of her year traveling to Sundance, Berlin, SXSW, Cannes and beyond in the name of supplying Neon’s film slate with titles that will soon be Letterboxd’s new obsession (see: Oliver Laxe’s Sirāt and the long-awaited doc Once Upon a Time in Harlem). Raised in New Mexico by artist parents, young Colvin would spend whatever free time she had with friends at Santa Fe’s one art house cinema. She laughs, “We thought we were so highbrow.” But she took that passion to NYU, where her professor, indie producer David Hinojosa, helped her land an internship at Neon, right as the then-upstart distributor was releasing its first success, I, Tonya. “There was no formal end date to the internship,” she says. “Eventually, Tom [Quinn] was like, ‘You should probably have a job here, then.’ ” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “A blend of PeeWee Herman and Griffin Mill from The Player.” THE TALENT I’D KILL TO WORK WITH IS “Wile E Coyote.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “The great equalizer that is the valet stand after the Academy Awards.”

- Dylan Conklin, 34 Entertainment 360, manager LOGLINE Guides the careers of clients like Kaia Gerber and Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story star Ella Beatty. THE ARC Conklin was studying international business in China for a summer when he realized the path wasn’t for him. Fortunately, a TV class with guests from Breaking Bad and Mad Men opened his eyes to a career in the entertainment field instead. Following a stint as an assistant to producer Tripp Vinson and some good advice from mentor attorney Howard Weitzman, he landed at 360 in 2016. A decade later, the dad of two has an impressive roster of talent clients, including Costa D’Angelo, for whom he’s lined up back-to-back shows (East of Eden, The Sticks, We Were Liars), and Ji-young Yoo, whose post-KPop Demon Hunters path includes a Paramount movie and Presumed Innocent season two. BEST ADVICE ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Don’t chase hits. Champion exceptional artists, nurture their talent, and the hits will follow.” IT WAS FROM… “Mo Ostin.” THE TALENT I’D KILL TO WORK WITH IS “Danny DeVito.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Making PB&J sandwiches in the office kitchen with Jennifer Garner.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “Jerry Bruckheimer.”

- Kai Dolbashian, 33 1.21, Film & TV development head LOGLINE Identified filmmaker Michael Shanks and helped develop Together from script to splashy Sundance sale. THE ARC While attending Chapman’s film school, Dolbashian landed an internship at MGM TV. The problem: The job was an hour away on a good day, and he had no car. Though he racked up credit card bills renting Zipcars, the bet paid off. He scored a post-grad gig and found a mentor in producer Andrew Mittman. And when Mittman launched his own banner in 2020, he was there on day one. Now, as the company’s head of film and TV development, Dolbashian has a slew of projects in development, including Warner Bros.’ remake of Attack of the 50 Foot Woman with Margot Robbie and Tim Burton. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Arno from Uncut Gems. We’re both impatient Armenians and both desperately want to do business with Adam Sandler.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “The first time I had lunch with Christoph Waltz, he cut and ate his strudel exactly the way his infamous character Hans Landa does in Inglourious Basterds. Thankfully, unlike Hans, Christoph is one of the nicest human beings.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Bill Hader. There is literally no one else who could write and direct that epic motorcycle chase and shootout from season three of Barry, yet also perfectly embody the unhinged role of Officer Slater in Superbad.”

- Carly Elter, 32 Hidden Pictures, senior vp film and TV LOGLINE The architect behind The Housemaid is also behind lit-centric packages based on best-sellers from Rebecca Yarros and V. E. Schwab. THE ARC When Elter first walked into the house at the center of her 2025 movie The Housemaid, she cried. “It was such a surreal moment,” she says. “In my apartment, I read a book that I thought was a good idea for a movie, and now we have 100 people-plus employed making that movie.” Elter sold the film adaptation when it was self-published by author Freida McFadden; it would later land a publishing deal and sell 6 million copies, while the movie earned more than $400 million and quickly scored a sequel, which is in production. It’s not the married New Jersey native’s only claim to fame. While still an assistant — with stints at WME, Pascal Pictures and Mandeville — she also founded Women Wednesdays (now The Real Champions), where she’d screen films from women and nonbinary filmmakers for fellow assistants with the goal of getting the directors studio jobs. Later, Elter — who lives in Playa Vista with her husband and mutt Archie and also counts TV as a part of her remit with MGM+’s Robin Hood — started a mentorship program that’s helped place over 150 people into jobs. MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Being approached by a famous actor on a red carpet who told me he was a huge fan of mine. Turns out he thought I was Alana Haim.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Amanda Seyfried. She has built a life where she makes incredible movies and TV shows and then goes home to her farm to hang out with goats and emus. She’s cracked the code.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “You have to work hard to build the version of Hollywood you want to be a part of.” IT WAS FROM “Sara Scott.”

- Anna Flickinger, 34 UTA, motion picture lit agent LOGLINE From Mary Beth Barone to Sterling Point producer Raffi Donatich, she gets funny women’s work to screen. THE ARC “I read these goddamn think pieces like, ‘Comedy’s dead,’ ” says Flickinger, whose response is often: “Really?! There’s always going to be a big theatrical comedy that gets people back in the seats.” She saw it happen firsthand when writer client Ilana Wolpert’s Anyone But You made over $200 million at the box office. Initially, the Chicago native and oldest of eight thought she’d pursue a career in politics, but after interning in the office of Sen. Dick Durbin (“loveliest man in America”) and a DC lobbying firm (“fucking depressing”), she realized her love of The West Wing was more about an interest in entertainment than government. After temping her way around L.A., she landed at UTA, where she ultimately found a home in the motion picture lit group. Now, Flickinger, who lives with her husband and their Rottweiler and Chihuahua, guides clients like Sammi Cohen (You Are So Not Invited to My Bar Mitzvah) and Barone, who’s writing and starring in her own rom-com. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “C.J. Cregg sun, Josh Lyman rising, Toby Ziegler moon.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “The public transit infrastructure of New York in L.A.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Why it takes women making their first, second, third and fourth movie to get the compensation and resources that men get to make their second movie.”

- Carly Frankel, 32 WME, digital agent LOGLINE Brokers deals for top podcasts, including Giggly Squad’s nine-figure pact with SiriusXM. THE ARC An L.A. native, Frankel got an early taste of agency life while booking comedy shows, including Chelsea Peretti’s, as an undergrad at UC Berkeley. It led to an assistant gig in UTA’s comedy touring department, then another at then-podcasting startup Wondery. But after greenlighting Wondery shows including Baby, This Is Keke Palmer, Frankel was called back to the agency side at WME, where she’s helped Maria Sharapova launch a podcast with Vox Media and brokered Tinx’s deal with SiriusXM and Dr. Mary Claire Haver’s deal with Audacy. As more and more people consider starting a podcast, Frankel advises talent about the hard work required, including recording a minimum of 45 episodes a year. “I think the number one thing is someone who is genuinely enthusiastic about it,” she said. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Chasing comedians down Melrose to introduce myself after their stand-up sets. Saying hi on behalf of the agency was my cardio.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Truly anywhere that offers a 16-ounce cup. The ‘default 10-ounce latte’ trend is killing me.”
BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Your reputation is your greatest currency. Work hard and be kind.”

- Katie Giarla, 35 Cut To, founding member/partner LOGLINE Building a slate of hot projects, including the upcoming Elle Fanning-Nicole Kidman legal thriller Discretion, for the A24-based company. THE ARC Raised by a psychologist and a lawyer in Pittsburgh, Giarla’s only link to the entertainment business was her childhood birthday parties at the local movie theater. “I thought I’d be a lawyer,” she says, “and then I did some internships in law and realized I could make money and I would hate my life.” Upon graduating from University of Pennsylvania, Giarla parlayed her love of reading into a gig in the books department at WME. The trouble, she’d soon learn, was that she was more interested in the books than the dealmaking. So, she shifted groups before segueing to Endeavor Content (later, Fifth Season), where she championed projects including East of Eden as a series for Netflix. Giarla would later jump with boss Joe Hipps to Cut To, a red-hot company that will soon have more shows than executives. Among its recent sales, all of which prompted frenzied bidding wars: the Joel Edgerton-led crime drama Trigger Point and a two-season order for a Gwyneth Paltrow drama. At press time, however, Giarla was more focused on her other major project, her newborn son, with whom she’s now home on maternity leave. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Lady Olenna Tyrell. I’ve been rewatching GoT on maternity leave. She’s inquisitive, sharp-tongued and loyal to a fault.“ MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “When I realized there was a typo on a deck that my boss was en route to present to Obama — at the White House. That was a crazy two hours.”
PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “Andy Cohen. The writers’ strike was in full swing when Scandoval hit, which gave me way too much downtime to stumble into the Bravoverse.”

- Jordan Gorelick, 34 UTA, talent agent LOGLINE Steers the career of rising stars Odessa A’zion and Alien: Earth lead Sydney Chandler. THE ARC As an undergrad at Colgate, Gorelick had his sights set on a career in screenwriting. The dream shifted, however, once he stumbled upon HBO’s Hollywood show Entourage and David Rensin’s book The Mailroom: Hollywood History From the Bottom Up. Suddenly, agenting was the goal, which led to an early gig in UTA’s mailroom. It was everything Gorelick had hoped for: “Watching the agents, the intensity, being a 21-year-old kid and driving around Hollywood and seeing the billboards on the Sunset Strip — I loved being in it.” Eleven years on, he’s constructing a list of rising stars (Nicholas Braun, Ray Nicholson, Lili Reinhart) and helping craft the next stage for established actors (Lizzy Caplan, Adam Scott, Timothy Olyphant, Paul Bettany). He feels his abandoned writing ambitions are actually key to his success. “The way I analyze and interpret and discuss material, that comes from a writer’s perspective and has set me apart in the way I work with actors.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Kevin McCallister eating that cheese pizza in the stretch limo.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Buddy from Air Bud.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Driving a young Chalamet to general meetings.”

- Angie Haney, 31 Netflix, director, film LOGLINE Supplies Netflix with rom-com hits like Voicemails From Isabelle and People We Meet on Vacation. THE ARC Haney was outside the Vatican on vacation when she saw two girls filming themselves doing a choreographed dance featured in her latest movie, Voicemails for Isabelle. “I was like, ‘There’s no way that’s what they’re doing!’” She approached the girls in St. Peter’s Square and that was exactly what they were doing. While Haney is now Netflix’s romantic comedy whisperer, she grew up envisioning a career in politics. In high school, the L.A. native and future Columbia poli-sci major was a congressional intern for outgoing L.A. Mayor Karen Bass. But a series of entertainment internships — not to mention a childhood watching classics like Singin’ in the Rain with her voiceover actress mom, theater director dad and screenwriter twin brother — prompted a change of heart. After a cold email led to a stint at Disney, she landed a job as the assistant to then-Lucasfilm head Kathleen Kennedy as the Star Wars series were starting to populate Disney+. She’d later jump to Netflix, where she has found success with rom-coms and coming-of-age films. Up next: a reimagining of 13 Going on 30. “I’ve heard it said before that we should all make movies for our 12-year-old self,” she says, “And that is very true for me.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Watching George Lucas meet Grogu on the set of The Mandalorian.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR “Nora Ephron to have written 20 more movies.”

- Louie Hayes, 35 LuckyChap, vp TV LOGLINE The on-set producer for the summer smash Sterling Point. THE ARC Hayes’ family moved half a dozen times before he left for college. The constant in his home growing up was TV, which he claims he watched “an unhealthy amount of.” Eager to put down roots after graduating from Northwestern, he settled in L.A. with some college buddies. “At the time, everyone started at a talent agency,” he says, so he dutifully lined up a gig at Gersh. And while agenting wasn’t Hayes’ calling, it was there that he’d meet his future wife (and fellow Next Gen honoree), Samantha Militante, who’d later follow him to FX. But after nearly a decade as a buyer — working on hits like Dave and Alien: Earth — he jumped to LuckyChap, where he’s built an impressive roster. In fact, one of Hayes’ very first projects at the uber-successful Margot Robbie outfit was the runaway hit Sterling Point, which he was intimately involved with every step of the way. Up next: series Sex Criminals, from Kumail Nanjiani and Emily Gordon, and an adaptation of The Retrievals from Molly Smith Metzler. PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Jeff Probst. I consider Survivor America’s fifth major sport, and I have some ideas.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Arnold from Hey Arnold! An idealist with an oversized head and a compulsive need to help.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Don’t date anyone in the industry. My wife is on this list.”

- Julia Iglesias, 34 Focus Features, VP LOGLINE Shepherds artistic films including Sense and Sensibility and Nosferatu, along with the upcoming Werwulf and the adaptation of The Bell Jar. THE ARC Growing up in South Florida, Iglesias would regularly make her little sister act in her home movies. It wasn’t until she landed at Boston University that she learned how to turn her passion for storytelling into a career. “I did tons of internships,” she says, “and took all of the screenwriting and production classes I could get my hands on.” After a brief, post-grad stint as an unscripted postproduction coordinator at Relativity Media, she landed at NBCUniversal. A job working for then-Universal Filmed Entertainment Group chairman Jeff Shell turned into a gig at Focus Features, where Iglesias has been ever since. Now, the newly engaged exec — her fiancé proposed at this year’s Sundance Film Festival — cherishes seeing projects through to the end with auteurs like Sarah Polley and Robert Eggers. BEST ADVICE ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Pick your boss, not your job.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “The dog handler on Sense and Sensibility.”
THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Somewhere neither person has to valet.”

- Ben Iguchi, 32 Netflix, manager, original series, live-action comedy LOGLINE Champions buzzy comedies including Cobra Kai and Doozer Productions’ upcoming I Suck at Girls and Nick Kroll’s A Hundred Percent for Netflix. THE ARC Iguchi can’t remember a time when comedy wasn’t a central focus in his life. As he tells it, his Ph.D. dad had proposed to his dancer mom during an episode of The Golden Girls, and every memory in his childhood home seems to feature a sitcom of some kind. In fact, by the time Iguchi turned 13, Jewish comedy became his bar mitzvah theme. “It definitely was not cool,” he jokes as he recounts the Groucho Marx glasses with the mustache that adorned every table. Still, the L.A. native turned up at Georgetown thinking financ

items.title: Chris Harrison Says Being Fired From ‘The Bachelor’ Was a “Blessing,” Not a Cancellation
items.description: Chris Harrison is back as host of a TV dating competition, but he won’t be handing out any roses.
items.author: Tony Maglio
paragraphs: Chris Harrison is back as host of a TV dating competition, but he won’t be handing out any roses.

Harrison, the former longtime host of The Bachelor (and its in-universe spinoffs), is launching his own spin on the genre with Chris Harrison’s The Vow from Lionsgate Alternative Television, which streams on Fox News Channel’s companion platform Fox Nation. You’ll remember Harrison from getting fired from The Bachelor for defending 2021 contestant Rachael Kirkconnell for attending an antebellum-themed fraternity formal three years before she appeared on the ABC series.

Five long years later, Harrison is bringing his own (second) bride with him. Lauren Zima, the former Entertainment Tonight host, and Harrison were married in 2023. Harrison and Zima created The Vow together and executive produce it.

“It feels really a little cathartic,” Harrison told The Hollywood Reporter of his Hollywood comeback vehicle, which has more than flicked at his old job in its marketing materials — earning Lionsgate and Fox a cease and desist from The Bachelor studio Warner Bros. Television.

Chris Harrison’s The Vow curates the dates between its hero and his prospects, setting up “real-world compatibility challenges,” according to its synopsis. It’s all pretty faith-based and longterm focused: “At a time when much of modern dating culture is driven by fleeting connections and social media attention, the series offers a different approach by placing the focus on meaningful relationships, commitment and building a life together.”
The six-episode Chris Harrison’s The Vow premieres its first two episodes today on Fox Nation; read more from our interview with Harrison below.
Five years later, how do you now feel about your very public split with The Bachelor?

I know this sounds weird because it was so tumultuous and it was a crazy time in my life, but I look back at it as a bit of a blessing. I was in a contract negotiation with them. I was talking to my wife: “Is it time to move on? What do I do?” And I don’t know if this lightning-bolt moment hadn’t happened, if I would have stepped away. Having that divorce and that breakup was a blessing. It allowed me to step away. However humbling all of that was, it allowed me time to hit the pause button and watch my kids graduate high school, fall in love, get married in my own life — tell my own love story for a minute — and then kind of get the fire burning again and get excited about creating my own show because The Bachelor wasn’t my baby.

Being able to create this with my wife and with the people I choose to do it with, and be there every step of the way to executive produce, host, sit there and go through the post-production process — it is a painstaking process to get something there, and it’s a great achievement. We’re very proud of it and very excited.
Do you believe your contract situation played more of a role in you being let go from The Bachelor than was initially reported?

Probably. But in any divorce, you only know your side, right? The rest is speculation. They have their story, and then somewhere in the middle is probably the truth. I’m guessing it had some impact on it all, but how much I have no idea. It definitely played in it for me, and gave me that chance to break away from that, and come back and be so refreshed and excited and involved from the ground up and create [a new show]. Again, it’s weird to call something like that a blessing, but when you’re humbled and you move forward and you come back bigger and better, feel the excitement in the air — timing is everything, and the timing now is so good.
Do you believe you were “canceled”?

I don’t. I know people say that because of the time, and that term really came on strong then. I don’t say that, and I don’t think that. In my opinion, it makes me seem like a victim, and I wasn’t. I had a messy public divorce with the people I worked for. It was a very humbling moment for me, and I think a little humility and getting knocked down is good in life. Look, as I tell my kids, life’s not a hockey stick — it’s a roller coaster ride. The ups and the downs. I’m glad I don’t define my life by being the host of a certain show. Again, I go back to my faith. I go back to my friends and family, and you carry on and come back bigger and stronger and hopefully smarter. If you don’t learn from something like that, God, you’ve done yourself a disservice. I do feel like a better host, a better producer, a better husband, a better friend because of all that.
Do you feel that the industry has typecast you into this host-of-reality-dating-competition role? Or is this genuinely what you want to be doing right now?

It is. I got to a very blessed place in my life, and it’s very rare you can get there in business. And that is being able to choose the project, and also choose who you would like to do that project with. Going back to The Bachelor, I was a hired host, so I didn’t get to choose who I was working for, with, etc. You go in, you do your job, and you are so happy to get the paycheck in this business. But along the way, I did Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? I hosted Miss America, The Walking Wallendas.

I did a bunch of other shows, and really, what I love is twofold: I love hosting and producing TV. I find it so invigorating, intriguing. I love telling stories, being a part of stories — but I also love love. I’ll admit, I’m a little bit of a hopeless romantic. I love rom-coms — those are my favorite movies — and I love diving into these people’s lives, kind of exposing them and telling their stories and hopefully helping them find love, as romantic and silly as that may sound. I love being a part of those stories. When you see it work, that’s the addiction. When you see it work, you’re just like, man, that lightning in a bottle, that love story that we’re all clamoring for, that we all enjoy. It’s worth it. It makes it all worth it.
Forgive me for not remembering his name, but how did you find this show’s “bachelor”? He’s frustratingly handsome and seems like a good dude too.
Right and he has a cool fucking name. It’s not fair.

He could be a spy. He could be a stunt man. He might be the next James Bond. We we like to say he’s if Tim Tebow and [Rob Gronkowski] had a baby, that’s what Jace looks like. He has the looks, and yes, he has the abs. He really was that diamond in the rough, and that’s what set the tone.

We had this amazing casting director, Lindsay Liles, who was a producer on The Bachelor and left to go do her own casting agency. I had this great relationship with her, but she thinks like a producer, and that was really important to understand— as the kids say, she understood the assignment. She really knocked it out of the park, and we took more time, more energy, probably more money on casting than anything. We really wanted to do our due diligence on every aspect of these people, and make sure that this is who we wanted to launch this show with. In our case that diamond in the rough was from Canby, Oregon, of all places, and he is a man of faith, a man of values, high morals. Not perfect — he’s a human being. And he’s a little bit older. He’s 30 years old. That was important to us as well. The frontal lobe is formed, and he knows what he wants.
Faith is a big part of the show. Jace and his bachelorettes, for lack of a better word, pray together on camera. Fox Nation’s audience should be into that. Tell me about your own faith.

My wife and I — faith very much plays a part in our lives. It’s a big part of our marriage. I think it’s the foundation. Definitely as a man, it’s my foundation. It’s something I always fall back on. But our faith wasn’t the impetus for the show, but what I do think is, it made Lauren and I good stewards of how to create this environment.

That was why we ended up partnering with [Fox Nation] because that is part of their brand. They have other faith-based shows. All of us thought it was important that this wasn’t a cocktail joke. It’s not. “Hey, look, we’re doing a show about faith and look how crazy and silly this can be!” No, I wanted the intention there, and it was important that we understand that world to create the environment so they can actually feel able to let go. Like they— you know, I guess pun intended, they had to put their faith in us to come on this show, talk about their faith, feel comfortable doing that. And I think we were trusted to create that world for them that they could let go and really try to find love and talk about it freely.
So the season is wrapped as we speak. Did any of the 11 participants sort of expose themselves as maybe not being there for the right reasons?

What I was hoping for as a producer was, if we did a show involved that involved people of faith, that if we brought 11 humans on, we’d have 11 different opinions, experiences, and I was hoping that we would get the conversations that we have. And this is one thing I’m really excited about. You are going to see and hear conversations and topics covered you’ve never heard on reality TV, and it is raw. It’s rare. You’re going to see people pray, and you will see people called into question about their faith.

Some people, like the people at Warner Bros., will call this a ripoff of The Bachelor, and I believe it’s a fair criticism. That said, pretty much every dating show since The Bachelor has been, to some degree, a ripoff of The Bachelor. You, more than most people, should get a pass on that. But you’ve removed a bunch of the tropes, like a formal elimination ceremony to end each episode, and Jace is not expected to propose in the finale…

We took all those hurdles and safeguards that honestly, you probably should have as a producer, because it’s smart. Like an elimination ceremony. “OK, it’s 10 o’clock. Kick two girls out, so I know I can end episode one with a break up.” We didn’t do that. We felt any contrived, produced moment is going to [feel like a contrived, produced moment].

Well episode one does kind of end with a break up, but I’ll concede that the elimination feels more authentic. Jace’s marching orders are to eliminate a potential mate when she stops seeming like a potential mate.

It’s what a gentleman should do. It’s what women should expect. If you’re going to break up, look her in the eye. Don’t shoot a text. Don’t go on your keyboard. Don’t just ghost somebody. Let’s raise the level, guys — come on!

But that intentionality is very important to us, but it’s scary because if you take your hand off the wheel, you don’t know what you’re going to get. But what we found was the unpredictability is the drama. You don’t know when those breakups are going to happen, and even as producers, Jace would be talking, and all of a sudden we’d be like, “Whoa, OK, he’s up right now. Here we go.” And it turned out to be great TV.

In the sizzle reel for the remainder of the season, it is revealed to (those of us who don’t watch The Bachelor) that one of the women was on The Bachelor. I’m guessing that was after your time, so did you know?

Yeah, yeah. Yeah. We talked about that in casting, and we had a long talk between all the executive producers and our casting agent. And again, it was very intentional. Why her faith in where she is in her journey and what she wants, and it felt like none of that was really given a fair shake [on The Bachelor], and she wasn’t really able to talk about that and show that. So we thought, “You know what? OK.” And we had a long talk with her, and we felt like that was a very intentional, good choice to add to the mix.
Was it a challenging decision to cast the woman who sells penile implants for a faith-based Fox Nation show?

It’s what she does for a living. I wanted to show what people of faith really look like in this world. This generation, these are women are unbelievably dynamic, incredibly diverse, and come from all walks of life. One is a penile implant salesman. So be it. That’s her job. She’s really — and I mean this sincerely — she’s passionate about it.
No spoilers, but are you happy with the arc of the season and the results, whatever they may be?

I am. I am very proud of the show. We are very proud of the show. We’re proud of what we created. On one side, because this business is so hard, and to get a show created, sold, and produced, and on air…it’s tough right now. And to put people to work and all those things. There’s that side of it that we’re really proud of. But then the product we created, the show, the idea we had — to watch that come to fruition really was a dream. The show’s not predicated on the fact that it’s going to work. It’s not guaranteed.
Chris Harrison’s The Vow streams weekly on Wednesdays on Fox Nation.

items.title: ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy Elevate Peacock’s Overly Familiar Southern-Fried Thriller
items.description: We all have our television pet peeves and, for me, red flags abound in Peacock‘s new limited series, The Good Daughter.
items.author: Daniel Fienberg
paragraphs: We all have our television pet peeves and, for me, red flags abound in Peacock‘s new limited series, The Good Daughter.

Adapted by Karin Slaughter from her book of the same name, The Good Daughter is interchangeable, in terms of title, plot or structure, with a dozen recent limited series — most conspicuously, Amazon’s The Better Sister and Netflix’s His & Hers.
Cast: Rose Byrne, Meghann Fahy, Brendan Gleeson, Olivia Williams, Harper Steele, Michael Dorman, Audrey Grace Marshall, Drew Cheek

It’s a story set in and filmed in the Deep South, but its central cast is populated by actors from Australia, Ireland, Massachusetts and basically anywhere other than the Deep South, leading to a succotash of colorful and, to put it politely, inconsistent accents.

And it’s a story instigated by a school shooting and pushed forward by multiple instances of sexual violence, all propping up a mystery that’s barely mysterious — at least until the characters all sit down to explain everything in a series of weakly staged monologues.

That The Good Daughter is so full of tropes I find tedious or annoying and yet somehow ends up being compulsively entertaining is a tribute to Slaughter’s gift for characterization and dialogue, the confident hand of series director Steph Green, and particularly the committed, emotionally exposed and often funny performances from leads Meghann Fahy, Rose Byrne and Brendan Gleeson.
The Good Daughter begins with a double dose of trauma, the better to winnow away squeamish viewers.

First, in flashback, devoted sisters Sam (Audrey Grace Marshall) and Charlie (Drew Cheek) witness a horrible act of violence perpetrated on their doting mother (Olivia Williams’ Gamma), perhaps the latest retaliation against their father (Gleeson’s Rusty), a defense attorney prone to rubbing people the wrong way.
Their lives will never be the same.

Jump to the present. Charlie (Fahy) has grown up to follow in her father’s footsteps, working out of his ramshackle office in the same Georgia town populated by people who still hate him and don’t feel too kindly toward her. She’s separated from hubby Ben (Michael Dorman, endearingly normal in a show populated by broad portrayals) and making various self-destructive choices, including a one-night stand with Huck (Jake McDorman), whose ponytail and scruff let you know he’s a bad idea.

Charlie and Huck accidentally swap phones, which leads her to discover that he’s a high school teacher. In the process of returning his phone, she is present when Kelly (Shayna Benardo, an impressively grounding force) shows up and shoots and kills the well-liked principal and a freshman.

Rusty, who has a bad cough and a history of heart problems, and likes to wear — for reasons that are never explained — a red clown nose, shows up to represent Kelly, whose cognitive issues haven’t stopped the local powerbrokers from eyeing the death penalty.

Sensing everything is going astray, Rusty also calls elder daughter Sam (Byrne), now a patent lawyer in New York City and left with a permanent limp and partial blindness stemming from the incident with her mother. Sam hasn’t seen or talked to Charlie in 10 years, but she quickly finds herself back in Pikeville, caught up in the mystery of the shooting, as well as several additional mysteries from her family’s past.

If you just look at the bones of the series, The Good Daughter is beyond rudimentary, with a crime in the present and a crime in the past that just coincidentally happen to be directly connected. The story can barely even decide what twists are supposed to be surprising and, as a result, nothing is really “guessable” or revelatory.

Instead, The Good Daughter works best as a dirtied-up — though confusingly racially whitewashed — version of To Kill a Mockingbird, with Rusty as a lawyer doing noble things in a disreputable way, constantly looking like he slept at his desk, bottle in hand, eschewing Atticus Finch’s seersucker and moral rectitude. He stands up to threats from his adversaries that are violent and gory rather than ominous and insinuated, investigating cases in which the rape and persecution of the handicapped and impoverished play out on the surface rather than being buried in euphemism. It almost certainly works better on the page than on the screen, where we’ve seen too many versions of these generic rednecks in their generic pick-ups and these generic drawling, obfuscating lawmen to take them seriously.

Green and the series’ cinematographers are able to embed in the rundown streets of Pikeville and take us into the “holler,” capturing this community within a community. But when every main cast member talks like the closest they’ve ever been to a holler was a quick drive-through during rehearsal, the verisimilitude suffers.

What holds the show together is Slaughter’s grasp on the characters and their relationships. When Sam, Charlie and Rusty talk, it’s in a vernacular that mixes in-jokes, deeply felt family history, snooty literary references (lots of Flannery O’Connor and Emily Dickinson), amusingly unsnooty pop culture references (from Die Hard to Buffy the Vampire Slayer), and an awareness of how to hurt or heal the people they know best. Byrne, Fahy and Gleeson don’t talk like they come from the same place, but the energy among them gives the series its energy and its authenticity.
Sure, Fahy is doing a variation on her bad sister character from Netflix’s Sirens, but she’s tremendous at playing these open books of damage.

A little too much of Byrne’s performance consists of actorly takes on disability, but she makes those notes of artificiality pay off. Everything Sam does is a put-on; her attire, hair and speech are defined in opposition to the place she left behind and hoped never to return to, with aspects of her natural self returning as she spends more time in Pikeville.

It’s easy to buy them as sisters, in both the parts evoking pain and the parts where they bicker humorously. Plus, it’s easy to see the toll taken by trauma and time because Byrne and Fahy are well-matched by Marshall and Cheek.
Gleeson isn’t as convincing in the flashback segments, and his Southern-ish intonations kept reminding me of somebody I couldn’t quite place, but he makes Rusty rascally and flawed.

Like the actors, the characters are occupying roles — the city mouse, the bad girl, the folksy country lawyer — but when they’re together, they can be themselves. It’s a nice touch that one of the few characters who doesn’t have a public role to play, Rusty’s longtime assistant Lenore, is played by Harper Steele — you know her from the documentary Will & Harper — who isn’t an actor and comes across not as studied but as gentle and natural.

For five episodes, Green maintains the flow between past and present smoothly, and is able to modulate most of the agonizing parts of the story so that they feel tense but not exploitative. Too bad the finale collapses under the weight of all its over-explaining.
I never quite cared who did what and why, but Fahy, Byrne and Gleeson at least made it possible to care about the people to whom these things were happening.

items.title: To Penny, or Not to Penny?
items.description: Few shoes are as essential in the modern menswear landscape as the classic leather loafer. Whether you’re dressing up or dressing down, it is the “the Swiss Army Knife of shoes,” an any-occasion solution to many footwear conundrums. But within the broader loaf
items.author: Tyler Chin; Gerald Ortiz
paragraphs: Few shoes are as essential in the modern menswear landscape as the classic leather loafer. Whether you’re dressing up or dressing down, it is the “the Swiss Army Knife of shoes,” an any-occasion solution to many footwear conundrums. But within the broader loafer genus, one particular species—the penny loafer—includes a divisive design feature: a small, coin-shaped slot in the leather strap “saddle” across the vamp of the shoe.

As the lore goes, Ivy Style pioneers and sock-hopping teens in the mid-20th century liked to store a penny in their shoes as “payphone change.” But now that payphones are a thing of the misty-eyed past and the American one-cent penny is no longer minted for circulation, is it still cool to put a penny (or any other coin, or coin-shaped object) in your penny loafers? What is the line between timeless and passé?
We invited two of GQ’s most well-heeled staffers, associate grooming and wellness editor Tyler Chin and senior style commerce writer Gerald Ortiz, to ponder the pros and cons of the penny loafer.

Tyler Chin, associate grooming and wellness editor: Sure! I’ve seen so many guys wearing loafers these days, and yet still haven’t seen any of them harking back to the shoe’s origins with a penny in them. Maybe I’m not looking hard enough or I’m not in circles where they are doing that, but it’s an inoffensive and easy way to accessorize the shoe. Plus, I had an English teacher in high school who did it, and while she wasn’t particularly cool, I did think the sartorial choice was neat.

Gerald Ortiz, senior style commerce writer: No. I feel like guys who put pennies in their loafers are either try-hards, or just learned about that particular piece of prep trivia. The only acceptable instance to wear a penny in your loafers is if you’re really about that prep/Ivy style, like Preppy Pete, or the guys who frequent Alfargo’s Market (shout out).

TC: I think the penny would be the most boring and obvious choice. If a quarter could fit in there, I think it’d be so funny if you were at a vending machine and short a few cents and settled up with the coin in your shoe. One time, the button on my pants fell off on the street and I lost it, but imagine I had a spare button in my shoe? I could reattach it right there and then! In the hypothetical I’d also need to be toting around a sewing kit, but hey, I’d love to think I could be MacGyver in that scenario.

GO: It doesn’t have to be anything at all. But if you’re going to do it, I don’t see why it couldn’t be another coin or object. It could be a Chuck E. Cheese token. Whatever you put in the slot, it would still be wack.

TC: I just got back from a trip to Tokyo, and I had a lot of leftover yen coins. Two of them—the five and 50 yen—have a hole on them, which differentiates them from your boring American coin. I’d throw one of them in my shoe and be one of those people who never stops talking about their travel abroad.
GO: I saw on Instagram someone stick a hundred dollar bill into their loafer and that was funny for a second. Then I scrolled on to the next meme.

TC: I’m pretty sure a coin that is that close to the ground will surely have a patina before the end of the day. Also, I can’t remember the last time I’ve seen a shiny new coin—who carries loose change these days anyway?!

GO: You know, it might be kind of cool to see a penny completely covered in verdigris slotted into your loafers. But maybe the coin should match the sheen of your loafers. I dunno, just don’t do it and you won’t have to think about it.

TC: Everyone I know is very familiar with my love of penny loafers. Lately I’ve been wearing them with bootcut jeans that are just a little longer than usual, so they have a nice drape over the shoe. Top-wise, I’d go with a tucked-in button up, T-shirt, or sweater. Pretty much anything that would go well with sneakers would be equally suited for wearing with loafers. Which is nearly all outfits.

GO: Penniless or not, a pair of wide khakis with a clean-to-slight break and a striped button-up is a failsafe outfit. It wouldn’t be very inventive, but it would pass muster for most conceivable situations. Vintage straight-leg jeans with good fades, a fucked-up band tee, and a sportcoat is also a great look. But the best looks are always the unexpected pairings.

TC: It’s sort of like how guys will go on and on about having functional sleeve buttons on a suit jacket. Is there any situation where you’ll actually need to unbutton those or do you just leave one or two undone to “stunt” on your unimpressed bros? If you really want to put a coin in your shoe for the sake of accessorizing your footwear, then by all means get a shoe with a functioning penny slot and use it! But if you’re doing it just so you can say “Yeah, these joints are the real deal!” and use it as an excuse to talk about the history of the shoe and why yours are superior, then I’d rather you wear lace-ups.
GO: I think it’s fine, even preferable to have a faux penny slot. It’s like how jeans still come with the watch pocket. It’s purely vestigial at this point, but would feel incomplete without it.

TC: One of these days, I’ll be telling my great-great grandchildren about the origins of the penny loafer and they’ll be confused because they would’ve never heard or seen the one-cent coin before. I’ll whip one out of my shoe and instead of being impressed they’ll chalk it up to another one of Old Man Ty’s tales from his youth, and tuck me back into the nursing home they checked me into.

GO: Lol. I guess it’ll make the penny more covetable. But it’ll be a long time before the penny becomes that desirable. That said, I love this British brand Six 95 that’s designing cool pieces using coins, so I can absolutely see more labels farming pennies for their clothes and accessories.
TC: Men will break up anything other than a toxic relationship. Loafers did nothing wrong and sometimes it’s just the person wearing them that needs to hit the curb.

GO: It makes sense. It’s like any trend, really. Even if they’re as versatile as we’ve been propping them up to be, loafers reached an inflection point where, for some guys, they’re just not the vibe anymore. But I don’t think they’ll dip so low to be thought of as cringe or as an emblem of the 2020s. They’re as classic as it gets and they’ll go through their own ebbs and flows.
TC: A quarter to increase my net worth 25-fold.

items.title: The 73 Best-Ever Celebrity Fits From Every GQ Men of the Year Party
items.description: It’s the best time of the year: GQ’s annual Men of the Year Party. For three-plus decades and counting, November in Los Angeles has been punctuated by the starriest, most show-stopping event of the season. (Actually, there have been a few exceptions—like MOTY
items.author: The Editors
paragraphs: It’s the best time of the year: GQ’s annual Men of the Year Party. For three-plus decades and counting, November in Los Angeles has been punctuated by the starriest, most show-stopping event of the season. (Actually, there have been a few exceptions—like MOTY 2002, which honored that year’s magazine cover stars Denzel Washington, Hugh Grant, and Ralph Lauren—that took place in New York City. As an event, it’s sort of spiritually bicoastal.) And when we’re talking about the biggest menswear red carpet of the year, let’s just say that “big menswear” has meant a lot of different things through the high-octane 1990s, the freaky-deaky early aughts, the buttoned-up 2010s, and the no-rules 2020s.

With the latest iteration of the Men of the Year bash just around the corner, we’re taking a look back at a smattering of the biggest, boldest looks to ever strut the MOTY red carpet, from OutKast’s galactic-level fits in ’02 to Dwayne Johnson’s take on the post-WWE modern cowboy in 2024.
Which burgeoning style icons will earn their rightful place in this hall of fame this year? Keep a close eye on GQ.com this month to find out.

items.title: Scientists May Have Discovered a Massive Starless Galaxy
items.description: Some galaxies appear to contain all the ingredients needed to make stars, yet have failed to produce almost any.
items.author: Jacklin Kwan
paragraphs: Some galaxies appear to contain all the ingredients needed to make stars, yet have failed to produce almost any.

Scientists have puzzled over why for years. Recent findings suggest that these “dark galaxies”—that is, galaxies that contain gas and dark matter but few or no stars—may be lurking throughout the cosmos. Finding them could help astronomers understand why some galaxies form stars while others remain dark, and test the best models of galaxy formation.

Researchers’ most successful model of the cosmos, known as Lambda-CDM, assumes the existence of two invisible ingredients: dark energy, the mysterious property thought to be driving the accelerating expansion of the universe, as well as cold dark matter, a hypothetical substance that physicists think makes up about 85 percent of the universe’s matter.

Clumps of dark matter, called haloes, provide the gravitational scaffolding for galaxies to form and grow, according to the model. Gas collects inside these haloes, eventually cooling and collapsing to form stars. But astronomers are still trying to understand why this process appears to happen in some haloes but not others.
One possibility is that some contain vast quantities of hydrogen gas, yet form very few stars. That would make them extremely difficult to spot.

Now, researchers have found a promising candidate for such a dark galaxy and published their findings in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. The object, known as AGC 322753, contains roughly 2 billion times the sun's mass in hydrogen, yet appears to have no stars, though the researchers note that it is too big to be totally starless. However, if confirmed, it would be an unusually massive example of a starless galaxy.

Researchers at Swinburne University of Technology in Australia made the discovery by comparing observations from two existing radio surveys, one conducted by the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico and the other by China's Five-Hundred-Meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope. Both telescopes had picked up a massive cloud of hydrogen.
Although other researchers have identified several dark galaxy candidates over the past decade, this one stands out for another reason: It may be rotating.

Hydrogen gas emits radio waves at a signature wavelength, which shortens when the gas moves toward Earth and stretches when it moves away. The signal from AGC 322753 shows two distinct peaks, suggesting that one side of the gas cloud is moving towards us while the other is receding.
This could mean that the gas has settled into an organized, rotating structure, much like the discs in ordinary galaxies, despite apparently having formed no stars.

"The theoretical models and the simulations show us that dark galaxies shouldn't rotate, so this is extremely interesting," says Marco Monaci, an author of the study at Swinburne University of Technology.
If AGC 322753 really is a rotating disc with no stars, astronomers will have to explain how the gas organized into such a structure without producing them.

That isn’t the only puzzle. Most models of galaxy formation predict that a cloud holding this much hydrogen should have formed at least a few stars, as its densest patches collapse under their own gravity and ignite.

The paper’s coauthors suggest it may be very unlikely that AGC 322753 contains absolutely no stars. So, instead, they think it may contain stars too faint to see–an “almost dark” galaxy. If so, they must be very faint indeed, because even deep optical images from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, which search for starlight rather than the hydrogen gas detected by radio telescopes, reveal none.
From this, the team estimates that AGC322753 contains at least 40 times more mass in hydrogen than in stars, raising questions about what exactly suppressed stars from forming.
But further observations, such as ones made by the Very Large Array, a network of radio antennas in New Mexico, will be needed to confirm whether AGC 322573 is truly a dark—or almost dark—galaxy.
"Finding out more about it really is an essential next step at the moment. It's intriguing, and I want to know more," says Robert Minchin at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory.

Minchin knows how misleading such signals can be. He was involved in the discovery of VIRGOHI21, a dark galaxy candidate found in the early 2000s that was later reinterpreted as a long stream of hydrogen gas pulled from a nearby galaxy by gravity, known as a tidal tail.

Gas torn away like this can keep some of its original motion and mimic the signature of rotation, so Minchin says more observations are needed to rule out the same explanation for AGC 322753. Yet there is no obvious nearby galaxy it could have come from.

Rhys Taylor, an astronomer at the Astronomical Institute of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague, says tidal debris is unlikely to explain the observations. Reproducing the candidate dark galaxy’s distinctive double-peaked profile through such a process “is technically possible, but it’s fantastically unlikely,” Taylor says.

Taylor and Minchin both flag another concern, though. The two radio surveys that the researchers used placed the hydrogen at noticeably different positions in the sky. That suggests AGC 322753 may be an extended cloud of gas rather than a compact galaxy, another possibility that follow-up observations could help untangle.

Whether AGC 322753 turns out to be completely dark or merely exceptionally faint, understanding objects like it could still help astronomers work out why some galaxies form stars while others apparently do not, says Elisabeth Adams at the Planetary Science Institute.

One possible reason is a galaxy that spins so fast that its gas stays too spread out to collapse. Another is that ultraviolet light from the universe’s earliest stars heated the gas, keeping it too warm to condense. Studying such almost-dark galaxies could help tell these phenomena apart, revealing how the conditions of the early universe shaped the galaxies we see today.
“Once it’s no longer a dark galaxy, people seem to stop caring, and I actually think that’s not the right approach,” says Adams.

But if AGC 322753 truly is starless, it would be one of the most massive dark galaxies ever identified, potentially helping explain where the missing galaxies predicted by Lambda-CDM have been hiding. It could even help astronomers understand why some gas-rich galaxies form stars while others don't, providing a valuable test for models of galaxy formation—and perhaps even offering new clues about the nature of dark matter itself.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Leather Jackets Confessed Before He Did
items.description: The latest “Are we living in a Veep subplot?” headline to grip the nation involves Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who, over the weekend, admitted to having an extramarital affair with a businesswoman suspected of moonlighting as a Chinese spy. The New York Times rep
items.author: Emma Childs
paragraphs: The latest “Are we living in a Veep subplot?” headline to grip the nation involves Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who, over the weekend, admitted to having an extramarital affair with a businesswoman suspected of moonlighting as a Chinese spy. The New York Times reported that the woman, Alice Huang (same last name but no relation), was recruited by China’s ministry of state security to collect information on Nvidia’s artificial-intelligence chips. Jensen, a close friend of Donald Trump’s, is currently under investigation by his employer and has been summoned to Congress for a closed-door session next week.

While an international honey trap targeting a close Trump ally who runs a $4 trillion company might sound far-fetched, one thing should have told us long ago that something was amiss: Jensen’s proclivity for very expensive leather jackets.

Huang is known among the Patagonia-vested dweebs of Silicon Valley as something of a luxury-leather-jacket aficionado — they are to him what black turtlenecks were to Steve Jobs. He wore one on the cover of Time magazine in 2021. He sports them onstage for Nvidia’s keynote speeches, often tossing in a corny thumbs-up to the crowd. He collects leather jackets from Tom Ford, a luxury fashion designer synonymous with sex.

A $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution. That’s a man in a midlife crisis with an active Raya profile and a Harley in the garage. If someone had consulted me years ago, I’d have said Huang is clearly someone who drinks wine with his mistress in the middle of the day. (The Times uncovered a 2023 photo of Jensen appearing to do exactly that at a luncheon in Shanghai with Alice.)

As if his bicep-hugging expensive leather were not offensive enough, Huang has blamed his jacket habit on his wife of 40 years, Lori Huang, and his daughter — he claims they dress him. I imagine the game plan there was to cultivate a cool and edgy image, not the aura of a divorced dad in the club buying 20-somethings tequila shots. It’s also hard to believe. You’re telling me two women picked out this outfit?

If Lori and Jensen do get divorced after all this (though, to be clear, they haven’t shared any updates on the status of their relationship), she could be in for a historically high divorce settlement. I hope her lawyers factor Jensen’s leather jacket collection into his net worth; This July, one of Huang’s pre-worn and signed Tom Ford jackets sold at a Sotheby’s auction for $960,000.

items.title: The Best Gift Ideas for the Friend Who’s All About Wellness
items.description: For more of the Cut’s favorite fashion, beauty, and home finds, sign up for the weekly Cut Shop newsletter.
items.author: Hanna Flanagan; Lauren Adhav
paragraphs: For more of the Cut’s favorite fashion, beauty, and home finds, sign up for the weekly Cut Shop newsletter.

We all have that friend who can’t seem to stop talking about Erewhon hauls and sound baths (it’s me — I’m that friend). So now’s the season to show them how much you love their manifesting mind by presenting them with with an intentional wellness gift. These days, wellness can mean everything from hiking and Pilates classes to smearing on a face mask, lighting a candle, and calling it a day. Meditating, journaling, and even sleeping can be categorized under the W-word too because they’re all ways to take care of yourself from the inside out.

Whether your friend is embarking on a new wellness journey or just looking for the best way to help improve their inner self, we’ve rounded up the best wellness-gift ideas ahead of the 2026 holiday season, from nonalcoholic spirits and sleep gummies to workout gear and top skin care that your favorite health-conscious friend — your everyday wellness guru or the one just entering their Goop era — will appreciate.
