items.title: This Melbourne-born social club is making Amsterdam's chess culture social, noisy, and young again
items.description: It’s a Thursday at No Man’s Art Gallery in Amsterdam. Patrons are hunched over chessboards. In the middle of it all, a DJ is mixing, while the hosts of the monthly Acid Chess Club – 27-year-old Tayla Iakovidis and 29-year-old Matt Bodger – greet arrivals and p
items.author: Ilze Vitola; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: It’s a Thursday at No Man’s Art Gallery in Amsterdam. Patrons are hunched over chessboards. In the middle of it all, a DJ is mixing, while the hosts of the monthly Acid Chess Club – 27-year-old Tayla Iakovidis and 29-year-old Matt Bodger – greet arrivals and pair them up. “I try to sense who’s here to socialise and who wants to play seriously – and whether they would rather face someone at their level or more advanced,” says Bodger, who works in wearable climate tech and first came here as an attendee.

Like Iakovidis, the club hails from Melbourne, where it was founded in 2021 by artist Jack Irvine and James Benjamin, a festival organiser and musician. Acid Chess Club is also Benjamin’s DJ name – he carries a chessboard in his bag that he whips out at parties. The idea arrived after James helped Irvine sharpen his game. In Melbourne, the club has grown from three players to about 150 who flock to twice-monthly nights.

Its international reach grew as regulars moved overseas and took the format with them. “We’re about to start one in Tokyo and three more in Australia,” says Benjamin. “I can’t keep up.” The first international edition launched in London in August 2024, followed by Amsterdam in December 2025, set up by Iakovidis and Tal Sardone, a chef from Melbourne. “Amsterdammers are such doers, so I figured it was the kind of place where you could set something up easily,” says Sardone. Like many chess enthusiasts, he started playing online during the pandemic, partly inspired by Netflix series The Queen’s Gambit, and came to the Melbourne events to play against people in person. “Clubs like ours have changed the stereotypes of chess – it’s not just a game for quiet people in quiet rooms any more.”

“This is one of the busiest nights yet,” Iakovidis tells Monocle, estimating that there are about 50 participants here. The club is now seeking a bigger venue or perhaps even its own space. Every night ends with a tournament: 16 players compete for a block of cheese from the local deli.

It’s a way for young people to connect without screens. “When every tech lord is trying to put AI in our toothbrushes and earrings, being offline is a luxury,” says Bodger. “We’re regaining our freedom.”
No Man’s Art Gallery, Bos en Lommerweg 88-90, Amsterdam

items.title: The Tech-Right Preps for a Blue Wave
items.description: It’s election Tuesday, and after years of lying low, the tech left is ready for its big comeback. “We’re gonna wipe the floor pretty aggressively,” Democratic consultant Cooper Teboe boasted to me late last week. Meanwhile, a DC tech lobbyist I caught up with
items.author: Julia Black
paragraphs: It’s election Tuesday, and after years of lying low, the tech left is ready for its big comeback. “We’re gonna wipe the floor pretty aggressively,” Democratic consultant Cooper Teboe boasted to me late last week. Meanwhile, a DC tech lobbyist I caught up with told me, “For my Republican friends, it’s like the fall of Saigon. Everyone’s trying to get the last chopper out.”

After the votes are all counted, I expect the postmortems coming out of Silicon Valley to start getting spicy. After all, the tech right hardly sat this one out. Elon Musk alone spent a reported $474 million on midterms races. A billionaire coalition including Sergey Brin, Patrick Collison, and Eric Schmidt spent more than $333 million to prevent the so-called billionaire tax in California. A swirling cadre of PACs and dark-money groups were caught using less-than-aboveboard tactics to combat a rising tide of public fury around AI. Spoiler: It didn’t work.

Over the last few weeks, I’ve been reporting on Greg and Anna Brockman, two of the tech mega-donors who’ve thrown the most money at this chaotic election cycle. While OpenAI cofounder and president Greg Brockman’s story has been told pretty extensively, Anna remains one of the last great mysteries on the AI frontier. As The Wall Street Journal put it this spring, “She is intensely private: Almost no information, including her maiden name, is available online.” Until now.
Read on to learn more about their AI-fueled love story, their slow-motion political misfire, and one of the more surprising twists in my journalism career: I went to college with her.

Mentioned in this issue: Citrini Research, Greg Brockman, Diane von Furstenberg, Tina Brown, Alex Karp, Instacart, Darren Aronofsky, Kathryn Murdoch, Daniela and Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, Anna Brockman, Peter Thiel, Mira Murati, Donald Trump, James Blair, OpenAI, Sam Altman, DoorDash, Intel, Binance, Edna Mode, Subvocal, Meta, Ilya Sutskever, Y Combinator, Walter Isaacson, and more.

Over the weekend, the buzzy macro research firm Citrini Research threw a Halloween party at the notorious “Torture Townhouse,” a luxurious eight-bedroom home in SoHo where two crypto investors allegedly kidnapped and tortured a man in an attempt to steal millions of dollars worth of Bitcoin. Dark.

Last week, Diane von Furstenberg, Tina Brown, Darren Aronofsky, Kathryn Murdoch, and others came out to fête Walter Isaacson’s new podcast The Builders, which features lengthy interviews with figures like Alex Karp, Daniela and Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, and Peter Thiel. “When we started this podcast, I was an AI optimist,” Isaacson told the crowd. But after learning more about the technology’s progress—and interviewing more than a couple of people he noted seem to “lack the empathy gene”—he became more fearful of what might happen when we unleash “swarms of agents that we allow to get out of our control.”

Buried in The Atlantic’s excellent profile of Donald Trump’s former White House deputy chief of staff and top Republican strategist James Blair was the tidbit that Meta had hired Blair to advise on its data-centers communications strategy. Meta did not respond to a request for comment.
OpenAI is already rolling out its post-midterms rebrand: Data centers are heretofore to be known as “compute campuses.” Good luck with that, guys!
DoorDash has acquired its grocery-delivery competitor Instacart for $17 billion—if regulators allow the deal to go through.

Frantic crypto investors are pulling their money out of Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, following a $6 billion cyberattack that the FBI attributed to North Korea. (About half that money was successfully frozen.) Binance has reported $3.64 billion in user withdrawals since restoring user access after the incident.

As if San Francisco’s street scenes weren’t surreal enough already, now you can expect to see people wandering around murmuring inaudibly to themselves while looking like Edna Mode. At least that’s the hope over at lipreading-to-text smart-glasses maker Subvocal, which just raised $1.3 million from Y Combinator and Afore Capital.
-25%: Chipmaker Intel’s stock took a tumble Friday along with other tech and AI stocks, as some investors began to hedge on big AI bets.

items.title: Dua Lipa Settles 'Levitating' Lawsuit With Talk Box Musician
items.description: Dua Lipa has settled a copyright-infringement and breach-of-contract lawsuit with the producer Bosko Kante over her hit song “Levitating.”
items.author: Jon Blistein
paragraphs: Dua Lipa has settled a copyright-infringement and breach-of-contract lawsuit with the producer Bosko Kante over her hit song “Levitating.”

Lawyers for both parties signaled a settlement had been reached in court documents filed Monday, Nov. 9. The case was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be brought again, and both sides will cover their own costs and attorneys’ fees. Additional details of any settlement — such as whether it would include monetary damages or song credits — were not disclosed.

“We’ve resolved Bosko’s disputes with Warner,” Kante’s lawyer, Na’il Benjamin, said in a statement. “We’ve always maintained that Bosko’s contributions to ‘Levitating’ were important. More broadly, we believe cases like this matter to all artists who produce, perform, and collaborate on projects released by large labels. Artist contributions are valuable, and proper use, credit, and compensation should be provided accordingly.”
Lawyers for Lipa and the other defendants — including Warner Records and producer Stephen “Koz” Kozmeniuk — did not return Rolling Stone’s requests for comment.

Kante brought his suit over “Levitating” in 2023. The musician and producer specializes in making music with a “talk box” voice modulator; over the years, he’s invented his own ElectroSplit device, collaborated with artists like Kanye West and Big Boi, and composed the theme music for the hit Nineties sketch-comedy series In Living Color. Kante claimed that in 2019, while working on “Levitating,” Kozmeniuk reached out and asked him about “creating and performing a talk-box performance” for the song.

According to the suit, Kante eventually struck a licensing agreement that would allow his performance to feature on the track. But Kante claimed the agreement only covered the original version of “Levitating,” released March 26, 2020. It did not cover, he claimed, any future remixes of “Levitating,” of which there are several, including a smash-hit version featuring DaBaby.
Kante’s suit was one of several to be filed over “Levitating.” It’s also the only one to end in a settlement, with Lipa prevailing in the other cases.

The first was brought in March 2022 by a Florida reggae band, Artikal Sound System, who claimed Lipa stole the hook of their song “Live Your Life” for her hit. That case was dismissed after a judge ruled that Artikal Sound System had failed to prove that Lipa and her collaborators had ever heard “Live Your Life.”

Additionally, songwriters L. Russell Brown and Sandy Linzer claimed that “Levitating” ripped off their 1979 disco song “Wiggle and Giggle All Night.” That suit was also dismissed, with a judge ruling that “Levitating” did not bear enough similarity to “Wiggle and Giggle” to warrant a trial.

items.title: The Real Housewives of Potomac Recap: Beach Please
items.description: Hosting a group vacation is a delicate art: you’re tasked with managing a collection of competing tastes, budgets, and interests, all while ensuring that nobody feels aggrieved enough to start a group chat without you. Naturally, most people are terrible at it
items.author: Shamira Ibrahim
paragraphs: Hosting a group vacation is a delicate art: you’re tasked with managing a collection of competing tastes, budgets, and interests, all while ensuring that nobody feels aggrieved enough to start a group chat without you. Naturally, most people are terrible at it, and the women of Potomac are no exception (I am still recovering from Angel’s comically disastrous outdoor adventure in Denver last year). But even by the franchise’s extraordinarily low standards, Ashley Darby seems uniquely ill-equipped to understand what actually makes a vacation enjoyable. You would think that after subjecting the women to the hellscape that was Austin, where they were literally standing in kitchen shit, Bravo would have imposed a permanent embargo on any new travel ideas originating from her, yet in a decision that defies belief, here we are again, indulging Ashley’s delusion that a rainy beach weekend in Delaware in 50-degree weather is something that even remotely resembles a fun getaway for a girls’ trip.

What Ashley doesn’t seem to understand is that you can upgrade the accommodations and propose absurd luxury flourishes like a helicopter ride (which was mercifully canceled), but none of that changes the fundamental problem: you’re still sitting on a cold, gray beach in Delaware. This is not a Nancy Meyers movie, where everyone can wander around a picturesque California coastline in cashmere turtlenecks; the Delaware coastline in early spring has all the charm of a municipal parking lot, and Diane Keaton is nowhere in sight. No number of bathrooms can compensate for the indignity of spending a spring weekend at the beach in freezing rain so cold that it’s waking Karen Huger’s nipples up from the dead.

First, however, we have to get there, and the girls all meet at Ashley’s to pile into sprinters and settle into a 3-hour commute to what is effectively a beachside sleepover. At the same time, Monique talks their ear off about every conspiracy under the sun, and while I am not surprised in the slightest that a woman who started a business selling essential oils believes in random detox pseudoscience, I’d rather hear her prattle on about the nonsense she heard on an RFK Jr. podcast over yet another update on the status of her divorce and fallout with Cookie, someone who has never been an official cast member of the show. Yet, we are continuously forced to discuss as if she’s the Suge Knight of Maryland Jack & Jill. I could not possibly care less about the activities of two people who aren’t even on my television screen anymore, and I was barely interested in the comings and goings of Chris Samuels even when he was on my screen. Do I think it’s poor form of Karen to admit to remaining friends with a woman who seems to only exist to spread rumors and sow discord amongst these women for attention? Certainly, but I only care as far as Karen’s inability to admit that she did something wrong showcases that her sobriety work, which should be focused on acknowledging and taking accountability for her actions, is far from over.

After the women settle into their accommodations, the conversation shifts to Tia’s marriage, where the women are still litigating the circumstances under which she found out that Robert had been on dating apps. This all feels like a transparent setup to try to nail Stacey to the wall for bringing Tia’s struggles on camera, but none of it is making sense at all. Yes, Stacey was definitely a bit shady in her delivery of the news, but what does that matter when Ashley was the one who ran to gossip about what Gizelle shared with her at a recorded event, so what does Gizelle’s claim that she “never planned to discuss it” even mean? Tia herself defends Stacey, pointing out that Stacey had sent her a screenshot privately before the matter became a group spectacle, and Wendy points out that Stacey didn’t bring it up at the reunion as a jab, waiting until Tia asked to share what she knew.

Unfortunately, Wendy cannot resist using the conversation as another opportunity to revisit her disastrous double date with Tia and Robert, and I am yet again left at a loss as to the point of this conversation. How, exactly, have we arrived at a place where Robert is the sympathetic party in this situation? Let Wendy tell it: Tia held Robert down at that dinner with a custom muzzle, and only let him up for air every few minutes. Robert may not have a functioning mirror, but he is ostensibly a grown man with an executive career and, presumably, a functioning vocabulary to match. If he wanted to communicate his unhappiness, he could have found a way to do so without maintaining dating profiles for a year; he mumbled about nothing because in what world does he owe Wendy a public explanation for his marriage when he has yet to come up with an answer for his own wife? I am sorry, but it is nothing other than misogyny to suggest that Tia’s dominant personality has rendered her husband incapable of expressing himself. These are your husbands, not your children; please stop infantilizing them.

Nevertheless, Tia maintains that Robert’s actions, while hurtful, aren’t necessarily sufficient grounds to dismantle their family, despite this being the second time she’s had to confront similar behavior. That’s her decision to make, but I find myself agreeing with Monique as a voice of reason, against all odds. It isn’t Tia’s responsibility to rehabilitate Robert’s behavior; it’s his responsibility to be accountable to her and their kids and demonstrate that he’s capable of changing. Monique delivers the core thesis of Real Housewives in a single soundbite: “You have to live a life that you don’t have to lie about. And a lot of times in marriages you’re doing a bunch of lying. Whether you’re lying to people to seem like you’re happy, or you’re lying to yourself.” While I wouldn’t necessarily trust Monique to pet-sit for me, her divorce does seem to have forced a degree of honesty about the trap of prioritizing a marriage over your own well-being.

That evening, the women gather for dinner on the rooftop of their vacation rental — since it’s too early in spring to go to a picturesque waterfront restaurant, we’re treated to thirty minutes of forced leisure in a cramped, windswept gathering organized by someone who forgot to check the weather forecast while preparing the group’s pre-dinner plans. Once they finally admit defeat and traipse back downstairs for a Cinco de Mayo-themed dinner, Stacey takes the reins and starts to dig into friction between Ashley and Robyn, much to Gizelle’s chagrin. Feigning innocence, Stacey guilelessly tells Ashley that Robyn suggested that Ashley was threatened by her return.

It’s true Robyn and Ashley have never been particularly close; their alliance has largely been sustained by their shared relationship with Gizelle and a rotating list of mutual enemies, from Monique to Candiace to Wendy to Mia. But the underlying tension is obvious now, which Robyn reveals is at least in part because Ashley is still upset about being called out for her interactions with Charrisse’s son (who recently revealed that he is in recovery from a battle with cancer). Now that those shared grievances are gone, they’re back to their tilted three-person friendship where two people are really only friends with the third, and Gizelle naturally resents Stacey bringing this to the surface.

Later in the night, Ashley and Courtney venture out for drinks. Guys, I know that the Eileen Davidson accords are up, but I feel like we haven’t seen enough of Courtney yet to discuss her in any meaningful way. She’s a walking contradiction, but so are all of these other women — Courtney isn’t even the first scandalous church member on cast. She’s clearly image-conscious, but to what end? She doesn’t want to be caught drinking on camera, yet is willing to gossip about Stacey being a disfellowshipped Jehovah’s Witness while canoodling in the hot tub with Ashley? I have more questions than answers at this point, and will have to continue to reserve my verdict on Courtney until a little further into the season, but the obvious one at the moment, of course, is why join Potomac if you are this concerned about protecting your public reputation? This is not exactly a franchise known for that.

If Stacey did leave the Kingdom Hall, that strikes me as a reason to approach her with empathy more than anything else. But that’s ultimately the recurring problem with this group — women like Ashley are so accustomed to treating one another’s vulnerabilities as ammunition that they struggle to recognize when a situation calls for compassion rather than confrontation. Instead of opening up about their own vulnerabilities, they are stockpiling evidence against each other, hoping to use it as a distraction the next time they are put under the microscope, and wondering why they only end up looking malicious and not supportive. Monique may have returned to Potomac with enough baggage to fill an entire sprinter van, but she has them dead to rights when she calls out their hypocrisy: the women have lied to themselves for so long about the reasons behind their actions that the only thing they have left to keep them company is their misery and resentment.

Next week, Karen and Robyn try to find common ground, Chanel Ayan resumes her job as the resident town crier of the Bravoverse to discuss Wendy’s payola magazine cover, and Courtney is asked to explain her Hot Girl Minister lifestyle. See you all there!

• Of all the possible comedians I would have imagined Stacey Rusch to be a fan of, Tiffany Haddish and her sailor mouth was definitely quite far down the list. Not to sound like Ashley Darby, but I really wish we could see the real Stacey at some point, and not the eccentric performance that she gives us.

• Watching Stacey plan to leave a group trip for Vulture’s Reality Masterminds shoot while I’m writing a Vulture recap of the trip in mention is entirely too meta, but this only means I am one step closer to reality fame of my own. Andy, I’m ready for my close-up! (Just kidding, I would rather swim 10 laps in the Potomac River naked.)

• I don’t really understand why Wendy is being so vocal about her ongoing legal circumstances. I can only hope that she is making her statements with the advice of legal counsel, but I cannot imagine that any lawyer would think it would make sense for their client to get on camera and mention whether a plea deal has been offered yet or what their chances are of vindication. It just goes to show that education has nothing on hubris; two years ago Wendy was advising Karen to take the plea deal, only to not heed that very same advice in her own circumstances.

• Monique and Karen address the deterioration of their relationship, but did anyone for a second believe that Karen and Monique were off-camera friends? Monique is rightfully upset that Karen has maintained friendly ties with her ex-husband during a hostile divorce, but instead of choosing just to apologize and move on, Karen hems and haws her way around accountability like usual.

• I understand why Stacey might have preferred that Wendy not repeat her shady remark to the group, but let’s not pretend she wasn’t milking the moment when she originally delivered it; even if Wendy hadn’t repeated it, production would have found another way to bring it back by the reunion.

• I know it’s hard to believe that Ray may prefer drunk Karen, but if you have ever had close people in your life who deal with addiction, you know that enabling relationships can allow one partner to occupy the roles of victim and beneficiary simultaneously, and sometimes an addict’s partner feeds into that dynamic in their own way. Ray may have suffered because of Karen’s drinking while also enjoying aspects of her behavior that allowed him to feel like a hero, which sobriety has now eliminated.

• Who did Stacey team up with for her newest confessional look? Auburn beach waves, dewy complexion, and a black cutout bodycon dress? Someone gave Stacey the Porsha Williams glam makeover — I’m going to guess it’s Paris Chea.

items.title: Cupertino Recap: Drivin’ ’n’ Testifyin’
items.description: A lot of people consume network television via streaming services these days, and often in batches rather than one episode a week. So it’s probably not that meaningful that Cupertino’s sixth episode debuted on a Sunday night, rather than at the show’s usual Th
items.author: Noel Murray
paragraphs: A lot of people consume network television via streaming services these days, and often in batches rather than one episode a week. So it’s probably not that meaningful that Cupertino’s sixth episode debuted on a Sunday night, rather than at the show’s usual Thursday time. But I still find the switch interesting, if only for what it says about CBS’s faith in this show. The network put this episode in a prime slot, after a day of football and 60 Minutes. Then they followed it with reruns of two more Cupertinos. Clearly they’re hoping to hook some new viewers.

CBS picked an especially hooky episode for this too. “Harper” is named for an uncommon Price, Siffre & Associates client: a young woman who is one of Christy’s many roommates, and not someone who has been recently harmed by a tech company. Michael and Olivia represented Harper in an insurance claim, convincing Judge Hornstein (Peter Riegert) to order her insurer to pay for a liver transplant that had already been scheduled.

But then, seconds before the operation is about to begin, another patient cuts the line. The purported reason? The algorithm that generates the transplant list ruled against Harper. Now that’s a case for PSA!

This plot is classic TV courtroom drama fodder. With the clock ticking on the donated liver — which needs to be transplanted into someone within four hours — two sets of lawyers hustle to make their arguments. In one corner: Harper Irvin, a young woman with her whole life ahead of her. In the other: Albert Ensler, a middle-aged husband and father who runs a hugely successful business as a venture capitalist. Both have a fair claim on the organ. But that’s not what the attorneys are debating. Their respective cases have to do with whether an AI-driven algo can be trusted.

Because this is a Michelle and Robert King-produced show, there are, of course, multiple twists — and I don’t just mean in the plot. The credited screenwriter Keith Eisner and director Rosemary Rodriguez stage this case-of-the-week cleverly, with nearly all of the testimony and arguments happening on cell phones via Zoom, while the judge and the lawyers are stuck in post-49ers game traffic. Complicating matters further: Judge Hornstein is in a ride-share car that picks up another passenger along the way, while Ensler’s lead attorney, the sleazy Ry Vance (in his first appearance since the series premiere), is in a self-driving taxi.

Eisner and the Cupertino writers don’t miss many opportunities to work technology into this story at odd angles — often making fun of the nagging inconvenience of all of our modern conveniences, from the noisy GPS devices that don’t seem to know where they’re going to the cell phone that dies in the middle of crucial testimony. (Judge Hornstein has to leave his car to find a charge and ends up in a noisy auto body shop, where the first they ask him is, “USB or lightning?”)

But again: The main technology under debate here is AI, and whether it’s capable of properly determining who should get a human organ. And what’s ingenious about this episode is that before the hearing’s four hours are up, both Ry Vance and PSA will end up arguing both sides of the issue.

When the case begins, Olivia and Michael are putting their former client and occasional employee, Vik Malhotra, on the virtual stand to claim that AI is biased against young women with a modest income. PSA also tears apart Vance’s witness Dr. Marjorie Wellington for phoning in her testimony from a nudist colony at Burning Man. Then another witness — who is in the actual courtroom! — testifies that the AI actually picked Harper, and that a human doctor overruled it. Suddenly, PSA is siding with Dr. Wellington and accusing Vic of being an unreliable druggie. (“I micro-dose!” Vik protests. “So does Elon Musk!”)

What eventually sinks the Ensler team is the testimony of Dr. Dexter Stimson, the man who overrode the algorithm. He claims to Judge Hornstein that he considered things the AI couldn’t, like the patients’ respective recent medical histories and the size of the donated liver. Sounds reasonable, right? Unfortunately, Stimson is undone when one of his disgruntled former assistants mentions that the doctor overrules the algo a lot, for patients who always end up dying. Oh, and before making this particular decision, Stimson’s cancer research program got a huge donation from the Ensler Charitable Foundation.

There are — somehow — two subplots running through this episode, even though nearly every major character is inside various cars for nearly the whole time. Olivia is in traffic because she just picked up her brother Jacob (Gilles Geary) from the airport. During the ride, she discovers that Jacob is very likely the victim of a pig-butchering scam, as he has sent thousands of dollars overseas to a girlfriend he’s never met.

Meanwhile, Michael’s in a car with Nichole, his ex (and lately his greatest legal rival), who is trying to find a moment to talk with him about an offer she just received. A boutique Silicon Valley law firm named Pandas & Associates — which handles “reputational” cases for all of the “Magnificent Seven” tech companies — wants her to come on board and become their dedicated anti-PSA attack dog. (And this company apparently loves dogs, given that every touchy-feely employee Nichole meets there has a pooch by their side.)

Both of these subplots in their own way speak to what Cupertino has been up to through its first half-dozen episodes — what those Sunday night CBS viewers might’ve been missing, in other words. In one storyline, we see how deep fakes and social media have led to a nice young man getting fleeced. In the other, we see how the friendly face of a Silicon Valley business masks ruthlessness. In both cases, the utopian promise of technology has curdled into crass money-making.

What’s been fascinating about all this over the past month-plus of Cupertino is that Michael seems to think that the only way he can sell his firm is to act as though PSA’s “standing up for the little guy” pitch is also just about profit, ultimately. When he tells Nichole that prosecutions of white-collar crime have dropped from 350 a year to 95 a year over the past decade, he says he sees that as an untapped market. Idealism be damned.

Does he really believe this, or is he just speaking the language of his peers? I think Michael’s body language may be telling us what we need to know. After Harper’s surgery finally begins, her mom hugs Christy, who brings Olivia into the embrace, who then reaches out to Michael, who stays stock-still. The ladies have to scoot over to him. He’s not doing this job for the hugs.
• Alas, any viewer whose first Cupertino episode is “Harper” will be deprived of Busy Philipps’s delightful performance as PSA’s rich benefactor Natalia — absent from this story.

• We also didn’t get as much of Christy as usual in this one, although it was a good running gag to have the nurses constantly snapping at PSA’s chief assistant for being on her cell phone while racing through the hallways.

• Olivia explains the presence of condoms, lube, and a sex toy to her brother by saying that one of her roommates borrowed her car. I’m not sure I buy that. I believe there’s much more to Olivia’s backstory and personal life than we’ve been told. For example, doesn’t she seem unusually hard-bitten when she warns Jacob not to trust every needy person?

• I’m glad Nichole Ferebee is sticking around, and that she will apparently be working for a firm that plans to aggressively and proactively antagonize PSA. I enjoyed Nichole and Michael’s bickering banter in her fancy rental car this week, poking at each other over who’s had a more privileged upbringing and whose legal strategies are more effective. (I also like how, when they part ways, Nichole says, “Come work with me!” and Michael answers, “At the Panda Express?”)

items.title: Saturday Night Live Recap: Druski Struggles to Do It Live
items.description: Druski is the most famous comedian in the country whom you possibly haven’t heard of. The host of last night’s episode of Saturday Night Live, who made history as the first “digital creator” to host the show, is undoubtedly on the rise. His self-described “ski
items.author: Charu Sinha
paragraphs: Druski is the most famous comedian in the country whom you possibly haven’t heard of. The host of last night’s episode of Saturday Night Live, who made history as the first “digital creator” to host the show, is undoubtedly on the rise. His self-described “skits” have amassed millions of followers on Instagram and YouTube and garnered him a multiyear deal with Netflix. It tracks that SNL would seek him out to host, given the show’s commitment in recent years to recruiting internet-famous comedians to join the cast. It’s a logical move on Lorne Michaels’ part, likely rooted in a desire to keep the show’s finger on the cultural pulse.

But what works on Instagram is not necessarily what works on live television. Though Druski brought a palpable enthusiasm and energy to this hosting gig, it became increasingly clear throughout the night that he is not a seasoned live sketch performer. Which, to be clear, is not a requirement by any means of an SNL host — there are myriad ways that the show can work with and around a host’s natural talents and abilities, whether or not they include live comedy. However, the show’s insistence on having every sketch of the night revolve around Druski only made more obvious the fact that this type of performance is not his strong suit. It became difficult, in fact, to keep track of the flubbed lines and awkward comedic timing that plagued so much of the episode, from the monologue right down to the last sketches of the night. It makes sense that the strongest moments of the show came in the pre-tapes, which perhaps share more DNA with Druski’s internet comedy than the live sketches.

The middling nature of last night’s episode also has something to do with the fact that the show didn’t do much at all with the current events of the week. Despite the writers having plenty of topical political material to mine with the midterm elections, the episode didn’t do or say anything interesting with it. Nowhere was this more evident than the cold open, which was weirdly inert, again featuring James Austin Johnson’s Trump and Colin Jost’s Pete Hegseth saying a bunch of nothing. And while I love JAJ’s Trump with all my heart (and will not comment on Jost’s Hegseth), the whole open felt like a missed opportunity to comment meaningfully on the blue tsunami. Even a cameo appearance by newly elected Senator James Talarico couldn’t save the thing.
Nonetheless, here are the highlights…

Far and away the high point of the evening, this pretape saw Druski donning whiteface (one of his favored bits) to play Elizabeth Holmes in a parody of You Can See Everything. Druski delivered his funniest performance of the night as a deadeyed Holmes opposite Jane Wickline (who also nailed it as Holmes) and Ben Marshall as Billy Evans. Druski’s understated delivery of “You trying to fuck me?” perhaps proves that he’s at his best when he’s not doing too much. Prepare to see this sketch clipped on Instagram Reels for the foreseeable future.

Another pretape that made good use of the night’s host. This sketch has a sort of convoluted premise (the weird guy on your corner gives you updates on your health by making unwanted comments on your body), but it works regardless. Maybe it’s because of the good character details— like the corner guy always having a fully charged Beats pill.
Weekend Update: Democrats Win Control of Congress, Trump Blames Poor Quality GOP Candidates

Update had a lot to work with this week, and while it didn’t quite knock it out of the park, Jost and Che still got some jokes in (though I’d like to note that the bits about Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed felt lazy). Special shout-out to the Epstein reference, “Infinity Watergates,” and the observation that Trump will live on in all of us in the form of long COVID.
Two People Who Just Hooked Up

This recurring Update desk bit remains a favorite, even if it follows the same beats every time and doesn’t really ever break its form. Is it possible that I just want to watch a romantic comedy starring Andrew Dismukes and Ashley Padilla? Yes! It is purely a delight to see these two onscreen together, and I hope we see them again.

The last sketch of the night made the smart choice of placing the host in an ensemble, as part of the socially conscious hip-hop group Lenny & The Street Smart Crew, played by Druski, James Austin Johnson, Ben Marshall, Kam Patterson, and Tommy Brennan. The sketch is smartly heightened, and the music doesn’t overstay its welcome.

• This episode had a number of cameos (Talarico in the cold open, Emma Stone during the monologue, and Walton Goggins during The Strokes’ performance). The goodnights revealed that apparently Dave Chappelle, Chris Rock, Austin Butler, and Michael B. Jordan had also been there, though they didn’t appear in the actual episode for some reason.
• Jeremy Culhane stopped by Update with an Elon Musk impression, which was solid, though not as memorable as his take on Tucker Carlson.

• The clearest example of the weird comedic timing of this episode appeared at the end of the Wedding Photographers sketch. I don’t know if there was a cue card flub or a missed line, but the ending of that sketch was truly odd.

items.title: Dexter: Resurrection Recap: Attention Economy
items.description: Change has never been Dexter’s strong suit. The O.G. series’ familiar formula turned it into a serialized show with a distinctly procedural vibe — not that there’s anything wrong with that. After several years, however, a series that had once kept us on our to
items.author: Louis Peitzman
paragraphs: Change has never been Dexter’s strong suit. The O.G. series’ familiar formula turned it into a serialized show with a distinctly procedural vibe — not that there’s anything wrong with that. After several years, however, a series that had once kept us on our toes became surprisingly predictable. How many times did Dexter take on a burgeoning serial killer partner while another Miami Metro cop tried to pin him as the Bay Harbor Butcher? And then came Dexter: Resurrection, a radical revamp that actually recaptured the joy of the show’s glory days. Sometimes change is a good thing! It’s fitting, then, that the second episode of the season sees Dexter learning that the best way to counter a midlife crisis is by doing something different.

Harrison is also all in on change, having evolved from impulsive murderer to police officer working homicide. And while some might consider that a lateral move, he does get to spend more time with his one-night stand, Fiona, who turns out to be his field training officer and Captain Mixon’s daughter. This makes for a delightfully awkward moment at Brooklyn Diner when a clueless Dexter asks Harrison, “Is your officer one of those old-school types who’s gonna ride you hard day and night?” Double entendres aside, Dex is right to rain on his son’s parade about Harrison’s plum homicide assignment. It does seem more likely that Wallace wants to keep a former suspect close than that she was simply impressed by his test scores. Harrison’s frustration soon gives way to fear with the sudden arrival of Charley Brown, crashing their dinner and sporting a much calmer demeanor than when she was Prater’s right-hand woman. “Be cool, I’m not a threat,” she says when Dexter instinctively reaches for his knife. It’s such a thrill having Uma Thurman back, and the chemistry between her and Hall is electric from the jump.

Once Charley assures both Morgans there’s no need for police intervention, Harrison leaves so she and Dexter can have a one-on-one. “I’m here to help tie up some loose ends,” Charley explains. If we take her at her word (and that’s a big “if”!), she’s had a dramatic change of heart. Before her mother died, Charley confessed all of her serial killer-wrangling in the hope of absolution. Instead, she got the appropriate amount of judgment, and now she’s determined to make things right — which starts with eliminating the last remaining members of Prater’s club. Charley has no interest in hunting down the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger and the JawSplitter herself, but she can coax them out of hiding and into Dexter’s crosshairs. “I have no reason to trust you, so forgive me if I don’t jump at this opportunity,” Dex answers. He’s right that Charley could be lying, but what would her end game be? And on some level, he wants to believe her. While she can’t sway him with cash, Charley is probably right that these killers will strike again if Dexter doesn’t take them out first.

Back at home, Dex debates his next move with Harry, who has become a lot more open-minded between seasons. (Given that Harry is not an actual ghost but a reflection of Dexter’s psyche, I think that makes sense.) When you’re stuck in a rut, Harry reasons, it’s good to try something different. As hard as Charley may be to trust, there may be worse ideas than partnering up with her. Dexter points out that Harry has advised against this sort of arrangement in the past, and that’s certainly true of Lumen, Hannah, and Mia, among others. “That was true then, but things feel a little different now,” Harry notes. “Maybe being alone all the time has become part of the problem.” As it turns out, Dexter won’t be alone for long. Right on cue, there’s a knock at the door from none other than Joey Quinn. Both men look like they’ve seen a ghost.

Over drinks at a nearby bar, the former colleagues catch up. Quinn has left Miami Metro — does anyone still work there? — and he’s now a private investigator. Because the NYPD has not made any progress in finding Prater (good luck with that), Quinn is now working to find him and his serial killer pals on behalf of their victims. Last week I mentioned my concern that the Quinn storyline was going to play out exactly as Batista’s did last season, so I’m encouraged by a different angle here. At the same time, I don’t buy that Quinn isn’t also suspicious about Dexter, who famously faked his own death after Deb died. That’s not a normal thing to do! Quinn also makes a point of mentioning that Prater had a ton of memorabilia from notable Miami serial murderers like the Ice Truck Killer, Arthur Mitchell, and Travis Marshall, but nothing for the Bay Harbor Butcher beyond a James Doakes nameplate. Dexter smartly realizes he needs to keep Quinn close, and to that end, suggests working together on finding Prater. The theme of this episode may be change, but there’s a throughline of unlikely partnerships, too.

As Dexter mulls over Charley’s offer, he decides it’s worth trying to get the ball rolling on the New York Ripper. When he spies on Don Framt, he discovers that the octogenarian has groupies — though he’s not fessing up to his crimes, Framt has been publicly identified as the city’s most brutal serial killer, which has the hybristophiliacs out in full force. It’s fun watching Dexter wrestle with his complicated feelings here, balancing his repulsion toward the Ripper with his jealousy at another serial killer getting so much adulation. Dex follows Framt into a strip club, where he fans out over the New York Ripper and presses him for details that Framt is smart enough to hedge on. One thing Framt is clear about, however, is how much he’s loving his new fame. “Attention, adoration… that’s awesome, man,” an envious Dexter says. There’s a flash of the Ripper’s dark side when he harasses a waitress, a reminder that he’s likely still more dangerous than he looks. After Framt gets kicked out of the club, Dex fantasizes about doing what the cops can’t.

The problem, of course, is Harrison, whose admiration for his superior, Detective Wallace, means he can’t let Dexter take out the Ripper — she needs to be able to put Framt in prison herself. Thankfully, Harrison is accepting of the fact that Dex will have to get his jollies going after the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger and the JawSplitter instead. As much as I don’t need to see these two at odds again, I have doubts that a loving relationship between a serial killer father and his homicide detective son can last. On the other hand, it’s possible Harrison sees real value in what his dad does, especially given how much the NYPD is struggling to find the Five Borough Killer. The department is in hot water for not warning baseball game attendees about the first threat FBK called in — especially after Oliva’s daughters share on TikTok that their dad tipped them off — and Wallace’s casual remark that the killer could be a one-off prompts FBK to deliver his next warning. “I promise you, I’ve barely gotten started,” he says. “Someone will die on Broadway tonight. A very special show.” The cops have nothing to go on, beyond that the suspect is of average height and wearing smart glasses, so they take the drastic step of shutting down the theater district. It’s that or risk the cast of Other Desert Cities.

Elsewhere, Dexter decides he’s ready to accept Charley’s offer. “Maybe Harry was right,” he reasons. “Maybe I can change more than I think.” In this case, that involves discussing plans for offing the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger over a very expensive bottle of wine. (Charley has been draining Prater’s bank account, which she counts as her severance.) Dex’s one condition is that he needs to do the killing on his turf, which means Charley will have to be more involved than she’d intended. Under the pretense of a Prater dinner party, she will invite the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger (real name Ray Ballard) to a new venue, where she’ll introduce him to “Red Schmidt.” Dexter will take care of the rest. As part of the plan, Charley rents a townhouse that isn’t quite as upscale as Prater’s mansion, but will work in a pinch.

Ballard seems like a worthy next target for the Bay Harbor Butcher. Charley details his M.O.: watching his victims while they sleep, gaslighting them with barely perceptible changes to their home over multiple nights, and finally stabbing them to death with an ice pick. She also admits he creeps her out more than the others. “I think if you were to peel back the layers, you wouldn’t find an actual human in there,” Charley says. Even as they discuss a homicidal sociopath, there’s no denying the spark between Charley and Dexter, who quickly fall into a mutual respect that sure looks a lot like attraction. “It’s nice to work with a professional,” she tells him. Dex, who has spent these first two episodes desperate for attention, responds, “It’s nice to be recognized.” Kiss already!

To be clear, I love a slow burn, and I’m here for whatever course the relationship between Dexter and Charley takes. But the show is clearly leading us in a specific direction, as evidenced by the final scene of the episode, in which the two meet again at an outdoor restaurant and get mistaken for a couple by the waiter. When Dexter says it might be safer to let people think they’re a couple, Charley grabs his hand. (A “fake dating that leads to real feelings” trope? It’s almost like the Dexter writers knew AO3 would be down.) Charley asks what led Dex to agree to work with her, and he shares his new outlook. “I think I just finally came to a point in my life where I felt like it was okay to do things a little differently,” he says. “Be open to change.” They look like they’re about to lock lips for real after Charley learns that she and Harrison are the only two people alive who know Dexter is the Bay Harbor Butcher. “I’m honored,” she tells him, which is a funny way of saying, “I’m horny.” Am I falling into an obvious trap? Is Dexter? Before anything can happen, though, they’re interrupted by a body being thrown off the roof above them and splattering on a nearby newsstand. Nothing like the next FBK murder to kill the mood.

• FBK hasn’t earned the serial killer title yet, because, as Dexter repeatedly notes in frustration, it takes three kills. Earlier in the episode, he tells Harrison, “He’s killed one person, putting him in the same category as Aaron Burr and Phil Spector.”

• Was anyone else thrown when Wallace mentioned that the Ryan Foster case was a few years ago? I clearly hadn’t been paying enough attention to the timeline. For fellow confused folks, there was, indeed, a three-year jump between seasons.
• Harrison gets to flex some of his Spanish, along with a reminder that he grew up in Argentina with Hannah. Fiona looked pretty impressed!
• The song playing at the strip club while Dex buddies up to the New York Ripper is, hilariously, “Pony.”
• Speaking of Brian Cox, the sequence of the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger casing his next victims’ house reminded me of the Tooth Fairy in Manhunter, which feels deliberate.

• Care of Charley, Dexter finally has a new boat to dispose of bodies with, and he’s named it the Slice of Life Too. As Harry taunts, “You expect me to believe this isn’t part of your midlife crisis?”

items.title: Is ‘I Play Rocky’ Original or Adapted? Stallone’s ‘Rocky’ Origin Story Faces a ‘Barbie’-Style Oscar Dilemma (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Sylvester Stallone wrote “Rocky” in three days. Figuring out which Oscar screenplay category the movie about him writing it belongs in is taking a lot longer.
items.author: Clayton Davis
paragraphs: Sylvester Stallone wrote “Rocky” in three days. Figuring out which Oscar screenplay category the movie about him writing it belongs in is taking a lot longer.

Amazon MGM Studios’ “I Play Rocky” has been the subject of multiple conversations among the studio, the Writers Guild of America, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and the film’s creative team over whether Peter Gamble’s script will compete as an original or adapted screenplay. No determination has been made.

Thursday, Nov. 12, is the final deadline for studios to submit Official Screen Credits (OSC) forms to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences for the 99th Academy Awards in the best picture, animated feature and general entry categories. No films afterward will be considered.

Gamble conceived and wrote the script as an original, and it isn’t based on a book, article, memoir or any other single published work. He drafted it on spec, and Bellevue Productions, shared it with Christian Baha of Baha Films. Baha came aboard as a producer alongside Toby Emmerich, and director Peter Farrelly, who helmed best picture winner “Green Book” (2018), eventually signed on. It’s Gamble’s second produced feature script after “Office Uprising” (2018).

But “Rocky” is one of the most established pieces of IP in Hollywood, and sources say some within each organization are weighing whether the screenplay is a better fit for adapted, the category for scripts built on previously established material. Rocky Balboa, Adrian and Apollo Creed are preexisting characters and Farrelly’s film restages some of the 1976 movie’s best-known scenes, written half a century ago.
Amazon MGM and the Academy declined to comment.

“I Play Rocky” expands nationwide Nov. 20, the same day WGA submissions close, but the guild won’t be weighing in. The film wasn’t produced under a WGA signatory agreement, so the guild can’t classify the screenplay or consider it for the WGA Awards, even though Gamble is a member. That leaves the decision entirely to the Academy’s Writers Branch executive committee, which makes its own determinations and has broken with the WGA before.

Elsewhere on the circuit, the question will carry less weight. The Golden Globes put all screenplays in a single category, while BAFTA and the Critics Choice Awards, which split original and adapted, generally go with the category the studio submits.

According to the Academy’s screenplay submission FAQ for the 99th Oscars, films don’t submit to a specific writing category. Instead, the Writers Branch executive committee reviews each eligible title and generally defers to the WGA’s classification, except when the guild hasn’t classified a film, as is the case with “I Play Rocky” or its classification “has been called into question.” The guidelines cut both ways for Gamble’s script.

A script is generally deemed adapted if it’s based on a sequel, a remake, an existing film or “pre-existing characters,” but it’s considered original if it tells a true story in which the writer “performed their own research and used multiple sources.” While a determination is under review, the committee may ask the film’s credited writers for a statement. Once it rules, the decision is final and no appeals or additional materials are accepted.
We seem to have one of these every awards season.

In January 2024, Greta Gerwig’s “Barbie” was moved to adapted after Warner Bros. campaigned it as an original and the WGA classified as well. Barbie and Ken existed as Mattel dolls long before Gerwig and Noah Baumbach turned them into a billion-dollar sensation, and there were multiple cartoons that existed with the characters. Ultimately, the script earned an adapted nomination and lost to Cord Jefferson’s “American Fiction.”

Category reversals aren’t new. Barry Jenkins’ “Moonlight,” Damien Chazelle’s “Whiplash” and Joel and Ethan Coen’s “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs” all carried original labels from the WGA before the Academy shifted them to adapted. The Academy has also long treated sequels as adaptations because their characters come from earlier films, which is how “Before Sunset,” “Toy Story 3,” “Top Gun: Maverick” and “Glass Onion” all landed in adapted.

That rule is being tested again this season. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” which dramatizes whistleblower Frances Haugen’s 2021 Facebook leak and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz’s coverage of it, was initially marketed as a sequel to “The Social Network” (2010), which won Sorkin the adapted screenplay Oscar. The WGA has classified the new film as an original. There’s no word yet on whether the Academy’s committee will accept that designation.

That’s the precedent Gamble’s script has to get around, and there’s a strong counterargument. “I Play Rocky” isn’t a sequel, a prequel or a spinoff. It’s a biographical drama about a real person, and biopics have routinely competed as originals. Dustin Lance Black won original screenplay for “Milk,” even though Harvey Milk’s life had already been chronicled in the Oscar-winning documentary “The Times of Harvey Milk.” Anthony McCarten’s “Darkest Hour” also competed as an original, despite covering Winston Churchill’s first weeks as prime minister, a chapter that fills every high school history textbook.

Movies about the making of movies are interesting territory, and they have produced originals, too. “Saving Mr. Banks,” about the making of “Mary Poppins,” competed as an original but didn’t land a nomination. Neither did Jason Reitman and Gil Kenan’s “Saturday Night,” which follows the 90 minutes leading up to the first televised episode of “Saturday Night Live.” Netflix’s “Mank,” written by the late Jack Fincher, father of director David Fincher, chronicles screenwriter Herman J. Mankiewicz’s work on Orson Welles’ “Citizen Kane” (1941). It was also deemed an original, and it also missed in the category, even as the film led the field with 10 nominations.

When a making-of film does land in adapted, there’s usually a book behind it. Scott Neustadter and Michael H. Weber’s “The Disaster Artist,” for example, was based on Greg Sestero and Tom Bissell’s 2013 nonfiction book of the same name. A public figure’s life, however, is fair game, as illustrated by A24’s Chris Hansen story, “Primetime,” which Ajon Singh based on an article by Luke Dittrich.

Interestingly, Amazon MGM owns the “Rocky” franchise. The 1976 original earned 10 Oscar nominations and won best picture, and Stallone was nominated for best actor and original screenplay. Director Farrelly knows the original side all too well, as he shared the original screenplay Oscar with Brian Hayes Currie and Nick Vallelonga for “Green Book,” another true story that drew from no single published source.

Where the film lands could reshape its trajectory, and both races are stacked. In original, Jesse Eisenberg (“The Debut”), Jordan Firstman (“Club Kid”), Mike Leigh (“Tender Loving Care”), Martin McDonagh (“Wild Horse Nine”) and Simon Rich (“Artificial”) are all in the conversation. A move to adapted wouldn’t clear the road. It would put Gamble up against Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Drew Goddard’s “Project Hail Mary” and Rashida Jones and Will McCormack’s “The Invite,” along with Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra” and Denis Villeneuve’s yet-to-be-screened “Dune: Part Three.”

“I Play Rocky” has been gaining momentum since its world premiere at TIFF. It finished first runner-up for the People’s Choice Award behind “La Bola Negra” and was the runner-up at Middleburg. It was also the audience choice winner at Cinéfest Sudbury International Film Festival, and recently Ippolito was honored with the breakthrough award at SCAD Savannah Film Festival. It recently opened on Nov. 6 in seven theaters, capturing $345,000 from seven theaters, averaging $49,200 per location. The film has also made one category call already: it’s submitted at the Golden Globes as a musical or comedy, joining a field that includes “Wild Horse Nine,” “The Debut” and Amazon MGM stablemate “Project Hail Mary.”

The Academy’s final word likely won’t surface until nominations voting opens Jan. 11, 2027. Before that, the WGA announces its screenplay nominees Jan. 8. Oscar nominations will be announced Jan. 21, and the 99th Oscars take place March 14.

items.title: Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Comeback: A Smaller $5 Million Salary, Optimistic Theater Owners and More
items.description: Four years ago, Johnny Depp‘s fans and detractors descended on the sleepy town of Fairfax, Virginia, to cheer or jeer the actor in his ugly defamation case against ex-wife Amber Heard. Now, when local cinema operator Mark O’Meara probes his patrons about “Eben
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: Four years ago, Johnny Depp‘s fans and detractors descended on the sleepy town of Fairfax, Virginia, to cheer or jeer the actor in his ugly defamation case against ex-wife Amber Heard. Now, when local cinema operator Mark O’Meara probes his patrons about “Ebenezer,” a new take on “A Christmas Carol” featuring Depp as the coldhearted miser Scrooge, he’s met with decidedly less intensity about the embattled star’s first major movie role in nearly eight years.
“Some people can’t wait. They love Johnny Depp. And others are just like, ‘Meh,’” says O’Meara, who owns Fairfax’s University Mall and Cinema Arts Theatres. “I don’t think it’s a polarizing thing.”

“Ebenezer” isn’t expected to ignite the box office à la “Michael,” a musical biopic about a controversial figure. The Dickens adaptation, which opens on Nov. 13, is tracking a modest debut of about $20 million domestically and another $20 million overseas from 63 markets. But O’Meara doesn’t get the sense the public sees Depp as persona non grata, even though the actor’s career has been derailed by personal drama, including domestic abuse allegations leveled by Heard.

Paramount, meanwhile, is betting that moviegoers have been missing Depp, whose last Hollywood outing was 2018’s “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald.” (He was forced by Warner Bros. to exit the “Harry Potter” spinoff series in 2020 after losing a libel case against the British tabloid The Sun, which called the actor a “wife beater.” Depp won the subsequent defamation trial in the U.S.) An April 2026 study by the National Research Group suggests his fans never turned on him. Participants ranked Depp among the top 10 actors — ahead of Tom Hanks and behind Margot Robbie — who “would make you most interested in seeing a new movie in a cinema in the future.”

“Audiences don’t care. He’s still one of the biggest movie stars on the planet,” says Kevin Goetz, founder and CEO of audience research firm Screen Engine/ASI. “That, to me, is very telling about how often Hollywood perpetuates its own self-fulfilling prophecies.”

As Hollywood has kept a distance, Depp has remained a popular figure around the world, receiving career achievement and tribute awards from international film festivals and retaining a $20 million brand deal with Dior. Onscreen, he has appeared in underseen indies like the 2020 drama “Minamata” and the 2023 period piece “Jeanne du Barry,” and he directed the 2024 biopic “Modì, Three Days on the Wing of Madness.” And Depp’s fans have been vocal on social media, supporting the actor through his professional struggles and bizarrely rallying in 2021 to nominate “Minamata” for the Oscars first (and only) fan favorite award.

Lately, the town seems willing to forgive Depp. His next film is Lionsgate’s 2027 action thriller “Day Drinker,” co-starring Penélope Cruz. Meanwhile Disney is looking into “Ebenezer” and the potential backlash, as it contemplates another “Pirates of the Caribbean” movie, according to sources. Depp has said he’s open to returning to the franchise, but he noted “the only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note.”

“Ebenezer” doesn’t need to electrify the masses to justify its price tag. Given the uncertainty, Paramount cautiously spent $38 million to produce the Dickens tale. Depp was paid $5 million, a fraction of what he’s earned on prior studio movies, with the promise of bonuses tied to box office performance. Marketing expenses were around $50 million, including stops at San Diego Comic- Con where the actor made a surprise appearance, dressed in character, and threw handfuls of candy at the foot of attendees. (Paramount declined to comment on budgets.) Directed by Ti West, known for the “X” horror trilogy, “Ebenezer” spins the oft-told yarn of the curmudgeonly businessman who is visited by the ghosts of Christmas past, present and future.

“I’m optimistic for a few reasons,” says Regal’s CEO Eduardo Acuna. “Even though this story predates him, it feels like the character was written for Johnny Depp. And it’s good IP from a very distinctive filmmaker.”

Cinema operators like Acuna suggest the box office haul will speak less to Depp’s appeal and more to the movie’s quality. After all, there’s been no shortage of takes on “A Christmas Carol.” Scrooge has been a staple of holiday moviegoing for decades, with popular versions including the 1951 classic with Alastair Sim and 1988’s “Scrooged” with Bill Murray. The most recent entry, Disney’s 2009 “A Christmas Carol,” starring Jim Carrey, brought in $325 million against an overinflated $200 million budget.

“It’s a story that’s been told a number of times, so it’ll be more about whether this one is compelling,” says Classic Cinemas CEO Chris Johnson. “I don’t know if I’ve heard anyone saying they won’t see it because of Johnny Depp. The public seems to be pretty forgiving.”

For Depp, embodying a misanthrope like Scrooge — in the trailer, he’s seen scaring villagers and being stingy with Christmas bonuses — jibes with the other offbeat or unlikable characters he’s spun into the stuff of contemporary cinema classics. His real-life rebellious persona has helped sell his most famous roles, from the chaotic Captain Jack Sparrow from “Pirates of the Caribbean,” eccentric Willy Wonka from “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” and the mercurial Mad Hatter in “Alice in Wonderland.”
“Johnny’s image was built on being a bad boy,” Goetz says. “He ain’t America’s dad. We don’t want him to be that.”

items.title: MCU Surprise: ‘VisionQuest’ Finale Teases the Return of [SPOILER] in ‘Avengers: Doomsday’
items.description: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “Forever,” the finale of “VisionQuest,” now streaming on Disney+.
items.author: Adam B Vary; Angelique Jackson
paragraphs: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “Forever,” the finale of “VisionQuest,” now streaming on Disney+.

The “WandaVision” Saga has come to a close with the final episode of the Disney+ series “VisionQuest.” But it seems as though the story of the ultra-powerful Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen), the synthezoid Vision (Paul Bettany) and their super-powered children will continue in the MCU.

The season finale sees Vision reunite with his and Wanda Maximoff’s grown-up sons, Ruaridh Mollica’s Tommy Maximoff (who was key to “VisionQuest”) and Joe Locke’s Billy Maximoff (whose eleventh-hour arrival completes the family reunion). Then, the post-credit scene replays the ending of 2022’s feature film “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness,” where Wanda eradicated the Darkhold from all of the multiverse before (seemingly) being crushed from within a mountain.
However, this time, the scene continues with the appearance of Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom, who lifts the rubble off Wanda and addresses her.
“Scarlet Witch, awaken — your power will be mine,” Doom says, as Wanda gasps and opens her eyes.

The coda confirms fan speculation that Wanda would return as the Avengers face off against Doom in “Avengers: Doomsday,” out Dec. 18. And she’s not the only powerful hero that Doom has now rounded up. In “Avengers Endgame: Encore,” Doom kidnapped the Hulk (Mark Ruffalo) in a newly added post-credits scene.

Ahead of the finale, Marvel tweeted a message written in binary code, which fans were quick to decode as a quote from “WandaVision.” Though the tweet was written with a series of 0s and 1s, it translated to: “We could never truly leave each other, even if we tried.” The line is from the show’s 2021 finale.

Olsen first appeared as Wanda in the post-credits scene for 2014’s “Captain America: The Winter Soldier,” which set up her full-fledged debut in 2015’s “Avengers: Age of Ultron.” Despite her wide-ranging powers of telekinesis and mind manipulation, Wanda’s first forays in the MCU were laden with tragedy, including the death of her brother Pietro (Aaron Taylor-Johnson), the devastation of her home country of Sokovia in “Age of Ultron,” and then the death of her beloved Vision (Paul Bettany) in 2018’s “Avengers: Infinity War.”

That trauma led to 2021’s “WandaVision,” Marvel Studios‘ first TV series for Disney+, in which Wanda’s overwhelming grief led her to take over an entire New Jersey town and transform it into a recreation of American sitcoms — complete with a reconstituted Vision and two twin sons, Billy and Tommy. By the end of the series, she had to let go of Vision and her sons, all while her interactions with the witch Agatha Harkness (Kathryn Hahn) revealed Wanda to be the Scarlet Witch, one of the most powerful beings in the Marvel universe. Agatha’s witchy, post-“WandaVision” escapades continued in the 2024 Disney+ series “Agatha All Along,” which introduced Joe Locke as Wanda and Vision’s grown-up son Billy Maximoff.

Wanda’s story continued in 2022’s “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness,” in which her grief from the loss of her children led her to turn fully evil as the film’s central villain. She brutally killed anyone standing in opposition to her desire to find her boys within the multiverse, fueled by the corrupting book of magic, the Darkhold. By the end, Wanda understood all the harm she had caused, and she eradicated the Darkhold from all of the multiverse before (seemingly) being crushed from within Wundagore mountain.
When asked by Variety in 2022 whether she hoped to play Wanda again, however, Olsen sounded optimistic.

“It’s weird that I’m expecting to return, but no one’s told me I’m doing anything!” she said with a laugh. “But in my mind, I’m just making the assumption that they’ll have me again. I don’t know to what capacity, but I hope I’m back. I hope there’s also more fun to be had in something different.”

items.title: ‘You’ve Got Mail’ Reboot in the Works at Warner Bros.
items.description: Warner Bros. is rebooting the classic 1998 rom-com “You’ve Got Mail,” with Jason Orley attached to direct, Variety has confirmed.
items.author: Jack Dunn
paragraphs: Warner Bros. is rebooting the classic 1998 rom-com “You’ve Got Mail,” with Jason Orley attached to direct, Variety has confirmed.

Plot details remain under wraps. Orley is currently drafting a script based on a previous take by Deborah Kaplan and Harry Elfont. Neal Moritz and Tania Landau are set to produce under the Original Film banner.

Nora Ephron’s original starred Tom Hanks as major bookstore capitalist Joe Fox, who threatens to put Meg Ryan‘s Kathleen Kelly, an independent children’s bookstore owner, out of business with his new location. While their in-person rapport is naturally confrontational, over the now-defunct AOL Messenger, they spark an anonymous romance. Other cast members include Greg Kinnear, Parker Posey, Jean Stapleton and Steve Zahn. The film was a major box office success following a Christmas-time release, earning $250 million against a budget of about $65 million.

“You’ve Got Mail” was inspired by the 1937 play “Perfumeire” by Miklós László, which was previously adapted into the 1940 comedy classic “The Shop Around the Corner” with Jimmy Stewart and Margaret Sullavan.

Orley joins “You Got Mail” after recently wrapping post-production on “Close Personal Friends,” an Amazon comedy film starring Brie Larson, Jack Quaid, Lilly Collins and Henry Golding. He made his feature directorial debut with “Big Time Adolescence” in 2019. He followed that with 2022’s “I Want You Back.”
On the small screen, Orley directed six episodes of Pete Davidson’s 2023 Peacock series “Bupkis.” He also collaborated with Davidson on three of his comedy specials.
Orley is repped by UTA, Rise Management and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman, Newman, Warren, Richman, Rush, Kaller, & Gellman L.L.P.
Deadline was first to report the news of the “You’ve Got Mail” reboot.

items.title: As Russell Brand’s Begins a 10-Year Prison Sentence, Why Celebrities Fear the Power of an Exposé
items.description: Standing in the glass dock at Southwark Crown Court in London, awaiting his sentence for one rape and three sexual assaults to be handed down, Russell Brand was addressed directly by the judge. “No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behavi
items.author: K J Yossman
paragraphs: Standing in the glass dock at Southwark Crown Court in London, awaiting his sentence for one rape and three sexual assaults to be handed down, Russell Brand was addressed directly by the judge. “No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behaviour that only you could get away with,” Justice Bennathan said, referencing an incident in which Brand had launched himself on an unknown woman in the middle of a studio corridor as his entourage looked on. “It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offence. And as it turns out, you haven’t got away with it.”

Brand may well have gotten away with it had it not been for a joint investigation by Channel 4 documentary strand “Dispatches” and The Sunday Times of London. Their reporting, published in Sept. 2023, contained numerous serious allegations, including that the former comedian had sexually assaulted four women between 2006 and 2013. Brand denied any wrongdoing (none of the women who made the allegations in the documentary were involved in the recent criminal trial although it is understood the Met Police are now investigating at least one of those complaints and Brand may face yet more charges).

The former comedian, who’d appeared in Hollywood movies and had a short-lived marriage to Katy Perry at the height of her success, had long cultivated an air of degeneracy as part of his persona, enabling him to operate in plain sight. Yet it wasn’t until the Channel 4/Sunday Times investigation was published that police opened an investigation. Whether it’s because the reporting had prompted more women to come forward – as Brand’s lawyer in the trial, Ian Winter, repeatedly argued — or because the media spotlight gave the authorities the resolution they needed to investigate a celebrity will probably never be known.

But Brand is not the only celebrity to have found themselves in the dock after being accused of wrongdoing in the media. In 2023 news anchor Huw Edwards, once the best-known and highest paid journalist at the BBC, was the subject of an exposé by The Sun, who revealed he had been in an inappropriate text-based relationship with a teenager during which he’d paid for nude photographs.

Although he had not acted unlawfully in that instance, Edwards was arrested less than a year later and eventually convicted of making indecent images after police found videos of children as young as seven being abused on Edwards’ phone. It emerged he had been sent them by a pedophile to whom he’d, apparently unrelatedly, gifted numerous instalments of cash.

Kevin Spacey has also faced an endless series of legal battles – both criminal and civil on both sides of the Atlantic – after he was accused of sexually assaulting a 14-year-old boy in a 2017 Buzzfeed interview. None have resulted in any finding of liability or criminality and Spacey has always denied any allegations of sexual misconduct but his career has never recovered. In the U.K. Spacey was, like Brand, tried at Southwark Crown Court, where he was on trial for nine charges of sexual assault against four separate men. He was acquitted on all counts. After the trial, some of the jurors asked to meet the Oscar-winner and shake his hand.

So it’s unsurprising that David Walliams, a comedian, bestselling children’s author and former “Britain’s Got Talent” judge, sought an injunction last month to prevent the same newspaper from publishing an investigation into his alleged sexual misconduct. Lawyers for Walliams told London’s High Court he would be likely to commit suicide if the story was published. The judge held that suicidal ideation is not a ground on which to prevent the publication of an article potentially in the public interest, although he noted his decision to dismiss the injunction does not mean the allegations are true.

Published today, the Guardian’s report accuses Walliams of grooming young fans and harassment. One woman told the newspaper she was 15 when she alleges Walliams drove her to his house and engaged in behavior that she now considers to be sexual assault. Walliams has denied all the allegations. There is no police investigation into Walliams nor any suggestion he may face charges, but, like Spacey, his career now lies in ruins. (Walliams has been dropped by his agent and his books will no longer be published).

Brand’s celebrity loomed large throughout his trial: some of his victims were fans who were initially thrilled to meet him, others were vulnerable because of his disproportionate power over them. In his sentencing remarks, Justice Bennathan accepted the former comedian’s fame was “an intrinsic part of each offence” as it allowed him to carry out his crimes. But, he noted, “I also need to be careful I am not punishing you more because you are famous.”

Coddled by their managers, obeyed by their assistants and adored by their fans, some celebrities have been able to abuse their exalted status. But when an intrepid journalist turns that spotlight to expose alleged misconduct, whether criminal or otherwise, fame can also be their undoing.

items.title: Dua Lipa, Tame Impala, SZA and Daddy Yankee to Headline 2027 Coachella Festival
items.description: The mystery is over: the lineup and headliners have been revealed for next year’s Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival in Indio, California.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: The mystery is over: the lineup and headliners have been revealed for next year’s Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival in Indio, California.

The headliners set to hit the stage for two weekends, April 9-11 and April 16-18, 2027, are Dua Lipa on Friday, Tame Impala on Saturday and SZA on Sunday. Daddy Yankee has also been tapped as a fourth top-billed headliner to showcase a special production.

Other artists for Friday include Madonna, Zara Larsson, Steve Lacey, JISOO, Kehlani and Leon Thomas. As for Saturday, Phoebe Bridgers, Weezer, Tiësto, Martin Garrix, Role Model and Adéla are set to take to the Coachella stages. And finally, on Sunday, other performers include Don Toliver, Dom Dolla, Kygo, The Neighbourhood and Becky G. See the full lineup below.
The official Coachella Instagram account wrote in the post’s caption, “The return to innocence.”

The 2027 headliners follow the chart-topping artists who headlined the 2026 iteration of the famed music festival, which included Justin Bieber, Sabrina Carpenter, Karol G and Anyma. Last year, Carpenter delivered a theatrical production that featured a dazzling, vintage Hollywood-style set and several celebrity cameos. As for Bieber, he brought a more intimate set, leaning heavily on his Swag era while also playing some classic hits via YouTube clips from his laptop onstage. Karol G, who became the first Latina solo artist to headline the festival’s main stage, brought the energy back up on Sunday with a visually stunning and electric performance.
Passes for Coachella 2027 go on sale Nov. 13 at 12 p.m. PT. YouTube also returns for its 15th year as the exclusive livestream partner for both weekends.

items.title: ‘You’ve Got Mail’ Reboot in the Works at Warner Bros.
items.description: A new take on the beloved rom-com You’ve Got Mail is in the works at Warner Bros., The Hollywood Reporter has learned.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: A new take on the beloved rom-com You’ve Got Mail is in the works at Warner Bros., The Hollywood Reporter has learned.
Rather than a remake of the original 1998 film starring Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan, the new film will follow a new story, though plot details are being kept under wraps.

Jason Orley (Close Personal Friends, Bupkis and I Want You Back) has been tapped to direct the project. He’s also writing the current draft based on a screenplay by Deborah Kaplan and Harry Elfont. Neal Moritz and Tania Landau from the original movie are also returning to produce.

The 1998 pic, based on Miklós László’s 1937 Hungarian play Parfumerie, follows book superstore magnate Joe Fox (Hanks) and independent book shop owner Kathleen Kelly (Ryan) as they fall in love in the anonymity of the Internet. However, they’re both blissfully unaware that he’s trying to put her out of business. Greg Kinnear, Parker Posey, Jean Stapleton, Steve Zahn, Heather Burns and Dave Chappelle also starred in the film helmed by Nora Ephron.

Upon its release, You’ve Got Mail grossed more than $250 million at the global box office, not adjusted for inflation. It became Ephron’s highest-grossing film to date, behind Sleepless in Seattle (1993). Ryan also earned a Golden Globe nomination the following year for best actress in a motion picture — comedy or musical for her performance as Kathleen.
Orley is repped by UTA, Rise Management and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman, Newman, Warren, Richman, Rush, Kaller, & Gellman L.L.P.

items.title: Brandon Sklenar on ‘Iron Jane,’ Body Dysmorphia and His Rapid Hollywood Rise
items.description: Brandon Sklenar is taking a moment to catch his breath. Over the past few years, the 36-year-old actor has watched his career explode with co-starring roles in Taylor Sheridan’s Paramount+ series 1923, the much-discussed Blake Lively drama It Ends With Us, the
items.author: Patrick Brzeski
paragraphs: Brandon Sklenar is taking a moment to catch his breath. Over the past few years, the 36-year-old actor has watched his career explode with co-starring roles in Taylor Sheridan’s Paramount+ series 1923, the much-discussed Blake Lively drama It Ends With Us, the South by Southwest sensation Drop and The Housemaid, Lionsgate’s $400 million-grossing erotic thriller starring Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried.

And he has four more star vehicles expected next year — Paramount’s contemporary Western The Rescue, Warner Bros.’ special forces thriller F.A.S.T., scripted by Sheridan; Ramin Bahrani’s romantic thriller Vegas: A Love Story, opposite Maika Monroe; and Lissette Feliciano’s female bodybuilding drama Iron Jane, co-starring Eiza González.

“I’ve pretty much been going nonstop for the last few years, and only just very recently, in the last couple months, have I had a moment of stillness to take stock,” Sklenar says. “And now that I can stop and look around, I’m like, ‘What the fuck? This is crazy.’”
