items.title: Michael Bloomberg and Diana Taylor Get Married After 26 Years
items.description: Sometimes it takes a quarter-century, but he will be down to DTR. A spokesperson for former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg announced on Monday that he and his longtime partner, Diana Taylor, have married after 26 years together. It was “a small, private
items.author: Grace Klara Marshall
paragraphs: Sometimes it takes a quarter-century, but he will be down to DTR. A spokesperson for former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg announced on Monday that he and his longtime partner, Diana Taylor, have married after 26 years together. It was “a small, private ceremony at their home on the Upper East Side,” and Bloomberg’s daughters from his first marriage, Emma and Georgina, were there alongside other family members.

Bloomberg and Taylor met in 2000, when he was first running for mayor. They were seated next to each other by chance at the notoriously romantic Citizens Budget Commission meeting. Thankfully, fate struck a second time when they were dining at the same restaurant later that night. In Taylor’s telling, Bloomberg saw her, approached her table, and asked her to have a drink afterward.

Bloomberg, who’s 84, served as the city’s mayor for three consecutive terms from 2002 to 2013. During his tenure, Taylor, a 71-year-old business executive who was married once before she met Bloomberg, served as the city’s unofficial First Lady. (She was also the New York superintendent of banks from 2003 to 2007.) Taylor has described herself as a “step-whatever” to Bloomberg’s children.

Why now? In 2020, when Bloomberg was running for president, Gayle King asked about his relationship with Taylor and whether he planned to be the first modern-day unmarried president. “We’ve only been living together for 19 years and, I think it’s fair if I can speak for her as well, neither of us have any plans to change,” he replied coyly. Their domestic partnership came up a few times during his presidential run — in her own interview with the Washington Post, Taylor said she hates the term girlfriend “because it sounds so temporary” and “junior high” but finds partner too business-y. “Nobody’s come up with language around what we are,” she said.

Well, now we can officially call them man and wife. Could death and taxes have brought them to the altar? Or as one X user theorized, maybe it took two decades to lock in their prenup? Whatever it is, good for them. It really is never too late to get hitched.

items.title: Rhea Raj Is Building Her Own Path to Stardom
items.description: Summer is over. Class is back in session. Catch up on our Star Study series here.
items.author: Cat Zhang
paragraphs: Summer is over. Class is back in session. Catch up on our Star Study series here.

The West’s fascination with South Asian culture has been driven to the max: White fashion girls are tossing dupattas over their shoulders, going to yoga, and embracing Ayurvedic wellness rituals like hair oiling and breathwork. But why not let South Asian creatives take center stage instead?

Twenty-six-year-old Rhea Raj, the singer-producer-dancer and older sister of Katseye’s Lara Raj, could be your next pop favorite. Her luxe electropop anthems broadcast a life of first-class flights, VIP access, and general baddie-dom; they pull from trap, R&B, and club music and recall Timbaland’s Bollywood-sampling 2000s productions, though actually made by a Desi person. Rhea grew up in the Dallas suburbs to Tamil parents. Her mother taught Bharatanatyam, a type of Indian classical dance. She started dancing at 2, singing at 10, and producing at 11. “I just wanted to record YouTube covers,” Rhea says. “I told my parents, ‘I learned about this thing called Logic. It’s like a nicer version of Garage Band. Can you guys please get it for my 11th birthday gift?’” She inspired Lara to follow in her performance footsteps: “I remember she was like my little art project. I would be like, Let’s direct music videos in the room and try on costumes and makeup.”

Fast-forward to today, and both of them are pop performers on the rise. Fans of Katseye may be familiar with Lara and Megan Skiendal’s hotly anticipated unreleased demo, “First in My Bloodline,” which was co-produced by Rhea. But Rhea has her own projects in the works. Just a few weeks ago, her song “Dream Girl” was teased during the halftime segment of the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. “I self-produced it in my bedroom at 3 a.m., the week after I came home from India in January,” she says. It’ll be the lead single on her upcoming album.

Listen if you like: Extravagant Bollywood films; 2000s Timbaland-produced bangers; Ariana Grande’s “7 Rings” era; pretending to have an Amex Black Card; the self-confidence of Love Island (UK)’s Jasmine Muller.

Her top artist: Rosalia. “I discovered her when I was 17 or 18, just starting college in New York and studying music. I remember really studying everything she did: her music videos, interviews, and the narrative thread connecting her music from album to album. Seeing her evolution as an artist and watching her become her truest, most openhearted self is really inspiring”

Her biggest “pinch-me” moment: “I was about 20 and studying at NYU when I met a publisher named JKash. He was visiting from L.A. and came to speak to one of my business classes. I ended up playing him a demo off my laptop, and he said, “This is so cool.” We stood outside in the snow for two hours after class, playing demos off my phone. They were super-electronic, very Fast & Furious vibes. He said, ‘Why don’t you come to L.A. and meet my wife, Jaime? She’s an incredible publisher. Come to L.A. tomorrow.’

I flew out the next morning. This was in 2020, and I’ve since signed a publishing deal with them. They’re like my second family in L.A. When I arrived, Jay put me in a session with Charlie Puth. It was one of my first times ever writing with someone else, and I was blown away.”
On her producer icons: “So many. I mean, Pharrell is my birthday twin. I also love Mike Dean. I love big, dramatic synths, and it’s my dream to be in a room with him and create. I’d also add Arca.”

On what’s on the mood board for her next album: “I’m describing the visuals as ’70s vintage Bollywood cinema meets cyberpunk and sci-fi. Think high saturation, fun visual effects, and those two worlds coming together because they’re both essential to who I am.

I grew up watching sci-fi movies. When I was 8, I was already insisting that we watch Terminator. I loved Mad Max and anything tech related. Now I love anime too. What’s interesting is that when I watched Dream Girl, a Bollywood film from the ’70s, I noticed how futuristic the title track’s music video was. The visual effects, coloring, and overall aesthetic felt so ahead of its time. It was really cool to see how these two worlds could come together.”

On her favorite Bollywood films: “Om Shanti Om (2007) and Sholay (1975). I really look at the coloring and set design. There’s so much incredible set design in Bollywood films. And the dance breaks! I love watching a crazy dance moment.”

On the South Asian creatives that made her feel like she could do it too: “I remember watching Priyanka Chopra come from India to the U.S. and build her career here. My mom and I were so inspired by her journey. The week after I appeared on American Idol at 15, my mom reached out to her manager, Anjula, saying we were big fans of what Priyanka was doing and would love to meet her.

Fast-forward ten years, and I signed with Anjula for management this year on the exact ten-year anniversary of that email. We checked the dates on my contract, and it was February 8, 2026, exactly ten years after February 8, 2016. It was incredible.”

On having a sibling in the industry: “It’s surreal. Yesterday, we hadn’t seen each other in a week, and then we met on the pink carpet at the Victoria’s Secret show. We hugged and cried because we couldn’t believe how busy we are now and how we’re meeting at the places we grew up dreaming of being.”

On her favorite thing about Lara: “Aside from being incredibly talented and creative as an artist, she’s so true to herself and such a great friend. That’s something I really value about her as a person.

Everyone in her life says the same thing: She’s working 20-hour days, traveling, and going to incredible places, but she always makes time to sit with people and make them feel like the most important person in the room.”

On what she’d do with 24 hours in Chennai: “There’s a street in front of a temple near my house that I love visiting with my family. It has so many shops selling filter coffee, which is our South Indian coffee, and flower stores. There are cats everywhere, too. I’d go for a walk there with my family, spend 15 or 20 minutes at the beach meditating with my grandfather, and then enjoy a big home-cooked South Indian spread at my house.”

On her signature dish: “I love making tofu scramble. I’m a vegan, so I also love figuring out how to make Indian dishes vegan. My family will make malai kofta with sweet potato and tofu, as well as cashew or coconut cream, at home. We’ll be in the kitchen cooking up a storm, with everyone making a completely different extravagant dish at the same time. It’s so funny.”

On her evolving personal style: “I’d describe myself as maximalist in the way I love putting pieces together. My Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show look was one of my favorites. It was a deconstructed, sari-inspired gown made up of six different pieces that came together to create a really cool reconstructed sari. I love experimenting like that.”

On the South Asian creative peers she’s a big fan of: “There’s Rowi Singh, a makeup artist and one of the OG makeup girls creating fun, vibrant, maximalist looks. She’s from Australia, and we actually just met in New York. She did my glam for some Diwali parties.
I also really love Tanya Ravichandran. She’s a fashion ‘It’ girl and South Indian like me. We also met for the first time recently in New York.”

On her bucket-list travel destinations: “There are a few international shows I’m dying to play. I’m doing Lollapalooza India in January and Weverse Con, also in India. Playing in my hometown, in my motherland, has always been a lifelong dream. I’m also dying to play Mexico City and see my fans there, as well as London. That’s been years in the making. Ultimately, I want to play more international shows and go on an international tour.”

On whether there will be an official release of “First in My Bloodline”: “I wish! I love that song. It’s a banger. I posted about it last week because I love it so much. Maybe the fans need to keep asking for it!”

items.title: Meghan and Harry Put on a Brave Face in Belgium
items.description: Meghan Markle and Prince Harry touched down in Brussels, Belgium on Tuesday to open the Lost Screen Memorial, an art installation dedicated to the memories of children who “lost their lives as a result of the harm they suffered on social media.” It was also th
items.author: Sam Reed
paragraphs: Meghan Markle and Prince Harry touched down in Brussels, Belgium on Tuesday to open the Lost Screen Memorial, an art installation dedicated to the memories of children who “lost their lives as a result of the harm they suffered on social media.” It was also their first public appearance since Markle’s father, Thomas Markle, was arrested in Florida by the FBI last week and charged with one count of possession of child pornography.

Thomas was arrested following a tip about a storage unit he owned in L.A., which police found contained sexually explicit images of him with prepubescent girls. In a statement last month, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations against Thomas, which were first brought to her attention in 2018 in a letter from the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan said.

Harry spoke to Parliament on behalf of the couple on Tuesday, and also participated in a panel titled Beyond Promises: Building a Digital Future That Works for Children. Meghan was originally slated to deliver the speech, but, according to British tabloids, she pulled out ahead of the visit. An “insider” told The Telegraph she’s “not strong enough, emotionally, to be doing any public speaking right now.”

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex first opened the Lost Screen Memorial in New York City in 2025 as part of the Archewell Foundation’s No Child Lost to Social Media campaign. The installation is made up of 50 lightboxes resembling smartphone screens, each of which features a child’s face. Per the organization’s website, “These images represent the ones their parents have on their phone lockscreens. Their faces serve as a constant reminder of what has been lost.”

“If technology really can change the world for the better,” Harry said during his address, “let’s begin by making it safe for children.” The couple did not answer reporters’ questions as they arrived in Brussels, but both were dressed in black and wore red poppy pins associated with Remembrance Day in the UK.

items.title: ‘Foot Undies’ Put a Pep in My Step
items.description: The internet has found its new favorite micro-trend: “Foot undies,” a term used to describe lace socks peek-a-boo-ing out of a shoe, ranging from Chantilly slip-ons bordering ballet flats to DIY’d hosiery whale tailing in between the second and third toe. Yeva
items.author: Emma Childs
paragraphs: The internet has found its new favorite micro-trend: “Foot undies,” a term used to describe lace socks peek-a-boo-ing out of a shoe, ranging from Chantilly slip-ons bordering ballet flats to DIY’d hosiery whale tailing in between the second and third toe. Yeva Kouzouian, founder of digital magazine Tourist Souvenirs, first coined the phrase in an September Instagram carousel of such sock moments, with a title card reading, “Foot Undies Fall.” At 75.6k likes, it’s the fashion moodboard’s most popular post to date. Kouzouian believes “the name is really what caused such a commotion;” The internet is, of course, where the freaks go to congregate, so any mention of feet and-slash-or underwear will do numbers. “But it’s also aggressively been the year of feet,” Kouzouian tells me.

It’s true. Fashion really has let the dogs out as of late. Chanel’s heel-only sandals opened up a new frontier of naked shoes. (Do they even count as a shoe? With three-fourths of the foot making direct contact with the ground, they’re more like the concepts of a plan of a shoe.) Saint Laurent sells PVC piggy-peepers, recently worn by proud weirdo Alexander Skarsgard on the Wicker red carpet. Accentuating your feet with unnecessary accessories is also in: On the streets of New York City this summer, I saw countless ankles dripped out in chains and flip-flops bejeweled with toe rings. Foot undies feel like the natural next step in this procession, especially heading into colder weather where tootsies can no longer be laid bare.

Alexus Shefts, a Los Angeles-based wardrobe stylist, received a request for a pair of foot undies after her client, Delilah Hamlin, saw Tourist Souvenir’s viral post. Hamlin — the daughter of Lisa Rinna and Harry Hamlin and sister to Amelia Gray — wanted hers hot pink, so Shefts bought a white pair and dyed them to fit the bill. “Foot undies just make things more interesting,” Shefts says. “There’s this notion of no-show socks being unflattering. Foot undies are an ironic play on that, where something that was looked at as Ugh, cringy, is now super cool-girl.” And unlike the other fashion trends percolating in the ether, foot undies are intuitive and easy to style: Sock plus shoe, and you’re good to go.

It was at this point, after speaking with Shefts, that I went to Etsy and bought myself a pair in blush pink. I’m always interested in trends that lean slightly left-of-center, especially those that are idiot-proof enough for when I only have T-minus ten minutes to leave the house. My foot undies arrived five business days later. Immediately, I was presented with a styling snafu, which was that these low no-show socks did a great job at not showing. I did my best to pull the lace out from my black Larroudé ballet flats, but I wanted a much lower vamp. Paloma Wool’s Joelia pumps were more successful, revealing slices of scalloped lace at each edge. Satisfied, I wore the combo out to my nearby coffee shop and found that I walked with a pep in my step. Not only did my blister-prone feet have a barrier of protection, I felt like I had a sexy little secret, similar to the rush I get from wearing a Real Bra. I ordered my iced oat milk vanilla latte, thinking to myself, I’m not like other girls — I wear a footie negligee with my kitten heels!

Though the best shoes to wear with foot lingerie, I’ve decided, would be Paloma Wool’s toe-cleavage heels from its spring 2027 runway. Even better would be Evelina Kryvopust’s barely-there shoes, which eliminate the need for socks altogether. The Ukrainian designer hand-sculpts each pair from lace hosiery into a “second skin” for the foot, and she recently partnered with Area creative director Nicholas Aburn to make her now-signature shoes for the brand’s spring 2027 show. Afterward, her barely-there heels went viral and earned stand-alone coverage in Vogue and a co-sign from cult-favorite fashion photographer Nadia Lee Cohen. “I think their appeal is in that they don’t look like a conventional shoe,” Kryvopust says of her design. “They’re made from something very familiar, lace hosiery, but used in a way you wouldn’t necessarily expect. I don’t want to create something that looks completely new at first glance, but rather something that makes you look twice.”

Ultimately, it’s that double-take effect that makes foot undies so alluring. My heels on their own are cute. With an assist from a scrap of lace, they became something more titillating and intentional, understated but still flirtatious. It’s likely no one even noticed them during my quick Brooklyn neighborhood excursion. But I knew they were there, and that was enough. As I’ve learned in my years of womanhood thus far, sex appeal is at its strongest when it’s subtle and mostly private.

items.title: CoverGirl’s Newest Mascara Survived Rain, 10-Hour Days, & My Picky Standards
items.description: I’ve genuinely reached flow state with my makeup. Maybe it’s not the most exciting thing for a beauty writer to admit, but I’m perfectly happy admiring the experimental glam girls from afar. My own routine is pretty much down to a science: 15 minutes flat (yes
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: I’ve genuinely reached flow state with my makeup. Maybe it’s not the most exciting thing for a beauty writer to admit, but I’m perfectly happy admiring the experimental glam girls from afar. My own routine is pretty much down to a science: 15 minutes flat (yes, I’ve timed it), using the same products, in the same order, every single day. Sometimes, I’ll swap my mauve blush for terracotta — groundbreaking, I know. But the way I see it, why mess with a good thing?

Of course, I’m not opposed to trying something new in the name of journalism. But the barrier to entry in my permanent makeup bag is pretty high — particularly when it comes to mascara. I’ve already found a formula I love, so any serious contender has to offer something different. CoverGirl’s new Lash Blast Showstopper Mascara caught my attention for exactly that reason: I’d never seen an applicator quite like it, combining fiber bristles and silicone ones on the same wand.

In theory, the combination is meant to give maximum volume while also separating lashes so they don’t look clumpy. (Essentially, everything I’m looking for in a mascara.) As a longtime drugstore makeup enthusiast, I had high hopes — but if I spotted so much as a single flake, I was ready to throw in the towel. Spoiler: I haven’t reached for my regular mascara in a week. Ahead, my full review.
- Best for: Buildable volume, lifted lashes, and long-lasting wear.
- What I like: It doesn’t smudge or flake (even after 10 hours), and the brush makes it easy to coat every lash evenly.
- What I don’t like: The formula is a little thick, so I prefer wiping off any excess product before applying.
CoverGirl Lash Blast Showstopper Mascara

At this point, you don’t need to be a makeup guru to recognize CoverGirl’s Lash Blast. The iconic orange tube has been a drugstore staple for years, thanks to its ability to deliver fuller-looking lashes. The latest addition to the lineup, the Showstopper Mascara, offers the same focus on volume — just with a slightly different approach.

The biggest selling point? The Double Act brush. Unlike Lash Blast’s chunky silicone wand, this one is slimmer, making it easier to reach even those tiny hairs in the inner corners. It also combines fiber bristles with silicone ones in a 360-degree twist — almost like a volumizing wand and a lengthening wand rolled into one. The idea is to build up thickness while combing through lashes for a more separated, defined finish. (In other words, if you found the OG Lash Blast a little clumpy, the Showstopper Mascara might be more your speed.)

The formula comes in a regular and waterproof version — with both promising flake-free, transfer-proof wear. They also contain a conditioning complex with peptides, vitamin B5, and castor oil to help nourish your natural lashes underneath. To apply, CoverGirl recommends starting at the roots, then twisting and rotating the wand as you pull it through your lashes instead of just wiggling it so both types of bristles get a chance to do their thing.

My lashes are naturally thick, so I've never really given much attention to volumizing mascaras. Typically, I'm more interested in getting a little extra length and making sure everything washes off easily at night. (Urban Decay's Tube Job is my tried-and-true.) But, TMI warning: After dealing with a stye this summer, my lashes aren't quite as full as they used to be. There are a few sparse spots, and adding more length without volume makes them look spidery.

Naturally, when I tried the Showstopper Mascara before a night out, I was hoping to get some of that fullness back — and I wasn’t exactly shy with the application. I went in with two coats, and my lashes were basically touching my eyebrows. Even better, they still looked like individual lash clusters instead of five or six giant hairs clumped together. The brush did a good job of separating them, so there wasn’t just a bunch of product sitting at the root.

Of course, with my luck, it started raining halfway through the night — which really put this mascara to the test. But thankfully, there wasn’t a ring of black around my eyes when I made it home. In fact, there wasn’t even a single flake. Still, it came off like a breeze when I took a shower. (Considering how many mascaras smudge throughout the day and then refuse to budge when you're actually trying to wash them off, I was sufficiently impressed.)

The next day, I decided to go for a more natural lash look. The formula is on the thicker side, and the brush picks up quite a bit of product, so I wiped off the excess on a paper towel before applying (a trick I learned from Makeup by Mario, thank you very much). With a lighter coat, it looked even less clumpy, but my lashes still looked fuller and more defined — almost like I'd gotten a fresh lash lift and tint.

After testing CoverGirl's Showstopper Mascara for a week — through several 10-hour days, might I add — I'm happy to report that it's consistently good. Not once did I have to worry about smudging or flaking, and taking it off at night was just as easy. More importantly, I genuinely liked how my lashes looked: thicker and more lifted, but never spidery.

For my everyday routine, I'll probably stick to using less product, even if it means taking an extra second to wipe off the excess. Still, I like knowing I can build it up when I'm in the mood for something more exaggerated. If you want a reliable mascara that can do both (for less than $13, too), this is the one to try.

items.title: Sherri Shepherd Has Some Very Sherri Shepherd Ideas For Her 'Aladdin' Genie
items.description: As the Genie in Disney’s Broadway production of Aladdin, Sherri Shepherd’s character has gotten a lot of sleep after 10,000 years trapped in her lamp. In real life, the actor is trying to play catch-up. “Thank you for your patience — I just woke up,” she admit
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: As the Genie in Disney’s Broadway production of Aladdin, Sherri Shepherd’s character has gotten a lot of sleep after 10,000 years trapped in her lamp. In real life, the actor is trying to play catch-up. “Thank you for your patience — I just woke up,” she admits to Bustle, laughing, after joining our Zoom interview just a few minutes late. “I did not realize literally how much sleep you need after doing a Broadway show.”

It also takes a lot of energy to make history. In 2014, Shepherd made her Broadway debut by becoming the first Black woman to play the wicked stepmother in Rodgers + Hammerstein’s Cinderella. Now, more than a decade later, she’s the first woman to play the Genie in the long-running musical Aladdin, based on the 1992 film, at the New Amsterdam Theatre. It’s an honor she didn’t realize when she got the offer.

“When things scare me and an opportunity presents itself, I run, but not the opposite way. I run towards the fear,” she says. “And then I find out, ‘Oh, wait a minute, this is the first woman to play the Genie?’ That’s when I go, ‘What the hell did you say yes to? It’s too much pressure.’”

She seems to be doing just fine. Shepherd makes the Genie entirely her own, making timely wise-cracks when she can and infusing her numbers like “Friend Like Me” with pop culture references, from The Real Housewives of Agrabah (make this a reality, Disney) to her recent Emmy win for her eponymous talk show, which ended in May.
“When I say things like, ‘Oh, I got my very own star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame,’ the audience just goes crazy. Now I put in there, ‘my syndicated Emmy Award-winning talk show,’” she says.

However, some ideas didn’t make the final cut, specifically relating to a medley of classic Disney songs in the first act. “The director came in my dressing room and I’m singing [Cher accent], ‘Tale as old as time.’ He said, ‘Who are you?’ I proudly said, ‘I am Cher.” And he proudly said, ‘Yeah. No,’” she says. “At the end, I think I sang [Dolly Parton accent], ‘I want adventures in the gray.’ He said, ‘And who is that?’ I said, ‘That is Dolly Parton.’ And he said, ‘No, can you just go back to being the lounge singer?’ I just laughed so much because I don’t take things personally.”
While Shepherd may not be able to give her best celebrity impressions, her turn in Aladdin is already having the kind of impact on fans that performers dream of.

“A little girl came last night — she was three years old and dressed as the Genie,” she says. “She had her own little lamp, her dad said they asked her, ‘Is this the Genie from the movie?’ And she said, ‘No, the Genie from Broadway.’ I took her on a tour and gave her a real Aladdin lamp. It brought tears to my eyes. Everybody doesn’t want to be a princess — they want to be a genie. I love that now they’re dreaming like that.”

The first person I called was Kristin Chenoweth. I left a message on Michelle Williams’ voicemail. I called Wayne Brady. Steven Boyer was with me in a show called Trial & Error, and I called him and said, “What am I supposed to start doing?” Kristin sent me a video that was about 19 minutes long — no, it was longer than that — saying, “These are all of the things that you need to do, I’m sending you this.” Thankfully, I have a lot of friends on Broadway who told me what I was supposed to do — probably three-quarters of them I never did, but I do now, like sleep.

I do my vocal warmups, because Kristin said that’s the most important thing, and I stretch, then I listen to some soft music. Some people have to listen to rap, rock, and heavy stuff — not me. I have to center myself. I look at my son Jeffery’s picture, because he calms me down. When I try to call him, he’s like, “Bruh, what are you calling me for? Is this going to go on every day?” And I just stare at myself in the mirror. I will run through the show and picture it successful.
On mastering the choreography:

This is a team that really cares. They accommodated me with the dancing. I wish I could tap, but I get to say [to Aladdin], “Hey, do you know how to tap? Well, you do now. Don’t embarrass me.” I get to sashay off that stage and come on back in. They carry me through, and it’s an organized cacophony behind the scenes.
On her haunted Broadway theater:

I found out there’s a ghost, Ollie, in New Amsterdam. She used to be a Ziegfeld dancer, and was married to one of the silent screen film stars. Her picture is on the wall when you come in the theater. When I was rehearsing, part of the ceiling just fell on the floor, and I screamed. Everybody went, “Oh, that’s just Ollie. She's upset about something.” I said, “Do I need to do an exorcism?” And they said, “No, she’s very friendly. You just have to say good morning to her.” So I came in that theater and said, “Look here, girl. How are we going to do this?”
On her stage-door requests:

There’s a lot of fans who bring me things and hand it to me, and that’s kind of scary — somebody just throws something in your face. But I’ve had all kinds of gifts. Somebody printed out maybe 20 or 30 pictures of different things that I’ve been in — 30 Rock and The Sex Lives of College Girls — and wanted me to sign them. I’m like, “Can I keep these for myself?” A guy wanted me to take a picture and kiss him. I was like, “I’m going to decline because I don’t need no wife showing up.”
On the Aladdin she wants to see:

If they had a younger Genie, there would be more chemistry with Aladdin. It’d be like, “Jasmine who? I’m here.” In my season, it’s more maternal, big sister. But if a younger female Genie came in, she’d be like, “Honey, I’ll give you three wishes and more. Who are you going to choose?” That would be a lot of fun. I think now that I’ve done it, and they’ve seen we can incorporate different things to fit a Genie that’s not run-of-the-mill, the possibilities are endless.

items.title: Exclusive: Xochitl Gomez Reveals How Marvel Helped — & Hurt — Her Career
items.description: Xochitl Gomez has been working in Hollywood for almost a decade, but she’s not afraid to fangirl every now and then. For Halloween, the actor transformed herself into Euphoria scene-stealer Maddy Perez after finding the same dress that Alexa Demie wore while d
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Xochitl Gomez has been working in Hollywood for almost a decade, but she’s not afraid to fangirl every now and then. For Halloween, the actor transformed herself into Euphoria scene-stealer Maddy Perez after finding the same dress that Alexa Demie wore while discovering Nate Jacobs’ death in the desert.

“I am a victim of overpriced Depop sellers, I fear,” she tells Bustle over Zoom from her living room in Madrid, Spain. “Her outfit was absolutely iconic, and I love Alexa. I feel like she doesn't get enough recognition.”

You can make the same argument for Gomez, who has put in work that fellow rising stars could only dream of. The 20-year-old made her onscreen debut in Disney Channel’s Raven’s Home in 2018 and led one season of Netflix’s The Baby-Sitters Club before jumping to the Marvel Cinematic Universe at just age 16, starring as America Chavez in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.

Despite building quite the acting resume in her teens, Gomez’s star power got another big boost thanks to Dancing with the Stars, kicking off the show’s resurgence in 2023 when she took home the Mirrorball trophy with partner Valentin Chmerkovskiy at 17 years old. As one of the youngest winners in the show’s history, Gomez brought in Gen Z fans while winning over longtime viewers. “I really had to introduce people to Xochitl Gomez,” she says. “Especially after Marvel, it was very hard to allow myself to be myself because people were expecting a character.”

With a new following under her belt, Gomez is back to embracing new characters. Her latest role in the animated adaptation of Dr. Seuss’ The Cat in the Hat (in theaters Nov. 6) is a full-circle return to her childhood. “My grandma was a teacher and would read the book to me whenever I’d come over, but I was so young that now the only thing I remember when it comes to Dr. Seuss is Seussical,” she says. “I was maybe 10 and playing this super flamboyant character named Mayzie. She wears this huge outfit, and her project is to make this new awesome bird, Gertrude.”

This time, she voices Gabby opposite America Ferrera as her onscreen mom, Carmen, marking another childhood dream come true. “The first time I ever met America was in the White House because we were visiting, and I remember being in total awe,” she says. “Her answers are always so clear, thoughtful, and precise. I want to be like that.”

Like Ferrera, the Mexican American actor uses her platform to advocate for Latinx representation in film, which, combined with playing a Marvel hero, has drawn her fair share of racist criticism. But as she enters her 20s, she’s setting boundaries — including creating a healthy distance from Hollywood. When she’s not filming or doing press, Gomez flies back to Madrid, where she’s hoping to stay long enough to obtain a visa and reside in her downtime. And when it comes to building her repertoire, she’s not afraid to follow her instincts.

“Sometimes there are cool projects, but something's off about it, and I end up saying no. Then later on, a story comes out, and I’m like, ‘I was saved by the bell,’” she says, declining to name names. “I’ve seen so many young people lose their spark, and I don’t ever want to be in a situation where that’s me. If that means saying no to the project, then so be it.”
Below, Gomez opens up about the pros and cons of Marvel stardom, her time on DWTS, and what’s next on her vision board.
Your first onscreen role was Raven’s Home. What do you remember about being on set for the first time?

How much of an operation it was. It was a live taping. Everyone knew their thing. I was like, “If I flub up, that means these kids have to do it again.” I was nervous because I kept forgetting one word and was like, “I never want to feel that again.”
What Disney Channel show or movie would you like to see revived next?
Sonny with a Chance. When I was a kid, I loved Demi Lovato because of her hair and her outfits, and I just want to bring that back.
Then you ended up joining Marvel. How was that transition, especially with it happening so quickly at such a young age?

I was definitely nervous. It was scary and frightening. But also, I was working with people I looked up to. After that, I had a hard time getting roles because they were like, “She's too expensive. What if she’s in this and that, her schedule?” And I'm like, “Guys...”
Yes. It was a gift and a curse because I was like, “Wait, I want to do the cool indie movies. Give me a chance, guys.”
Did you feel any pressure from that huge fan base, or did you use it to your advantage?

The pros of being in a franchise are that people are excited, and there’s a literal map of what people expect. So if you study that as much as they have, they’ll appreciate how much thought you've put into it. But there are people controlling what is being written. We were changing scripts like crazy. I was a huge fan of Doctor Strange, so I knew people expected a certain thing, and it was really hard, as a 14-year-old girl, to be like, “Wait, the character wouldn't do something like that.”
Is there a possibility that you could return for Avengers: Doomsday?
Well, they own the rights to my image, so it's possible.
If America Chavez ever returns to the MCU, which I feel like she will at some point, what part of her journey would you be most excited to show?
We left her at a really interesting place where she finally understood her powers and what she's capable of, so I want to see what’s going on there and how buddy-buddy she and Wong are.
Is there anybody from the Avengers universe you would be excited to share a scene with?
Florence Pugh. Even if I don't say anything, I would love to watch her process because her choices are always so solid, clear, and good.
Your season of Dancing with the Stars introduced it to a younger generation. Looking back, why do you think you won?

In my head, I was like, “There's going to be Olympians, pro-athletes,” so I went into it knowing I probably wouldn't make it very far, but I wanted to make an impression. I had the amazing ability to do that for 11 weeks in a row and introduce my culture to America. And I had an amazing partner [Chmerkovskiy] who allowed me to control a lot. I designed all the costumes.
I love hearing you talk about Latinx representation. Why is it still important for you to fight for it?

Going back to franchises with books, there’s a lot of criticism and hate that caused me to shell up. I was trying to let people know who I am, but I was also putting restrictions in place. Some of those things were limiting my comments and only responding to certain people, which was hard to navigate at 16. But what really helped me was people telling me, “Hey, your representation and seeing you onscreen is everything to me.”
You've already achieved a lot before 20 years old. Do you take pride in that, or do you still have a lot more you want to go after?

Sometimes I see other people's careers, and you can’t help but compare, and then you have to remember, “Oh, I'm not a white girl, so there are only so many opportunities.” But I also have to look back and be proud because 10-year-old me didn't think this is where I would be.
What is still on your vision board?

Broadway has been a dream since I was 5. There’s a special thing about Bye Bye Birdie. That was my first lead role. I played Rosie. I was supposed to be a 35-year-old woman, and I was 10. I had my little French twist and suit that my mom made me. It’d be super cool to revisit that someday.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: 25 Gifts For The Woman Who Has Everything & Wants Nothing
items.description: 25 Gifts For The Woman Who Has Everything & Wants Nothing
items.author: Irina Grechko; Victoria Montalti
paragraphs: 25 Gifts For The Woman Who Has Everything & Wants Nothing
Lola Blankets Wild Moss Medium Lola Weighted Blanket

We're starting strong (and heavy) with one of Lola Blankets' weighted blankets. The beloved luxury blanket brand always has its praises sung with fans declaring that it's worth every penny. Your giftee may already own an original cozy blanket from the brand, so consider one of the weighted styles in a variety of sizes and designs if your budget allows for it.
Brighter Day Pigments DIY Watercolor Paint Set with Travel Pouch

2026 was the year of analogue hobbies, and we think the desire for hands-on activities will continue well into 2027, so why not purchase a sweet watercolor paint set? This one has a few Anthropologie-exclusive postcard prints and pouch designs to pick from. The neat watercolor pen and travel-sized paint tin are chef’s kiss for the friend who likes to get creative wherever they go.
Flamingo Estate Personalized Heritage Olive Oil

You've probably seen Flamingo Estate's iconic heirloom tomato candle in almost every gift guide (or have gifted one already), but the luxury lifestyle brand has so much more to offer. And its food, like the olive oil, shouldn't be slept on, making this personalized EVOO bottle an amazing gift for a mother, holiday host, or home chef. Write a short, sweet note and leave a long-lasting effect with your giftee.
Maison de Sabré The SABREMOJI Fruit Charm

Whether she’s a seasoned jet-setter... or a forgetful person, you can upgrade her AirTag game with these joyful fruit charms, intended to keep AirTags safe and stylish, personalizing everything from house keys to suitcases (I wear one on my work bag!). Pair it with a new AirTag for an extra thoughtful touch.
Free People Sunday Button Snood

A snood is the cozy solution to staying warm and stylish throughout the winter that isn't your everyday scarf (Because guess what? She doesn't need another one). This is a great option for your super stylish friend. She can wear it under her seasonal coat and oversized button-down top or over a cardigan for extra cozy coverage and dimension.
Shark ChillPill 3-in-1 Personal Cooling System with Fan

Shark's ChillPill fan was perhaps the most viral beauty tool of the year. And it is absolutely a little luxury, which many people say is worth the splurge. The portable fan stands out in price and quality because of the cooling plate and dry-touch mist for actually cold air. So if you're shopping for a giftee who runs hot, this is a gift they'll definitely need and want.

I've never met someone who doesn't love their Hulken rolling tote bag, including myself. While I use the large size for storage, others use it for laundry days, or opt for the smaller size for everyday commuting and grocery shopping. It's so versatile and practical, and with three sizes and multiple colors, you can pick the one that best fits your giftee's needs and lifestyle.
West Elm x Emma Chamberlain Pigeon Glasses Holder

Personally, I love Emma Chamberlain's quirky aesthetic, from her Architectural Digest home tours to her West Elm homeware collection. So if you have someone on your list with a similar aesthetic, check out the decor pieces for a gifting moment. This pigeon-shaped glasses holder is great for quirky decorators, sunglasses collectors, and NYC residents.
Bombas Merino Wool Blend Everyday Compression Knee High Socks

There's a high likelihood that your giftee already owns a pair of Bombas slippers or ankle socks. But the brand also offers compression socks that are perfect for the frequent flyer or avid hiker. And for an extra-luxurious touch, the merino wool options are extra comfy and warm.
MacKenzie-Childs Mocha Check Electric Salt & Pepper Grinder Set

Who doesn't love fancy salt and pepper shakers? These electric grinders from stylish hand-painted ceramics brand MacKenzie-Childs are an incredibly chic option to gift. Order and of the four checkered colorways to fit your giftee's space, then sit back, relax, and wait to receive shock and awe for the thoughtful present.
Ouai x Heaven Mayhem Fragrance Amulet Necklace

We can bet that even the woman who has everything doesn't have this new Heaven Mayhem necklace filled with Ouai perfume! The new collaboration consists of two vessel pendant designs and two fragrances (either warm and sensual Ibiza or floral & musky Rue St. Honoré) so that you can carry your favorite scent everywhere you go and reapply throughout the day in style.
LAnnodoMacrame Custom Hand Crank Photo Album

Especially when it comes to mothers and grandmothers, all they want is a simple, sentimental gift, like a photo album. But because you're trying to go above and beyond to impress them, consider this Etsy find, which is essentially a rolodex of your giftee's favorite memories and people. Customize the wood type, engraving, and number of photos you want, then send over a Google Photos link to the Etsy shop and they'll take care of the rest.
Miko Nest Towel Warmer with Aromatherapy

Upgrade something as simple as stepping out of the shower with a towel warmer for a not-so-expensive, spa-like environment. This bin can fit multiple towels or robes at a time, has adjustable timer and temperature settings, and releases a calming aromatherapy scent.
Big Night Aperitivo Spoons Set

For the hostess with the mostess or the girl dinner aficionado, check out Big Night's vibrant assortment of cutlery and serveware. This reusable tin set features three artsy spoons for scooping, smearing, and stirring. If you have an over-$50 budget, we also love the Snack Spreaders mini knives for a complete set perfect for charcuterie boards.
Checked Compression PackAway Closet

Travelers may not need another packing cube set, but they will appreciate a checked luggage organizer that holds their belongings and easily transforms into a hanging closet. The shelves and compartments help neatly organize an entire vacation wardrobe. Then just hook it into any hotel room to effortlessly see and pull your outfits without completely unpacking.
Granado Best-Sellers Perfume Suitcase

If you have a person on your list who loves experimenting with new fragrances or one who asks for a refill of their favorite scent year after year, go for something more unpredictable this time around. Brazilian brand Granado's tropical scents are a personal favorite (I'm still wearing the banana scent in the fall!). But if they're new to the brand, consider a suitcase full of mini perfumes so they can test and figure out their favorites before purchasing a full size.
Camp Snap Transparent Screen-Free Digital Camera

It's time to get nostalgic with a Y2K-inspired, colorful, jelly-looking camera. These Camp Snap options are like a hybrid of a digital camera and a disposable camera. While there's no screen (so you can't ruminate over getting the perfect shot), you can then connect a cable to your phone to upload the slightly grainy, retro-looking photos. It's a great companion for parties, concerts, and travels.
Quince Mongolian Cashmere Ribbed Wrap

Known for its luxe and budget-friendly cashmere, Quince needs to be on your radar when shopping for the woman who has everything. We’re thinking out of the box for your hard-to-shop-for giftee with this chic and versatile cashmere wrap.
Abbode Embroidered Dog Mom Small Croc Pouch

Abbode is a one-stop shop for the cutest and chicest personalized gifts. While there are so many styles to pick from, we've been eyeing this pouch for the dog moms in your life. This design can be personalized with several dog icons and text and used for everyday essentials, cosmetics, or travel must-haves so that your four-legged friend is never too far.

The woman who’s constantly traveling for work trips or vacations will appreciate this top-rated portable iron. The compact design — which comes in several cheerful colorways — quickly presses, steams, and irons six different fabric types, making it a practical, must-pack item.
Urban Outfitters Swan Shaped Metal Ring Holder

Sometimes we just need an unexpected design on an everyday essential, like a jewelry holder, to put a smile on our faces and make our daily routines a little less mundane. We can picture this swan ring holder, which can also hold stud earrings, elegantly perched on a bedside table or by a kitchen or bathroom sink to store rings while washing up.
Bobbi Brown x The Met Holiday-Exclusive Luxe Lipstick

Whether she's into makeup, art, or both since they often overlap, consider something from this new collaboration from Bobbi Brown and The Met. The festive holiday shades and whimsical packaging make everything — from the limited-edition eyeshadow palettes and the powder blushes to the creamy lipsticks — swoon- and gift-worthy.
Devyn Samara My Favorite Book Keepsake Necklace

You really can't go wrong with any gifts from Uncommon Goods, but these book locket necklaces stood out, especially if you're shopping for an avid reader. If you can't come up with a new book recommendation, consider this necklace, which highlights one of your giftee's favorite classic books, like Pride & Prejudice or The Great Gatsby.
Pura 12-Day Advent Calendar

While you may love carting up seasonal candles for yourself, we promise that the hard-to-shop-for woman in your life doesn't want another one. Instead, check out this unique advent calendar, which includes a Pura fragrance diffuser with 12 fragrances to unbox and try throughout the year. Then, she can keep the diffuser and re-stock her favorite scents to fill her space.
PalmRidge Custom Handcrafted Aluminum Matchbox Holder

At this point, you may have seen these custom matchboxes across many TikTok gift guides, and they're just so good that we had to include them here too! Pick from various embossed design options like cherries and butterflies or custom names and birth years. These are a sweet and unique gift (especially during the widespread matchbook obsession) to have lying around the house.

items.title: This Is What 2027 Will Smell Like, Based On Your Star Sign
items.description: All products featured on Refinery29 are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links.
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa
paragraphs: All products featured on Refinery29 are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links.

The leaves are changing color, matcha lattes are being enjoyed hot, and sweaters are coming out of retirement. Yes, fall is officially here — and as we enter the -ber months, we can’t help but get a little nostalgic as the year winds down. As any frag-head knows, scent and nostalgia are deeply connected, making this the perfect time to refresh your perfume wardrobe for a new season and an even newer year. (2027, you aren’t ready for us.)

In the season-one finale of Nose Dive, host Asia Grant sits down with celebrity astrologer and Astrolotea podcast host Aliza Kelly to discuss all things scent and stars, including what 2027 has in store for you, according to your zodiac sign. Think of it as your cosmic guide to finding a fragrance that feels written in the stars.

“Astrology is about embodiment [and] celebrating yourself. It’s about building confidence, knowing what makes you special, and understanding other people,” Kelly says. And what better way to celebrate your unique self than with a signature scent? Grant and Kelly kick things off with the fire signs — Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius — and the notes that best capture their bold, passionate energy. “This is giving something that’s pretty, spicy, and warm,” says Grant, who gravitates toward notes like incense, leather, and ginger. Ylang-ylang also makes the cut: “Something about it is so ’90s perfume coded. It feels very solar and fiery to me.”

Next up are the earth signs — Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn — whose grounded, no-nonsense energy calls for equally distinctive notes. “There’s like a control and unyieldingness,” Grant says. Think bold, specific scents with a strong point of view. For her, that means vetiver. Kelly is very much in agreement, noting, “It’s because it’s such a straightforward note. What you see is what you get. Yes. It’s like there’s not really that much wiggle room with a vetiver.” Translation: If you’re an earth sign, your fragrance doesn’t need to do the most to make an impression.

Then come the air signs — Aquarius, Gemini, and Libra — the zodiac’s more whimsical, cerebral bunch. Grant, a double Aquarius, gushes about one of her all-time favorite notes: jasmine. “But it is the scent that is a little itty-bitty cute white little flower. So intense, almost narcotic-like, goes into your nose, passages into your brain and, like, sticks there to the point where you can’t think about anything else.” In other words, never underestimate the power of a tiny flower with main-character energy.

Last but not least, the water signs — Pisces, Scorpio, and Cancer — bring a more intuitive, emotional sensibility to the fragrance conversation. Amber is one standout, with Kelly describing it as “very soft, plush, warm, cozy.” It’s an enveloping kind of scent, perfect for anyone who wants their fragrance to feel less like an accessory and more like a comforting second skin.

Of course, the stars aren’t the only inspiration behind this episode. Throughout the conversation, Grant and Kelly also explore the EOS holiday collection, which features three brand-new, highly giftable scents. Kelly even offers a fragrance forecast for each one, sharing what their signature notes might have in store for the year ahead.

First up is Cotton Candy Fleur, with notes of strawberry spun sugar, orange blossom, magnolia, patchouli, and midnight woods. Its forecast? Creativity. “This smells like creativity,” Kelly predicts. “This is for budding artists in 2027. This is for songwriters, musicians, people who want to be seen and heard.” Consider it a little olfactory inspiration for anyone ready to put their ideas out into the world.

Next, there’s Cozy Comfort, a plush blend of sueded vanilla, creamy amaretto, sheer skin-like musk, and mahogany woods. Its power word is romance. “It’s giving really nice faux fur blanket, like wrapped up nuzzling. It’s giving engagement. Under the tree,” Kelly says. Whether you’re manifesting a holiday proposal or simply craving a little more softness in your life, this scent is all about leaning into love.

Finally, Frosted Plum & Amber is what we can only imagine the Nutcracker’s Sugar Plum Fairy smells like. But beyond its festive sweetness, Kelly sees a scent synonymous with abundance and knowing your worth. “She knows her worth and is not afraid to walk away from a bad negotiation because she knows she’s valuable. And then everyone on the other side of the table is like, ‘Well, give her whatever she wants.’” Honestly, that’s the kind of energy we’re bringing into 2027.

Whether you’re looking to find your zodiac’s signature notes, manifest a little romance, or channel your most confident self in the new year, this Nose Dive finale makes a compelling case for letting fragrance be part of the ritual. After all, the right scent doesn’t just smell good — it can help you step into the version of yourself you’re ready to become.

items.title: The ethics of having a good time at Disney World, Florida | Psyche Ideas
items.description: The sun has set on Orlando, Florida, the theme-park capital of the world. Inside one of those parks, Walt Disney World’s EPCOT, thousands of visitors make their way toward a manmade lagoon surrounded by pavilions representing cultures and histories from around
items.author: Adam Kadlac
paragraphs: The sun has set on Orlando, Florida, the theme-park capital of the world. Inside one of those parks, Walt Disney World’s EPCOT, thousands of visitors make their way toward a manmade lagoon surrounded by pavilions representing cultures and histories from around the world. Of the many times that I have visited Disney World with my family, some of my favourite moments have come at this point in our trip, while we prepare for EPCOT’s fireworks display to begin. My daughter is generally sitting in her mobility chair as the rest of the family debriefs about the day’s activities, our legs tired from all the time we’ve spent on our feet. The temperature has usually cooled off a bit, and the collective nature of the experience is palpable. Around us, families and groups of friends are huddled together, anticipating the start of the show.
As lights begin to flash around the water, an opening narration sets the tone for what’s to come:

Everyone on this Earth is part of the great Symphony of Us. Each of us a unique instrument playing harmony to one another. And even though we are all playing different parts, it’s our unified heartbeat that connects us, reminding us that we are more alike than we are different. A rhapsody of rhythms that unites us and connects us through commonalities of the heart.

It’s high-minded, sentimental stuff for a theme park with rides featuring a talking snowman and a rat who becomes a chef. But at a time of rising scepticism about multiculturalism and universal values, it’s also a message that has come to resonate with me.

Like many families, we have formed meaningful memories at Disney World because of the entertainment-rich environment the Disney company has created. Its theme parks are enjoyable, in part, because they appeal to each member of my family. But our Disney memories are also meaningful because Disney World reflects my values: this is a place that is ostensibly committed to the idea that we are all, in some sense, citizens of the world bound together by a common humanity. It’s a simple ideal. But it’s one I believe in deeply and strive to embody, however imperfectly, in my life.

Of course, as a philosopher, I’m also keenly aware that all the experiences that have led to these moments at Disney World have been sold to me by a massive global corporation that strives to maximise its profits. Whether the Walt Disney Company genuinely believes in the cosmopolitan values it promotes is largely beside the point. What matters is whether portraying those values is a good business strategy. Disney is also a corporation that has received more than its share of criticism throughout its history. It has been criticised for its labour practices, for the cultural themes in its films, for the stands it takes (or does not take) on controversial public issues and, sometimes, simply for being a massive global corporation that strives to maximise its profits. This tension regularly leaves me puzzled. Is the value of my experience at Disney World undermined by the fact that it is, at the end of the day, a production of the Walt Disney Company? Can I trust a profit-hungry corporation to teach my children universal values? And does Disney’s message need to be sincere for it to really matter?

These sorts of questions are certainly not unique to Disney theme parks. In his book The Affluent Society (1958), the economist John Kenneth Galbraith coined the term ‘the dependence effect’ to characterise the process by which a business creates the desires that it seeks to satisfy. For example, you might not have wanted to buy a new sweater, but seeing a commercial on television makes you dissatisfied with your current wardrobe such that you hop online and order a new one. It likely never occurred to you to try iced tea with vodka until you saw the beverage advertised in a magazine, but now you find yourself on the way to the corner store to buy a six-pack. And Disney obviously wants to manufacture the desire to visit its theme parks because it will make money from everyone who wants to satisfy their newfound urge to ride Frozen Ever After and take pictures of their kids with Mickey and Minnie. For Galbraith, the dependence effect is problematic because it gives too much control over our lives to people who simply want to make money.

While contemporary critics of Disney might echo these concerns, the problem becomes more acute when the corporation in question has behaved poorly in other ways. The Walt Disney Company has long been the target of labour activists who criticise how Disney treats its employees. In 2024, unionised workers at Disneyland authorised a strike in contract negotiations where they argued that 73 per cent of their employees didn’t make enough money to cover basic living expenses, despite often working 12- to 14-hour days. That strike was ultimately averted, but it stands in a long line of labour controversies dating back to an animators’ strike in 1941, through protests about working conditions in the factories that produce Disney products, and most recently a series of layoffs across the company earlier this year.
There is a sense of something shared, however briefly and however manufactured, that I don’t find in many other places
Disney also has a decidedly mixed record on cultural issues. Writing in The Guardian in 2021, the journalist Steve Rose noted that:

Disney’s history of racist caricatures and ethnic stereotyping has been well documented and routinely criticised: the crows in Dumbo that drew on racist minstrel caricatures of African Americans; the Islamophobic tropes in Aladdin; the mockery of Native Americans in Peter Pan… the list goes on.
And its portrayals of women haven’t fared much better. As the media scholar Janet Wasko writes in her book Understanding Disney (2001):

Disney heroines are always beautiful, shapely, and often sexually attractive, while female villains are typically ugly and either extremely thin (Cruella) or grossly fat (Ursula), thus perpetuating norms of physical beauty prevalent in mainstream American culture.

Even this partial list of Disney’s foibles is enough to challenge the idea that it is a company deeply committed to the sort of cosmopolitan values that I’ve come to associate with its theme parks. And coupled with Galbraith’s more fundamental concerns about the dependence effect, the case for abandoning Disney World certainly can’t be dismissed out of hand.

In my mind, I try to balance these concerns with my experiences. There’s my daughter beside me on It’s a Small World, her eyes wide as she looks at all the animatronics moving to the attraction’s iconic song. There are the conversations I have with my son as we analyse a new ride or (just as likely) one we have ridden multiple times before. There are the various shows, parades and fireworks displays, all of which offer opportunities to feel part of something larger than oneself. There is a sense of something shared, however briefly and however manufactured, that I don’t find in many other places. And there is the belief that all of it is shaped by values that I wholeheartedly endorse.
But these experiences come with some trepidation. There is something undeniably risky about entrusting something of such value to a corporation whose track record is, at best, mixed.

While Disney sceptics might quickly dismiss that value as trivial, I think they are wrong to do so. My daughter is intellectually disabled, and there are not a lot of places where everyone in my family can enjoy a day on their own terms. When my kids were growing up, activities that might appeal to my daughter wouldn’t really interest my son. Some of this discrepancy was just a function of their age difference but, as they got older, their developmental trajectories also played a role. My daughter is 19 now, and the gap between what she and her brother want from a vacation has only widened. Moreover, while being a good parent may often require that adults sacrifice their own enjoyment for the benefit of their children, it is a sacrifice, nonetheless. Playing on monkey bars at the playground as a kid is a lot more fun than watching kids play on monkey bars as an adult. Finding activities that appeal to everyone in the family is a challenge, even when disability is left out of the equation.

A couple of years ago, we took a trip out west, visiting Las Vegas and some national parks on the way to southern California. Taken as a whole, it was an amazing vacation. However, the natural beauty of the Grand Canyon was somewhat lost on our daughter who is limited in her ability to hike long distances or navigate uneven terrain. The lights of Vegas were interesting enough for everyone, but full-blown family entertainment is not exactly the city’s calling card. When we finally made our first visit to Disneyland (having previously been to Disney’s parks only in Florida), everyone was able to engage. This didn’t necessarily make Disneyland the high point of our trip (for me, at least, that was the day we spent at Arches National Park) but it did highlight the fact that the universalistic design of Disney parks is central to their appeal.
What matters is not so much where our desires come from but whether the satisfaction of those desires makes our lives better

For example, there are numerous attractions throughout Disney theme parks that are thoroughly engaging for adults without being overwhelming for children. The Haunted Mansion is more bemusing than genuinely scary, and Pirates of the Caribbean gives everyone plenty of details to occupy their attention. Live shows, such as Festival of the Lion King, connect viewers to the artistry of Disney’s films in immersive and often interactive ways. If you haven’t seen any of the Star Wars or Avatar movies, you can still love every minute of the attractions they inspired. And even if someone in the family isn’t quite ready for rollercoasters like Space Mountain, there are plenty of tamer options on offer, ranging from boat rides like It’s a Small World and Jungle Cruise to the slightly more adventurous Seven Dwarfs Mine Train or Big Thunder Mountain Railroad. Every minute of every day might not be equally enjoyable for everyone, but visits to Disney World consistently leave a mark on our family that we have found difficult to replicate.
So, does it matter that these experiences are offered to us by a profit-seeking corporation?

In his response to Galbraith, the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek questions whether consumers should worry about the dependence effect. For Hayek, what matters is not so much where our desires come from but whether the satisfaction of those desires makes our lives better. He is an unlikely ally to reach for in defence of a place built on shared feeling and common humanity – Hayek spent much of his career warning against the kind of collective sentiment EPCOT is selling. And while I don’t generally align myself with Hayek’s libertarian views, I’ve come to think he’s probably right on this point. The same company that gave us decades of flattened stereotypes in its films also built a place where my son and daughter can spend a day on roughly equal terms. And in so doing, it gave us memories that largely stand apart from the commercial context in which they were created.

To be sure, the value of these experiences does not redeem Disney’s labour practices or its other missteps as a corporation. If anything, it gives Disney fans even more reason to challenge the company to live up to the ideals it portrays in its parks. Perhaps it also demonstrates that the value an experience has for people doesn’t require pure intentions on the part of those who create it. We are all something of a mixed bag, whether we are part of the crowd watching fireworks around the World Showcase Lagoon or part of the staff working in the offices of Disney’s corporate headquarters. And at a time when it can be difficult to feel connected to our fellow human beings, I think it’s OK to be thankful for whatever aspirational moments we might be able to grab, no matter how they might come to us.
