items.title: The Leather Daddy’s War Over Tom of Finland
items.description: For four decades, the Tom of Finland Foundation was headquartered in a 1911 craftsman house in the Echo Park neighborhood of Los Angeles that is stuffed with the artist’s illustrations of leather-uniformed men flashing rippling chests and throbbing bulges. The
items.author: Michael Waters
paragraphs: For four decades, the Tom of Finland Foundation was headquartered in a 1911 craftsman house in the Echo Park neighborhood of Los Angeles that is stuffed with the artist’s illustrations of leather-uniformed men flashing rippling chests and throbbing bulges. The work of other erotic artists lines the walls, and the ceilings are covered with frescoes of nude angels exchanging oral sex. A library holds thousands of vintage gay magazines such as Drummer and Honcho, and in the backyard is the Pleasure Park, a cruising ground and sculpture garden that has its own swing. “You could not possibly count the number of dicks on display,” says Carta Monir, who lived there as part of the foundation’s artist-in-residency program. “As a trans woman, I was very ready for it to be a very gender-essentialist experience. And it was wonderful. No weirdness; no discomfort. Incredibly welcoming. Durk gave us the first tour, actually.”

Durk is Durk Dehner, who bought the house in 1979 with his boyfriend, ex-boyfriend, and ex-boyfriend’s boyfriend. He met Tom of Finland in the late 1970s, and, for a time, they had a sexual relationship; mostly they were friends. Whenever Tom came to America, he stayed in a room on the third floor, sometimes for six months at a time. He and Dehner went into business together, first through a business partnership that split the revenues from licensing Tom’s imagery into Tom of Finland-branded products, and later by forming the Tom of Finland Foundation to oversee his work and papers. After Tom’s death in 1991, control of the foundation passed to Dehner, who ran it as a scrappy community hub, offering beds to artists and other castaways at the height of the AIDS epidemic.

Dehner convinced the German publisher Taschen to print several books of Tom of Finland’s work, got the government of Finland to put Tom of Finland on its official stamps, and, in addition to thousands of Tom originals, amassed a collection of queer erotic art spanning 6,000 works by over 800 gay artists, including Robert Mapplethorpe, Jean Cocteau, Bruce Weber, George Quaintance, and Michael Kirwan, whose ashes were planted at the base of a citrus tree in the backyard of his house. In all, the collection is estimated to be worth at least $40 million. Now 77, Dehner sees promoting Tom’s work as his life’s mission. “I was the tool for a gift, and the gift was Tom of Finland, and I wanted him to utilize me,” he says.

Then, last year, Dehner was pushed to resign as president of the foundation and to give up his seat on the board of directors. He had always been more of a public face than a traditional nonprofit director — the foundation, which never had more than a few hundred thousand dollars in assets, spent more money than it took in for three years in a row starting in 2021. But the reason for the dismissal was a recent photo Dehner had submitted as part of an application to judge an International Mr. Leather contest that featured him wearing a leather S.S. hat. He maintains the outfit was fetish-wear, not an act of hate speech. “My own board threw me under the bus, and didn’t give me a chance for any rebuttal, and that was unfair and not democratic,” he says. “But the way cancel culture works is that it isn’t democratic. It’s just: Off with your head.”

With his partner S.R. Sharp, who was then vice-president of the foundation, Dehner recruited new board members he hoped would be sympathetic to his cause. But the effort didn’t work out as planned. The new board members, a group of New Yorkers with limited nonprofit experience, encountered what they perceived as a mismanaged organization and seized control in order to course-correct. This past summer, they stopped paying rent on the house, fired most of the staff, and filed a complaint with the attorney general of California accusing Dehner of collecting royalties they said belonged to the foundation.

Dehner, who denies the charge, fired back with a website, Save Tom House, calling for the board’s ouster. The campaign has found favor among former artists-in-residence and employees, who have taken their grievances to social media. “It was almost like a private equity firm came in and just wanted to pick off all the social cachet and use the brand and use our resources for their own social gain,” says Craig Pratt, who worked part-time at the foundation last year.

The dispute between the board and the longtime caretaker has left the foundation on the brink of collapse and the original work of a seminal gay artist hidden from public view in a storage facility in downtown Los Angeles. The board of directors continues to fundraise as it looks for a permanent home for the nonprofit. For Dehner, who is at work on a book about his life with Tom, regaining control of the organization he cofounded is a deeply personal crusade. “This house has a kind of spirit that is very special, and when people come here for events, they feel it and they actually contribute to it. It really is about them feeling that they can be themselves, they can be anyone they want to be, and it’s okay here,” he says. “Tom House is not just a building. It’s an organic energy source.”

Tom of Finland, whose given name was Touko Valio Laaksonen, started composing erotic sketches of soldiers after he was drafted into the Finnish Army in 1940. He published his work pseudonymously, originally in American beefcake magazines such as Physique Pictorial, where publisher Bob Mizer gave him the cheeky nickname “Tom of Finland.” Reproductions of Tom’s sketches came to paper the walls of gay nightclubs and bars across the U.S. and Europe, and by the end of the century he had, through word of mouth, become the world’s most commercially successful gay erotic artist, influencing the designs of Jean Paul Gaultier and Tom Ford, and attracting admirers such as Mapplethorpe and the artists Mike Kelley and Catherine Opie.

In 1976, Dehner, a part-time model and waiter, spotted a flyer with one of Tom’s sketches at the Spike bar, a gay leather bar in Chelsea. The illustration was part of an ad for a bike run — a bar crawl for gay motorcyclists — and Dehner was captivated by the image, a visual of a shirtless man in black leather pants, his bulge almost comically engorged. The next day, a friend told him the artist’s name and shared his home address in Finland. Dehner and Tom began a correspondence and, a year later, when Tom was planning a trip to America, “I begged him to let me be his host,” Dehner says. Tom accepted.

The business they started together would eventually get Tom of Finland’s horny leather daddies plastered on bookends, mugs, tank tops, candles, shot glasses, jockstraps, and even clothes by high-end fashion labels such as JW Anderson and Diesel. After Tom’s death, Dehner raised money from gift-shop sales, donations, and rent from the artist-in-residence program, which charged fellows $690 a month in exchange for living accommodations. By 2023, his annual salary was $34,068. He also earned roughly $30,000 in rent payments from the foundation and between $10,000 and $30,000 in royalties from licensing Tom’s work.

For years, the board of directors was made up of a hodgepodge of Dehner’s friends and acquaintances: There was the Off-Broadway playwright Dan Berkowitz and the artist Cliff Benjamin; there was also an airline customer-service agent named Carl Porrino, whom Dehner said he “met on social media.” Sharp has served on the board off and on since the late 1990s. “I had to have some type of personal connection with the person,” Dehner says of the board members and employees he brought on.

The organization’s staff never amounted to more than six people, and the foundation budget was always below $1 million — often well below. Many of those who passed through the house spoke fondly of their experience. José Tinoco, who started volunteering at the foundation in 2019 before taking a full-time job there, often went to Dehner and Sharp for advice about dating and sex; on his 21st birthday, before a night out at the the Eagle, Dehner and Sharp gifted him a pair of leather motorcycle pants and a leather wrist cuff. “They walked me down the stairs like I was going to prom,” Tinoco says. Monir once invited a photographer over who was interested in working with her. She walked naked around the house, posing for photos while staffers and volunteers worked. “People were making lunch, and there was some kind of business meeting going on, and nobody even blinked,” she says. “That’s just the kind of environment it is.”

Others were less enthused by Tom House’s freewheeling spirit. When Dana Bramble, who was in charge of fundraising for the foundation, showed up for her first day of work, she was led to her desk in a corner of the attic. At one point, an older man in a bathrobe ducked into a crawl space beside her and disappeared behind a pair of white vertical blinds. Bramble was alarmed when he didn’t come out for hours and appeared to be napping. It was only a day later, when she asked a colleague who he was, that she discovered his name was Loyalty and that he lived there, in the four-foot-high crawl space by her desk.

Even Dehner’s supporters admit the house had seen better days. On hot days, they would huddle around a single ratty air conditioner in the attic. For a time, the ceiling leaked when it rained and bees took up residence in two hives at the house. A stale odor of cigarette smoke seemed to permeate every room. Meetings with the executive director took place in the bedroom where Tom died, which Dehner preserved intact, leather jackets, Finnish military uniform, awards, trophies, posters, and belt buckles all in their place. “I have to tell you, there’s something weird about being called into your boss’s office and there’s a bed between the two of you that a man died in,” says Pratt. “It was gay Gray Gardens, run by men who are stuck living in yesteryear.”

Around 2021, the board chairman Rob Hennig, an employment lawyer, told Dehner it was time to let a nonprofit professional take the helm. Hennig hired a consultant, who concluded the foundation also needed to offer some basic human resources benefits, like giving employees sick days. “Before then, I can’t say that we were adhering to all of the rules within California best practices,” Dehner says. Eventually, the board selected its treasurer, Edward Cella — an architectural historian who had worked across the nonprofit sector — to become chief executive. One of his first decisions was to move the foundation and its vast holdings out of the house in Echo Park.

For years, pieces from the world’s largest gay erotic art collection were hung in Dehner’s living room, which was neither temperature-controlled nor protected: The front door was often unlocked. The rest — fine artworks, framed sketches, and sculptures from Tom and other artists — was stored in a free-standing, air-conditioned POD in the driveway. Tom’s unframed illustrations, sketches, gauche paintings, letters and journals, VHSes, DVDs, photo negatives, and scrapbooks of magazine clippings are held in two giant bank safes in a converted garage. Though outside consultants had strongly encouraged better long-term storage, Dehner resisted the move, fearing he would lose access to Tom’s work.

Then, in January 2025, an Instagram user by the name Pup Diego Onyx surfaced a headshot of Dehner wearing the leather Nazi hat. The costume is common in leather fetish culture, which attempts to appropriate and eroticize symbols of hate and violence, but Dehner says Cella used the incident as an excuse to oust him from the board. “Edward really did not like me, and so when I had that social canceling situation, they just jumped on the opportunity,” says Dehner, insisting that, across two to three decades of wearing the hat to fetish events, no one had ever told him the outfit was offensive. It was an erotic outfit, not a political one, he says. “I didn’t even pay attention when I sent the photograph in.” For Cella, Dehner’s actions fit a pattern. “I’ve known this organization since 2013,” he wrote in a statement. “Durk has pushed out those board members, employees, and friends who questioned his authority or his decision-making about key aspects of the organization.”

Cast out of the foundation he’d spent his life building, Dehner was in a strange position. The organization remained headquartered at his home, and he continued to have lunch with staff. But he was excluded from meetings. “They wanted me gone, so in order to prevent them from having control over decisions, we brought on different people,” he says, referring to Sharp, his partner. Among the recruits were Brooke Wise, an independent curator who had helped plan shows for the foundation; Terence McFarland, who had previously worked at the theater nonprofit Los Angeles Performance Practice; David Aldea, a former Soho House executive perhaps best known for being Taylor Swift’s landlord when she lived on Cornelia Street in New York; and Robert Knox Hayes, a 37-year-old banker and financial adviser.

Hayes became involved in 2024 after meeting a foundation staff member at Aspen Gay Ski Week. He toured the house with Dehner soon after — his first time in Los Angeles — and was electrified by what he saw. “It feels like Tom is still there in the room with you,” he says. Dehner and Sharp, meanwhile, “felt like my gay grandparents.” Hayes was reaching the end of his term on the board of Equality New York, and he wanted to be part of an organization that could get him closer to the art world. “I didn’t want to be a finance guy, and I don’t want to be known as a finance guy,” he says. After joining, Hayes recruited Nolan Feng, a tech entrepreneur, which brought the total number of board members to nine, six of whom Dehner perceived as his allies. “I think Durk has always believed that we were going to put him back in the president position on the board,” Hayes says.

In July 2025, the new board voted not to renew Cella’s one-year contract. It was unanimous only because Hennig and another board member abstained, and a third resigned during the meeting. Aldea was announced as the interim executive director and, a month later, Hayes was appointed board chair. Besides a course they each had taken at the Aspen Institute for new directors of nonprofits, neither man had much professional experience in the field. The new board members set out to raise money for the foundation, which had only $69,312 in the bank at the start of the year.

Goals were modest. On the foundation’s website, five tiers of membership support were offered, from a $30-a-year “eNews subscription” to a $1,000-a-year package that includes a T-shirt and a house tour. The group had an eye for a glamorous party, but they were less savvy at actually making money from one. In December, a benefit at the design studio Apparatus in New York raised $12,000, but spent $10,000 on catering. For an event in Paris last month, the board secured $75,000 in sponsorship from the website PornHub; after expenses, it is expected to leave the foundation with “a surplus of several thousand dollars,” Wise wrote in an email earlier this month. Over the last two years, she continued, the board has raised hundreds of thousands of dollars. “I personally raised $95,000 over the last 60 days,” she says.

The board members are themselves not frequent donors, which has led to complaints from staff. “These social climbers from New York were really just doing nothing but stripping the foundation and the brand of its social value, and using that to parlay into parties that really turned into nothing,” Pratt says. Hayes has only given $1,000 since joining the board in 2024. “I’m a young professional, and I don’t come from a rich family,” he says.

The relationship with Dehner began to unravel in March when Hayes discovered what he considered an inconsistency in the legal arrangements around Tom of Finland’s work. Dehner had personally collected 50 percent of the licensing royalties, per the terms of a 1984 partnership agreement with the artist; the rest went to the foundation. In his 1991 will, Tom passed his 50 percent share down to Dehner in writing. But the will named their company as “Tom of Finland Inc.,” a business that didn’t technically exist yet. The two had set up a “doing business as” agreement under this name in Los Angeles County, but not as a formal company. Dehner wouldn’t register the company officially until 1994.

The new board interpreted this gap to mean that all of Tom’s licensing royalty belonged to the foundation, not to Dehner personally, and accused him of enriching himself with foundation assets. Hayes also claimed that a 2024 memo of understanding, which was intended to resolve the decades of legal and financial murkiness and to formally grant Dehner his 50 percent personal cut of all licensing royalties, was not valid because the board did not vote on it. (Dehner and Sharp maintain that the previous board actually had approved of the memo.) Hayes set up a meeting with Dehner to resolve the issue and extended an olive branch: Dehner could loan the 18 pieces of Tom’s art he personally owned—mostly, photos and sketches of Dehner himself—to the foundation in exchange for a fee. Dehner refused. “Pretty much after that, Durk and I stopped speaking,” Hayes says.

More sobering news arrived in May when Hayes got an assessment that the foundation was projected to spend around $250,000 over the next year in legal fees, a catastrophic obligation it could not afford. Much of the expense was attributed to a 2023 lawsuit Dehner filed against CultureEdit, a retail store he had hired to license Tom of Finland’s work for T-shirts, muscle shirts, and action figures. Dehner claimed the store owed hundreds of thousands of dollars in royalty payments. CultureEdit countersued, alleging the foundation had, among other things, cut the store out of deals it had negotiated. (Neither suit has been resolved.) “When we realized the dollar amount of those legal expenses, it just hit a point of like, enough is enough,” Hayes says.

The foundation stopped paying rent to Dehner and made plans to lay off most of the staff, which it did in June over a Zoom call. Catalina Bulgach, an archivist who had just finished several months of work cataloging all 1,722 pieces of Tom’s art, was asked to spend her last two weeks helping to move the collection to the offsite storage facility Crozier Fine Arts. That is where the artwork remains today. Hayes hopes to make it available to the public and to researchers again by digitizing it, a costly process, and potentially by donating it to an existing queer archive, such as the ONE Archives at the University of Southern California. “I understand it’s an emotional and painful process to have it move, but it was just very clear that we needed to do this, and it was in the best interest of Tom’s legacy,” Hayes says. He insists the board wants to reestablish a physical home for the Tom of Finland Foundation in Los Angeles, even if it’s not yet clear what form that will take. “What we’re trying to do is strengthen the foundation and make Tom’s legacy global, and we tried to do that while respecting Los Angeles and the house,” he says.

In August, after the board formally filed the complaint with the attorney general of California, Dehner wrote to friends informing them that the situation with the board “has deteriorated such that there is no longer any communication between me and the Foundation.” Tom’s papers — and the foundation’s collection of Kirwan, Cocteau, and Mapplethorpe — remain at the house in Echo Park, where Dehner still hosts artists despite the board’s cancellation of the artist-in-residency program. They pay him rent and plan on showing their work there in the coming months.

Tom House is quiet these days. There are no regular tours and the one remaining full-time staff member, the social media manager, works remotely. No one’s cruising the Pleasure Park anymore. Dehner and Sharp still live in the master bedroom on the second floor, and Loyalty is in his crawl space. When we spoke in October, Dehner was plugging away on his book about Tom, though he was reluctant to share the title because he was afraid someone would steal it. Even if he isn’t able to wrest back control of the foundation from the board, he plans to partner with other nonprofits to continue programming. He’s not retiring or going anywhere, that much is certain. He tells me that Tom, right before he died, warned him that running the foundation might take a toll. “If it gets too difficult, just walk away,” Tom advised. Dehner disagreed. “I’ve been through turbulent times here before. I could never walk away,” he says.

items.title: Democrats Must Probe Trump Corruption With Purpose
items.description: During a week of Democratic triumph and exultation, the only point of internal dissension was the battle among party members to out-hyperbolize one another on their newfound power to launch congressional probes. Representative Analilia Mejia vowed, “We’re goin
items.author: Elie Honig
paragraphs: During a week of Democratic triumph and exultation, the only point of internal dissension was the battle among party members to out-hyperbolize one another on their newfound power to launch congressional probes. Representative Analilia Mejia vowed, “We’re going to toss out subpoenas like Mardi Gras beads.” Senator Ed Markey boasted, “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.” Representative Robert Garcia, who will chair the House Oversight Committee, issued a two-word official statement: “Lawyer up.”

It’s good advice. Donald Trump and his supporting cast will delay and resist, of course, especially given the installment of the chromosomally bellicose Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff. And there are practical limits to what any congressional committee can accomplish. But the political landscape has shifted, and now Democrats, if they act strategically and quickly, stand poised to challenge and expose the worst abuses of the Trump administration. Elections have consequences.

These past two years, the Republican-led Congress has run wild with congressional oversight, hearings, and subpoenas. Investigators have compelled testimony from a MAGA wish list of purported enemies of the state: Jack Smith and members of his prosecutorial team, senior aides to Joe and Jill Biden, Dr. Anthony Fauci, Bill and Hillary Clinton. Little of substance came from these circus acts, which mostly provided drab anticlimaxes to long forgotten or laughably trivial causes.

But now the voters have spoken and the tables have turned. Democrats will take the gavel, and they’re ready to rip. Garcia immediately laid out his investigative priorities, starting with the “Trump crime family”: payments by a Russian oligarch for Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding, Jared Kushner’s private equity company and its receipt of $2 billion in Saudi investments, and Eric Trump’s position on the board of a company that won a massive Pentagon Defense contract. With sycophantic Attorney General Todd Blanche willfully averting his gaze, no government entity has even begun to explore this serial self-dealing. That’ll change soon. (Blanche has, however, shrieked about rhetoric from Democrats on impending investigations, vaguely suggesting that combative political talk might cross the line to criminality; either he knows he’s full of it, or he’s lost his mind.)

Garcia also vowed to probe the Department of Homeland Security’s immigration-enforcement tactics — singling out Miller for his role as “the architect of unconstitutional ICE raids” — and hold public hearings on the government’s Jeffrey Epstein investigation. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has pledged to investigate Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s management of the Department of Health and Human Services. Representative Jamie Raskin, who likely will chair the House Judiciary Committee, will examine the political weaponization of the Justice Department and the FBI. Representative Jared Hoffman has promised to scrutinize the White House ballroom and the president’s other prized construction projects. And Democrats reportedly are gearing up to interrogate Elon Musk and tech executives from Apple and Meta.

The Trump administration surely will resist, but there’s only so much their lawyers can do. Executive privilege — a legal protection for certain sensitive presidential communications — will be oft invoked but rarely successful.

Presidents since George Washington have claimed some variation of the prerogative. The courts have formally recognized the doctrine for the past half-century — ever since the Supreme Court in July 1974 agreed with Richard Nixon that executive privilege exists but found that it didn’t apply to his efforts to withhold White House recordings from Watergate prosecutors. (Nixon resigned two weeks later.)

But Trump has habitually overextended this privilege, leading to a series of precedent-shifting legal losses. The courts have in recent years rejected his invocations of it to avoid a criminal subpoena; to withhold documents from a congressional committee; and to block testimony by his advisers (including the vice-president) to Congress. Now, the president will reap his own litigious harvest, as the law has evolved to narrow the scope of executive privilege primarily through rulings in cases that Trump himself has chosen to pursue. And while the privilege can apply to the president and his advisers, it provides no relief to anyone outside government — Trump’s children or corporate CEOs or Musk, for example.

Regardless of its legal merits, count on the Trump administration to invoke executive privilege as a delay tactic. Complex constitutional litigation can take years, and that alone could be enough to run out the clock on the incoming 120th Congress.

Still, properly focused, the courts are capable of expediency. A dispute over Trump’s presidential records relating to January 6, for example, took just three months to be resolved, from the filing of a lawsuit in the district court in October 2021 to the final decision by the Supreme Court in January 2022. If the new Democratic Congress moves quickly and doesn’t let itself get bogged down in futile negotiations, and if the courts do their job with reasonable efficiency, then plenty of time should remain to resolve legal disputes and get on with the fact-finding.

Of course, subpoena recipients still might ultimately defy a court order, refuse to testify, and risk the consequences. If the House or Senate holds a witness in contempt, the matter gets referred to the Justice Department for potential prosecution. And Blanche surely will do nothing to prosecute anyone who ignores subpoenas from a Democratic Congress. But the statute of limitations for contempt of Congress is five years. So anyone who defies a congressional subpoena in 2027 or 2028 — banking on Trump’s DOJ to turn a blind eye — ought to remember that the next administration can still bring charges into the 2030s.

Even with last week’s seismic political reconfiguration, there are limits to what Democrats can accomplish. They won’t be able to legislate with Trump still holding the veto pen (though they’re now in position to negotiate, and they can send bills to his desk to force him to take politically fraught positions in opposition). Impeachment is possible in the House, but conviction and removal won’t happen in the Senate (which requires a two-thirds vote), and Democratic Party leaders have cautioned against the whole exercise.

But congressional oversight, and the accompanying subpoena power, will make a genuine, immediate impact. Trump and his political allies have expended hardly a thought on their excesses over the past two years, comfortable knowing there would be minimal accountability and no consequences. But now the era of scot-free malfeasance is over.

items.title: Susie Wiles Talks About the First Year of Trump’s Second Term (Part 1 of 2)
items.description: On the morning of November 4, 2025, an off-year Election Day, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles was meeting in the Oval Office with the president and his top advisers, men she calls her “core team”: Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio,
items.author: Chris Whipple; Christopher Anderson
paragraphs: On the morning of November 4, 2025, an off-year Election Day, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles was meeting in the Oval Office with the president and his top advisers, men she calls her “core team”: Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Stephen Miller, deputy chief of staff. The agenda was twofold: ending the congressional filibuster and forcing Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power. As she related it later, President Donald Trump was holding forth on the filibuster when Wiles stood up and started for the door. Trump eyed her. “Is this an emergency, that you have to leave?” he demanded. It was nothing of the sort—but Wiles left Trump guessing. She replied: “It’s an emergency. It doesn’t involve you.” With that, according to Wiles, she departed the Oval.
Click here to read Part 2 of 2 from Vanity Fair’s portfolio of Trump’s inner circle.

Wiles, wearing dark pants and a plain black leather top, met me in her office with a smile and a handshake. Over sandwiches from the White House Mess, we talked about the challenges Trump faces. Throughout the past year, Wiles and I have spoken regularly about almost everything: the contents, and consequences, of the Epstein files; ICE’s brutal mass deportations; Elon Musk’s evisceration of USAID; the controversial deployment of the National Guard to US cities; the demolition of the East Wing; the lethal strikes on boats allegedly being piloted by drug smugglers—acts many have called war crimes; Trump’s physical and mental health; and whether he will defy the 22nd Amendment and try to stay on for a third term.
Most senior White House officials parse their words and speak only on background. But over many on-the-record conversations, Wiles answered almost every question I put to her.

We often spoke on Sundays after church. Wiles, an Episcopalian, calls herself “Catholic lite.” One time we spoke while she was doing her laundry in her Washington, DC, rental. Trump, she told me, “has an alcoholic’s personality.” Vance’s conversion from Never Trumper to MAGA acolyte, she said, has been “sort of political.” The vice president, she added, has been “a conspiracy theorist for a decade.” Russell Vought, architect of the notorious Project 2025 and head of the Office of Management and Budget, is “a right-wing absolute zealot.” When I asked her what she thought of Musk reposting a tweet about public sector workers killing millions under Hitler, Stalin, and Mao, she replied: “I think that’s when he’s microdosing.” (She says she doesn't have first-hand knowledge.)
Wiles is the most powerful person in Trump’s White House other than the president himself; unlike any chief of staff before her, she is a woman.

“So many decisions of great consequence are being made on the whim of the president. And as far as I can tell, the only force that can direct or channel that whim is Susie,” a former Republican chief told me. “In most White Houses, the chief of staff is first among a bunch of equals. She may be first with no equals.”

“I don’t think there’s anybody in the world right now that could do the job that she’s doing,” Rubio told me. He called her bond with Trump “an earned trust.” Vance described Wiles’s approach to the chief’s job. “There is this idea that people have that I think was very common in the first administration,” he told me, “that their objective was to control the president or influence the president, or even manipulate the president because they had to in order to serve the national interest. Susie just takes the diametrically opposite viewpoint, which is that she’s a facilitator, that the American people have elected Donald Trump. And her job is to actually facilitate his vision and to make his vision come to life.”

It’s been a busy year. Trump and his team have expanded the limits of presidential power, unilaterally declared war on drug cartels, imposed tariffs according to whim, sealed the southern border, achieved a ceasefire and hostage release in Gaza, and pressured NATO allies into increasing their defense spending.

At the same time, Trump has waged war on his political enemies; pardoned the January 6 rioters, firing nearly everyone involved in their investigation and prosecution; sued media companies into multimillion-dollar settlements; indicted multiple government officials he perceives as his foes; and pressured universities to toe his line. He’s redefined the way presidents behave—verbally abusing women, minorities, and almost anyone who offends him. Charlie Kirk’s assassination in September turbocharged Trump’s campaign of revenge and retribution. Critics have compared this moment to a Reichstag fire, a modern version of Hitler’s exploitation of the torching of Berlin’s parliament.

Historically, the White House chief of staff is the president’s gatekeeper, confidant, and executor of his agenda. That often means telling the president hard truths. Upon taking office, Ronald Reagan was hell-bent on reforming Social Security. James A. Baker III explained to him that cutting Social Security benefits was the third rail of American politics. Reagan pivoted to tax cuts—and was ultimately reelected in a landslide. Donald Rumsfeld, Gerald Ford’s chief, explained: “The White House chief of staff is the one person besides his wife…who can look him right in the eye and say, ‘This is not right. You simply can’t go down that road.’ ”
Just how far will Trump veer off the guardrails of democracy?
The question around Wiles’s tenure under Trump has been whether she will do anything to restrain him. A better question: Does she want to?

Our first conversation took place little more than a week before the inauguration. Wiles called from the road, en route from Mar-a-Lago to her home in Ponte Vedra, Florida, in her BMW 530. She was in high spirits, basking in Trump’s victory. Not that she’d ever doubted the outcome. “At no point did I think we would not win,” she said. “Not in my core, not in my sleep, not in my rational mind.”

But on that January day, as his second inauguration approached, Wiles was determined to show the world a new Trump. “I told Hakeem Jeffries, ‘You will see a different Donald Trump when he gets there,’ ’’ she recounted to me. “I’ve not seen him throw anything, I’ve not seen him scream. I didn’t see that really horrible behavior that people talk about and that I actually experienced years ago.”

Wiles’s childhood had prepared her for difficult men. She was raised in Stamford, Connecticut, and Saddle River, New Jersey, the only daughter and eldest of three siblings. It was her famous father, Pat Summerall, who put Wiles on a path to the pinnacle of political power. Summerall had been a kicker for the New York Giants and afterward parlayed his knowledge and mellifluous baritone into fame and fortune as the “voice of the NFL.”

At her father’s knee, Susie Summerall became a football aficionado, rattling off win-loss records and player stats like a miniature John Madden—an ability she says Trump shares. “The president, it turns out, is a junkie of that and is like a statistical savant,” she said. “And I remember a lot of it.” As a child, Susie also absorbed the zeitgeist of her father’s 1970s Manhattan. “Much of what Donald Trump remembers about the New York of the ’70s I lived through with my dad,” she said. “So when he talks about Frank Sinatra’s bodyguard, I know that name.” Steve Witkoff, Trump’s real estate friend turned special envoy, says Wiles and Trump are creatures of that same bygone era: “That whole world of the Copacabana and Sammy Davis Jr. and all, those are things that he wants to talk about.”

The most valuable gift Susie got from her dad was hard-earned. Summerall was an absentee father and an alcoholic, and Wiles helped her mother stage interventions to get him into treatment. (Summerall was sober for 21 years before his death in 2013.) “Alcoholism does bad things to relationships, and so it was with my dad and me,” Wiles said.

“Some clinical psychologist that knows one million times more than I do will dispute what I’m going to say. But high-functioning alcoholics or alcoholics in general, their personalities are exaggerated when they drink. And so I’m a little bit of an expert in big personalities.” Wiles said Trump has “an alcoholic’s personality.” He “operates [with] a view that there’s nothing he can’t do. Nothing, zero, nothing.”

Susie Summerall got her first taste of politics in the late 1970s, interning as a college student in the Capitol Hill office of Jack Kemp, the New York congressman, who’d been a Giant with her father. Then, at 23, she landed a job in the Reagan White House as a scheduler, where she watched his chief of staff Baker in action. She married a GOP advance man, Lanny Wiles, and in 1984 they moved to Ponte Vedra. Wiles wanted to “start a family and a life outside politics.” But in 1988, Baker lured Wiles back to work with Dan Quayle, George H.W. Bush’s running mate. The couple had two daughters, Katie and Caroline. Wiles plunged into state politics—and over the next two decades became a formidable political strategist, serving as chief of staff to the mayor of Jacksonville, Florida, running Rick Scott’s gubernatorial campaign, and, briefly, leading Jon Huntsman’s campaign for president.

In 2015, Wiles was invited to Trump Tower to meet the real estate tycoon turned presidential candidate. The star of The Apprentice couldn’t believe he was talking to the daughter of the great Pat Summerall. “He’s said it a million times,” Wiles said. “ ‘I judge people by their genes.’ ” Wiles thought Trump was interesting and smart. “And they called me one night and said, ‘We’re serious about Florida now. Would you like to co-chair our leadership team?’ And I said, ‘Yeah, I would.’ ”
“I had become disenchanted with what we now call traditional Republicans,” she recalled.

Wiles’s relationship with Trump almost ended at his Miami golf club one night in the fall of 2016. Unhappy with a poll showing him doing worse than expected in Florida, Trump berated her in front of a gaggle of cronies. “It was a horrific hour-plus at midnight,” Wiles told me. “And I don’t think I’ve seen him that angry since. He was ranting and raving. And I didn’t know whether to argue back or whether to be stoic. What I really wanted to do was cry.”

Wiles steeled herself. “I finally said, ‘You know Mr. Trump, if you want somebody to set their hair on fire and be crazy, I’m not your girl. But if you want to win this state, I am. It’s your choice.’ ” Wiles walked out. Trump turned on a dime. “Lo and behold, he called me every day.” Wiles never looked back. Trump carried Florida, the first big prize in his stunning 2016 upset over Hillary Clinton.

Then, in a fateful turn of events, Wiles went to work in 2018 for an ambitious gubernatorial candidate named Ron DeSantis. (Trump urged DeSantis, then his protégé, to hire her.) She led the underdog candidate to victory. But afterward, DeSantis turned on her, denouncing Wiles publicly and bad-mouthing her privately. To this day, Wiles doesn’t know what triggered the governor’s vendetta. “I think he thought I was getting too much attention, which is ironic,” she told me. “I don’t ever seek attention.”

Wiles landed on her feet, organizing Florida for Trump’s 2020 reelection bid. Trump had rescued Wiles, recently divorced, at a dark moment in her life. (Wiles and her husband divorced in 2017—due, she has said, to his bad financial decisions.) Looking back on DeSantis’s behavior, Wiles reflected: “Had he said, ‘Look, thank you. I appreciate your help. We’re done here.’ I believe the course of his history would have been different. I might or might not have gone to work for Donald Trump.”

On Trump’s first day in office, the president signed a flurry of executive orders, 26 in all, withdrawing the US from the World Health Organization and the Paris climate agreement, rescinding birthright citizenship, sending troops to the southern border, freezing foreign aid, and stopping federal hiring. Then Trump issued pardons to almost everyone convicted in the bloody January 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol, in which nine people ultimately died and 150 were injured. Even rioters who’d beaten cops within an inch of their lives were set free. (Fourteen people convicted of seditious conspiracy had their sentences commuted.)
Did she ever ask the president, “ ‘Wait a minute, do you really want to pardon all 1,500 January 6 convicts, or should we be more selective?’ ”

“I did exactly that,” Wiles replied. “I said, ‘I am on board with the people that were happenstancers or didn’t do anything violent. And we certainly know what everybody did because the FBI has done such an incredible job.’ ” (Trump has said his FBI investigators were “corrupt” and part of a “deep state.”) But Trump argued that even the violent offenders had been unfairly treated. Wiles explained: “In every case, of the ones he was looking at, in every case, they had already served more time than the sentencing guidelines would have suggested. So given that, I sort of got on board.” (According to court records, many of the January 6 rioters pardoned by Trump had received sentences that were lighter than the guidelines.) “There have been a couple of times where I’ve been outvoted,” Wiles said. “And if there’s a tie, he wins.”

In the West Wing, Wiles is surrounded by young MAGA men. “She is a ‘go to church every Sunday, uses a swear word very, very rarely’ ” person, said James Blair, Wiles’s 36-year-old deputy chief of staff. “She doesn’t raise her voice. But she likes being around junkyard dogs.” Indeed, Wiles has seemed content to let her pit bulls—deputy chiefs of staff Miller, Blair, and Dan Scavino—run loose as she watches.

During Oval Office events, Wiles almost always sits just off camera. “There’s the president and then there’s whoever the three high-ranking people are on the sofa,” she said. “And then there’s a chair at the corner of the sofa, which is my chair, which means I’m the one that gets hit in the head with the boom mic.”

For all the chaos in the Cabinet, Wiles has kept palace intrigue and shivving to a minimum in the White House. Trump has empowered her; when Wiles weighs in, everyone knows she is speaking for him. She has in turn empowered her team: Blair, Miller, Scavino, and Taylor Budowich, who departed in September.

“First and foremost, she brings no ego,” says Blair. “And that is the starting point from which just an immense amount of power flows. There’s so much ego and testosterone around her, there wouldn’t be any room for hers anyway.”
From day one, Wiles had to grapple with another power center: Elon Musk.

“He is a complete solo actor,” said Wiles of Trump’s billionaire pal who led the scorched-earth blitz known as the Department of Government Efficiency. Wiles described Musk as something akin to a jacked-up Nosferatu. “The challenge with Elon is keeping up with him,” she told me. “He’s an avowed ketamine [user]. And he sleeps in a sleeping bag in the EOB [Executive Office Building] in the daytime. And he’s an odd, odd duck, as I think geniuses are. You know, it’s not helpful, but he is his own person.”

Musk triggered the first true crisis of the Trump presidency and an early test for Wiles. Trump’s chief was shocked when the SpaceX founder eviscerated USAID, the United States Agency for International Development. “I was initially aghast,” Wiles told me. “Because I think anybody that pays attention to government and has ever paid attention to USAID believed, as I did, that they do very good work.”

In his executive order freezing foreign aid, Trump had decreed that lifesaving programs should be spared. Instead, they were shuttered. “When Elon said, ‘We’re doing this,’ he was already into it,” said Wiles. “And that’s probably because he knew it would be horrifying to others. But he decided that it was a better approach to shut it down, fire everybody, shut them out, and then go rebuild. Not the way I would do it.”
Wiles knew that fixing this was on her. “The president doesn’t know and never will,” she told me. “He doesn’t know the details of these smallish agencies.”

Wiles says she called Musk on the carpet. “You can’t just lock people out of their offices,” she recalls telling him. At first, Wiles didn’t grasp the effect that slashing USAID programs would have on humanitarian aid. “I didn’t know a lot about the extent of their grant making.” But with immunizations halted in Africa, lives would be lost. Soon she was getting frantic calls from relief agency heads and former government officials with a dire message: Thousands of lives were in the balance.

Wiles continued: “So Marco is on his way to Panama. We call him and say, ‘You’re Senate-confirmed. You’re going to have to be the custodian, essentially, of [USAID].’ ‘Okay,’ he says.” But Musk forged ahead—all throttle, no brake. “Elon’s attitude is you have to get it done fast. If you’re an incrementalist, you just won’t get your rocket to the moon,” Wiles said. “And so with that attitude, you’re going to break some china. But no rational person could think the USAID process was a good one. Nobody.”

The shuttering of USAID crippled the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR). The antiretroviral program, launched with $15 billion by George W. Bush in 2003, was credited with preventing millions of deaths. It depended on USAID grants. In an interview with The Financial Times, Bill Gates remarked: “The picture of the world’s richest man killing the world’s poorest children is not a pretty one.”
Privately, another drama was playing out.

Bush himself had gotten wind of the gutting of PEPFAR. He called Rubio to express alarm, according to a former aide close to Bush. “He’s been appalled by Trump from the beginning and he’s determined not to weigh in,” the aide said. But Musk’s attack on one of his legacy achievements was too much. Bush, said that person, “cares deeply about the PEPFAR program. That and Wounded Warriors are the two things where he will weigh in, not publicly, but with intention.”

Did Rubio have any regrets about the untold number of lives that PEPFAR’s evisceration might cost? “No. First of all, whoever says that, it’s just not being accurate,” he told me. “We are not eviscerating PEPFAR. PEPFAR has been rearranged and reorganized in such a way where we’re now going to be able to deliver aid in a way that has a goal. The goal is to help countries become self-sustaining.” With a note of “America First,” he added: “Let’s begin with the premise: Is it the United States’ fault? Why isn’t China paying for more immunizations? Why isn’t the UK or Canada or any of the G7 countries?” (The UK, following in the footsteps of the US, slashed foreign aid in 2025. In November, China, which funded the Africa CDC, pledged $3.5 million in AIDS prevention in South Africa alone.)
When I repeated Rubio’s comment to a former GOP White House chief of staff, he remarked: “I find that immoral.”
“Our job is lethality and readiness and war fighting.” —Pete Hegseth on his first day at the Pentagon, days after Vance cast the tiebreaking vote in his Senate confirmation

For Trump, Wiles has helped pick a Cabinet of MAGA hard-liners: Pete Hegseth, secretary of war (formerly defense); Kash Patel, FBI director; John Ratcliffe, CIA director; Pam Bondi, attorney general; Tulsi Gabbard, director of national intelligence; and Kristi Noem, head of Homeland Security. Wiles calls them “a world-class Cabinet, better than anything I could have conceived of.” Trump’s Cabinet members are either one of the least qualified presidential teams in history or, to hear Wiles tell it, disrupters—the only people with the balls to take on an entrenched deep state.

“People talk about the deep state being at the State Department,” Wiles said. “It’s not. It’s the military-industrial complex.” Hegseth, in her view, is just the guy to take on the powers that be. She referred to Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., another world-class disrupter, as “my Bobby” and “quirky Bobby.” In Wiles’s view, RFK Jr.’s shock treatment of HHS is warranted. “He pushes the envelope—some would say too far. But I say in order to get back to the middle, you have to push it too far.” (In December, Kennedy’s federal vaccine panel voted to end the decades-long recommendation for newborn vaccinations against hepatitis B, which is highly infectious and causes liver failure.)
“US deports hundreds of Venezuelans to El Salvador, despite court order.” —NPR

In mid-March, after Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents (ICE) shackled and herded 238 immigrants onto transport planes and flew them to a notoriously brutal Salvadoran prison. According to Trump, the men were members of Tren de Aragua, a violent Venezuelan gang, but the evidence was sketchy (often based on tattoos alone). Most had committed no serious crimes; one, Kilmar Abrego Garcia, was deported by mistake, the Trump administration admitted.
“I will concede that we’ve got to look harder at our process for deportation,” Wiles told me at the time.

When we spoke again in April, in cities across the country, masked ICE agents were snatching people off the street, throwing them in vans, and zip-tying and frog-marching them into makeshift deportation camps. Many were US citizens or entitled to be here. (ProPublica documented 170 cases in the first nine months of 2025 of US citizens being caught up in ICE’s dragnet.)

“If somebody is a known gang member who has a criminal past, and you’re sure, and you can demonstrate it, it’s probably fine to send them to El Salvador or whatever,” Wiles told me. “But if there is a question, I think our process has to lean toward a double-check.” But as the usa.gov site itself notes, “In some cases, a noncitizen is subject to expedited removal without being able to attend a hearing in immigration court.” Not long after the El Salvador deportation fiasco, in Louisiana, ICE agents arrested and deported two mothers, along with their children, ages seven, four, and two, to Honduras. The children were US citizens and the four-year-old was being treated for stage 4 cancer. Wiles couldn’t explain it.

“It could be an overzealous Border Patrol agent, I don’t know,” she said of the case, in which both mothers had reportedly been arrested after voluntarily attending routine immigration meetings. “I can’t understand how you make that mistake, but somebody did.”
“Long-threatened tariffs from U.S. President Donald Trump have plunged the country into trade wars abroad….” —PBS News
The president declared April 2 “Liberation Day,” bragging about billions of dollars that would flow into US coffers from tariffs, refusing to acknowledge that the levies were a tax on consumers.

“So much thinking out loud is what I would call it,” said Wiles of Trump’s chaotic tariff rollout. “There was a huge disagreement over whether [tariffs were] a good idea.” Trump’s advisers were sharply divided, some believing tariffs were a panacea and others predicting disaster. Wiles told them to get with Trump’s program. “I said, ‘This is where we’re going to end up. So figure out how you can work into what he’s already thinking.’ Well, they couldn’t get there.”

Wiles recruited Vance to help tap the brakes. “We told Donald Trump, ‘Hey, let’s not talk about tariffs today. Let’s wait until we have the team in complete unity and then we’ll do it,’ ” she said. But Trump barreled ahead, announcing sweeping “reciprocal” tariffs, from 10 to 100 percent—which triggered panic in the bond market and a sell-off of stocks. Trump paused his policy for 90 days, but by that time the president’s helter-skelter levies had given rise to the TACO chant: “Trump Always Chickens Out.”
Wiles believed a middle ground on tariffs would ultimately succeed, she said, “but it’s been more painful than I expected.”
At the time this article went to press, shortly before the December holidays, a Harvard poll showed 56 percent of voters think Trump’s tariff policies have harmed the economy.
“National Guard mobilizes 800 troops in DC to Support Federal, Local Law Enforcement—Trump declared a crime emergency in the nation’s capital.” —US Department of War

During the summer, Trump ordered the National Guard into four Democratic-led cities, claiming the troops were needed to crack down on crime and protect federal immigration facilities. In June the president deployed some 4,000 guard troops to Los Angeles; later he sent them to Washington, describing the city’s crime rate as “out of control.” “This was like a vitamin boost of ICE, of the [National] Guard, of the Park Service police, who actually have more authority than the DC Metro Police,” Wiles said. “And the idea was to right the ship and then slowly back off. And that’s what we’re doing.”
Critics denounced the deployments as unconstitutional, performative, and ineffective, and many feared Trump had another, more sinister plan up his sleeve.
Will the president use the military to suppress or even prevent voting during the midterms and beyond?
“I say it is categorically false, will not happen, it’s just wrongheaded,” she snapped.
“Do you understand where people who think that are coming from?” I asked.
“I do a little bit, but not fully. I mean, I think they hate the president. They think he’s too wrapped up in what happened in 2020.”

The president and his team were pushing almost every legal and constitutional boundary and defying courts to stop them. But would Trump obey the Supreme Court? “Do you think he will adhere to whatever the courts decide in the end?” I asked Wiles. “I do,” she replied. But Wiles made a prediction: “The smart lawyers around us think that we will be slowed down, as we already have been, but we will ultimately prevail.”
Click here to read Part 2 of 2 from Vanity Fair’s portfolio of Trump’s inner circle.

items.title: A Blue Wave Rejected Trump. Will Democrats Confront His Racism?
items.description: This article was produced by Capital & Main. It is co-published by Rolling Stone with permission.
items.author: Erin Aubry Kaplan; Ryan Bort
paragraphs: This article was produced by Capital & Main. It is co-published by Rolling Stone with permission.

The historic shellacking voters delivered to President Donald Trump and the GOP Tuesday already has many names — stinging rebuke, rejection, repudiation, reset. Analysts’ consensus is that the blue wave was a response to what so many Americans could see and feel every day — soaring prices, the effects of a needless war, blatant corruption at the top, all led by an erratic and increasingly unpopular president who openly dismissed the concerns of average people. The message was: enough.

For anyone alarmed about the country’s Trump-led decline, the midterm results are beyond heartening, the best possible outcome. At the very least — and this is still huge — a Democratic takeover of Congress puts a serious check on the chaos. At most, it is a generational opportunity to change direction. But what remains undiscussed is what the election results will mean for the country’s most intractable and corrosive problem, what powered the rise of Trumpism 10 years ago and powers it still: racism.

Will Democrats insist the country re-embrace diversity? And if so, how? In the last two years, many norms have been degraded and discarded with astonishing speed, chief among them the ideal of racial equality that is at the heart of America itself. Undoing diversity, equity and inclusion programs was the first agenda item of Trump’s second term, because it was dear to his base, but more importantly, because he intuited that dividing the country racially would weaken it and make it vulnerable to his authoritarian ambitions.

In his overarching campaign against DEI, Trump crossed lines and broke norms in ways detrimental and devastating for people of color, from sweeping federal job cuts that disproportionately hit Black workers to the targeting of Haitian immigrants for deportation to the recklessness and violence of ICE. It was the contempt and anything-goes lawlessness white authorities perpetrated on Black people during a century of Jim Crow segregation, but with the whole country drawn in this time.

Were the midterms a repudiation of this? Dorian Warren, co-president of the civil rights organization Community Change, is cautiously optimistic they might be. When we spoke in 2016 Warren told me that the crisis of Trump’s election was racial, a white problem that only white people could ultimately resolve. While that hasn’t happened, he now thinks the midterm results are a mark of notable progress.

“Though there were multiple motivations for voters, this was a definitely repudiation of Trump and MAGA,” Warren said in an interview on Thursday. “Think about it — now we have five Black governors. Keisha Lance Bottoms is the first Black female governor in history . . . It’s astounding.”
Warren said that this could be the moment that the Democratic Party finally realizes the magnitude of debt it owes to Black voters, who turned out in force, especially across the South.
“It’s like we’re saying, ‘Enough! We saved your butt many times,’” said Warren. “‘Stop running away from race.’”
In other words, Democrats need to unapologetically own the diversity of their party, and of America itself.

While it isn’t yet clear how much antiracism factored into the Democrats’ sweeping victory, there is no doubt about the role of Black Americans in pushing back. Black voters turned out in big numbers and shifted markedly to the left compared to 2024. That is at least in part an angry reaction to the GOP’s bald attempts to wipe out Black political representation with gerrymandering that disappeared Black-majority districts after the Supreme Court’s latest gutting of the Voting Rights Act.

That was perhaps the sweetest victory of all on Tuesday: that not only was a racist strategy ineffective, it backfired. Remarkable as that was, it’s also consistent with the resolve that has long characterized Black history.
“It’s amazing how resilient we are,” said Warren. “They tried to shut us down, and we said, ‘No, we’re not doing this.’”

Even if voters’ repudiation of Trump and the Republicans wasn’t chiefly about their racism, it was about morality. Candidates from Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico to Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton spoke about restoring decency, humanity and neighborliness to politics and American life. Talarico is a Presbyterian seminarian and Hamilton a Methodist pastor, but you didn’t have to be Christian to call out the moral rot of the Trump era, or to hear the message.

While few white candidates actually talked about racism — Talarico has called Christian nationalism “fundamentally un-Christian” and racism “immoral and wrong” — Democrats have generally been reluctant to talk in detail about spirituality or race. The moment demands they do both.
But even if the Democratic Party leaders don’t step up, Warren believes people of color will.

“My first thought after the election was, ‘This is a rainbow coalition,’” he said. “People are calling the increase of Black and Latino Democratic voters ‘blacklash’ and ‘brownlash.’ But that’s a coalition.”

While the Latino voters’ shift away from Trump was crucial, Warren said Black voters remain the anchor of the Democratic coalition. The question is whether their status within the party will change from being “captured” — taken for granted — to being “anchors” involved with directing the party and its mission.

The answer has great implications for the larger existential question about whether the U.S. will finally decide to champion its diversity as a permanent political and cultural good. Even at this moment of uncertainty and inflection, those answers are probably not coming anytime soon.
“As Black organizations and activists, we can’t wait around,” he said. “Now is the time we have to make demands and apply pressure. We have to get to work.”

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Recap: The Price of Loyalty
items.description: Just when Henry and Julia think they have a little breathing room to figure out how to get back to the 1900s, a new wrinkle appears to blow up their plans. And this wrinkle, whether it actually happens or not, is surely going to have some major ramifications f
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Just when Henry and Julia think they have a little breathing room to figure out how to get back to the 1900s, a new wrinkle appears to blow up their plans. And this wrinkle, whether it actually happens or not, is surely going to have some major ramifications for Blood of My Blood going forward. Friends, Lord Lovat is totally going to try to kill Julia.

Let me back up a quick second: The lairds of loyalist clans — including Uncle Grant and Lovat — have gathered at the Duke of Sandringham’s Scottish Estate to meet with King George I. They are being celebrated and thanked for putting down the Jacobite rebellion. Lord Gerard Grey, who isn’t in attendance because he’s out hunting Dougal MacKenzie, gets elevated to Duke of Pardloe. Lovat gets his title and lands back and is named Governor of Inverness. Lovat could not be more smug about being the guest of honor. He’s especially thrilled to clock that Uncle Grant is bestowed with only a bronze medal, not a silver like him. And that’s not the only thing Lovat’s clocking: He meets Margaret Grant and is immediately taken by her.

You’d think this would be welcome news for Julia. It is initially, mainly because when Lovat makes up an excuse about Julia not feeling well to signal that he wants her to scram, it means she gets to sneak off with Henry. It does seem wild that everyone is cool with Julia being even remotely close to the dude they all think just tried to kidnap her, but I guess that just shows you how little Lovat actually cares about her. Sure, he makes a joke about demanding his head, and Henry gets big mad and begs him to try, which is objectively hot, but other than that, kidnapping, schmidnapping.

Julia and Henry do use Lovat’s fixation on Margaret and Uncle Grant’s fixation on Lovat’s fixation to their advantage. They sneak into a spare room so Julia can drop that bomb she discovered at the end of last week’s episode: According to Maisri, who has been right about everything else, Julia only traveled through the stones because she was pregnant with William, who does not have the power to travel. Leaving Julia behind is a nonstarter for Henry. It doesn’t take long before he’s like, Well, why don’t we just get you knocked up again? It sounds like an obvious conclusion to make, but Julia immediately shuts it down. She reasons that they shouldn’t have a child just to use it for their own needs, but I’d think a bigger reason is that there’s no guarantee the baby will be able to travel, and if not, they just brought another child into a very dangerous situation. But these two have never really concerned themselves with the nitty-gritty of time travel.

The next option they have is, of course, to grab William and run away together. But Lovat wants that baby — his future king — and if they run, he will never stop hunting them. Instead of feeling overwhelmed by the current situation, they take a moment to dance like they used to, remember how much they love each other, and remind themselves that for now, both of them are in safe situations and they have those gemstones ready to go in case of emergency. They have time to figure out what to do next.

Meanwhile, Lovat and Margaret have found a quiet place to make out. Uncle Grant bumps into them and is mostly disgusted by the whole thing, but it doesn’t take long for both Margaret and Grant to take control of the situation. Lovat wants to have sex with Margaret immediately, but she refuses to let Lovat do anything until he promises to marry her. She seems like the only woman he’s ever kowtowed to — and he likes it. God, he really is the worst.

We know that Uncle Grant has been looking to off-load his sister, so when Lovat sidles up to him, he starts talking about how Margaret would make a good wife, what with her sizable dowry and connections to some powerful people in London (she knows the king’s mistresses), but wow, isn’t it such a shame that Lovat’s already married … to his former maidservant. Whatever Grant is up to here, he’s good at it. Twisting the knife about how low-class Lovat’s wife is plays right into Lovat’s insecurities about his status. You see his wheels — okay, it’s like, one wheel — turning now. He wants Margaret, and he’s a man who gets what he wants. So he decides to build a little trust with Uncle Grant: He “lets” it slip that Ellen was handfasted to Brian before her wedding to Malcolm and the MacKenzies lied about it. Something tells me Uncle Grant isn’t just going to move on with his day after learning that piece of information.

Now that Lovat knows Grant is onboard with him marrying Margaret, he just starts spending time with her out in the middle of the room, for all to see. And “all” includes Julia. The moment she sees the two standing so close, she knows exactly what is happening here. Thankfully, Henry is nearby so she can tell him, too: Lovat wants to get rid of her, and the only way to do that and keep the baby without any type of scandal is for her to die. Seems like their whole plan to take a breath and figure things out, since they’re both safe for the moment, just got tossed out the window.

There are some death threats happening over at Castle Leoch, too. Lord Grey — now Duke, it seems — has arrived at Leoch looking for Dougal. (You’d think that would’ve been his first stop, but never mind me.) When Colum plays dumb about his brother’s whereabouts, Grey decides to arrest him. He doesn’t care that Colum stayed neutral in the rebellion — it’s still treason by omission and punishable by death. He agrees not to commandeer Leoch for the crown since the deed is under Ellen’s name and she had no power to fight for the king or stop Dougal from joining the Jacobites (Ellen’s plan worked!), but when Dougal rushes in to nobly save Colum from having to pay for crimes that aren’t his own, Grey takes it as an opportunity to kill two MacKenzie traitors.

Once again, Ellen has to clean up her brothers’ messes. At least this time, she’s going to take a little something for herself, too. She calmly gets Grey to agree to give Colum and Dougal time to pray before they’re taken off to be executed and then pays those boys a visit in the chapel. She will bargain for their lives — and she’ll get Grey to agree — but with a few conditions. First, Colum is going to be the sole laird of the clan. Dougal put them all at risk, and he can’t be trusted with any decision-making. Second, she’ll sign Leoch back over to Colum, but only if he agrees to give her the parcel of land that abuts Fraser land — the exact piece of Fraser land where Brian will be building their home. Colum and Dougal are livid that she’d even ask these things, which is especially rich because she could just let Grey take them, and Leoch and all the land and money that comes with it would be hers. These two are the biggest ding-dongs to ever ding-dong, and it is a wonder that they’re still around decades later in Outlander. Dougal can call his sister “a black-hearted bitch” all he wants, but they really have no choice but to agree to Ellen’s demands.

And Ellen makes good on her promise. She meets with Grey, and after flattering him for a bit, she reminds him that if he does go along with these executions, the story behind them will get out too. That story is, of course, that a rebel Highlander escaped Grey’s prison, killed a bunch of his men, and remained hidden and then gave himself up to save his family. Dougal will become a legend to the cause, and Grey will be humiliated. She also tosses in a bunch of money for good measure. It remains as true as ever: Ellen is the only MacKenzie really suited to be laird.

With Grey satisfied and Colum and Dougal saved, Ellen has one final condition for them: They are never, ever allowed to set foot on her and Brian’s land. At first, both of her brothers react to the rejection with anger. Colum refuses to pay her dowry, and Dougal makes a dig at Brian (who just saved his life, by the way) before storming out. But it becomes quite clear that they’re feeling more than anger, and if I had to guess, it would be that they’re embarrassed and heartbroken. Everyone on this show needs therapy, but especially the MacKenzie brothers.

You know what? There is one caveat to my previous statement. You know who is almost fully self-actualized? Ned. Sweet Ned! Colum may hide his tears when Ellen walks away from him, but not Ned. He finds Ellen one more time to say a real good-bye. He’s not afraid to tell her that he’ll miss her. The two used to sit by the fire and read and perform plays, and so, tearfully, he gives her a bit of Titania’s monologue from A Midsummer Night’s Dream — a bit in which he can tell her he loves her. “I do love thee,” she returns. She makes sure he knows he isn’t just the family lawyer and adviser to her. And hey, she never said Ned had to keep off her property. Fingers crossed these two best buds will get to perform Shakespeare again someday soon. Honestly, Brian would make a great Bottom.

• Have we been too hard on Colum? When Ellen tells him he’s not allowed to set foot in her home, he quietly tells her that she is always free to return to Leoch. When Ned remarks that he was actually worried Colum would turn Dougal over to Grey, he responds with a small but adamant “never.” Is he a secret softy inside, worried that he’s becoming a monster?

• Gah! John Cameron is headed to the West Indies (without Jocasta) to manage a sugarcane plantation he just bought, and he’s forcing Grace to go with him. Murtagh is beside himself when he finds out. He gets very Daniel Day-Lewis in The Last of Mohicans with his whole “I will board a ship! I will find you!” declaration. This can’t be the end for these two, can it?

• When Murtagh first goes to surprise Grace and she refuses to kiss him out of fear of them getting caught, he tells her that he’ll settle for his name on her lips. Murtagh is such a goddamned dreamboat. Nobody hurt him!!
