On the first Saturday morning of the school year, Horacio and three of his children — Margoth, 8; Maithais, 6; and Noah, 5 — walked up 139th Street in the Bronx toward the charter school the kids attend. At the top of the hill, a pair of gray doors (which have since been painted blue) swung open, and the family stepped inside. “I’ll be back around 2,” he told the safety officers sitting behind a desk in the lobby. One was Ellen Coleman, whom everyone knows as Ms. Ellen. She leaned back in her chair, grinned, and greeted each kid by name. “You sure you don’t want to leave them for longer?” she asked. “We’re getting dinner.”

The school, called Strive Charter School, opened in August. It was founded not with a lofty pedagogical mandate or unique classroom-behavior strategy but with the goal of making life significantly easier for working parents. The founder, Eric Grannis, takes pride in Strive’s academic offerings but knows that the school’s main selling point is its hours of operation. Horacio learned about Strive over the summer, when he was handed a pamphlet at the entrance to a subway station. “Open from 7am to 7pm,” the paper read. “7 days a week, 12 months a year.”

During the regular school year — from September to late June — class is in session five days a week, from 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The extended part of the schedule (early mornings, evenings, weekends, and July and August) is optional and free of charge. Those hours will be filled with a variety of programming: tutoring, sports, art, music, viewings in a planetarium, and free play. In the summer, the full week will run like a classic day camp with some additional academic components, including required reading periods, tutoring, and enrichment. Dropping off and picking up a child outside of regular school hours, according to Grannis, should be as simple as stopping by Starbucks for a preordered cup of coffee.

In Strive, Grannis has embraced a dual role for schools as both centers of education and an integral form of child care that many teachers and administrators have long resisted. But the vast majority of working parents in America depend on schools to do their jobs, and Grannis believes educational institutions can and should do even more to help parents stay employed. Across the United States, there are about 23 million kids unable to access after-school programming whose families would enroll them if they had the option. And in New York City, the demand for free or affordable after-hours programming far outstrips the availability. In the 2023–24 school year, there were around 150,000 complimentary after-school slots for the over 643,000 children enrolled in the city’s K–8 public schools. The city comptroller’s office estimates a shortfall of more than 390,000 seats next school year. What’s more, around 30 percent of employed people work over the weekend, which makes Saturday and Sunday child care a necessity too. Strive, which serves grades K–4, aims to bridge these gaps and then some while sticking to a standard public-school budget.

Grannis started the school with assistance from his wife, Eva Moskowitz, co-founder and CEO of New York City’s largest and arguably most controversial charter-school network, Success Academy. The two met in high school and dated through college. He worked for Success Academy early on and explains, with some enjoyment, that when his wife was hired to lead the organization, his first and only recommendation for her was to fire him. (Grannis still does pro-bono work for Success Academy.) Moskowitz has spent years openly criticizing the city’s teachers union, and Grannis shares her sense of embattled disdain. Both say they are looking to serve students and this task has been impeded by complacency and bureaucracy. “This is how it is,” he wrote atop an email exchange he forwarded me between himself and the city Department of Education. “They always make things impossible for us.”

To create Strive, Success Academy’s board voted to transfer one of their charter-school licenses to Strive’s board of trustees, whose members Grannis had recruited. The move was then approved by the SUNY board of trustees — one of the governing bodies overseeing charter schools in the city. The transfer was subsequently challenged in court by the United Federation of Teachers, who argued that the license transfer violated a citywide cap on the number of charter schools in operation. Grannis, unbothered, expects a judge will throw out the case soon. With the school now open, he is focused on the practical challenges of delivering on the promises he made to the parents who took a risk on an untested enterprise and enrolled.

“I work anywhere from five to seven days a week,” Horacio said, straddling the doorstep at Strive that Saturday morning. “And even if it’s five, the weekdays are so crazy. Weekends are my only real time with the kids.” But on Saturday, he was using the school’s open-door policy to keep his older kids busy while he accomplished some errands with his youngest son. He just wanted a little bit of time. “Whatever you need,” said Ms. Ellen. “You run your errands. We’ve got them up there doing art.”

In the 19th century, the school calendar varied widely across America and even within individual states. Schools in one district might run for three months of the year, while those just a town over were in session for ten months. But one commonality all schools shared, wrote historian Kenneth Gold in his essay “The Myth of Summer Vacation and the Agrarian Calendar,” was that they were open in the summer. In fact, in many urban schools, attendance numbers during those months were the highest of the year. It is a fallacy that the modern-day public-school schedule — with its long summer break, weekends off, and early-afternoon dismissal time — came about to encourage seasonal farmwork. In reality, as the century progressed, the modern schedule arose from what Gold describes as a perceived “inferiority of summer term teachers” (the vast majority of whom were women); a series of summer illness outbreaks and heat waves that drove wealthy urbanites to flee cities for country homes; the need to expand, construct, and repair more school buildings as the city’s population grew; and eventually, a decline in student attendance, and a desire for standardization. By 1867, summer vacations in New York City were seven weeks long.

School leaders did worry about teachers’ skills growing soft over the break (concerns over a student “summer slide” didn’t take shape until the 1920s) but eventually justified it as a time for renewal and professional training. Summer education conferences flourished. By the dawn of the 20th century, the school-calendar model had become largely standardized: “A 180-day school held during the fall, winter, and spring; punctuated by a 2-3-month summer vacation,” Gold wrote.

By 1918, every state had some form of legislation making school compulsory, though what compulsory meant varied greatly. At nearly the same moment, early versions of after-school programs began springing up across New York, especially in immigrant neighborhoods. Settlement houses provided food and activities for children in lower Manhattan. A playground movement in the late 1800s prompted the construction of outdoor play spaces often overseen by city-employed supervisors who organized games and saw to the children’s safety. Starting in the 1930s, the city created what has become one of the largest publicly funded in-school after-school programs in the country. The school day began, almost universally, at 9 a.m. until the 1960s and 1970s, when some districts began to move the drop-off time earlier to accommodate parents who needed to commute to work afterward.

Schools across the United States have experimented with the calendar for decades, although none has gone as far as Grannis. In 2018, about 3 percent of public schools in the U.S. maintained year-round schedules. The Center for American Progress has been advocating for a school day that runs from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. for at least a decade (though without an even earlier drop-off and later pickup option, this tweak would still leave most parents scrambling for child care). KIPP Public Charter Schools used to have a program that required all enrolled students to attend school one Saturday a month, but it has mostly been phased out. No school has attempted the one-stop shop Grannis envisions. The closest competitor to Strive in New York City is the Harlem Children’s Zone charter-school network. It has an academic calendar that stretches from September into late June and offers a summer program in July and August, all in the hopes that truncated breaks will help limit learning loss. It also offers free after-school programming until 7 p.m. Monday through Thursday and until 6 p.m. on Friday. The schools aren’t open on the weekends, but they do offer Saturday programming at select central HCZ community centers. But overall, schools in the U.S. are almost uniformly closed over the weekends, which makes Strive’s Saturday and Sunday hours arguably its boldest, most appealing feature.

On the first Saturday of the school year, I followed Maithais and Margoth into Strive’s weekend programming. Grannis had warned me that he was still working out the kinks. For example, there had been problems with a missed bus stop, and the kitchen was still not operational; meals were sandwiches and other packaged foods that didn’t require cooking. The building Strive occupies is owned by St. Luke’s Catholic Church, which doesn’t allow the school to use the space on Sundays, and Grannis was still searching for an alternative. The DOE, he complained in an email, had been opaque and unhelpful. (In October, Grannis reported that the kitchen was now functional and that he had found a likely home for his Sunday programming— a Success Academy campus.) Grannis has hired a soccer coach for the weekends, but he’ll only work on Sundays. There will also be basketball, eventually, but the school’s gym has not yet been set up.

So far, Grannis has hired a staff of 40 teachers and assistants. Especially for experienced teachers, the school’s salaries are markedly lower than in New York City public schools. There, veteran teachers can earn more than $128,000 per year, and entry-level salaries range from $71,314 for those with no experience and no master’s degree to $80,166 for those starting with a master’s degree. Strive, by contrast, offers full-time assistant teachers $60,000 per year for 50 hours per week and $80,000 per year to lead classroom teachers with two years of experience; each subsequent year of experience adds only $2,000. And importantly, teachers at Strive are required to be at school for 210 instructional days, as opposed to the standard public school’s 180. The remainder of the extended hours at Strive are staffed largely by teaching assistants paid about $25 per hour. “There are lots of people who have experience in the world of education who don’t have Harvard degrees or a B.A., necessarily,” says Grannis. At most DOE schools, teachers leading after-hours programming or summer enrichment earn an additional $63.04 an hour. Its salary structure has all but ensured the Strive faculty will be inexperienced compared with that of a typical public school.

Grannis estimates that keeping the school open on Saturday and Sunday will cost Strive around $5,000 each week, or $250,000 over the course of the year. When I visited, Grannis pulled out his phone to check the math and informed me that, working from a budget of around $9 million a year, weekends will take up just 3 percent of his overall budget if he can attract 325 students to the school. “If we stick to the current enrollment,” he told me, “I will have to do some fundraising.” A shrinking student population is one of the most pressing difficulties city schools face.

Before I arrived that morning, Grannis sent me a barrage of emails. Among them was a message warning that attendance might not be high. “I honestly don’t care if you report that attendance was low because my view has always been that the point is to give parents optionality,” Grannis wrote. “Even if only a relatively small number of children come on any given optional day, that may be totally critical to that family.”

When Horacio arrived with his children at 9:15 a.m., there was a steady trickle of parents coming in and out, early proof that the demand Grannis predicted is real. One mother came in asking to order a school shirt for her son, another to retrieve a student who had gotten sick. “He’s not feeling his best,” Ms. Ellen told me sympathetically. A pile of boxes sat near her desk —all packages of books and LEGO sets Grannis had ordered. Myasia Ennis, the head of Strive’s after-school programming at the time (she has since left, and three lead teachers have taken over the project), came in and out of the lobby, keeping tabs on everyone.

Margoth and Maithais stood uncertainly in front of Ms. Ellen’s desk, both wearing their Strive polo shirts, as their father chatted with other parents. Margoth was quiet and wide-eyed as she followed Ennis, looking slightly unsure about what she had gotten herself into.

The first-floor hallway was quiet. The kindergarten classes were brightly decorated and carpeted; purchasing the rugs was a particular preoccupation for Grannis over the summer. Down the hall was the activity room, where the younger children built block towers and worked with Play-Doh under the supervision of Emprise Williams, a first-grade teaching aide and weekend teacher who sat on a chair at a slight remove. “You guys are doing great,” Williams told her charges. “Take a minute and kiss your brains.”

As Margoth settled in, an older group of children played Uno and drew with markers. She sat quietly on the rug while a teacher’s aide played name games with the kids. A group of girls watched in awe as Margoth pulled a pack of cheddar fries out of her backpack. “You got cheddar fries?” asked one girl, starting to play with Margoth’s hair. Margoth nodded.
“You’re lucky,” said the girl. She introduced herself as Emma. Her friend, she said, was named Phoenix.
The girls discussed whether they liked the school so far. They had heard rumors about a basketball program and soccer.
“I like it here,” said one of the girls. “I might just come every day.”
“You’re joking,” said Emma. “Who wants to wake up at 6 every morning?”
They squealed in horror at the thought. Then the aide told them it was time for lunch.

I first met Grannis in March in a coffee shop in South Harlem not far from his home. By the time I arrived, Grannis had parked his bike outside, ordered breakfast, and set out a copy of the book he co-wrote with Moskowitz, A+ Parenting, to give me. Grannis is an ideas man in the classical mold. He has theories about classroom layouts and teaching math, about meal plans, student engagement, and the value of the movie musical 1776. In a near-ubiquitous button-down and slacks, he doesn’t look like a fitness buff, but he is, in fact, an avid biker. Even when he’s not exercising, he is often slightly out of breath from either enthusiasm or activity.

Strive’s educational philosophy was shaped by Grannis’s own experience, what he likes to call “the tasting tour of American pedagogy” (or, more accurately, elite education). He went to the famous West Side Montessori School for nursery school and P.S. 145 and then Collegiate for elementary school. He transferred to the Bank Street School during middle school and attended Exeter and later Stuyvesant for high school. His fondest memories, he says, were at Bank Street, where he outpaced his classmates in math and the teacher gave him and another classmate a textbook so they could study independently. It’s an experience he says he wants to recreate for students at Strive.

Much of the curriculum Strive is using has already been tested at Success Academy, which has a track record of high scores on state tests but also a reputation for harsh discipline strategies and a fair amount of attrition as students move into later grades. The school’s math curriculum is based on a series called Context for Learning Mathematics and focuses on mathematical understanding rather than rote memorization. (Grannis happens to know the creator and author of Context for Learning, Cathy Fosnot, and on one of my visits to the school over the summer, she was there training teachers herself.) The literacy program, Grannis says, embraces a spirit of independent inquiry he hopes will set Strive apart.

The first principal Grannis hired, Rebecca Goodsell, previously worked as an assistant principal at Success Academy, but she left halfway through the summer to tend to a family emergency. Her replacement, Shaniqua Sonnee, was formerly the director of enrichment at Hunter College Elementary School, a highly selective K–12 school in New York. Sonnee has recruited several of her former co-workers from Hunter to lead, among other things, Strive’s science classroom and after-school programming. Grannis also hired a recent college graduate to help him build an app for families, called Strive Arrive, that he says will eventually enable parents to log on and alert the school they are on their way to drop off or pick up their child. Through location tracking, the app will estimate the parent’s time of arrival and, theoretically, with around ten minutes’ advance notice, enable staff to pack up the child’s backpack and get them to the front door for a seamless pickup. “Then they can just walk right out when you arrive,” Grannis told me. So far, the app is not fully operational and the school is handling arrival and dismissal in the usual analog way.

“What they’re offering us has been priceless,” Daniel Ramirez, a father of a Strive first-grader, told me over the phone when I asked how his daughter’s first month has gone. “This idea with this school, it’s just brilliant. And it’s not only brilliant, it’s considerate. It’s considerate of the lives of hard-working people.”

In the months I spent following Grannis as he got Strive off the ground, all of the parents I spoke with who were considering the school faced formidable familial and logistical challenges. More than one had to quit a job over the summer to care for their children. They told me about their children’s strengths, struggles, and interests; the quirks of their work schedules; and the impossibility of efficiently managing their days.

Ramirez lives in the Bronx and works in security in Yonkers, and he chose Strive after the charter school his daughter attended for kindergarten announced it would admit kids to the after-school program by lottery with no guarantee of admission. “My wife and I both work,” Ramirez told me. “I’m not in the business of ‘see if it happens or not.’ I need some certainty.” When a co-worker mentioned he was moving his daughter from Success Academy to Strive, Ramirez decided to follow suit. When I spoke to him in October, he was thrilled with his choice. “They give my daughter a lot of homework,” Ramirez told me. “And we are on top of what’s going on. We ask her a lot of questions. And Aria loves it. She loves her teachers already.” Ramirez and his wife have been using the school’s Saturday hours, although sparingly. “At the end of the day, she’s our child. She’s not the school’s child,” he said.

Raychelle, whose name has been changed to protect her children’s privacy, works a hybrid job in hospital administration. She moved back to the Bronx from upstate New York over the summer. “But working from home doesn’t mean the kids can stay with you. My mom used to help, but now my mom is older,” she explains. She found what she described as a perfect school for her son, who has autism, in the Bronx. But she wanted an academically rigorous fit for her 7-year-old daughter and knew she needed it to be convenient since she was handling both of her kids’ transportation to school herself.

A few weeks into the school year, Raychelle said she had come to love the Saturday program at Strive. Her daughter wanted to go every week, Raychelle told me. “She’s like, ‘No, I want to go to school. They have dance or soccer or Monopoly.’ One day, I was so proud, she was upset that I came to pick her up too early. She said, ‘Mom, I had four properties.’” But Raychelle also shared concerns about the school’s ability to smoothly deliver its curriculum and the meager class sizes in the older grades. “I worry about this learning process as they go through the kinks,” she told me. “I hope they can feed that gift that she has.” She confessed to me that she feels slightly guilty about picking a school primarily because it fits her own schedule, rather than her daughter’s interests and strengths. “That’s my greatest fear. I was up last night thinking about it. I couldn’t go to sleep thinking about it.”

Horacio, Margoth and Maithais’s dad, works in a bodega in the South Bronx. During our first conversation over the phone, someone in the background interrupted him, cursing. He politely asked me to excuse him. He put down the phone and I heard him telling the man to leave. “Get out of the store,” he said sternly. And then again, there was yelling. After some commotion, Horacio picked up the phone again. “I’m sorry for that,” he said.

Last year, as Horacio’s family went through a rough patch, his children did not attend school at all. “I’m just trying to create more stability for me and the children at the moment,” Horacio told me. “The best way we can is through education and keeping them busy.”

He believes in consistency. He believes that, while you may have all the talents in the world, you’re nothing without routine. He is proud of the fact that aside from a bout of the flu and hand, foot, and mouth disease, they’ve had perfect attendance at school this academic year. Horacio lives in a family shelter, where kids may not be left home without adult supervision. He is hoping to find housing somewhere in the South Bronx so his children can stay close to Strive.

He told me that his job as a parent — in addition to giving his kids love and a stable routine — is finding out what they excel at and encouraging them. He wants them to know how to be with other people in the real world, rather than online. Margoth loves to draw, so Horacio fosters it. His youngest, he predicts, will end up in construction or demolition because of his tendency to take things apart. “He’s my little bull in the china shop,” Horacio laughed. His middle child is, at the moment, obsessed with dinosaurs.
“I can see already that Strive is taking care of the academic needs that the babies have,” Horacio told me.

In an idealized America, parents would be available to collect their children when the school day ends and to then oversee their kids at home with the benevolent calm of the mothers of our imagined past, watching them play as the afternoon light dwindles, no iPads or Xboxes in sight. For real working parents, however, the search for child care — after school, on weekends, in the summer, when the babysitter calls out sick, when camp is too expensive — is perpetual and stressful.

Teachers may be wary of conflating education with child care; they may feel the association denigrates or mischaracterizes their expertise and impact. But as the pandemic and its exodus of mothers from the workforce demonstrated, schools function as the most widely used and most effective form of child care we have in America. The overlap of education and child care doesn’t have to look exactly like Strive. The program could be teacher-led or built through partnerships with community organizations. It could be implemented in established and better-funded public schools that give enrolled families more confidence in their infrastructure and academics. But Grannis’s notion to expand in-school child care into the weekends and summer is so intuitive that it’s hard to believe he’s the first to get it off the ground.

On Strive’s first free Saturday, lunch (sandwiches and fruit) was followed by recess. After that, Grannis gathered all the kids, younger and older, and had them help unpack the LEGOs he had ordered. The last student left at 7 p.m., after dinner. By the end of the day, just over 40 of the school’s around 200 students had passed through the doors. He sent an email afterward thanking parents for dropping off their kids and included a video of the unboxing. “We didn’t have a lot of formal programming because we haven’t gotten everything in place yet, so children engaged in a lot of informal play, but that can actually be very educational,” he wrote. “If you ask a class of students if any of them want to help with something, all of their hands shoot up. It is so important to give children opportunities to do work.”

There is a part of me that is loath to see children spending time in any single institution for a 12-hour day. Watching students go in and out of Strive on a Saturday was bittersweet; although they looked excited and their parents relieved, I was struck by the fact that none of these families could afford, as Grannis put it, to “buy time” with their children. “Lower-income parents can’t afford to free up their time the way more affluent families can,” Grannis told me when we first met as he explained why a school like Strive is necessary. Parents, for example, may not have the resources to move closer to their jobs or hire help for time-consuming chores, nor do many have the autonomy to set a work schedule that accommodates their children’s needs. In situations like these, a flexible and familiar school where children feel safe and comfortable is an obvious and ideal child-care solution. Unlike many charter schools in New York, Strive does not weed out kids and families unable to meet attendance expectations or strict homework requirements. Any child who wants to enroll at Strive is welcome (though Strive is currently unable to accommodate students with certain individualized education plans), and in fact, the school is seeking more students.

Grannis is aware of the challenges involved in keeping the school running and funded. While the parents and teachers I interviewed attributed the difficulties of the start of the year, including faculty resignations and facility problems, to growing pains, outsiders — especially those opposed to charter schools in general — have questioned the scrappiness of this kind of venture and the benefit of extending the presence of a new, untested school in any child’s life. There were moments when I, too, strongly questioned whether Grannis and Strive could succeed. On one sparsely attended school-tour day at Strive, the operation had the feel of a start-up venture. A welcome video for touring parents, played inside an inflatable planetarium, featured a Star Wars–style yellow scroll and AI avatars of then-principal Goodsell and her vice-principal. Grannis hired a video editor in the Ukraine to help him produce it. He told me Goodsell moved too much in the regular recorded version, rendering it unusable.

The parents I spoke with early in the year have had somewhat mixed experiences in the time since. By the end of October, Raychelle, the parent who had been worried about the school’s academics, had moved her daughter to another school. “It wasn’t a fit,” she told me. “But I still believe in the school’s mission. I’m still a fan.” Ramirez and Horacio, however, remain happy with their choice. Their kids are settling in, doing homework, and learning.

And within the school, Grannis’s optimism has proven contagious. With Sonnee, he has managed to recruit a staff of aides and teachers who, when I spoke with them, were overtly enthusiastic about the school’s aims. Strive’s assistant principal and science department chair, Andrea Coleman, told me she has arranged a partnership with the Bronx Zoo. “We’re going to do real data collection,” she said. “We’re trying to create the scientists of the future.” Williams, the weekend teacher, said she felt blessed to have found the place. Ms. Ellen told me her employer, a security company, tried to relocate her to another school, but she refused to go. When she’s at work, she likes to imagine how much a school like Strive would have helped when her own children were still at home.

With school well into its second month, Grannis says he has already stepped away from classroom operations, which are now in the hands of Sonnee and an assistant principal. Sonnee smiles patiently while he talks. “We work well together,” she told me as the two reviewed a color-coded weekly schedule. His focus now is on tracking enrollment, ordering supplies, and staying abreast of changes that need to be made. And now that his first school is up and running, Grannis has set his sights on expansion. He recently started discussions with another charter school interested in adopting the Strive model.

items.title: Hegseth Impeachment Headlines a Messy Lame-Duck Session
items.description: Washington is abuzz about the upcoming 120th Congress with its new Democratic management and the pending drama with a defeated but still dangerously powerful president over the next two years. Indeed, freshly elected House and Senate members are already arrivi
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Washington is abuzz about the upcoming 120th Congress with its new Democratic management and the pending drama with a defeated but still dangerously powerful president over the next two years. Indeed, freshly elected House and Senate members are already arriving in D.C. for orientation sessions and finding places to live and hiring staff for their exciting new adventure. But in the meantime, the outgoing 119th Congress is fully empowered to conduct business, with the now-repudiated GOP trifecta still in place. This so-called lame-duck session begins today — and it could be very consequential. It will also feel ghostly in important ways. House Speaker Mike Johnson, who isn’t even bothering to compete in this week’s GOP leadership elections for the next Congress, will hold onto his gavel (assuming he doesn’t decide to resign as Speaker) and preside over potentially big happenings before he reenters the obscurity whence he emerged just over three years ago. (“I’m sorry that the voters made the wrong choice,” he told reporters on Monday.) Here’s what is or could be on tap now that the lame duck is officially on.
The Impeachment of Pete Hegseth

In September, renegade GOP congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who is himself a lame duck after being purged by Trump, filed an impeachment resolution aimed at Secretary of Defense (or as the administration calls him, Secretary of War) Pete Hegseth alleging illegal executive overreach in his pursuit of an equally illegal Iran War. Under the arcane rules of the House, this is a “privileged” resolution that goes straight to the floor for a vote on an expedited timetable. Johnson managed to avoid this vote in September by adjourning the chamber prematurely (though giving endangered members extra time for campaigning, which they clearly needed, was the principal motive), but it will begin the lame-duck session at the top of the queue, triggering a vote this very week unless Republicans can find some way to delay it. (A temporary adjournment is always possible.)

But if and when the vote comes, the odds are very high Hegseth will find himself behind the eight ball. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says he is a “hard yes” on doing this, and every House Democrat is expected to vote for impeachment, given the partywide belief that ending the Iran War is the most immediate mandate Democrats were given by the midterm electorate. It will take only two Republicans other than Massie to pass the resolution and trigger a Senate impeachment trial with absences among defeated Republican members being a strong possibility. Even if it’s somehow stopped or delayed now, a Hegseth impeachment will become a slam-dunk once the new Democratic majority takes office in January. Trump may have to choose between going to the mats for his erratic, testosterone-loving war fighter (which he seemed inclined to do during his 60 Minutes interview with Ross Douthat) and ushering him out to avoid an early the confrontation.

If Hegseth is impeached, the Senate trial would occur during the lame-duck session, sucking up precious time and attention needed for other urgent matters. It’s very unlikely that the necessary 20 Senate Republicans can be found to convict Hegseth of impeachment articles, but it could increase pressure on Trump to get rid of this particular problem and possibly become a factor in broader bipartisan negotiations over the Iran War.
Another Government Shutdown?

It’s not as immediate as the move to impeach Hegseth, but both parties in Congress have to deal with a December 11 deadline for extending or replacing the stopgap funding bill signed by Trump on September 8 that kept the federal government operating past the midterm elections. Even without their new majority, Democrats will be able to block government funding via a Senate filibuster. Preliminary bipartisan negotiations on a new funding bill prior to the midterms went nowhere because of predictable and longstanding party differences over the relative level of Defense and non-Defense spending, dramatized by Trump-Hegseth demands for a massive $1.5 trillion Defense buildup. Now Democrats from every party faction are promising to use their spending powers to end or at least wind down the Iran War.

While there has been no announcement of strategic intentions from Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer on their willingness to countenance a government shutdown as part of this effort, it’s significant that the top House Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, told Politico, “Democrats will absolutely not fund Trump’s war of choice with Iran that has increased costs on American families and made us less safe.” Appropriators hate government shutdowns like sin itself, so the fact that DeLauro is talking tough could mean a tough Christmas for federal employees. It’s always possible Democrats agree to another short stopgap bill and take up the fight again in January, when they will have even more leverage over appropriations, but they will face grassroots and activist pressure to take a stand right now.
Leadership Elections (which could get heated)

The two parties in Congress have different deadlines, and different prospects, for choosing their future leadership. Mike Johnson is officially on his last legs, and this week House Republicans are expected to choose between current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and long-time conservative firebrand Jim Jordan to succeed him. The outcome could signal whether what’s left of House Republicans are inclined towards accommodation to reality (Scalise) or last-ditch obstruction of the new Democratic majority (Jordan), but whoever wins is likely to continue the House GOP’s subservience to Trump’s orders. So far no organized opposition to Senate GOP leader John Thune has emerged, indicating that he’s not being blamed for the party debacle on November 3. But some hard-core MAGA senators like Rick Scott and Mike Lee are talking about delaying their leadership election to assess prospects for dumping Thune.

House Democrats are holding their leadership election on November 18 or 19, and while there is desultory talk among progressives about dumping Hakeem Jeffries, it’s not very promising. In theory Chuck Schumer might be more vulnerable to a challenge given his advanced age and less than sterling communications skills, and Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is said to be open to taking him on, but it still remains unlikely given the party’s huge 2026 gains under Schumer’s direction.

Aside from fending off Hegseth’s impeachment and following Trump’s directions on a possible government shutdown, Republicans need to decide what they want to accomplish before they hand over power to their enemies in January. In addition to final Trump judicial confirmations before Democrats gain the power to block them, there are three significant “holdover” issues they could decide to prioritize: a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill still under construction that people in both parties consider a way to show action on “affordability” concerns; Senate-passed college sports legislation being backed by Trump but that’s opposed by unions and many Black lawmakers; and an always-difficult defense authorization bill setting long-term strategy and funding levels for the military.

But there is also considerable MAGA pressure for lame-duck Republicans to enact another big and consequential budget reconciliation bill in the final days of their trifecta, as GOP Senator Bernie Moreno signaled before the elections:

“We will do a reconciliation bill — one way or the other we will,” the Ohio Republican told reporters at the Capitol, referring to the simple-majority budget process. “Obviously, if we lose control of Congress, it’ll be the Last Supper.” Such a bill, he added, would be “giant” and would include “all the Republican priorities that we can get done.”

Those might include another defense or ICE spending build-up; cuts in domestic programs; tax goodies for favored GOP constituencies; or even the “election integrity” measures the courts would not let the administration pursue immediately prior to the midterms. Technically speaking Democrats can’t do anything to stop a budget reconciliation bill, but time will be short, GOP discipline would be critical, and all sorts of distractions could derail the whole effort. Rick Scott, the Senate’s leading MAGA zealot, wants Republicans to devote every moment to exploiting their fast-dissipating power:

But Scott will unquestionably defer to Trump on this key strategic decision. Ironically, how “lame” the lame duck session turns out to be will depend heavily on the president who led Republicans to their midterm debacle. He is after all, now the Lame Duck in Chief.

items.title: The Spy Who Loved Jensen Huang: Everything We Know So Far
items.description: Artificial-intelligence giant Nvidia announced on Sunday that it has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang after he admitted to the board that he’d had an affair with a business executive whom the U.S. government believes is a spy for Ch
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: Artificial-intelligence giant Nvidia announced on Sunday that it has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang after he admitted to the board that he’d had an affair with a business executive whom the U.S. government believes is a spy for China. In a companywide letter, Huang told employees: “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He also said he supports the investigation “and will cooperate fully” and that “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

Given Nvidia’s dominance in the AI industry, its clout on Wall Street, Huang’s ties to Donald Trump, and the whole suspected Chinese spy at the center of it all, this is obviously not your typical workplace affair.

So what has the president said about all this? Have Democratic congressional leaders, what with their newfound power come January, weighed in? How has the stock market reacted? Has Huang’s family spoken out? Here’s what we know so far.

Huang is the Taiwan-born co-founder of Nvidia, which he started in 1993 with two friends. (They came up with the idea for the company at a Silicon Valley Denny’s.) Today Huang is one of the most powerful industry players, having “transformed Nvidia from a maker of video-game graphics chips into the world’s dominant supplier of AI processors.” Nvidia has a market capitalization of roughly $4.5 trillion. Huang himself was worth approximately $150 billion prior to the Sunday revelation; he lost a few billion to his name after the affair went public. He’s known for wearing black leather jackets, which have been purchased as collector’s items.

Alice Huang (or Huang Le) is a business executive whom U.S. intelligence began electronically surveilling more than a year ago. “Information on Ms. Huang’s background is largely absent from the Chinese internet,” according to the New York Times, which noted that an online biography said “she worked in China as a TV reporter before becoming a top executive at a Singapore-based data center company that had become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia,” buying “more than $4.8 billion in chips since June 2024.”

That company, Megaspeed, has been under investigation by the Commerce Department since last year “for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China.” The Times reported that “as Megaspeed’s chip purchases rolled in, Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang” — who are unrelated — “began spending time together.”

In June 2024, he joined her at a bar in Taipei after a local technology trade show. They drank whiskey alongside other A.I. executives. A year later, they dined at a restaurant in Taipei with other executives. Taiwanese media captured her giving him a kiss on the cheek and standing behind him as he spoke to journalists.
Officials in Washington were said to be intensely worried about the relationship, especially given that they were “already alarmed by the large volume of Megaspeed’s purchases.”
Who is Huang apologizing to in his companywide letter?

The Nvidia CEO has been married to Lori Huang since 1985. They met at Oregon State University, where he has said he got into her lab group and attempted to impress her with his brain. “I walked up to her and said, ‘Do you want to see my homework?’” he recalled in 2024. “Then I made her a promise: ‘If you do homework with me every Sunday, I promise you, you’ll get straight A’s.’”

On the podcast How I Built This, Juang said that while he was building Nvidia, “Lori took care of everything and I don’t remember her complaining one time. That’s the gift that she gave me.” (It is not clear if the couple have a prenup. California, where they live, is a community-property state that dictates all assets and debts acquired during the marriage are divided equally in a divorce.)
The Huangs have two children, Madison and Spencer, who work for Nvidia, as does their son-in-law.
Did the Nvidia CEO say anything publicly about the relationship before Sunday?
Indeed he did, telling Bloomberg News last month that any interactions he had with Ms. Huang had been “related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.”
Did anyone in Washington sound any really loud alarms about the affair?

As it happens, Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly “oversaw the drafting of the highly classified memo this past spring warning top Trump administration officials that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.” That memo, per the Times, was written after U.S. officials determined Ms. Huang “had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security.”

The memo was reportedly sent to officials with high-level security clearances prior to a trip the president took to China in May, and it may or may not have played a role in Jensen Huang not initially being invited to join Trump, per the Times.

Huang was initially left off the list of major business and tech executives invited to join Mr. Trump in China. It is unclear whether the exclusion was connected to the memo. By that point, a number of people inside the administration were concerned about Mr. Huang’s influence on the president’s policy of only lightly regulating A.I., people briefed on the matter said.

After Mr. Trump saw media coverage about Mr. Huang being absent from the delegation, the president asked him to join the trip by meeting Air Force One during a layover in Alaska. The president drafted a social media post saying that it was an honor to have “the Great Jensen Huang,” and other business leaders “journeying to the Great Country of China where I will be asking President Xi, a Leader of extraordinary distinction, to ‘open up’ China so that these brilliant people can work their magic.”
“The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday.

He sure has, in his typical way, telling reporters, of Huang, “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong” and that “he dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.” (Did the president mean “everybody” has affairs with suspected Chinese spies? That “everybody” has affairs generally? Unclear.) The president also said he believes the Nvidia CEO is “an honorable guy” and “probably has an excuse for it.” He added that he did not regret not acting on earlier intelligence.

Hakeem Jeffries, who will likely become House majority leader in January, told CBS News on Monday that the matter is “a significant issue of concern.” He said there is a classified briefing being held at the White House today, where he expects the affair will be a topic of conversation. On Saturday, Democratic senator Chris Coons, who is expected to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, wrote on X that “Congress will investigate and get answers.”

Representative Michael McCaul, a Texas Republican who serves as vice-chair of the House Committee on Homeland Security, wrote on X on Saturday: “The U.S. should immediately pause the shipment of advanced AI chips to China until we can get to the bottom of this incident and ensure our national security is not being undermined.”
Huang has resisted calls for stronger government regulation on the export of advanced AI chips.
Has Elon Musk offered his two cents?
Who is running the investigation?

The company said on Sunday the board will choose an outside counsel to probe the affair and that Huang will not be part of selecting who that counsel will be. Also worth noting, per the Times: “At Nvidia, Huang is the sole public face of the company and has no clear second-in-command. He decides which projects are a strategic priority, and frequently sends short emails to individual engineers about details. Huang has said he has 60 direct reports and reviews every employee’s salary.”
Any suggestion that Huang will be replaced at the company is “comedy,” Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC on Monday.

items.title: 6 Stunning Moments From Trump’s 60 Minutes Interview
items.description: Donald Trump’s discussion with Ross Douthat on 60 Minutes, which aired Sunday night, was the most interesting interview the president has done in some time. Theoretically, Trump was on friendly turf. The conservative columnist, who joined the CBS newsmagazine
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Donald Trump’s discussion with Ross Douthat on 60 Minutes, which aired Sunday night, was the most interesting interview the president has done in some time. Theoretically, Trump was on friendly turf. The conservative columnist, who joined the CBS newsmagazine program over the summer after 17 years at the New York Times, may not be Trump’s biggest booster. But the entire show has just undergone a MAGA-y makeover under new CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss, and Douthat is a far cry from, say, recently departed CBS correspondents Anderson Cooper and Scott Pelley.

That may be why the president was relaxed and (relatively) introspective through nearly the entire interview, even as Douthat asked unusual and probing questions on topics like immigration, Trump family corruption, and forgiving your enemies.

As always, everything Trump said must be taken with a grain of salt. The interview was taped Friday afternoon, and since then, the president has already made moves that contradict what he told Douthat. But it’s still a fascinating snapshot of where Trump’s head was at the end of the Susie Wiles era and how he responds when someone respectfully pushes him to slow down and reflect on the wild things coming out of his mouth. Here are some of the most notable moments.
Trump acknowledges Republicans lost due to “bad messaging, maybe by me”

Trump started with the same explanations he’s been giving all week for the GOP’s midterms drubbing, pointing to the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot and his decision to go to war with Iran (which he defended). When Douthat pushed him to drill down on what went wrong, he eventually wound up at “I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me.”
The correct answer is actually “bad leadership, definitely by me.” But it’s unusual for Trump to admit blame at all.

The president has already reversed himself since the interview. On Truth Social on Monday morning, he baselessly suggested that Republicans lost the midterms because they were rigged, not because he did anything wrong.
Trump admits his immigration policy “might be too tough”
When asked about something he might work on with Democrats, Trump pointed to immigration and acknowlwedged that his deportation agenda was perhaps too harsh.
“I think it might be too tough, yeah,” he said. “I think ultimately that hurt me.”
Trump went on to suggest that law-abiding undocumented immigrants should maybe be able to stay in the country:

When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that’s worked there as– you know, as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress, a lotta good things, great jobs, and all of a sudden, they’re being taken outta the country, it’s tough. It’s a tough thing. But there’s a group of people that I would say on the sort of pretty far right that would like everybody taken out.

Which politician vowed to deport 11 million people or more back in 2024? Trump doesn’t remember! He may have already forgotten what he said to Douthat too. Hours after the interview was recorded, he made Stephen Miller his new chief of staff.
Trump says he’s “not necessarily” going to endorse anyone in 2028

A week ago, Trump saying he might not endorse a successor might have made J.D. Vance’s soul leave his body (well, more so than it already has). But after Tuesday, maybe it’s better if Trump keeps his 2028 opinions to himself, as he noted.

Trump said that, aside from the vice-president, he thinks Marco Rubio would be a “great” 2028 nominee and that “there’s some senators that are excellent. I know ’em all. I like ’em a lot.” He added, “I may or may not get involved. I don’t know. Maybe I’m better off not getting involved.”
Trump dismisses corruption allegations as a problem “going back to George Washington”

Trump did get a bit testy when Douthat deftly pushed him on corruption. Douthat pointed to the Trump family’s ownership of World Liberty Financial, noting that if the Bidens had a cryptocurrency company tied to the government of the United Arab Emirates, the president would have lost his mind.

Trump said the two scenarios are different because he divested from his family’s companies (“But no, you didn’t,” Douthat countered). Plus, he added, “Every president has had this problem.” Trump suggested that even Washington was sullied by his financial ties to “whatever crypto was at the time, okay?”

Trump also asserted nonsensically that he’s only getting so much flak for his corruption because he’s such a monumental historical figure. “I’m a bigger name than other presidents, whether we like it or not,” he said.
Trump reveals he’s heard “things that are very strange” about UFOs

Douthat snuck in one weird question that a lot of people want to ask: What does the president know about aliens? The president said he’s “not too much of a believer,” but it kind of sounds like he is:

I sat in the Oval Office first term and a little bit second term meeting with Air Force pilots that are really good, solid people. These are not people that you would say are conspiracy theorists. But they’re great, great pilots. They’re the real deal. And they’ve told me things that are very strange. They said that — in, in certain cases — they said yes, there’s something going on out there. Because they’re flying an F-22, which is the best there is, the fastest, the best plane that anyone’s ever seen. And something goes by them at three times their speed and it’s round. It’s not aerodynamic; it’s round.
Trump thinks, “in theory, I go to Heaven” — unless that entails forgiving his enemies

The president has been offering sporadic updates on his odds of getting past the pearly gates for several years now. When asked on his current chances, Trump said, “I’m a religious person, so in theory, I go to Heaven.”
Douthat pressed him to go deeper, asking if he’d give up on hating foes such as James Comey and Nancy Pelosi if that was his only path to Heaven.
“Honestly, Ross, can I — can I be honest?” Trump said after some deliberation. “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”
Here’s the full interview:

items.title: 17 Eye-Popping Facts About Tuesday’s Midterms
items.description: While polling largely predicted Tuesday would be a good night for the Democratic Party, few were prepared for the sheer extent of the party’s successes in the 2026 midterms — victories that extended from the U.S. Capitol to statehouses across the nation. But b
items.author: Nia Prater; Chas Danner
paragraphs: While polling largely predicted Tuesday would be a good night for the Democratic Party, few were prepared for the sheer extent of the party’s successes in the 2026 midterms — victories that extended from the U.S. Capitol to statehouses across the nation. But beyond the marquee wins of a blue Texas and Congress returning to Democratic control, the night saw some other eye-catching developments. From an Iowa Democrat who won their race despite dropping out weeks earlier to the defeat of the Republican Party’s congressional campaign head, here are some notable details you might’ve missed about the results.
The congressman who ran the House GOP’s midterms strategy lost his seat

North Carolina was home to some of the Democratic Party’s most notable wins, including Democratic governor Roy Cooper flipping Republican senator Thom Tillis’s seat and winning several U.S. House races despite a statewide gerrymander designed to prevent those wins. Most notably, one of the seats lost in the blue tsunami belonged to Richard Hudson, a 13-year incumbent who was also the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the party’s House campaign arm. Hudson, who was tasked with leading Republicans’ House campaign strategy, lost his 13th Congressional District seat to Richard Ojeda, a Democratic retired U.S. Army major.

Hudson’s loss is reminiscent of what happened to Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee chairman Sean Patrick Maloney in 2022 as the congressman lost his bid in New York’s 17th Congressional District to then–Republican state assemblymember Mike Lawler.
Cindy Hyde-Smith likely lined up her own demise

One of the most unexpected stories of the night is undoubtedly Scott Colom, the Democratic Mississippi district attorney who is on the brink of becoming the state’s first Black senator elected since Reconstruction. While the slim margin between him and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith is still being tallied (as of Friday afternoon, Colom currently leads by just under 2,000 votes), a Colom win would allow him to get a little revenge over the sitting senator.

In 2022, Colom’s nomination to be a federal judge on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi was blocked by Hyde-Smith, who refused to return her blue slip, a Senate custom that allows senators to sign off on judicial nominations for their state. With Colom being only 43 years old, it’s likely he’d still be on the bench today had Hyde-Smith let his nomination through.
Marsha Blackburn nearly lost the Tennessee governors’ race

Republican senator Marsha Blackburn is poised to make history as Tennessee’s first female governor. But her victory nearly failed to come to pass as her Democratic opponent, Memphis councilwoman Jerri Green, came within striking distance. With 95 percent of the vote in, Blackburn received 45.5 percent of the vote to Green’s 43 percent, a figure likely too close for comfort.
A Democrat almost won Bill Cassidy’s Senate seat in Louisiana

The blue tsunami that saw Democrats flip Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, and Maine was close to sweeping Louisiana away from Republicans as well. Republican congresswoman Julia Letlow, who defeated incumbent Bill Cassidy following an endorsement by President Trump, just barely held on to become Louisiana’s next senator. With 95 percent of the vote tallied, Letlow stands at 50.9 percent to her opponent, Democratic farmer Jamie Davis, who received 49.1 percent, a nearly two-point difference.
Early votes for Talarico, Cooper, and Ossoff surpassed their opponents’ total votes.

Texas’s official election results showed James Talarico received 4,397,474 early votes. The figure is actually larger than the total number of votes Ken Paxton received overall at 4,249,373, a difference of 148,101. The incoming senator-elect could’ve made history even with just the early vote. NBC’s Decision Desk discovered similar dynamics for Georgia senator Jon Ossoff as well as North Carolina senator-elect Roy Cooper, who received more votes in early voting than his Republican opponent, Michael Whatley, won in total.
The Indiana GOP’s resistance to gerrymandering may have saved them from a blowout

Indiana Republicans found themselves out of President Trump’s good graces as the state legislators resisted a push from the White House to adopt an aggressive gerrymander aimed at making the state’s districts redder ahead of the midterm elections. But as one Indianapolis city councilor noted on social media, Democrats likely would’ve swept through the state had the gerrymander gone through:
One of the admirals Pete Hegseth purged won Nancy Mace’s House seat in South Carolina

Last summer, Vice-Admiral Nancy Lacore, then the chief of the Navy Reserve, was fired from her role by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth as part of his ongoing purge of U.S. military leadership and top officials. On Election Night, Lacore won her race to be the next congresswoman from South Carolina’s First Congressional District, flipping a seat previously held by outgoing Republican congresswoman Nancy Mace.
An Iowa Democrat won the race he dropped out of

On September 7, Eric Armstrong, a Democratic candidate for Iowa’s House District 20, announced that he would be stepping down from his campaign, citing “personal health issues that require my full attention and immediate care.”

By Election Day, Armstrong somehow found himself a winner, emerging victorious in a race he dropped out of and defeating Republican Keith Jones by about ten points, per the Des Moines Register. The surprise result was, no doubt, a signal of the strength of Democratic enthusiasm in Iowa, a wave that helped carry Josh Turek, whose seat Armstrong won, to the U.S. Senate.
In an interview with the New York Times following his unexpected win, Armstrong said he was “going to do my best to represent” his district even amid his continuing health issues.
The top Republican in the California Assembly almost lost his seat to a Democrat who spent nothing
A progressive is crushing a six-term House GOP incumbent by a 2-1 margin in central California

David Valadao, a moderate representing the heavily Latino 22nd Congressional District in California’s Central Valley, has served six terms in the House and is the sole remaining Republican in Congress who voted to impeach President Trump.

He’s only once before lost his seat, in the 2018 midterms, by 862 votes. (He then won the seat back in 2020.) This year, with 57 percent of the vote in, Democratic challenger Randy Villegas is beating Valadao by more than 33 percentage points.
Data centers were rejected in 40 out of 41 ballot measures

While data centers emerged as a top issue among voters relatively late in the election cycle, a clear message was sent on Tuesday as states across the country approved measures limiting the facilities. The Washington Post reports that voters in at least 38 different jurisdictions voted in favor of ballot measures that placed restrictions on data centers or even outright banned them from their communities.
According to a CNBC analysis, only one of 41 ballot measures across ten states centered on restricting data centers failed.
Democrats will now run the elections in 16 out of 17 swing states
Democrats made significant gains in secretary of State races Tuesday night, keeping the chief election-official roles in party hands ahead of the 2028 election cycle. Bolts magazine has a breakdown:

Out of the states that elected a secretary of state this fall, Democrats swept the swing states, and then some. They won all blue states, plus every state that Trump had won by up to 12 percentage points just two years ago.
They also secured the power to choose who runs elections in many other states — such as Texas, or Pennsylvania — where the secretary of state is appointed.

Out of all 17 states with the tightest 2024 presidential margins, the only one where the GOP is on track to control election administration moving forward is North Carolina — and that’s only because of a Republican power-grab in late 2024 to seize control from the Democratic governor.
75 percent of Americans will now be governed by Democrats
The vast majority of Americans will have a Democratic governor after the party flipped seats in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada, and Iowa while holding onto power in states like Wisconsin and Michigan.
Two teen Democrats won state races

Two young Democrats were among Tuesday’s winners in their state races. Maricopa County, the fourth-most-populous county in the nation, just elected 19-year-old Sebastian Matta to become the next Superior Clerk for Maricopa County. Matta, a student at Arizona State University, defeated his opponent, Republican Jeff Dial, to win the seat.

In Massachusetts, Daniel Darris-O’Connor, also 19, defeated incumbent Republican state representative Marc Lombardo, who has held his seat since 2011. Darris-O’Connor was elected to his hometown’s select board last year, becoming its youngest member.
Joe Manchin went 0-6 in midterm endorsements

Joe Manchin, the former Democratic senator turned independent, has focused his post-congressional life on helping to support and elect independent political candidates largely through the Independent Leadership Council, which he founded with his daughter. Through the organization and in his personal capacity, Manchin expressed his support for a number of candidates across the political spectrum.

In the Senate, he said he supported former congressman Mike Rogers in Michigan and went on to endorse Maine Republican senator Susan Collins’s reelection bid, as well as Seth Bodnar’s Independent campaign in Montana. Then in the House, Manchin endorsed long-standing moderate Republican Brian Fitzpatrick’s reelection bid in Pennsylvania as well as Independents like Michael Bridgford in Iowa and the reelection campaign of California incumbent Kevin Kiley, who left the Republican Party earlier this year. But all six candidates would go on to lose their races.
Morris County. NJ just elected its first Democratic commissioner since 1973

Democratic Morristown councilman Christopher Russo defeated incumbent Republican County Commissioner Tayfun Selen, making Russo the first Democratic county commissioner on Morris County’s board of commissioners in 1973. According to the New Jersey Globe, the last Democrat elected to the board was Doug Romaine, who defeated a Republican incumbent on a wave of Republican backlash following the Watergate scandal.
Democrats will soon control more state governments than Republicans
In addition to their federal gains, the Democratic Party strengthened its presence in state legislatures across the country. Politico breaks it down:

Democrats flipped more than 500 state legislative seats and won control of at least a dozen legislative chambers, establishing new governing trifectas in Michigan, Arizona, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Nevada. They captured legislative chambers in Texas, Georgia and North Carolina — states long dominated by Republican lawmakers. And they picked up even more legislative seats in deep blue strongholds like New York, California and Illinois.
Democratic strategist Matt McDermott says the party is poised to hold 22 trifectas in state governments nationwide:
- Hegseth Impeachment Headlines a Messy Lame-Duck Session
