items.title: Dior Enlists Rihanna and Robert Pattinson for a Hand-Drawn Holiday Fantasy
items.description: It is never too early to get into the holiday spirit. Everyone knows the Christmas season can be stressful, but the more you prepare ahead of time, the more you can enjoy all the magic. So while it may seem too early to start considering your gifts, in reality
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: It is never too early to get into the holiday spirit. Everyone knows the Christmas season can be stressful, but the more you prepare ahead of time, the more you can enjoy all the magic. So while it may seem too early to start considering your gifts, in reality, you’ll just be saving your future self a lot of stress. And luckily, the brands are, once again, ahead of schedule, already rolling out their holiday content for our benefit. Ferragamo, Dior, Chanel, and more have released their 2026 holiday campaigns, and the images are getting us in the yuletide mood. So while the leaves may just now be falling off the trees, soon they’ll be on the ground, covered in snow—and there’s no time like the present to dive into the 2026 holiday campaigns.

“It was a quiet night at the atelier at 30 Avenue Montaigne,” begins the animated short film, Christian Dior’s Night in Color. The seven-minute movie, directed by award-winning French filmmaker Sylvain Chomet and narrated by Robert Pattinson, tells a fictional story that weaves together key moments from the fashion house’s history.

Jonathan Anderson was inspired by the cinema’s transition from black-and-white to Technicolor for the Dior cruise 2027 collection. Christian Dior’s Night in Color once again explores that shift. The narrative follows Christian Dior as he rushes to make a dress for Marlene Dietrich and her Technicolor film.

The cast is filled with familiar voices: Louis Garrel as Dior, Josh O’Connor as a talking chair, LaKeith Stanfield as a director. Greta Lee pops up as a busy atelier bee, and Rihanna even makes an appearance as the star atop a Christmas tree. “Shine bright...like a Christmas tree,” she exclaims.

In the end, Dior is able to create a dress—the famed Junon style—and deliver it to Dietrich just in time. It’s a heartwarming story, filled with nostalgia, whimsy, and craft—all hallmarks of both Dior and the holiday season.

Louis Vuitton’s 2026 holiday campaign is an ode to those who travel for their winter festivities. The Oliver Hadlee Pearch images take place in a train station, the setting of magical reunions and exciting departures.

The campaign captures the last five minutes before a grand departure. Stories unfold on the platform and within the train cars. Friends reunite, children play, travelers rush around carrying their Louis Vuitton luggage. It’s a suspended moment that perfectly embodies Louis Vuitton’s Art of Travel.

Burberry is opening the doors to a gorgeous English country home for its 2026 holiday campaign, inviting Pierce Brosnan, Dwyane Wade, Gabrielle Union, and more friends of the brand to gather for an afternoon of winter fun.
“We wanted to celebrate 170 years of Burberry with a proper party,” said Daniel Lee, Burberry chief creative officer. “Family, friends, great gifts, and everyone dressed up.”

Set at Longleat House in Wiltshire—a historic, stately home built in the 16th century—the images capture a festive celebration of party games, gift exchanges, and, of course, a whole lot of Burberry check.

It’s time! The holiday season is officially upon us, which means Queen of Christmas Mariah Carey has taken the spotlight—and her rightful place on her holiday throne. Of course, preparations must be made, and the Gucci team is on it, making sure everything is ready for Carey to ring in all the merriment.

The iconic singer stars in Gucci’s holiday campaign video, directed by Harmony Korine and set to Carey’s hit song, “All I Want for Christmas Is You.” Accompanying images star friends of the house as they wait in anticipation of Carey’s arrival.

When Carey arrives at the party, she does so in Gucci’s new Butterfly special collection. Inspired by the insect, the collection embodies the iridescence of the butterfly, while paying homage to Carey’s signature motif and her 1997 album, Butterfly.

Chloé’s latest campaign is festive, but not in an obvious way. Shot by David Sims and starring friend of the house, Claudia Schiffer, the images capture a nocturnal spirit through a cinematic, after-dark atmosphere.
Schiffer’s enduring personal allure is reflected in the imagery, as her natural presence and distinctive character bring a singular perspective to the campaign.

Fashion, humor, personality, and New York energy collide in Marc Jacobs’s winter 2026 campaign, Let It Joy. Actor Meg Stalter stars in the campaign video, holed up in her hotel room during a snowstorm. When Mel Ottenberg invites Stalter over for a party, there’s only one issue: She doesn’t know his room number.

Chaos ensues as Stalter attempts to locate the party. Luckily, the comedienne does not give up and is able to follow the music. She eventually makes it to the holiday bash, ready to celebrate in her black Marc Jacobs shift dress alongside New York personalities and cultural figures like Knicks center Andre Drummond and model and actress Kai Schreiber.
Tory Burch presents a guide to the holidays, along with tips to celebrate the upcoming season the Tory way: with optimism, joy, and presents piled high.

Tory Burch’s holiday campaign comes with a list of rules to follow. Number two pertains to gifting (and receiving), suggesting we give generously and react dramatically. Number four urges us to embrace the festive spirit, while the last rule is a bit of a warning: Pace yourself; it’s a long holiday season ahead.

Alongside the tips, you’ll find more holiday inspiration in the form of images from Anthony Seklaoui. The shots are full of beaded sparkle, cozy knits, and community—the perfect recipe for a joyous season.

Michael B. Jordan, Yerin Ha, and Inde Navarrette star in the David Yurman 2026 holiday campaign. The three actors gather in snow-covered Washington Square Park for shots that capture the joy of togetherness and the magic of the holiday season in New York City.

Jordan and Ha face off in a spirited card game, while Navarrette searches for the perfect holiday gift. Of course, all three are bedecked in David Yurman designs, including 18-karat gold cable bracelets and pieces from the brand’s Starburst and Armory collections.

Fresh off her buzzy turn in You Can See Everything, Amanda Seyfried has returned to New York from Texas, just in time for the holiday season. The actor is Tiffany & Co.’s newest House ambassador and the star of its holiday campaign, “Love Is a Gift.”

As part of the campaign, Seyfried acts in a short film, “You & Me,” which tells the story of two different Christmas celebrations: one taking place in the present day, and one in 1992. Between these two moments passes a Bird on a Rock ornament, originally gifted decades ago and still a prized possession all these years later. It’s a story of tradition, holiday memories, and the connection between generations.

“I’m thrilled to join the Tiffany & Co. family as their newest House ambassador and to be part of a campaign that celebrates love, family, and the traditions we carry with us through generations,” Seyfried said in a statement. “‘You & Me’ captures beautifully how a meaningful gift can hold memories and become part of a family’s story. It was incredibly special to bring that idea to life with Tiffany this holiday season.”

The holidays are all about family, so it makes sense that Kim Kardashian enlisted her very famous sisters to star in the Skims Holiday campaign. Shot by frequent Kardashian collaborator Nadia Lee Cohen, the campaign takes inspiration from nostalgic holiday portraits, placing Kim, Kourtney, Kylie, Khloe, and Kendall in scenes you may recall from your own home videos.

The sisters are styled in pieces from the Skims holiday shop, wearing outfits with varying degrees of coziness. Khloe and Kourtney are covered head-to-toe in their respective patterned onesie and red long johns. Kylie and Kendall, meanwhile, show off more skin in bras boasting classic holiday prints. All the girls don retro glam—bouffants and old-school glasses. The result is a vintage scene with no clear time stamp. But it doesn’t matter, because Santa still clearly approves.

Gigi Hadid, Louisa Jacobson, and more gather in a grand townhouse to celebrate the holidays. The polished wood walls are covered in wreaths, the tree is bedecked with ornaments, and everyone is dressed in Miu Miu.

The wardrobe highlights contrasts between lifestyle archetypes and seasonal themes. Silk dresses are paired with upcycled knits and sportswear-inspired zip-front blousons. Cropped sweaters reveal button-down shirts, and utilitarian cotton canvas separates are layered over sequined bralettes.

But the models are not alone in this uptown space. They are joined by plush toy bears, rabbits, geese, and more. Treated like treasured guests, these additions provide whimsy to the scene, a composed portrait of bourgeois behavior subverted by humor and play.

Friendly furry creatures are not unique to the Miu Miu campaign this season—they pop up in the Prada world as well. This time, though, the woodland pals are hand-drawn by a team of artists led by cinematic animator John Pomeroy.

Sadie Sink gets down on the ground with a trio of mice to admire a patterned, calf-hair loafer. Maya Hawke faces off against a sly fox as she braves the elements of a frozen setting. There is a whimsy to these wintertime scenes, which emphasizes Prada’s humanity and a connection to craft that lies at the heart of the brand’s approach to creation.

Kris Jenner is the matriarch of the Ferragamo family in the brand’s 2026 holiday campaign, The Joy of Loving. “Ferragamo is all about family,” says creative director Maximilian Davis. “And when I design, I am always thinking about that, too: how a collection can be worn by different generations, but also how pieces you love will be held onto and passed down through them.”

The momager stars as the director of a fictional film, leading screen tests featuring the campaign’s various faces. There’s Paloma Elsesser and her brother, Sage; girl group The Womack Sisters; and Sofia Testino with her dog, Syko. Actress Joan Chen is joined by her daughter, Audrey Hui, while acting coach Nancy Banks poses with her son, actor Benny Buckley.

The campaign connects back to the roots of Ferragamo, and founder Salvatore Ferragamo’s original desire to build a better life for his family through his love of invention and creativity. “One of the founding values of Ferragamo has always been of beauty that develops from craftsmanship, humanity, and joy,” says Salvatore’s son, Leonardo Ferragamo. “This campaign is telling that story.”

Loro Piana invites you to a weekend at the cabin, where the elegantly falling snow outside matches the chic inhabitants’ wardrobes. Models are dressed in the brand’s holiday collection, an expression of style that plays out across textures, hand-finished prints, exclusive patterns, and elaborate stitches.
Loro Piana’s usually muted color palette is realized once again, this time in the form of dark greens and earthy browns. They are highlighted with pops of winter-white and marigold.

Warm jersey tops and trousers form the foundations of these après-ski looks. On top, classic Loro Piana outerwear like the Spagna jacket and Konny vest are crafted in wool and finely detailed with needlework; the wearer stays warm while also making an enviable sartorial impression.

Chanel is hitting the slopes for its 2026 Coco Neige collection. Bright-red knits and colorblocked puffers stand out against snow-capped mountains. The images have a retro flair, but the clothing is distinctly modern.
A snowball fight adds even more joy to this already playful campaign, while penguin and polar bear-shaped purses and earrings provide the perfect amount of whimsy.
Shearling caps keep ears warm, while winter whites are embraced with aplomb. It’s a reminder that dressing for warmth does not mean sacrificing style or charm.

Indulge in your sweet tooth with Dior’s 2026 holiday campaign, which sees the brand’s famous 30 Montaigne store reimagined as a sugar-dusted gingerbread house. Anya Taylor-Joy and Deva Cassel star in a joyous musical video. The house’s ambassadors prance around the store, snacking on Dior cookies, spritzing the brand’s famed fragrances, and trimming the icing-lined cookie Christmas tree.

items.title: Ads in Chatbots Have Arrived. Here’s What’s Working—and What’s Not
items.description: Anthropic is holding firm on the pledge made in its Super Bowl commercial this year to keep Claude ad-free. The company’s recent IPO filing didn’t even mention the possibility of selling ads to make money from the AI chatbot. It’s easy to maintain the high gro
items.author: Paresh Dave
paragraphs: Anthropic is holding firm on the pledge made in its Super Bowl commercial this year to keep Claude ad-free. The company’s recent IPO filing didn’t even mention the possibility of selling ads to make money from the AI chatbot. It’s easy to maintain the high ground with about $112 billion in investor cash.

The chatbot industry, though, may find selling ads necessary to defray the high costs of generating AI responses. OpenAI is all in, with over 100,000 customers advertising in ChatGPT since ads debuted there in February. Last week, Google expanded ads in its search chatbot AI Mode to 10 more countries beyond the US and declared that users “find them highly relevant.” Advertisers are far from satisfied with the experience, but they expect it to improve.

Ads stand to be particularly vital for the long-term viability of niche chatbot platforms, which can’t rely on the same degree of venture capital largesse as the top AI labs or the massive revenues of tech giants. I recently spoke with Koah Labs, one of a number of new ad technology companies focused on AI experiences. The San Francisco startup markets itself as bringing ads to over 200 apps, such as DeepAI, which offers tools for creative queries, and Liner, which focuses on providing citations in AI answers. It works with brands like telehealth giant Hims and flower delivery service UrbanStems.

Koah has attracted just a tenth of the advertisers OpenAI has, but CEO Nic Baird still believes he’s getting a good sense of what’s working and what’s fuzzy as chatbots take over from traditional search engines—and what their rise will mean for your AI experiences.

Ads composed partly by AI rather than fully by a human generate double the clicks, Baird says. It’s difficult to assess exactly why, but AI-generated marketing copy likely feels more natural next to the output of an AI model.

Because ads shown by Koah are grounded in product details and imagery supplied by the advertiser, users don’t seem to be encountering AI-hallucinated, erroneous information. But some advertisers, such as drugmakers, face government requirements on what they must—or cannot—say in ads, Baird says. These companies default to more human control over their ads, generating weaker results, according to Baird.

Since ads with dull messages or that feel like clutter could drive users away, the onus is on ad tech companies to find a middle ground that’s engaging to users without triggering risk-averse brands. That balance might be harder to strike when a human is out of the loop.

Google searches for “help with stress” are likely to bring up ads for therapists. Chatbots can get more creative, in Baird’s view. For instance, ads for spas have performed well within Koah’s network when shown after users’ prompts related to “stress,” he says.

The key difference, according to Baird, is that Koah can select and customize the ad based on “not only the prompt, or the Google search, but also the response from the AI platform, which brings context from the rest of the conversation thus far.” In addition, chatbot prompts tend to be at least double the length of Google queries, giving Koah more information to determine a relevant ad.

Baird claims users are accustomed to navigating through multiple topics within a chatbot conversation, which could make them more receptive to adjacent marketing than they are in traditional search. Koah says users are clicking on about 3 percent of ads, about on par with the performance of the more mature Google ads system.

When called on to show an ad, Koah generally receives a user’s entire conversation up to that point to help inform what it displays. While traditional search queries generally look for specific information, people often use chatbots as not just conversation partners but confidants. It’s unclear whether users will accept the privacy trade-offs that come with personalized chatbot ads as they begin to proliferate.

Baird says Koah anonymizes the queries it receives and stores them in a de-identified way, but he declined to comment any further on the data collection and storage. While acknowledging that personalization can become intrusive, he argues that there are benefits for users and advertisers alike as the tech matures. Nonsensitive information about chatbot discussions, for instance, could inform personalized content on the page that loads after an ad click. Perhaps someone expressed interest in a specific feature, or the AI model didn’t highlight a particular downside of a competing product. The advertiser could fill in the gap.

Koah doesn’t have data on whether people actually want these customized pages, but the tech industry has long argued that people prefer when ad experiences feel relevant. Having the conversation history also could benefit advertisers when Koah enables retargeting, or repeating, an ad to the same user.

By Koah’s estimate, one out of every four chatbot queries about a retailer or brand concerns a return, exchange, or other support issue. Baird believes chatbots provide an opportunity not replicated easily elsewhere for advertisers to address what they might politely call a “customer success” matter.

He expects manufacturers and retailers will eventually target disappointed customers to remind them about warranties, engage them in an AI-intermediated support, and potentially steer them away from a more costly customer service interaction. It’s possible that the AI chatbot’s response may provide users with similar help, but buying an ad guarantees companies get their message across.
The ideal outcome is users reaching resolution they can live with more swiftly than through other means. In the worst case, it's a wasted ad buy and a more irate consumer.

None of the apps Koah currently serves ads in offer users AI agents that can shop on their own. However, apps like Instinct and Meta’s Muse are starting to take over shopping chores for some users. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently said Muse could become the company’s biggest source of revenue but suggested it would come from transaction fees rather than ads.
That doesn’t mean advertising will be entirely cut out from bot-dominated ecommerce, with initial studies suggesting that ads could influence AI agents.

Baird expects an opportunity to give “the user's agent the best possible recommendation, and that’s going to be a combination of a great discount, a really relevant product,” and an easy digital path to make the purchase. The chatbot must make “abundantly clear” to the agent what content is sponsored or else risk losing user trust, Baird says.

It’s also possible the chatbot ad market fizzles out before agents take hold if more AI developers adopt Anthropic’s stance. Kevin Baragona, CEO of DeepAI, says while ad revenue has been meaningful, he’s not committed to it because the experience just doesn’t feel right yet in terms of privacy, design, and more.
“I don’t think the ads are working terribly well for anyone,” he says.
This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

items.title: Finding New Drugs Is Laborious. This AI Startup Is Skipping The Lab Work
items.description: A new British startup believes that artificial intelligence is the key to speedrunning the slow and temperamental process of drug design.
items.author: Joel Khalili
paragraphs: A new British startup believes that artificial intelligence is the key to speedrunning the slow and temperamental process of drug design.

Potential Sciences plans to build large-scale chemical datasets by using basic principles of physics to simulate interactions between atoms, then small molecules, then complex amino acids and proteins. With that data, it’s betting it can train AI models and prediction systems capable of identifying highly targeted drugs for specific diseases, bypassing costly and time-consuming lab experimentation.

“We want molecules that are never going to work in the clinic to fail fast,” Hatem Helal, Potential Sciences founder and CEO, tells WIRED. “That means having better predictors of how they will behave as they interact with human biology.”

The startup, which launched on November 5, says it has seed funding in the tens of millions of dollars from SovAI—the UK government’s AI venture capital fund—and Twin Path Ventures, among other investors. The founders declined to disclose the precise figure or valuation.

If things pan out as Potential Sciences hopes, it could pave the way for the accelerated development of new treatments for all sorts of diseases. By reducing the cost of experimentation, Helal says, the company’s approach could also make it economical for pharmaceutical companies to pursue drugs for rare conditions that have previously gone untreated.
“We want to make it possible to have more bespoke treatments for diseases—this idea that medicines can be one-off molecular combinations that are tailored to your unique human biology,” he says.
The question is whether Potential Sciences will be able to predict how well drug candidates will bind to disease-related proteins as accurately as it hopes, which would require a marked leap forward.

“I’m sure it will be an improvement,” says Peter Wolynes, a professor of chemistry at Rice University. But currently, “the engineering is at the level of the Romans, not of the Renaissance, in terms of how protein engineering is done,” he says.

Industry luminaries like Demis Hassabis, who won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for his work at Google DeepMind, have long said that advances in AI will eventually lead to momentous scientific breakthroughs, in the same way the technology has recently carved up mathematics. The hope among startups like Potential Sciences is that drug discovery will be one of the first scientific frontiers to be transformed by the technology.

At the moment, a large proportion of AI drug discovery labs are developing models on top of a single public database of 3D atomic structures—the Protein Data Bank—which researchers have expanded over decades with the results of new experiments. The problem, according to Helal, is that the dataset remains too small to train AI models advanced enough to reliably accelerate the search for viable drug candidates.

“Of all the atoms in the universe, there’s around 1060 ways that you could assemble them into molecules that you could potentially give to a human,” says Helal. “Think of drug discovery as a search problem; it’s about how fast you can navigate and prune that space into promising molecules for a particular disease.”

To address that issue, Potential Sciences is trying to construct far larger datasets made up of synthetic data, produced by simulating interactions between different chemical compounds. From far larger pools of data, the theory goes, the startup will be able to train far more advanced AI models and prediction systems.

Academics see the potential in the simulation-based approach that Potential Sciences has adopted. “If we could calculate accurately the interactions between all molecules in the cell and the fluctuations in their structure we could predict where molecules would bind and that would indeed revolutionize drug development,” says Alan Fersht, an emeritus professor of chemistry at the University of Cambridge who specializes in protein engineering. “I am optimistic that this will eventually happen.”
In receiving investment from SovAI, Potential Sciences joins fellow AI drug discovery companies Basecamp Research and Isomorphic Labs, and materials discovery startup CuspAI.

The UK government established SovAI earlier this year with a mandate to invest in British startups capable of becoming indispensable components of the global AI supply chain, affording the country vital geopolitical leverage. The fund has at its disposal roughly $800 million and the ability to offer its portfolio companies access to the UK’s national AI supercomputer.

“Coming at drug discovery from a physics angle—the physics of chemistry—sets [Potential Sciences] apart from other companies,” says Joséphine Kant, head of ventures at SovAI, who has joined the startup’s board as part of the investment. “Giving them access to computing resources, they can do this work at a scale that would be very difficult otherwise for a small startup.”

However, AI drug discovery is a crowded market. Even with a leg up from the UK government, Potential Sciences will face steep competition from a multitude of entrepreneurs and academics racing to solve the same bottlenecks from varying angles of approach.

Nor does the ability to more quickly identify promising drug candidates eliminate the cost and time required to test their safety and efficacy, meaning new treatments will continue to take a long time to come to market, regardless of advances in AI. “The cost of designing a drug is nothing compared to figuring out what it will do to mice; to really sick patients; to normal people,” says Wolynes. “In some sense, it’s not the rate-limiting phenomenon.”

As the field progresses, startups like Potential Sciences will also have to contend with the prospect that technologies able to identify effective treatments could be abused to develop highly dangerous chemicals, too. “If we can design tools that perfectly minimize toxicity, it’s a bit flip to maximize it as well,” Helal says.

Potential Sciences doesn’t yet have all the answers. The startup hasn’t settled on a way to generate revenue from the various technologies it’s developing nor decided whether to make its models freely available, given the potential for misuse. But Helal is convinced that there are few more worthwhile problems to try to remedy with AI.
“There have been many waves of promising breakthroughs that don’t quite have an impact in drug discovery,” says Helal. “It’s a fundamental, high-impact problem for us to try and solve.”

items.title: I Used NYT Cooking’s New AI-Powered Recipe Modifier, and It’s Actually Pretty Good
items.description: In an aside in the New York Times Cooking video I watched recently, where Melissa Clark made her lemony white bean soup with turkey and greens, the food reporter and recipe columnist invited viewers to leave a comment telling her what they do with the kale ste
items.author: Joe Ray
paragraphs: In an aside in the New York Times Cooking video I watched recently, where Melissa Clark made her lemony white bean soup with turkey and greens, the food reporter and recipe columnist invited viewers to leave a comment telling her what they do with the kale stems. It highlighted this sweet, funny relationship between a media brand’s personalities and its audience, a warm-casual vibe.

I am not among the multitudes in the Cooking section's commenter army, but a few days later I was very surprised to see some of them in open revolt. I was even more surprised to see why: In an iOS-only beta, the Times is now using AI to allow subscribers to modify recipes.
Below the article announcing the change on October 23, commenters loudly aired their grievances, threatening to cancel subscriptions, asking who wanted this, and how to turn it off.
After four days and 172 almost exclusively angry comments, commenting for the story was turned off.

The Times doesn't share Cooking's subscriber numbers, but NYT executive communications director Jordan Cohen said the site and app were visited 514 million times in 2025, and its YouTube channel has over 1.4 million subscribers. Reading over the section's AI plans and thinking about how many bungled attempts I'd seen to mush technology into places where it doesn't need to be in the kitchen, I guessed that I would side with the commenters. Then I tried the new AI feature, and found that it worked surprisingly well.

My writing for WIRED over the past decade has shown me again and again that adding tech to a kitchen product is risky at best. I've repeatedly watched companies try and fail: Bluetooth connections for all the appliances, apps that lean too heavily on crummy recipes, toasters with optical sensors or touchscreens that still couldn't toast particularly well. Just about anything that was part of the "smart kitchen" tended not to be very smart at all.

Developing dependable, delicious recipes is hard, expensive work that can require a whole staff. Yet skimping can hurt the brand. Two notable companies with a deep bench—The New York Times Cooking and America's Test Kitchen—are cooking content makers. Recipes, which is to say delicious, high-quality, tested recipes, are what they do.
Since AI is often a lousy chef, giving it a role in the presentation of NYT's gold mine of content is a big risk.

Earlier this year, the Times allowed AI to help with a recipe-scaling feature (modifying ingredient quantities so "serves 4" turns into "serves 6") and converting from imperial measurements to metric—cups, tablespoons, and Fahrenheit to grams, milliliters, and Celsius. Now, in the iOS-only beta, a "customize this recipe" field appears just above the ingredient list.

If you want to make banana bread but tell it you don't have a loaf pan, it'll ask you what kind of pans you do have, then modify the recipe to suit. All the changes throughout the recipe are noted in a visible red-orange text. Over several days of testing, I saw how you can do relatively simple things like swap ground pork for ground beef, or make more complicated demands like asking it to tailor things to your dietary needs. The modifications it makes are very visible throughout the recipe. If you ask it for something too out there—like turning Eric Kim's gochujang buttered noodles into a cookie—it gives you a "hard redirect" and points you to a better-suited recipe, which in this case is Kim's gochujang caramel cookies.
"We put a lot of effort into trying to tell you when not to do something if it's no longer in the spirit of the recipe," says Camilla Velasquez, the general manager of NYT Cooking.

For its recommendations, the LLM looks at the recipe itself, the Times’ ingredient substitution guide, user comments, and then what it calls AI "drawing on our expertise," in that order. Velasquez says the AI should be a helper, not the main act, noting, "You shouldn't be chatting with it."
She explains that when the Times built the AI functionality, recipe editors helped create the original rule set, then evaluated how it worked at the end.

When I ask what this means for the jobs of 60 editors, writers, video journalists, and other employees—the team that creates the recipes people use and curates the vibe readers relate to—Velasquez stresses that NYT Cooking has been "hiring more than ever" and that it has "zero intention of publishing fewer recipes."

So far, she says people are mainly using it for ingredient and equipment substitutions, along with adjusting recipes for dietary needs. "Some people use the chatbot to scale, or they'll scale to match an ingredient," giving the example of someone who had only one cup of oil for a recipe that needed more.
As a food writer whose career has taken some substantial turns due to AI recently, I wouldn't say I've been clamoring for this, but I find the Times’ measured approach works pretty well.

I started testing it out by making chicken and dumplings using a five-star Alison Roman recipe with more than 6,000 ratings. I asked the AI tool to swap out bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs for boneless, skinless breasts. It thought about it for a moment—"simmering" in AI Cooking patois—and then offered up "Chicken Breast and Dumplings," with the "breast" in the title rendered in the red-orange color that indicates a modification. Just below the title, it said it was "Joseph's version made with AI. Not tested or endorsed by the original recipe's creators." Along with those visible changes, I could also toggle back and forth between my version and the original.

Once I started cooking, things went smoothly. I'm a recipe follower, not an improviser, and the Times’ recipes are easy to follow. The modifications were too. I was also impressed by how the app flagged that the chicken breast simmering time would be reduced because it cooks faster than thighs, and since they don't render as much fat as skin-on thighs do, it added some butter to the roux. These changes were incorporated into the right places in the recipe.

It all made sense except for one bit. It suggested the shredded, cooked breast go back into the pot for about another 30 minutes while the sauce thickens and the dumplings cook. I saw this coming and, well, I wasn't going to do that to my dinner. I put a handful of shredded meat in as directed so I could see what happened and reserved the rest. The shredded bits that were in for that extra half hour weren’t bad per se, but their texture was notably less succulent than what I'd reserved and way less than thighs would be.

This was the largest issue I encountered in all of my testing. If I had been the creator of the Times' original recipe, I'm not sure how I'd feel about the option to use a breast instead of thighs, which is not unheard of, but not very common in classic chicken and dumpling recipes. Perhaps it's something that could be fine-tuned or simply not offered as an option.

From there, it was fairly smooth sailing. I had it turn a Francis Lam roasted mushroom and broccoli grain bowl into a roasted mushroom, cauliflower, and squash grain bowl. The crucifer crisscross was an easy one-to-one, but I also told it to add a pound of delicata squash. It had me slice the squash into half moons so everything would finish at the same time, then upped the total amount of olive oil. Lam's poetic voice was preserved in both versions of the recipe, telling you to heat the olive oil "until it slips around the pan like water" before adding beaten eggs for festive dish-topping egg ribbons. My buddy Dave had come by for cribbage night, and this made for an enjoyable, healthy, pregame dinner before he went on to skunk me twice.

I'd been curious how it would handle batters, and it capably transformed Yewande Komolafe’s Toasted Sesame and Scallion Waffles into a yeasted version, which, unlike the original, gets an overnight in the fridge, letting the active dry yeast get bubbly and add an appealing tang.

A friend suggested Colu Henry's pasta and chickpea stew. I swapped canned diced tomatoes I had in my pantry for whole, and asked it to "add more vegetables." It gave options in line with the recipe—carrots, celery, onion, zucchini, mushrooms, and extra greens—then put what I chose into the right spots throughout the procedure so everything went in at the right time. It made for a healthy, hearty dinner.

Having been to the Portland Fermentation Festival recently and wanting guidance on incorporating a few extra ingredients, particularly garlic, into my sauerkraut, I used the AI to modify Lidey Heuck's original, saying "add carrots, garlic, and kale," which it suggested grating, thin slicing, and mincing, respectively, all in the right-feeling proportions. It also added more salt, since I was making more kraut. The big jar is sitting next to me as I type, and while it's several days from being ready, a sniff test tells me it's on its way to being a good batch.

Finally, I turned Sue Li's peanut noodles with spicy tofu into peanut udon with tofu, whitefish, and cucumber. I started by asking it to make the original less spicy, add veggies, and "keep the tofu," but add some good-looking rockfish I found at the grocery store. Impressively, since the fish was an add-on, it had me cook it, then set it aside and wipe out the pan (!) before cooking the tofu. Since I swapped udon for the original bucatini, it customized the noodle-cooking guidance, too.

It seems pretty natural that the Cooking section ran into some resistance when launching this feature. The NYT employs some of the best recipe creators in the business. Using AI to help us make substitutions is helpful, and the way the app integrates those changes into the recipes is impressive, but this tinkering with the original is essentially a subtractive process. How many of us are going to make substitutions and land on something better than Melissa Clark, Yewande Komolafe, or Francis Lam set out to make by design?

Instead, it's saving us a trip to the store, or helping us use something we have on hand, or making it gluten-free, serving as a good and rare example of how you can use technology to make a product incrementally better.

It also sounds like the commenters’ concerns have been heard. Velasquez let me know right away when we spoke that people will be able to hide the AI feature in the app if they want. The Times is also keeping the whole thing in iOS-only beta for now, and not saying when it would be available on other platforms.

That bond that you can see between the Cooking team and its users is a pretty sweet thing. Deep down, I'm guessing the upset Cooking commenters felt worried they were going to lose some of that human connection. I hope it never goes away.

items.title: Wandrd’s Magnetic Camera Straps Are My New Favorite Accessory
items.description: More than a decade ago, Peak Design rethought the humble camera strap. This was a necessary development. When you buy a camera, manufacturers almost always toss in a chintzy, uninspired strap with their logo on it. These cheap straps have cheap mounting system
items.author: Julian Chokkattu
paragraphs: More than a decade ago, Peak Design rethought the humble camera strap. This was a necessary development. When you buy a camera, manufacturers almost always toss in a chintzy, uninspired strap with their logo on it. These cheap straps have cheap mounting systems that make it hard to quickly remove the strap from the camera when you need to, like when you're attaching your camera to a tripod or gimbal and you’d rather not have a dangling strap whacking you in the face.

Peak Design solved this with its Anchor Links system, small circular nubs you leave attached to camera eyelets that make detaching or even swapping straps easy. The quick-connect mechanism is now the de facto industry standard and has inspired countless copycats.
Now, Wandrd has outdone that design using magnets.

“We're photographers ourselves, so we're constantly ideating, tinkering, thinking of ways that things can be better,” Ryan Cope, Wandrd cofounder, tells WIRED. “A camera strap like this has been at the back of our minds for a while.”

Wandrd—known for its camera bags—launched its Magnetic Camera Strap system on Thursday. It features a circular anchor similar to Peak Design, called “Torus Links.” The anchors attach to your camera’s eyelets and are rated to carry up to 198 pounds—so unless you're bench-pressing your camera, they'll do the job. If the cord does start to wear down over time, you'll first see yellow under the black fabric—a sign you should replace the Torus Link. If it's red, you should stop using the link immediately—a warning system borrowed from Peak Design. (Wandrd offers a two-year warranty.)

Unlike Peak Design's anchors, the Wandrd anchors look like donuts, with a hole in the middle. When you attach the strap, the embedded magnets guide the Torus Link into the strap's CoreLock mechanism, which pinches into the hole to secure the camera body. The magnets make connecting a strap easier, and they keep the strap fastened to the anchor, but you can’t just pull the strap off like you’re pulling a MagSafe accessory on your phone. You’ll need to use the strap’s dual-pinch mechanism to remove it from the Torus Link, a design that’s more secure.

It’s a much faster way to connect and disconnect a strap, and that speed pays off in the field. This week, I had to photograph a product during a press briefing. Usually, I use Peak Design's Leash and, instead of taking off the strap, I bunch it up in my hand when it's not around my neck. It's not that it's hard to remove—it's just an extra step I have to think about. But Wandrd's magnetic system felt faster to unlock mid-shoot when I wanted to lower the camera for an awkward, low-angle shot, and reattaching the strap was practically instantaneous. I did the whole swap one-handed, with the magnets doing most of the work.

“I love magnets, man,” Cope says. “I love the simplicity they create—guiding things into place. You don't always have a place to put your camera down; I like that magnets help guide them and are a lot more secure, and they're also just fun.”

I have two Torus Links on my camera body, one on the right eyelet and another on the tripod baseplate. But my favorite configuration turns the strap into a single-point sling. The strap has a built-in “Torus Loop” on the buckle—clip one end directly into it to create a closed loop worn across your torso, leaving just a single magnetic connector to snap onto your camera. When you unclip the camera to shoot freely, the strap stays neatly in place across your body instead of sliding off your shoulder.

The nylon felt comfortable across my chest and near my neck—there's no padding, but that's intentional. Cope says Wandrd spent two years developing this custom “liquid nylon” tubular webbing that is softer along the edges, so it won't feel like the strap is cutting into your neck after a long day of wear. The lack of metal throughout the strap system also prevents the strap from scratching up your camera gear.

Best of all, you don't have to replace your strap to use Wandrd's system. If you have a strap you love—maybe a fancy leather strap someone gifted you—Wandrd is selling a DIY kit ($29) that lets you attach its Magnetic CoreLock system to the ends of your preferred strap. Otherwise, the strap kit comes in a 30-mm size ($69), a 15-mm “Lite" ($49), and a wrist strap ($39).
I don't know if Wandrd's system will see the same success as Peak Design's Anchor Links, but I don't see myself switching back anytime soon. Magnets are just too dang cool.

items.title: There’s a Scapegoat for Jacob Elordi’s Blond Hair
items.description: Nobody asked for a blond Jacob Elordi, and yet here we are. Elordi was photographed on a date with Kendall Jenner over the weekend where, seemingly against his will, his new bleach job was first brought to the public’s attention.
items.author: Sam Reed
paragraphs: Nobody asked for a blond Jacob Elordi, and yet here we are. Elordi was photographed on a date with Kendall Jenner over the weekend where, seemingly against his will, his new bleach job was first brought to the public’s attention.

The couple attended a performance of Paranormal Activity on Broadway, which is billed as an “immersive” experience based on the horror franchise. Romantic. Jenner and Elordi are too tall and beautiful to go truly incognito, but they both did their best to keep a low profile in all-black attire that was also on theme. In photos published by Deuxmoi, Elordi can be seen wearing a black beanie with some undeniably bleached hair peeking out underneath.

The most likely scapegoat for this sudden change of pace is, of course, Scapegoat, the Ari Aster movie Elordi is filming in New York right now. Little is known about the plot, but it’s rumored to focus on a surgeon who operates on an internet celebrity. Why exactly this needed to involve damaging Elordi’s perfectly nice head of hair remains to be seen.
God willing, all will return to normal once Scapegoat wraps. Order will be restored. Brunet Jacob Elordi will rise again.

You can save on everything from beauty and skin-care tools to home appliances and bedding. So far, retailers including Ulta, Net-a-Porter, Nordstrom, and Target have early Black Friday deals you won’t want to miss, below. Last year, Glossier, Tatcha, Gap, and more joined in on the early discounts, so check back here for updates throughout the month.
Holiday glam essentials for less
The Best Early Black Friday Beauty Deals
