items.title: Amanda Seyfried Is Posting About Her Divorce
items.description: Amanda Seyfried is still shy about discussing You Can See Everything, but she’s not afraid to post about her divorce. Seyfried, who announced in September that she and her husband, Thomas Sadoski, had been “been separated for a while,” made a pair of Instagram
items.author: Grace Klara Marshall
paragraphs: Amanda Seyfried is still shy about discussing You Can See Everything, but she’s not afraid to post about her divorce. Seyfried, who announced in September that she and her husband, Thomas Sadoski, had been “been separated for a while,” made a pair of Instagram Stories about how peaceful this breakup really is.

Seyfried reposted an Instagram Thread from Olivia Howell, the CEO of a divorce registry, arguing that “the most radical thing we can do is make divorce boring. Make it normal. Make it accessible.” The quote urged people to think of divorce as “just another life transition—like a wedding, like a graduation.” That way, Howell wrote, “the patriarchy loses one of its most effective weapons.” In case it wasn’t clear what she was talking about, Seyfried followed up that repost with a black-and-white photo of her and Sadoski embracing.

Seyfried and Sadoski were married for nine years. They met in 2016 while co-starring in an Off Broadway play, eloped in 2017, and had two children together, Nina in 2017 and Thomas in 2020. In their joint statement to People back in September, they said, “We’ve got each other forever — and it’s GOOD.” Based on her Instagram Stories, that’s more true than ever.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 9, 2026
items.description: After last night’s Scorpio new moon, expect to be tired. You may tell yourself you have no excuse for feeling so drained — that nothing major happened recently and you haven’t worked hard enough to deserve a break. But trying to muscle through exhaustion is li
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: After last night’s Scorpio new moon, expect to be tired. You may tell yourself you have no excuse for feeling so drained — that nothing major happened recently and you haven’t worked hard enough to deserve a break. But trying to muscle through exhaustion is likely to backfire. Make your decisions based on how you’re actually feeling, not how you imagine you “should” be feeling. Particularly in the early afternoon, when the moon and Mars come into conflict, taking it easy can help you avoid stress and stay on an even keel.

If you see your friends succeeding this week, part of you will be genuinely happy for them — but another part might get jealous. You’ll imagine the good things happening to them should be happening to you instead, or that their achievements somehow make you look bad in comparison. A little envy is completely normal, but make sure you don’t act on it in a way you’ll regret. Refocusing on your own goals will help you remember that you’re running your own race and that other people’s progress doesn’t stand in the way of your own.

You don’t tolerate disrespect from anyone in your life. If someone shows they don’t value your time or your opinions, then you’re not about to waste any energy on that relationship. But remember there’s a difference between maintaining healthy boundaries and expecting absolute perfection from the people in your life. Sometimes others will make mistakes or express themselves clumsily, but that doesn’t mean they don’t care. As long as they’re genuinely willing to try, give them a chance.

Today, you’ll want to avoid anything that strikes you as tedious. You’re not afraid of working hard; you just don’t want to be bored. You’re eager to be challenged, to learn something new, to try something you’ve never done before. You’re much less keen to check dull tasks off a list. But sometimes, those dull tasks are important, and if you procrastinate now, you’ll regret it later. They probably won’t take long once you actually commit to handling them, so don’t put them off any longer.

Some people wear their feelings on their sleeves, but you tend to be more private. When you’re stressed or angry, you usually keep that to yourself; you wouldn’t want to put others on the defensive. Even when you have good news, you’re thoughtful about who you share it with because you don’t want anyone to think you’re bragging. But today, you’ll only isolate yourself if you refuse to let people know what’s going on with you. You don’t have to overthink it — just say what’s on your mind.

If you feel underappreciated today, try to let it go. This might conflict with your instincts — you’ll want to speak up and highlight your talents, to make sure it’s impossible for anyone to ignore you — but you’re unlikely to make much headway. For now, be patient. Focus more on doing good work than on getting credit for it. You won’t have to wait long: If you keep showing up and making valuable contributions, the people around you will take notice soon.

As much as possible, you try to be objective in your thinking. You do your best not to let your biases override your ability to assess situations accurately. But today, you could struggle with this. Your emotions are too powerful right now for you to simply set them aside — and you’re probably better off not even trying. As long as you’re aware that you’re seeing the world subjectively and that others might have different (but no less valid!) perspectives, then you’ll do fine.

Make it a priority to enjoy yourself right now. That might mean spending time with the people you care about, relaxing quietly at home, exploring new places and activities, or sticking to the things you already know make you happy. Whatever you need at this moment, try to give it to yourself. While you shouldn’t necessarily prioritize your own enjoyment all the time, you’ve been dealing with a lot lately. For now, you deserve to do what feels good.

Today, remind yourself that not everything is about you. Some interpersonal conflicts are more about what the other person is feeling than anything you have (or haven’t) done; some problems don’t actually affect you at all (so there’s no reason for you to weigh in). Give yourself permission to step away from the issues that don’t involve you. That way, you can devote your energy to the ones where your voice and perspective will make a difference.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You struggle sometimes to reckon with the “bad” parts of your personality. You’d rather ignore your flaws than assess them head-on; it seems easier to pretend everything’s fine than to admit there are parts of yourself that need improvement. But today, try to be honest with yourself about what you’d like to work on. This doesn’t mean you should fixate on what’s “wrong” with you, nor should you try to be perfect. But look for ways you can grow as a person today.

Usually, you’re more likely to give advice than receive it. The people around you see you as someone who has life figured out, and you worry that asking for help would spoil that illusion. But today, asking for support and advice is the best thing you can do. It’ll strengthen your relationships, but more than that, it’ll actually help you solve your problems. Your friends have valuable insights to share. You have a lot to learn from them if you can put your pride aside long enough to ask.

If you’re trying to be something you’re not today, the people around you will notice. They might not know what is off, but they’ll recognize that something is different — and they’ll respond to you with hesitation or outright suspicion. So right now, focus on being yourself. Even if you fear that you’re “too weird,” or that you’re not clever enough to hold people’s attention, it’s still better to be genuine than artificial. And you’ll probably discover that your peers like your real self more than you expected.

Nobody has all the answers — but sometimes, you feel like everyone pretends to. You find yourself wondering if it’s embarrassing to have gaps in your knowledge; it feels like you’re supposed to act like you know everything, even when you have doubts. But today, be honest about your own ignorance. When you’re uncertain, admit it. When you have questions, ask them. You’ll feel so much better when you drop the pretense of knowing everything. Once you do, you’ll be able to start learning.
Buy Claire Comstock-Gay’s book, Madame Clairevoyant’s Guide to the Stars, here.

items.title: Your Childhood Horse Girl Era Is Back — In Tattoo Form
items.description: Horse girls, get ready for your redemption arc: Your childhood obsession is becoming everyone’s favorite tattoo.
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: Horse girls, get ready for your redemption arc: Your childhood obsession is becoming everyone’s favorite tattoo.

On TikTok, one video featuring a slideshow of horse tattoos, set to The Rolling Stones’ “Wild Horses,” has racked up over 350K likes. The comments are full of people showing off their own ink, from tiny herds on the backs of their arms to foot tattoos and even tramp stamps.

So, what's behind the sudden equestrian craze? Maybe it’s tied to the country music renaissance (call it the Ella Langley effect). Maybe it’s because 2026 is the Year of the Horse. Or maybe, in the age of ironic tattoos and Y2K-inspired placements, a horse just feels perfectly tongue-in-cheek.
Horses have long symbolized freedom — the idea of running wild with nothing tying you down. And who couldn’t use a little more of that energy?
Whether you galloped around in elementary school gym class or not, consider this your sign to embrace your inner horse girl. Ahead, the designs worth saving for your next tattoo appointment.

Horse tattoos are nothing new, and there’s no shortage of styles to try — traditional, fine line, abstract, you name it. But one design in particular seems to be everywhere this year: three horses galloping in a row, each at a different point in its stride. (Think of it like a flipbook.)
The lower back and hip are particularly well-suited to the design, since they give the horizontal tat plenty of room to run. Bonus points for being able to show off your new ink in low-rise jeans.

Another trendy way to try the motif? Foot tattoos are making a comeback, and a little horse is the perfect detail. Whether you place it on the side of your foot or right on top, it’s versatile: hide it when you want or flaunt it with a pair of ballet flats.

For larger designs, try something more photorealistic, like a horse rearing up on its hind legs or a close-up portrait with intricate detailing. Paired with red accents, it gets an extra dose of Wild West flair.

If cowgirl isn’t your thing, you can always lean into the fantasy aspect instead. Think winged horses and illustrations that look like they belong in a medieval storybook. If you’re ready to go full Pegasus, a procession of mythical horses makes for a pretty epic back piece.
Bottom line: A horse tattoo can be dainty or dramatic, kitschy or meaningful — there’s no wrong way to wear it. Turns out, being a horse girl was never something to grow out of.

items.title: Rachel Bloom Loves A Musical That's A Little "F*cked Up"
items.description: Callback With Rachel Bloom
items.author: Christina Amoroso
paragraphs: Callback With Rachel Bloom
The Crazy Ex-Girlfriend star and co-creator, now on Broadway in The Imaginary Invalid, talks dark comedy, complicated characters, and four works that inspire her craft.
As an actor and comedic writer, Rachel Bloom has a zest for exploring things that don’t always appear as they seem.
“I love things that are gift-wrapped in a genre that doesn’t necessarily fit the actual content,” she says. “Happy musicals that are actually quite f*cked up. Horror that’s actually quite funny.”

She’s also fascinated by absurdity and deluded characters, which makes her Broadway debut — as Toinette, a maid to a severe hypochondriac, in The Imaginary Invalid — the perfect fit for the Golden Globe-winning co-creator and star of Crazy Ex-Girlfriend. Bill Irwin’s brisk (and timely) adaptation of the 1673 Molière comedy explores medical quackery, family scheming, and the lengths people go to in pursuit of good health.
“For the most part, people want to be the hero of their own story,” she says. “And so they have justifications.”

Bloom also has another role in mind when The Imaginary Invalid wraps its run at the Todd Haimes Theatre on Nov. 22. “I’d love to play The Baker’s Wife [from Into the Woods], especially now that I am older and have a kid,” she says. “That’s actually the role that I identify with the most. I would love to do it. I’m tech avail!”
Below, for Bustle’s new series, Callback, Bloom goes deep on four influential plays and musicals and how they’ve shaped her career as an actor and writer.

Her first selection is Kander and Ebb’s iconic 1975 musical Chicago about murder and fame in the 1920s. Bloom says she fell in love with the show during middle school. “The thing that resonated with me was it combined things that felt really happy, like vaudeville, with very dark things like murder and faking a pregnancy,” she says. “I think that, as a kid, growing up in a very sunny place where everyone was really happy, I also really liked happy musical theater. I had a dark side of me as well and I couldn’t marry the two.”

Bloom credits playing Roxie Hart during her senior year of high school with shaping her development as an actor. “That show is where I learned to start taking my personal emotions and putting it into a character,” she says. “The show’s so sexual and I was a virgin in high school, but I remember singing the song Funny Honey and being like, ‘OK, well what if I’m singing this about my boyfriend?’ And I hadn’t really done that before.”

Roxie’s pursuit of fame and attention also hit home. “That whole song is unabashedly, ‘Look at me, look at me, look at me, look at me!’” she says. “And look, that’s at the core of why I went into performing — and I think at the core of why most people go into performing.”
The Goat, Or Who Is Sylvia?
Her next pick is Edward Albee’s 2000 play The Goat, or Who Is Sylvia?, in which a seemingly perfect family is thrown into chaos when the patriarch’s affair with a goat comes to light.

Bloom says she found the work at a formative moment in her life. “What I loved about it, because it was also simultaneously while I was learning comedy writing and comedy performing, was that you could take an almost sketch-like premise, right? Your husband’s f*cking a goat. It’s so insane. And treat it as real as possible and treat it deadly, with deadly realism,” she says. “I loved taking a premise that sounds so outlandish and just doing it the way that it would actually happen.”

It also brought her closer to a theater legend. “I did a workshop in college. It was with Kathleen Turner, and I chose a monologue from The Goat, Or Who is Sylvia?,” she says. “I got to get coached on that by her, and that was an unbelievable experience.”

Her third show is Avenue Q, a 2004 cult-classic musical comedy about the harsh realities of young adulthood performed with Sesame Street-style puppets. “I started listening to the soundtrack to Avenue Q when it first came out and I was instantly obsessed,” she says. “[The year] 2004 was this legendarily amazing year for theater. Avenue Q and Wicked were the same year, and actually Avenue Q won Best Musical over Wicked [at the Tonys].”

Bloom also has dreams of a revival. “I think every woman wants to play Kate Monster,” she says. “She has unbelievable songs. I mean, ‘There’s a Fine, Fine Line’ is just a really good song about a breakup. And yeah, it happens to be sung by a puppet — but what an earnestly good breakup song.”

Her final pick is Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s 1986 musical Into the Woods which imagines a set of fairy tale characters after their “happily ever afters.” In high school, Bloom played The Witch. “I’m pretty proud of the old lady voice that I was able to do,” she says. “I’m excited to be 80 and finally play the roles I want to play. There’s something that I really connect with senior citizen roles.”

Bloom says it was thrilling to get to act out The Witch’s thirst for revenge. “Because I’m a people pleaser, I don’t want to be the bad guy. I fear being seen as mean...I think that there’s a part of my rage that I still am uncomfortable expressing in earnest life because I don’t want to be seen as unstable or crazy,” she says. “Into the Woods allowed me and roles like that allow me to be angry and rageful and petty and evil in a safe space.”

items.title: Jung Kook's Calvin Klein Holiday Campaign Is So Internet Boyfriend-Coded
items.description: Jung Kook Has The Perfect Internet Boyfriend-Inspired Holiday Wardrobe
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: Jung Kook Has The Perfect Internet Boyfriend-Inspired Holiday Wardrobe
The BTS member’s new Calvin Klein campaign is the answer to your gift-giving needs.

It's Christmas come early. While finding a pair of BTS concert tickets under the tree is on every ARMY's wish list, getting a front-row look at Jung Kook in his Calvin Kleins is the gift you can enjoy right this second. And it might just give you some inspo in the process.

The youngest BTS member stars in the brand's new Holiday 2026 campaign, extending his successful partnership as a Calvin Klein global ambassador following the first buzzy collab that sold out within minutes. Launching today, Nov. 9, the collection offers a personal edit of his seasonal wardrobe. It serves as a cheat sheet for anyone needing gift ideas for their partners, family members — or even yourself. Think cozy knits, timeless denim silhouettes, and effortlessly cool staples.

“There are certain Calvin Klein styles that I always come back to — especially the denim,” Jung Kook says about his capsule in the official press release. (Can confirm: Throughout the recent US and Europe legs of BTS’ Arirang World Tour, the singer consistently sported his fave silhouettes from the label, including baggy, barrel, and ‘90s-inspired straight-cut jeans.) “For this holiday edit, I had fun taking some of the most iconic fits and styling them in new ways for the season,” he shares, adding that the versatile pieces can easily be dressed up or kept simple to make each look “your own.”
The "Internet Boyfriend" Layered Knit

In one layout, BTS’ “Golden Maknae” gives everyone a master class in cozy dressing, layering a chunky gray marbled yarn sweater over a white undershirt. He pairs it with nondescript black trousers and a belt for a sleek look, finishing it off with chunky noir leather shoes and silver accessories. It’s the kind of laid-back ‘fit that works for basically any type of situation: meeting the parents, lounging with your childhood bestie at home, or simply running out for an iced coffee.
The Street-Style Denim Edge

The “Standing Next To You” singer’s love for a jean jacket is well documented. Jung Kook even launched his own ‘90s trucker-inspired silhouette as part of his previous CKJK collab. Naturally, a denim jacket has a prominent spot on his current holiday wish list. This time around, however, he skips the matching jeans in favor of slacks and shiny leather shoes for extra polish. By layering a white shirt under a black top beneath the jacket, he gives the effortless attire a structured look that’s perfect for hitting the town — possibly on his motorbike.
The Modern Gentleman Silhouette

In a separate look, Jung Kook takes a sleek, dapper turn in a noir pantsuit and crisp white button-down. A skinny black tie adds a timeless, gentlemanly charm to the ensemble while maintaining a decidedly modern edge.

items.title: Your Horoscope For The Week Of November 9 – 15
items.description: Get ready for some serious and much-needed energy shifts as the middle of November approaches. Things start off strong, as there’s a new moon in Scorpio kicking off the new week. November’s lunar reset peaks at exactly 2:02 a.m. ET on Monday morning, injecting
items.author: Nina Kahn
paragraphs: Get ready for some serious and much-needed energy shifts as the middle of November approaches. Things start off strong, as there’s a new moon in Scorpio kicking off the new week. November’s lunar reset peaks at exactly 2:02 a.m. ET on Monday morning, injecting a glimmer of hope into an otherwise sludgy and exhausting couple weeks. Emotions do run deep with this one, so explore your feelings and connect with your soul-level desires throughout the first few days of the week. This new moon can be great for making plans and setting intentions, so long as they come from a place of reflection, self-awareness, and truth.

As the middle of the week comes around, you’ll really start feeling the effects of November’s rare triple conjunction between Mars, Jupiter, and the release-centric South Node in Leo. Expansive planet Jupiter lands directly on the South Node overnight on Wednesday, while assertive Mars follows suit two days later. This aspect can turn up the volume on the restrictive nature of your comfort zone, making it painfully clear what’s inhibiting your growth and holding you back from your destiny. Resist the urge to get defensive, and accept that some things need to change in order to get onto the path you know is meant for you.

Between the new moon and the cosmic flush of the Mars-Jupiter-South Node alignment, the work week might feel intense — but fortunately, Friday the 13th appears to be bringing some good luck. That’s because both Venus retrograde and Mercury retrograde come to an end on that day, just a few hours apart. Love planet Venus has been backspinning for nearly six weeks, recalibrating everyone’s relationships and values. Mental planet Mercury only shifted into reverse for the latter half of that, but it sure packed a punch when it came to stirring up misunderstandings and timing misalignments. Now that both of these influential personal planets are moving forward again, you’ll find that you’re able to think more clearly and feel more in tune with yourself and others.
Here’s each zodiac sign’s horoscope for the week ahead.

You’ve been exploring complexities in your relationships and with your own boundaries, and these emotional journeys are finally beginning to resolve. You’ll find that you can start showing up for yourself and others with a greater awareness of your own needs, so make sure you don’t backslide into self-abandonment after making so much progress.

It’s almost impossible not to bring old baggage into relationships — even new ones — but it’s a whole lot easier to deal with when you’re aware that it’s happening. Sit with your worst hang-ups and habits this week and try to figure out where they stem from. Your past experience may shape the present, but they don’t have to dictate your future.

Your daily routine has been undergoing a recalibration, and this week, you may finally find yourself settling into a new groove. Just remember that what works for you may not work for others and vice versa, so while advice is always nice, you’re probably better off conducting your own experiments as you figure out what motivates you to stay on track.

What truly makes you feel happy, fulfilled, and impassioned? Before you default to a list of stock answers, take a moment to check in with yourself. As you evolve and grow, so will your values — which in turn will shape your desires. This week, practice seeking the feeling instead of a specific experience. You might be surprised by what lights you up.

If you want to level up in your life and align with a new frequency, you’ve got to start from the bottom up. Think back to some of the foundational experiences and desires in your life. How are those manifesting now? If there are inner child issues you haven’t healed or parts of your past you haven’t dealt with, now’s the time to start trying.

Perhaps not every coincidence is a sign from the universe and not every misspoken word is a Freudian slip — but what if some of these things have more meaning than you think? Pay more attention to casual conversations, random connections, or passing thoughts that cross through your awareness this week. Some part of you may be trying to express itself.

What’s meaningful to this week may be a much different list than it would have been two months ago, as your values have been shifting in a big way. As you figure out what feels most worth your energy and time, you may find that you feel a little less aligned with certain friends or social groups. If you need a little distance to figure out your feelings, take it.

Is the image you’re projecting out into the world aligned with the way you see yourself? It’s OK to have a public persona, but don’t give yourself an identity crisis by hiding who you are under a million layers of disguise. You can retain your patented air of mystique and still drop the facade every once in a while. There’s no reason to hide your truth.
Sagittarius (Nov. 22-Dec. 21)

Just because you believed something wholeheartedly yesterday doesn’t mean it still resonates with your worldview today. Such is the beauty of gaining perspective! You’re beginning to see that dogmatic views and rigid paradigms are limiting your ability to explore new corners of life freely, so open your mind and let your opinions be a little more fluid.
Capricorn (Dec. 22-Jan. 19)

There are so many new social connections opening up to you this week, but it’ll require you to work through some emotional entanglements before you can fully open yourself up to them. Building group relationships through shared passions and interests is great, but it’s important to be vulnerable enough to create a deeper bond, too.
Aquarius (Jan. 20-Feb. 18)

You’re finally ready to push past the professional barriers that you’ve been hovering on the threshold of for a long time now, but will you trust yourself to know what to do once you’ve overcome it? Just because you’re facing a new situation doesn’t mean you’re ill-equipped to deal with it. Draw on experiences from your personal life to help guide you in your career.

You have the power to achieve unimaginably big things, but you may need to restructure parts of your daily life if you want to make real magic happen. Reaching sky-high aspirations requires discipline, intention, and consistency, so find ways to show up for your dreams every single day until doing so becomes a natural part of your routine.

items.title: Luxury Gifts Under $50 That’ll Impress Anyone (Without Breaking The Bank)
items.description: Luxury Gifts Under $50 That’ll Impress Anyone (Without Breaking The Bank)
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa; Victoria Montalti
paragraphs: Luxury Gifts Under $50 That’ll Impress Anyone (Without Breaking The Bank)
Piecework Puzzles Happy Hour Puzzle

2026 emphasized more than ever our craving for analogue activities and hobbies that pull us away from our phones. So puzzles, especially ones as beautiful as the artwork from Piecework Puzzles, make for thoughtful gifts. It's a relaxing, time-consuming activity that leaves your giftee with a stunning piece of art. There are numerous designs to pick from, but we're eyeing this colorful cocktail tablescape.
Quince Lightweight Cotton Cashmere Crew Cardigan

If you want to impress your gift recipients with high-quality yet budget-friendly gifts, you have to look to Quince. The selection of under-$50 gifts spans accessories, home decor, and, our favorite: cashmere sweaters. Consider a cozy cardigan that's a bit more versatile and can be worn across seasons.
Anthropologie Bistro Tile Stoneware 24k Gold Accent Pitcher

The entirety of Anthropologie’s Bistro Tile collection is stunning with its mosaic look and artisanal feel, making tons of items perfect for gifting to your holiday party hosts… or yourself. This under-$50 pitcher is a classic style for holding Thanksgiving gravy, signature Christmas cocktails, or flower bouquets year-round.

Lush's viral massage bars are viral for a reason. I myself got persuaded and purchased a citrus scent over the summer and couldn't get over the super-moisturizing formula, which left me with glowing skin, or the invigorating scent, which gained me many compliments. There are many many scents to pick from, including calming and meditative scent combos. (Tip: Purchase a $5 oval tin online to hold the bar too. They're usually sold out in-store!)
JW Anderson X Uniqlo Wool Cashmere Stole

Uniqlo knows how to do a designer collab right, and its latest with JW Anderson is full of high-quality pieces at reasonable prices. Gift these wool-cashmere scarves in multiple color combos, stamped with the JWA logo. This functional and fashionable unisex design is great for nearly everyone on your list.
GloryByAbbey Custom Photo Strip Wood Frame

It was truly the year of photo booths. Friends and couples scoured their cities for the best photo booths, leaving with vintage-style photo strips. Because of this, we've also noticed an influx in photo strip frames. Whether you DIY one or support a small business on Etsy and customize it online, there are tons of designs available to display you and your giftee's favorite shared memories.
Nécessaire The Hand Cream + The Tube Key

Anyone would be delighted to be gifted anything from bodycare brand Nécessaire. We recommend the bestselling hand cream, but elevating it more with the brand’s stainless steel tube key to help squeeze out every last drop of the moisturizing goodness.
Lululemon Metallic Nano Crescent Bag

For the Lululemon lovers on your list, consider this new metallic mini bag-keychain hybrid. It can be hooked onto a larger Lululemon bag for extra personalization. The festive design is small but practical (it can fit your coins, earbuds, lip balm, or house keys).
Staub 16 oz. Petite Tomato Cocotte

This mini heirloom tomato-shaped cocotte doubles as a mini Dutch oven and statement serving bowl (perfect for side dishes) that’ll instantly enhance any meal or tablescape. It’s so beautiful, no one will guess how much (or little) you spent on it.
Fotofoto Zero Waste Recycled Disposable 35mm Film Camera

Whether you're shopping for a Gen Z giftee, a nostalgia lover, or a frequent traveler, a disposable film camera is a great under-$50 option to help them document special moments in an instant without taking 30 identical photos on their phone. Even better, this particular camera is made from up-cycled materials and comes with a mailer from Fotofoto to send the camera back to get photos developed (and recycle the camera after the fact).
Free People Frostbite Fur Pillbox Hat
Your giftee will look like they're stepping out of a luxe '80s ski resort with this retro faux fur pillbox hat. Pick from leopard print, caramel, or cream designs to best fit your giftee's style.
Fishwife The Spicy Trio with Gift Tin

Tinned fish lovers assemble! Fishwife’s gift tins — like this smoked salmon, albacore tuna, and sardines trio spicy olive oil and hot pepper — will delight foodies. Because who doesn’t love unwrapping niche treats during the holidays?
BaubleBar Bubble Letter Custom Necklace

Baublebar’s custom charm jewelry was a reader-favorite last year, so we had to spotlight it again. Opt for a more modern and youthful version of a nameplate necklace with these puffy letter charms in either gold (for $48) or sparkly gold pavé (for $50).
Godonlif Candle Warmer Lamp with Timer

A candle warmer is one of the best gifts I’ve ever been given. It quickly fills up my space with my favorite scent, and doesn’t wear down my candle like a flame does, so I can reheat it over and over again. And from the gift-giver perspective, it's a low-lift, high-reward option!
Julie Pedersen The Bread Baker's Seasoning Kit

At this point, we probably all know someone who has taken up sourdough bread-making in the last couple of years. We think an ideal gift for spicing up their baking is this bread seasoning kit, which contains 15 jars of sweet and savory seasoning blends like Tuscan Tomato, Green Tea Sesame, and Dill Caraway.
Ugg Men's Suede Clamshell Logo Gloves

Who knew you could find Ugg gloves under $50. Well, you can at TJ Maxx, and these men's suede gloves are calling our names. Cart them up for your father, brother, partner, or friend and leave them in awe over the very generous gift.
Kylie Cosmetics Mood Stones Mini Trio Gift Set

Kylie Jenner knows a thing or two about viral moments, and her fragrances are no exception. The mogul released these new mood stone scents over the summer and got everyone hooked. On the chance that your giftee hasn't already carted up one of these perfumes, consider buying this mini trio scent so they can test out their favorites. They're also the perfect travel size for throwing in weekender bags and suitcases.
Charles & Keith Croissant Charm

A bag charm that's also a coin purse that's also a croissant? What more do we have to say? We're loving this design, but Charles & Keith has so many adorable bag charms to pick from that'll put a smile on your giftee's face.
Crocs Classic Cozzzy Slipper

Unless you look closely, you’d never know these faux-fur shearling slippers are from Crocs. Super cozy and plush, they’re the perfect option for the homebody on your list! And even better, they’re currently on sale!
Lilly Pulitzer 2027 Large 12 Month Agenda

Just because your budget is $50 doesn't mean you need an inexpensive version of a luxury gift. Instead you can get a super luxe version of an ordinary gift, like an agenda. And this chic zebra-print 2027 agenda calendar is just that! It'll add a bit of whimsy to your giftee's everyday routine.
Maison Balzac Hand Cake Server

From chrome fortune cookies to sparkling ornaments, Coming Soon offers some of the most unique and elevated under-$50 homeware gifts. But we’re eyeing this kitschy hand-shaped cake server for the baker, host, or sweets-lover on your list.

items.title: Your Horoscope This Week: November 8 To 14
items.description: Cosmic beings, this may be the most exciting week of November, and after weeks of retrograde reflection, the cosmos is finally giving us something to celebrate! The week begins with a powerful Scorpio New Moon in the early hours of November 9th, kick-starting
items.author: Dossé-Via Trenou
paragraphs: Cosmic beings, this may be the most exciting week of November, and after weeks of retrograde reflection, the cosmos is finally giving us something to celebrate! The week begins with a powerful Scorpio New Moon in the early hours of November 9th, kick-starting a six-month chapter of profound transformation and renewal. This is one of the most emotionally significant New Moons of the year, inviting us to get radically honest about what we’re ready to change and who we’re becoming in the process. With Scorpio’s traditional ruler Mars in passionate Leo and its modern ruler Pluto in innovative Aquarius, there’s a fiery, intellectual edge to this lunation that encourages us to blend intuition with action. The intentions we set over the next ten days could deeply influence the direction of the next six months, so dream boldly, own your power, and be willing to take the first steps toward what you want.

Then, on November 13th, we receive a double cosmic blessing as Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio and Venus ends its retrograde in Libra. Hallelujah! After weeks of crossed wires, relationship revelations, financial delays, and perhaps a few unsolicited trips down memory lane, we can finally start making sense of everything we’ve experienced. Mercury retrograde may have exposed conversations we needed to revisit or truths we’d been avoiding, while Venus retrograde pushed us to reconsider what we value, how we love, and where our energy is being reciprocated. Now, with Mercury moving forward in Scorpio and Venus moving forward in Libra, we can use those insights to make clearer decisions, repair connections where there’s mutual willingness, and move on from situations that have run their course. We’ve spent weeks figuring out what needs to change. Now we get to do something about it.
Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

Aries, your next financial breakthrough could come from thinking beyond what you can accomplish on your own. The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th activates your investments and wealth-building realm, opening a six-month chapter of financial transformation. You may feel inspired to explore a business partnership, apply for funding, or develop a strategy for creating long-term financial security. With your ruling planet Mars in Leo energizing your creativity, an idea you’re passionate about could become an unexpected source of income. Think about the resources, expertise, or support you could leverage to bring your vision to life. There’s power in knowing when to collaborate, Aries.

On November 13th, Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, helping you make progress with financial applications, contracts, or negotiations that have required extra patience. You may finally receive information about an investment, insurance matter, or shared financial obligation that’s been difficult to sort out. Meanwhile, Venus direct in Libra brings renewed momentum to your partnership realm. If you’ve been reconsidering a romantic or professional commitment, you may feel more confident about what you want moving forward. The second half of November could be especially promising for agreements that benefit everyone involved, so pay attention to who shares your vision.

Taurus, two heads may be better than one, especially when it comes to your biggest ambitions. The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th activates your partnership and collaboration zone, launching a six-month chapter that could introduce important new alliances into your life. Perhaps you’re ready to find a business partner, work with a mentor, or team up with someone whose skills complement your own. With Mars in Leo energizing your home and family realm, you may also be considering a joint investment in property or a project involving relatives. Think about what you could create with the right person by your side, Taurus. An exciting partnership could open doors you hadn’t previously considered.

Then November 13th brings a welcome turning point as Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, helping you finalize agreements, revisit proposals, or clarify expectations with someone you’re working closely with. A connection that seemed uncertain may finally start taking shape. Your ruling planet Venus also ends its retrograde in Libra, bringing fresh energy to your work, wellness, and daily-routine realm. If you’ve been questioning your professional environment or how much time you’re dedicating to other people’s priorities, you may feel ready to make some changes. Your schedule should leave room for your own ambitions, Taurus, and this is a promising time to create that balance.

Gemini, what if your next career breakthrough came from completely reimagining how you work? The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th activates your productivity and wellness realm, launching a six-month chapter of professional and lifestyle improvements. You may feel inspired to transition into a new role, develop a specialized skill, or explore technology that could make your work more efficient. With Mars in Leo energizing your communication and learning zone, opportunities involving writing, teaching, marketing, or digital media could be especially appealing. Think about what your ideal workday would look like and which changes could bring you closer to experiencing it.

On November 13th, your ruling planet Mercury finally ends its retrograde in Scorpio, helping you move forward with job applications, workplace negotiations, or projects that have been stuck in revision mode. You may receive useful feedback from a supervisor or discover a more effective way to manage your responsibilities. Meanwhile, Venus direct in Libra brings a refreshing boost to your creativity, pleasure, and self-expression zone. A hobby or artistic project you’ve neglected could suddenly feel exciting again, and you may even discover an opportunity to share it with a wider audience. There’s room for both professional success and personal enjoyment in your next chapter, Gemini. Make space for both.

Cancer, that creative idea you’ve been sitting on deserves a bigger stage. The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th activates your creativity, fame, fate, and self-expression zone, opening a six-month chapter where your talents could take you further than you imagined. Whether you’ve been considering launching a passion project, sharing your work publicly, or turning a hobby into a business, this lunation encourages you to take your gifts seriously. With Mars in Leo energizing your income realm, there’s also potential to connect your creativity with greater financial independence. Think about what you’d love to have created or accomplished by next spring, and give yourself permission to be ambitious about it.

On November 13th, Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, making it easier to pitch ideas, revisit creative collaborations, or finally get feedback on something you’ve been developing. A project that lost momentum could find its spark again. Meanwhile, Venus ends its retrograde in Libra, bringing greater clarity to home and family matters. If you’ve been weighing a move, negotiating household arrangements, or trying to make your living environment more comfortable, you may feel ready to settle on a direction. Your private life and creative ambitions can support each other, Cancer, and this week helps you figure out how.

Leo, your home may be ready for an upgrade, and we’re talking about more than a new couch. The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th begins a six-month chapter of transformation involving your living situation, family, and sense of belonging. You could be preparing to relocate, considering homeownership, or thinking seriously about how you want your household to function. With Mars in your sign, you’re feeling more motivated to take charge of these decisions, while Pluto in Aquarius brings important questions about partnership and shared responsibilities into the picture. What kind of home would make your everyday life easier, happier, and more aligned with your future plans?

Then November 13th brings relief as Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, helping stalled housing decisions, family logistics, or property-related paperwork move forward. You may finally receive information that makes your next steps easier to plan. Venus also ends its retrograde in Libra, bringing renewed momentum to your communication, learning, and immediate environment. An application, writing project, or conversation you’ve been revisiting could start gaining traction. You may also feel more inspired to explore your neighborhood or connect with people who can oﬀer useful advice. Sometimes the right information arrives just when you’re ready to put it to use, Leo.

Virgo, you could be sitting on an idea that’s worth sharing with a much bigger audience. The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th activates your communication, writing, and learning realm, opening a six-month chapter of intellectual growth. Perhaps you’re ready to launch a newsletter, start a podcast, learn a language, or develop an expertise that could open professional doors. With Mars in Leo moving through your behind-the-scenes zone, some of your best work may begin privately, while you’re researching, experimenting, and figuring out what you want to say. You have time to develop your voice, but don’t underestimate how far one well-executed idea could take you.

On November 13th, your ruling planet Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, helping you move forward with submissions, presentations, contracts, or educational plans that have required multiple revisions. You may finally feel ready to send something out into the world after weeks of fine-tuning it. Meanwhile, Venus direct in Libra brings welcome clarity to your finances and earning potential. If you’ve been reconsidering your pricing, negotiating payment, or evaluating the financial value of a skill, you could feel better equipped to advocate for yourself. Your knowledge has value, and the second half of November is a good time to start treating it that way.

Libra, what if the next six months completely transformed your relationship with money and your sense of self-worth? The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th activates your income, security, and abundance zone, encouraging you to set intentions around the kind of financial freedom you want to create. With Mars in Leo energizing your friendship and future-goals realm, a collaboration or connection within your network could help you see new possibilities for building wealth. Think about what you want your financial life to look like by next spring, including how much you want to earn, save, or invest. The more specific you get about your goals, the easier it’ll be to recognize opportunities that can help you achieve them.

Then November 13th brings a major turning point as your ruling planet Venus finally ends its retrograde in your sign, alongside Mercury ending its retrograde in Scorpio. If the past several weeks have felt like one long identity crisis, you may be more than ready to come up for air! Venus direct can help restore your confidence in your appearance, relationships, and personal direction, especially if you’ve been questioning decisions you once felt certain about. Meanwhile, Mercury direct in your financial realm could bring clarity to delayed payments, negotiations, or important money conversations. Give yourself credit for the ways you’ve grown through this retrograde season, Libra. You’re entering the second half of November with a stronger sense of who you are and what you’re worth.

Scorpio, your solar return season’s getting increasingly better. Your annual New Moon arrives on November 9th, and this one has “fresh start” written all over it. Think of yourself as emerging from a chrysalis, with the next six months offering you the chance to spread your wings in ways you may have only dreamed about until now. This New Moon in your sign is ideal for setting intentions around your identity, confidence, appearance, and the experiences you want to invite into your life. With Mars in Leo activating your career and public-image realm and Pluto in Aquarius transforming your home and family zone, you may feel inspired to reinvent both your public persona and your private world. Let yourself get excited about what’s possible, Scorpio. You’ve done plenty of reflecting lately, and now you get to start creating.

Then November 13th brings another reason to celebrate as Mercury finally ends its retrograde in your sign, while Venus ends hers in Libra. Mercury direct can help you regain momentum with personal projects, important decisions, or conversations you’ve been postponing. You may find that people are more receptive to your ideas or that expressing yourself feels easier after weeks of second-guessing. Meanwhile, Venus direct in your solitude and spirituality realm could bring a welcome sense of inner peace, especially if you’ve been processing complicated feelings about someone from your past. You may realize that a situation you once obsessed over simply doesn’t occupy as much space in your mind anymore. Enjoy that freedom, Scorpio. Your birthday season deserves to feel like a celebration of everything you’re becoming.

Sag, what if some of your biggest breakthroughs over the next six months happen when nobody’s watching? The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th activates your solitude, spirituality, and behind-the-scenes realm, making this a powerful time to nurture ideas that aren’t quite ready for the spotlight. You may feel inspired to work privately on a creative project, explore a spiritual practice, or make plans for a personal reinvention that you’ll reveal when the timing feels right. With Mars in fellow Fire sign Leo energizing your travel and expansion zone, your imagination may be running wild with possibilities. Give yourself permission to experiment without needing immediate feedback or approval.

On November 13th, Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, helping you gain clarity about plans or decisions you’ve been considering. You may finally connect the dots on an idea that seemed too complicated a few weeks ago or find a more practical way to bring it to life. Meanwhile, Venus direct in Libra brings renewed energy to your friendships, collaborations, and social life. An invitation, introduction, or opportunity to reconnect with someone could lead to something promising, especially if you’ve been craving more inspiring company. With your birthday season beginning next week, Sag, you may feel your enthusiasm returning in full force. Enjoy the anticipation, and start making room in your calendar for the adventures ahead.

Capricorn, what if the right people could help you accomplish in six months what you’ve been trying to do alone for years? The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th activates your friendship, community, and future-goals realm, opening a powerful chapter for collaboration and collective success. You may feel inspired to join an organization, build a stronger professional network, or turn a shared vision into something tangible. With Mars in Leo energizing your shared-resources zone, conversations about funding, investments, or pooling resources could become especially relevant. Think about the kind of support system your next big goal actually requires, and be willing to let others contribute.

On November 13th, Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, making it easier to coordinate group projects, finalize plans with collaborators, or reconnect with contacts who went quiet. Meanwhile, Venus direct in Libra brings welcome momentum to your career and public image. A professional relationship that felt strained may improve, or you could gain a clearer understanding of how to position yourself for an opportunity you’ve been pursuing. You may find that someone who previously overlooked your work is suddenly paying attention. Stay open to conversations that could lead somewhere promising.

Aquarius, your next career move could change how people see you, and more importantly, how you see yourself. The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th illuminates your career, reputation, and legacy zone, launching a six-month period of professional reinvention. You may feel ready to pursue a leadership position, launch a business, or take your expertise into an entirely new field. With Mars in Leo activating your partnership realm, an important collaborator, client, or romantic partner could influence the direction you choose. This is a powerful moment to consider what you want your name associated with and which opportunities deserve your full commitment.

Then November 13th brings relief as Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, helping stalled professional negotiations, applications, or decisions involving authority figures gain traction. If you’ve been waiting for feedback or clarification about a project, you may finally get some answers. Venus also ends its retrograde in Libra, bringing fresh perspective to your travel, education, and publishing realm. A delayed trip, academic application, or international opportunity could become easier to navigate. You may realize that expanding your skills or exploring a different environment is exactly what your professional growth requires.

Pisces, your world is about to get bigger, and the Scorpio New Moon on November 9th wants you to be intentional about where you go next. This lunation activates your travel, publishing, and spiritual expansion zone, opening a six-month chapter of discovery. Perhaps you’re considering relocating, pursuing a qualification, sharing your work with a wider audience, or exploring a culture that’s always fascinated you. With Mars in Leo energizing your daily-routine realm, the challenge is finding practical ways to make room for these experiences. Start researching the logistics, costs, and commitments involved. A dream becomes much more exciting when you can see a realistic path toward it.

On November 13th, Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, bringing greater clarity to travel arrangements, educational paperwork, or publishing matters that have been delayed. You may receive news from someone abroad or finally feel ready to commit to a direction you’ve been researching. Meanwhile, Venus direct in Libra helps untangle questions involving shared finances, loans, or financial support from others. If money has been a deciding factor in your plans, you may have a better understanding of what’s available and what still needs to be arranged. There’s plenty to look forward to, Pisces, and this week can help you move from possibility to preparation.

items.title: The ethics of having a good time at Disney World, Florida | Psyche Ideas
items.description: The sun has set on Orlando, Florida, the theme-park capital of the world. Inside one of those parks, Walt Disney World’s EPCOT, thousands of visitors make their way toward a manmade lagoon surrounded by pavilions representing cultures and histories from around
items.author: Adam Kadlac
paragraphs: The sun has set on Orlando, Florida, the theme-park capital of the world. Inside one of those parks, Walt Disney World’s EPCOT, thousands of visitors make their way toward a manmade lagoon surrounded by pavilions representing cultures and histories from around the world. Of the many times that I have visited Disney World with my family, some of my favourite moments have come at this point in our trip, while we prepare for EPCOT’s fireworks display to begin. My daughter is generally sitting in her mobility chair as the rest of the family debriefs about the day’s activities, our legs tired from all the time we’ve spent on our feet. The temperature has usually cooled off a bit, and the collective nature of the experience is palpable. Around us, families and groups of friends are huddled together, anticipating the start of the show.
As lights begin to flash around the water, an opening narration sets the tone for what’s to come:

Everyone on this Earth is part of the great Symphony of Us. Each of us a unique instrument playing harmony to one another. And even though we are all playing different parts, it’s our unified heartbeat that connects us, reminding us that we are more alike than we are different. A rhapsody of rhythms that unites us and connects us through commonalities of the heart.

It’s high-minded, sentimental stuff for a theme park with rides featuring a talking snowman and a rat who becomes a chef. But at a time of rising scepticism about multiculturalism and universal values, it’s also a message that has come to resonate with me.

Like many families, we have formed meaningful memories at Disney World because of the entertainment-rich environment the Disney company has created. Its theme parks are enjoyable, in part, because they appeal to each member of my family. But our Disney memories are also meaningful because Disney World reflects my values: this is a place that is ostensibly committed to the idea that we are all, in some sense, citizens of the world bound together by a common humanity. It’s a simple ideal. But it’s one I believe in deeply and strive to embody, however imperfectly, in my life.

Of course, as a philosopher, I’m also keenly aware that all the experiences that have led to these moments at Disney World have been sold to me by a massive global corporation that strives to maximise its profits. Whether the Walt Disney Company genuinely believes in the cosmopolitan values it promotes is largely beside the point. What matters is whether portraying those values is a good business strategy. Disney is also a corporation that has received more than its share of criticism throughout its history. It has been criticised for its labour practices, for the cultural themes in its films, for the stands it takes (or does not take) on controversial public issues and, sometimes, simply for being a massive global corporation that strives to maximise its profits. This tension regularly leaves me puzzled. Is the value of my experience at Disney World undermined by the fact that it is, at the end of the day, a production of the Walt Disney Company? Can I trust a profit-hungry corporation to teach my children universal values? And does Disney’s message need to be sincere for it to really matter?

These sorts of questions are certainly not unique to Disney theme parks. In his book The Affluent Society (1958), the economist John Kenneth Galbraith coined the term ‘the dependence effect’ to characterise the process by which a business creates the desires that it seeks to satisfy. For example, you might not have wanted to buy a new sweater, but seeing a commercial on television makes you dissatisfied with your current wardrobe such that you hop online and order a new one. It likely never occurred to you to try iced tea with vodka until you saw the beverage advertised in a magazine, but now you find yourself on the way to the corner store to buy a six-pack. And Disney obviously wants to manufacture the desire to visit its theme parks because it will make money from everyone who wants to satisfy their newfound urge to ride Frozen Ever After and take pictures of their kids with Mickey and Minnie. For Galbraith, the dependence effect is problematic because it gives too much control over our lives to people who simply want to make money.

While contemporary critics of Disney might echo these concerns, the problem becomes more acute when the corporation in question has behaved poorly in other ways. The Walt Disney Company has long been the target of labour activists who criticise how Disney treats its employees. In 2024, unionised workers at Disneyland authorised a strike in contract negotiations where they argued that 73 per cent of their employees didn’t make enough money to cover basic living expenses, despite often working 12- to 14-hour days. That strike was ultimately averted, but it stands in a long line of labour controversies dating back to an animators’ strike in 1941, through protests about working conditions in the factories that produce Disney products, and most recently a series of layoffs across the company earlier this year.
There is a sense of something shared, however briefly and however manufactured, that I don’t find in many other places
Disney also has a decidedly mixed record on cultural issues. Writing in The Guardian in 2021, the journalist Steve Rose noted that:

Disney’s history of racist caricatures and ethnic stereotyping has been well documented and routinely criticised: the crows in Dumbo that drew on racist minstrel caricatures of African Americans; the Islamophobic tropes in Aladdin; the mockery of Native Americans in Peter Pan… the list goes on.
And its portrayals of women haven’t fared much better. As the media scholar Janet Wasko writes in her book Understanding Disney (2001):

Disney heroines are always beautiful, shapely, and often sexually attractive, while female villains are typically ugly and either extremely thin (Cruella) or grossly fat (Ursula), thus perpetuating norms of physical beauty prevalent in mainstream American culture.

Even this partial list of Disney’s foibles is enough to challenge the idea that it is a company deeply committed to the sort of cosmopolitan values that I’ve come to associate with its theme parks. And coupled with Galbraith’s more fundamental concerns about the dependence effect, the case for abandoning Disney World certainly can’t be dismissed out of hand.

In my mind, I try to balance these concerns with my experiences. There’s my daughter beside me on It’s a Small World, her eyes wide as she looks at all the animatronics moving to the attraction’s iconic song. There are the conversations I have with my son as we analyse a new ride or (just as likely) one we have ridden multiple times before. There are the various shows, parades and fireworks displays, all of which offer opportunities to feel part of something larger than oneself. There is a sense of something shared, however briefly and however manufactured, that I don’t find in many other places. And there is the belief that all of it is shaped by values that I wholeheartedly endorse.
But these experiences come with some trepidation. There is something undeniably risky about entrusting something of such value to a corporation whose track record is, at best, mixed.

While Disney sceptics might quickly dismiss that value as trivial, I think they are wrong to do so. My daughter is intellectually disabled, and there are not a lot of places where everyone in my family can enjoy a day on their own terms. When my kids were growing up, activities that might appeal to my daughter wouldn’t really interest my son. Some of this discrepancy was just a function of their age difference but, as they got older, their developmental trajectories also played a role. My daughter is 19 now, and the gap between what she and her brother want from a vacation has only widened. Moreover, while being a good parent may often require that adults sacrifice their own enjoyment for the benefit of their children, it is a sacrifice, nonetheless. Playing on monkey bars at the playground as a kid is a lot more fun than watching kids play on monkey bars as an adult. Finding activities that appeal to everyone in the family is a challenge, even when disability is left out of the equation.

A couple of years ago, we took a trip out west, visiting Las Vegas and some national parks on the way to southern California. Taken as a whole, it was an amazing vacation. However, the natural beauty of the Grand Canyon was somewhat lost on our daughter who is limited in her ability to hike long distances or navigate uneven terrain. The lights of Vegas were interesting enough for everyone, but full-blown family entertainment is not exactly the city’s calling card. When we finally made our first visit to Disneyland (having previously been to Disney’s parks only in Florida), everyone was able to engage. This didn’t necessarily make Disneyland the high point of our trip (for me, at least, that was the day we spent at Arches National Park) but it did highlight the fact that the universalistic design of Disney parks is central to their appeal.
What matters is not so much where our desires come from but whether the satisfaction of those desires makes our lives better

For example, there are numerous attractions throughout Disney theme parks that are thoroughly engaging for adults without being overwhelming for children. The Haunted Mansion is more bemusing than genuinely scary, and Pirates of the Caribbean gives everyone plenty of details to occupy their attention. Live shows, such as Festival of the Lion King, connect viewers to the artistry of Disney’s films in immersive and often interactive ways. If you haven’t seen any of the Star Wars or Avatar movies, you can still love every minute of the attractions they inspired. And even if someone in the family isn’t quite ready for rollercoasters like Space Mountain, there are plenty of tamer options on offer, ranging from boat rides like It’s a Small World and Jungle Cruise to the slightly more adventurous Seven Dwarfs Mine Train or Big Thunder Mountain Railroad. Every minute of every day might not be equally enjoyable for everyone, but visits to Disney World consistently leave a mark on our family that we have found difficult to replicate.
So, does it matter that these experiences are offered to us by a profit-seeking corporation?

In his response to Galbraith, the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek questions whether consumers should worry about the dependence effect. For Hayek, what matters is not so much where our desires come from but whether the satisfaction of those desires makes our lives better. He is an unlikely ally to reach for in defence of a place built on shared feeling and common humanity – Hayek spent much of his career warning against the kind of collective sentiment EPCOT is selling. And while I don’t generally align myself with Hayek’s libertarian views, I’ve come to think he’s probably right on this point. The same company that gave us decades of flattened stereotypes in its films also built a place where my son and daughter can spend a day on roughly equal terms. And in so doing, it gave us memories that largely stand apart from the commercial context in which they were created.

To be sure, the value of these experiences does not redeem Disney’s labour practices or its other missteps as a corporation. If anything, it gives Disney fans even more reason to challenge the company to live up to the ideals it portrays in its parks. Perhaps it also demonstrates that the value an experience has for people doesn’t require pure intentions on the part of those who create it. We are all something of a mixed bag, whether we are part of the crowd watching fireworks around the World Showcase Lagoon or part of the staff working in the offices of Disney’s corporate headquarters. And at a time when it can be difficult to feel connected to our fellow human beings, I think it’s OK to be thankful for whatever aspirational moments we might be able to grab, no matter how they might come to us.

items.title: How to take notes that actually help you learn | Psyche Guides
items.description: is an associate professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience at Saint Louis University School of Medicine in Missouri, US. Her research focuses on the use of effective learning strategies and individual differences in learning. She is
items.author: Cynthia Nebel
paragraphs: is an associate professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience at Saint Louis University School of Medicine in Missouri, US. Her research focuses on the use of effective learning strategies and individual differences in learning. She is a member of The Learning Scientists and co-author of Ace That Test: A Student’s Guide to Learning Better (2023).

is an associate professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience at Saint Louis University School of Medicine in Missouri, US. Her research focuses on the use of effective learning strategies and individual differences in learning. She is a member of The Learning Scientists and co-author of Ace That Test: A Student’s Guide to Learning Better (2023).

Notetaking is a versatile skill. Perhaps you take notes during lectures in class, or as part of your job, or when you’re reading an insightful book, or when you have an important meeting. If you’re a notetaker, in any case, you want your notes to be as useful as they can be. And that starts with thinking about their function. Since taking notes is such a common activity, it’s easy to overlook the question of what notes are actually doing for us.

Many people assume that just by writing information down, they are doing something useful. But the cognitive processes involved in taking notes and the way you take them can make a big difference in terms of what you ultimately get out of them.

There are two broad goals of notetaking: recording and learning. The first is when you try to take down as much information as you can so that you don’t miss anything and can review it later. This might be necessary sometimes – for instance, if you are going to be tested on the information presented in a lecture, and you won’t have a recording, text, or slides to refer back to later. Similarly, if you are in charge of meeting minutes or want to do more research on what you’re hearing from your doctor, you may need to simply record as much information as possible.

But in many situations, the most effective and efficient way to take notes is to treat them as a tool for learning: that is, to use them to help you retain and understand the information by putting it down in your own words and organising your thoughts about it. This is the kind of notetaking that I’ll focus on in this Guide.

What do good notes look like, and how can you get better at notetaking? There is not one right answer to these questions, but knowing a bit about how and when notetaking is effective will help you to decide what kind of notes to take when, and what to do with them afterward. As a cognitive psychologist and director of learning services at a medical school, I have a lot of experience with the most effective strategies for notetaking and why they work. Below, I’ll explain how to use some of these strategies and the reasoning behind them.

Taking notes to learn is different from taking them to record. Sometimes you need to take down as much as possible. But if you hope to internalise the information, you’ll want to process it as you take notes.
Use paper if possible. Since it slows you down, you have to decide what the most important pieces of information are before putting them on paper, which supports learning.

Experiment with ways of processing. Organise the information in your own way – try making summaries, bulleted lists, drawings or charts – and note links between what you’re learning and other things you know.
Try a structured approach. In the Cornell notetaking system, you complement your main notes with a summary at the bottom and cues to practise recalling the information later.
Adopt a better review strategy. Don’t just reread or copy your notes – reorganise them in some way. Then test your memory and understanding and check your notes to see what you’re missing.
Use AI tools selectively. They can be helpful for creating detailed records, but don’t rely only on AI notes if you’re trying to learn.

You may have heard before that taking notes by hand, on paper, is better than typing them on a laptop. There is truth to this, but it is due to more than just the effect of handwriting. Writing on paper can be more effective because it is much slower than typing. It’s difficult to write down every word or detail, requiring you to decide what the most important pieces of information are before putting them on paper. When you do this, you’re engaging in a type of mental processing that leads to better learning. Taking notes on paper also allows you to easily jump back and forth between different concepts and to organise them visually (using a diagram, for example).

These things can be done electronically, but most people find that it’s clunkier. If you must use a device, my recommendation is to not simply copy what you hear or read verbatim, but rather to prioritise what seem to be the most important points, and to ensure you process the information by doing some of the things I’ll describe next.
Experiment with ways of processing

When you’re taking notes to learn, it’s essential to organise the information in your own way and to think about how it relates to other things you know (even examples from your own life). You could make bulleted lists, write summaries in your own words or write questions about the material. Maybe you also want to draw pictures or flow charts, or connect different parts of a lecture with arrows. All these activities involve somehow mentally processing the information, which leads to actual learning rather than just recording.

For example, some of my students will create a high-level outline of the main topics from a lecture; under each heading, they write a summary of the information in their own words once that part of the lecture ends. Other students try to anticipate how they might be quizzed on the material and write practice test questions in their notes.

Here’s an example from outside the classroom – let’s say I’m reading a book about a historical figure and want to better retain the information. How might I start? As I go from chapter to chapter, I could take notes in the margins, or in a separate notebook, about how each part of the book relates to contemporary events, other history that I know, or situations in my own life. I might find certain areas interesting or inspiring and write in my notes about why those things caught my attention. Again, these all involve mentally processing, or what we can call active (vs passive) reading.

Coming up with your own way of taking notes may seem like a big challenge. The good news is that there are existing notetaking strategies that can help you with this process. One of the strategies that is supported by research is the Cornell notetaking system, created by the Cornell University education professor Walter Pauk.

In this approach, you separate a page into three parts. On the main part of the page will be your ‘notes’. At the bottom of the page, you include a ‘summary’. In the lefthand margin, you label an area for ‘cues’. Here’s an example:
As you’re taking in the information (eg, in class or during a discussion), you use the ‘notes’ area to keep track of important points and ideas.

Afterward, you fill out the ‘cues’ section, which is primarily used to help guide your study later on, when you go back to review your notes. You might write down questions to help you think about the material that was covered, or prompts related to what is most important. These serve as retrieval cues to help you practise recalling the information later, which is a highly effective learning strategy. It could also be helpful to note in the cues section anything you don’t understand, to clarify what you might have to review further or follow up about. Sometimes, depending on the context, you might be able to fill out the cues section while you’re still taking down your main notes.

Last, you fill out the ‘summary’ section, writing down the big-picture ideas that came out of what you heard or read, in your own words. This allows you to take a step back and think through what all of this means and how it fits with other things you’ve been learning.

What’s great about this notetaking system is that it requires you to process the material in multiple ways. The system is also very adaptable. If, for example, you attend a lecture that’s very dense, you could take verbatim notes first and then take Cornell notes later, based on your initial round of notes. And if you need more space, you can reserve a whole page for the ‘cues’ section and subsequent pages where you put your notes, including a summary at the end.

While the Cornell approach is a reliable technique, there are other structured ways of taking notes that you might want to explore as well. For example, mind-mapping is a strategy in which you put the main idea in the centre of a page and organise related material around it using branching connections. With sketchnoting, you take advantage of the powerful interaction between verbal and visual material by creating notes that involve lots of pictures. And outlining can be an effective strategy because it requires you to consider what is most important and how various pieces of information support each topic. Each of these strategies is evidence-based and they work in different ways to support deeper processing.
Adopt a better review strategy

Once you have your notes, what should you do with them? Hopefully it’s clear by now that processing the information is key, so just rewriting the same notes is mostly a waste of time. When you do that, you don’t really have to think about the notes you’ve taken. However, if you reorganise your notes in some way – such as by summarising them, or creating diagrams, flow charts, or hierarchies – that is likely to be more useful, especially if you had to take verbatim notes at first. For example, after hearing about how the heart works, you could draw a picture with arrows showing the direction of blood flow, or you could create appropriate headings and subheadings to organise the main ideas and supporting facts.

Similarly, just rereading your notes doesn’t require a lot of mental effort. It feels like you’re learning, and you might get better at it over time. But if you’re trying to internalise and retain information for later (for example, if you want to be able to retrieve answers on a test), then the best way to prepare is to practise doing that. Instead of rereading, you could try using your ‘cues’ from the Cornell method to bring as much of the information to mind as you can. Then you can go back to your main ‘notes’ section to see what you missed.

If you’re using a different notetaking strategy, you could write quiz questions based on your notes that you can then answer from memory. Or, you could use your notes to make flashcards. Instead of just copying down the notes onto the cards, try using the front side of the card for questions that you could get someone to ask you, or for different ways of comparing and contrasting the information. For example, you could write: ‘Compare and contrast the upbringings of Alexander Hamilton and Aaron Burr.’ This will give you a processing benefit while you’re creating the cards, as well as the retrieval benefit when you use them later.

You could also do a ‘brain dump’, where you try to write down everything you can remember about a topic and then check your notes for accuracy and to fill in any gaps. All of these strategies involve more productive mental effort than rereading does, and they come with the advantage of helping you figure out what you do and don’t know.

If you’re recording a lecture or a conversation and you want a thorough transcription and summary that you can revisit later, AI tools can be useful for that. However, when you use AI to take notes rather than doing it yourself, you are bypassing the kinds of mental processing that will help you learn. Because of this, I don’t recommend relying on AI for notetaking if your goal is to retain the information. In situations where it’s important to have a detailed record and you use AI to create one, just make sure that you go back to those notes later and apply one or more of the review strategies above if you hope to remember the material later on.

Notetaking is not just one thing and you should adjust your approach depending on the situation. If the information is very dense and it’s not contained anywhere else, then trying to take down as much as you can makes sense – but you’ll still need to revisit and make sense of those notes later on. And when your aim is not to copy but to internalise what you’re hearing or reading, then the best way to take notes is to summarise, organise and make connections between the material and what you already know. Ultimately, the key is to think about what you’re learning, both as you’re taking it in and when you come back to it later. The best way of taking notes is the one that helps you do that.
