items.title: Aftershocks, Stephen Miller, and Even More Democratic Wins: Midterms Aftermath
items.description: The wave crashed. A roiling aftermath followed. As the country waited for the final results in many key races, the brutal postmortems came out, the resignations started, and everyone — including the victorious Democrats and the Trump administration — tried to
items.author: Intelligencer Staff
paragraphs: The wave crashed. A roiling aftermath followed. As the country waited for the final results in many key races, the brutal postmortems came out, the resignations started, and everyone — including the victorious Democrats and the Trump administration — tried to make sense of what it all meant. Also: Stephen Miller, of all people, got promoted. Here’s our running account of the first few days after Democrats trounced Trump and the GOP in the 2026 midterms.
“Susie keeps the trains running on time. I don’t know what this looks like moving forward.’
CNN reports on a White House in disarray:

Trump, who initially appeared unfazed by the results of the Tuesday night midterms, has become angrier as he’s watched coverage of the historic losses, according to the people familiar with his response. That sour mood has spread throughout the West Wing, which has become increasingly factionalized in recent days.

Trump made his displeasure with his political team known starting at a tense election night reception in the East Room, according to one of the people familiar with the matter. He vented that deep Republican losses were the result of their strategy. Wiles was among those Trump blamed for the Republican losses, the person said. …

Since the midterm wipeout, Trump had heard from several allies and associates who urged him to make changes to his senior staff in response to the losses, a source familiar with the matter said. But the move nonetheless came as a shock to many in the administration, and multiple White House officials told CNN it left them concerned about the rest of Trump’s second term.
“Susie keeps the trains running on time. I don’t know what this looks like moving forward,” one official said.
Another Trump ally called it a “catastrophic loss” for the president.
Revenge of the Epstein Files
The Atlantic’s Sarah Fitzpatrick reports that Jeffrey Epstein did factor into Trump and the GOP’s losses:

The president’s decision to go to war with Iran and the resulting spike in gas prices may have been the front-of-mind issues for most voters in the 2026 midterms. But members of Congress, pollsters, political operatives, and campaign staff all told me that Trump’s mishandling of the Epstein issue meaningfully contributed to the GOP’s drubbing. The Republican pollster and strategist Brent Buchanan told me that Epstein became “a proxy for corruption” in the midterms. Another Republican close to the White House described the Epstein issue to me as the “nuclear fuel” that accelerated a new form of American populism. First, it boosted Trump. But on Tuesday, it worked against him, helping bring him to the lowest point of his presidency. Many of Trump’s voters viewed his handling of the matter as a betrayal. Pollsters told me it had cracked the bond between Trump and his coalition—and changed the course of the midterms.
It’s almost like you can’t trust him
Trump’s 60 Minutes interview is going to be a little out-of-date:
When 60 Minutes Correspondent Ross Douthat asked Mr. Trump whether he expected to fire anyone after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress, the president said: “I do, yeah. Little bit.”
“I love my Cabinet. I think they’re good,” he said. “But I’ll … be doing maybe a few changes.”

Mr. Trump suggested Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is safe for now, despite CBS News reporting that he asked advisers this week whether the Pentagon chief should stick around. When Douthat asked whether he has confidence in Hegseth, Mr. Trump said: “I do.”

“Look, we’ve won two wars. We’ve won Venezuela and taken out billions and billions and billions of dollars already. And we will be taking out many billions of dollars and get along very well. And, you could call it a territory, you could call it whatever you want. We won that war in less than one hour,” Mr. Trump said.

Venezuela was not a war, of course, it was an arranged abduction. The other war is a war, and it’s not over, and the U.S. has not won it. Also “little bit” isn’t firing the Chief of Staff who has run the Trump Team for years.
Three out and counting at the Justice Department

High-profile leaders resigned from the department Thursday and Friday, including Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon, National Security Division chief John Eisenberg and U.S. Attorney for Southern Florida Jason Reding Quiñones, who led prosecutors in the so-called “grand conspiracy” case President Donald Trump hoped to mount against his longtime adversaries.

Two people familiar with the personnel changes, granted anonymity to describe internal decision-making, said the departures were not surprising. One person said Blanche had grown frustrated with some of the department’s leadership amid struggles to bring high-profile indictments or score big wins in litigation connected to the president’s top priorities.
So they’re out because they failed to deliver substantive trumped-up charges?
Colom’s lead just keeps growing
Steve Kornacki fasts during Election Night
America’s favorite election nerd did this week’s Grub Street Diet. From his entry about Tuesday night:

On big event nights like this, when everybody is working late, they usually bring in pizzas. They’ll keep a stack of like 30 pizza boxes out in the hallway. I never eat before the broadcast, but I always tell my producer that when we’re done, we’ll go all in on the leftovers; we always go through the boxes, and they’re always empty.

Because I’m on-camera basically nonstop, I don’t really eat anything during the broadcast. I make it for ten and a half hours straight, which is a personal record for one of these livestreams. There’s only time for one bathroom break! The crew keeps refilling a ceramic NBC mug with water for me the whole time. It doesn’t seem like such a strenuous thing on paper, but being on your feet for ten hours talking almost nonstop takes more of a physical toll than you might think.

Whatever it is, I sort of hit a wall at about 3:30 a.m. Things have also slowed down dramatically resultswise at this point, too. So after I take a break, I huddle with the producers and we decide it’s actually the logical time to call it a night. They bring some random snacks over to me: a thing of trail mix, some grapes, and Cheez-Its. I chug a big can of lemon-lime Gatorade. I think it’s around 5 a.m. when I finally get home, and I’m too exhausted to eat anything else.
An ominous sign of things to come
As I argue in my new post, the Miller pick is a chilling indication of what awaits us in the final two years of Trump’s presidency:

Miller is deeply responsible for losing 2024 Trump voters who supported border control and deportation of violent criminals but never bargained for the terror ICE has inflicted on immigrant communities or the unapologetic racism that underlies Miller’s approach.

And that may be the scariest thing of all about his new base of power: He has two more years to act on his deep belief in the Great Replacement theory. This is the idea that traitorous liberals are deliberately destroying the country through a conspiracy to drown native-born white Americans in a sea of shiftless immigrants who trade illegal votes for welfare benefits and the opportunity to commit crimes. Trump talks about this nightmare scenario all the time as part of his demagogic pitch to the MAGA base. But for Miller, it’s an article of faith.

Some Trump defenders will try to rationalize Miller’s elevation as insignificant, a semi-automatic move up the ladder for the Trump loyalist who was technically Wiles’s deputy. It’s true that he may bring more discipline and fewer leaks to the White House staff. But it will likely be the discipline of sheer fanaticism and intolerance for dissent.

Trump’s big decision in the wake of the midterms is whether to learn something from his party’s setback and seek to wind down his final term in office in a dignified manner or instead try to implement the worst and most divisive elements of his agenda come hell or high water. There’s little question Miller would take the administration down this second path, and his promotion will give him that chance.
Another ominous sign of things to come
Does this make renewing the Iran War more or less likely?
Notes the Stimson Center’s Emma Ashford:
Miller probably the most Jacksonian of all Trump’s close advisors, which means – when it comes to Iran – that things could just as easily go to escalation as de-escalation.

But Maggie Haberman reports that “Miller’s pitch for the job, according to people who heard it, was that the president needed to wind down the Iran war, which the president’s core supporters viewed as a betrayal.”
Eurasia Group Analyst Gregory Brew adds:
FWIW there are a couple of different routes to “end the war” but somehow I doubt Miller’s pitch to Trump was to go back to the MOU and let Iran have the strait.
Stephen Miller says ‘the mission is now more clear than ever’
His first statement as Chief of Staff suggests a bunker mentality:
President Trump is the most transformative political leader in American History — and he has single-handedly saved America from those who would destroy it.
It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff.
I want to thank the incomparable Susie Wiles for her years of devoted service to the President and the Country, and for her friendship.
The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic.
RFK Jr. wants to ‘unleash the Kraken’
A totally normal statement of praise from a totally normal HHS secretary:
Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.
The latest post-midterms margins
The Democratic majorities will be 260 in the House and 56 in the Senate:
Hegseth better polish his resume

He’s blasting out how psyched he is about his fellow MAGA zealot Stephen Miller now being in charge of the White House, but Pete Hegseth is looking more and more like a post-midterms sacrificial lamb. Congress is already on the case with Thomas Massie’s impeachment resolution, which will go live the minute the lame-duck session begins. And now it’s increasingly clear Trump’s inner circle has decided the Iran War is the expendable part of the second-term agenda.

J.D. Vance, who never does or says anything that will dismay the boss, has blamed the entire midterm debacle on the war. And now Miller has reportedly argued that ending the war is how Trump wins back his base. Dumping the Warfighter In Chief at the Pentagon could simultaneously please the MAGA folk who never liked the war to begin with, while giving congressional Democrats an early trophy. Maybe Hegseth can be given some phony-baloney diplomatic post like Kristi Noem was given.
Trump and Miller’s mandate of the mind
Vox’s Astead Herndon cautions:
Why I’d urge caution on declaring the Trump era over. The second term project hasn’t just been about retribution, but also unchecked presidential power — with Miller and Project 2025 its architects.

They didn’t really try and sell their agenda to the public. They tried to gerrymander a win before voting started. And they worked hard to empower the executive, and to minimize the role of Congress/Courts altogether.
So in a weird, undemocratic way, the WH has been building to this moment for two years.
Trump reportedly sped up Wiles’s exit
According to a CBS News report, Wiles’ sudden departure was not exactly what she had planned:

Wiles had planned to stay on as chief through Congress’ lame-duck session and exit after that, likely at the end of this year or early next year, according to sources familiar with her thinking. The president accelerated her departure.
Targeting Minneapolis was Miller’s ‘passion project’

Here come the leaks. The Washington Sun reports that Miller “pressed administration officials for evidence of fraud related to immigrants, Minnesota and the state’s Somali population nine times in a span of about 10 minutes during a December 2025 call”:
The president’s fierce loyalist, at the time his deputy chief of staff, , according to a recording obtained by The Washington Sun.

Miller cut one official off as they were describing a fraud problem in Florida, a hot spot for bad actors who siphon off government benefits, according to the government’s own data. He appeared uninterested in the official’s description of fraud when it didn’t prominently feature immigrants.
At one point, Miller was told about an active criminal investigation into a national fraud case out of the Eastern District of Virginia.
“I hear you, but that’s a long way off from Minneapolis,” Miller responded.
The call is one of several previously unreported instances since the fall of 2025 in which Miller pushed administration officials to target a small population of immigrants in a single state. …

Miller has repeatedly sought to wield the full weight of the federal government against the roughly 100,000 Somalis who live in Minnesota, targeting the state’s federal funds, installing an ally of his immigration agenda in a key position at the Justice Department and clashing with career and political officials in the process.
“It’s like a passion project for him,” one source close to the White House said.
Who needs strategy when you’ve got American carnage
“Stephen Miller should lawyer up”
From the likely new head of the House Oversight Committee:
Hegseth is in full ‘F*ck Yeah’ mode
‘American blood on his hands’
Democratic leaders have unsurprisingly, rejected the Miller pick.
Hakeem Jeffries, the likely incoming Speaker of the House, has weighed in on Miller’s new role as chief of staff, saying he has “American blood on his hands” and calling for him to be fired.
Chuck Schumer, who is expected to be Senate Majority Leader once again, vowed that the new Democratic-led Congress will “fight him every step of the way.”
‘I just wanted to make a change’
“We gotta make moves,” Trump said, like this move didn’t mean much, to reporters outside the White House:
It’s not fully clear what “change” actually means to Trump right now, however.
The White House hatchet man is thrilled
The bunker meme has returned

Sources told Axios that her departure was a mutual decision, but driven by Tuesday’s midterm losses, for which Trump blamed her. Trump did not ask for her resignation, said one informed source who spoke with Wiles, “but he couldn’t get it out of his head that she was to blame, not him.”“Susie could’ve stuck around, but what’s the point?” that person said. “Whether it’s right or wrong, Susie knows that serving the president means it’s at his pleasure. And if she couldn’t change the way he felt, there was no reason to stay.” …

Wiles’ strength was understanding how to navigate Trump rather than trying to control him. She avoided public confrontations, offered disagreements privately and sought to carry out Trump’s priorities rather than restrain them.But her influence had limits. She was a critical voice against the war in Iran and repeatedly questioned the hardline immigration tactics championed by Miller.

One of the disconnects right now is that the Republican midterm losses were a decisive rebuke of the president and his actions in office. But Trump has two years left of the term, and putting in Miller — who is deeply ideological and also the most powerful policy staffer in the modern history of the presidency — is doubling down on Trump’s agenda, not switching course.

Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff. Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.
More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.
The cruelty is still somehow Trump’s point
Comments Ron Brownstein on X:

I’m sure Vance and Rubio are feeling confident today that Miller is just the man to steer their way back to support from all the voters who thought Trump was too extreme, chaotic, cruel, reckless and ineffective this week. Who better to recapture straying Latinos?

The GOP loses everything beyond deep MAGA terrain (+andeven some there), suffers big reversals with all the groups that moved to Trump in 2024, swing voters & even non-MAGA Republicans, and Trump’s answer is to elevate Stephen Miller as Chief of Staff, with his unerring instinct for outreach and consensus.
Below-the-radar midterms feats
We collected a bunch of eye-popping details about election results from across the country, including:
Early votes for Talarico, Cooper, and Ossoff surpassed their opponents’ total votes.

Texas’s official election results showed James Talarico received 4,397,474 early votes. The figure is actually larger than the total number of votes Ken Paxton received overall at 4,249,373, a difference of 148,101. The incoming senator-elect could’ve made history even with just the early vote. NBC’s Decision Desk discovered similar dynamics for Georgia senator Jon Ossoff as well as North Carolina senator-elect Roy Cooper, who received more votes in early voting than his Republican opponent, Michael Whatley, won in total.
Trump has made Stephen Miller his new Chief of Staff
Wiles is out. Miller is in, Trump says on Truth Social:

I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026. Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job! President DONALD J. TRUMP
I wrote about the midterms most difficult to please constituency, the swing voters who hate both parties:

Donald Trump will not be on the ballot in 2028, and between now and then Democrats need to convince double haters to hate them less than Republicans in a comparative context, including one in which Democrats will be entirely in control of Congress. This challenge may be intensified by a wide-open 2028 Democratic presidential-nominating contest in which candidates may be focused more on appealing to reliable party-primary participants rather than the swing voters they will need in November. If conditions in the country worsen and such emerging existential issues as AI-related job loss explode into prominence, it’s even possible that long-suppressed support for minor parties, old or new, could finally threaten the two-party duopoly or at least affect the balance of power between Democrats and Republicans. So leaders and activists in both parties need to get over the midterms quickly and focus on the sales pitches they have to develop to win over voters who aren’t very fond of any of them.
Jeffries made his own way to the gavel

[W]ithin the Democratic Party, the new House majority represents the victory of realism over rhetoric. For all the headlines given to the supposed influence of socialists and ultraprogressives, Jeffries’s majority was created by painstakingly recruiting and supporting the kind of candidates who can defeat Republicans. In New York, while the Democratic Socialists of America were attacking mainstream Democrats like Adriano Espaillat and Antonio Reynoso, and debating over who was first to use the word genocide to denounce attacks on Gaza, Jeffries was lining up candidates in red-to-blue districts that included ministers, combat veterans, farmers, prosecutors, and other centrists from blue-collar backgrounds.
The right-wing media meltdown is well underway
The Bulwark’s Will Sommer observes:

RIGHT-WING MEDIA has always been a fractious place even under the best of circumstances, featuring combustible personalities with flexible ethical standards clashing with one another in the pursuit of influence, followers, and money. A civil war has roiled the podcast right for over a year, turning intertwined issues like the Epstein files, Charlie Kirk’s murder, and the Iran war into the stuff of both conspiracies and blood feuds.

But the midterm rout, which none of these folks seemed to see coming, has cranked the stakes up to eleven. That’s partially because right-wing media figures are worried about their future. If no one wants to be a Republican anymore, who’s going to watch their podcasts and buy their brain pills? But it’s also because there’s a genuine belief that the fate of their ideological projects is at stake.
Rubio denies he’s planning to bounce
He spoke with the New York Times today:
Responding to the news reports that he was mulling an exit, Mr. Rubio said, “I don’t know where these things come from, to be honest with you.”
“I love the work I’m doing,” he continued. “And plus I always laugh when they say he’s going to leave his job. I go, ‘Which one?’”
Mr. Rubio, who is also Mr. Trump’s national security adviser, declined to answer questions about whether he was considering running for president in 2028.
“I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore,” he said in the interview, in his White House office. “I just won’t do it.”
Democrats’ other astounding nationwide feat

They are on track to seize control of a majority of America’s state legislative chambers for the first time in 16 years — since 2010, when the GOP swept to state power on the coattails of the anti-Obama Tea Party movement. Notes Axios:
If current leads hold, 75% of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governor, and 53% will live in Democratic trifectas. …
The party is set to flip 12 legislative chambers, dismantle five Republican state trifectas, shatter 11 GOP supermajorities and build 12 of its own, according to AP returns as of 6pm ET on Wednesday.

If leads hold, Democrats will control the governor’s office and both chambers in five of the seven 2024 presidential battlegrounds: Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.They have also broken Republican one-party rule in the sixth (Georgia) and flipped the House in the seventh (North Carolina).Democrats flipped five GOP-held governorships (Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas) and lead in Alaska.
Colom’s lead is still inching up
In case you missed it, the Senate candidate endorsed a very state-appropriate vote-counting method yesterday:
Let’s hear it for the failures
I just ranked the 13 biggest losers of the midterms, including:
3. The White House Political Team

Probably no one group of Americans in politics has received more undeserved credit for brilliance than Donald Trump’s White House political team. To be sure, Susie Wiles and Chris LaCivita, the co-chairs of Trump’s 2024 comeback campaign, and James Blair, that campaign’s political director, did a fine job of plucking the ripe fruit of the Biden administration’s many problems, and guiding the 45th president through to his inauguration. And on the most superficial level, Trump 2.0 was less chaotic under their management than Trump 1.0. But in many respects, that just meant Trump was very free to pursue his own worst instincts, and his political team did little if anything to restrain him. Now in the wake of the midterm disaster, the long knives are out for these erstwhile geniuses, as Jake Lahut reported.
Pete Hegseth will not be able to parachute into the Senate
The governor of Tennessee has rejected the wild idea that she would help Trump get rid of the embattled Defense Secretary, per a source who spoke with Punchbowl’s Jake Sherman:

[Pete Hegseth] is not being considered [for Senate]. This is nothing more than Washington, D.C., spin from a bunch of consultants with nothing better to do. The Blackburn team is focused on the transition, not entertaining baseless speculation. Dc won’t pick the next senator.
I’ve done a close read of the president’s social posts in the aftermath of the midterms rout, during which he appears to be trying a new tack:

This rebranding attempt is glaringly obvious if you scroll through Trump’s Truth Social feed. It actually won’t take long at all. Pre-election, @realDonaldTrump “truthed” and “retruthed” dozens of times per day. His posts often reflected the worst of the MAGA cesspool, from racist and Islamophobic diatribes to bizarre AI-generated trolling.

In contrast, Trump only put up three posts on Wednesday. The first featured screenshots of a New York Post story praising him for saving the Western hemisphere with his “Donroe Doctrine.” The next said, “Stock Market just hit another Record High,” without noting that might have something to do with the election results. Then on Wednesday night, Trump put up a post highlighting his effort to make daylight saving time permanent.
Meanwhile in President Trump’s mind
Yep, this really happened, and check out the new “VETO” hat on his desk, too:
Meanwhile at the White House
One of the GOP’s only gains
Rubio may resign from his 17 roles in the Trump administration

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is weighing whether to leave the Trump administration, people familiar with the matter said, as he considers his next moves following Republicans’ midterm elections wipeout this week.

Rubio and his advisers are going over options for his future, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing internal deliberations. He hasn’t made a decision about whether to quit his posts as top US diplomat and national security adviser, and there is no timetable on a possible departure.
An earlier report from the Independent suggested he was also considering a 2028 run.
Maybe Trump just sucks at politics
On Tuesday night, our former colleague Jonathan Chait argued that the results have demonstrated, again, that Donald Trump is not some savvy political magician:

Whatever misgivings some Republicans may have about Trump’s character or his policies, many subscribe to the theory that, if nothing else, the man knows how to win. And his aura of mastery has extended beyond his followers to the Americans who most detest him. The disgust with which many liberals regard Trump is mixed with fear and envy. His powers of persuasion are a source of endless fascination. They have launched a thousand diner safaris to explore his mystical hold on Real America, and inspired innumerable Democratic activists and intellectuals to ponder how they could create a Trump of their own.

But Trump is not a winner. He is, for the most part, a loser. In 2016, he lost the national popular vote—that is, the measure of which candidate Americans wanted to win the election—by two percentage points. His party lost control of the House in the 2018 midterms. Trump lost reelection in 2020. His sole unambiguous victory came in 2024, when he faced the clumsy fill-in candidate for an unpopular administration, against which he prevailed, almost by default.
And now he has lost again.
‘Events actually mattered’

I had a long conversation with with the Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter about the meaning of the midterms. One of her big takeaways was how this election showed once again how nothing in politics is set in stone:

Events actually mattered. We went through COVID and January 6th and inflation in 2022 and Harris being the new nominee in 2024, and it didn’t move the partisanship much. Not to say that this is a permanent reshuffling of it, but it is a marker now for just how far a president can push unpopular policies and agendas without backlash. It is a good, healthy reminder that our politics is never as set in stone as those of us who have to watch it every day often think it is, and that there’s no such thing as a permanent coalition in politics, even when it seems, as I said, that there is a calcification that’s impossible to break. Every now and then, it does. And it is an extraordinary thing to witness.
Colom’s small lead has grown in Mississippi
It’s now up to 1,724 votes as of Thursday afternoon.
What Democrats did well to win: Message
Here’s what Democratic pollster David Shor told our old friend Eric Levitz over at Vox:

I think the Democratic leadership and both wings of the Democratic Party — the left and the “establishment” or whatever — deserve a lot of credit for making big, concrete shifts in their messaging; specifically, focusing more on economic issues that affect people’s everyday lives. That was not a given. It was not uncontroversial at the time. And it paid dividends.

Right before the 2024 election, Republicans had a 12-point trust advantage on the cost of living. Today, among 2026 voters, Democrats actually have the trust advantage on the issue, which continues to be voters’ No. 1 concern by far.

We ask voters questions like, “What do you think the Democratic Party cares about?” And when we asked that question a year after the 2024 election, voters thought Democrats prioritized catering to their base over the cost of living by 4 to 1.

When we ran that survey again right before this year’s election, voters thought Democrats cared about the cost of living more than anything else, just like them. They thought Democrats’ second concern was fighting Donald Trump, which maybe wasn’t a total positive. But then No. 3 was healthcare and No. 4 was the economy. And so Democrats really did execute a big pivot.
How did El-Sayed fare among Jewish voters?
At a quiet Huntington Woods polling

items.title: Del Casher, Guitarist Who Invented the Wah-Wah Pedal, Dead at 88
items.description: Del Casher, the guitarist and inventor whose innovations included the wah-wah pedal, has died at the age of 88.
items.author: Daniel Kreps
paragraphs: Del Casher, the guitarist and inventor whose innovations included the wah-wah pedal, has died at the age of 88.
Casher died Oct. 1 following a battle with cancer, according to a GoFundMe to raise money for his widow, Eiko. TMZ was first to report on Casher’s death.

Born Delton Kacher in Hammond, Indiana, Casher first performed with artists like Gene Autry, Lawrence Welk, and the Three Suns, while also experimenting with new techniques and technologies in an effort to make his own electric-guitar playing stand out.

In the early Sixties, while playing with the Thomas Organ Company’s Vox Ampliphonic Orchestra, Casher asked about making his guitar sound like the trumpet, complete with the ability to mildly suppress the instrument mid-playing. While Casher often credited Thomas Organ’s Brad Plunkett as the engineer of the device, the wah-wah pedal was considered Casher’s brainchild.

First dubbed the “Cry Baby” pedal, Casher also recorded a demo for instrument stores showcasing how to use the pedal, as well as an accompanying single. Both the pedal and the single failed to catch on with the music-playing public upon release in 1967.
However, Frank Zappa, who used the wah-wah pedal in 1966 when Casher sat in with the Mothers of Invention, gifted a pedal to Jimi Hendrix, solidifying the wah-wah’s place in music history soon after.

Hendrix would employ the pedal throughout his classic Electric Ladyland — including on “Voodoo Child,” “Burning of the Midnight Lamp,” and “All Along the Watchtower” — while fellow guitarist Eric Clapton wah-wah’d on Cream tracks like “Tales of Brave Ulysses.”

Soon after, many of the great rock guitarists of the era, like Jimmy Page, Tony Iommi, David Gilmour, and more, were experimenting with the wah-wah pedal. By 1971, the wah-wah pedal had featured on a Number One single and Oscar-winning song thanks to its use on Isaac Hayes’ “Theme From Shaft.” Generations of guitar players have used the pedal since.

Outside of inventing — Casher is also credited with contributing to the creation of the Ecco-Fonic and the Fender Electronic Echo Chamber — the guitarist also found work with artists like Elvis Presley, appearing in his 1964 film Roustabout. Casher also contributed film scores later in his career.
“I feel gratified that I was there at the beginning,” Casher told The New York Times. “I would just like guitar players to think of me once in a while. The only thing I ask is: remember me.”

items.title: Andy Richter Claims U2's the Edge Wrote an 'Elf' Sequel Screenplay
items.description: Andy Richter, who had a small role in the 2003 Christmas classic Elf, revealed in a new interview that U2’s the Edge wrote a screenplay for the sequel to the Will Ferrell-starring film.
items.author: Daniel Kreps
paragraphs: Andy Richter, who had a small role in the 2003 Christmas classic Elf, revealed in a new interview that U2’s the Edge wrote a screenplay for the sequel to the Will Ferrell-starring film.
For over two decades, Elf fans have clamored for a sequel to the film, and while an Elf 2 came close to happening in 2013, Ferrell ultimately decided against reprising the role of Buddy.

At some point after the film’s release and rise to holiday favorite, as Richter told Obsessed: The Podcast, Elf producer Shauna Robertson received a phone call from an unlikely screenwriter pitching a meeting about Elf 2.

“Somebody reached out to her and said, ‘The Edge from U2 has written a sequel to Elf, and he wants to talk to you about it,’” Richter said. “It’s the weirdest story, but apparently it was fully written somewhere in the world. There is an Edge-penned Elf 2 out there.”
Richter added that the meeting “never happened.” “It’s one of those things where she’s like, ‘All right, sure, I’ll meet him,’ and then it just petered out and never happened,” Richter said.

While the Edge has hundreds of credits on his IMDB page thanks to his work with U2, “Screenwriter” is not among “Composer,” “Soundtrack,” and “Actor” (as himself) in his filmography. However, the Edge has served as a producer on a handful of occasions on non-U2 projects, including documentaries and short films.
The Edge has not commented, ever, on his Elf 2 script. U2, however, will gives fans an early Christmas present next week with the arrival of their new album Carnaval de Luz.

items.title: U2 Sound Revitalized on 'Carnaval de Luz'
items.description: In the 1988 documentary Rattle and Hum, B.B. King chats with Bono, then 27. The bluesman reflects on his station in life: “[People] say, ‘There he is, a 62-year-old — and what is he trying to do?'”
items.author: Kory Grow
paragraphs: In the 1988 documentary Rattle and Hum, B.B. King chats with Bono, then 27. The bluesman reflects on his station in life: “[People] say, ‘There he is, a 62-year-old — and what is he trying to do?'”

It’s a question that U2‘s members may have asked themselves as they worked on Carnaval de Luz, their 16th full-length and first album of original music in nearly a decade. They were teens when the group formed in Dublin half a century ago, in their thirties when their art-damaged rock started to “fuck up the mainstream,” middle-aged when they reinvented themselves with “Beautiful Day,” and old enough to know better when they brute-forced Songs of Innocence onto your iPhone. Their resume boasts multiplatinum Number One hits, instant sellout tours, and household-name status. But now, here they are, sixtysomething years old — and what are they trying to do?

U2 show they’re nowhere close to a finish line on Carnaval de Luz, whose central theme seems to be “it’s not too late”: It’s not too late to party (“Go [Carnaval de Luz]”), not too late to find God (“Midnight Sunshine”), not too late for empathy (“Torn”), not too late to save a relationship (“If the World Is at War We Better Not Be”), not too late to save the world (“Street of Dreams”), and just plain not too late (“Can’t Stop Us Now”).

Each song is tight and punchy, memorable and melodic. The music is the opposite of the blues, as well as U2’s legend-making hits; it’s big, bright pop music with more silver linings than clouds and only a few minor keys. As always, U2 work best when they’re not trying too hard. The songs on Carnaval never recall “Pride (in the Name of Love),” or “One,” or “Stuck in a Moment,” but they do sound like U2 every time Bono opens his mouth and croons something profound (“Nobody is alone but nobody knows that,” on “La Reina”) as much as when he belts something a little corny (“Sing-a-ling the reggaeton,” also on “La Reina”). They sound like U2 whenever the Edge‘s guitar echoes and chimes (“Street of Dreams,” the intro to “The Mirror Maker [Rosalía]”), when Adam Clayton‘s bass stabs and undulates (“La Reina”), and when Larry Mullen Jr. plays a propulsive, march-like rhythm (“Can’t Stop Us Now”) — affectations that come to them naturally.

Carnaval’s best song, “The Greatest Show on Earth,” does resemble The Joshua Tree’s big singles, thanks to an ambient soundscape assisted by that album’s producer, Brian Eno. But it also fits in with the lean, hook-focused essence of the rest of the LP, produced by Jacknife Lee. The band’s last collection of originals, 2017’s Songs of Experience, suffered from a bit too much experience — nine credited producers — and the songs went in too many directions. This time, they kept the production relatively simple and achieved a cohesive feel.

They seem refreshed. Carnaval de Luz is an ambitious endeavor, connecting the previously released EPs Days of Ash and Easter Lily into a conceptual arc. Carnaval, at least the way they spell it, is Brazil’s colorful festival preceding Lent (which good Catholic boys like U2 know means Ash Wednesday, a day of ash) and, later, Easter.

Days of Ash featured the punk rocker “American Obituary,” mourning the death of Renée Good at the hands of an ICE agent, and the powerful, Roy Orbison-like “The Tears of Things,” which obliquely addresses the divide between Gaza and Israel. Easter Lily, the better of the two EPs, featured “Song for Hal,” a classic-sounding U2 song about never feeling alone (“You are not alone when you close your eyes,” sings the Edge) and “In a Life,” which features more traditional U2 drama and sparkling guitar. The final song, “Coexist,” ends with the opening analog-synth notes of Carnaval, starting the cycle over again.

When taken as a whole — and a deluxe edition of Carnaval de Luz does pair the LP with the EPs — the songs present an alternative argument to pop-culture doomsaying, since, as always, U2’s central message is preaching peace, hope, and love. And, well, the music is fun. Right from the word “Go,” the upbeat dance song that kicks off Carnaval, they fuse Nile Rodgers–style disco guitar, Suicide-inspired keys, and hooks galore into a dance-rock anthem with lyrics about how they “came to find other people who feel like this.” Best yet, the song runs under three minutes.

“La Reina” and “Street of Dreams” borrow the spirit of Latin pop without becoming Latin pop (though there is a little hip-hop on “Street of Dreams”), and Bono still aspires to transmit universal truths like “Everyone is on their own, everybody knows that” on the former and “Don’t you give up, and your dreams won’t give up on you” on the latter. On “The Mirror Maker (Rosalía),” Bono may be drawing inspiration from Rosalía, but the Edge is thinking of Pete Townshend as he strums big wind-milling chords on acoustic and electric guitars.

The album’s best songs come toward the end, and they’re anything but quiet. The intro the Edge plays on “The Greatest Show on Earth” begins like a Joshua Tree single but then the guitar echoes shift out of phase, similar to Refused’s “The Shape of Punk to Come,” perhaps to show they’re in a new era. Then they settle into a gentle rumination on love, aging, and God. “Is this a church of love or fear?” Bono sings. “Have we made God feel like a stranger here?” Meanwhile, he repeats words for extra hooky oomph on the Martin Garrix co-produced “Glorify,” singing, “They’re looking for you to glorify, glorify.” And “Midnight Sunshine” feels like it could be both a sex jam and an end-of-the-world party song, since Bono’s lyrics — “In the dark, we discover midnight sunshine” — are open to interpretation.

Carnaval ends with “Torn,” a country-ish duet with Dolly Parton in her final recorded vocal, which recalls Johnny Cash’s appearance on the band’s Zooropa. Just like “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” U2’s chronicle of the division wrought by Ireland’s troubles decades earlier, it’s not a “rebel song” but a humanitarian plea. Parton sounds emotional and cracked, and Bono deepens his voice for maximum gravitas as they describe “a family at war.” Neither Parton nor Bono calls out Republicans and Democrats, Catholics and Protestants, or any other ideologically divided people. It’s clear that Parton and U2 just want everyone in the world to try to understand one another on a fundamental level, before it’s too late. That is what U2 are trying to do.

items.title: Black Doves Recap: Grasping the Concept of Undercover
items.description: Rescue heist! At last, the rescue heist is upon us! And son of a gun if it’s not a riff on Helen’s chapter in “The Opportunity to Become Savage”: Helen and Sam are Helen and Wallace; Williams and Eleanor are Ollie and Jacqueline; Reed is Franz; and Laila is Na
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: Rescue heist! At last, the rescue heist is upon us! And son of a gun if it’s not a riff on Helen’s chapter in “The Opportunity to Become Savage”: Helen and Sam are Helen and Wallace; Williams and Eleanor are Ollie and Jacqueline; Reed is Franz; and Laila is Nanny Marie. Mum and Dad are trying to get their fractious children to settle down, the opinionated children wear down their parents to ensure they can listen to their music, the target is acquired and delivers a monologue that answers some questions and raises others, and then the energetic nanny arrives to get everyone back in order.

I’d never heard of a kill mix (or a murder mix) before, but in these days of algorithmically generated playlists, I love that Williams has a hand-selected mix of psych-up jams to get her in the right headspace for her contract work. The gig economy is so competitive; any little advantage you can give yourself sets you apart from the rest. No intergenerational group project can move forward without a bit of conflict, and Sam seems more than ready to go several rounds today. First, he puts on some Nick Cave (strong marks thematically; you’ve got a solid chance of firing up a murder ballad even if you hit “play” on a Nick Cave song at random), then trolls Eleanor by suggesting a bunch of Welsh artists (“You fucking racist!” she yells). (“No Gorky’s Zygotic Mynci?” I wonder aloud.) After some podcast bickering and the kids mocking Helen for even suggesting her kids’ favorite artist, Olly Murs, Sam and Helen finally agree to return to the murder mix, leading to Williams and Eleanor rocking out while “Nobody Speak,” by DJ Shadow feat. Run the Jewels, rings out.

Sam being Sam, he’s got a full armory in the boot of his car, including walkie-talkies, and urges everyone (1) to be mindful of their tone of voice so as to be respectful of Williams and her hangover and (2) to approach the house where Reed is being held with caution. Let’s keep everything as low-key as possible and not attract maximum attention from the 20-to-40 armed guards the Black Doves have outsourced this job to, okay? Absolutely not. Williams and Eleanor have bigger fish to fry, specifically, the pros-and-cons list that could be about their nascent relationship or about taking the contract to kill Sam. What’s the difference, really? Degree of difficulty, concerns about regrets and potential damage to their friend/colleague group — all relevant for both topics when you think about it.

Eleanor and Williams spend the remainder of the episode doing what they’ve always done: bickering and bantering at high speed, quipping while dispatching foes, and working their way toward sincere emotional conversation. Their screwball antics are so funny and heartfelt, and the balance of tartness and sweetness is calibrated just right. How can Eleanor take Williams’s declaration of love seriously if she has never told Eleanor her first name? Learning it’s Fionnula sends the two of them down a rabbit hole of family history and cultural allusions punctuated liberally by the casual gunning down of the faceless gunmen and occasional bludgeoning with a darling retro dusty-pink telephone.

It’s all intercut with Helen and Sam’s adventures, in which our besties are having the most serious argument of their friendship. Sam has been holding back information from Helen, partly for her safety and partly to forestall conversations like this one. She resents his making decisions about what information she can and can’t access, and as is usually the basis of arguments like this, they’re both partly right and partly wrong. He’s right: Helen often is impulsive, and her now-firm decision to fight for the life she has built affects him, too. The revelation of what a joyless, bleak vacuum Sam’s life has become now that he has “pushed every person who ever threatened to love [him] away, and the ones that [he] didn’t push away are killed” hits hard. He has nothing left to give her, but like his admirable fellow countryman Rick Astley, he’s also never gonna give her up, let her down, run around, and desert her. Their argument isn’t over, but he’s going to hold off these hired goons as long as he can. There are so many of them. Sam, Eleanor, and Williams are mowing them down, but Conteh (whom Reed sniffily describes as “suffer[ing] from a terminal lack of imagination”) keeps sending more.

It’s very interesting to hear Reed explain what has been going on to Helen. The mask of cool detachment and unflappability she has worn for so long is too precisely fitted to remove, but some glimmers of normal human feeling do come through. Her admission that she didn’t lose Vita but abandoned her and that she deleted all references to her daughter from the operation’s file is about as self-lacerating as Reed can get. Even that is delivered in a smooth, even tone of voice as if she were reading aloud from a field report, and it’s really no different from what she did with all official traces of Helen’s existence prior to her joining the Black Doves.

The piece of her story that is more fleshed out than what we’ve seen already pertains to Vita, Franz, and Alexi Chernov. Franz popped up on Reed’s radar when it became clear that he had been blackmailing Chernov for vast sums, threatening to expose his attempted defection in 1988. This wasn’t just for fun but to resurrect Kestrel and pass it down to Vita herself. Alert viewers will have already made a reasonable guess as to the current identity and location of the woman formerly known as Vita.

Meanwhile, the waves of hired goons keep coming, so Helen hands Reed a small shotgun and the two sally forth to try to rendezvous with Sam, Williams, and Eleanor. If only Laila could see how decidedly Helen is kicking the asses of the heavily armed guys standing between her, Reed, and the exit. Shooting, knifing, kicking! Who’s a spy wife now, huh? Eleanor and Williams are squabbling their way toward fully mutual love confessions. Nothing says a love built to last like addressing your beloved as a twat and then throwing a grenade out the window at the bad guys. Romance is alive and well among the professional assassins of the greater London metropolitan area!

Although there’s a brief moment when it looks as if our anti-heroes will be gunned down by Conteh’s forces, Laila shows up to save the day. Huzzah! I love how she’s framed in this moment: a small woman in profile firing a very large gun. It reminded me of how Teyana Taylor appears in a memorable scene of One Battle After Another. Immediately after dispatching the remaining goons, Laila checks in with Mrs. Reed, and I love the juxtaposition of her one-woman murder squad with sincere care for her (once and future?) boss. Laila’s arrival reenergizes the whole group, which is handy because they’ve got one more round of mercenaries to deal with before making it back to London, where they all agree a round of drinks is in order.

Reed makes Sam’s life easier by letting him know that she knows this hasn’t been a rescue mission after all. Leila does the same with Eleanor, and even Patrick extends a similar professional courtesy to Sam with a timely heads-up about the contract out on his life. None of these people will be as easy to kill as any of the folks Sam has been hunting all season. Before she and Sam head out on their fateful walk home, Reed offers Helen her best attempt at sincere warmth, giving her a tiny shoulder squeeze and thanking her protegée. This should set off some very high-decibel alarms to Helen, but I can’t blame her for being just a bit too tired to hear them.
Strange Times to Be Nefarious

• I hope Sam finds it in himself to believe Helen when she says his strength and friendship strengthen her, too. He has been walking around believing Patrick’s claptrap about the strong needing others to be weak, but that’s all it is.

• The pain at the heart of Helen and Sam’s relationship finally comes to the fore in this episode, something Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw reflected on in our interview. Whishaw said it was interesting to play “because it’s the first time they really argue seriously — they have some real disagreements,” with Knightley picking up the thread that “the whole root of the relationship is these are two people that can’t be themselves with anyone other than each other, and all of a sudden in this season they’re keeping things from one another.”

• Was this our most Wallace-forward episode so far? This has to be the most we’ve seen of him without Helen. Perryman makes the most of his private audience with Wallace and might have gotten somewhere with his latest pieces of Heleniana, especially the photos Wallace has clearly never seen, had he not been preempted by the commissioner from the Met. Wallace did well to save Helen’s and his own bacon after instantly recognizing Sam’s face in the surveillance photos by asking to have them sent to his secretary. The commissioner doesn’t bat an eyelash, and why would he? Wallace has this summit to pull off tomorrow; he’s going to let the man get back to work!

• There’s something off about the scenes with Cecile Mason. Neve Campbell’s performance seems built on top of her approximation of Kim Dickens’s voice as Joanie Stubbs in Deadwood run through a filter set to Aaron Sorkin–esque. Every time she’s onscreen, I wonder if this character was more significant in earlier drafts or if the role got pared down in editing. The way she’s talking and the influence and access she clearly thinks she ought to have seem disproportionate to the way everyone else perceives her. Then again, that may well be the point.

• Reed easily gets the line of the episode, sighing to Helen, who has just blown a hole in the door to the room where she’s being held, “Sometimes I wonder if you have ever truly understood the concept of undercover.”

items.title: John Oliver Dunks on Midterms Losers Elon Musk and Haley Stevens
items.description: After issuing an urgent warning prior to the midterms about the GOP’s increasingly troubling ties to neo-Nazis (with a little dig at Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans, of “You Can See Everything” infamy, thrown in for good measure), John Oliver returned to the
items.author: Marlow Stern
paragraphs: After issuing an urgent warning prior to the midterms about the GOP’s increasingly troubling ties to neo-Nazis (with a little dig at Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans, of “You Can See Everything” infamy, thrown in for good measure), John Oliver returned to the “Last Week Tonight” desk on Sunday to bask in the Democrats’ blue tsunami that saw them wrest back control of Congress in imposing fashion.

“It has been a busy week and, given the midterm results, a pretty good week, too!” Oliver exclaimed at the top of his HBO show. “Democrats won so big on Tuesday it was sometimes genuinely hard to take all the positive results in.”

Oliver opined how it was “genuinely hard to believe Texas had just turned blue,” adding it was “hard to process” all the wins, including 22 state trifectas, Chris Pappas becoming the first openly-gay man elected to U.S. Senate, Deb Haaland of New Mexico being the first Native American woman elected governor of a U.S. state, and Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms elected the first Black woman governor of a U.S. state.

The comic also applauded how, “Abdul El-Sayed won in Michigan, meaning all the hateful shit thrown his way did not work, and also that this woman [Haley Stevens] imploded her own political career for nothing. Then, you realize Susan Collins lost too! A decade of having to listen to her express reservations about something before going ahead and doing it anyway are finally fucking over.”

But wait, there’s more: “Then it hits you that Elon Musk wasted so much money! The half a billion dollars he spent to try and buy the election just went up in flames faster than a parked Cybertruck. Speaking of which: we also learned this week he’s ending production of Cybertrucks, which isn’t an election result but kind of feels like one.”

Yes, Musk spent nearly $500 million during the midterm election cycle, including $200 million to (unsuccessfully) defeat Senator-elect James Talarico in Texas; while Stevens, a supposed Democrat, backed GOP candidate Mike Rogers over her primary rival (and eventual winner) El-Sayed.

items.title: Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Roars With $31 Million Debut, ‘Cat in the Hat’ Fizzles With $20 Million
items.description: The Cat in the Hat was no match for the mighty Godzilla. “Godzilla Minus Zero” climbed to the top of box office charts with $31.6 million from 3,254 theaters, a roaring start for a foreign-language epic in North America. Meanwhile, “The Cat in the Hat” stumble
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: The Cat in the Hat was no match for the mighty Godzilla. “Godzilla Minus Zero” climbed to the top of box office charts with $31.6 million from 3,254 theaters, a roaring start for a foreign-language epic in North America. Meanwhile, “The Cat in the Hat” stumbled with $20 million from 4,003 locations, a weak debut for an animated movie that’s based on one of the most well-known children’s books of all time.

Ticket sales for “Godzilla Minus Zero” register as the largest opening for a live-action foreign-language film in North America, shattering the record set by China’s martial arts-inspired “Hero” with $17.8 million in 2002. The R-rated “Godzilla” sequel benefited from sterling reviews and strong audience scores (a 90% on Rotten Tomatoes and “A” grade on CinemaScore exit polls), as well as outsized interest from premium large formats. It’s the first Japanese production ever filmed for Imax, and the company’s bigger and brighter screens have contributed a huge $12.7 million, or 40% of domestic grosses. It wasn’t just Imax that appealed to audiences. PLFs, including Dolby, accounted for a staggering 74% of ticket sales. By comparison, “The Odyssey” collected 53% of opening weekend returns from PLFs.

“We’re so happy to see audiences embrace ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ at an unprecedented scale for an international film,” says Chance Huskey, VP of distribution for Gkids, which distributed the movie in the U.S. The movie was produced by Japan’s Toho. “This landmark release is the result of a thoughtful campaign by Gkids and Toho that emphasized the ‘must-see’ intensity of the theatrical experience.”

“Godzilla Minus Zero” built on the success of the prior kaiju adventure, 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One.” That sci-fi epic secured a better-than-expected $11.4 million start and powered to $57 million in North America and $113 million globally, in addition to winning a visual effects Oscar. Directed by Takashi Yamazaki, the movie takes place two years after the previous installment as Godzilla regenerates and resurfaces to combat a new monster that’s tormenting postwar Japan.

“‘Godzilla’ is a hit,” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “Critics’ reviews and audience scores are once again outstanding. This weekend’s opening takes the Japanese production to a new level.”

“The Cat in the Hat” was well received by audiences, earning an “A” grade on CinemaScore, which could help in terms of box office longevity. Critics weren’t as kind, saddling the movie with a 45% on Rotten Tomatoes. Bill Hader voices the titular character in the cartooned version, which revolves around the shenanigans that occur after a mischievous cat (donning a hat) arrives to cheer up two siblings who move to a new town. Overseas, “The Cat in the Hat” collected just $10 million from 60 international markets for a global start of $30.5 million. Unless “The Cat in the Hat” rebounds in the coming weeks, the $92 million-budgeted movie will rank as another dud for Warner Bros. (Theater owners keep roughly 50% of ticket sales.) The studio, which recently merged with Paramount Skydance, has endured a brutal year at the box office with flops, including “Digger,” “The Bride!” and “Supergirl,” which have resulted in hundreds of millions in theatrical losses.

This is the second adaptation of the Dr. Seuss classic following 2003’s live-action comedy, starring Mike Myers as the Cat. That film opened to $38 million, not adjusted for inflation, and ran out of steam with $134 million, a disappointing result given the budget was above $100 million. More recently, Dr. Seuss adaptations like 2018’s “The Grinch” (which opened to $67 million) and 2012’s “The Lorax” (which opened to $70 million) were big hits for Universal and Illumination. Yes, the theatrical landscape has changed a lot since those films were released. But “The Cat in the Hat” is based on popular IP, and it didn’t have any competition. (Families with young kids haven’t had much to see since Universal’s “Forgotten Island” in September.) Even this spring’s “Hoppers,” an original offering from Disney and Pixar, managed to debut to $45 million.

“This is a soft opening,” Gross says. “However, family animation does extremely well in ancillary windows, earning more in digital sales and rental, streaming and TV licensing than in theatrical. That is where the film should recover its costs.”

Overall, this weekend reached $114 million across all films, up 86% from the same frame a year ago when “Predator: Badlands” was No. 1 at the box office. Meanwhile, year-to-date revenues hit $8.6 billion, 20% above the same point in 2025, according to Rentrak. Exhibitors are hoping the momentum continues through November, which sees the release of Paramount’s Christmas fantasy “Ebenezer,” starring Johnny Depp, Lionsgate’s “Hunger Games” prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping,” Universal’s comedy “Focker in Law,” with Ariana Grande joining Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, and Disney’s animated “Hexed.”
“It’s another encouraging sign as we head toward the all-important holiday movie season,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian.

Also this weekend, Searchlight’s dark comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell and directed by Martin McDonagh, opened at No. 8 with $6 million from 1,100 theaters. It’s a promising debut for the Oscar hopeful, which has a much larger initial footprint than McDonagh’s prior film, 2022’s “The Banshees of Inisherin.” After starting in limited release, “Banshees of Inisherin” became a slow and steady box office hit with $10.5 million domestically and $50 million globally. “Wild Horse Nine” follows Malkovich and Rockwell as CIA officers who are dispatched from Santiago to Easter Island shortly before a Chilean military coup.

Another newcomer, the Indian epic “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” earned $8.6 million over the traditional weekend and $12.1 million during its first four days in theaters. Sony is distributing “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” in 1,300 theaters, marking the widest North American release for an Indian film. Nitesh Tiwari‘s two-part adaptation of the ancient Hindu epic are the most expensive Indian films ever made, costing a combined $500 million to bring to screens. Globally, the movie bowed to $55.7 million, led by India with $32 million followed by the United Kingdom with $3 million.
“Indian epics do some business in English-speaking countries, but they can make a fortune in India,” says Gross. “It’s going to need to make a fortune there.”

“Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” opened in fifth place behind of A24’s electric Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything.” The zeitgeist-capturing movie has earned $8.8 million from 2,473 theaters in its fourth weekend of release, boosting its domestic tally to a staggering $79.8 million. “You Can See Everything” will leave theaters as one of the biggest documentaries in decades. And it will be very profitable for A24, which produced the nearly three-hour movie for $7 million.

“Drummer Boy,” a Christian musical from Angel Studios, landed at No. 3 with $9.3 million from 2,850 theaters. “Jimmy,” a faith-based biopic starring KJ Apa as the actor and military vet Jimmy Stewart, finished the weekend in 12th place with just $2.2 million from 1,470 theaters.

Elsewhere, A24’s heartwarming comedy “Club Kid” and Amazon MGM’s drama “I Play Rocky” scored in limited release. “Club Kid” earned $390,583 from six screens in New York and Los Angeles, translating to $65,097 per location. Jordan Firstman wrote, directed and stars in the film, which revolves around a hard-partying club promoter who finds out he has a 10-year-old son. “I Play Rocky” captured $345,000 from seven theaters, averaging $49,200 per location. Directed by Peter Farrelly, the movie depicts the real-life story of Sylvester Stallone bringing the 1976 classic “Rocky” to the big screen. Both films will expand nationwide around Thanksgiving.

“We’re incredibly encouraged by the response to ‘I Play Rocky’ so far,” says Amazon MGM Studios head of domestic distribution Kevin Wilson. “The enthusiasm from audiences reinforces our belief that we have a film with both awards potential and commercial appeal.”

items.title: Denis Villeneuve Teases James Bond Progress at LACMA Art + Film Gala: ‘I’m Having a Great Time’
items.description: When Denis Villeneuve arrived at LACMA on Saturday night, his black Gucci tuxedo made him look more like James Bond than a director who’s spent the last decade in the desert of Arrakis. Perhaps that’s fitting since the filmmaker is currently putting the final
items.author: Angelique Jackson
paragraphs: When Denis Villeneuve arrived at LACMA on Saturday night, his black Gucci tuxedo made him look more like James Bond than a director who’s spent the last decade in the desert of Arrakis. Perhaps that’s fitting since the filmmaker is currently putting the final touches on the 70mm Imax print of “Dune: Part Three” while simultaneously starting work on his Bond movie.

“It’s a very personal film and a project that is very close to my heart,” Villeneuve told Variety about wrapping up his “Dune” trilogy. “It’s also the project that is the completion of 10 years of work in the deep desert. I can just say that it has been a privilege of a lifetime to spend, and I enjoy every minute of it.”

On the topic of James Bond, news broke Friday that Villeneuve and producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman are inching closer to selecting the new 007, with finalists including Robert Pattinson, Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden.
On the red carpet, Villeneuve politely declined to comment about the casting speculation.
“I should not comment right now because every word I’m going to say is going to be scrutinized,” Villeneuve said. “I would just say that I’m having a great time.”

But inside the gala, he was ready to make some news. “For many years, LACMA has been a temple for me. Tonight feels like home, and to express my gratitude. With the blessing of my new friends at Amazon, I will reveal to you tonight who will be the next James Bond,” Villeneuve began, causing an audible stir in the crowd.
“The actor who will play the next James Bond is…” Villeneuve continued, pausing dramatically.
“And I will stop right now because Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack,” he said, laughing. (Yes, the Canadian director was only joking.)
Read on for more from Villeneuve’s remarks and a peek inside the high-fashion gala.

- Nicole Kidman and Denis Villeneuve Nicole Kidman admitted that she was sweating bullets as she prepared to present to Denis Villeneuve. “I’m just going to disclose I have sweaty armpits,” Kidman, wearing Chanel, joked. “Let’s keep it real here.” Then, Kidman revealed that she’d traveled 15 hours from Australia (overnight!) to make the event because she’s such an admirer of Villeneuve — even though they haven’t worked together yet. “About six years ago, I made a commercial for a little company called AMC Theaters,” Kidman said. “So much of what inspired me to be a part of that campaign and to champion the importance of returning to cinemas was the opportunity to experience films from the likes of tonight’s honoree, Denis Villeneuve.”

- Nicole Kidman Despite the fact that Kidman and Villeneuve had never really met before Saturday night, the Oscar winner said she feels like she’s gotten to know “the deepest parts” of Villeneuve through his films. “That is what extraordinary filmmakers do. They let you in. They reveal themselves to us through their work,” Kidman said. “They invite you into their imaginations, into their dreams, into their questions, and into their fears.” She continued: “I feel like that transcends anything that needs an introduction, because his films explore the great mysteries of our existence: time, memory, identity, destiny, the things we cannot explain, and the possibility that there is something that we do not understand. That we will never understand.” Kidman also recalled her experience watching an 11 p.m. screening of “Dune” at her local cinema and plans to return to the theater for “Dune: Part Three” when it hits theaters on Dec. 18. “I will always be one of your audience,” she said.

- Denis Villeneuve Onstage, Denis Villeneuve reflected on a fortuitous visit to LACMA while he was preparing to film 2016’s “Arrival.” “I was looking for guidance. Then I walk into the James Turrell exhibition … I watched people standing in a room in front of a brilliantly colored light in silence and in awe. And then I thought, ‘OK, I know how to direct the film now.'” Villeneuve shared that he discovered the power of images early in life. “My first contact with the English language as a boy in Quebec was through cinema,” he explained. “I didn’t understand the words, so I watched the images, and I imagined what the characters were saying.”

- Timothée Chalamet, Tanya Lapointe, Denis Villeneuve and Nicole Kidman In addition to the support from his “Dune” star Timothée Chalamet and Kidman, Villeneuve was also saluted in a clip reel that included filmmakers Steven Spielberg, James Cameron, Chloé Zhao, Alfonso Cuarón, Alejandro González Iñárritu, composer Hans Zimmer and producer Mary Parent. “When I was 12, all my friends were raving about hockey, and all I cared was about Steven Spielberg,” Villeneuve said. “He became my hero. Steven is the reason I’m standing here today, and I’m lucky enough now to call him a friend. “Then came James Cameron,” Villeneuve continued. “These are titans. James has always been ahead of his time, and I hope he was wrong when he predicted Skynet, the self-aware artificial intelligence Terminator. These friendships meant the world to me because I’ve always felt isolated as a director in my own bubble.” He saluted Zhao, Cuarón and Iñárritu as “three phenomenal artists pushing the boundaries of cinematic expression in the most original ways.” Villeneuve also thanked his frequent collaborators and his crews. “It takes many people to bring cinema to life. I want to honor their contribution in making my dreams come to life on screen,” he said.

- Tanya Lapointe and Denis Villeneuve At the heart of each of Villeneuve’s films, there’s a question that he seeks to answer. “Dune Part Three,” Villeneuve (seen here with his wife and producing partner Tanya Lapointe) centers on Chalamet’s Paul and Zendaya’s Chani fighting to give their children a better world than the one they were given. “We are at the crossroads, asking what defines a human being and what human expression is worth,” Villeneuve said. “Every parent on Earth is a little worried about the world our children will enter it.” “For a filmmaker today, it is very real. I have a choice. I can create something with a prompt,” Villeneuve said, referencing the advent of AI tools. “Or I can go into the desert with actors, with a crew, and go on a real adventure where I learn about life and become better at my craft. Those are two different things.” Even though one of those options is “more expensive than the other,” Villeneuve cracked, he firmly believes that the process of filmmaking is more important than the result. “The process is how the human experience acquires its meaning,” Villeneuve said. “In this moment in time, it is more important than ever that human beings keep making art together. That is the heritage I want to leave to my children.”

- Anya Taylor-Joy and Denis Villeneuve Anya Taylor-Joy dropped by the gala to support her “Dune: Part Three” filmmaker Villeneuve. What makes him unique? “It’s the vision,” Taylor-Joy told Variety. “But it’s also the fact that when you’re working with him, he makes you feel that you’re a part of something bigger than yourself. He never makes anybody feel small, and he leads with such love and conviction, and I adore him.”

- Anya Taylor-Joy Anya Taylor-Joy, looking like a piece of art in archival Pierre Cardin, also weighed in on Villeneuve’s Bond movie. “I’m excited to see what he’s going to do with all the fight sequences. I think he got a taste of it on ‘Dune,’ and I think he might be really, really good at it,” Taylor-Joy said. The actress has also co-starred with four of the five reported finalists — Robert Pattinson (in “Dune”), Nicholas Hoult (“The Menu”), Josh O’Connor (“Emma”) and Callum Turner (“Emma”). “I’ve been very lucky with my older brothers in film,” Taylor-Joy added. “They are delightful. They have taken very good care of me, and they’re all wonderful to watch on screen. So I’m excited to see who it’s going to be.”

- Viola Davis and Julius Tennon Viola Davis — here with Julius Tennon, both in Gucci — recalled working with Villeneuve on 2013’s “Prisoners.” “Denis is one of the greatest directors I’ve ever worked with,” the Oscar winner told Variety. “My favorite thing is when he loved a take and he said ‘Perfect,’ but in a French accent. I would say, ‘Say it again, Denis.'” For her next act, Davis will star in “The Children of Blood and Bone,” reuniting with “The Woman King” director Gina Prince-Bythewood and star Thuso Mbedu. “She’s an extraordinary talent,” Davis said. “I think this is going to be her time.”

- Jordan Firstman “Club Kid” filmmaker Jordan Firstman told Variety he most admires Villeneuve’s “restraint” as a director. “He really knows how to hold back and when to go for it and let you ride the worm,” Firstman, wearing Ferragamo, told Variety. “That’s what I tell all my students.” As Villeneuve pivots to the Bond franchise, Firstman has a pitch: “I want to be a Bond gay. Like, instead of the Bond girls, I think they should make them gay guys.”

- Benito Skinner Benito Skinner, wearing ERL, joked that he was on a mission to figure out who Villeneuve chose to play the new 007. “He must be so over it, like I have to stop fucking reading about it. We gotta just pick it. Are we close? I’m gonna ask him tonight,” Skinner told Variety, laughing. (For the record, he’d like to play Bond’s tech genius, Q. “I’m like, use that pen. It’s a gun.”) Why does Skinner admire Villeneuve? “He builds worlds so beautifully,” Skinner said. “We don’t get that anymore. We need blockbusters. We need butts in seats at AMC the Grove. He’s just a true visionary, and we don’t have many, and that scares me. Even if [the world] is as insane as ‘Dune,’ you still feel the humanity in it.”

- Jessica Williams Jessica Williams (sparkling in Phan Huy) chose “Arrival” as her favorite Villeneuve film. “I just really liked the way people responded to aliens,” Williams told Variety. “People were so overwhelmed with it, and I thought that was a really cool take.” As a fan of the filmmaker, the “Shrinking” star quickly conjured a pitch to join his Bond movie. “I’d be a really cool-ass logistics person. I feel like I’d be really good in the Bond office,” she said. “I play a lot of parts where I’m like a lady that knows stuff, and I’d like to be a lady that knows stuff in that universe.”

- Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvó “La Bola Negra” filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvó (aka Los Javis), both in Gucci, said Villeneuve’s 2010 film “Incendies” was a key reference to their 2023 series “La Mesías.” “He’s one of the best directors,” Ambrossi told Variety, noting the innovative ways Villeneuve uses music and stages his scenes. Calvó added: “He’s so full of idea and the way he works with actors — with the small parts [or] with the big parts, like the stars — it’s amazing. He’s a master.”

- Ashley Park, Anthony Ramos and Alex Garcia Ashley Park — seen here with Anthony Ramos and Alex Garcia and wearing Prabal Gurung — said her favorite Villeneuve projects are the “Dune” movies and “Sicario.” “Watching that film really shook me in a lot of different ways,” the “Emily in Paris” star told Variety about “Sicario.”

- Denis Villeneuve, Nicole Kidman, Vija Celmins and Michael Govan Vija Celmins (seen here with fellow honoree Denis Villeneuve, presenter Nicole Kidman and LACMA CEO Michael Govan, CEO) delivered a charming acceptance speech. “You guys are just crazy party people,” Celmins said onstage, as the well-heeled crowd burst into laughter. The recognition from LACMA is special, Celmins explained, because “Los Angeles had a big influence on me. I had never lived next to the ocean, and I have never seen the land, and it sort of crept into my work.”
- Rachel Kushner, Vija Celmins and Michael Govan After Rachel Kushner presented the award to Vija Celmins, the pair posed with LACMA CEO Michael Govan.

- Eva Chow, Michael Govan and Timothée Chalamet During the program, Art+Film Gala co-chair Eva Chow announced she’d be stepping down from her post after 15 years. “Together, we have raised close to $60 million for LACMA. That is something we can all be incredibly proud of,” Chow said. (She co-chairs the event with Oscar winner Leonardo DiCaprio.) “It is difficult to put 15 years of memories, friendship, experiences into a few words,” Chow added. “To have started with an idea and to see it grow into one of Los Angeles’ most celebrated traditions has been one of great privileges of my life. I leave this chapter with tremendous pride, wonderful memories, and above all gratitude.”

- Sienna Miller, François-Henri Pinault and Salma Hayek Pinault Sienna Miller smiles alongside Kering board chairman François-Henri Pinault and Salma Hayek Pinault. Gucci has been a presenting sponsor of the gala since its inception in 2011.
