items.title: There’s No Sex Recession on It Gets Worse
items.description: Scrolling through 12 streaming platforms but still can’t find something to watch? You’re not alone. Our television columnist Michel Ghanem, a.k.a. @tvscholar, watches over 160 seasons of television each year, and he is here for you. Perhaps you’re in the mood
items.author: Michel Ghanem
paragraphs: Scrolling through 12 streaming platforms but still can’t find something to watch? You’re not alone. Our television columnist Michel Ghanem, a.k.a. @tvscholar, watches over 160 seasons of television each year, and he is here for you. Perhaps you’re in the mood for a hidden gem that’s sitting undiscovered on a streamer or a series with mysteries so tantalizing you can’t stop thinking about them long after the credits roll. It’s all about carving out time for the shows that are actually worth it — your appointment viewing. Fire up that group chat because we’ve got some unpacking to do.

We love a comedy about a group of messy 20-somethings figuring it all out. We’ve previously covered FX’s Adults and Tubi’s Big Mood in this column. It Gets Worse is a promising new addition to the canon and a worthy successor to Girls — even Lena Dunham, who appears in the series, approves. Leo Reich’s A24-produced comedy is finally available to stream on Paramount+.

“It Gets Better” was the promise Dan Savage’s nonprofit anti-bullying campaigns made to LGBTQ+ people back in 2010. I remember the testimonials vividly as a young closeted person. Saturday Night Live even spoofed it a few years ago. Queer people often run up against this promise that any self-hatred you have as a young queer person will certainly be replaced with love, community, and unlimited happiness as you get older. In some ways, the prophecy was fulfilled. Some things did get better for queer people: Gay marriage is legal in the United States; PrEP, first approved by the FDA to prophylactically work against HIV in 2012, is now widely accessible; I can get takeout, condoms, and a bottle of wine delivered to my door within the hour from a single app. But what about the existential angst young queer people face and continue to cope with as they enter adulthood?

This is what comedian Leo Reich’s It Gets Worse, a new six-episode series airing on Paramount+ in the U.S. after premiering on Channel 4 in the U.K., aims to tackle. Reich stars as Ethan, an obnoxious middle-class 24-year-old living in East London with his two besties. They’re being kicked out from their flat, and there is a traitor in their midst. Abi (Emily Fairn), who works at a start-up, is gearing herself up to come clean about her plans to move in with her boyfriend, Sam (Sean Delaney), even though she doesn’t seem particularly in love (and they’re not very sexually adventurous together). That leaves Ethan and Sam (Olive Gray), a tutor–slash–Substack writer, in quite the housing predicament. Ethan tries to move in with his situationship while Sam rents a bedroom in an “anarchist” communal living space in which her ex-girlfriend resides. Naturally, chaos ensues in these arcs as each character gets their own episodic perspective (narrated thoughtfully by Zadie Smith).

“Ethan had one of the easiest lives in recorded history,” Smith narrates in the opening frame of the pilot. This is followed by “You’re just a hole for daddy,” which is uttered by a therapist–cum–Grindr hookup played by Andrew Scott as he spits in our twink protagonist’s mouth. I’m happy to report the full series is just as spicy as that scene might suggest. It Gets Worse is raunchy, angsty, and chaotic — just like the experience of being broke and in your mid-20s, navigating the ups and downs of crushes and relationships.

The series suggests that young people are more than capable of making things worse for themselves, whether that’s by hopelessly pursuing someone emotionally unavailable or throwing a flat’s security deposit out the window because you zonked out on TikTok instead of figuring out how to fill a hole in the drywall. As the old adage goes, it gets worse before it gets better, and sometimes being put through the self-esteem wringer is just par for the course on the journey to adulthood. It Gets Worse mainly explores this adage through sex. (Gen-Z sex recession where?) After Girls brought ass-eating to the forefront of heterosexual consciousness, It Gets Worse finds a new angle on that very sexual act — right when I was wondering if it had been taken off the menu for straight consumption. The show also has fleshlights, lesbian porn, and a sex party. So much of these three characters’ arcs revolve around exploring the particular awkwardness their sex lives. It’s clear to me that Reich understands how sex, in a shit economy with unreasonably expensive rent prices and pricey door covers for parties, remains one of the few free, offline spaces of connection.

In this way, It Gets Worse fits in perfectly with the current messy Gen-Z television universe. I’m talking about Adults, Overcompensating, and I Love LA. But there is something unfiltered about It Gets Worse and each of the lead performances that sets it apart. What made Girls so successful in all of its autofictional glory was the ways in which its characters were self-involved but still affable and relatable. It Gets Worse pokes fun at zoomer stereotypes, but it also has a lot of empathy for being a 20-something right now. As Reich told The Guardian, “All of these traditional institutions like marriage and climbing the career ladder don’t really exist, or if they do exist you can’t trust them. There’s a vague sense of massive anxiety.” Who wouldn’t spiral into ennui under those conditions?

• Keep an eye out for some great cameos, including the one and only Lena Dunham. Reich played a minor character in her (underrated) 2025 Netflix series Too Much; she repays the favor by reciting some of the most unhinged lines of her career as Abi’s boss.
• Lebanese director Mounia Akl is behind the camera of every episode of It Gets Worse — one to watch for sure.

• This is the second time Fiona Apple’s “I Want You to Love Me” is featured in a show set in London this fall after HBO’s Youth, so I’d like to declare a moratorium on the use of that (excellent) song.

• In the pilot, It Gets Worse captures the uniquely annoying experience of waiting way too long in line to get into a club only to abandon that quest and just go home instead. Isn’t that what being young is all about?

items.title: The Birkin of Leather Journals
items.description: Skylar Davis took her lunch break early to race to the Sézane store in Nolita before it opened, but when she arrived, the line already stretched down the block. The 24-year-old waited for over an hour, hoping that she’d still be able to get her hands on the jo
items.author: Eve Upton-Clark
paragraphs: Skylar Davis took her lunch break early to race to the Sézane store in Nolita before it opened, but when she arrived, the line already stretched down the block. The 24-year-old waited for over an hour, hoping that she’d still be able to get her hands on the journal of her dreams: a fully customizable leather Honoré folio in the color azul from the Parisian stationery and leather-goods brand Louise Carmen.

Staff handed out croissants and tote bags, but more than an hour later those on line were informed there wouldn’t be enough stock to sell past a certain point. Though Davis returned to work empty-handed that day, she was able to snag an appointment at the Brooklyn pop-up later that same week. With the embossing of her initials and additional charms, her two purchases, the Honoré and the Pocket notebooks, came to $445.29.
“This is something that is going to grow with me over time,” Davis tells me. “It becomes part of my life rather than, like, Oh, here’s something I’m holding on my arm.”

For the journaling community, a Louise Carmen has become a coveted accessory. But for those unfamiliar, a leather journal that runs the same price as a midrange designer bag might come as something of a shock.

Fans can customize the notebooks, starting at $160 for a basic version of the trifold leather cover, with embossing, different styles of paper, and charms, which can run hundreds of dollars more. Multiple thin notebooks fit neatly inside the reusable leather cover, secured in place by elastic bands, and can be swapped out and rearranged indefinitely. Those who buy it see the journal folio as an heirloom worth investing in.

The French artisanal-leather stationery and notebook brand was founded in 2016 by Nathalie Valmary; her husband, Fabien; and their daughter, Victoire and has steadily grown in popularity via social media. Videos documenting the purchasing experience often gain hundreds of thousands of views, and Americans are now responsible for 60 percent of the brand’s online orders, Valmary told CNBC earlier this year.

Davis has been journaling for much of her life but had never really considered investing in anything fancy. “I usually just grab a notebook and call it a day,” she says. But over the past few years, she started seeing Louise Carmen tours and journal-ecosystem videos online and was influenced to buy one.

While the brand does take online appointments and ship worldwide, the in-store experience of customizing the journal to your exact specifications is what justifies the price point to those like Davis. In the store, customers are encouraged to feel the paper and choose the exact leather their journal will be created from.

“Louise Carmen is mostly about the in-store experience because, let’s be honest here, there are tons of amazing Etsy sellers making leather journals,” Sophie Pav, a 30-year-old freelance marketing consultant and content creator, tells me.

Pav had been aware of the brand for a few years when she heard it was coming to New York City to offer this in-person design experience. Her husband offered to secure her spot on line. He arrived at 8:30 a.m., and she finally entered the store more than five hours later at 2 p.m.
“I love collecting stationery. I love writing, I love journaling, I do it every single day,” she says. “For me, this is the category that I’m ready to splurge on.”
Once inside, Pav purchased the Honoré notebook in plum-colored leather. She added a gold leather pocket, embossed her lucky numbers, and attached a single charm to the pink cord for a total of $370.

And the splurge has become a phenomenon. Theodora Helgason, the store manager at the New York stationery chain Goods for the Study, tells me she’s seen a huge influx in customers looking for luxury journal covers and notebooks in the past few years. The shop hosted a Louise Carmen pop-up in 2024 and still has shoppers asking after the brand every day.
“People are just obsessed with them, and I get it,” she says.

But why spend so much when similar options from brands like Traveler’s Company won’t even run you $100? The notebooks fit into what brand strategist Mara Dettmann recently called the “medium treat economy,” defined as “non-essential purchases substantial enough to feel like indulgences, but still affordable enough to justify.”

According to Dettmann, these splurges can be defined as “collectibles, premium accessories, or products connected to our hobbies and interests,” she writes in her newsletter In Interesting Times. Unlike a “small treat,” these are items we can cherish for years, adding a bit of luxury to something we already enjoy.

Helgason purchased her own Louise Carmen notebook two years ago and believes the quality of the leather and the level of personalization makes it feel like a worthwhile investment. To her, it’s more satisfying than buying, say, a leather handbag for the same price.
“To use a Louise Carmen, you need to be writing,” Helgason says. “That feels more profound to me.”

The notebook’s popularity also aligns with a widespread return to analog that’s seen so-called “grandma hobbies” like flower pressing, needlepointing, and crafting experiencing a surge as we all attempt to slow down and get off our phones. For Davis, being off a screen is one of the main reasons she fell in love with journaling.

“There was a period of my life where the convenience of just putting everything into my phone outweighed the joy of actually putting pen to paper,” she says. “But now I’m working to appreciate it more.”
Davis uses one notebook in her new journal for stream-of-consciousness writing, a second to jot down quotes from movies and books, a third for manifestation, and a fourth for learning Italian.
While some might scoff at the high price tag on an otherwise free activity — scribbling down your thoughts on paper — for Davis, either you’re willing to spend the money or you’re not.

“Whether you go to a local coffee shop or you go to a chain like Dunkin’ Donuts, everything you do to some extent is signaling your values and what you care about,” Davis says. “It is an investment, and I think people are gradually starting to understand that an investment can be a daily object. It doesn’t have to be in the stock market. It doesn’t have to be a Birkin bag. It can be something as simple as an expensive leather journal.”

items.title: Susie Wiles Is Leaving the White House
items.description: Another woman has bit the dust in the Trump administration. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, the first woman ever to serve in the role, announced on Friday that she’s stepping down from her post. She will be replaced by Stephen Miller, one of President
items.author: Andrea González-Ramírez
paragraphs: Another woman has bit the dust in the Trump administration. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, the first woman ever to serve in the role, announced on Friday that she’s stepping down from her post. She will be replaced by Stephen Miller, one of President Trump’s closest allies and the architect of most of his far-right and extremist domestic agenda.

Wiles’s resignation comes after Republicans suffered embarrassing losses in the midterms, with Democrats taking control of the House, Senate, governor mansions, and many state and local seats. The president is reportedly blaming Wiles for the debacle.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump posted on Truth Social. “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Wiles, who co-ran Trump’s 2024 campaign, was diagnosed with breast cancer in March and worked through her treatment. Six months later, she announced she was cancer-free. As chief of staff, she has reportedly tried to temper the president’s worst instincts. Anticipating massive election losses, she tried to steer Trump away from the hardline mass-deportation efforts championed by Miller, according to the New York Times. Now she’s out, and Miller is in.

Miller, who has long-standing ties to white-supremacist groups, has been one of Trump’s closest companions since the 2016 election. He was the mastermind behind some of the most virulent anti-immigration efforts of Trump’s first term, including the family-separation crisis and the Muslim ban. During Trump 2.0, he has continued his campaign of terror against immigrants and has pushed for taking foreign territories in a new vision of American imperialism.

Wiles, who is 69, is the latest in a string of high-profile women who’ve exited the Trump administration this year alone, most of whom have been replaced by men. In the spring, Trump fired both Attorney General Pam Bondi and Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem, who were replaced by Trump’s former personal attorney Todd Blanche and former senator Markwayne Mullin. Lori Chavez-DeRemer also resigned from her post as Labor secretary amid an investigation into alleged misconduct on her part; she was replaced by Keith Sonderling. In May, Director of National Security Tulsi Gabbard resigned to take care of her husband, who is battling cancer. Gabbard was then replaced by Jay Clayton.

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is the only woman whose replacement hasn’t been a man. Leavitt stepped down from the job in August. Her replacement, Katie Zacharia, was appointed in October. She lasted five days on the job.

items.title: Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd Broke Up Over a Year Ago
items.description: After months of speculation, WNBA players Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd confirmed they are no longer together and haven’t been for over a year. On Friday, the Dallas Wings teammates appeared together in a new episode of Fudd’s podcast, Fudd Around and Find Out,
items.author: Brooke LaMantia
paragraphs: After months of speculation, WNBA players Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd confirmed they are no longer together and haven’t been for over a year. On Friday, the Dallas Wings teammates appeared together in a new episode of Fudd’s podcast, Fudd Around and Find Out, to break the news that the split happened before Fudd was drafted by the Wings with the No. 1 pick in 2026, meaning they played the whole WNBA season on the same team as recent exes. Lesbians are so strong!

“We were not together before she got drafted. So all of those narratives can go to bed,” Bueckers said on the episode. “She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She’s an amazing human, amazing basketball player. And we’re still friends. We’re still cool. We played an entire season together. We’re the utmost professional. We care about basketball.”

The pair became “official” in July 2025, though hopes and dreams of a Bueckers-Fudd relationship had been swirling online, especially on TikTok, for plenty of time before that. They played together at UConn during the 2025 NCAA tournament, and Bueckers brought Fudd as her plus-one on draft night in 2025. Still, the two of them kept most of their relationship private, and it looks like they are going to keep it that way. “We know you guys are curious and probably have a ton of questions, but we’ve addressed everything that we need to and the rest will stay with us,” said Fudd. TikTok may be in mourning, but at least these two are fine.

items.title: Exclusive: Harry Shum Jr. Wants The 'Glee' Reboot To Have This Mike Chang Twist
items.description: The Harry Shum Jr. Renaissance Is Nigh
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: The Harry Shum Jr. Renaissance Is Nigh
The actor opens up about being on Dancing with the Stars as Glee and Crazy Rich Asians return — from the set of Grey’s Anatomy.

Harry Shum Jr. has the best of both worlds — well, kind of. The actor is spending countless hours rehearsing for Dancing With the Stars, with his pro partner, Jenna Johnson, choreographing routines that get more intricate every week. But right now, just hours after landing a perfect score on Disney Night, he’s on the set of Grey’s Anatomy in full scrubs doing a whole lot of nothing in the ABC medical drama’s operating room. It’s safe to say he’s exhausted.

“We just shot a scene for three hours straight standing,” the 44-year-old actor tells Bustle from his car, taking a quick lunch break still in costume. “It’s crazy how we think dancing is tiring, which it is, but you’re moving a lot. I give it up to doctors and surgeons that stand for eight hours. I would rather be moving right now. And then when I’m dancing, I’d rather be standing.”

Shum Jr.’s hip-hop skills are well-documented on Glee, with his character Mike Chang carrying the New Directions on his back when it came to choreography. But on DWTS, he’s also proven himself a ballroom master, with him and Johnson becoming the first duo this season to earn two perfect scores in a row, positioning them as undeniable frontrunners. “I’m just flabbergasted,” he says.

Shum Jr. says the scores are even more “meaningful” because he and Johnson have focused more on creating dances they’re passionate about rather than strategizing how to win. “There was a switching point halfway through where I was trying to figure out what Dancing with the Stars is in terms of being on the back side, figuring dances out, whether it's creative,” he recalls. “Jen and I looked at each other like, ‘Let's just dance for ourselves and do what we want to do.’”

Whether or not he wins the Mirrorball, DWTS is just the beginning of the Shum Jr. renaissance. While he’s been in the ballroom, the return of Glee became official, and the long-awaited Crazy Rich Asians TV series was finally announced, giving him two easy ways to keep dominating our screens. Luckily, he’d jump at the chance to return to his roots in both franchises, especially Glee.

“That show did a lot,” he says. “It tapped into the zeitgeist, but also had this crazy anticipation before the pilot ever came out, then went on tour, had this cultural effect, and charted on Billboard, and also spotlighted things we never really address in terms of bullying and gay rights. I enjoyed being able to show the dynamics of an Asian family in a different way and having it still be entertaining.”

But for now, Shum Jr. is simply focused on spreading his love of dancing for as long as he lasts in the ballroom. “It's cool hearing how families are rooting for me and finding their entry point to dance,” he says. “Even guys who only watch sports are actually invested in this competition. That's awesome. I embrace the people trying to figure out what this all is, maybe being their own judge and holding their own paddle. That makes it fun.”
Below, Shum Jr. opens up about his most meaningful dance, his relationships with the Glee cast, where he sees Mike Chang on the revival, and his future on the Crazy Rich Asians series.
Which DWTS dance are you most proud of so far?

It always feels like I’m most proud of the last dance because it's the closest, but I have to say Dedication Night. I'm going to hold that forever as the most memorable thing, having three generations on that stage. I don't think my parents ever thought in their lifetime they would be on stage, especially on national television. And to dance with my wife [actor and dancer Shelby Rabara]... 20 years ago, we tried to audition for this dance commercial, and I didn't know how to partner and I messed it up for her.

During those times, anytime you try to get a job, it’s like paying rent. You need that job. And I lost it for her because I was stepping on her toes. I wasn’t doing the lifts right, and I froze. So for 20 years we didn't partner, and this was the first time we did on this show. Our relationship is great, but repairing that part of it was very meaningful.
You're currently filming Grey's Anatomy. How’s it been balancing the show and rehearsals? Are you dancing on the set when you're not filming?

A lot of that is happening. Jenna comes and tries to teach me some of the dance, but honestly, it's so hard to focus because I still have to perform well on the show and make sure I'm giving my all to the scenes. Today we have a long [operating room] scene, so there's absolutely no time for that. It’s a lot of work, I’m not going to lie, but I feel so privileged to be able to do both and to have the support of both productions and my team. It’s not just a one-man show.
Chris Colfer was telling me how amazing it was to be with your daughter watching you dance. How does it feel to have your Glee cast’s support all these years later?

It means the world. Especially in Hollywood, where you do a job and move on to something else and everyone lives different lives, to still be in contact and come out and support each other says a lot about the bond that we have. Honestly, no one knows what we experience fully other than us. It’s beautiful because everyone’s been so successful in doing the thing they've been wanting to do.
Has your daughter seen Glee?
She did watch the pilot and was blown away, so I don’t know when we're going to start that train.
Amber Riley and Heather Morris have been on the DWTS journey before. Did they tell you anything before you joined the season?

Amber said it’s a lot, and to remember who you are, and Heather said the same thing. I’ve never done anything like this before in my life, but a lot of people have opinions about what they want you to be for them. I love to take constructive criticism, and sometimes I look at things like, “Oh yeah, I need to do that a little more.” But in other ways, I took that advice.
How do you feel about Glee returning? Has Ryan Murphy given you any details about it?

I don’t know too many details about what he’s trying to do other than him writing the pilot. He’s really excited about it. When that show came out, the arts were being defunded, and the world was trying to figure out how to transition into a different era. We never really saw that type of humor in a musical. Everyone’s a lot more mature now. I’m still trying to figure out what it is, but I’m glad they’re getting everyone talking about it, and we’ll see if I’m involved.
In your head, where do you see Mike Chang today?

I feel like all of my characters play into the multiverse of what am I living. It’d be kind of funny if he just stopped dancing. I’m already playing a surgeon and dancing right now on another multiverse, I don't want to bleed too much into that. But there’d be something interesting if Mike stopped dancing and became a plumber or something, just to go against everything that his dad wanted him to do, and then seeing how he can find his rhythm back.
The Crazy Rich Asians TV show being announced the same week is also divine timing. Have you been in touch with the cast or showrunner Adele Lim since that was announced?

Adele’s my friend. We talk about wanting to work together on different projects. The character that I play is tied to another character [Gemma Chan’s Astrid], so we’ll see if they write that in, because there are so many storylines in the books. [Adele] wrote the first episode, so I don't know what it’s all looking like, but I still talk to her a lot, and I would love to reprise Charlie Wu. In the books, it’s such a fun storyline that I think a lot of fans want to see come to life.
Next week is Grammy Night. Can you give us a peek at what you have planned?
I can say that finally we get to dance to something where the style really fits into the song.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Exclusive: Maya Hawke & Lili Taylor Tease Easter Eggs In 'The Hunger Games' Prequel
items.description: Maya Hawke & Lili Taylor Bring Calm To Sunrise On The Reaping
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Maya Hawke & Lili Taylor Bring Calm To Sunrise On The Reaping
The stars of the Hunger Games prequel open up about becoming Haymitch Abernathy’s mentors.

Maya Hawke and Lili Taylor entered the Hunger Games universe in very different ways. Taylor, 59, saw the films through the eyes of her teenage daughter, Maeve, before becoming a fan herself. “I almost felt a little bit like a kid,” she tells Bustle. Meanwhile, Hawke, 28, watched the Hunger Games movies “so many times” in high school that she can’t “even begin to remember” her first viewing.

However, she has a special memory with Suzanne Collins’ novels. “When I read the first book, I was on a family vacation,” she tells Bustle. “I was the most melancholy teenager, didn’t want to talk to anyone, wanted everyone to just leave me alone and let me read my book. And I was obsessed.”

More than a decade later, the two actors are joining Panem as the rebellious mentors of future District 12 victor Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), showing how The Hunger Games brings generations together. In the new prequel Sunrise on the Reaping, set 24 years before the original trilogy, Hawke assumes the role of brainy District 4 victor Wiress from Amanda Plummer, while Taylor steps into the late Lynn Cohen’s shoes as the nurturing Mags.

Like the film’s other blockbuster actors, fans who grew up with these characters praised both Hawke’s and Taylor’s casting. Naturally, that brings a certain level of pressure. “I’m glad that they’re excited,” Hawke says. “Maybe because of my experience on Stranger Things, you’re constantly like, ‘How much do I let this information influence me? How much do I take in?’ I’ve really made an effort not to take it in at all.”

As for Taylor, who has experiences in franchises like The Conjuring and The Maze Runner, she says the fans “fueled” her performance. “It felt like walking into a really warm room of people who want you to succeed,” she says. “Anyone could do well with that vibe.”
Below, Hawke and Taylor open up about channeling their characters’ trauma, their memories with the younger cast, and the Easter eggs they felt were important to include.
How did your characters resonate with you?

Hawke: Wiress resonated with me personally for a long time because of her behavior in her own games. I’m certainly a pacifist now and was a deeply moralistic child. The idea that someone had the strength of character to care more about protecting their morals than about prolonging their own life is just a beautiful thing to me.

Taylor: My kid plays soccer, and I love going to the games. I love supporting the girls. And it felt like on some level, Mags is there to support and help. When I talked to [director] Francis [Lawrence] and I brought up loving the girls playing soccer, that resonated with him for Mags.
Wiress is only a year out from her Hunger Games win, and it’s clear she’s still processing it. Tell me what it was like channeling that trauma into this performance.

Hawke: Having to send children down the same path that you had to walk down is a deeply painful and complicated process. I don’t relate to it at all, just because of the high stakes of that experience. But even though I wasn’t a child actor, when working with young actors, not even children, I often have some feeling of wanting to tell them the things that I was able to do that helped me protect my mind. I have all these younger siblings, and wanting to protect young people from pain and being unable to is such a human experience.
Lili, Mags is a helpful guide to the tributes. Similarly, did you give the young actors any advice when you were on set about tackling a movie this big and what was to come of it?

Taylor: The young actors are really mature and could probably teach some of the older actors some stuff. But if anything, I felt like I needed to let Joe [Zada] know that what he was going through was real, and that as an actor, there’s no way around it. You have to suffer it, and that’s the paradox. I understood what he was going through as a human being. It was really hard on him.
Maya, you’re mentoring these tributes in the film, but in reality, you’re not much older than them. How did that dynamic play out on set when working with these actors?

Hawke: What’s amazing is that, especially in actors, you never lose the kid in you. So the group of people hanging out in my scenes — Joe, Billy [Porter], Glenn [Close], Mckenna [Grace], Ben [Wang] — felt the same age. We were all so relaxed around each other, chatting and joking together.
Lili, did you have any favorite bonding moments with the cast when you all were filming?

Taylor: I actually went out with the kids a couple of times. I really love younger people. There are these Christmas fairs in Berlin. They’re a big deal all over the city, Mckenna’s obsessed with them, and they have rides and stuff. It was just so much fun being with them.
Is there anything you added to your performance that wasn’t scripted, or an Easter egg about your character that you wanted to make sure was in the movie?

Taylor: Mags came from a fishing village, and one of their things was that they could make things out of anything. So I wanted to make sure that she could make things if she had to in the moment, but I didn’t get a chance to show that.

Hawke: I really cared about Wiress having a mechanized watch, with her connection to Beetee. I wanted it to feel like something really unique and special that she had. And also, the “tick tock” is iconic. You got to pay tribute to the “tick tock.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Corn Porn, White Shirts, & 9 More Korean Perfumes You Should Know About
items.description: It’s no secret that K-beauty is everywhere. From salmon sperm to cushion foundations, Korean skin care and makeup have made their way into just about everyone’s routine. Fragrance wardrobes, though, have been slower on the uptake — at least, until recently.
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: It’s no secret that K-beauty is everywhere. From salmon sperm to cushion foundations, Korean skin care and makeup have made their way into just about everyone’s routine. Fragrance wardrobes, though, have been slower on the uptake — at least, until recently.

According to Spate, interest in Korean perfume has jumped 147.3% year over year. In Seoul, perfume boutiques have become just as much of a destination for beauty lovers as Olive Young. And now, plenty of Korean fragrance houses are expanding stateside — meaning you no longer need a plane ticket to discover your next scent.

But what do Korean perfumes actually smell like? “Koreans often want people to lean in closer to smell them,” says Jun Lim, founder of BornToStandOut. “Nobody wants their perfume announcing their arrival on a crowded subway.”

That doesn't mean the category is all barely-there scents, though. “People love describing Korean fragrances as clean, subtle, delicate, and minimalist — which is funny, because anyone who’s spent a Saturday night in Seoul knows Korea is anything but quiet,” says Lim. “We’re a country of contradictions: deeply traditional yet obsessed with what’s next, extremely disciplined yet wonderfully chaotic.”

That push and pull is part of what makes Korean perfumery so interesting. As Elorea co-founder Su min Park explains, traditional Korean fragrance practices emphasized harmony between the body, mind, and surroundings — a philosophy that continues to influence how contemporary perfumers approach scent.

The results can be deliciously unexpected: toasted sesame, Korean rice wine, even buttered corn. With inspiration spanning everything from the kitchen to traditional Korean rituals, Korean perfumery is anything but one-note. Whether you're a minimalist who wants to smell like you (but better) or a gourmand lover with a sweet tooth, keep scrolling for 11 Korean fragrances worth checking out.

If you've always found floral perfumes a little cloying (or even old-ladyish), Elorea’s Prelude might change your mind. It's not the kind of rose fragrance that immediately gives you a headache. Instead, Korean wild rose and woody musks come together for a dry-down that's fresh and a little earthy. It stays close to the skin, making it inoffensive to wear every day — even to the office.

A perfume that smells like corn on the cob? Maybe it’s not the first thing that comes to mind when you think of smelling good enough to eat, but BornToStandOut is here to change that. “Imagine a steaming cob of corn absolutely drowning in melted butter,” says Lim. “Salty, sweet, sticky, almost obscenely delicious.” Basically, your Thanksgiving comfort food, bottled up.

Sandalwood perfumes have a reputation for smelling like luxury hotel lobbies (looking at you, Santal 33), but Nonfiction’s Santal Cream feels more like a chill afternoon at home. It’s still sophisticated, with cardamom and vetiver adding some spice and depth. But a hint of fig balances out the rest of the notes, making it feel creamier and cozier than other drier sandalwoods.

For anyone balling on a budget, Etleé should be on your radar. With prices ranging from $10 to $20, the fragrances are surprisingly well-rounded. Case in point: Sweet Lychee, which puts a fun twist on fruity floral scents. It opens with a tart burst of apple and lychee before settling into something warmer and more mellow, thanks to jasmine, vanilla, and sugared musks.

Craving the scent of freshly washed clothes? White Shirts by Loe is the next best thing to doing a load of laundry. Soapy and cottony with a hint of floral, it smells less like you just sprayed perfume and more like you hung your favorite T-shirt out to dry in the spring. And just like that tee, you’ll probably find yourself reaching for it on a regular basis — with a $45 price tag, why not?

Don’t let the boozy notes fool you: Elorea’s Cloud Daze is just as good for daytime as it is for a night out. Inspired by makgeolli, a Korean rice wine, it has that creaminess balanced by the freshness of lemon and juniper — which almost smell floral in this composition. In fact, everything blends so well that it’s hard to pick out one note. Instead, you get something that’s worthy of a signature scent: unique enough to get people to ask you what you’re wearing — plus, it lasts all day long.

K-pop stans, this one is for you. Tamburins’ Chamo is the reported favorite of Jennie — and for good reason. Imagine a cup of chamomile tea with a spoonful of honey stirred in: herbal but light, with just enough woodiness from the clary sage to balance out the sweetness. In other words, it’s perfect for a rainy day — or any day when you want something soft and skin-like.

On the opposite end of the spectrum, there are plenty of K-fragrances that offer a little more bite. Just take Pesade’s Oud Nights — a blend of leather, cumin, and saffron. It’s sultry (and quite unisex), but less heavy than your usual oud-and-leather perfumes thanks to the bright grapefruit opening.

Another perfume that wouldn’t feel out of place in a smoky cocktail bar? BTSO’s Drunk Lovers, which Lim describes as “a romantic evening where the lovers cannot keep their hands off each other.” Juicy red berries make that first impression — not overly sweet, but a little flirtatious as the cognac starts to settle in. Then, when the vanilla finally comes through, everything gets warmer and more intimate, like the moment you’ve stopped being nervous around each other and moved to the same side of the booth.

Looking for a morning pick-me-up instead of a nightcap? SW19’s 6am is a good place to start. It opens with crisp citrus, while basil adds a green, slightly peppery twist — like walking through a garden at sunrise. Even better, it settles into a woodier, musky scent that’s just as fitting after lunch.
11The Sophisticated Gourmand

If you want to dip your toes into gourmands without smelling like a sugar overload, try Dosigoh’s Sesame Shower. At first spritz, it smells like a black sesame cookie: toasted, nutty, and warm. But instead of getting sweeter, it gets fresher as it dries down. Vanilla and floral notes come to the forefront, giving it an almost soapy quality. Think dessert, minus the sticky fingers.

items.title: Exclusive: Jordyn Woods' Game Day Style Guide Has 6 Important Rules
items.description: Whether you’re a hardcore basketball fan who can give a play-by-play recap of the NY Knicks’ historic 2026 championship run, or a fashion girlie who can do a similarly in-depth analysis of unforgettable WAG ’fits, chances are you’ve heard of Jordyn Woods’ A+ a
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: Whether you’re a hardcore basketball fan who can give a play-by-play recap of the NY Knicks’ historic 2026 championship run, or a fashion girlie who can do a similarly in-depth analysis of unforgettable WAG ’fits, chances are you’ve heard of Jordyn Woods’ A+ accessory game. More specifically, you know about her “lucky bag” — the orange, ostrich-leather-inspired clutch from her brand, Woods by Jordyn Woods, that became the team’s unofficial good-luck charm.

But Woods’ chic game-day style goes far beyond one viral accessory. Throughout the season, she was a courtside fixture, marrying polished luxury tailoring with sporty pieces. Now, following an epic victory parade and a dreamy Malibu wedding to the Knicks’ Karl-Anthony Towns (KAT), she’s entering a brand-new era — and already giving fans inspo.

Between wrapping up her brand’s first NYC pop-up, launching new styles like a “Trophy Gold” edition of her famous clutch, and running a campaign with Love Island’s Aniya Harvey, the multi-hyphenate is busier than ever. She’s also making wellness a priority, staying hydrated, taking her vitamins, and moving her body. “Whether it’s Pilates class or cardio, fitness helps a lot,” Woods tells Bustle. She even teamed up with Walgreens for its “Don’t Get Benched by the Flu” initiative: “The flu shot was super helpful for me because I really can’t afford to get the flu right now.”

She’s even picked up a few wellness habits from her husband, including a love for infrared saunas. Her wardrobe strategy, however, is entirely her own. While she figures out her aesthetic for the next playoff run as a returning champ’s wife, the entrepreneur is sharing her foolproof guide to serving a game-day slay.
Keep It Cozy On The Sidelines

You may not be playing the sport, but comfort should still be a priority when getting dressed. Arena layouts typically require a lot of walking and climbing steep stairs, so you need an ensemble you can actually move in. “The perfect courtside outfit is really whatever you feel comfortable with,” Woods says, noting that you never know when your competitive spirit might take over. “I love something that you can jump around in if you need.”
Make A Statement With Your Outerwear

For Woods, a stylish coat is an instant confidence booster. “I always feel like a boss in a blazer and good tailoring,” she says. “I love outerwear — a good coat, a good trench — and accessories.” Plus, it handles a very practical problem: “It’s always so cold in there, and I’m always cold, so I love a good jacket.”
Shop Like A Fashion Insider

Team merch isn’t the only way to show up with a winning look. While some fans started bedazzling bags or even screen-printing matching tees (hello, Taylor Swift), Woods prefers a highly curated approach.

“I haven’t been shopping too crazy, but I did go to my first sample sale, the Alaïa sample sale. It’s a very New York thing. I got some really good ready-to-wear pieces,” she says. The style star modeled one of her finds recently, too. “The outfit I wore to Forbes’ [30/50 Summit], I actually got at the sample sale.”

Woods loves showing team spirit as much as the next fan, but she recommends pacing yourself when the season kicks off. An all-out fan look belongs in the postseason. “I don’t really go full orange and blue decked out until the playoffs,” she admits.

Instead, she’s treating the early months of the season as a trial run to fine-tune her game-day attire. “I would love to have a uniform and figure out my exact silhouette, but right now it’s just using an excuse to experiment and try different silhouettes.”
Bench Your Good-Luck Pieces

Every fan has their rituals — like wearing a jersey or carrying a literal lucky charm. But according to Woods, you don’t have to break out the superstitions just yet. She, herself, is keeping her trusty orange Tux Clutch Mini out of rotation for the time being.

“The bag can never be replaced, but it’s definitely retired for now,” she says. “For me, superstitions don’t really come until the playoffs. We’re very fresh in the season for me to put the pressure on 80-something games.”

Rather than forcing anything, she’s open to letting more lucky pieces develop naturally as the games go on. “I don’t really have fashion superstitions this early in the season. They are developed months down the line,” she shares. “For me, it’s just about getting to wear my clothes. If I have something I’m excited to wear, I have an excuse.”
Make Room For The Aesthetic Fans
Whether someone is a lifelong season-ticket holder or a bandwagon fan who jumped on board because the outfits were cute, Woods believes everyone deserves a seat at the table.

“I love it. The more the merrier,” she says. “I’m not here to tell someone they can’t be a fan of something, because all it takes is one game to become a fan. I don’t have ownership of the fandom. Any support is good support. People should be allowed to do whatever they want.”

At the end of the day, the arena is just another runway, and she’s here for the creativity. “New York is full of so many different characters, and there’s something fun and exciting every time,” Woods says. “There are always fun videos of people’s outfits, or even the phone accessories people would make.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Krysta Rodriguez Won’t Back Down
items.description: Krysta Rodriguez Won’t Back Down
items.author: Christina Amoroso
paragraphs: Krysta Rodriguez Won’t Back Down
In Broadway’s A Few Good Men, the theater vet plays a woman who knows how to make herself heard. In real life, she’s learning to do the same.

In the Broadway revival of Aaron Sorkin’s legal thriller A Few Good Men, Krysta Rodriguez plays Lt. Cmdr. Joanne Galloway — one of just two female roles in the play, which opened at the Vivian Beaumont Theater last week. She’s used to being one of the only women in the room.

“I often find myself in those positions, and you’re grateful to be in the room, but when push comes to shove, you don’t always have the allies who you might need,” says the actor, 42. “I’m very fortunate this group of men that I’m working with are all so lovely, and we’re having a great time. But as far as groups of people you want to look for when you need to feel like someone understands you, that’s not going to happen every once in a while — and so I definitely relate to Jo in that.”

The starry Lincoln Center Theater production, which runs through Jan. 10, features Bradley Whitford (who starred in the original in 1990 on Broadway) and Tom Blyth, who’s making his Broadway debut. Sorkin wrote much of the play on cocktail napkins while bartending at the Palace Theatre. And while its initial run wasn’t a hit — with critics or the box office — the 1992 movie, starring Tom Cruise, Jack Nicholson, and Demi Moore, was a smash that launched one of the most iconic lines in movie history: “You can’t handle the truth!”
“What’s been crazy is how many younger people know the line but never saw the movie,” Rodriguez says of the show’s new audience.

Rodriguez’s extensive TV and theater credits include Smash (both the NBC series and the Broadway musical) and Spring Awakening (the original production and the 2015 revival). She also recently wrapped up a turn as Roxie Hart in Chicago and moonlights as an interior designer, having fixed up dressing rooms for Broadway stars Jeremy Jordan, Megan Hilty, and Lily Rabe. For Jordan, she created a Jazz Age-inspired space for his run in The Great Gatsby.
So what does Rodriguez’s own dressing room look like?
“To be honest, I haven’t been able to focus on it yet. I always make this joke that the cobbler’s children have no shoes.”

Jo picked this career because there is a sense of meritocracy in it. Even with all the bullsh*t, she can still put together the right paperwork that will get the right thing done. So I relate to the desire to be in a system like that. I think I give off this appearance of being relaxed and cool, but I am the most anal, the biggest rule follower. I don’t know why I’m an actor, because I wish I lived in a meritocracy. I wish I lived in a world where A plus B equals C, and it just never does.

My life is so different day to day — I’m playing someone who’s skipping through the fields or I’m traveling to Budapest to shoot something or I’m working on my interior design business. What I wanted to tap into is the structure and the rigidity of somebody who went in through the academy, who woke up at six every morning, made their bed, did the routine, and made sure they didn’t step out of line or the whole house of cards would fall apart. For me, my whole life has been about stepping outside the line. If I stay too rigid, my life will fall apart. So I tried to find tiny things that would be a big deal for me, like making my bed every morning and making it really meticulously, or making sure I went to the gym every day — something that I noticed that I have committed to and I stay firm on.

Due to the rank Jo has, people have to listen to her. She gets to be less polite. Whereas in my life, I have to make sure I lead with a smile and am nonthreatening — kind of tiptoe around an opinion. And sometimes that can build up until the one time you do give an opinion, it actually backfires because you’ve presented yourself as so docile. I don’t think anyone believes I’m docile, but you do try to sand those edges so that you’re palatable. And when you do ask for what you need, it actually works against you. You could be nice for 400 days, and the one day you’re a little surly, that’s what they’re going to remember.

So what I’ve tried to learn in my life is that it’s actually helpful to be honest and clear from the beginning. And that’s what I need to learn from Jo — she’s clear, she is not presenting any sort of front. It’s actually impossible for her. And it has taken her far. She, through all of her chutzpah, makes everyone come in line with her.

What I love about Jo’s ambition is that it’s pure. She is there because she believes in justice. There is no altruistic motive in acting. When you’re young, you want to be a star. And then as you start to realize what that means and what you sacrifice for that — is it satisfying at all? So you start to recalibrate. And as I started to get older, some of the roles that were coming to me were less exciting, just as I became more interesting and complex. I wanted the parts to meet me there.

My mom likes to talk about balls and strikes, and sometimes ambition can mean waiting. It can mean making sure to do things that align with your values and what you want to spend your time doing. So my dream expanded. Like, the dream initially was to be on Broadway — OK, I got that. Like, the dream was to be a lead — OK, I got that. The dream was to be at the Tonys — I got that. Now the dream is like, can I enjoy my life? Can my career be positioned in a right-sized manner with the rest of my life? Can the ups and downs of it affect me in the same way as the ups and downs of the rest of my life? And will that keep me more curious, more relaxed, more free, and let me wait for the parts that really speak to me so that they are more worth my energy and my care? So I think my ambition has turned more caring.
On working with younger actors:

We have, like, 11 Broadway debuts in the show, and I’m lucky to be in it with a lot of young people who are just starting out. It’s so fascinating to see that ambition on display — “I want this and I want that.” It’s exciting, but you also want to hug them and be like, “This is gonna wear off.” So either use it now, or learn to make friends with it.

Tom is making his debut, but he went to Juilliard, so he’s not afraid of the stage. A lot of people who have only done film or TV take this opportunity because they really want to hone their chops in a new way, and I think this experience for Tom of just being able to show these chops now to people, or to get to pull them out of storage, is fun. Both he and Bradley are just so lovely to get along with, and it’s so nice because you never know what you’re going to get with a show where you don’t know a lot of people. I do so many musicals, so it’s almost impossible for me to do a show where I don’t know three-quarters of the cast. So for this to be a bunch of people who I’ve never met, and they’ve never met me, has expanded my life, but I think it’s been good for the show.

We don’t know anything about Joanne’s life outside of this show. Everybody’s got a backstory, and Jo has nothing. It’s literally a joke in the show — “Jo, you do whatever it is you do when you’re not here.” And while that’s a funny punchline, it is something that I think people are recognizing now, that maybe the female characters don’t get as much backstory. So I like to play around with this idea that Jo’s actually kind of fun at home. She’s a real good-time gal. Like, she can be married. She could have one-night stands. She could be going to the bar every night.

I like to make a playlist about what I think Jo might be doing at home. She’s got a little something rolling around underneath, and that’s what makes her rigidity so much more fun. I want Jo to be the most solid woman you’ve seen, and for women who come to see the show to be like, “That’s my bitch. I wanna be her.” So I have Beyoncé’s “Formation.” And anything that has some militaristic feel, like “I have got to wrangle people,” is on there. And some Lily Allen.
On memorable audience interactions:

What’s rare is to have a show where you have so many rules that could be followed — there are rule books after rule books about the uniforms and the bars and the salutes. What’s particularly moving is how many service members who have seen the show, and so many of them became service members or became JAG because of the movie. At some point I was at the stage door where this woman got my signature, and then she ran to the end of the line and went, “Uh, your skirt’s too long.” And I said, “Oh, we have a uniform consultant,” but he’s male, you know? And she said, “I’ve been JAG for 29 years, that skirt’s too long.” And this other woman who was next to her — and they weren’t together — says, “I’m Air Force. She’s right.” So I went to my costumer, and he raised the hem. So we have tried our best, but we want to make sure we reflect properly to the people who we're representing.

Every show is a little different, and I haven’t figured it out quite yet. Right now, I go home and go to sleep — I’m in my bed within 20 minutes of arriving at home. Anything else I need to do is happening while lying down, and it might be emails or planning for the next day or whatever. But my favorite way to unwind is grabbing food after the show with friends, people who have come to see it, and maybe having a nightcap. Right now, those things are not available to me as I learn how to train for this particular show, but I’m hopeful that those things will arrive. As the kids say, touch grass — and for me, touching grass is spending time with my friends.

Another fun thing is learning the spots around Lincoln Center. Vanguard Wine Bar is a spot that’s also in Midtown, so that feels comfortable — you’re like, OK, great, I know what I’m gonna get here. The Empire Hotel rooftop bar is really special. And I’ll go with my friends to Shun Lee, this really classic Chinese place around the corner, when we go to the opera and get dressed up. That’s like our ritual. We actually had a day during tech where Tom and Nick, who plays Sam, and I went to Shun Lee and had a defense team dinner, and it was so fun. We just had a blast and ordered as much kung pao chicken as you can possibly eat.

items.title: Scorpio Season Is All About Death, Sex & Rebirth. Your Tarotscope Explains Why
items.description: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
items.author: Tatianna Tarot
paragraphs: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
Beautycon is a global platform that brings together beauty enthusiasts, brands, and industry leaders to explore the latest trends, innovations, and conversations shaping the future of beauty.

November opens with the dead, particularly our ancestors and beloved spirit guides. On November 1 and 2, Día de Muertos fills homes with marigolds, candles, and the favorite foods of those who came before us. At the same time, in Haiti and across its diaspora, Fèt Gede honors the Gede, the spirits of death in Haitian Vodou. They’re known for their dark humor, their unapologetic sexuality, and their power to heal. Neither tradition treats death as something to fear. Both treat it as part of life, a doorway, and a reason to celebrate.

This month, we are also deep in Scorpio season, ruled by the very things most people avoid talking about: death, desire, and transformation. Scorpio knows that nothing is reborn without first being let go, and that pleasure and power live in the places we’ve been taught to hide. The New Moon in Scorpio on November 9 plants the seed of who you’re becoming. Meanwhile, on November 13, Venus and Mercury both station direct, ending the review of your love life and your truth that began in October. What you learned in the dark is now ready to be lived.

Death, sex, and rebirth aren’t taboo. They’re sacred themes that help us embrace more life. Something in your life is ending. Something in you is craving more. And someone new is emerging from what you’re finally ready to release. You can’t fully live until you’re willing to let something die.
These tarotscopes will show you what’s ending, what you’re desiring, and who you’re becoming. Read for your sun, moon, and rising.
