Lace, lingerie and leather are now completely red carpet-worthy. Slinky close fits and strong tailoring are forever. And so, apparently, is fashion’s idolization of Zendaya. We could have easily included three or more of her looks, but to keep the list varied and fun, we chose only one top fit per actor or actress. The methodology behind the list included tabulating the top 10 looks chosen by 50-plus stylists, prioritizing by the number of votes each look received, and then, to break ties, bringing in rankings. The result: a realistic look at coming trends and which designers and designs rank the highest for Hollywood, by the world’s top tastemakers.

- 1. Zendaya At the NYC premiere of The Odyssey on July 14, America’s favorite zillennial stunned in Matières Fécales’ “Ange” gown. Styled by Law Roach, the micro-hand-pleated chiffon creation sported white rooster feather wings designed to evoke Zendaya’s character in the movie: Greek goddess Athena. “What I loved most about the Matières angel look,” says stylist Ilaria Urbinati (her clients: Dwayne Johnson, Barry Keoghan) “is how cohesively ethereal it felt from head to toe. It didn’t look costume-y. She looked like a painting. Not many could pull it off.” Adds stylist Tara Swennen (Kristen Stewart, Ali Wong), “It literally took my breath away.”

- 2. Emma Chamberlain At the Met Gala on May 4, Chamberlain grabbed the limelight in custom Mugler by Miguel Castro Freitas. Inspired by impressionist painters, the one-of-a-kind rainbow dress, styled by Jared Ellner, took 40 hours to paint and four days to dry. “It really embodied the ‘Fashion Is Art’ Met Ball theme without feeling like a costume,” says stylist Tracy Shapoff (Molly Parker, Bill Maher). “The gorgeous hand-painting texture on the dress felt as though they’d painted a one-of-a-kind piece directly onto her body. I really felt like I was looking at a piece of artwork.”

- 3. Chase Infiniti Styled by Wayman + Micah, last Oscar season’s breakout Infiniti radiated in custom Thom Browne at the May 4 Met Gala. Made of 1.5 million hand-embroidered sequins and over 600 shades of silk fringe, the gown was inspired by the Greek sculpture of Venus de Milo. “There’s something surreal about it,” says stylist Avigail Collins (part of a team with husband Damian; they work with Elizabeth Olsen and St. Vincent). “Like wearable art, almost sculptural, the way the sequins, beading, intricate embroidery, craftsmanship and embellishments create an abstract silhouette, pushing the boundaries of fashion.”

- 4. Teyana Taylor Also wearing custom Thom Browne and also styled by Wayman + Micah, another of last awards season’s standouts, Taylor, grabbed fashion mindshare at the Actor Awards on March 1. The surrealist molded gown in gray and off-white was meant to evoke an abstract painting of a naked woman’s body, with ribbons dripping down the back. The “naked” anatomical bodice was made from over 160 pattern pieces put together via intarsia and tonal shading to mimic carved musculature; the gray tulle mermaid skirt was embellished with over 400,000 sequins in gold and white gold.

- 5. Nicole Kidman In a ruby-beaded, liquid-looking Chanel confection, Kidman, styled by Jason Bolden, turned heads at the Met Gala on May 4. Chanel’s Matthieu Blazy created the dropped-waist silhouette, with feathers at the hips and cuffs, a long dramatic train and surprising long sleeves. “What I loved most about that gown,” offers stylist James Yardley (Connor Storrie, Hannah Waddingham), “was its simplicity. Immaculate fit, and the placement of the feathers had such an impact. The cherry on top: the spinel and lapis lazuli ring, also from Chanel.”

- 6. Daisy Edgar-Jones Wearing this Miu Miu crystal corseted gown at the Oct. 1 Sydney premiere of Sense and Sensibility, Edgar-Jones, as styled by Dani Michelle, perfectly referenced Jane Austen’s era, with delicate ribbons as shoulder straps. “This strikes all the right notes,” declares stylist Ariel Tunnell (Rachel Bloom, Stephanie Beatriz). “The color, the sheer elements, the tones against her skin — so flattering. Add in the historical dressing of corsets and lacing, and it comes together in the coolest and most gorgeous way.”

- 7. Charli XCX Modelling custom Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello at the Sept. 27 MTV Video Music Awards and styled by Chris Horan, the music provocateur reminded that the midriff is an erogenous zone. Goth and glam at the same time, Charli embodied a modern Morticia Addams. “I can’t think of anyone who knows who they are better than Charli XCX,” stylist Michael Fisher tells THR (Ethan Hawke, Jon Hamm, Jake Gyllenhaal). “Every time I see her on a carpet, she’s perfectly herself and looks effortlessly cool.”

- 8. Rihanna Styled by Jahleel Weaver, she wore a custom metallic architectural creation by Maison Margiela artistic director Glenn Martens for the May 4 Met Gala. Inspired by the medieval buildings of the Flanders region of Belgium, it was sewn from duchess silk, recycled metal threads and 115,000 crystal beads alongside antique jewels and chains. The label’s Paris atelier spent 1,380 hours of handwork on what Rihanna described as “looking like a pearl emerging from an oxidized oyster shell,” a reference to her home country of Barbados.

- 9. Bella Hadid The Schiaparelli couture lace gown worn by the model multihyphenate and styled by Mimi Cuttrell for the Cannes Film Festival was an homage to Jane Birkin. It required 130 artisans to create. Stylist Molly Dickson (Sydney Sweeney, Lana Del Rey) offers: “Everything Daniel Roseberry does at Schiaparelli is incredible. This dress balances delicate proportions and contrast perfectly. The crochet is intricate; the V of the neck is the perfect line. And let’s not forget the back! It has a black ribbon corset lacing up to the neck, providing the tiniest bit of edge.”

- 10. Charlize Theron Only badass Theron, as styled by Leslie Fremar, could sex up this suit from Dior men’s fall 2026 collection, which she wore to the April 22 NYC premiere of Apex. “This look stood out to me,” says stylist Lee Harris (Helen Mirren, Drew Barrymore), “because in this red carpet world in which so many try to go over the top for attention, this was razor sharp and clean, with just one powerful accessory. She wore the look — the look didn’t wear her.”

- 11. Paul Anthony Kelly In Celine at a Good Morning America appearance in February promoting Love Story, Kelly wowed stylists and fashion luminaries of all genders. Styled by Warren Alfie Baker, the combo of jacket, rep tie and jeans hearkened back to his character, JFK Jr. “I love when well-worn denim makes its way into celeb dressing because it’s always unexpected,” says stylist Erica Cloud (Robert Downey Jr., Mia Goth). “The homage to JFK Jr. in the ’90s was a great intro to Paul’s fashion presence. The little Celine details — minimal loafers, squared-off tie — were icing on the cake.”

- 12. Tilda Swinton Swinton’s striking Chanel couture cocoon silhouette, complete with vertical pleating and a soft, body-conscious drape, was styled by Jerry Stafford for Cannes. Notes stylist Sarah Slutsky Tooley (Maya Hawke, Emma Watson, Elizabeth Olsen): “I’ve looked to Tilda as a style icon since I began in fashion. This look has unexpected proportions, matching tomato red with white kitten heels. It’s so thoughtful, though so easy. She looks so cool, completely refreshing and unexpected. Fashion is so natural to her DNA.”

- 13. Jacob Elordi At the Jan. 28 L.A. Wuthering Heights premiere, Elordi drew admiration as a very tall, masculine figure in a Chanel cropped jacket, all styled by Wendi and Nicole Ferreira. “This Chanel look masters understated luxury with a relaxed, modern twist,” notes stylist Chris Brown (David Beckham, Luke Evans, Leo Woodall). “The oversized blazer, soft knitwear and cream trousers create an elegant tonal palette, while the loose fit keeps things effortlessly modern. It’s a lesson in quiet confidence.”

- 14. Troye Sivan In Erdem at the MTV Video Music Video Awards, Sivan sported tuxedo suiting with sharp shoulders and a stiff, upturned collar, but from the waist down was adorned with ostrich feathers and satin and tulle trim. Styled by Marc Forne, this look was adapted from an Erdem dress in the spring/summer 2027 collection that was inspired by 1920s American aerialist Barbette, who performed in drag. Erdem used that as a jumping-off point to play with masculine and feminine tropes, combining strict tailoring and dramatic stage costume.

- 15. Pharrell Williams In a custom pink, plush velvet double-breasted suit with flared pants by Louis Vuitton, Pharrell cut an appropriately high-fashion figure at the Feb. 1 Grammys. Styled by Matthew Henson, the Vuitton men’s creative director also made matching suits for Clipse — the hip-hop duo also known as Malice and Pusha T, who were named by Pharrell himself — for their Grammy-night reunion. Pharrell also donned two Jacob & Co. Georgian-style yellow and white diamond riviera necklaces and diamond stud earrings.

- 16. Zoë Kravitz In an intricate Saint Laurent black-lace ballgown at the Met Gala, Hollywood’s perennial cool girl was in top form, as styled by Danielle Goldberg. “The silhouette creates a striking contrast between sleek sensuality and vintage drama,” comments stylist Brown. “It’s a look that feels mysterious, tactile and unapologetically individual, with Saint Laurent’s signature rock ’n’ roll attitude running throughout.” Kravitz’s Met Ball date was not her fiancé, Harry Styles, but one of her most-worn designers, Saint Laurent creative director Anthony Vaccarello.

- 17. Jenna Ortega In 36-year-old Turkish fashion designer Dilara Findikoglu at the Met Gala, Ortega played up her Goth character Wednesday Addams with a full-on peekaboo look, styled by Enrique Melendez. “I love that the chest is covered and the cutouts are on the sides of this gown,” says Dickson. “It’s like a reverse of the expected, creating an interesting moment on the carpet.”

- 18. Margot Robbie Pairing a vintage John Galliano brocade feather-cuffed coat with a micro-mini and red tights for the Feb. 5 London premiere of Wuthering Heights, Robbie caught lightning. Styled by Andrew Mukamal, the head-to-toe look is a brilliant study in dissonance, pairing modern and Gothic. “What we loved about this look,” says stylist Avigail Collins, “was the contrast between the romance of the 1992 archival Galliano coat and the sexiness of the black mini, red stockings and that clashing pink ribbon. An unexpected combination that works beautifully.”

- 19. Lady Gaga Styled by Nick Royal and Peri Rosenzweig of Hardstyle, the original little monster wore a black feathered gown with a train by Matières Fécales to the Grammys. “The cut sold me,” says stylist Nico Amarca (Atticus Ross, Chase Hudson). “Feathers go straight up the neck, lock around her jaw like armor, a hard look. Gaga’s biggest looks have always been about shock. This one was about control: one material, all black, no gimmick. Choosing a young, independent house like Matières Fécales over a legacy name made it even better.”

- 20. Dua Lipa Donning a white Schiaparelli suit with broad-brimmed hat while marrying Callum Turner at a London civil wedding on May 31, the singer-songwriter struck a Lorenzo Posocco-styled iconic silhouette. THR artistic director Alison Edmond explains, “It was all the more stylish by the location being so low-key; I loved that for them. She owned that Bianca Jagger reference, but made it Dua: the suit, hat, gloves, pumps, the flowers — perfection. There’s so much reality (in the dictionary sense of the word) about this couple: real love, real bodies, real sexiness … no fake relationship here.”

- 21. Pedro Pascal Styled by Jamie Mizrahi, Pascal shone at the Academy Awards in a custom Chanel jacketless tuxedo shirt with a white floral brooch made of silk and feathers, as unconventional as an Oscar look can get. “A guide to how to be a stylish man in formal wear, without being garish,” says stylist Melendez (Jenna Ortega, Inde Navarrette). “He hit the perfect medium. The exquisite tuxedo shirt with flower brooch moment added subtle drama we love to see in a carpet look, and that we always appreciate in men’s styling. The accentuated waist with the cummerbund showcased the fine tailoring.”

- 22. Shaboozey Styled by Anastasia Walker and showcasing a cropped tux by Mexican designer Patricio Campillo, the country hip-hop star made quite an impression. “Shaboozey walked into the Oscars and turned black-tie into a full showman moment!” says stylist Chaise Dennis (Tramell Tillman, Edward Norton.) “It’s impeccably tailored, totally distinct, so much fun. He put on a show. I also love the support of a small brand like Campillo on such a big stage.”

- 23 (tie). Jennifer Lawrence and Keri Russell The Jan. 11 Golden Globes was the first time J.Law went sheer. Styled by Ryan Hastings, the custom semi-transparent Givenchy gown was designed by Sarah Burton. “The look was both floral and sheer,” enthuses stylist Melendez, “which doesn’t sound too exciting until you actually see it! The perfectly placed appliqués made this look the perfect blend of sultry and sweet, and the addition of the silk embroidered shrug instantly made it even more captivating — an almost street-style element added in the most elevated way.” The Khaite backless custom leather halter-neck gown at the Emmys, as worn by The Diplomat star Russell and styled by Frank Fleming, was one of a number of edgy appearances. Her accessories matched the toughened look: high black stilettos, Buccellati garnet and diamond gold jewelry, and a slicked back, low ballerina bun. “This is a perfect look,” notes Cloud. “Equal amounts of nonchalance and edgy sexiness.”

- 24 (tie). Demi Moore, Michael B. Jordan and Renate Reinsve Moore was on the judging panel at the Cannes Film Festival, and her red carpet entrances encompassed 10 amazing looks styled by Brad Goreski, including this full-on ballgown by the provocative Paris duo of Matières Fécales. “A hot-pink Matières Fécales gown at Cannes, before most people knew the brand — perfect irreverence,” says stylist Britt Mccamey (Tracee Ellis Ross, Sadie Sink). “I respect how much Demi and Brad care about art in fashion. No algorithm could have picked this for her, that was the whole point. It’s fun to have fun!” “I enjoyed the detailing of this look,” says stylist Chloe Takayanagi (Sterling K. Brown, Kumail Nanjiani) of the details on Jordan’s custom-tailored Louis Vuitton Nehru-collar suit, styled by Jason Bolden for the Oscars. “I loved the brooch on the back of the neck and the watch chains, which seemed like a light nod to his character in Sinners. The mandarin, stand collar jacket was also a refreshing take on a classic-cut suit.” Styled by Karla Welch, Reinsve wore a number of Louis Vuitton dresses throughout awards season, all of them stark and revealing at the same time. The one she wore to the Oscars was a red strapless column gown with a sweeping train. “This was one of my favorite looks of Renate’s, the simplest dress, so effortless,” describes stylist Jessica Paster (Emily Blunt, Quinta Brunson). “It’s a beautiful dress — the sleekness of the slit up the leg — and the color. Sooo chic.”

- 25. John Malkovich “I adored seeing Malkovich walk down the carpet in this look in Venice,” says THR’s Edmond of the actor’s Dior suit at the film festival. “He has a touch of the genius in his work, and stylist Jeanne Yang is certainly talented enough to know how to showcase the theatrical via the sartorial. The beautifully oversized suit with the tied and pleated collar: What a perfect mix of fashion and film, putting Jonathan Anderson’s flourishes on this incredible actor.”

- 26. Florence Pugh The corsetry and exaggerated shape of Pugh’s Vivienne Westwood at the Sept. 30 NYC premiere of East of Eden strongly references her character’s early 20th century wardrobe. “This is the power of a strong silhouette,” observes Swennen of stylist Rebecca Corbin-Murray’s work. “The volume’s deliberate, yet does not overwhelm her. The fabric is so regal and opulent and the color — lime green/chartreuse — that’s something you don’t see often on the red carpet. I love it when people take risks, when they’re bold. It’s a very regal, luxurious look.”

items.title: Can a Radar-Equipped AC Actually Cut Your Power Bill?
items.description: With rolling heat waves sweeping the globe, 2027 is shaping up to be the hottest year on record. As the health risks of extreme temperatures mount, there's never been a better time to rethink sustainable cooling.
items.author: Sophie Charara
paragraphs: With rolling heat waves sweeping the globe, 2027 is shaping up to be the hottest year on record. As the health risks of extreme temperatures mount, there's never been a better time to rethink sustainable cooling.

Air conditioners and electric fans account for around 20 percent of electricity used in buildings worldwide—3 to 4 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions—and, as demand for cooling in homes, workplaces, and schools grows, the number of AC units in use could reach 5.5 billion by 2050.

The solution isn't one magic fix, but a suite of emerging technologies heading for living rooms and apartment windows. From radar sensors tracking your body to compact heat pumps and climate-safe refrigerants, here is how the next generation of air-conditioning plans to keep us cool without cooking the planet.

In 1994, Mitsubishi Electric was zooming past the air-con competition, introducing the first motion and occupancy sensors for AC, with infrared 3D sensing eventually following in the mid-2010s. Fast-forward to 2026 and AI-powered ACs now track people in the home with millimeter-level precision.

AC makers have launched intelligent, targeted air conditioner units all year, from Samsung’s Bespoke AI system in March to Dyson’s Find+Follow feature for its Purifier Cool fan in June. At IFA in September, we got a whole sweep from Chinese companies like Hisense, Dreo, and Midea.

LG’s latest DualCool AI AC has a 5-meter radar sensor for people detection plus targeting based on your everyday movement patterns. Hisense’s Companion Living AC also uses data from smart home sensors to identify and precool “target paths” within the home, based on your routines. So if you always head from the couch to the kitchen for a midnight snack, your AC can cool that particular zone before you even get up.

The real-time cooling features aim to improve comfort inside sticky homes. A secondary benefit is that precisely locating people and delivering cooling directly to them could reduce energy consumption. “It definitely has the potential to reduce the total energy use for air-conditioning,” says Björn Palm, senior professor in energy technology at the KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. By how much? That's less clear.

Dyson’s Find+Follow purifier and fan uses a simple, low-resolution camera, feeding the “stick figure”-like, anonymous coordinates of its 17-point person detection into an algorithm, all instantly processed on-device and deleted, without any face recognition. “It can tell that you’re a human, whether you’re sitting or standing, which direction you’re moving," says Alex Hudson, an environmental care engineer at Dyson. "It might map your arms and shoulders.”

The Purifier Cool can oscillate 350 degrees between “up to six people” in the space, directing airflow for personalized cooling. One hour after it detects that everyone has left the room, the appliance will switch to Auto mode and—if there is no big pollution spike for the purifier to deal with, like a truck driving past an open window—it’s a "considerably lower power draw than when it’s in fan mode, so there’s definitely a benefit there,” Hudson says.

Samsung’s Bespoke AI WindFree Pro adds a motion radar sensor, which can recognize and track two occupants. “AI Direct Wind” can follow and blast you for immediate cooling, whereas “AI Indirect Wind,” you guessed it, cools the spot you’re in without blowing air right in your face. Samsung’s residential environment tests claim energy savings of “up to 30 percent” with its overall AI energy mode switched on. At IFA, Samsung added wearable data: a Galaxy Watch or Galaxy Ring can signal to the AC when you’ve fallen asleep, triggering a gentler Windfree Cooling mode overnight.

Midea’s VitaBreeze AC, launching in early 2027, combines user photos with millimeter-wave radar sensors to personalize cooling. During setup, the user manually uploads a series of room images to the app, indicating the air conditioner placement. The AC then uses those images with radar data to create a 3D virtual grid of the room and furniture position.

Millimeter wave (or mmWave) radar—the kind used in 5G cellular technology—bounces short-wavelength radio waves, typically 1 to 10 millimeters, to detect an object's distance and angle, as well as tiny movements in real time. Here, the Midea app’s Follow Me feature, similar to Samsung's, can pinpoint your real-time position in the room, triggering louver adjustments as you move around. Manuel Seethaler, head of Midea's Residential Air Conditioning product strategy in Europe, says that its technology can save more than 30 percent of energy in cooling mode compared with units without these algorithms.

The average AC sold in 2024 was already about 20 percent more efficient than an equivalent model in 2014. However, there’s still plenty of room to grow, as the IEA predicts that “cooling demand” will grow by 1,600 terawatt-hours by 2035—Japan and South Korea’s total electricity combined. But this kind of proximity sensing could also result in marginal energy savings.

“There is a performance improvement you can get if [targeted AC] is done well,” says Vincent Romanin, founder and CTO of San Francisco–based Gradient, which makes 120-volt all-weather window AC/heat pumps. “But we’re going into buildings where we’re reducing the energy by 85 percent and to design another feature that gets us to 87 percent? I personally have never used a product with an occupancy sensor that I feel like worked well.”

For Palm, to reach sustainable home cooling by 2050, we need three major changes: cheaper, compact heat pumps for all home sizes; fewer toxic natural refrigerants (fluids and chemical compounds that absorb and release heat); and newly designed systems with low charge to ensure safety.

Heat pumps have become a modern, efficient option for heating and cooling. For heating, it's a four-stage process: absorbing outside heat to produce gas via a refrigerant; compressing to raise the temperature; condensing, where heat is passed to the water in your home’s heating system; and cooling back into a liquid via an expansion valve to drop the pressure. When cooling is needed, the reversing valve switches back to run the process from inside to outside for air-conditioning.

The key is to persuade renters and people living in smaller homes to make the overall switch. “For the domestic market, we need heat pumps which fit into an apartment without being too noisy or bulky,” Palm says. It's also critical to reduce the price.

Gradient units typically use one-third less energy than a standard window AC, mostly for heating but with cooling efficiencies too. They’re a quick self-install option that lets apartment renters get their window back, see lower bills, and run a quieter AC system than older models.

But fixing the form factor only solves part of the equation. Palm’s other criteria—replacing toxic synthetic refrigerants with natural alternatives like propane (R290), as in Bosch's Climate 6000iP, which launched in September—present a tougher engineering challenge. Leaking refrigerants alone account for an estimated 720 million metric tons of CO2-equivalent emissions every year. Natural refrigerants dramatically curb the potential for global warming, but their flammability demands complex, spark-free redesigns and low-charge systems that US regulators and supply chains are still cautious about embracing.

Reaching sustainable cooling by 2050 won’t be glamorous, Palm says. Ultimately, the future of home cooling won't hinge on an air conditioner that tracks you to the kitchen for a midnight snack—it depends on the unsexy, invisible mechanical work happening deep inside the compressor.

items.title: This Smart Ring Wants to Be a Remote Control for Your AI Agent
items.description: Apoorv Shankar believes that in the very near future, humans will interact with technology through a series of approvals and rejections. AI agents will proactively come to us to complete tasks, and humans will say, “Yes, order that Uber,” or “No, don't get lun
items.author: Julian Chokkattu
paragraphs: Apoorv Shankar believes that in the very near future, humans will interact with technology through a series of approvals and rejections. AI agents will proactively come to us to complete tasks, and humans will say, “Yes, order that Uber,” or “No, don't get lunch from that spot.”

But if you get multiple pings from an AI agent throughout the day, taking out your phone to say yes or no every single time will be a “bottleneck,” he says. That's why he made the Aina Ring. It has a small display and a joystick-like button that lets you quickly accept or reject an AI agent's actions with your hands. Your phone can stay in your pocket.

Aina has been in stealth for the last 15 months, though the company debuted a few experimental products at CES 2026 under a different name: Project Mirage. One was called Dune—think of it as the precursor to the Aina Ring. Connect it to your Mac and the three buttons become context-aware controls based on what you're doing. In a meeting? The buttons can turn into shortcuts for mute, camera off, or record.

Aina studied how people used Dune and developed the Aina Ring, which it’s announcing today. Preorders are live now, and the ring costs $399 for a limited time before the retail price rises to $499 when it starts shipping in January 2027.
“Approvals are going to be the future of interfaces and interaction, and we wanted to build a device that just made it easy to approve stuff,” Shankar says.

This isn't Shankar's first time with a smart ring—he previously was the vice president of hardware at Ultrahuman, a fitness- and health-tracking ring that competed with Oura. (Ultrahuman was briefly banned in the US after a patent dispute with Oura.)

The team explored other gadgets like smart glasses and pendants, but ultimately decided the ring was the most convenient way to interact with agents. The titanium Aina Ring connects to Macs or iPhones, and at any moment, the onboard assistant is looking for the three things you need next. It learns your routines from your personal data, like location, calendar, and email, and after you connect various third-party services in the Aina app, like Uber or Spotify.

If you usually go for a run at 6 am, as soon as you put on your running shoes, it will suggest continuing the podcast you started last night, or play music—the ring's joystick doubles as a music-playback controller. If it's 8:30 am and you usually take an Uber to work, it'll suggest the ride—flick yes on the ring, and it'll handle the task right away. If you're running late for a Zoom meeting, Aina will ask if you want the assistant to send an email saying you'll be late. Shankar calls these “Aina Cues,” powered by the ring's Context Aware Operating System.

Many of these actions will likely be limited based on what apps and features are supported, though Shankar says users can create their own Cues using natural language. So if you want the ring to prompt you about turning on the coffee machine every morning at 8 am, you can configure that. If your favorite app or service doesn't work through Aina, you can connect your preferred AI agent—like Muse or Instinct—to Aina, and they will handle the task through virtual browsers.

The display is crucial to make sure the user knows whether an action went through. “Agents today don't respond immediately,” Shankar says. “For us to trust these devices—that what I said actually just happened—you need display confirmation.”

These Cues aren't the only capability on the Aina Ring. Aina Voice lets you quickly talk to your AI agents by pressing the center button, or ask Aina to take notes, similar to smart rings like the Sandbar Stream or Pebble Index 01. The ring also has a tiny speaker, so you can take phone calls—initiate the call with a voice command, then bring your hand to your ear, like you're James Bond talking through an earpiece. (Bond would strongly advise against the gesture.)

Like the experimental Dune gadget, the ring also turns into a context-aware remote based on what you're doing. If it knows you're in a Zoom call on your Mac, it will offer up Zoom controls on the ring. If you're watching TV and can connect your TV system to Aina, it can act as a TV remote.

Many companies have tried and failed to be the next gadget for the AI revolution. Humane and Rabbit are two notable examples, but nothing has stuck so far. OpenAI is developing such a product with ex-Apple designer Jony Ive. But many of these devices claimed to replace your phone, and some, like the Rabbit, just felt awkward to carry around alongside the smartphone.

The Aina Ring isn't trying to replace anything—Shankar says phones are “too perfect.” Instead, it's just a means to stop you from being a bottleneck, so your AI agents can keep working on your behalf.

“We are seeing a major shift in how we operate with things—agents are able to do so much, and everything is waiting on us," he says. "I don't have an easy way to approve—we're going to see that a lot more once we see what the potential of proactive AI is.”

items.title: Motorola Wants to Sell You a $1,600 Phone That Doesn't Fold
items.description: How much is too much to pay for a smartphone? Prices have climbed globally—IDC forecasts a nearly 30 percent rise this year alone amid ongoing memory supply crunches—but would you pay $1,600 for a Motorola?
items.author: Julian Chokkattu
paragraphs: How much is too much to pay for a smartphone? Prices have climbed globally—IDC forecasts a nearly 30 percent rise this year alone amid ongoing memory supply crunches—but would you pay $1,600 for a Motorola?

That kind of money typically buys a folding phone with a bendable screen—where steep manufacturing costs justify the markup—or a maxed-out “candy bar” slab from an established premium brand like Apple or Samsung with gobs of internal storage. Motorola hasn't pushed into this price bracket outside of its latest Razr Fold or Razr Ultra folding devices, but that's changing with the new Motorola Signature 27.

It marks Motorola’s first unapologetic, ultra-premium candy bar in the US in six years, harking back to the Edge+ from 2020. And this time, rather than settling into the comfortable value-flagship tier, Motorola is taking direct aim at the highest-end Galaxies and iPhones on hardware alone. Preorders open on November 19, and the phone goes on sale November 26.

So what exactly do you get for $1,600? The Signature 27 has contoured edges, a thin design, and an “integrated” camera plane—similar to the iPhone 18 Pro’s Camera Plateau—finished in ceramic and brushed aluminum. It comes in two colors: Pantone Capulet Olive with a textile-inspired finish and Pantone Coal Smoke with a tactical-weave finish. The front glass is Corning's Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3, and the phone has an IP68/69 rating for top-of-the-line dust and water resistance.

Most notable is the 6.8-inch screen. Motorola claims its “Extreme AMOLED Duo” panel is the brightest smartphone display on the market, peaking at an eye-searing 12,000 nits. Underneath, it uses tandem OLED tech—stacking two panels on top of each other—similar to what Apple debuted on its iPad Pro and touchscreen MacBook.

Even so, Apple's new display peaks at around 2,000 nits, and most smartphones today top out around 3,600 nits, which is more than enough nits to read the screen in harsh sunlight. Chinese phone brands like Honor and Huawei have recently touted 10,000-plus max nits of brightness, but those ratings rarely apply outside of tiny slivers of the display during HDR playback. Treat Moto’s brightness statement as pure spec-sheet marketing.

The tech does deliver better energy efficiency, meaning the display uses less power and could improve battery life, plus a 121 percent longer lifespan than normal AMOLED panels. The screen also has a 1.5K resolution, Dolby Vision support, and “Pantone Validated” color calibration for accurate colors.

Once a handicap, the company's camera tech has become more competitive in recent years, and Motorola hopes the Signature 27 will stand out with its top-end image sensors. There's a 50-megapixel Sony Lytia L910 main camera—Sony's first sensor with LOFIC (Lateral Overflow Integration Capacitor) technology, which can dramatically improve dynamic range in a single exposure. Basically, it should perform better in challenging lighting conditions, with fewer crushed blacks and blown-out skies.

Next up is a 200-megapixel periscope 3X telephoto camera with up to 100X digital zoom, enhanced with generative AI, similar to what Google and Samsung offer on their respective devices. Rounding things out is a 50-megapixel ultrawide camera and a 50-megapixel selfie camera with 4K video support. Speaking of video, Motorola says its new video enhancement engine uses AI to optimize color, contrast, and dynamic range, and improved stabilization should make footage look smoother.

But wait, isn't there a fourth camera on the back? No, that's actually a dedicated “Event-Based Vision Sensor” (EVS), which Motorola claims is a first on a smartphone. It works with Motorola's Action Shot mode, freezing motion so photos of moving subjects look perfectly crisp and sharp with no motion blur.

The Signature 27 is among the first phones to use the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip, announced in September, the top-end processor you can expect to see in most flagship Android smartphones in 2027. Motorola cites better cooling performance with a 40 percent larger thermal chamber to keep the processor running longer. It comes with 12 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage.
It's one of the first phones with Wi-Fi 8. (Yes, you'll need a Wi-Fi 8 router to take advantage, and those barely exist on the market right now.)

A massive 7,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery sits inside—relatively new technology that enables denser yet slim batteries. That size should get you around 66 hours of battery life—more than two days. It supports 90-watt TurboPower fast charging—the company claims 12 minutes of charging will get you 12 hours of use—and wireless charging (but still no Qi2 magnetic wireless charging).

To help justify that $1,600 price, Motorola is partnering with premium audio brand Bang & Olufsen for the phone's speaker system, with a new speaker architecture promising the kind of “deep bass” and “clear vocals” every phone maker claims in their latest and greatest.

On software, Motorola promises 7 years of software updates. Motorola has historically lagged in updates, but it is changing its tune with higher-priced devices like the Razr Fold and now the Signature 27. This is also Motorola's first smartphone to support GrapheneOS—a de-Googled version of Android that focuses on protecting your privacy. (You can just stick with stock Android if you want.)

The Signature also gets a few Gemini Intelligence features that Google introduced this year with Android 17. You can ask Gemini to tackle tasks on your behalf, like booking an Uber or ordering food through DoorDash; create widgets using generative AI; and translate American Sign Language into English in real time with Google's Gboard and Live Transcribe apps. Google is also lending Motorola its Rambler feature that until now was exclusive to the Pixel 11. Rambler dramatically improves speech-to-text dictation.

Will all of that be enough to convince someone to part with $1,600? Motorola's Nicole Hagen, head of global product marketing, thinks so. She tells WIRED that Motorola has positioned itself as a lifestyle company for the last few years by leaning into luxury partnerships with brands like Pantone and Swarovski and pushing into the premium tier.

She points out that revenue is up 15 percent year over year in the second quarter of 2026, with a third of that coming from the “premium” category. She also says that the Signature model launched outside the US earlier this year alongside the Razr Fold saw the highest net promoter scores in the company's history, suggesting greater customer satisfaction and brand loyalty.

“Historically for Motorola, higher pricing has been tied to the foldable form factor, but we wanted to offer that set of consumers seeking the highest-quality smartphone where no technical specification has been overlooked,” Hagen says. And if the price is off-putting? Hagen points to Motorola's entire portfolio, from the budget and midrange Moto G series to the upper-midrange Motorola Edge phones.

Nabila Popal, senior research director at research and consulting firm IDC, isn't convinced that Motorola can successfully command such high prices. In the US, Apple captured 80 percent of the premium smartphone market in the second quarter of 2026, with Samsung sitting at 16 percent. Lenovo, Motorola's parent company, had just one percent.

“The average consumer—even the premium consumer—is not seeing which phone wins on a spec sheet,” Popal says. “Regardless of how great this phone is, it's going to be quite hard for Motorola to compete.”

Still, Motorola has seen success in this bracket. Its pricey folding phones are the most popular in the US, leading with 78 percent of the folding market. (Apple is expected to dramatically chip away at Motorola's lead with the new iPhone Duo.)

Motorola’s new handset does fall in line with the current “premiumization” trend in the hardware industry, though, where devices get a glow-up so companies can charge higher prices and preserve profitability in the memory-crisis era. Amazon's slate of October announcements is a good example—its new tablets, Echo devices, and Kindles all have higher starting prices but are made with nicer materials and more powerful components.

If the premiumization playbook works, Motorola will have proved that luxury doesn't have to bend. But it’s an uphill climb in this economic climate—especially when $500 can still buy you a fantastic phone.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 6, 2026
items.description: Astrologically speaking, you’re likely to have a quiet day ahead. But that could change if Mercury and Saturn (in Scorpio and Aries, respectively) stir up stress and anxiety tonight. Especially if you’re up late, you might start spiraling, convincing yourself
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: Astrologically speaking, you’re likely to have a quiet day ahead. But that could change if Mercury and Saturn (in Scorpio and Aries, respectively) stir up stress and anxiety tonight. Especially if you’re up late, you might start spiraling, convincing yourself you’ve made bad choices or even that you’re a “bad person.” But you’re not likely to reach any useful conclusions thinking this way. If you’re trying to work through a dilemma, you’re better off sleeping on it. You’ll have more clarity and a more positive outlook in the morning.

Today, you might overreact to minor disagreements and small inconveniences. Even if you know, rationally, that none of these issues are significant in the long run, your emotions might run hot anyway. But if you try to suppress your “bad” feelings, you’ll inevitably fail. Whatever you try to bottle up today will end up coming out one way or another. So instead, make it your goal to find a healthy way to channel your energy today. It’ll serve as a powerful motivator if you can use it for good.

When your close relationships feel strained or contentious, you prefer to address the problem rather than avoid it. But today, the solution might be for everyone involved to take some space. With a bit of distance, you might realize that your issues aren’t nearly as serious as you feared. More than that, time apart will give you a chance to remember what you actually like about each other. Deep and difficult conversations can wait. For now, simply letting the issue rest might be all it takes to feel better.

Most of the time, you’re good at rolling with the punches. Even in the most stressful of circumstances, you can typically find something to work with. Today, though, you might not be as flexible as usual. If your routines are off, you’ll be more bothered by it than you normally would be; if your living space is untidy or uncomfortable, you’ll easily get distracted. So take some time to put the details of your day in order, to the extent that you can. It’ll make everything else flow more smoothly.

You make a point of considering your words carefully before you speak. You don’t want your ideas to come out wrong or to accidentally offend anyone. You’re not afraid of being controversial; you just want to be intentional about it! But today, give yourself permission to be spontaneous. If you take too much time to plan out what you want to say, the conversation might move on by the time you’re ready. So trust yourself, and if the moment comes to speak up, seize it.

You struggle not to wrestle with FOMO. Sometimes, you imagine that if you want to have interesting experiences and enjoy your life, you need to constantly chase the action whenever and wherever it’s happening. But today, try to slow down a bit. If you make a point of looking around with an open mind, you’ll realize that there’s plenty of excitement in your own community and your own life. You don’t need to go anywhere else to find what you want; you have everything you need already. You just need to notice it.

Sometimes, when you’re stressed out, you need to commit to doing less — bowing out of the obligations you don’t have to to fulfill, making fewer plans, and cutting down your to-do list. But if you try to do that today, you’ll only wind up feeling bored and dissatisfied. Don’t attempt to shrink your life down to a smaller, more manageable size at the moment. Instead, refocus your energy, and remember you’re capable of more than you give yourself credit for.

Taking the path of least resistance might seem, to you, like a form of laziness. Those who refuse to buck convention strike you as scared and tired, even boring. But today, you’d be wise to consider their perspective. Keeping things simple, straightforward, and “normal” right now might actually be the smartest move you can make. There’s no need to overcomplicate processes or to exhaust yourself simply so that you feel like you’ve done something different and “unique.” Do what comes naturally. You’ll get the best results that way.

This could be one of those days when everything feels a little off. You’ll struggle to shake the sense that you’re messing up, even if you can’t pinpoint how or even what you’re “messing up.” Right now, it’s likely that your problem stems from your own expectations: They’re too vague, and you keep shifting your own goalposts. Give yourself specific, tangible targets to work toward, and you’ll have a much better sense of what is and isn’t working. And once you’ve reached those goals, give yourself permission to celebrate.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

Usually, you’re not especially thin-skinned — but today, don’t be surprised if you’re more sensitive than usual. Comments that might not normally make an impression could move you deeply; your own feelings will be easily hurt. There’s nothing wrong with this, but try to be aware of it. It might be a good idea to avoid the more brash and callous people in your life. You’ll probably need some extra care, so spend time with the people most likely to give it to you.

Be thoughtful about who you spend time with today, because other people’s moods are likely to affect your own. Hanging around your most cynical friends could quickly make you feel jaded, too. And others’ anxieties could easily spike your own stress levels. Being influenced by your peers is normal — and just as likely to lead to positive shifts in your own mind-set! — but try to be discerning about who you’re taking your cues from.

You have a strong sense of self. You know who you are and what you believe in, and you’re more interested in staying true to yourself than being popular. But today, remember it’s okay to want to be liked. Sometimes it feels good to fit in. Even if you usually enjoy being the one to voice unpopular opinions or go against the grain, consider relaxing that stance for now. You don’t need to change who you are, but it’s worth considering how you can best relate to those around you. Focus today on building positive, supportive relationships.

Your own fear of making mistakes could hold you back today. If you’re so nervous about making a wrong move, you’ll end up convincing yourself you shouldn’t try anything new, just in case it’s a bad idea. But that’s no way to live — it’ll ensure that you never learn or grow. Today, take a breath and remember that errors are part of the process. Trust that if you do make a mistake, you can also make things right again.
Buy Claire Comstock-Gay’s book, Madame Clairevoyant’s Guide to the Stars, here.

items.title: The New Moon In Scorpio Is Here — & This Is Your Opportunity To Reconnect With Yourself
items.description: The New Moon occurs on November 9th during the last weeks of Scorpio Season. This lunation will bring a mix of versatile vibes, some volatile and some favorable. We can pick and choose our own adventure and how we wish to navigate the New Moon, as long as we'r
items.author: Lisa Stardust
paragraphs: The New Moon occurs on November 9th during the last weeks of Scorpio Season. This lunation will bring a mix of versatile vibes, some volatile and some favorable. We can pick and choose our own adventure and how we wish to navigate the New Moon, as long as we're careful not to get pricked by the venomous stingers of the scorpion. To evade the drama, it's imperative that we stay in our lanes and do not honk our horns in traffic — basically, keep the commentary that doesn't involve us to a minimum and opt to take the high road, when in doubt of how to proceed.

Mars, Scorpio's traditional planetary ruler (modern ruler: Pluto), squares the New Moon. Mars in Leo aspecting the New Moon in Scorpio creates an intense external reaction to internal forces. We may feel as though other people are triggering us with their actions, stirring frustration in our auric field and prompting us to voice our annoyances and assert ourselves, even though we know the best move is to walk away from confrontation. The reason is that words can cut deep during this transit; we may not be able to take back or apologize for things that are said in the heat of the moment.

Getting carried away with our emotions is part of the vibe. IKYK that Scorpio is a sign that is penetrating and oozing with passion; when Mars comes into play with it, the exuberance intensifies, giving us the ability to accomplish our goals and set an aspirational path forward. Impulsivity runs high, so we tend to take shortcuts to achieve greatness and skip necessary steps. Working our way up the corporate ladder or starting a relationship slowly isn't a bad idea — to be real, it encourages us to know the criteria and scope of the job and provide companionship to someone we are familiar with. Wanting to rise to the top without understanding the requirements and prerequisites can lead to our downfall — so tread lightly. More importantly, do not rush the process. Savor the moment. Test the temperature of the water by dipping our toes in first, rather than jumping in.

Mercury retrograde in Scorpio and Venus retrograde in Libra are still moonwalking in the sky, creating erratic sentiments; this is a call to hone in, as the energy is unpredictable, meaning the unforeseen can come to fruition. A great way to harness this is to listen before speaking and think through the best response; also, don't commit before you know the details and expectations. That way, we know the rules of the game, and we can act accordingly. Of course, this won't be easy. But through discipline, we can control our behavior to ensure we conduct ourselves with dignity and treat others with respect.

The following day, Venus retrograde in Libra and Mars in Leo align, setting the stage for a grand journey that promises growth and development in matters of love. However, we'll do our due diligence to heal and transcend. Consider the New Moon as the catalyst for this venture. Forgiving others — especially ourselves — will be freeing because it lifts a burden from us. We no longer have to carry embarrassment, fear, resentment, and heartache. We are moving past it into a state of newness that replenishes our lives. The hurt we feel are in the natural rhythm and flow of mending themselves, offering hope and optimism for the future.

The asteroid Ceres, which is in Cancer, harmonizes with the New Moon. The mythology of Ceres is that of a mother whose daughter, Proserpina, was abducted by Pluto, unbeknownst to her. As the goddess of agriculture and fertility, Ceres stopped tending the Earth, which affected the harvest and caused famine when Proserpina went missing. She revolted against the Roman gods to get their attention and make them search for Proserpina. After finding Proserpina, Ceres struck a deal: she'd visit her daughter in the underworld for a few months and do her job to aid Earth the rest of the time, creating the cycle of seasons. We see Ceres as a testament to unconditional love and the depths we go to for those we care about. In this case, we are both Proserpina and Ceres. The New Moon is our opportunity to reconnect with ourselves or old friends, but only if we are ready to evolve. Let's get moving!

items.title: Welcome to the mixed-up, joyful world of AuDHD | Aeon Essays
items.description: How would it be if you woke up one morning around 4 am, consumed by an idea that felt like the Best Idea You Ever Had. You spend the next two hours fervently researching said idea, watching videos, reading in-depth articles, compiling a spreadsheet comparing c
items.author: Sarah Hendrickx
paragraphs: How would it be if you woke up one morning around 4 am, consumed by an idea that felt like the Best Idea You Ever Had. You spend the next two hours fervently researching said idea, watching videos, reading in-depth articles, compiling a spreadsheet comparing costs, techniques and options, then buying a whole load of books and equipment, and signing up to courses to teach you how to bring this fantastic, life-changing idea to fruition. You book a viewing for the new house in a new country that you are going to buy after investigating climate, housing options and work opportunities. You book the flights for that trip, to a Pacific island, where you will learn to scuba dive and set up a business as a dive instructor having fully understood the tourism industry and its legal implications. You sign up for that master’s programme in hypnotherapy/mushroom-growing/road-building after comparing the cost and quality of all colleges offering these courses. Your research is deep, your conclusions well justified. These are all good choices.

Buzzing on your own brilliance at finding the answer to all of your problems, your true calling in life and, basically, frigging nirvana, you are desperate to wake your beloved, who is lying beside you, blissfully unaware that their world is about to be rocked. You think about waking them because you can’t contain all this excitement alone and need to share it, but it’s only 6 am and you know from experience that this wouldn’t end well. So you sit, fidgeting, watching the clock until 6:30 am. Surely, that’s late enough? Perhaps if you bring them coffee, they won’t be so mad. Yet how could they be mad, when what you’re about to reveal to them will make them say: ‘Why didn’t you wake me up sooner, you genius?’

But as you sit impatiently waiting for an acceptable hour to rouse your beloved and blow their mind, your whole self shifts sideways, like someone just turned the TV over to another channel or a changeling took over your mind. You suddenly realise that your previously designated Best Idea Ever is full of holes and is actually a Terrible Idea. You are puzzled that you didn’t see this sooner. What were you thinking? You can’t move house because your kids are in school here, you have a full-time job and bills to pay, and you don’t have the attention span to read your horoscope, let alone do a master’s. And you can’t even swim.

What idiot thought that any of this was a good idea? Oh… it was me. OK… time to cancel it all and hope that you didn’t lose too much money and that it will all be back in the bank account before ‘they’ wake up.
And hope that you don’t do the same thing again tonight.
Welcome to the world of AuDHD.

You will likely have come across the term AuDHD used as a shortcut to describe those given the dual diagnosis of autism and attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). It is a relatively new label and for good reason – until recently, no one individual was clinically permitted to be given both diagnoses and therefore there was no one to whom the term ‘AuDHD’ could officially apply.

In 1994, a mere 32 years ago, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th edition (DSM-IV), included Asperger Syndrome for the first time. In 2013, the diagnosis was removed from the 5th edition (DSM-5) and subsumed under the broader category of ‘autism spectrum disorder’. Asperger Syndrome had identified individuals who met the social and behavioural aspects of the diagnostic criteria for autism but who did not have intellectual disability or the language-development differences then associated with an autism diagnosis. As a result, an autistic person reading this magazine today would have been unlikely to receive an autism diagnosis in the past: there was simply no diagnostic category that fit their profile. That helps to explain the huge rise in adult diagnoses in recent decades.
Autism and ADHD were long considered mutually exclusive

Alongside this, diagnosis of ADHD in adults has been a similarly recent arrival. Having been considered a predominantly childhood condition for most of its history, the idea that children can continue to experience ADHD features into adulthood was not seriously considered until the early 2000s. Earlier versions of the DSM required that symptoms had to have been present prior to the age of seven years, and focused almost entirely on childhood behaviours to form the diagnosis. In 2013, with the publication of the DSM-5, the onset age of ADHD symptoms was raised to 12 years, and fewer symptoms were required for adults to meet the diagnostic threshold – which took into account development changes and challenges within adult settings, such as work – thus opening up ADHD diagnosis to adults.

This means that a person without intellectual disability and with relatively typical language development has been eligible for an autism diagnosis for only 32 years. And the ADHD criteria have been explicitly adapted to better recognise the disorder in adults only since 2013. That history is one part of the AuDHD issue.

The second part is that autism and ADHD were long considered mutually exclusive. It was thought that their apparently contradictory traits of rigidity and impulsivity effectively cancelled each other out. This meant that a person – either child or adult – could not be officially diagnosed with both conditions until 13 years ago, when the DSM-5 removed this exclusion and allowed both diagnoses to be given to the same person – opening the way for what is now widely called AuDHD.

At first glance, existing diagnostic criteria for each condition may look like contradictions of each other. While a stereotypical autistic person may present as socially awkward, precise and cautious in language and behaviour, requiring predictability, sameness and calm, our ADHDer looks like the complete opposite. ADHD diagnostic criteria typically present as someone socially driven, scattered and impulsive in language and behaviour, seeking novelty, variety and stimulation. How can it be that both of these seemingly opposing traits can exist in one person, and what is it like for that person when they do?

Given the relatively recent formal recognition of this comorbid profile, research into its impact is unsurprisingly scarce and, aside from a small handful of papers, has been focused on children and adolescents. The earliest research into this overlap I could find was published in 1999; those investigators concluded that autistic features were common in those with ADHD, and that a dual diagnosis should be considered in some cases, even though this was not clinically permitted at the time. This overlap has been one of the most frequently studied aspects of AuDHD.

A 2023 systematic review identified 9,050 articles and ultimately included 23 studies; across these, estimates of the prevalence of ADHD symptoms in autistic young people without intellectual disability ranged from 2.6 per cent to 95.5 per cent. Another paper suggested that 50 to 70 per cent of autistic people present with comorbid ADHD. If you are reading this article with a diagnosis of autism or ADHD, you may want to think about whether you may be both, because it’s looking increasingly likely that you are.

Of course, there have always been differing opinions and concerns about the pathologising nature of diagnosis in neurodiversity. Where does one neurodivergent condition end and another begin? Can we really separate these aspects of ourselves into neat clinical categories – often deemed necessary to permit access to a particular support service, therapy, fund or setting to meet the often-disabling needs of being neurodivergent in a neurotypical world? The reality is that no one knows the answers, so here we are with our rigid clinical diagnostic criteria, which – as we can see from the alterations in the DSM-5 – are changing as understanding grows. Forgive me for working within these uncomfortable neat boxes, but they are all we have right now; and, for at least some people, they can be a helpful way of understanding the contradictions of living with AuDHD.
My former life had failed to meet my autistic need for routine but had satisfied my ADHD need for novelty

The example at the top of the article is one from my own life and it has resonated with many of the 69 AuDHD adults and parents of AuDHD children whose stories and words I had the privilege to gather for my new book, The Complete Guide to AuDHD (2026).

My own AuDHD story is a typical one. I was diagnosed as autistic in my 40s after having written five books on autism and neurodiversity and achieving an MA in autism – I knew my stuff, and myself, or at least I thought I did. Yet I had led a chaotic life of multiple jobs, house moves and plans and schemes of one kind or another – I am known for it by those who know me; they take bets on how long I will stay in one place/job/course/project – which upsets me, but which is hard, logically, to take umbrage at.

I had never considered that I would meet the criteria for ADHD diagnosis because I was too logical, too organised and too set in my ways. I am the Queen of the Spreadsheet, the Mistress of the Plan. After bringing up two kids, I worked as a trainer and speaker for 15 years, travelling the country and overseas on a crazy schedule of driving, hotels and public speaking. Not surprisingly, I crashed horribly into years of panic attacks, agoraphobia and severe physical and mental burnout. Eventually, I gave it all up and began working locally and remotely, removing 90 per cent of the stress and unpredictability of my former life. At first, it was wonderful, I remembered what it was like to wake up without a brick of dread and anxiety on my chest. I slept in the same bed every night and knew what each day would bring. Perfect. Until… a few weeks into this blissful new existence I recall a feeling that I verbalised at the time as ‘I feel like I’m dead.’ I felt flat, blank, nothing, emotionless. Over a period of reflection, I realised that I had never actually sat still my whole life. While my former parenting and working lives had failed to meet my autistic need for routine and predictability, they had entirely satisfied – what I now understood to be – my ADHD need for constant dopamine in the form of novelty, variety and excitement.

Those who have the same experience of a second diagnosis of either autism or ADHD share the same feeling I did – it’s the final piece of the puzzle. The first diagnosis made sense of a lot, but it didn’t explain it all. There were questions and gaps: ‘I’m too social to be autistic.’ ‘I need too much order to be ADHD.’
This sense of two selves, of the push and pull of opposing wants and needs, is the core of the experience

Since the dual diagnosis of the two conditions is fairly recent, it is still unusual for both diagnoses to occur at the same time, with most adults currently having received one diagnosis first and the second at some point later, as did I. And although autism and ADHD were deemed contradictory for much of their joint history, both sets of diagnostic criteria need to be met for each diagnosis to be given: there is no allowance made for ADHD characteristics masking those of autism, for example – which they often do – during the diagnostic assessment.

Which diagnosis comes first varies from person to person, with either autism or ADHD often appearing as the primary profile. Perhaps ADHD appears more ‘visible’ for a child challenged by sitting still at school, or autism for an adult struggling with the social and flexibility requirements of a job – with the other lurking behind ready to throw a spanner in the works or offer a helping hand. Given that the second diagnosis was simply not an option for so long, the thought of it was generally never given the time of day, although a number of AuDHD people I have assessed often say they’d felt that the first diagnosis had answered some of the questions they’d had throughout their lives about why they were different, but not all. For others, it was a complete surprise. As one person I interviewed for my book explained:
My ADHD assessor said: ‘Many of these symptoms could be explained by the autism,’ to which I replied: ‘What autism?’

For many, this ‘primary’ profile is not fixed. Female hormones are known to affect the severity of ADHD. The time of day and associated stress and fatigue play a role. And the impact depends on the activity contemplated – does it require speed and creativity, or accuracy and focus?

The idea of the autistic and ADHD selves as separate entities is hardly definitive, and experts differ here. Some research finds autism and ADHD symptoms to be largely segregated along existing diagnostic boundaries; others that they have overlapping features; while others suggest that the co-occurrence of autism and ADHD may represent a distinct combined phenotype. Regardless of the thoughts of academics, this sense of two selves, of conflict and contradiction and the push and pull of opposing wants and needs, is one that formed the core and essence of the experience of the participants in my own research.

An article by Siân Boyle in The Guardian in 2024 described this contradiction in the AuDHD label as one of ‘oxymoronic nature, perpetual internal war and rollercoaster of needs’, which nicely sums things up.

The realisation that there is a name and an explanation for the persistent inconsistency that accompanies the AuDHD lived experience can be liberating – it’s a relief to know that you are not actually crazy, because that’s the way it can feel. In the words of my research participants, it is:
Having to keep two different beasts fed and cared for, after having spent most of my life being told by others that neither beast existed.

A lightbulb moment when I realised that my hectic brain being pulled in two different directions at all times throughout my whole life actually had a reason and it wasn’t that I was stupid or incapable as I always believed before.

Despite this sense of contradiction, the two conditions do share some characteristics. Both are highly heritable and run through families. As far back as 2009, a team led by the child and adolescent psychiatrist Aisling Mulligan at Trinity College Dublin found that autistic traits in children with ADHD ran in families, along with the ADHD itself. More recent research shows that mothers with ADHD are six times more likely to have a child with ADHD – and 2.5 times as likely to have an autistic child. Other studies suggest a shared genetic base between autism and ADHD, explaining the high prevalence of both conditions in the same families. Twin studies provide further evidence of this genetic overlap.

People with either autism or ADHD may find it challenging to read subtle social nuances and engage in reciprocal conversation, making it harder to sustain friendships and relationships. Both often have intense passions and interests, although these tend to last longer in autism than in ADHD. And while sensory features are not mentioned in the diagnostic criteria for ADHD, both groups may have atypical sensory profiles. As a very broad generalisation, autistic people find sensory experiences overwhelming, leading them to avoid some sensations and seek out comfort. On the other hand, ADHD people may seek sensory input and stimulation to feel grounded and focused. Although it is early days for research and the number of papers looking at AuDHD are small and focused almost entirely on children and adolescents, the general consensus is that the combination of autism and ADHD makes things worse socially, adaptively, behaviourally and mentally. I could not find any research-based evidence that sought or found examples of the dual diagnosis making life better. It seems that, in academic studies, questions relating to the advantages and joys of AuDHD were not asked, and that the focus was entirely on problems, challenges and deficit, as is often, disappointingly, the case.
Every day needs to be filled with entertainment and stability, learning and fun

The inconsistency brought by these apparently opposing sets of features does cause considerable frustration for the typical AuDHDer, who lives switching – often rapidly – between seeking both order and disruption, sameness and variety, impulsivity and risk-aversion, social motivation and solitude, single focus and multi-focus. When needs and wants shift so quickly and vary so wildly, decision-making and balance can feel impossible, leading to a far more chaotic life than would be expected from someone with an autism diagnosis. As one of the research participants said:
For my child, it’s like living with Bert and Ernie from Sesame Street in his head at one time. Bert wants quiet but Ernie needs noise… The internal tension is real.

Yet the participants in my own research reported the joys of AuDHD as well. For me, the combination of the detail and diligence of autism and the creativity and impulsivity of ADHD have likely led to my deeply interesting and varied life, because I couldn’t have tolerated it any other way. Every day needs to be filled with entertainment and stability, learning and fun. Others in my research agree:

The absolute chaos and rhizome-like thinking enables me to be very creative in all aspects of my life and see things in a way that others don’t. The ability to feel and see so much; a complete all-encompassing joy over very small tiny things and details that most other people miss, sometimes it feels like I can almost see or feel an extra dimension compared to those around me, and it brings me so much joy.

For me, it feels like a life of two halves, like living as a pair of twins who argue a lot but now and again will sit on the couch together and watch a movie. We know we have to have a schedule, eat the same foods and get things done. We know we have to physically move – a lot – keep switching tasks, and force ourselves to stop when we’re just done. We know we find it hard to begin, hard to keep going and hard to stop, and we’re continually developing ways to work with all of that at any given time in all given circumstances.

And although Autism has to step in to keep ADHD in check, and force it to sit down and do the dull, important things for a few minutes – rather than spending all day watching videos about giant tortoises on the Galápagos Islands – ADHD also needs to break through the rigidity of Autism’s need for productivity, tell it to lighten up – and come watch some of these great videos on giant tortoises on the Galápagos Islands. And then, once ADHD has piqued Autism’s interest with today’s Best Idea Ever, Autism can become a world authority on tortoises, research the climate, food, cheapest flights and best hotel on the islands, and build a spreadsheet to get this trip on the road. What a team!
We only have to hope that Autism knows where the passport is.

items.title: The Nue Black Aesthetic explores the many voices shaping Black design
items.description: At London's Design Museum, collective objects bring us closer to the people behind them, their influences and the knowledge that makes their work possible. 'The Nue Black Aesthetic' (until 8 August 2026) guides visitors through the narratives shaping Black des
items.author: Jamilah Rose-Roberts
paragraphs: At London's Design Museum, collective objects bring us closer to the people behind them, their influences and the knowledge that makes their work possible. 'The Nue Black Aesthetic' (until 8 August 2026) guides visitors through the narratives shaping Black design, from earlier masters and Larry Neal's writing to the conversations taking place in studios and workshops today. Along the way, it asks whose creative contributions are remembered, how knowledge lives on between generations and who has been denied the leeway to tell their story.

Guest curated by Charlene Prempeh, alongside co-curator Tiya Dahyabhai of the Design Museum, the exhibition brings together over 100 objects by 16 contemporary Black designers. Spanning furniture, architecture and fashion, their work challenges Black erasure while granting agency to the individual experiences and endeavours that shape a practice.

The exhibition builds on discussions of a Black aesthetic in the 1960s and a New Black Aesthetic in the 1980s, focusing on Larry Neal's 1968 essay 'The Black Arts Movement', and a collection of seminal essays on the arts, Any Day Now: Toward a Black Aesthetic, published by David Zwirner Books, placing today's practices within a continuing discussion about cultural identity and artistic self-determination.

Here, 'Nue' stands for nuance. The designers, many of whom belong to diasporic communities, draw on shared but dispersed experiences and the distinct traditions of their particular heritage. Their work reveals how differently those influences can be felt and communicated, with historical research running throughout the exhibition.

Designers including Andu Masebo, Samuel Ross and Ini Archibong bring their own approaches to objects, while fashion by Foday Dumbuya, Feben, Saul Nash, Bianca Saunders and Rachel Scott return our attention to 'the dressed body'. Taiba Akhuetie's braided objects and Phoebe Collings-James' ceramics offer further ways into the relationships between material, form and making. There is plenty to absorb as the exhibition continues to unfold and these connections accumulate. Spending time with each practitioner account deepens the show's proposition: Black design is not monolithic.
Here, we look at five key objects from the exhibition, and the stories they tell.
Lantern House by Tosin Oshinowo

For Nigerian architect and designer Tosin Oshinowo, the conversation begins with the conditions of a Lagos home. Featuring 'Lantern House', the building expresses her approach to Afrominimalism through the everyday experience of living back home: an extended focus on how light enters a room, how it transforms, while also considering how a home feels to those inside it.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Assemblage takes a more explicit form in Mac Collins' 'Open Code'. Drawing on his Jamaican heritage, Collins's reconstruction of the dominoes table for Harewood House, an estate with historical connections to slavery, gives the game's familiar expression of Jamaican communal life particular resonance. The table's significance extends through the people who sit and the discussions that follow.
Strang Notes by Giles Tettey Nartey

In the exhibition's wider conversation, British-Ghanaian architect and designer Giles Tettey Nartey's 'Strang Notes' presents his reinterpretation of the balafon, a gourd-resonated West African xylophone, examining how inherited forms continue to develop through contemporary making, along with a further development of Assembly, continuing the idea of gathering unity.
Resting Figure Bench by Simone Brewster

Simon Brewster continues her exploration of the Black female body through sculptural form. Visitors may already know her work from the museum's PLATFORM display. In many ways, her new piece, 'Resting Figure Bench' materialises earlier conversations, drawing attention to the relationship between Black female body, everyday life and the customary constructs that support.
Oríkì (Act III): Whispers of a Trail by Nifemi Marcus-Bello

For Lagos-based designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello, the starting point is material. 'Oríkì (Act III): Whispers of a Trail' follows copper through countries' politics of extraction and the practical difficulties of sourcing it in his community. Working with traders and craftspeople, the artist procures reclaimed metal from Lagos's scrap markets and reworks it into functional sculptures, bringing the expertise of those who sourced and worked the metal, alongside questions about who can access Africa's resources and who benefits from their circulation.

Jamilah Rose-Roberts is Wallpaper’s Social Media Editor. Alongside shaping the brand’s social media presence, she writes about arts and design, focusing on cultural narratives, the diaspora, and contemporary practice. She enjoys meeting artists and designers, visiting exhibitions, and conducting interviews.

items.title: How Peter Copping is rebuilding Parisian couture house Lanvin
items.description: ‘I think they wanted a good, solid designer who would bring stability,’ says Peter Copping when asked why he believes he was selected as the creative director of Lanvin – Paris’ oldest, continuously operating haute couture house – in 2024.
items.author: Jack Moss
paragraphs: ‘I think they wanted a good, solid designer who would bring stability,’ says Peter Copping when asked why he believes he was selected as the creative director of Lanvin – Paris’ oldest, continuously operating haute couture house – in 2024.

It is a modest understatement: the British fashion designer, who was born in Oxfordshire and went on to study at London’s Central Saint Martins and Royal College of Art, has one of the industry’s most distinguished CVs. His career began at Christian Lacroix, where he interned in the 1990s; roles at Iceberg and Sonia Rykiel followed; and in 1997, he began a 12-year tenure at Louis Vuitton under Marc Jacobs (Copping ended up as head of womenswear). In 2009, he stepped into the spotlight as creative director of Nina Ricci (he is often credited with revitalising the house), before being personally selected by Oscar de la Renta as his successor in 2014. More recently, he served as head of couture at Balenciaga under Demna, after the Georgian designer relaunched the line in 2021.

Copping commands so much respect within the industry that his appointment was marked not with the usual lively internet debate, but a rare positive consensus. The ovation after his first show – held in January 2025 at Paris’ Pavillon Gabriel as a precursor to the wave of creative director debuts that would follow in September that year – was equally emphatic. There, he posited a contemporary vision of founder Jeanne Lanvin’s 1920s heyday, all louche silhouettes and decadent details, with the addition of menswear on the runway (the latter came with a similar spirit, seeing swathes of sequins spread across the shoulder of a shirt or patches of intarsia shearling adorning a sweater).

But there is truth to the fact that, after two years at the house, Copping is a steadying force – and not simply in his demeanour (he is softly spoken and thoughtful, far from the mercurial figure often associated with designers in his position). ‘I know how to run an atelier,’ he says from his office in the new Lanvin HQ in Hôtel Botterel de Quintin, a listed 18th-century building in Paris’ 10th arrondissement. ‘My primary focus is always the clothes, working with the design team, finding the fabrics. That always has to be the anchor of a collection.’

A safe pair of hands was much needed for Lanvin, which had been in a state of decline since the exit of Alber Elbaz in 2015, following a 14-year tenure. The late Israeli designer brought an after-dark insouciance to the house, with jewel-tone cocktail gowns cut with ruffles, bows and drapes, and adorned with gobstopper costume jewellery; by 2019, four years after his exit, annual sales had slumped from €143m to €41m, and a stream of creative directors followed, including Bouchra Jarrar, Olivier Lapidus, Bruno Sialelli and Chemena Kamali. When Copping started, Lanvin had been without a creative director for 14 months.

His approach was to begin in the house’s archive, which comprises both clothing and ephemera, including fabric and embroidery swatches, a particular obsession of Copping’s. Paris’ museums and curators also ‘opened their doors to him’, including Alexandre Samson at the Palais Galliera. ‘Jeanne Lanvin’s work is so incredibly detailed,’ he says, noting that her garments would often appear as one thing from afar, and another close up. ‘You might see a sequin dress, but when you actually look at it, it’s layers of different geometric sequins’ (the technique inspired Copping to create constellations of embellishment in his first collection). The antique fabrics that Jeanne Lanvin had sourced on trips to Egypt and Venice, as well as those developed by the designer herself, proved equally inspiring: in a pioneering move, she would go on to create her own dyeing workshop outside Paris, which would lead to the advent of the house’s signature blue.

‘She was really forward thinking,’ Copping says of the proto-multi-hyphenate, who was an early adopter of menswear (Lanvin-Tailor-Shirtmaker was introduced in 1926), childrenswear (she started making miniature versions of her clothing for her daughter Marguerite in 1908), fragrance (Lanvin Perfumes was established in 1924), and interiors (she co-founded Lanvin Décoration with Armand-Albert Rateau in 1921). ‘Jeanne came from humble beginnings, and I have a huge admiration for her for starting so young. She began as a milliner and then used her daughter as a muse to make clothes that people started to see, and then wanted. She understood women’s lives were changing.’
