items.title: Is This Luxury Diaper Brand Leaving Babies With Burns?
items.description: Kaylyn Bradford started using Millie Moon diapers when her oldest daughter was born three years ago. She liked how soft and fluffy they were, and they seemed to fit her two daughters well. Anytime another mom would ask what diapers she used, “I’d be like, ‘You
items.author: Erica Schwiegershausen
paragraphs: Kaylyn Bradford started using Millie Moon diapers when her oldest daughter was born three years ago. She liked how soft and fluffy they were, and they seemed to fit her two daughters well. Anytime another mom would ask what diapers she used, “I’d be like, ‘You have to get Millie Moon.’” That is, until a few months ago, when angry red bumps suddenly appeared all over her younger daughter’s private area. Bradford was used to the occasional diaper rash, but these looked like blisters. Their pediatrician was stumped; at first, she wondered whether Bradford’s daughter could have hand, foot, and mouth disease that spread to other parts of her body. The doctor told Bradford to mix a topical antibiotic with diaper cream and prescribed an antifungal medication, but nothing helped until Bradford switched diaper brands. A few days later, the rash was gone.

Bradford figured her daughter must just have especially sensitive skin. But then she started to see other moms on social media saying the exact same thing had happened to them after using Millie Moons. According to Consumer Reports, more than 700 similar incidents involving Millie Moon diapers have been submitted to the Consumer Product Safety Commission this year, at least three of which resulted in trips to the emergency room. Parents in Indiana told a local outlet that their 2-year-old developed a rash so severe after wearing a Millie Moon potty-training diaper that he needed skin grafts. In October, Millie Moon customers filed a class-action lawsuit against the brand’s parent company, Zuru Consumer Brands, alleging that the diapers have a defect that has resulted in “severe rashes, redness, blistering, skin-peeling, pleading, and burn-like injuries.” While Consumer Reports recently called on the brand to issue a recall, Millie Moon has stood behind its diapers, writing in a statement posted to Instagram that its products have passed extensive safety testing and that, as of last week, the brand has “not identified a product-related cause for the reported reactions.” Meanwhile, parents are furious. “I’m absolutely shocked,” says Bradford. “I’ve been using these diapers for so long. How could this happen?”

Millie Moon launched at Target in 2021, marketing itself as a more affordable alternative to luxury diaper brands like Coterie, HealthyBaby, and the Honest Company. Bradford says she was won over by the brand’s claims of using “clean” ingredients: “You hear all these stories about bleach and chlorine and stuff causing rashes.” Millie Moon emphasizes that its diapers are made from elemental-chlorine-free pulp and are “free from nasties such as lotions, latex, or fragrance.” In paid posts, doctors say that Millie Moon’s transparency about ingredients and OEKO-TEX certification make its diapers a good choice for babies with sensitive skin. Last year, the brand partnered with Ms. Rachel to launch a line of potty-training pull-ups designed “for ultimate comfort” and absorbency.

But the parents I spoke to said the rashes their kids developed after wearing Millie Moon diapers were unlike anything they’d ever seen. Danielle Vero, a mom of two in Staten Island, usually uses Coterie diapers for her daughter. But when her family was traveling for Labor Day, she grabbed a pack of Millie Moon diapers from Walmart. Almost immediately, her toddler developed a severe rash. “Her skin was bleeding. It was blistered and cracking,” she says. “It was as if, God forbid, she had a curling iron put up against her private area.” When it was time for a diaper change, her daughter screamed and refused to lie still. Vero racked her brain trying to figure out what could have caused such an extreme reaction. Did she eat something new? Could it be the water? “I never would have thought a diaper could possibly do this.”

Catie Giblin, a mom of three in Texas, recently switched her two younger kids to Millie Moon since they were cheaper than the Pampers and Honest Company diapers she’d used previously. They both immediately got a rash. Her daughter had open wounds that started scabbing, and she would cry whenever Giblin tried to wipe her. The fact that both her kids got rashes convinced her the diapers were to blame. “And as soon as we stopped using them, we had no issue.”

In its statement last week, Millie Moon said that it had conducted an independent investigation and “no harmful bacteria were detected in the samples tested, and the products met the requirements assessed under the US Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act.” But parents are convinced the diapers must have changed. Roya Alkafaji, a mother of a 2-year-old in Chicago, says her son used Millie Moon diapers for more than a year with no issue. A few months ago, when she opened a new box she’d bought at Target, she thought the diaper seemed different. “It felt more papery. It wasn’t as soft or luxurious-feeling. It felt rougher,” she says. She compared the new diaper side by side with an older version, and it also looked different: The new diaper had the print going all the way up past the waistband. And sure enough, as soon as her son started using the new diapers, he got a persistent red, itchy rash.

According to Millie Moon, the only recent change to its diapers is aesthetic. A company spokesperson told Consumer Reports that starting in February, the brand rolled out a new design where the pattern on the diaper now extends past the waistband, but said the brand hasn’t changed the materials, suppliers, or construction of its diapers. But Alkafaji isn’t buying it. “Shrinkflation is totally a thing. Things are getting more expensive, and companies are cutting corners,” she says. “Clearly, the diapers look different.”

Jody Levine, a pediatric dermatologist in New York, agrees that something in the diaper must have changed, though she’s skeptical of the theory that the new diapers contain some sort of dangerous chemical. If that were the case, she thinks there would be far more parents reporting issues. It’s true that baby diapers aren’t regulated by the FDA, and diaper brands generally aren’t required to disclose their ingredients. That may be changing: In recent years, New York, Illinois, and California have passed laws requiring manufacturers to list the ingredients in their diapers online or on their packaging. Hilary Swank — the chief innovation officer at the diaper brand HealthyBaby who lobbied for California to pass its diaper-transparency law — recently called the lack of regulation for diapers “horrific and frightening and not okay.” Levine, however, says she’s not convinced that most diapers actually contain toxic ingredients. “In general, you don’t usually hear about problems like this from diapers,” she says.

Many babies do have allergies to the dyes commonly used in diapers. But Levine’s best guess is that the new Millie Moon diapers are somehow less absorbent than the original version. With less absorbent diapers, the skin stays wet longer, and urine and stool can cause severe irritant dermatitis that can look like a burn. Levine says that’s something she sees often when a baby has diarrhea and isn’t changed frequently enough. When this happens, the irritation “isn’t coming from any chemicals in the diaper,” she says. “It’s really the chemicals in the urine and stool that are causing it.” And some babies are more susceptible than others — especially those with eczema or other damage to their skin barrier. “I think there should be a recall of this batch,” Levine said. “It is not normal to have 600 people complaining about severe, what they call burns from a diaper.”

But while Walmart has stopped selling the diapers online, Millie Moon hasn’t indicated any plans to pull its diapers from store shelves. In a statement to The Cut, a spokesperson for Millie Moon reiterated that the brand has found no issues with its diapers. “We stand fully behind the safety and quality of Millie Moon products, supported by an extensive body of independent testing and investigation.” The brand said that they will continue to cooperate with the Consumer Protection Safety Commission, but that to date, “skin irritation complaints represent fewer than .1 percent of Millie Moon diaper packs sold.”

But Vero thinks the fact that so many moms experienced the same rash can’t be a coincidence. She claims the brand deleted her comments from its Instagram and only replied to her emails after she mentioned that her husband was looking into taking legal action against the company. A response from the brand told her some babies were probably more sensitive than others and offered her a $50 refund. “I was like, ‘I don’t care about the money. You’re burning babies,’” she says. “I have absolutely zero trust in that company,” she added. “If it were the last diaper on earth, I’d put leaves on my child before I would use one again.”

items.title: My Disordered Eating Had Nothing to Do With My Weight
items.description: For years, I’d built a functional system around my gut. In my 20s, I’d been diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome with constipation, or IBS-C, which can cause everything from abdominal pain and bloating to infrequent bowel movements, hard stools, and straini
items.author: Johanna Ferreira
paragraphs: For years, I’d built a functional system around my gut. In my 20s, I’d been diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome with constipation, or IBS-C, which can cause everything from abdominal pain and bloating to infrequent bowel movements, hard stools, and straining. There’s also the persistent feeling that you haven’t fully emptied your bowels, or what I call “the groundhog” — when it feels like something is sitting right at your rectum but refuses to come out — the most uncomfortable and most mortifying feeling ever.

It was mostly manageable, though. I ate twice a day, lunch and dinner, and I had months when, depending on what was going on in my life and how stressed I was, IBS episodes were frequent. Whenever I had these episodes — in which I felt the worse symptoms all at once without any remedy other than going to bed and starting over the next day — I’d cut down on foods that were harder to digest. Rice, starchy carbs, legumes, dairy, and gluten were out, and I’d avoid coffee. I’d make sure to drink plenty of water, ginger, and green tea throughout the day and eat fiber; string beans, spinach, pineapple, and kiwi often did the trick. I also had stretches of time, even years, when I felt completely normal and could tolerate foods I couldn’t always, like dairy, pasta, or bread.
I thought it was all working well enough until about four years ago, when I experienced some bad food poisoning.

It was the first holiday season since coming out of the pandemic lockdown, so I had plans every week, often including eating out and drinking wine. In fact, I was eating out so much it was hard to even track what had caused the food poisoning. I just remember one week around the holidays waking up with a bloated belly filled with gas, an urge to use the bathroom, and not being able to actually go for days. By January, most days I was bloated, in pain, and struggling to pass a complete bowel movement no matter what I did or what I took.

Even four months later, at my younger sister’s wedding in Playa Mujeres, Mexico, I felt like death. I was burnt out, both from work and the chronic constipation, bloating, abdominal pain, and even rectal pain that had worsened since the presumed food poisoning.

I gritted my way through the ceremony, but at the reception I told myself, Fuck it, we’re going to eat, we’re going to dance, we’re going to enjoy the night. By midnight, I was in level-8 pain. Once the reception ended, I speed-walked to my resort room and sat in my outdoor hot tub for hours until the symptoms reduced enough for me to actually go to bed. The following morning, I called my gastroenterologist and made an emergency consultation for when I got back to New York. He scheduled me to get a colonoscopy and blood work done. But because everything came back okay, my doctor told me exactly what I had expected him to say: “I think it’s just your IBS.”

So I did all the “healthy” things I needed to do for my gut to get myself back to good enough: taking probiotics, digestive enzymes, colostrum, black seed oil, oregano oil, and more; working out regularly; doing red-light and hot-sauna sessions at my local recovery center; eating a mostly clean diet; and avoiding trigger foods as much as possible. At one point, I saw an acupuncturist and a Chinese-medicine doctor, who suggested I give up alcohol altogether. I haven’t had any since the wedding.

My doctor would tell me over and over again that my IBS had just gotten worse, but I knew there had to be something else going on. I got MRIs and blood work to rule out colitis, Crohn’s disease, or colon cancer, but I didn’t have the time or the energy to investigate further. I was too consumed with work and also convinced there was nothing a doctor could do to help me. In many ways, I kind of gave up. I gave up on the idea that I could heal this and just gave in to the idea that I was going to live a limited life that always revolved around my stomach and my bowel movements.

Instead, I learned to live with it. I would get up between 7 a.m. and 8 a.m. most days because getting up too early somehow affected my ability to pass a bowel movement in the morning, which often led to really bad bloating and gas buildup by 10 a.m. Any kind of commitment with anyone before noon was completely off the table, and when I traveled for work, I’d beg for a later flight. More than once I had to go into graphic detail in order to prove I wasn’t just trying to be high maintenance or lazy. If my job hadn’t been remote, I don’t know if I would’ve made it through the nearly five years I did.

Eating would inevitably result in immediate bloating that was often accompanied by abdominal pain, so I avoided it if I had to. It didn’t matter what plans I had that night, whether it was a concert, a media event, an in-person interview with a celebrity, a panel I was moderating or speaking on, a red-carpet event, or even just regular dinner plans with a friend; if I had evening plans, I’d fast for most of the day. Because the only way to avoid canceling was to fast. I avoided daytime plans; evenings are easier because I’m rarely out all night. I can stay for two or three hours, then I make my Irish exit, go home, and nurse my symptoms in private.

I’d have water with electrolytes and bone broth throughout the day so I wouldn’t pass out, waiting until either after the event to eat or, if I had dinner plans, depending on how I felt, sometimes I would take an edible or hit my THC/CBD vape beforehand to avoid nausea, trigger an appetite, and actually be able to digest the meal. And if I didn’t feel great afterward, I often knocked myself out before bed with an edible, too.

I had so much anxiety around making plans with people — whether food is involved or not — because eventually, I still have to eat. I almost never ate without fear or calculation. My anxiety worsened when I was around other people, because at home, at least, I’m the only one who witnesses what happens when my symptoms flare.

Then, this past January, I lost my job as content director for the Latine vertical of a women’s-interest digital-media site where I worked for almost five years. Before being laid off, I’d been in fight-or-flight mode. Not only did I run my vertical as a one-woman team while managing a pool of regular freelance writers, but I also felt an even bigger responsibility to thrive because my work felt so personal. I was representing an entire community and demographic at a time when more and more media sites were getting rid of identity verticals and no longer prioritizing diverse audiences. And being the ambitious perfectionist that I was, the goals set for me at work weren’t enough. I wanted my vertical to attract sponsors and advertisers. I wanted the stories to go viral. I wanted to publish celebrity exclusives every month. I wanted to be on top of the trends. I wanted it to be something that the community and the industry respected. So I never slowed down. I attended numerous events a week. I blocked time on Fridays for external calls with publicists and my contributing writers. I spent much of my after-hours researching ideas, brainstorming, networking, and, in some cases, even writing. I did this all while pushing past my symptoms.

Every year, I compromised more. I went from being a supercautious eater to becoming very comfortable going hours without eating and revolving my entire schedule around my bowels. I never thought I needed to eat less to be thinner; I’ve always been a relatively thin person. But I did believe I needed to eat less to function. There were periods when I simply wasn’t eating enough, leaving me exhausted, weak, physically depleted, and unable to concentrate. So many times, I’d tell myself that when things felt more secure at work, I’d make time to really investigate, find a homeopathic doctor, and figure this out. But things never felt more secure.

My diet became so limited that the only people I was truly honest about it with were my mom and my sister. Outside of meat protein and very few vegetables like potatoes, carrots, cooked greens, and, on good days, white rice, there were very few foods that didn’t upset my stomach. Most of my friends had no idea that on some days or even weeks I was eating only one meal a day, usually dinner. I’ve been called a hypochondriac and accused of being obsessed with my health. I’ve had women — especially women who struggle with weight-loss or body-image issues — tell me they were triggered by my lack of eating or by me eating significantly less than them at restaurants or for skipping the bread basket, assuming I was dieting. The hardest part of it all was how my symptoms often prevented me from being really present even at special moments like my sister’s wedding and my niece’s first birthday.

I smoked so much weed at my niece’s birthday party so that I could eat with everyone without immediately experiencing abdominal pain. I was so focused on being able to enjoy the meal that I wasn’t even affected by the criticism I received from my younger brother, who was furious that I was smoking outside where my niece and nephews could see me. For years, no one believed that the entire reason cannabis had even become part of my lifestyle was because it allowed me to eat, digest, and manage my pain.

When my layoff happened, my symptoms soon got worse. Even fasting stopped working. I would suddenly wake up bloated and stay that way all day, even if I didn’t eat. Cannabis no longer helped, either. It dawned on me that everything I’d been doing in order to function and have a life was no longer going to cut it.

Even though I hadn’t had any luck with gastroenterologists, I called one of my close guy friends in tears one evening and asked for his doctor’s info. He has ulcerative colitis and had found tremendous relief after he started seeing his doctor. At my initial appointment, Dr. Matthew McNeill said it was very likely that I had SIBO, or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. He described it as an overgrowth of intestinal or pathogenic bacteria in the small intestine that results in gas production, stomach distension, bloating, and irregular bowel movements in the form of diarrhea or constipation. Patients with SIBO often go long periods of time undiagnosed, he explained, in some cases even years, because the symptoms are often mistaken for IBS — in my case, worsened IBS — or other common digestive disorders.

The most common presenting symptom in SIBO is bloating right after eating. Dr. McNeill explains that patients, both male and female, often describe themselves as feeling as if they are pregnant after eating. That’s how significant the bloating and stomach distension is.

So many patients with SIBO go undiagnosed, it turns out, because most doctors don’t even mention it, and it requires a very specific breath test. The SIBO test measures sequential levels of various gases, specifically hydrogen, hydrogen sulfide, and methane. They measure them over time and compare them to a baseline after you ingest a carbohydrate load. After weeks of research and barely being able to eat in May, I scheduled an appointment with Dr. McNeill in June and shared my suspicion that what I’d believed for years was worsening IBS might be SIBO. Dr. McNeill said that, based on symptoms alone, it was very likely.

But because there are no FDA-approved treatment options and many insurance plans refuse to cover dedicated SIBO testing, my only option was to pay out of pocket, which he warned could cost hundreds of dollars. As an underemployed freelancer, that wasn’t an option for me.

He explained that because SIBO testing can be expensive and difficult to access, gastroenterologists sometimes treat patients for SIBO without dedicated testing, particularly when they present with IBS-like symptoms. He ordered blood work, a stool test, along with other tests to rule out other conditions; I had also undergone a CT scan during an emergency-room visit a few weeks earlier, which I shared with him. Eventually, Dr. McNeill prescribed me two antibiotics commonly used to treat SIBO: Xifaxan (rifaximin) and neomycin.

After my first 14-day round of antibiotics in July, which I took while following a low-FODMAP diet for about six weeks, my symptoms improved significantly, signaling that the treatment was working. Dr. McNeill warned me, however, that SIBO has a high recurrence rate and that I would likely need another round of antibiotics by the fall. I felt almost healed in August — until I learned that the freelance contract that had been essentially paying my rent was ending and that my landlord didn’t want to renew my lease despite my having paid every month for five years, citing “personal reasons.”

The stress quickly took a toll on my nervous system and appetite. By mid-September, my symptoms had returned; I was barely eating — often just one meal a day — and I was looking increasingly frail again. You could see it in my face. I was losing so much weight that my cheekbones became more pronounced, and, for the first time, I developed hollow eyes, something I’d made it to 40 without ever having to worry about. “The presence of SIBO in and of itself doesn’t likely affect the appetite, but the symptoms associated with SIBO might,” Dr. McNeill said. “If someone feels bloating or discomfort after eating, they may be less likely to eat certain foods, less likely to eat large quantities of food, and could theoretically have decreased appetite across the board.” There is scientific research that shows the connection between psychological stress, the gut-brain axis, the vagus nerve, intestinal motility, and digestive symptoms associated with SIBO. The body’s response to stress can inhibit intestinal movement, and the vagus nerve plays a role in gut-brain signaling.

Eventually, through talking with a holistic coach and following gut experts and homeopathic doctors on TikTok, I learned that restricting my food intake so severely, and going hours without eating, may have compounded my GI issues — potentially contributing to malnutrition, functional impairment, and even worsening my constipation by leaving me without enough food to produce a bowel movement. The muscles and nerves that move food and waste through the digestive tract don’t work as efficiently as they should when there isn’t consistently enough to process, making it harder to clear food and bacteria from the small intestine and move stool through the large intestine toward the rectum.

When you struggle with motility, you can experience everything from prolonged fullness after eating, bloating, and abdominal discomfort to constipation, infrequent bowel movements, hard stools, straining, incomplete evacuation, and that groundhog feeling. Looking back, I think the combination of food poisoning and already struggling with motility issues is likely how I developed it. The hardest part about having SIBO is being able to actually eat enough. Some days I feel too full from lunch for the rest of the day, with no desire or room to eat again. I don’t count my protein or fiber intake like most people because I’m still in survival mode here, and having two nutritious meals a day every single day so far hasn’t been possible. This is what a lot of my undereating and disordered eating is triggered by.

“Any condition that leads to uncomfortable symptoms following eating can affect one’s relationship with eating and specific foods,” Dr. McNeill told me. “While this doesn’t universally lead to pathological disordered eating, it certainly can contribute to a degree of disordered eating that may cause weight loss or become clinically significant.”

In September, I did another 14-day course of neomycin and Xifaxan, and I’m just now finally seeing the light at the end of the tunnel. I still don’t feel normal. I’m still struggling with bloating, but instead of it being every day after every single meal, it’s just some days now and some meals. I’ve also noticed I have to go to sleep on a relatively empty stomach or I wake up feeling awful, so dinner these days has been more like a snack and I have to eat it at least three hours before bed.

Sometimes it’s hard to imagine a life in which I don’t have to think about any of this shit — no pun intended. A life that doesn’t revolve around my stomach and bowel movements. A life where I can wake up whenever I want, get on a plane without worrying about developing a sour stomach, and simply enjoy a meal without dreading the painful consequences that might follow. I honestly don’t know what that feels like anymore. It’s been close to five years of having to completely revolve my habits and way of life around eating, digestion, and my morning bowel movements. I hardly remember how my body physically felt before all this. But I yearn for that life, and I’m hopeful that it’s coming soon.

And as long and consuming as healing may be, my doctor and everyone I know who have dealt with SIBO have assured me that with treatment, patience, and time, I can get there. When I finally do, I know exactly how I’ll celebrate: with one of my favorite foods that I haven’t been able to fully enjoy in years — a nice, greasy New York slice of pizza.

items.title: Travis Scott Reveals Limited-Edition Nike Air Force 1 Low "GTA 6"
items.description: Travis Scott has revealed a limited-edition Nike Air Force 1 Low celebrating 'Grand Theft Auto 6' and Rockstar Games
items.author: Joyce Li
paragraphs: Travis Scott has revealed a limited-edition Nike Air Force 1 Low celebrating 'Grand Theft Auto 6' and Rockstar Games
The design features black patent leather camo ripstop panels pink accents and a six-star Wanted level graphic
While the revealed pair serves as a Friends and Family exclusive additional colorways arrive November 19 for $130 USD

Grammy-nominated artist Travis Scott has revealed a limited-edition Nike Air Force 1 Low “GTA 6”, celebrating the iconic gaming franchise in collaboration with Rockstar Games. The Houston rapper debuted the custom GTA 6-inspired sneaker himself on his Instagram, announcing plans to gift pairs directly to longtime supporters, gaming fan pages, and close friends rather than staging a public retail drop.

Constructed with a premium mixed-material upper, the sneaker features sleek black patent leather complemented by camouflage ripstop nylon along the quarter panels and vibrant pink overlays. Scott’s signature reverse Swoosh is executed in oversized white tumbled leather, while the traditional “AIR” embossed lettering on the lateral midsole is swapped for custom “GTA” text. Medially, six bright pink stars wrap around the midsole in homage to Grand Theft Auto’s maximum Wanted level, mirrored by an identical six-star graphic embedded into the rubber outsole.

Emphasizing its limited nature, Scott instructed dedicated fans to message him their locations directly for an opportunity to receive pairs. While this Friends and Family colorway will not see a traditional retail rollout, additional colorways from the broader collaborative collection are slated to hit shelves in the coming weeks.
While this limited-edition Friends and Family iteration remains exclusive, other Travis Scott x Nike Air Force 1 “GTA 6” colorways are scheduled to release on November 19, 2026, for $130 USD.

items.title: The 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Custom In-Game Cars Have Come to Life
items.description: West Coast Customs helped recreate the in-game custom cars of 'Grand Theft Auto VI'
items.author: Eddie Eng
paragraphs: West Coast Customs helped recreate the in-game custom cars of 'Grand Theft Auto VI'
Each car comes with its own backstory, including stats, figures and details
'Grand Theft Auto VI' finally arrives on November 19
Grand Theft Auto VI is finally coming, and one of the best, most detailed components of the game is coming to life. Literally.

The iconic West Coast Customs of Los Angeles was brought in to recreate some of the most recognizable in-game cars with real life counterparts. The detail that went into replicating the replicas must have been painstaking, as we even had a bit of difficulty differentiating the in-game shots (above) from the real life photos (below).

And what’s even better is that each car is baked with stats and IRL figures, bridging their digital and real-life connections even stronger. Ever wonder what the engine was under the Coquette? Or how much horsepower the Tempesta cop car has? Check out the breakdown of each car and judge for yourself how close each car got to its in-game version.

The Grotti Cheetah is quintessentially Miami. The classic mid-engined ’90s supercar is clean, with Italian-styled lines broken only by intakes feeding a 4.9L naturally-aspirated V8. West Coast Customs lowered it on track-ready tires, gave it a “Vice City fade” paint job, and trimmed the cabin with custom-stitched Italian leather.

The Buccaneer is a fully restored 1960s lowrider with a 7.5L V8, paired with hits of mahogany and gold trim throughout. The candy apple green paint, laid down in large metallic flake, carries bespoke airbrushing and pinstripes for the ultimate custom look. Air-ride suspension and gold multi-spoke rims sit under a cream ragtop and a leather interior with zebra-print inlays, because Vice City.

Perhaps the wildest build in this list, the Emerus is a track-ready thoroughbred, with aero bodywork and fighter jet-style vents built around a twin-turbo 4.0L V8. It’s painted candy orange with an even louder orange interior to match. One of the largest aero wings on the market, plus custom suspension and racing tires, keeps it planted when you’re five-star and on the run.

The icon and probably most recognizable. The mid-engined Coquette packs a 6.2L naturally aspirated V8 we all secretly know and love. Its “Yeti Camo” livery for the game in flamingo pink and vibrant purple definitely stands out in your garage. It also gets custom rims, lowered suspension and a fully custom leather interior.

The Manana is a 1970s classic with a 7.7L V8, stripped down and rebuilt with bold, straight panels for a fresh take on donk. It’s coated in large-flake Vice City blue paint with gold bumpers and trim. A sky-high custom suspension sits on oversized gold-and-chrome rims, and the matching blue leather cabin is edged in gold for added flair.

The aggressive, mid-engined Invetero Tempesta runs a flame-spitting 4.0L naturally aspirated V10. It wears a Vice Beach Police Department livery over lowered suspension and custom rims, because even one time deserve some style. Inside, the cockpit takes after a fighter jet, packed with custom leather, buttons and cutting edge police tech. All we have to say is: good luck.
Grand Theft Auto VI arrives on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S on November 19.

items.title: Анна Громова: Между дисциплиной и свободой: как меняется подход к детскому балетному образованию
items.description: В балете результат виден на сцене: движение кажется легким, хотя за ним стоят годы повторений. У частной балетной школы похожая логика. За выступлением учеников остаются невидимыми методика, организация занятий, работа с родителями и ежедневные решения руковод
items.author: Анна Громова
paragraphs: В балете результат виден на сцене: движение кажется легким, хотя за ним стоят годы повторений. У частной балетной школы похожая логика. За выступлением учеников остаются невидимыми методика, организация занятий, работа с родителями и ежедневные решения руководителя. Мне было интересно поговорить с человеком, который знает обе стороны — творческую и предпринимательскую.
Моя собеседница — Лилит Барсегян, педагог-хореограф, основательница детской школы балета «Жемчужина» в Анапе.

Она училась в Ереванском государственном театре танца и музыки, Ереванской государственной консерватории имени Комитаса и Челябинском государственном институте культуры. В 2023 году получила Гран-при международного конкурса педагогического мастерства «Признание — 2023» в номинации «Лучший педагог — 2023». Мы поговорили о том, как вырастает собственная школа, что можно и нельзя стандартизировать в обучении и почему для нее успех ученика важнее внешней эффектности.
Про выбор профессии и первые управленческие решения
Лилит, вы говорите, что впервые задумались о балете в пять лет. Что осталось от того детского впечатления сейчас, когда вы уже руководите собственной школой?

Тогда я впервые оказалась в театре и почувствовала, что хочу связать жизнь с танцем. Конечно, в пять лет невозможно представить себе все сложности профессии. Позже были учеба, репетиции, работа над техникой. Но то ощущение интереса и радости от балета осталось. Наверное, поэтому для меня так важно, чтобы дети приходили на занятия не только ради результата, но и потому, что им действительно нравится танцевать.
Ваш первый коллектив появился в 2011 году. В какой момент вы поняли, что умеете не только преподавать, но и организовывать работу других людей?

Меня пригласили работать в сельскую школу в районе Анапы, и там я создала коллектив «Ритмы планеты». Это был очень важный опыт. Недостаточно придумать постановку: нужно выстроить занятия, распределить время, поддерживать интерес детей и отвечать за общий результат. Я стала смотреть на работу шире отдельного урока. Именно тогда начала формироваться моя самостоятельность как руководителя.
Позже вы работали в школе сети Lil Ballerine. Что этот этап изменил в вашем представлении о балетном образовании?

В 2022 году я пришла в Lil Ballerine и получила возможность работать с коллективом, который участвовал в конкурсах и фестивалях. Со временем я стала гораздо отчетливее понимать, какие педагогические решения работают, как важно наблюдать за развитием ребенка в динамике и почему одних красивых постановок недостаточно. Появилось желание создать школу, в которой подход к обучению будет отражать именно мои принципы.
Про школу, которую нельзя строить на страхе
Почему вы назвали собственную школу «Жемчужина»?

Для меня это образ ребенка, у которого уже есть индивидуальность и способности. Задача педагога — заметить их и создать условия для развития. Я не хотела строить школу вокруг жесткого сравнения учеников друг с другом. Балет требует дисциплины, но дисциплина не равна давлению. Мне хотелось, чтобы серьезная подготовка сочеталась с уважительным отношением к детям.
Часто родители представляют классический балет как строгую систему с жестким отбором. Вы пытаетесь изменить это восприятие?

Я не считаю, что классическую базу нужно упрощать до обычной разминки. У балета есть техника, последовательность и требования к качеству движений. Но можно объяснять ошибки без унижения, учитывать возраст и физическую готовность, давать ребенку время освоить элемент. Моя задача — сохранить содержание балетного образования и сделать сам процесс более бережным.
Что отличает вашу методику от обычных занятий танцами?

Урок имеет четкую структуру: сначала мягкий разогрев и партерная гимнастика, затем работа у станка, упражнения на середине зала и танцевальные комбинации. Отдельная часть — музыкальность. Я преподаю не только классический балет и индивидуальную хореографию, но и сольфеджио. Мне важно, чтобы ученик понимал, как устроено движение, знал терминологию и слышал музыку, а не просто повторял за педагогом.
Как вы понимаете, что ребенок готов двигаться дальше по программе?

Не по дате рождения. Я смотрю, насколько устойчиво освоены базовые навыки: координация, осанка, баланс, музыкальность. Для одного ученика важным достижением станет сложная комбинация, для другого — уверенность в простом движении, которое раньше не получалось. Если усложнять программу слишком рано, можно потерять мотивацию. Поэтому переход на новый уровень должен опираться на реальную готовность.
Про творческий бизнес и качество обучения
Вы открыли школу в 2024 году. Что оказалось самым неожиданным в роли предпринимателя?

Когда ты педагог, твоя основная ответственность — ученики и качество уроков. Когда создаешь собственную школу, к этому добавляются организация процесса, развитие программ и решения, от которых зависит устойчивость проекта. Оказалось, что балетная дисциплина помогает и здесь: нужно уметь долго держать внимание на цели и последовательно работать с деталями. Но управлению все равно приходится учиться отдельно.
Можно ли масштабировать школу, если ее сильная сторона — ваш личный подход к детям?

Это, пожалуй, один из главных вопросов для творческого бизнеса. Сейчас я сама веду занятия, поэтому хорошо вижу успехи и трудности учеников. Но для развития школы нужно формулировать принципы так, чтобы они были понятны не только мне: структура урока, критерии прогресса, бережная обратная связь. Масштабирование имеет смысл лишь тогда, когда качество обучения остается на первом месте.
Вы развиваете онлайн-формат. Какая часть балетного образования, на ваш взгляд, может существовать за пределами зала?

Онлайн дает возможность делиться знаниями с теми, кто находится в другом городе или стране. Но я не считаю, что дистанционный формат во всем заменяет очное обучение, особенно когда речь идет о постановке техники и контроле нагрузки. Важно понимать, какие задачи можно решать дистанционно, а где необходима непосредственная работа педагога с учеником. Для меня развитие направления — это прежде всего расширение доступа к обучению, а не отказ от его качества.
В 2025 году вы получили документ о предоставлении лицензии на образовательную деятельность. Почему это было важно для школы?

Я хотела, чтобы школа развивалась именно как образовательный проект, а не только как место, где готовят номера к выступлениям. Поэтому оформление лицензии стало важным организационным этапом. Для меня это часть ответственности руководителя: выстраивать работу последовательно и серьезно относиться к тому, что получает ученик.
Про признание, учеников и международный опыт
Какие награды вы считаете наиболее показательными для своей работы?

Мне особенно значим Гран-при конкурса педагогического мастерства «Признание — 2023», потому что это оценка именно педагогической деятельности. Для «Жемчужины» важны достижения учеников: в 2025 году школа получила диплом лауреата I степени на Sochi Art Start, а на конкурсе «Звездный шаг» — специальный диплом за сохранение традиций классического танца. Для меня важно не количество дипломов, а то, что за выступлениями стоит содержательная подготовка.
Есть ли ученик, чья история особенно ясно показывает, ради чего вы работаете?

Я часто вспоминаю Яна Горбунова. Он пришел ко мне в класс в девять лет и прошел большой путь подготовки. Сейчас Ян обучается в Московской государственной академии хореографии. Я горжусь тем, что смогла участвовать в его становлении. Когда ученик продолжает профессиональное образование, понимаешь, что годы совместной работы имели значение.
У вас есть и международный преподавательский опыт. Что дает работа с детьми в другой культурной среде?

Мне интересно видеть, как дети воспринимают музыку и движение в разных условиях. В 2026 году я работала преподавателем музыки и балета в Umka School в Дананге, во Вьетнаме. Такая работа еще раз показывает, насколько важны ясные объяснения, доброжелательная атмосфера и внимание к индивидуальным особенностям. Эти принципы понятны в любой стране.
Про будущее творческого образования
Каким вы хотели бы видеть свой проект через несколько лет?

Я хочу продолжать развивать «Жемчужину» и онлайн-направление, сохраняя индивидуальный подход. Для меня важно, чтобы школа оставалась местом серьезной работы, но без страха перед ошибками. Не каждый ребенок станет профессиональным артистом, и это нормально. Если занятия помогут ему лучше чувствовать музыку, владеть телом и увереннее выражать себя, значит, мы уже сделали многое.

items.title: Is Trump Trying to Save the Oval Office From Himself?
items.description: Since Tuesday’s catastrophic GOP midterms losses, Donald Trump has been soothing himself with his favorite hobby: turning Washington, D.C., into a gaudy shrine to himself. Soon, he may not even have that: Democrats are already talking about ways Congress might
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Since Tuesday’s catastrophic GOP midterms losses, Donald Trump has been soothing himself with his favorite hobby: turning Washington, D.C., into a gaudy shrine to himself. Soon, he may not even have that: Democrats are already talking about ways Congress might thwart his White House ballroom project, and on Thursday a judge blocked construction on Trump’s arch near Arlington National Cemetery as legal challenges make their way through the courts.

So it makes sense, on an emotional level, that Trump is trying to protect the Oval Office, as it’s the one renovation project he has near-total control over. But in the realm of logic, nothing about his proclamation designating the Oval Office and adjacent Cabinet room as national monuments makes a lick of sense.

The proclamation itself really has no legal force. As the AP noted, “Trump himself has reversed national monument designations made by his predecessors.” Trump said he would ask Congress to ratify the proclamation. But it’s unclear why Congress would rush to adopt the president’s wording when he’s repeatedly refused to obtain their authorization for his various D.C. construction projects.
Talking to reporters on Thursday afternoon, Trump said the goal of his first post-midterms executive action was to make these spaces “a landmark for the ages.”

“It won’t be able to be taken down, destroyed, touched, or anything else,” Trump said. “It’s a federal landmark. And when completed, and when we get the documentation fully done, legally binding, it’ll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space.”

All the proclamation actually does is “proclaim the Oval Office as the Oval Office National Monument.” The document acknowledges that the entire White House is already “recognized as a National Historic Landmark,” but it says the Oval Office still “merits specific recognition” as a “discrete historic structure of national significance.”

You might assume Trump is trying to preserve all the gold junk he’s put up in the Oval Office, some of which he superglued with his own two hands. However, it specifically states that future president can redecorate as they please:

Nothing in this proclamation shall be construed to restrict the President’s authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument’s historic structure or architectural character.

The proclamation directs the Interior secretary to form a management plan that “prioritizes the preservation of the monument’s structural and significant architectural features,” and ensures that there’s a thorough review before any action that would “substantially alter or demolish” the rooms.
Basically, the goal is to make sure no one tears down the Oval Office. Trump gave reporters the example of a future president saying “Let’s make it square,” adding, per the Daily Beast:

I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come in and take it down and try and do something with it, because every once in a while they’ll look and they’ll say, “Oh, maybe what we’ll do is we’ll put some glass that’s a little bit better or something.” And I’d say, “No, you’re not going to do anything.” We’re going to leave this as it is.

The only person you could imagine doing such a thing is Donald Trump himself. If the president really wants to preserve the Oval Office, he’d be better off putting a Post-it on his bathroom mirror that says, “Do not destroy more parts of the White House today.”

items.title: The Midterm Wave Was Hate-Powered
items.description: It’s a political truism that midterm elections are referenda on the party controlling the White House, and thus Donald Trump’s dreadful job-approval ratings are the simplest explanation for the huge Democratic gains posted on November 3. But in what that means
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: It’s a political truism that midterm elections are referenda on the party controlling the White House, and thus Donald Trump’s dreadful job-approval ratings are the simplest explanation for the huge Democratic gains posted on November 3. But in what that means for future elections, it’s important to understand that voters who reject a president’s party in the midterms won’t necessarily support the opposition party in future elections. In an era with a serious substratum of unhappiness with politics and government generally and a mistrust of any and all institutions, party affiliation can be a slippery thing. And thus many political observers have focused on voters who dislike both major political parties as important to the competition between them.

More often than not, these so-called double haters have been relatively friendly to Trump, perhaps because he has always posed as an anti-Establishment “disrupter” or simply because he’s a world-class hater himself. In 2016, one of the keys of his upset win over Hillary Clinton was that he carried the 18 percent of voters who had unfavorable views of both candidates by a robust 17 percent margin. It was significant in 2020 that the number of “double haters” dropped all the way to 3 percent of the electorate, though Trump still won them by 17 percent. In 2024, voters who didn’t like either Trump or Harris represented 8 percent of the electorate, and Trump won them by a smashing 20 percent. Double haters split evenly in the 2018 midterms, but Republicans won this 11 percent of the electorate by 17 percent in 2022.

So it’s definitely worth noting that in 2026, according to the latest exit-poll data, double haters bounced back up to 15 percent of the electorate and Democrats carried them by 28 percent (61 percent to 33 percent). Will these voters stick with Democrats in 2028? We obviously don’t know yet, but there’s no reason to assume they will. Presidential elections are typically comparative by nature instead of a referendum on the people running the country. Despite a Democratic skew in the 2026 electorate (those who previously voted in 2024 tilted to Kamala Harris by 5 percent, though some may be misremembering or misrepresenting their votes), the Democratic Party’s favorability rating was 47 percent positive and 52 percent negative. Only 16 percent of 2026 voters were “strongly favorable” toward the Democratic Party, while 35 percent were “strongly unfavorable.” Democrats rightly celebrating their wave election shouldn’t start singing “Happy Days Are Here Again” just yet. They may control Congress in 2027 but don’t command a reliable majority in public opinion or any positive mandate.

Donald Trump will not be on the ballot in 2028, and between now and then Democrats need to convince double haters to hate them less than Republicans in a comparative context, including one in which Democrats will be entirely in control of Congress. This challenge may be intensified by a wide-open 2028 Democratic presidential-nominating contest in which candidates may be focused more on appealing to reliable party-primary participants rather than the swing voters they will need in November. If conditions in the country worsen and such emerging existential issues as AI-related job loss explode into prominence, it’s even possible that long-suppressed support for minor parties, old or new, could finally threaten the two-party duopoly or at least affect the balance of power between Democrats and Republicans. So leaders and activists in both parties need to get over the midterms quickly and focus on the sales pitches they have to develop to win over voters who aren’t very fond of any of them.

items.title: The 13 Biggest Losers of the 2026 Midterms, Ranked
items.description: The 2026 midterms may have been a stunning string of victories for the Democratic Party, but it’s important that we also commemorate all the failures. Here’s a baker’s dozen, ranked in reverse order of loserhood:
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: The 2026 midterms may have been a stunning string of victories for the Democratic Party, but it’s important that we also commemorate all the failures. Here’s a baker’s dozen, ranked in reverse order of loserhood:
The Schumer-Jeffries Haters

White-hot progressive (or insurgent) rage at the two New Yorkers who head the minority caucuses in Congress was a regular feature of political life in the past two years of Democratic discontent. For years, Schumer has been widely mocked as an inept party messenger and strategist, and who can forget the excited progressives on New York’s primary night in June chanting “You’re Next!” when Hakeem Jeffries appeared on their television screens? Schumer’s getting pretty long in the tooth, and Jeffries may indeed be vulnerable to a primary challenge in his own district. But neither is going to be “purged” from a leadership post following this massive win. It’s probably already dawning on those hoping the democratic socialist “bloc” would form a powerful faction in the House that Jeffries’s majority will dwarf their numbers and also include a ton of new centrists representing districts Trump carried in 2024.

One very happy democratic socialist, though, is Nithya Raman, who is now projected to become the next mayor of America’s second-largest city, Los Angeles. But that means a very big 2026 loser is incumbent Democratic mayor Karen Bass, whose fortunes dropped rapidly when the outbreak of catastrophic wildfires in her city caught her on an overseas junket to Ghana. Raman was a Bass ally on the city council whose candidacy surprised, and then eventually removed, the mayor. More than likely, this is the end of a storied Bass career that flourished in the California legislature and in Congress before she came home to run her city.

At this point, Stevens still professes to be a Democrat despite talk of booting her out of the House Caucus during her final weeks in Congress. But her shocking last-minute endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers against the candidate who defeated her in Michigan’s August Senate primary, Abdul El-Sayed, turned out to be, among other things, a very bad bet. El-Sayed won by 7 percent, more than his lead in some preelection polls, and it’s possible Stevens’s effort to sabotage him actually increased his votes. In any event, her treacherous behavior and the erratic character it exposed have left her with a lot fewer friends and virtually no admirers.
Conservative Judicial Activists

A lot of people who otherwise aren’t big fans of Donald Trump have nonetheless supported him because of his success in stacking the federal judiciary–and most crucially the U.S. Supreme Court–with constitutional “originalists” and other products of the conservative legal movement. His power to do so (at least without lots of compromises with Democrats) ended with the destruction of the GOP’s Senate Majority. And the stubborn refusal of Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas to retire and give Republicans a chance to choose younger successors will now create a significant drought of SCOTUS appointments, particularly since the size of Democratic Senate gains makes it unlikely that Republicans will retake the chamber in 2028. Too bad Alito ruled out a 2026 retirement that might have created the brief opportunity to confirm a Trump appointment during the upcoming lame-duck session.
Republican Congressional Leaders

If Schumer and Jeffries are now secure, for a while, in their leadership posts, their GOP counterparts are toast. Perhaps in reality, Republicans can blame Trump almost entirely for the midterm debacle, but (a) John Thune and especially Mike Johnson did little to interfere with his agenda and his domination of GOP messaging and (b) culpability aside, you don’t get to continue as leaders if you lose that precious gavel and do so by such an enormous margin. It’s unclear to whom House and Senate Republicans will turn given their shared responsibility for toadying to Trump and pursuing a failed message. But in any event, they’re probably stuck with the current leaders during the very significant lame-duck session that will begin next week. That can’t be great for party morale.

The self-styled Secretary of War was already slated to be an impeachment target during the soon-to-convene lame-duck session thanks to a resolution from outgoing anti-Trump Republican Thomas Massie. More generally, Hegseth is by far the most convenient target for congressional Democrats, whose leaders will almost certainly try to create alternatives to a third impeachment of Trump himself. Aside from his regularly obnoxious conduct and his over-the-top Christian nationalist worldview, he’s very much the symbol of an unpopular Iran War that Democrats want to exploit if they cannot end it. And even if Hegseth cannot be convicted by the Senate, the heat could convince the president to sack him, as some reports indicate he is already thinking about doing.

One of the most shocking developments of the midterms was the U.S. Senate victory of Democrat Annie Andrews in the conservative bastion of South Carolina, flipping a seat Lindsey Graham and Strom Thurmond had held for 68 years. While the national Democratic wave and Trump’s constant interventions in South Carolina elections had something to do with this GOP catastrophe, some of the blame must be assigned to Lindsey’s little sister, appointed and then defeated senator Darline Graham. It was understandable that she received a courtesy appointment to serve out the final months of her brother’s term after his sudden death in July. But she then insisted on running for a full term despite limited political experience and no known views on major issues (especially the foreign-policy issues on which Lindsey was most focused). This definitely annoyed the horde of Palmetto State Republican pols who would have done anything to occupy a precious Senate seat, and some even openly slow-walked any support for Darline. In the end, she inherited both her brother’s baggage (he never fully earned the trust of South Carolina conservatives) and Trump’s, and added some of her own. In a terrible year for her party, she sank to the occasion.

This health-care billionaire came out of nowhere to push aside Trump’s designated candidate for governor of Georgia and then outspent Democratic candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms by an enormous margin, yet ultimately led his party to an ass-kicking unlike anything outside of Texas. Outgoing two-term Republican governor Brian Kemp probably remains the most popular politician in his state, but Jackson and his ticket mates squandered all that political capital, losing every single statewide office, not even coming close to threatening Senator Jon Ossoff, and astonishingly losing control of the statehouse in the bargain. It was by far the worst election year for the Georgia GOP since 1998, and defeated Republicans will long be haunted in their dreams by Jackson’s incredibly redundant autobiographical ads.

The hypereccentric and intensely reactionary trillionaire was doubly involved in the 2026 midterms. His wildly destructive DOGE regime tainted Trump’s second term indelibly, right off the bat. And then having feuded with and reconciled with the president, Musk made a vast and unprecedented personal investment in the GOP midterm campaign. He spent an estimated $474 million on GOP races and super-PACs — close to half of it in Texas alone, mostly in an effort to rescue Senate candidate Ken Paxton. His ROI was next to nothing, and indeed, he might have personally proved for all time that money cannot buy an election without a lot of help from smart politicians and, well, objective reality.

The giant money sink and scandal magnet named Ken Paxton may deserve his own spot on this list, but I dunno, the many losers among Texas Republicans are all worthy recipients of a raspberry. Governor Greg Abbott typified the arrogance and extremism of the Texas GOP during his 12 years in office. Unlike Paxton, he didn’t have to wage a wildly expensive primary fight this year. And for all of Gina Hinojosa’s many merits, she didn’t have James Talarico’s national buzz and incredible fundraising chops. Yet Abbott lost to her by over 700,000 votes and took the entire statewide Republican ticket, and his party’s control of the statehouse, down with him. Their humiliation was richly earned over a long, long time.
The White House Political Team

Probably no one group of Americans in politics has received more undeserved credit for brilliance than Donald Trump’s White House political team. To be sure, Susie Wiles and Chris LaCivita, the co-chairs of Trump’s 2024 comeback campaign, as well as James Blair, that campaign’s political director, did a fine job of plucking the ripe fruit of the Biden administration’s many problems and guiding the 45th president through to his inauguration. On the most superficial level, Trump 2.0 was less chaotic under their management than Trump 1.0. But in many respects, that just meant Trump was free to pursue his own worst instincts and his political team did little if anything to restrain him. Now, in the wake of the midterm disaster, the long knives are out for these erstwhile geniuses, as Jake Lahut reported.

In assessing J.D. Vance’s political chops in view of what just happened, it’s important to remember that he ran for office only once before catching a ride on Trump’s 2024 coattails and by most accounts underperformed in his own 2022 Ohio Senate campaign. As vice-president, he has tried to carry out the traditional attack-dog chores of a veep but has been consistently outclassed by his boss in the hard work of lying and smearing opponents, while showing himself to be an awkward communicator who is dangerously too online for real-world politics. Now, his political shortcomings have been graphically illustrated by the GOP’s poor performance in Vance’s home state; one moment that stands out was Vance’s aggressive defense of a nasty Vivek Ramaswamy ad that some Republicans condemned and virtually all regretted. With his Ohio base devastated, the big question now is whether the mantle of heir apparent to Trump as leader of the MAGA movement and presidential front-runner is still his and still worth its obvious downside. Unfortunately for him, Vance is still stuck in Trump’s shadow, chained to his unpopular agenda, and more or less powerless without his blessing. He can’t break with Trump but perhaps can’t really live down to his legend, either. He’s looking screwed.

This leads inevitably to the unquestioned author of the midterms, the president whose unpopularity afflicted every GOP candidate yet who insisted day after day that voters forget about the actual names on the ballot and instead think only of him. His brash 2024 promises about lowering living costs came back to bite him again and again, and instead of doing anything about it, he expressed fury at struggling Americans for their lack of gratitude toward his incredibly successful and benevolent rule. He loaded his Cabinet with personalities so clownish you expected them to show up in public with big floppy shoes and round red noses. He began a war of choice with Iran that made all his other problems immeasurably worse, and he appeared helpless to stop himself from waging it ineffectually. And his personal conduct and rhetoric steadily deteriorated to the point where even his legendary rallies were filled with empty seats and restless people. Ending the midterm campaign with a long speech touting the monuments to himself that he was building capped it all off perfectly.

Going forward, the question is whether Trump has lost interest in the non-ceremonial parts of his job and is equally incapable of fighting or working with the Democrats who now firmly control Congress. It’s going to be a long two years before his scheduled departure from office, and he’s looking more and more like poor, lost George W. Bush in the sad denouement of his own presidency. It may even be worse. Perhaps for the country, that sort of presidency is better than a return to furious relevance for Donald Trump, but for his party, it’s as bad as the Election Night returns so terrible that he couldn’t even pretend to have won.
