items.title: Trump Launches Triumphal Arch Website Right As Judge Blocks Construction
items.description: After his party suffered a brutal loss in the 2026 midterms, Donald Trump has tried to find solace in his attempts to remake Washington, D.C. But thanks to one federal judge, Trump is beginning to learn that exerting his will over the forces of state bureaucra
items.author: Jack Crosbie
paragraphs: After his party suffered a brutal loss in the 2026 midterms, Donald Trump has tried to find solace in his attempts to remake Washington, D.C. But thanks to one federal judge, Trump is beginning to learn that exerting his will over the forces of state bureaucracy may not be as easy as it once was.

Late on Thursday, Judge Tanya Chutkan of the District of Columbia brought one of Trump’s prize beautification projects to a screeching halt, ruling that construction on Trump’s triumphal arch must be stopped pending the outcome of a combined legal case that names both Trump himself and the federal National Parks Service as defendants. The timing of Chutkan’s ruling couldn’t have been worse: As it came down, the White House was in the process of rolling out a glossy new website for the project, featuring 3D renderings and sweeping views of a grand structure that now may never actually be built.

This is not Chutkan’s first run-in with Trump or his administration. In 2023, Chutkan oversaw the criminal trial against Trump for his attempt to overturn the 2020 election, a case that was only dismissed after Trump won the presidency in 2024, on the basis that the federal government could not prosecute sitting presidents.

But she hasn’t been an unequivocal Trump opponent. The following year, in 2025, Chutkan declined to block the so-called Department of Government Efficiency from accessing federal employee data, saying that the plaintiffs trying to block DOGE’s power failed to prove the agency would cause “immediate, irreparable harm.”
On this ruling, however, she did not find any merit to what the government was arguing — and her opinion was unsparing on that count.

“Defendants also assert — belatedly — that the Arch represents ‘a generational national defense opportunity,’ and that the Arch may assist in combating or deterring assassination attempts on the President,” Chutkan wrote in her ruling. “The court appreciates the government’s significant interest in national security. But these recent and unsupported attestations of security … appear nowhere in the planning documents on which the project was reviewed and approved. Indeed, they materialized, for the first time, when Defendants filed their opposition brief last week.”

In less-legal terms, Chutkan is basically noting that, as opponents of the arch have suggested for months, Trump and his cronies made up some utter flimflam about the “security” opportunities of an enormous arch in the middle of D.C. and tried to shoehorn it through legal review. Chutkan has said in no uncertain terms that that’s not going to cut it.

“The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission’s decision to fully approve President Trump’s historic vision to build a much-needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, D.C.,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle posted after the ruling. “An activist district court thereafter blocked the construction of the project.”

The judge’s posture toward the flimsy legal work of the Trump administration mirrors that of another federal judge, Ana C. Reyes, who exploded at administration lawyers in court a few weeks back after they tried to pull a fast one on her during Trump’s renovation of the East Potomac Golf Links. Reyes’ beef with the administration was more explicit — she accused them of explicitly betraying her trust — but similar to the core of Chutkan’s argument here. In essence, the administration’s lawyers can’t be trusted because they are making up whatever excuse they can to enact the president’s will.

Trump is, as we all know, someone who is used to getting what he wants. For his entire career, he has employed legal teams to help him accomplish those things, whether they be sweeping aside sexual assault allegations, dodging taxes, or finding ways to enrich himself from the Oval Office. Federal judges have been less amenable to this than the private courts Trump worked with as a civilian, but now, with Trump’s mandate across the government eroding by the hour, it seems unlikely any justice with a gavel is going to allow him an inch.
That won’t stop him trying, of course, as it’s very likely that building an arch or an unnecessary ballroom is the only solace he has left.

items.title: Willi Carlisle Says Life Is Dead Serious, Life Is a Joke on the Brilliant 'Universal Bubba'
items.description: This week, states that most people never imagined could ever turn blue did just that, as part of a massive Democratic sweep in the midterm elections. Most people, that is, except for the residents actually living in them. Texas, Kansas, Iowa, possibly even Mis
items.author: Marissa R Moss
paragraphs: This week, states that most people never imagined could ever turn blue did just that, as part of a massive Democratic sweep in the midterm elections. Most people, that is, except for the residents actually living in them. Texas, Kansas, Iowa, possibly even Mississippi. No place is a monolith, and our country is a rich, vibrant, and diverse place in every corner, where real people rarely line up with the stereotypes we thrust upon them. They may not all be Instagram-glamorous, but they believe in meaningful work, family (chosen, born or both), and a good joke. They love hard, they struggle, and they get shit done.

That’s who Willi Carlisle, the Kansas-born country songwriter, is singing about on his new Tyler Childers-produced double album, The Universal Bubba. It’s the place he is writing from, the stories he tells with equal parts craft, tenderness, and a lot of humor, and it proves that celebrating our differences is what helps us live in harmony. “I sing America old and weird, wide open borders and pioneers,” Carlisle sings on “The Universal Bubba, Part Two,” one of a pair of glorious Southern rockers. “Sing on a doubleshift ‘til I’m outta breath, a song about freedom, a song about death.”

America old and weird is the story of the brilliant Universal Bubba. It’s folk songs for the people in the Ozarks and Appalachia and hollers in between who get their story sung thanks to Carlisle’s endlessly vibrant mind. Recorded in a makeshift studio in the Bywater District of New Orleans with Childers and members of his ace band, the Food Stamps, The Universal Bubba feels both otherworldly and hilariously real, maybe because so many of us can easily be both things at once. You can explore Eastern religion and still top your yerba mate with a splash of bourbon on “Marlboro Vinyasa,” but you better be able to laugh at the absurdity. You can love your country but still think it’s brutal as hell as he does on “Master’s Hammer,” a folk offering to any wayward souls ready to rip it all up and start anew.

“I’m filled with grief, but I’m wild enough to win,” Carlisle sings as the harmonies ring like a wavelength we can all tap into to, humming out of the darkness. None of these things are actually paradoxes, unless you think people can’t be complex, strange, surprising. Carlisle sure as hell does, and he wants them all to shine.

The Universal Bubba was the first time that the equally complex and probing Childers has produced a record other than his own, and it’s a delightfully perfect fit: the two artists met while Carlisle was on tour supporting Childers in Australia, and they quickly found a musical and spiritual kinship. Carlisle is a skilled picker, but he he’s not married to tradition — nor does it feel like he’s trying to intentionally escape from it either. Banjo and fiddle (on one song, “Bigger’n Dallas,” via Amanda Shires) are the record’s heart, but never its casing. It grooves, swings, it dances to the accordion on “Old Milwaukee Onestep.” And it all ends at the Chinese food buffet.

“I wish you luck and health in business, in passion and divorce/I wish you imitation crab, wish you moo-shoo-pork,” Carlisle sings on his end-of-life prayer “Golden Dragon Buffet,” where his last request is to be sliced up and tossed in a pile of fried rice. It’s both absurd and heartbreaking, but maybe he has a point: How many of us spend more hours hunched over a greasy meal than we do with our fingers in the dirt? Life is dead serious, life is a total joke. Somewhere in between is what makes us human, and that’s where The Universal Bubba lingers.

items.title: Remix Albums Are Helping Pop Acts Live in the Moment Longer -- And Feel Less Alone
items.description: When Underscores joined Porter Robinson on the Smile! : D tour in 2025, she noticed something unusual about his set. “Perfect Pinterest Garden,” a showy deep cut from the musician’s third studio album, didn’t sound quite the same.
items.author: Larisha Paul
paragraphs: When Underscores joined Porter Robinson on the Smile! : D tour in 2025, she noticed something unusual about his set. “Perfect Pinterest Garden,” a showy deep cut from the musician’s third studio album, didn’t sound quite the same.

“You’re playing it one semitone down,” she told him. Underscores would know — it’s her favorite song on the maximalist pop record released in 2024, and she has an affinity for any song played in its original key. When Robinson made the adjustment during his next soundcheck, he saw her beaming.

That exact level of perception and specificity made Underscores a perfect recruit for Smile! : D Plus+, an ambitious remix album that dismantles and reassembles Smile! : D with appearances from 16 artists. During his hunt for collaborators, Robinson looked for people who bleed music. “They just care, and they’re actually deeply passionate, and the details matter,” he tells Rolling Stone. “The things that people might not even be able to hear — those things matter to them.” Underscores put her expertise to work on an explosive new version of “Perfect Pinterest Garden” alongside fellow pop disrupter Ninajirachi.

“[Underscores] and Nina just brought all of the life back into it,” Robinson says. “The added verses, the re-recorded parts, the way it’s kind of turned into an electro dance remix — it’s just brimming with life now.”

Remix albums have been common practice for decades, but as audience attention spans dwindle and artists look for creative partnerships that are more personal than transactional, the pop remix album has an even greater function. Smile! : D Plus+ follows recent releases from PinkPantheress, Zara Larsson, Charli XCX, and more in pouring a little more love and a little more life into community and collaboration.

After the Smile! : D tour ended, Robinson passed his time playing DJ sets that turned up the energy on some of his most contemplative songs. Smile! : D is his most cerebral release, a meticulous assessment of parasocial fan culture and external pressure that turns inwards. “I realized that a lot of people in the world had this notion of me that was just a totally incomplete piece of the picture, and that was scary to me,” Robinson says. He communicates so much on the record, but figured if anyone didn’t get it the first time, Smile! : D Plus+ might break through to them. “I care so much more about my pop songs than about high energy DJing,” he says. “I like both, but I care about my songs the very most.”

Robinson gave his Smile! : D Plus+ guests their pick of the original track list. “I didn’t want to force it,” he says. “I didn’t want to make them do a song that they weren’t feeling.” This applied even to songs already claimed by other artists — it’s why there are four new versions of “Cheerleader” and three of “Is There Really No Happiness?”, including one from Frost Children. The electronic duo of Angel and Lulu Prost are the only featured guests who also appeared on the original album. But where “Mona Lisa” takes a classic pop approach to affection, their distortion of the melancholic “Is There Really No Happiness?” amplifies progressive trance gate elements Robinson hinted at on his own. He’s always felt the song never got its proper due.

“I always thought if you stripped the instrumental and just heard the vocal, you would hear it as this beautiful EDM melody,” says Lulu. “I wanted to pick one that wasn’t already pretty hype and turn it into something a lot more crazy.” Angel started by crafting a melody out of vocal chops from Robinson’s acapella recording. Frost Children’s dance music DNA took over from there. The final version runs for seven minutes, nearly twice as long as the original. “You could play this entire thing in a set and it takes you on a journey you get lost in,” Lulu adds. “Old trance songs are like 10 minutes long, and it’s just looping, and then finally a euphoric melody comes in.”

Frost Children attempted to trim their edit down, but found themselves wondering, “What’s the point of making a remix if you’re gonna compromise everything again, anyways?” These days, the duo have an influx of remix requests coming in. Signing on for Smile! : D Plus+ was an obvious yes — Lulu got a tattoo for Robinson’s album Worlds when they were 17 and attempted to hide it from him while they worked together. “In high school, that era of Porter’s music meant a lot to us and still does,” they say. “I was too embarrassed to show him.” When Lulu finally revealed it, Robinson admitted he knew the whole time.

“Within this last year, we’ve seen the rise of so many artists who I think themselves would say that they grew up on my albums,” Robinson says. Being able to call on those artists now positions him as something of a mentor, but he’s also a fan. “Ninajirachi, Underscores, Frost Children, they’re forging their own path,” he adds. “They have a machete and they’re cutting through the wilderness and discovering something new.” The admiration is mutual, even as they become collaborators and friends. “All of us are gagged that we’re talking to him,” Angel says.

Robinson liked the Frost Children version of “Is There Really No Happiness?”, but suggested they change just one chord to create a more euphoric feeling. It made all the difference. Before, Frost Children were never really sure how to make notes without overstepping. It’s something they’ll carry into their own work. Compromise is an essential component of collaboration — like when producer Margo XS had to sacrifice some of the ambient dreamscape French musician Malibu created for “Saturn’s Return” from Zara Larsson’s expansive remix album Midnight Sun: Girl’s Trip.

“It was definitely too sleepy to get everybody, including the label, on board to put on a mainstream pop remix album,” Margo says. She restructured the song with songwriter Helena Gao, but saved Malibu’s mystique for the end, which brought an airy feel to its introspection. Margo and Larsson went into Girl’s Trip imagining what it would be like to make Midnight Sun over again, this time with the creative familiarity they’ve fortified in the past year. In that time, the album marked a true, long-awaited breakout for Larsson. Girl’s Trip allowed her to let that moment breathe, and share it with 13 other artists, including Margo, JT, Tyla, Robyn, and more.

Larsson initially planned to release a traditional deluxe edition of Midnight Sun, with a few remixes and new songs. But Margo and MNEK, who also worked on the record, “felt a lot of freedom and excitement by being able to take these stems and flip them on their head.” It’s how they ended up with an elevated R&B version of “Blue Moon” featuring Kehlani. Robinson felt similarly revitalized by stripping back to the bare bones. “Some of the remixes are speaking to the DNA that was in the song from the very beginning in a roundabout way,” he says. “Easier to Love You,” for example, started as a Eurodance song inspired by Gigi D’Agostino’s “I’ll Fly Away With You,” but ended up as a sensitive guitar ballad. Smile! : D Plus+ brought that original sound back through Dutch hardstyle DJ Vertile.

Margo describes the art of the remix album as community building, and sees it as a response to years of indifferent pop features that seemed to serve little creative purpose beyond boosting streams. “OK, you got this feature — but the production doesn’t change over it. It feels phoned in. It feels like you were just trying to maybe combine audiences and get some more love from the algorithm gods,” she says. “People got a bit fatigued from that way of working.” A remix album, on the other hand, “makes it feel very intentional in these collaborations and allows people’s identities to really flourish, and then continue to create a community around a certain style of music.”

The creation of Girl’s Trip overlapped with the release of Fancy Some More?, a remix album from PinkPantheress that revamped her mixtape Fancy That? “We were definitely inspired by her willingness to platform alternative producers and alternative voices on a pop record,” Margo says. The project features everyone from JADE and Anitta to Basement Jaxx and Kaytranada. “It just made it feel like the sky was the limit in terms of what we could do in terms of production and features.” Like, Smile! : D Plus+, Fancy Some More? includes multiple configurations from different artists. There’s a version of “Stateside” with Kylie Minogue, another with Bladee, another with Groove Armada, and of course, the breakout remix featuring a killer verse from Larsson.

After trading aesthetics in the “Stateside” video, PinkPantheress and Larsson appear together again on the Girl’s Trip version of “Midnight Sun.” An innovative producer herself, PinkPantheress and her collaborator Count Baldor worked closely with Margo to shape the song. “I really relate to how committed she is to doing a sonic aesthetic across a whole record,” Margo says. Charli XCX was in the same headspace when she released Brat and It’s Completely Different but Also Still Brat in 2024. “There’s still so many different versions of that song that could be made using a tiny element of the production from the original, or a tiny reference to a lyrical concept, or a literal lyric,” she said at the time. “It can all be deconstructed and put back together again. Why not? Why just be like, ‘It’s the album, and it’s done?’”

The possibilities are endless, especially when it comes down to locking down features. For Girl’s Trip, Larsson reached out to potential collaborators via DMs, shifting her approach depending on whether she already had an existing relationship with them. Sometimes MNEK made the connection. Margo can’t quite remember which route led to Shakira featuring on “Eurosummer,” but does recall the craziness of that particular yes. “We gotta figure this out,” she thought. “We gotta make this a bop.” It wasn’t the only version they made. There’s a “Eurosummer” remix with Romanian dance-pop stars Alexandra Stan and Inna sitting on a computer somewhere. “I know that has been very wanted by the internet, and there were a lot of rumors going around about it,” Margo says. “It does exist. That’s all I can say.”

Robinson’s process was far more free-flowing in comparison. He primarily reached out to friends and people he thought would be cool to spotlight, like the indie-pop singer EJEAN who he found through a twist of fate (read: Instagram Reels, in an incredibly rare instance, he says). “I would love to hear your version of ‘Year of the Cup’ because I think you would make the most heartwrenching version of this,” Robinson said in a message to EJEAN.

“Year of the Cup” is not really the kind of song you can flip. The original ballad samples a Lil Wayne interview from 2009 in a way that is both disjointed and completely enchanting. “It’s almost impossible to make a dance remix of it,” Robinson says. EJEAN covered it instead. Their stripped back acoustic version is the standout moment on Smile! : D Plus+.

It struck Robinson to process someone else singing words that hold so much weight to him. “When I heard them say ‘something’s in the air like vanilla,’ or these experiences where I know specifically where my two feet were in the world when those moments happened in my real life,” he says, “it gave me this twisted up feeling inside. It was like, ‘I wonder what that means to them.’” Even beyond lyrics, the sheer tone of a voice can communicate emotion so differently. Turnstile showed as much with Never Enough: Versions, a 22-track cover project with a host of guests including Hayley Williams, Elton John, and A. G. Cook. “You put everything into making an album,” Robinson says. “Anything that you can do to refresh it and remind people of its importance and remind people of what it means to you, and extend its lifespan culturally — I think there’s good reasons to do that.”

There’s a certain trust and vulnerability required to let another artist reconfigure songs born from such specific experiences and perspectives. Sometimes, doubt gets in the way. Robinson considered reaching out to Jane Remover to participate in Smile! : D Plus+ through the rapper-producer’s EDM side project, Leroy. There were threads of influence and connection there, but they hadn’t properly met before, so he decided against it. “I was too shy to ask,” he says. “I should have just asked.” He would have also loved to hear something from Smile! : D reimagined by a K-pop artist, like KiiiKiii or Aespa, similar to how PinkPantheress recruited Seventeen for “Illegal.”

These crossovers are as exciting for the artists as they are for the audience. They offer something new without completely compromising the original listeners fell for, while also potentially expanding their palette. “It’s a non-algorithmic, non-AI way of finding new things you like, and you’ll never find the end of things that you like,” says Angel. The special moments created on these projects — whether something as explosive as “Stateside,” or Lorde and Charli XCX working it out on the “Girl, So Confusing” remix, or Robinson pouring back into a lineage of his own influence — are the product of true connection.
“It’s so amazing for me to be able to hold hands with those people and the respect is so mutual,” Robinson says. “And doing it as a way of celebrating the album, it’s a win-win for everybody.”

items.title: Adam Driver Won’t Return for ‘Girls’: ‘I Wish Them the Best of Luck’
items.description: Adam Driver had a major breakout thanks to his role on “Girls,” but the actor shut down the idea of returning for the reboot of the iconic series in a recent interview.
items.author: Pat Saperstein
paragraphs: Adam Driver had a major breakout thanks to his role on “Girls,” but the actor shut down the idea of returning for the reboot of the iconic series in a recent interview.

While talking about his role in James Gray’s new movie “Paper Tiger,” Driver was asked by Cinema Blend if he will be returning for the revival. “No, but I wish them the best of luck,” he told the outlet.

News of the new “Girls” series broke in mid-October, with creator and star Lena Dunham set to return as Hannah Horvath alongside co-stars Allison Williams as Marnie Michaels, Jemima Kirke as Jessa Johansson and Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna Shapiro. Andrew Rannells also returns to the role of Elijah Krantz.
The series will have a limited five-episode run on HBO with production starting in 2027.

Driver’s career took off after his run as Hannah’s boyfriend on “Girls.” In addition to his role as Kylo Ren in three “Star Wars” movies, he starred in “Marriage Story” and “The Meyerowitz Stories” for Noah Baumbach; “The Last Duel” and “House of Gucci” for Ridley Scott; “Ferrari” for Michael Mann and this year’s “Misty Green.” He’s also worked with director Jim Jarmusch on “Paterson,” “The Dead Don’t Die” and “Father Mother Sister Brother.”

In her recent memoir “Famesick,” Dunham described her tumultuous relationship with Driver, saying, “He could be short-tempered and verbally aggressive, condescending and physically imposing. He could also be protective, loving even,” Dunham writes. After the last episode of “Girls” wrapped, Dunham says Driver told her, “I hope you know I’ll always love you” before he said goodbye.

items.title: James Bond Surprise: Robert Pattinson Screen Tested to Play 007
items.description: In a surprise few saw coming, Robert Pattinson has emerged as a contender for 007. The actor, 40, is among those who have screen tested for the role of James Bond, multiple sources tell The Hollywood Reporter, joining hopefuls Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Jo
items.author: Borys Kit; Aaron Couch
paragraphs: In a surprise few saw coming, Robert Pattinson has emerged as a contender for 007. The actor, 40, is among those who have screen tested for the role of James Bond, multiple sources tell The Hollywood Reporter, joining hopefuls Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor.

Conventional wisdom has been that the next man to get the license to kill would not be a globally recognized star like Pattinson, one of the biggest actors of his age cohort, and already the face of DC Studios’ Batman franchise. The screen tests are said to have occurred the weekend of Oct. 24. THR previously reported that four, possibly five actors were in the mix but only three names surfaced at the time.
Another name now surfacing as one of the Bond mystery men is Nicholas Hoult, a runnerup to Pattinson for Batman years ago.

Pattinson is a favorite of auteurs from Robert Eggers and the Safdie brothers to Christopher Nolan, whose 2020 spy movie Tenet might feel like a Bond audition in hindsight. And more importantly, he worked with Bond director Denis Villeneuve on the upcoming Dune: Part 3, which bows Dec. 18 and is said to have gone well for the two men.

The actor is in the midst of the biggest year of his career, with a key role in Nolan’s The Odyssey and as the co-lead of A24 hit The Drama and anchoring the well-reguarded movie Primetime, also from A24. He’s currently filming The Batman Part II in London, where screen tests have been taking place.
Amazon had no comment on the testing.

While conventional wisdom goes against a world famous Bond, these are unprecedented times in the franchise. It is the first Bond movie made under the control of Amazon, which bought out the creative rights from the Broccoli family in February 2025. And producing are Spider-Man‘s Amy Pascal and David Heyman, producer of the Harry Potter movies. A young Pattinson broke out with a tragic role in 2005’s Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, before gaining global fame a few years later in Twilight.

The Bond casting search comes 21 years after Daniel Craig was set as the next James Bond back in October 2005. He retired from the role after five films with 2021’s No Time to Die, his tenure including the franchise’s first and only $1 billion hit, the 2012 feature Skyfall.

items.title: ‘The Bachelor’ Returns, ‘The Rookie’ Moves as ABC Sets Midseason Schedule
items.description: ABC had previously announced premiere dates for The Rookie and its spinoff, The Rookie: North. Both shows are set for Wednesday, Jan. 6 — a move from The Rookie’s Tuesday home of the past few seasons.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: ABC had previously announced premiere dates for The Rookie and its spinoff, The Rookie: North. Both shows are set for Wednesday, Jan. 6 — a move from The Rookie’s Tuesday home of the past few seasons.

The network has now released it full midseason lineup, and the move for The Rookie is not a temporary one: It and The Rookie: North will form a two-hour block on Wednesday nights, giving the veteran show an earlier time (9 p.m. instead of 10 p.m.) and the new spinoff a well-established — and presumably very compatible — lead-in as support.

Season three of Shifting Gears will join the two Rookie shows on Wednesdays. The comedy starring Tim Allen and Kat Dennings will premiere with two episodes on Jan. 6; Abbott Elementary will rejoin the lineup the following week.

Will Trent and High Potential are set to return in their usual Tuesday spots on Jan. 5. An ABC News Studios-produced unscripted show called Surviving a Scandal will fill the 10 p.m. hour. High Potential is also getting the post-Super Bowl showcase on Feb. 14.

At the far end of ABC’s midseason slate is the return of The Bachelor franchise to the network on March 21. With behind-the-scenes upheaval and last season’s scrapped Bachelorette season starring Taylor Frankie Paul, the Bachelor-verse has been absent from ABC since the November 2025 finale of The Golden Bachelor’s second season. The Bachelor last aired in March 2025.
American Idol is set to begin its 25th season (and 10th on ABC) on Feb. 8. The network has also set a retrospective special about the show for Feb. 1.
One other note: ABC has pushed the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff it ordered in the spring to the 2027-28 season. That’s not a surprise, considering the show hasn’t been cast yet.
ABC’s midseason dates, including those for the Grammys and Oscars, are below. All times are ET/PT unless noted.
10 p.m.: Surviving a Scandal
10 p.m.: The Rookie: North
8 p.m.: Celebrity Jeopardy!
8 p.m.: American Idol at 25 (working title)
7 p.m. ET/4 p.m. PT: Grammy Awards
10 p.m.: Shark Tank (new night)
6:30 p.m. ET/3:30 p.m. PT: Super Bowl LXI
7 p.m. ET/4 p.m. PT: The Oscars
10 p.m.: What Would You Do?

items.title: ‘I’m 100 Percent at War With Trump’: MAGA Revolts After Midterms Wipeout
items.description: Many MAGAworld figures are already pointing the finger of blame for their midterm losses squarely at President Donald Trump and his policies.
items.author: David Gilbert
paragraphs: Many MAGAworld figures are already pointing the finger of blame for their midterm losses squarely at President Donald Trump and his policies.
Trump spent Tuesday evening lashing out at Fox News for platforming the Democrats who swept aside their GOP opponents in deep red states and took control of the House and Senate.

“[Fox] bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse,” the president wrote on Truth Social. Later in the night, he called in to Fox News, where he congratulated the Democrats on their results.

Trump made clear that he doesn’t think the historic blowout was a reflection of his popularity, writing, “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” He then posted a picture of a red baseball hat with the word VETO embossed on the front.
But in the hours that followed, MAGA revolted.

Matt Walsh, a right-wing podcaster, called the results “a political catastrophe of historic proportions” and Trump “an 80-year-old lame-duck president.” Walsh blamed Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran and his focus on trivial matters like attempting to rename artificial intelligence super intelligence and the White House ballroom.
For right-wing commentator Mike Cernovich, it was Trump’s decision to ostracize libertarian voters that was partly to blame.

Mike Flynn, the disgraced former national security adviser who was among the most prominent voices pushing bogus conspiracies about the 2020 election being stolen, also blamed Trump, writing on X, “Someone needs to look in a mirror.” Flynn also blamed Christians for not showing up to vote.
But noted conspiracy theorist Alex Jones had another take on why Trump was to blame.

“I think he’s a Democrat. I’m gonna just say it right now,” Jones said on his show Tuesday night. “I’ve tried to salvage Trump. I’ve not been sure. I’ve invested so much—maybe I was blind to it—I think he’s the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell, and he works for them. I’m 100 percent at war with Trump.”
Other MAGA figures like right-wing commentators Jack Posobiec and Nick Sortor both blamed Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran for the losses but didn’t directly name Trump in their posts.

Unsurprisingly, Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former congresswoman who broke decisively with Trump earlier this year, also blamed the president. “Tonight was a total referendum on Trump. He told people to vote like he was on the ballot and they did,” Greene wrote on X.
One notable aspect of MAGAworld’s response to Tuesday’s GOP wipeout was the relative silence coming from some of Trump’s biggest supporters.

Elon Musk, who poured hundreds of millions of dollars into supporting losing Republican candidates, has not said who was to blame for the results. He did post a joke saying his “election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time” and commented that it was “interesting” that an exit poll showed the Iran war was a “massive losing issue.”

Rogan O’Handley, a vocal MAGA influencer known as DC Draino who posts incessantly on X about politics, has also not reacted publicly to the results. Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, who was reelected on Tuesday night, said the results were “not what we’d hoped and fought for” but failed to say what or who was to blame.

White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser Stephen Miller has also not commented publicly on the results, but his wife, Katie Miller, who boosted election conspiracy theories earlier on Tuesday, laid the blame on the media, which she called “a propaganda arm of the woke left.”

There were, however, a few right-wing figures who continued to publicly support Trump despite the losses, including MAGA influencer Laura Loomer, who wrote, “President Trump is a hero for stopping Iran from having a nuclear weapon, and now he should finish the job.” Instead of blaming Trump, Loomer spent Tuesday evening lamenting the end of America and the rise of communism.

Another right-wing figure continuing to back Trump was the former Fox News host turned conspiracy theorist Lara Logan, who blamed an anonymous group of Republicans who conspired to bring about the defeat so they could “get rid of the MAGA movement and the establishment would retake the party.”
Chaya Raichik, who runs the hugely popular LibsofTikTok accounts, blamed the losses on a years-long Democrat plot to import “millions of foreigners.”

Kari Lake, Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Jamaica, also refused to lay the blame at the president’s feet and was one of the few election deniers who continued to boost claims of a stolen election. “America, do you think that our elections are honest? Do you have complete confidence that only legal votes were counted?” Lake wrote in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

Others, like Harrison Smith, a host on Steve Bannon’s War Room show, turned their ire on their fellow right-wing influencers. He blamed Loomer, Ben Shapiro, Mark Levin, Will Chamberlain, and AIPAC, the prominent lobbying organization, for the losses.

But at least one former Trumpworld figure did take the blame on themselves. Former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem posted on X that the massive losses happened because “we were too successful in the first year of the Trump administration.”
